Hebrew University receives record $250 million donation from philanthropist John Paulson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
21:41:41 UTC
06:41:41 KST

American philanthropist and investor John Paulson announced a historic $250 million donation to the Hebrew University of Jerusalem at the university’s Board of Governors gala on Saturday evening, marking the largest gift in the institution’s history, the Calcalist reported.
The donation will fund the establishment of a new Faculty of Engineering, expand activities in medicine and biomedicine, and advance research and treatment related to trauma and post-traumatic stress.
In recognition of the gift, the university’s historic Mount Scopus campus will be renamed the Alina and John Paulson Campus, Mount Scopus, Jerusalem.
The contribution follows Paulson’s previous support for the university’s computer science and electrical engineering programs.
Paulson’s donation a 'profound expression of confidence in Israel’s human capital'
“This donation bolsters our ability to recruit world-class faculty, support outstanding students, equip laboratories with cutting-edge technology, and transform bold ideas into life-changing breakthroughs,” said Prof. Tamir Sheafer, president of the Hebrew University.
“This is far more than a historic act of philanthropy. It is a profound expression of confidence in Israel’s human capital.”
Paulson, founder of the hedge fund that bears his name, is known for his philanthropic support of higher education, including a gift of roughly $400 million to Harvard University about a decade ago, which remains the largest donation in the institution’s history.
“I made the choice to shift my philanthropy toward Jewish causes in general, and toward Israel in particular,” he told the Calcalist.
“Israel is currently facing numerous challenges. There is anti-Israel sentiment and a global rise in antisemitism. I decided it was crucial to demonstrate support for Israel, and a fantastic way to do so is by supporting Israel’s leading university.”

Israeli charity Save a Child's Heart marks 30 years, 9,000 children treated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
21:40:53 UTC
06:40:53 KST

The Talmud teaches that whoever saves a single life is as one who saved an entire world. If that’s the case, SACH (Save a Child’s Heart) can be credited with saving some 9,000 worlds.
SACH is Israel’s leading practitioner of medical diplomacy.
Founded in 1995 by the late Dr. Ami Cohen and headquartered in the Sylvan Adams Children’s Hospital at the Wolfson Medical Center in Holon, it provides free cardiac surgery for children with heart ailments regardless of their religion, ethnicity, or nationality. This includes children from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel, and youngsters from countries that are sworn enemies of Israel. To date, over 9,000 children from more than 75 countries have been brought to Israel for treatment. Each child is accompanied by a family member or nurse from the child’s home country.
In addition, medical personnel from third-world countries are brought to Israel to train in all aspects of cardiac surgery, so that children with heart problems can be treated closer to home. SACH teams frequently travel abroad to evaluate children with congenital and rheumatic heart diseases, and often perform urgent surgeries when the child’s condition is so serious that immediate treatment is required.
SACH volunteers and supporters met last Friday with President Isaac Herzog at his official residence to celebrate the 30th anniversary of SACH’s founding.
Along with the above were medical personnel, ambassadors and other diplomats from some of the African countries from which children have been brought to Israel for surgery, representatives of African hospitals whose pediatric cardiology teams were trained in Israel, representatives of international foundations which help fund SACH, and mothers with children who recently underwent successful surgeries and who will soon be returning home.
'We are celebrating 30 years of saving worlds'
SACH Executive Director Simon Fisher described the children who came under SACH care over the years as “living miracles,” adding, “We are celebrating 30 years of saving worlds.”
Fisher emphasized that SACH had grown from a small group of dedicated professionals to global proportions.
In explaining this, Fisher said, “A child in need is part of our collective responsibility.
Herzog, who has long been familiar with SACH's work, said that the organization deserved a Nobel Peace Prize and pledged to do everything he could to bring that about.
He declared that he was honored to host a milestone anniversary of “a remarkable Israeli humanitarian organization of which we’re very proud.”
Herzog characterized SACH’s achievements as “the triumph of human kindness which connects a wide heart of human effort.”
But it is more than simply healing a diseased heart, he pointed out. “From Iraq to the Palestinian Authority, all have been welcomed with wide open arms - simply because they are children in need.”
Herzog saw the effects of this a year ago when he paid a state visit to Zambia, and met with adults who as children had been healed in Israel, and were leading fruitful and meaningful lives.
“Few things leave me prouder to be Israeli,” he said.
“This is the essence of doing good in the world. This is something the international community should bear in mind when they accuse us of something else.”
In closing Herzog implied that SACH received its inspiration from the Biblical Noah - “one man who braved the current and ultimately saved the world.”
SACH co-chair Robert Baruch noted that over the years, SACH has given thousands of children a second chance at life, and has not been deterred by the child’s place of birth. Children come to Israel as the hope of families who cannot find treatment at home, he said. “It’s a reminder of what can happen when people decide to act. The impact of SACH is far greater than its size.”
Mega philanthropist Sylvan Adams, who, together with a group of other philanthropic families living in Israel, established the Sylvan Adams Children’s Hospital within the Wolfson Medical Center in Holon, shared some of his own SACH experiences.
The first time he visited, more than a decade ago, he was on a tour, and SACH staff asked whether he would like to spend a few minutes watching open-heart surgery. He agreed and was so fascinated by what he saw that he sat for hours and instantly became a donor. The children’s hospital that bears his name came into being because there was no children’s hospital in Holon before then. Since its inception, he has visited many times.
On that first occasion, he saw the surgeon being assisted by a doctor from Tanzania. What amazed him was that the two were conversing in Hebrew.
One per cent of all children are born with heart defects
Adams was shocked to learn that one per cent of all children are born with heart defects, which makes SACH’s work all the more vital.
During his visits, he has witnessed children from Gaza arriving with their parents and sometimes accompanied by their physicians. They were always treated with dignity - even after October 7, he said.
\In relation to the attitude toward Gazan children being treated in the same friendly manner as children from anywhere else, Adams is certain that there are people in Gaza who do not bear hostility toward Israel.
Along the entrance to the main building in the presidential compound, there were tall round tables bearing enlarged photographs of children who came with hope and left healed. Alongside each photograph was a round vase filled with white tulips. When the petals of a tulip first open, they form the shape of a heart. The message, though subtle, was clear.

BANGKOK, October 18. /TASS/. The World Bank recognizes Russia’s digital achievements and provides a platform to share this expertise with developing economies, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Overchuk told TASS, following the autumn meetings of the IMF and World Bank.
Overchuk noted that "Russia possesses vast experience and knowledge and has much to offer countries of the Global South," particularly regarding "digital transformation in public administration."
"The World Bank acknowledges Russia’s achievements in this area, understands how vital Russian expertise is for developing economies, and provides us with an international platform to work directly with these nations," he emphasized.
On the sidelines of the meetings in Bangkok, Russia organized two packed working seminars with World Bank support. "One seminar focused on digital transformation in land and real estate administration and geospatial data systems. The other addressed digital public services and digital transformation in tax administration," Overchuk said.
He noted that these areas crucially impact the business climate, investment attractiveness, and socio-economic development in the Global South. "The World Bank prioritizes these issues, and Russia is a global leader in digital governance," Overchuk said, adding that Russia ranks eighth in the World Bank’s GovTech Maturity Index.
"By learning from our experience, developing nations are seeking closer cooperation with Russia, which aligns with our interests."
Overchuk also pointed out that the World Bank primarily focuses on supporting developing nations and the Global South, the vast majority of which are friendly to Russia. "These nations form the core audience at World Bank meetings. They come here seeking access to financing, global best practices, and knowledge to develop their economies," the deputy prime minister concluded.

A Lebanese military delegation has prepared to present Beirut's demands for an immediate end to Israeli attacks in Lebanon at a trilateral meeting in Tampa, Florida, on 20 October, the Lebanese presidency confirmed.
President Aoun warned that Israel continues its assaults on southern towns and villages, demolishing homes, bulldozing land, and blocking farmers from their fields in direct breach of the US-brokered framework agreement.
He emphasised that ongoing occupation and border tensions prevent the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) from deploying down to the international frontier under UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
Aoun stated that the military delegation will put forward Lebanon's demands to halt Israeli escalation at the Florida talks, hoping to achieve tangible progress aligned with the framework accord.
He also underscored Beirut's desire to extend the mandate of international peacekeeping forces beyond their scheduled 2027 withdrawal, welcoming any UN mechanism that prevents an operational vacuum or direct friction between Lebanese and Israeli troops.
State authority
Aoun affirmed that Lebanese military and internal security forces are actively executing cabinet directives to extend state authority across the country, eliminate armed manifestations, and confiscate unauthorised weaponry and ammunition, referring violators directly to the judiciary.
He stressed that strengthening and equipping the army remains essential to fulfilling these national security responsibilities.
Lebanon and Israel have held several rounds of direct negotiations in recent months, aimed at ending hostilities following Israel’s attacks on Lebanon and its continued occupation of parts of Lebanese territory.
Under the framework pact reached through US-brokered talks, Beirut pledged to disarm Hezbollah, which was intended to lead to a phased withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon.
Israel has maintained its aerial strikes and military incursions across southern Lebanon.

Ay Yola brings Bashkir heritage to Grammy voting
Russian ethno-electronic band Ay Yola has advanced to the first round of Grammy Awards voting with its album "Ural Batyr" and single "Aihylyu," the group announced, Qazinform News Agency cites TASS.
The album has been submitted in the Best Global Music Album category, while "Aihylyu" is competing in the Best Arrangement, Instruments and Vocals category.
Inspired by the ancient Bashkir epic "Ural Batyr," the album features 12 tracks that combine traditional Bashkir vocals and folk instruments with contemporary electronic music. Band members described the Grammy recognition as a significant opportunity to showcase the cultural heritage of Bashkortostan on the international stage.
Ay Yola gained widespread recognition with its hit "Homay," which reached sixth place on Shazam's global Top 200 chart and topped music rankings in Russia, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan.
The group's debut album, "Ural Batyr," was released in October 2025 and has helped introduce Bashkir folk traditions to a global audience through a modern musical style.
It should be noted, Ay Yola was named the official ambassador of the World Nomad Games 2026 - Asia's largest cultural and sporting event.

Ukraine FM says Russian-held town is a 'death trap' with starving residents, Zelensky says genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
21:22:31 UTC
06:22:31 KST

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Saturday that Russian occupying forces were turning the Ukrainian town of Oleshky into a "death trap" gripped by starvation, and urged international organizations to help evacuate its residents.
Sybiha made his comments on X/Twitter a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin pledged, in a conversation with Pope Leo, to cooperate in delivering vital supplies into the town in southern Ukraine's Kherson region.
"Russians are trying to turn the Ukrainian town of Oleshky into a death trap. The hospital has run out of medicine. Dozens of bodies lie in the streets or in homes, as Russians forbid residents from burying them," Sybiha wrote.
"Families are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, preserves and even snails... Ukraine has repeatedly called for safe evacuation and international humanitarian access. These appeals cannot remain unanswered."
The Kremlin acknowledged in September that Oleshky had critical problems with food and medical supplies but said Russia's military was working to resolve them. Ukraine's military has twice used drones to deliver food and medicine to the town.
UN, Red Cross urged to secure evacuations, humanitarian access
Sybiha urged the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and other organizations to "secure safe evacuation corridors and immediate humanitarian access."
Oleshky lies on the east side of the Dnipro River in the Kherson region, which Russian forces mostly occupied soon after the 2022 invasion. A Ukrainian counteroffensive later recaptured large chunks of territory, including the city of Kherson.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy described the situation in Oleshky this week as "genocide."
Oleshky had a pre-war population of 24,000 people and is now home to around 1,700 residents, including 47 children, according to Danielle Bell, head of the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.
Local prosecutors said on Saturday Russian forces dropped aerial bombs on the city of Kherson, on the opposite bank of the Dnipro from Oleshky, killing an ambulance driver and wounding 40 people.

Photos: No Kings rallies in US urge midterm voters to cast ballots early
Thousands gathered at events throughout the country on Saturday, building on two years of No Kings marches.
Rallies organised by the No Kings network opposed to United States President Donald Trump were held Saturday in cities and communities across the US, with an aim of getting people out to vote early in the midterm elections.
No Kings has more than 3,000 events planned across the US. The planned events, this time dubbed “No Kings: Vote Early”, were billed as nonpartisan, though they sought to build on nearly two years’ worth of No Kings marches and demonstrations by people upset with Trump’s presidency.
“It’s a day of nonpartisan voter participation: we are bringing our community together to make a plan to vote early and ensuring every eligible voter understands their options for how to vote and has the opportunity to make their voice heard,” organisers said in a statement.
By advocating for voting early, the “No Kings” organisers hope to cut off the potential for any malfeasance once election day rolls around.
A band entertained what appeared to be a few hundred people in caps and coats at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, DC. Despite the chilly weather, many in the crowd danced to the tunes. “VOTE EARLY” and “HANDS OFF MY VOTE!” were among the many signs held aloft.
At an Atlanta rally, City Councilman Michael Julian Bond told the crowd to urge others to vote ahead of the November 3 general election.
“The Constitution gives you one power, right? That is the power to vote. Are you gonna use that power?” he said.
“You don’t see Superman giving up his power,” Bond continued. “You don’t see Black Panther giving up his power. You don’t see Wonder Woman giving up her magic lasso. So why would you give up your right, your power, your obligation to vote? Be a superhero, use your power. Go to the polls and vote.”
Trump has long been suspicious of mail voting and has claimed without evidence that voting fraud cost him the 2020 presidential election.
His administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for the midterm elections from people whom the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.
On Friday, the Department of Justice warned that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution.
Earlier that day, Democratic Senators Alex Padilla of California, Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Dick Durbin of Illinois wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche, demanding that the Justice Department commit to not seizing ballots or other election materials before the midterm elections are certified.

Cost of living protests hit Belgium, Italy, Portugal and France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
21:02:26 UTC
06:02:26 KST

Cost of living protests hit Belgium, Italy, Portugal and France
Hundreds of thousands of Europeans took to the streets for separate demonstrations putting pressure on governments across the EU.
Hundreds of thousands of Europeans have taken to the streets in separate, uncoordinated demonstrations to protest against the rising cost of living in their countries.
Saturday’s protests were in Belgium, France, Italy and Portugal in a wave of unrest that has put pressure on national governments across the European Union.
France experienced one of its most turbulent days of protests in decades, with over 550,000 people joining demonstrations and police facing off with protesters across the country – but it was not the only country to see significant demonstrations.
In Belgium’s capital Brussels – which has already seen weeks of protests by students against university registration fees – police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters, who they accused of launching missiles at them and setting fires.
In Liege, a smaller city east of Brussels, police also deployed water cannon to break up demonstrations. Police did not say how many people attended.
An estimated tens of thousands of protesters marched in Lisbon, the Portuguese capital, against the cost of living crisis, low wages and an inability to access housing in major cities. House prices in Portugal have more than doubled since 2017, while rents for new leases have increased nearly as much.
Portuguese Parliamentary Affairs Minister Carlos Abreu Amorim said on Friday that the “government will not yield to shouts from the street”.Protesters said their leaders are “out of touch” with the problem.
In Milan and Bologna, Italian police reported that, alongside peaceful cost of living rallies, protesters threw stones and clashed with officers.
Italian media reported several injuries and arrests.
French protests spill over
None of the protests reached the same scale as the nationwide rallies in France but they may be a sign of spilling over into other European nations, according to Alberto Alemanno, Professor of EU Law & Policy at HEC Paris business school.
“France is the epicentre of this movement … and there are signs now that this is spreading beyond France,” Alemanno told Al Jazeera.
He said Saturday’s protests may not be the last in many of these countries and new hotspots could emerge.
In Greece, Germany, and Austria, the “early stages” of a movement is emerging, with mobilisation expected “in the coming week”, he said.
They are not a single movement, he explained, but several protests happening at the same time, with some “shared grievances”: underfunded education, rising costs and, for students, uncertain prospects after graduation.
The unrest comes at a crucial time for Europe, as the continent prepares for what Alemanno called an “unprecedented super-cycle of national elections” in the coming 12 months, with votes scheduled in Spain, France, Italy and Poland.
“Inevitably, all these protests, all these mobilisations, are going to be at the centre of the political conversation,” Alemanno said.

Ukrainian guards busted on wrong side of Moldovan border (VIDEO)

2026-10-17

Ukrainian guards busted on wrong side of Moldovan border (VIDEO)
Ukrainian border guards’ pursuit of a draft dodger has landed them on the wrong side of the law in neighboring Moldova. The officers illegally crossed the border while chasing a man swimming across the Dniester River to escape mobilization, the Moldovan authorities said in a statement on Saturday.
The incident occurred on Thursday, the Moldovan Border Police stated. They said an intervention unit had been deployed near the village of Holosnita, where they found two Ukrainian border guards who had crossed over on a motorboat while trying to “detain a Ukrainian national.” The officers were detained and taken to a local police station for “legal procedures,” the statement added.
A boat with two border guards in it can be seen circling a man drifting in the water in a video that surfaced on the internet purporting to show the incident. The guards repeatedly start the boat engine before shutting it off as they appear to try to prevent the man from reaching Moldovan territory by blocking his way.
Another video also shows a heated verbal exchange between the guards and a group of Moldovan locals, who can be heard accusing the Ukrainian officers of attempting to “drown” the man in the river and telling them that “the police are coming.” Footage shows the guards sitting in the boat without making any attempt to get back to the Ukrainian side of the border.
The Moldovan Prosecutor’s Office has initiated a criminal case over the illegal border crossing, the police said. It is unclear if the Ukrainian guards remain in custody. The Moldovan authorities only said that measures regulated by existing legislation were applied to them.
Ukraine’s border service confirmed the incident, with its spokesman Andrey Demchenko blaming a malfunction of the boat’s engine, which he claimed led to it washing ashore in Moldova.
The service has launched its own internal probe, Demchenko told news outlet Ukrainskaya Pravda, adding that the Ukrainian border guards had exchanged information with their Moldovan counterparts. According to the spokesman, the alleged draft dodger was also detained by the Moldovan authorities.
Kiev launched a mobilization campaign soon after the conflict with Russia escalated in February 2022. Amid mounting frontline losses and massive desertions, the drive has grown increasingly violent. Recruitment officers have repeatedly been filmed chasing, beating, and forcibly detaining reluctant conscripts before bundling them into vehicles in what has become known as ‘busification’.
The draft effort has led to large-scale draft dodging. According to Euronews, around 1.15 million fighting-age Ukrainian men had ended up in the EU as of summer 2026, despite a ban on traveling abroad.
Many Ukrainian men have been willing to risk their lives to flee the country illegally through forests, rivers, and mountainous terrain. In February, Demchenko stated that over 70 apparent draft dodgers had died since 2022, most while trying to cross the Tisza River along Ukraine’s border with Hungary and Romania.
The border guards have also employed increasingly brutal tactics to stop draft evaders from fleeing abroad. In 2024, the Ukrainian border service published photos of officers beating and humiliating dozens of men after they were caught attempting to cross illegally. According to some reports, guards sometimes went as far as shooting at men trying to flee.

Belgium’s 10 F-16s bring Ukraine’s promised fleet to about 100 jets. Fewer than 40 are flying, as Russia’s jet drones run them ragged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
20:53:48 UTC
05:53:48 KST

- Belgium is speeding up the delivery of surplus Lockheed Martin F-16 fighters to Ukraine
- The 53 or so ex-Belgian jets are welcome, but the initial delivery for 2026 is for just 10 airframes, not all of which will be flyable
- The Ukrainian air force's sole F-16 wing is fighting hard with too few aircraft
Belgium has announced it will accelerate the delivery of surplus Lockheed Martin F-16 fighters to Ukraine. Instead of delivering three flyable F-16s before the end of the year, Brussels will ship 10.
It's unclear how many will be flyable. Previously, Belgian officials explained the first seven secondhand F-16s would include just three airworthy examples. The other four would be broken down for spare parts.
It's good news for Ukraine, but hardly cause for nationwide celebration. The handful of flyable F-16s that should arrive in the coming two months could make good recent F-16 losses. But those shipping-soon Belgian F-16s won't actually grow Ukraine's F-16 fleet by much, if at all.
The dozens of supersonic F-16s in action in Ukraine fly often and fight hard. They shoot down Russian drones and cruise missiles, tangle with Russian warplanes, and lob precision glide bombs at Russian forces on the ground. Russia launched about 2,000 jet-powered drones at Ukraine in September, up from some 350 in June, and F-16s are among the few weapons fast enough to catch them, the Wall Street Journal's editorial board noted. Every 300 flying hours, each jet must go abroad for a lengthy inspection.
The main constraint on the pace of F-16 sorties, besides maintenance demands and the availability of trained pilots, is munitions: running low or out of air-to-air missiles and glide bombs, the F-16s routinely aim their 20-mm guns at Russian targets. But even 20-mm ammunition sometimes runs low.
The busy F-16s and their equally busy pilots need reinforcement. But reinforcements are slow coming. Belgium is only slightly accelerating its F-16 shipments amid reports it will eventually give Ukraine all 53 F-16s it's gradually retiring as new Lockheed Martin F-35 stealth fighters arrive to re-equip the Belgian air force.
Further complicating the picture, Norway's six F-16s, promised in 2023, were still being refurbished in Belgium this spring. Some arrived there in pieces.
Yes, Ukraine got 24 fight-ready F-16s from the Netherlands and most of the 19 Denmark promised. But it's lost five of those jets since 2024. And others are so worn out from relentless flying that they're badly in need of maintenance. The Belgian firm Sabena, which services Ukrainian F-16s, has struggled to keep up, and President Volodymyr Zelensky has said about half of the jets spend long stretches abroad for repairs. That slows the return of repaired planes and further squeezes the front-line force.
One wing, too few jets
In short, it's possible the Ukrainian air force's 107th Aviation Wing, its sole F-16 unit, has fewer than 40 ready-to-fight F-16s. Those 53 Belgian F-16s will help grow the wing, but piecemeal. Ukraine should expect a handful of operational jets from Belgium this year. Under a schedule from May, the last 27, half the total, may not arrive until 2029.
To be clear, additional F-16s support the 107th Aviation Wing. The Netherlands sold 18 of its old F-16s to Romania for a token price in order to equip a training squadron, funded by a consortium of Ukraine's allies, that feeds trained pilots to the 107th Aviation Wing. But these 18 jets aren't available for front-line use. They don't even legally belong to Ukraine.
Ukraine is running short of its best missiles for hunting Russia’s jet drones. Now MiG-29s are firing 1970s weapons
The delays in supplies of combat-ready F-16s matter because the Ukrainian air force is under stress. Its last few dozen ex-Soviet warplanes, including Mikoyan MiG-29 and Sukhoi Su-27 fighters, are even older and wearier than the ex-European F-16s are. And they've suffered staggering losses in the air and on the ground in nearly 56 months of hard fighting in the wider war.
The air force does have a few ex-French Dassault Mirage 2000s that are at least as capable as the F-16s, but France has donated only a handful of the supersonic jets—and one has crashed. Any further supplies of Mirage 2000s could be complicated by the French presidential election in April 2027. The leading far-right and far-left parties are both friendly toward Russia and hostile to Ukraine.
Some relief is coming, although not quickly. Sweden has pledged 16 surplus JAS-39C/D Gripen fighters to the Ukrainian war effort; the first of these could arrive early next year. Later on, Ukraine also plans to buy 20 newer JAS-39E/Fs. Kyiv has also negotiated to purchase 16 new Rafale fighters from Paris, but the soonest these could arrive is 2028.
For now, F-16s are the main solution to Ukraine's air defense problems. Kyiv surely wishes it had more of them, sooner.

Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
21:53:00 BST
05:53:00 KST

Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
- Published
Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row.
Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests.
The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time.
Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration.
Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street.
The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday.
During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard.
Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days.
Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic.
Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks.
Black smoke from a burning vehicle and the sirens of police cars and ambulances split the afternoon.
As dusk fell, police special forces arrived to reinforce the riot police.
Many people have been injured on both sides, 80 people have been charged with disorder so far, and hundreds more have been arrested, or are under investigation.
The centre of the Tirana looks increasingly like a war zone, scattered with broken glass and burnt debris.
George, a 19-year-old medical student who works as an electrician to fund his studies, stood near the burnt-out education ministry building, a scarf wrapped round his face and goggles covering his eyes.
He is one of the thousands who have taken part in the increasingly intense protests which began in early June.
In his gloved hands he clutched two rocks intended for the police.
Asked if he was concerned about injuring them, he said: "We have mothers too. We have family too.
"We were peaceful for 135 days. Now we are trying to do like in France… we are trying to make a revolution.
"Our government doesn't want peace, so we are using violence."
Many of the protesters were even younger. Klea, 17, is in her first year of university in Tirana.
She said: "All the students are boycotting their university classes and left school to fight for our rights."
She alleged there were provocateurs among the protesters, smashing up stores and banks, to discredit the demonstrations.
Socialist Party Prime Minister Edi Rama has been in power for 13 years and has dominated Albanian politics, much like his main rival Sali Berisha, of the opposition Democratic Party, did for decades.
The students say they are against "the whole corrupt political class". So what is the alternative?
Osman Stafa, a prominent journalist for the News24 channel, who also describes himself as an activist for change, called for a "neutral, caretaker government for one year, to organise new elections".
The irony for the wider European community during this latest wave of unrest is that Rama has long been viewed favourably by the EU, which Albania aspires to join.
In a social media post on Saturday morning, he urged Albanian to "not forget that we have achieved extraordinary things".
He blamed the protests on the opposition Democratic Party, and on what he called "the sinister agenda of foreign actors, intent on halting our progress" towards EU membership, which he has promised by 2030.
He did not name which "foreign actors" he had in mind.
The latest protests have seriously tarnished Rama's carefully cultivated image as a charming leader, steering his country towards prosperity.
Parallel to the protests, a series of investigations by the special prosecution service also threaten his rule.
Set up under EU and US pressure in 2019, the prosecutors recently arrested the powerful secret service chief Vlora Hyseni.
She stands accused of helping a prominent businessman, former government official, and personal friend of Rama, Ergys Agasi, evade justice. The 39-year-old is under arrest.
Agasi, speaking through his lawyer, denied the allegations against him and said he had nothing to do with corruption. Hyseni told prosecutors that she contacted Agasi to try to recruit him to the intelligence services.
Several Albanian media outlets claim he acted as an intermediary between the prime minister and organised criminal groups.
Rama has admitted that he knows Agasi but denies any knowledge of illegal transactions.
"Edi Rama is caught between a rock and a hard place," Lutfi Dervishi, a political analyst and university lecturer, told the BBC.
"He's the victim of his own success. By concentrating so much power in his own hands, he has made himself the only person the people blame for their grievances."
Rama's Socialist Party has a comfortable majority, with 83 out of 140 seats in the Albanian Parliament. The next parliamentary elections are not due till 2029.

DOHA, October 17. /TASS/. Armed forces of the internationally recognized Yemeni government have neutralized over 800 members of the country’s rebel Ansar Allah (Houthi) movement over the past 24 hours, delivering over 1,400 strikes on their positions, Yemeni Armed Forces Spokesman Majid al-Nuzaili said.
"Over the past 24 hours, 1,417 precision and direct strikes were conducted using combat aircraft, drones, field artillery, and multiple launch rocket systems," he said in a statement.
In his words, "approximately 800 [enemy] elements were neutralized, including killed and wounded, and more than 190 pieces of armored vehicles were destroyed or disabled" as a result of the ongoing Operation Dawn of Yemen.
Al-Nuzaili said the strikes targeted Houthi manpower clusters, their fortified positions, firing points and drone launch sites.
The spokesman added that on the eastern front, government forces continued to clear enemy positions, establishing control over new tactical areas. Besides, in the Taiz Governorate in the country’s southwest, troops repelled continuous waves of Houthi attacks, while the Air Force delivered strikes on enemy positions and reinforcements, thus inflicting significant losses in terms of personnel and equipment.
The armed confrontation between the Houthis and government forces has been going on since August 2014. In September of that year, the Ansar Allah movement established control over the country’s capital Sana’a, and advanced southward. In March 2015, at the request of the then Yemen President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi, a coalition led by Saudi Arabia entered the conflict on the side of the government; the coalition declared its goal to be the restoration of the authority of the country’s internationally recognized leadership.
In early August 2016, the Ansar Allah movement intensified its offensive in the southwest of the country, and in September it established control over the port city of Mocha and the territories with access to the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait in western Yemen. On October 5, Rashad Mohammed al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, announced the launch of a large-scale military operation called the "Dawn of Yemen" to liberate the capital from the rebels; the operation is being carried out with the support of the coalition.
On October 12, the Houthis said they had gained control over a range of areas in the Taiz Governorate and had driven government forces out of these areas. On Wednesday, the armed forces of the internationally-recognized Yemeni government reported that they had neutralized around 1,250 militants and destroyed more than 460 their vehicles as part of Operation Dawn of Yemen.

Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze in France as over 1,000 arrested after protests
- Published
Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against education standards and the cost of living.
At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets.
In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds.
Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse.
Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeted against city halls and businesses also reported.
Sixty law enforcement officers were injured, including two who were taken to hospital unconscious, France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said.
In Paris, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC they were "pacifists" who are "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving".
However, as the day wore on some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles, including in iconic locations in the city centre like the Place de la République.
Shops were ransacked, at least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups.
Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons.
In Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy" for the city, telling BFMTV "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building".
Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze.
Fire crews also battled the fire at Limoges town hall, which the local prefecture said caused part of the building to collapse.
A young man "had his hand blown off by a grenade" in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media, adding: "Such a tragedy should never have happened."
The interior ministry said the protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers.
Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence.
Clothes and food shops were raided in Paris, while an Apple store in Lille was broken into and emptied.
Footage authenticated by BBC Verify showed a tourist train in Grenoble being driven by masked men along a narrow street in the city centre towards at least three riot police officers.
Hundreds of thousands of students have protested in recent weeks over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées - secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.
On Saturday, their numbers were bolstered by trade union members and other protest groups.
These groups include the so-called gilets jaunes 'yellow vest' movement, who demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.
While France is no stranger to outbreaks of protest and disorder, this round comes as the country heads into a period of deep political uncertainty.
French President Emmanuel Macron will leave office next year and polls suggest April's presidential election could come down to a fight between the leader of the National Rally, Marine Le Pen, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the hard-left La France Insoumise party.
The latter took part in demonstrations in France and later accused police officers of "unleashing" on protesters, while condemning looting and arson.
France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said his comments were "dangerous and cynical".
He earlier said police had faced "violence of extreme intensity" and some groups were using the protests as a "warm-up" for the presidential elections, adding: "No-one will impose their political agenda through violence."
Le Pen said "legitimate demands" voiced by protesters had been "held hostage by the far left", accusing Mélenchon of fuelling the violence.
French President Emmanuel Macron said: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished."
The government has made apparent attempts at concessions, with Education Minister Édouard Geffray promising 3,000 extra supply teachers, during a television interview on 8 October.
However, the protests have continued and intensified.

Mass protests in France spiral into worst riots in years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17

05:51:54 KST

Mass protests in France spiral into worst riots in years
FRANCE - Rioting erupted in cities across France on Oct 17 as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiralled out of control in some of the worst violence the country has witnessed for decades.
While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.
In Limoges, the city hall was set ablaze, as Marseille black-clad protesters broke into City Hall and defaced the building with anarchic graffiti and in Lyon protesters torched the city’s tourist office.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be “intimidated” by violence, and blamed the unrest on the “far-left” and criminals just months before a presidential election next year.
“To those who clearly want to use this violence as a ‘warm-up’ before the presidential election, I say clearly: We will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence,” he wrote in a post on X.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters that about 400 people had been arrested after violent incidents, most of whom were adults.
Around 550,000 people had participated in the demonstrations across the country, he said. The CGT union told Reuters it estimated protesters at 800,000 people.
French President Emmanuel Macron vowed to prosecute and punish people who had performed such attacks.
“We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who only seek to undermine our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so,” he wrote in a post on X.
Belgium, Portugal and Italy also faced smaller-scale protests on Oct 17 as living costs rise in Europe, while protesters in Albania again rallied against perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards.
Protesters said most people had marched peacefully, and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police. Many held signs bearing slogans against the police, the president and the wealthy.
“We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions,” said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris.
Tear gas, fire and looting
Most protests kicked off around midday, with some beginning before the official start of the demonstrations.
In some parts of Paris, police fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks and goggles to protect against tear gas.
Rioters tried to break into the Galeries Lafayette department store, smashed up banks, ransacked a Lacoste store as well as other boutiques and looted an SFR mobile phone shop. Protesters had been setting objects ablaze all day, including numerous cars.
In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people protested in Brussels, and some clashed with police. Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible.
In Albania, police fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down.
In Portugal, tens of thousands took to the streets of Lisbon following days of unrest to protest against housing and other living costs. Housing prices in Portugal have doubled since 2017, fuelling one of the worst affordability crises in Europe.
In Italy, a march against high costs of living in Milan degenerated into disorder, with police clearing the central cathedral square with tear gas. Police in Bologna used water cannons to try to disperse crowds and made seven arrests after another protest turned violent, the ANSA news agency reported.
French police response under scrutiny
The protests in France began in September, at high schools in Paris’ working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards.
In Paris on Oct 17, protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, recalling the Yellow Vest movement that marked French President Emmanuel Macron’s previous term in office.
The protests on Oct 17 eclipsed the size of the crowds at the peak of the Yellow Vest movement, though they were far lower than the levels seen at the protests in 2023 against Macron’s pension overhaul.
Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, facing a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy.
France’s efforts to reduce public debt have failed to reassure investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in over two decades.
Police tactics have drawn criticism following injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up a stun grenade. The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence.
Lecornu said more than 900 police officers had also been injured in previous protests.
Nunez said one person lost his hand in clashes with police on Oct 17. French media reported he tried to pick up a stun grenade.
The UNSA police union posted a video on X showing crowds attacking police vans with clubs and bricks in multiple locations. The union warned the government police forces were at breaking point.
“Today again, in every corner of France, our colleagues are being used as punching bags. Pelted with stones, injured, trapped in real ambushes,” the union said. “Let everyone take responsibility: this cannot go on indefinitely. The rope is stretched to its maximum.” REUTERS

Ousmane Dembele recovered from a missed penalty to score a goal and provide an assist as Paris Saint-Germain staged a late comeback to beat Strasbourg 3-1 away on Saturday in matchday seven of the French Ligue 1.
Strasbourg took the lead in the 17th minute when Giovanni Reyna's deflected shot beat PSG goalkeeper Matvey Safonov, giving the hosts a 1-0 advantage at halftime.
Dembele came off the bench in the 63rd minute, replacing Khvicha Kvaratskhelia as PSG searched for an equalizer.
The French winger had a chance to level the score in the 72nd minute after PSG were awarded a penalty following a VAR review, but the reigning Ballon d'Or winner sent his spot kick wide of the right post.
He made amends just five minutes later, delivering a cross from a quickly taken corner that Illya Zabarnyi converted from close range to equalize.
Dembele then completed PSG's comeback in the 85th minute, collecting a loose ball inside the penalty area before firing a left-footed shot past Strasbourg goalkeeper Filip Jorgensen.
Desire Doue sealed the victory in the third minute of stoppage time, tapping home Ferran Torres' pass after Dembele helped launch the attack.
The victory lifted PSG to second in the Ligue 1 standings with 14 points from seven matches, level with leaders Monaco ahead of their game on Sunday, while Strasbourg remained on seven points.

An additional £470 million is being spent on improving the security of critical military sites across Britain, alongside £240 million for an enhanced counter-drone system called Project PRESAGIUM, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Stuart Anderson, the Conservative member for South Shropshire, asked what progress had been made on building resilience to attacks and shocks since the Strategic Defence Review was published.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “Defence is strengthening the UK’s resilience to attacks and shocks through a range of measures, including an additional £470 million investment to improve the security of critical military sites across the UK. This is supportive of broader home defence planning to ensure the resilience of the UK’s most important CNI in the event of a crisis or conflict. We are working across Government in support of the Cabinet Office-led Home Defence Programme, to take a data-driven approach to identifying the CNI most essential to the UK’s ability to sustain and respond to conflict. By contributing Defence data to the Cabinet Office’s CNI Knowledge Base, we are fulfilling the commitments set out in the Resilience Action Plan and improving our understanding of the infrastructure, dependencies and vulnerabilities that would be most critical in a conflict scenario.
“This analysis is informing our Home Defence planning by ensuring that we align Defence resources and capabilities to the protection of the most important infrastructure against a broad spectrum of threats, from hybrid activity through to conventional conflict. It will also help to identify what Defence could contribute to support the protection of other priority CNI that is essential to the functioning of the country.
“Through the Defence Investment Plan and the wider Home Defence Programme, we are also investing in capabilities including Integrated Air and Missile Defence. Defence is investing £240m in Project PRESAGIUM, an enhanced counter-drone system, providing effective detection and defeat of emerging drone threats. We are growing and equipping the Reserves to support Homeland Defence tasks and enhancing capabilities to protect critical underwater infrastructure. Our Integrated Air and Missile Defence capabilities will be prioritised against the assessed threat as part of the future Integrated Force.”

Burc Eruygur
17 October 2026•Update: 17 October 2026
Moscow said on Saturday that the first tanker carrying Russian oil to world markets has departed its point of origin.
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told the political talk show Solovyov Live that Moscow has “no issues” as far as oil sales are concerned and that many countries are interested in becoming buyers of Russian oil.
“I am aware that the first tanker has already been loaded and dispatched from the port at Dikson,” Novak said, referring to the Russian Arctic seaport on the coast of the Kara Sea in the Krasnoyarsk region.
US President Donald Trump on Oct. 9 unveiled a diesel supply agreement following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, under which Moscow agreed to provide fuel to the US and global markets.
Putin said Russian diesel supplies to US and global markets would benefit the world economy, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the deal, warning that easing restrictions on Russian diesel exports could help finance its war effort.
In further remarks, Novak said the market is currently facing a shortfall of approximately 4-6 million barrels of oil per day, which has consequently raised prices.
Novak said that while the market hopes for a resolution, prices remain elevated, and will be driven even higher if the situation in the Strait of Hormuz does not improve.
“If the opportunity for supplies from Persian Gulf countries opens up, it seems to me that the market will rebalance within a year to a year and a half,” Novak added.
He argued that the ability to use oil reserves to stabilize the world market is “already being exhausted.”
The deputy prime minister said Russia expects to supply 39 billion cubic meters of gas to neighboring China through the Power of Siberia pipeline. “There is also an agreement in place to expand its supply capacity to 44 billion cubic meters of gas.”
He said the technical capability to restore gas supplies to Europe via the Nord Stream pipelines still exists “if decisions are made regarding the damaged pipelines.”
“Currently, three of the four lines are inoperable as a result of terrorist attacks and explosions. One line remains intact, and supplies could be delivered through it. However, this depends on the consumers – on our European counterparts,” he said.

Prominent Guatemalan anti-corruption lawyer killed in shooting
GUATEMALA – Guatemalan lawyer Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa, known for his high-profile fight against corruption in the Central American country, died after being shot on Oct 17 by two men while visiting a sports center in Guatemala City, a crime condemned by President Bernardo Arevalo.
Solorzano Foppa was a 43-year-old former prosecutor and anti-corruption lawyer who denounced wrongdoing by some of Guatemala’s most powerful politicians, business leaders and companies, and in 2023 briefly joined the defence team of a prominent journalist.
Shortly after the attack, Guatemalan police reported that they had detained two men and seized a carbine-style firearm and a motorcycle. According to the police, the arrests and seizure of the weapon were in connection with the case.
“I strongly condemn the cowardly murder of former prosecutor Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa. Both the direct perpetrators and those who ordered the crime must face the full weight of the law,” Arevalo said on his official X account. He added that he had instructed his government to coordinate with the relevant authorities to solve the crime.
“Those who believe that terror can intimidate the people of Guatemala and the government I lead are mistaken. In honor of Foppa, in honor of our homeland, in honor of justice.”
The lawyer was known for his anti-corruption work as head of the Criminal Investigations Directorate within the Public Prosecutor’s Office, and later as head of Guatemala’s tax authority, the SAT, from 2016 to 2018, when he helped prosecute dozens of powerful Guatemalan business figures and recover unpaid taxes.
In 2025, Solorzano Foppa alleged a connection between the Barrio 18 gang and the National Unity of Hope party, as well as links between criminal gangs and the judicial system. In 2023, he briefly joined the defense team of Guatemalan journalist Jose Ruben Zamora, who has become an international symbol of resistance to the criminalization of journalism and the erosion of judicial independence in Central America.
Solorzano Foppa had to leave the Zamora case after being accused by the Public Prosecutor’s Office of obstructing the proceedings and destroying or concealing information, a charge he denied but ultimately accepted as part of a plea agreement, saying he did not believe he would receive a fair trial.

Tajik scientist presents glacier research in Almaty
Dilorom Kayumova, a leading researcher at the Institute for the Study of Glaciers and Cryosphere of the Tajik National Academy of Sciences, highlighted the country’s scientific potential, glacier and water resource research in Central Asia, and the role of women in modern science at an international event held in Almaty, Qazinform News Agency cites Khovar.
The discussion brought together scientists and experts from Tajikistan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan representing fields including glaciology, cognitive sciences, medical technologies and artificial intelligence.
The event focused on the future of science in Central Asia, the region's capacity to define its own research priorities, generate globally significant knowledge and ensure the practical application of scientific findings.
Presenting research on Tajikistan's glaciers, Kayumova emphasized the importance of high-altitude glaciers for studying climate change and understanding the formation of regional water resources. She noted that the systematic collection of data on snow cover, glaciers and meltwater helps deepen understanding of natural processes and provides a scientific basis for decision-making on water security and climate adaptation.
Particular attention was given to the use of modern research methods, including isotope hydrology, which allows scientists to determine the origin of water, study its formation and trace its movement through natural systems.
According to Dilorom Kayumova, the development of such research expands the capabilities of Tajik scientists and strengthens the country's scientific potential in the study of glaciers and water resources across Central Asia.

tob.studio’s timber bike station in germany resembles stacked log pile

Unknown Publisher

20:35:02 UTC
05:35:02 KST

tob.studio’s timber bike station in germany resembles stacked log pile
the bike station integrates e-bike charging stations, repair facilities, and digital information, as well as public amenities including an accessible toilet and shower.
prefer designboom on google
LOG PILE GEOMETRY SHAPES TIMBER CYCLING HUB by ToB.Studio
Designed by ToB.Studio, the Burgsinn Cycling Rest Station establishes a public service hub along the D9 cycle route in Germany, positioned at the transition between the town and surrounding landscape. Drawing visual cues from local forestry history, the compact building reinterprets the form of stacked timber logs. Its solid volume features carved-out niches that accommodate sheltered seating areas, entrances, and service points beneath a broad overhanging green roof.
rough-sawn larch cladding wraps bike station’s exterior
The station, designed by ToB.Studio architectural practice, provides a range of amenities for cyclists, pool visitors, and local residents, including e-bike charging stations, a repair and wash area, digital information displays, and an accessible toilet and shower. The structure is built using a prefabricated timber frame according to Design for Disassembly principles, utilizing reversible mechanical connections to facilitate future maintenance and material-specific recycling. Constructed with locally sourced untreated larch cladding, wood-fiber insulation, and a membrane-free wall assembly, the building rests on a single reinforced-concrete slab that functions as the foundation, flood barrier, and finished floor surface.

NAIROBI, October 17. /TASS/. The number of confirmed Ebola cases in Kenya has risen to seven, including one fatality, Reuters reported, citing the country’s Health Ministry.

NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Saturday announced a compensation of Rs 25 lakh and a government job for the family of each person killed in a stampede at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal in north Kolkata.The state government will also bear the entire cost of medical treatment for the injured and provide Rs 5 lakh to each of them, Adhikari said, adding that a fact-finding committee would be constituted to investigate the incident."This is a tragic incident. 19 people have lost their lives, 17 of whom died on the spot... 25 people have been injured; 24 of them are out of danger, while one remains in critical condition," the chief minister said. He added that the government was making every possible effort to assist the affected families and that he had personally met relatives of the deceased.
'Appropriate measures against those who failed to manage crowd'
Adhikari said the state government would seek the intervention of the Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court to constitute a fact-finding committee, which would include special task force (STF) and forensic teams. The investigation would examine the circumstances leading to the stampede and identify those responsible for the crowd management arrangements.
Kolkata Police's Anti-Rowdy Section (ARS) has collected CCTV footage from the site, which will be examined as part of the investigation."We will check the footage and take appropriate measures against those who failed to manage the crowd. That could be a member of the puja committee, a homeguard, a temporary worker, a policeman, or a private company security guard. Nobody will be spared," Adhikari said.He said the state government was making arrangements for postmortems in accordance with the law and that six of the deceased had been identified so far. Officials were also coordinating with the families of the victims.The chief minister said the families who had met him had expressed faith in the state government. He added that the Prime Minister's Office had sought a report from the chief secretary, which had been submitted, and that the Centre and the state were working together to provide assistance.
'Some attempting to politicise this, but it will be to no avail'
Adhikari also criticised the previous state government over its handling of past tragedies, accusing some people of attempting to politicise the current incident."Everyone is well aware of the role of the previous government in similar incidents that occurred in the past. Some are attempting to politicize this, but it will be to no avail. I have met with the families of the deceased, and they have explicitly stated that they have full faith in the Chief Minister and the government... The PMO also requested a report from the Chief Secretary, which we have submitted. The Prime Minister has announced relief and compensation. He also referred to a devastating flood in north Bengal that killed 100 people, questioning the previous chief minister's response to those tragedies.
'An announcement by the organisers' led to the rush
The stampede occurred on Saturday evening, on Maha Saptami, at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal in north Kolkata. At least 19 people died and 25 were injured after a crowd surge amid rain, according to officials.A police officer said people waiting outside the pandal rushed forward as it began raining, causing some to fall on the road and triggering the stampede. Adhikari said an announcement made by the organisers of the community Durga Puja had led to a rush among revellers, resulting in what he described as a "painful incident".Officials of the organising club, private security guards and personnel on duty were detained for questioning, he said. The administration also advised several crowded theme-based puja pandals to temporarily close following the tragedy.
Union home minister Amit Shah, who had arrived in Kolkata and was scheduled to visit pandals on Sunday, cancelled his programmes following the incident. Art dealer who sold forged Warhols sentenced to nearly four years in prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
20:22:43 UTC
05:22:43 KST

A Miami art dealer who admitted to selling forged Andy Warhol artwork has been sentenced to nearly four years in prison.
Leslie Roberts, 62, created fraudulent invoices and authentication documents, as well as counterfeit stamps to deceive buyers, the US justice department said in a statement issued on Thursday.
The US district judge Roy Altman sentenced Roberts to three years and 10 months in federal prison on 2 October. The Associated Press reported that Altman also ordered Roberts to repay $2.6m stolen through his scheme centering on artwork falsely attributed to the leader of the pop art movement.
Roberts sold the fakes in question through his Miami art gallery, claiming he acquired the artwork from the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, according to the justice department. He provided fraudulent invoices that appeared to have been issued by the organization before pleading guilty in June to conspiring to commit wire fraud.
He also enlisted Carlos Rodriguez Melendez to pose as an employee of a New York-based auction company and falsely authenticate the work. The accomplice also pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud.
A statement from the southern district of Florida’s US attorney, Jason Reding Quiñones, said it was important to prosecute Roberts “because art fraud undermines confidence in the legitimate art market and victimizes buyers who rely on the authenticity of the works they purchase”.
Roberts “exploited the trust that collectors place in art dealers and the authenticity of the works they purchase”, Reding Quiñones said.
Reding Quiñones said Roberts’ prison sentence “sends a clear message: fraud is fraud, whether it happens on Wall Street or in an art gallery. Those who profit through deception will be held accountable.”
Others have also been convicted in recent months of selling fake Warhol work.
In April, a father and daughter in New Jersey, Erwin Bankowski and Karolina Bankowska, admitted to commissioning an artist in Poland to create at least 200 Warhol, Banksy and Pablo Picasso fakes and ultimately defrauding buyers of at least $2m.
The pair pleaded guilty to running a years-long counterfeiting scheme in which they tricked galleries and auction houses into buying the forgeries. When sentenced, they could face up to 20 years’ imprisonment as well as at least $1.9m in restitution, the US justice department said in a statement.

MOSCOW, October 17. /TASS/. Global oil prices may grow even further if attempts to stabilize the situation in the Strait of Hormuz are unsuccessful, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said in an interview to Marina Kim on the Soloviev Live television.
He recalled that the closure of the strait dealt a serious blow to the global energy and oil market. Earlier, this waterway accounted for approximately 18-20 million barrels per day, or 20% of the total global oil production and consumption.
"We see that the global oil market is currently facing a shortfall of around 4-6 billion barrels per day. That is why the price has risen; it is reacting to the deficit. Volatility is high," he said. "While the market expects things to stabilize there, prices remain high nonetheless."
"However, if this situation persists, in my view, it will drive prices up even further, because stockpiles are currently being drawn from various reserves," the Russian deputy premier added.
In his words, the capacity to use oil stockpiles to stabilize the global market has nearly been exhausted.
"Based on our assessments and those of experts, in fact, the potential to draw from reserves is effectively running out," the official said.

====================================================================================================

Two styles of meditation eased depressive symptoms in a four-week trial, possibly through different routes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
20:00:58 UTC
05:00:58 KST

A randomized controlled trial found that two different styles of meditation, one centered on focused attention and one on self-inquiry, reduced depressive symptoms over four weeks compared with a wait-list control group in adults without a depression diagnosis. Exploratory analyses suggested that the two practices may work through partially different psychological processes. The paper was published in Mindfulness.
Meditation has long been studied as a way to ease depression. However, an important question is why meditation works, and whether all forms of meditation work in the same way. Depression is often maintained by rigid negative beliefs about the self, habitual patterns of thinking, and a tendency to interpret experiences as threatening or personally damaging. Meditation may interrupt this cycle through cognitive decentering, which helps people observe thoughts and emotions without immediately treating them as facts or as reflections of who they are.
This shift may also contribute to a broader psychological state sometimes described as selflessness, in which the self is experienced as less rigid, less isolated, and less central to every experience. The idea has roots in Buddhist traditions, which regard attachment to a fixed and independent self as an important source of suffering.
Modern psychology has begun to translate this idea into measurable processes such as connectedness to other people and nature, along with the ability to adopt a more detached perspective on one’s own thoughts and feelings. However, meditation is not a single technique. Different practices may influence these processes in different ways.
Study authors Céline Stinus of the University of Navarra in Spain and Sophie Berjot of the University of Reims Champagne-Ardenne in France conducted a randomized controlled trial comparing the effects of two types of meditation on depressive symptoms and several related psychological characteristics. They expected the self-inquiry practice, which targets rigid beliefs about the self more directly, to produce larger benefits.
Focused-attention meditation involves sustaining attention on a chosen object, such as the breath, noticing when the mind wanders, and repeatedly returning attention to that object. Self-inquiry meditation is a practice in which people examine their thoughts, beliefs, and sense of self by asking questions about where these mental experiences come from and how they shape emotions and behavior. The self-inquiry program used in the study was secular and did not include Buddhist teachings.
The final sample included 147 adults recruited in France through social media, university campuses, and the researchers’ professional networks. People were not eligible if they were taking psychiatric medication, had previously been diagnosed with depression or any other psychiatric condition, or were experienced meditators.
Participants were randomly assigned to focused-attention meditation, self-inquiry meditation, or a wait-list control group, with 49 people in each group in the final analysis. The average age was about 49 in the focused-attention group, 46 in the self-inquiry group, and 44 in the control group, and each group was mostly made up of women.
Participants in the meditation groups were not told which type of meditation they had been assigned to, while those in the control group were told they had been placed on a wait-list. Each meditation program lasted four weeks and included five 60-minute online group sessions, all led by the study’s first author, plus 20 minutes of individual practice a day, five days a week. The two meditation groups attended sessions and practiced at home at similar rates.
Participants completed assessments a week before the programs began and within seven days after they ended. The assessments included measures of depressive symptoms (the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale), dysfunctional attitudes (the Dysfunctional Attitudes Scale), identity threat, or the perception that one’s sense of self is being undermined or devalued (the Threat Appraisal Subscale of the Cognitive Appraisal Scale), cognitive decentering (the Metacognitive Processes of Decentering Trait scale), connectedness to nature (the Connectedness to Nature Scale), and connectedness to humanity (the Connectedness to Humanity scale).
Both meditation programs led to greater reductions in depressive symptoms and identity threat than the wait-list condition, with moderate effect sizes, and both increased cognitive decentering. There were no reliable differences between the two meditation programs on these outcomes. Contrary to the researchers’ expectations, only the focused-attention group showed a reduction in dysfunctional attitudes relative to the wait-list group; the self-inquiry group did not.
The meditation programs did not differ reliably from the wait-list group in their overall effects on connectedness to humanity or nature. However, exploratory analyses found that only the self-inquiry group showed increases in both forms of connectedness from before to after the program.
Exploratory analyses of the processes behind these changes suggested that, in the focused-attention group, increases in cognitive decentering fully accounted for the reduction in depressive symptoms and partly accounted for the reduction in dysfunctional attitudes. In the self-inquiry group, increases in connectedness to humanity partly accounted for reductions in identity threat. Unexpectedly, increases in connectedness to nature in this group were linked to smaller reductions in identity threat, and none of the measured processes explained the self-inquiry group’s reduction in depressive symptoms. Because these analyses were run separately within each group, they do not allow a direct statistical comparison of the two practices’ mechanisms.
“Attentional and deconstructive meditation practices yield comparable benefits for depression-related outcomes but operate through partially distinct mechanisms. Cognitive decentering played a central mechanism in attentional meditation [the focused-attention meditation procedure] while deconstructive practice [the self-inquiry meditation procedure] showed exploratory associations with connectedness [to nature and to humanity], warranting cautious interpretation,” study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the mechanisms through which meditation practices might affect depressive symptoms. However, it should be noted that participants in the control group knew they were not receiving treatment, and all outcomes were based on self-reports, which leaves room for expectancy effects and self-report bias. Participants had not been diagnosed with depression or any other psychiatric condition, and their average depression scores were low and within the nonclinical range.
Both meditation programs were delivered by the same instructor, who was also the study’s first author, leaving open the possibility that instructor-related effects influenced the results. In addition, 20 participants dropped out of the wait-list group compared with four or five in each meditation group, the study was not preregistered, and there was no long-term follow-up. Participants were also mostly women who signed up for a meditation study and may have been especially receptive to it.
The paper, “Preventing Depression through Selflessness: Effects and Mechanisms of Attentional vs. Deconstructive Meditation in a Three–Arm Randomized Controlled Trial,” was authored by Céline Stinus and Sophie Berjot.

COP17: Kyrgyzstan suggests $10M fund to protect Issyk-Kul
Unknown

COP17: Kyrgyzstan suggests $10M fund to protect Issyk-Kul
Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov suggested establishing a special trust fund to protect Lake Issyk-Kul, pledging an initial 10 million US dollars from the state budget and calling on international donors and financial institutions to support the initiative, Qazinform News Agency cites Kabar.
Speaking at the Leaders' Summit during the 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17) to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity in Yerevan, Zhaparov stressed the need for stronger international cooperation to address climate change, biodiversity loss, and environmental degradation.
The Kyrgyz leader warned that glacier melt across Central Asia, driven by global warming, poses a growing threat to mountain ecosystems and regional biodiversity. He proposed four key initiatives to the international community: creating a dedicated mountain program under the Global Environment Facility, establishing a global mountain sustainability center in Bishkek, introducing debt-for-nature swap mechanisms, and strengthening regional efforts to protect endangered wildlife.
Highlighting concerns over the future of Issyk-Kul, Zhaparov said the lake's water level has fallen by nearly 14 meters over the past 170 years, with the decline accelerating to around seven centimeters annually during the last five years.
He outlined conservation measures already underway, noting that authorities have removed nearly 70 tons of waste and approximately 580,000 meters of illegal synthetic fishing nets from the lake over the past four years.
Zhaparov said Kyrgyzstan, with UN support, has launched efforts to create a dedicated trust fund to preserve the lake's ecosystem and appealed for international backing. The country is prepared to contribute 10 million US dollars as seed funding for the initiative.
The president also invited governments and international organizations to participate in the Second Global Mountain Summit "Bishkek+25," scheduled for October 21-23, 2027, in Bishkek.
Concluding his remarks, Zhaparov emphasized that biodiversity conservation must be integrated into economic policy, investment decisions, and regional development strategies, describing environmental protection as a shared responsibility for future generations.
Earlier, Kazakh President presented the Taza Qazaqstan initiative at COP17 Summit.
