(Hello Africa) Chinese hybrid rice takes root in Madagascar, boosts harvests, livelihoods
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
00:45:32 CST
01:45:32 KST

Chinese agronomist Hu Yuefang explains the growth of rice to local farmers at the China Hybrid Rice High-Yield Demonstration Base near Antananarivo, Madagascar, March 25, 2025. (Xinhua/Li Yahui)
Since a China-aided hybrid rice demonstration center project was launched in 2007, Chinese agricultural experts have introduced high-yielding rice varieties and cultivation techniques adapted to local conditions. To date, Chinese hybrid rice has been planted on a cumulative area of 90,000 hectares in Madagascar, with two to three times that of traditional local varieties. Madagascar now has the largest area under hybrid rice cultivation in Africa.
ANTANANARIVO, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- As the rainy season approaches, farmer Jean Jacques Landry is busy plowing his hybrid rice paddy near Lake Alaotra, about 300 km from Antananarivo, Madagascar's capital, in preparation for the new planting season.
Landry is among a growing number of Malagasy farmers benefiting from years of China-Madagascar cooperation in hybrid rice cultivation. Since a China-aided hybrid rice demonstration center project was launched in 2007, Chinese agricultural experts have introduced high-yielding rice varieties and cultivation techniques adapted to local conditions.
To date, Chinese hybrid rice has been planted on a cumulative area of 90,000 hectares in Madagascar, with an average yield of about 7.5 tonnes per hectare, two to three times that of traditional local varieties. Madagascar now has the largest area under hybrid rice cultivation in Africa.
BETTER SEEDS, BIGGER HARVESTS
Rice cultivation has a long history in Madagascar, yet domestic production has struggled to meet the country's staple food needs due to constraints including seed quality, farming techniques, and infrastructure.
Nineteen years ago, Chinese agricultural expert Hu Yuefang and other technicians arrived in Madagascar with hybrid rice seeds and cultivation techniques under the demonstration center project, aiming to help the technology take root on the island.
Given Madagascar's diverse climatic and environmental conditions, ranging from tropical rainforests and semi-arid regions to swamps and volcanic ash soils, finding suitable hybrid rice varieties was no easy task.
"For hybrid rice to take root here, we first had to find the right seeds," Hu said.
Carrying dozens of carefully selected rice seed samples, Hu and his team conducted a series of planting trials across the island's major rice-growing regions.
Years of painstaking work paid off when the team successfully developed five rice varieties suited to local conditions. The varieties combine high yields with resistance to drought, flooding, and lodging.
According to Hu, the rice varieties yielded two to three times as much as traditional local varieties. Impressed by their high productivity, villagers fondly nicknamed Chinese hybrid rice "Tsarabe," meaning "excellent" in Malagasy.
Chinese agronomist Hu Yuefang checks the rice seeds at the China Hybrid Rice High-Yield Demonstration Base near Antananarivo, Madagascar, March 26, 2025. (Xinhua/Li Yahui)
KNOWLEDGE SHARING BOOSTS PRODUCTION
"We must not only provide good seeds, but also teach farmers how to grow good rice," Hu said.
From sowing and raising seedlings to managing pests and diseases, he demonstrated each step of the cultivation process himself. To communicate more effectively with local farmers, he spent three years learning Malagasy.
Alongside field demonstrations, Chinese experts have also held monthly classroom training sessions at a local agricultural training center.
Over the years, Chinese agricultural experts have conducted hundreds of training sessions on hybrid rice cultivation in Madagascar, directly training more than 2,000 people and passing on techniques to tens of thousands of local farmers through indirect training and knowledge sharing.
In Mahitsy, about 35 km from Antananarivo, farmer Solomampionona Nantenaina Razafimalala has been growing hybrid rice since 2020. After switching to hybrid varieties and applying an appropriate amount of fertilizer, Razafimalala's rice yields can reach 10 tonnes per hectare.
Today, his family has enough rice to meet its needs throughout the year and earns additional income by selling surplus harvests, allowing it to gradually invest in more agricultural inputs.
Fellow farmer Mbolatiana Anjarasoa Rasolonomenjanahary has had a similar experience. A paddy that once yielded only about five bags of unhusked rice now produces 12 bags with hybrid varieties.
"Our lives have truly changed. We have gained valuable farming experience and become more independent, able to manage production on our own," she said.
According to Zhang Lijun, executive director of the Africa sub-center of the China National Hybrid Rice Research and Development Center, the project has benefited more than 5,000 farming households in Madagascar. The net income from cultivating traditional local rice varieties is approximately 2,000 yuan (about 300 U.S. dollars) per hectare, compared with more than 6,900 yuan per hectare for hybrid rice.
He added that if Madagascar devoted 150,000 hectares of its existing rice-growing land to hybrid rice cultivation, the country could achieve food self-sufficiency.
Farmers walk among fields of the China Hybrid Rice High-Yield Demonstration Base near Antananarivo, Madagascar, March 26, 2025. (Xinhua/Li Yahui)
DEEPENING AGRICULTURAL COOPERATION
In December 2024, the Hunan Hybrid Rice Research Center and the University of Antananarivo jointly established the China-Madagascar Belt and Road Joint Hybrid Rice Laboratory.
Through collaborative breeding of new rice varieties, personnel exchanges and training, as well as technology demonstrations and promotion, the two sides aim to strengthen Madagascar's domestic capacity for hybrid rice research and development.
Tiana Randriamihanta, Malagasy research project leader at the joint laboratory, said the facility would compare Chinese and Malagasy rice cultivation techniques to improve rice varieties and promote the local application of hybrid rice technology.
The laboratory currently has seven researchers and will focus on advancing hybrid rice research and education, boosting yields and training more technical professionals to support the development of Madagascar's hybrid rice industry.
Madagascar has also established an integrated hybrid rice industry chain encompassing breeding, seed production, cultivation, processing and sales, making it the first African country to commercialize hybrid rice. ■

Israeli forces, settlers damage 3,522 West Bank fruit trees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17

Breadcrumb
Israeli forces, settlers cause $1.9m in losses to Palestinian farmers in a week
Israeli forces and settler attacks damaged at least 3,522 fruit trees and caused agricultural losses exceeding $1.9 million over a period of a week in the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian Ministry of Agriculture announced.
The ministry's report for the week of 8 - 15 October showed that settlers had intensified their targeting of farmers and their crops during the olive harvesting season. At least 2,667 olive trees - three-quarters of the trees included in the survey - were reported damaged.
The damage varied between cutting down, uprooting, and burning trees, in addition to stealing and confiscating olive fruits, and destroying agricultural facilities and irrigation networks.
The report also noted that Palestinian farmers were prevented from accessing their lands, threatening their ability to harvest crops and compounding their losses during a season on which thousands of Palestinian families in the occupied West Bank depend as a source of income.
The ministry's report added that settlers stole 8,612 kilograms of olives, equivalent to approximately 8.6 tons.
The impact of this theft extends beyond the value of the olives themselves; farmers also lose a portion of their seasonal income and bear the costs of tree care and harvesting without any guarantee of safe access to their land or the ability to market their produce.
Hebron Governorate topped the list of the most affected areas with losses estimated at approximately $455,000, followed by Jenin with approximately $452,000.
The similarity in losses between the two governorates reflects the wide geographical extent of the damage, while the remaining losses are distributed across other areas of the West Bank.
The report comes after a week of even greater losses, with the Ministry of Agriculture's report for the period from 1 - 8 October documenting direct losses of approximately $3,678,000 and damage to 3,192 olive trees in seven governorates, with Jenin being the most affected.
The new report records damage in the following week, indicating continued losses throughout the harvest season.
The olive harvest is a primary source of income and employment in Palestinian villages, supporting tens of thousands of families wholly or partially.
The effects of the attacks go beyond the trees and the harvest, impacting family incomes and activities related to harvesting, pressing, and trade.

What interests him is not being the largest party in the bloc of those who serve, but being larger than Likud and entering negotiations to form a government with Netanyahu from a position of strength."

G7 pledges 260 million euros to repair Chornobyl’s shield after Russia pierced it. Full repair will require 500 million euros by 2030, before corrosion sets in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:40:46 UTC
01:40:46 KST

A Russian drone tore a hole in the shield over Chornobyl’s dead reactor. Now the G7 is paying to patch it.
The Group of Seven nations plans to allocate 260 million euros ($292 million) to repair the New Safe Confinement at the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant, First Deputy Prime Minister and Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal says on X.
The confinement, a 35-story steel arch sealing the reactor that exploded in the 1986 disaster, was damaged by a Russian drone strike in February 2025. Full restoration will cost at least 500 million euros, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) estimates, so the G7 pledge covers just over half, leaving about 240 million euros still to raise.
Shmyhal calls the decision an important step toward restoring nuclear safety at the plant, which the Russian strike had compromised. The money will go to priority work, including resealing the structure and restoring its ventilation system.
“Thank you to France and personally to Minister Roland Lescure for leadership in mobilizing international support,” Shmyhal says, crediting France and the EBRD with co-chairing the effort.
The night a drone pierced the sarcophagus
The damage dates to 14 February 2025. A Russian drone carrying a high-explosive warhead punched a hole through the arch’s roof and ignited a fire in the cladding, breaching the structure’s seal and ventilation.
The attack caused a 15 m² breach in the inner and outer cladding and damaged around 200 m² of panels.
"It was a targeted Russian attack on the Chornobyl station with a drone that is an analog of the Iranian Shahed," Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said at that time.
A bill only half-covered, and a 2030 deadline
The G7 money closes only part of the gap. Partners must still raise roughly 240 million euros more, and Ukraine hopes to secure it at a donor conference in Paris co-chaired by Ukraine, France and the EBRD, Shmyhal says.
The clock matters as much as the cost. The work must be finished by 2030 to limit corrosion and protect the arch’s 100-year design life, the EBRD says, turning a repair bill into a race against the rust the strike set loose.

It directs people to the BDS website, which details how Microsoft's technology is being used in Israel’s war on Gaza to carry out potential war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide.
“It has always been our intention for Big Walk to be played by groups of friends, and we know that keeping the game off Xbox runs counter to those intentions,” the statement from House House continued.
House House expressed regret at not being able to make the game available Xbox, but said it remains firm on the decision until Microsoft and, or Xbox have been removed as BDS boycott targets.
The decision has received widespread praise from activists, with many also calling on them to take their decision a step further by cutting any links they have to SONY, citing their sale of equipment to the Israeli military.
This is not the first time House House has supported the plight of Palestinians. In 2023, the developer released a statement emphasising the Palestinian right to self-determination following the start of Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave.
“Now that we're back on here, we want to express our support for the Palestinian people, and their right to self-determination, safety and happiness. An end to this genocide. An end to apartheid. Free Palestine,” they wrote.
The Big Walk game, which is a multi-player adventure that centres on teamwork, challenges and puzzles, is still available on other apps and platforms, including Steam and Nintendo.

Pope Leo returns to Vatican four days after lung cancer surgery

Pope Leo left the hospital in Rome on Saturday afternoon and returned to the Vatican four days after surgery for lung cancer, an illness that has prompted speculation about how it might affect his 17-month papacy.
The 71-year-old walked unaided to his waiting car, waving to well-wishers outside Rome's Gemelli Hospital. He stopped to speak to a 13-year-old girl named Varvara from Ukraine who has been in Italy for cancer treatment.
He was pictured smiling broadly and waving through an open window when his black SUV left the hospital. He waved again to crowds as he was driven back into the Vatican but did not speak to anyone there before re-entering the world's smallest country.
His doctors had said earlier on Saturday that he was well enough to return home after they carried out the latest blood tests and chest imaging, and that he was able to perform normal daily activities independently.
Leo, who had an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, will hold his first public engagement since surgery when he will lead weekly prayers with pilgrims in St. Peter's Square at noon (1000 GMT) on Sunday.
He has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis for a pope known to be relatively young and energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 caused shock and raised questions about the future shape of his papacy as he deals with the illness.
The pope's doctors have said his surgery was completed successfully, without complications. They have not yet disclosed the size of the tumor or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis.
Pope pursues packed agenda
The Vatican signaled on Friday that Leo, known for following a busy schedule, intended to keep up his commitments, as some cardinals began to publicly express concern about the pope's health.
In a sign the pope was back to work, Leo held a phone call on Friday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, urging a ceasefire to help get vital supplies into the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky.
The Vatican said work on Leo's November 6 to 17 visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, one of the most intense arranged for a pope in decades, was also "going forward." It released a list of journalists accredited to travel with Leo and cover the trip.
Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's secretary of state, said on Friday that Leo may need to adjust the pace of his schedule going forward "according to the condition of his health." It is unusual for a cardinal to say openly that a pope might need to modify his routine.
On Friday, the Vatican released the first images of the pope since his surgery, showing him celebrating Mass and standing unaided.

The problem with Israel’s hasbara is what it refuses to say - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:34:20 UTC
01:34:20 KST

Nearly every political party and research institute opposed to the current government is flagging better hasbara (public diplomacy) as a critical priority going forward and as a reason to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
But most politicians and analysts blabbing about this have failed to outline the tough messaging that must sweepingly replace Israel’s weak positioning of recent decades.
Perhaps because they are afraid to do so, or are incapable of recognizing the need to do so.
A few examples: former MK Dr. Einat Wilf, running third on the Reservists-Economic party’s Knesset list, is calling for a major expansion of the Foreign Ministry’s resources to combat anti-Israel narratives abroad, beyond the NIS 500 million that Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar has smartly invested.
Her recently unveiled seven-point national policy plan calls for integrating Israel’s “war of consciousness” into national security decision-making.
She proposes establishing a centralized information and intelligence hub for hasbara efforts, and using diplomatic, legal, and economic tools against supporters of terrorism.
She demands that Israel shift from reactive to “proactive” postures in public diplomacy, where Israel would shape the international debate rather than primarily respond to criticism and accusations.
All good. But what Wilf does not say is what the content of said hasbara would be.
She doesn’t explicitly outline the revolution necessary in Israel’s messaging: resolute messaging that matches Israel’s necessarily aggressive new strategic and defense posture, and messaging that restores Jewish faith to Israel’s diplomatic arsenal.
Similarly, Dr. Pnina Sharvit Baruch, former head of the IDF’s international law department and a senior researcher at INSS, has penned a 24-page proposal for restoring Israel’s international standing.
It calls for “building professional, factual, and legal capabilities to address allegations, institutional biases, and campaigns against Israel” that also “appeal to emotion,” and “adopting differentiated policies towards different audiences” – all correct approaches that I have advocated in these pages.
But she also shies away from biting the bullet, which is acknowledging that public diplomacy based on advocacy of the so-called “two-state solution” is a recipe for continued Israeli failure.
Instead, she misguidedly calls for renewed “presentation of a credible diplomatic horizon,” code for Palestinian statehood – as if nothing has changed in Israel’s diplomatic and defense world since the utter collapse of the Oslo Accords and since the October 7, 2023, massacre by Hamas.
THAT FACT IS that 25 years of Oslo-era diplomacy and hasbara epistles have not worked. It is simply insufficient to explain Israel’s security dilemmas or emphasize Israel’s past and potentially future diplomatic generosity towards the Palestinians.
Three additional themes are needed.
The changes needed for Israeli public diplomacy
The first is making Israeli public diplomacy more unequivocally and candidly “Jewish.” In the past, “secular” themes have dominated – Israel’s security needs and diplomatic bigheartedness.
This was because secular messaging was most comfortable for secular Israeli leaders and diplomats, and they also thought it was most relatable to foreign leaders and Jews of the Diaspora.
These days, given the ideological assault on Judaism and Zionism that underpins violent Palestinianism and its “progressive” fellow travelers, this must change.
We all must insist on a narrative that proclaims incontrovertible, indigenous Jewish rights in Israel – including in Jerusalem, and Judea and Samaria – and which speaks of Israel as a grand reunion of faith, people, and land.
We can win only if we speak about history, justice, and the Jewish nation. Jews abroad also need to recognize that one cannot escape core Jewish identities and claims in the Land of Israel in any effort to support Israel.
Indeed, in repeated visits to Dubai and Abu Dhabi, I have found that urbane Arabs like the Emiratis respect Israelis for their faithfulness to Jewish tradition, their belief in the power of Jewish history, their loyalty to ancient heritage, and their unique national identity.
The Emiratis seem to understand, better than we sometimes do ourselves, that these anchors of identity are the greatest source of strength and authenticity.
Second, there is no choice but to own up to and embrace Israel’s strength.
Israeli messaging must affirm Israeli power and articulate how that strength is justifiably and wisely being used to fight Iran, Islamic jihadism, and annihilationist-against-Israel Palestinianism.
The fact is that Israel is acting with overwhelming military power to reset the regional strategic architecture and roll back its enemies.
Israel is seeking to restore its dominance and deterrence across all its borders, and in Judea and Samaria as well, and it will yet act even more forcefully.
In fact, Israel is permanently resetting its borders with Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria for security reasons, without apology. Fiercer-than-ever takedowns of Iran and Hamas are surely coming, too.
Of course, this presents a heightened hasbara challenge for advocates for Israel, but there is no way to avoid Israel’s ferocity. The challenge must be met defiantly and unwaveringly.
David Ben-Gurion’s famous adage about the Messianic era when the lion will lie down with the lamb (as per Isaiah) is appropriate. “That will be great,” said Ben-Gurion, “as long as Israel is the lion!”
Supporters of Israel cannot be shy about Israeli military prowess. They must articulate the reasons why Israel must be the “lion” and use crushing force to destroy enemies and defend its homeland.
In my mind, this is a vital turnabout in Israeli public diplomacy and global pro-Israel activism. No apologetics or apprehension about Israeli power will improve Israel’s standing.
On the contrary, one can convey a deep sense of sincerity by clarifying Israeli red lines and owning up to Israel’s unavoidably hard-hitting defense posture.
People are forced to respect that, even if they do not contribute to Israel’s spectacular charity.
THE THIRD and hardest theme necessary in Israeli policy and public diplomacy is reintroducing realism and truth-telling into the global dynamic.
This means more than basic restatement of the Jewish people’s profound historic and national rights in Jerusalem and in the misnamed “occupied territories.”
It means more than clearly and constantly articulated outrage about genocidal anti-Zionist and anti-Jewish sentiment; and more than unabashed enunciation of Israel’s determination to decisively beat all enemies.
It means more than stopping to appeal for global sympathy because we were massacred by Hamas, and more than combating modern blood libels like the genocide and war crime charges with aggressive counter-facts and lawsuits.
It means explaining why the two-state concept is suspended and why the Palestinians do not deserve nor can be trusted with their own state – if they ever did or could.
It means demanding that the world dial back from the now evidently dangerous, impossible-to-implement, “everybody-knows-what-must-be” paradigm that imagined two democratic states living side by side peacefully after maximal Israeli withdrawals.
Israel will not yield to a stale formula based on wild Palestinian demands alongside minimal regard for Israeli security needs and national-historic claims; a discredited formula involving the uprooting of settlements, withdrawals from most of Judea and Samaria, and a division of Jerusalem.
Iranian-backed jihadism and Hamas-inspired rejectionism have thoroughly infected the Palestinian national movement and made such proposals passé.
There are no “demilitarization parameters,” “governance reforms,” and “deradicalization programs” (really, denazification curriculums) that are remotely realistic regarding Palestinians in this generation.
Perhaps under long-term Israeli sovereignty and military control, and only then, might Palestinians be freed from the venomous doctrines and ruinous theologies that have overtaken their society and politics.
Then they might find solace and solutions in cooperation with Israel.
Of course, it is politically incorrect to say these things bluntly. But it is the rock-bottom mandatory basis for authentic Israeli policy and public diplomacy with any chance of succeeding.
Israel cannot deflect boycotts and scuttle sanctions by fudging its defense policy and pussyfooting around with its diplomatic messaging.
Nothing less frank will reflect reality; nothing less audacious will ring true; nothing less bold will hold.
The writer is managing senior fellow at the Jerusalem-based Misgav Institute for National Security & Zionist Strategy. The views expressed here are his own. His diplomatic, defense, political, and Jewish world columns over the past 30 years are at davidmweinberg.com.

Israel must treat the media war as seriously as Iran’s nuclear threat, Gil Hoffman says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:34:10 UTC
01:34:10 KST

Three years after Hamas’s October 7 attack, Israel is still fighting a war it was never prepared for, one in which the weapons are not missiles or tanks but headlines, social media posts, and the narratives that shape how the world sees the Jewish state.
For Gil Hoffman, a veteran political analyst who has spent much of his career examining how Israel is portrayed abroad, this battle is not simply a public relations issue, but a strategic threat that the country’s leadership has repeatedly failed to recognize.
Hoffman covered politics for The Jerusalem Post for nearly a quarter century, before taking over as executive director and executive editor of HonestReporting to “lead the fight for Israel on the media battlefield.”
He spoke with the Post this week in the wake of the publication of his new book, The Blood Libel Machine, which argues that the spread of anti-Israel narratives and the surge in global antisemitism were not simply spontaneous responses to the war, but the result of a premeditated information campaign that had been in the works for decades.
On October 7, 2023, that media battlefield took on a new urgency. As Hamas terrorists crossed into southern Israel, the images and accounts of the massacre spread quickly around the world.
Israel failed on a major front: The media landscape
Hoffman saw that Israel had been caught off guard in two distinct but interconnected arenas. In his book, he describes October 7 as not only a military and intelligence failure, but also a failure on the media front.
Three years on, he said, Israel still fundamentally misunderstands how to communicate with the world.
Israel’s failure to prepare for the media battlefield
“Hamas planned this war in order to impact public opinion around the world,” he said. “Their goal was not Nova, which they did not know about; it was New York, and Israel played into their hands. They wanted Israel to respond with what they could call disproportionate force, no matter what it would be, and return the Palestinian issue to the international agenda.”
Israel not having a plan on this front, just like it didn’t have a plan on the military front, has harmed the Jewish state “tremendously,” Hoffman added.
“Every day since October 7 has become easier on the military battlefield. Every day since October 7 has gotten progressively harder on the media one.”
The contrast is central to his book. Israel has devoted enormous resources to its military prowess, but Hoffman argues that successive governments have treated public diplomacy as a secondary concern, despite its potential influence on both domestic security and the security of Jewish communities abroad.
According to Hoffman, the problem begins at the highest levels of government.
“They did not realize they need to be taking into account how the decision they’re about to make in Gaza, in Iran, against Hezbollah, how these decisions are going to impact the Jews in Golders Green and in New York. They did not take it into account whatsoever.”
Another strategic failure Hoffman identified is Israel’s tendency to remain on the defensive rather than challenge the credibility and motivations of those shaping the international narrative.
Much of Israel’s media strategy, if there is one, has focused on rebutting misinformation, disputing facts and figures, and pointing out flaws in logic.
Hoffman said Israel needs to be much more on the offensive.
In his book, he lays out four necessary strategies he believes must work together: offensive and defensive messaging, both within the context of the conflict and beyond it.
“I count four. It makes a Venn diagram that works all together. If you’re missing out on any of the four, then it’s inadequate. So, yes, we need to be blackening the names of the people fighting against us.”
For example, Israel should be “outing” international anti-Israel figures who are accepting huge amounts of money from Qatar, Hoffman argued.
“We need to be outing that. It’s not legitimate, the way that Qatar is influencing the world. Al Jazeera is not a legitimate news organization. It’s a propaganda mouthpiece of a terrorist-supporting state. People need to know that. People need to know what they can and they can’t trust.”
Qatar occupies a prominent place in Hoffman’s analysis. The Gulf state, which has hosted Hamas political leaders and played a central role in negotiations involving Israel and Hamas, funds Al Jazeera, one of the most influential Arabic-language news networks in the world. Hoffman argues that Qatar’s financial and media influence warrants greater scrutiny.
The offensive strategy also needs to be employed more on college campuses, where, for a very long time, the pro-Israel groups have been trying to be “nice,” and Hoffman says they “need to be less nice because the anti-Israel organizations on their campus are not nice.”
He believes pro-Israel students and organizations need to be more assertive in challenging anti-Israel activism rather than relying primarily on dialogue and attempts to persuade those already strongly opposed to Israel.
This also connects to Qatar, given the extensive reporting indicating significant academic institutional ties between the Gulf state and US universities.
How international institutions shape the narrative
One of the most challenging aspects of this media fight is combating the dominant narrative disseminated by human rights bodies and NGOs, Hoffman said.
The United Nations, Oxfam, Amnesty International, Doctors Without Borders, and others have been instrumental in legitimizing the anti-Israel rhetoric used in public and private spaces. Because of these organizations, buzzwords such as “genocide,” “apartheid,” and “ethnic cleansing” have become normalized in day-to-day discourse and in international media outlets.
Hoffman said he wanted to speak to journalists who covered the conflict during the war and “give them the benefit of the doubt.” He said he asked them why they believed Hamas.
“They said, ‘No, we didn’t believe anything from Hamas. We believe the organizations [like the UN].’ And they believed Hamas.
“These organizations were the ones who spread the propaganda and sanitized what a terrorist organization [Hamas] told them. Then the media quote these reputable organizations around the world, and it becomes a vicious circle. As Gerald Steinberg, the founder of NGO Monitor, understood way back at the Durban [Conference], this was going to cause damage to Israel, and now the entire world needs to understand that.”
The Durban reference is significant. At the 2001 UN World Conference Against Racism in South Africa, an accompanying NGO forum became the focus of controversy over antisemitism and the portrayal of Israel. Its declaration described Israel as an apartheid state and accused it of genocide and ethnic cleansing, language that would become increasingly prominent in subsequent campaigns against the Jewish state.
In Hoffman’s view, the events surrounding Durban were not an isolated episode but an early indication of how human rights terminology could be used as part of a broader campaign to delegitimize Israel.
“So, that’s part of that blood libel machine, the way in which – wittingly or unwittingly, and, unfortunately, too often wittingly – these NGOs were part of it. So the blood libel machine is the media. It is Qatar. It is Hamas. It is the anti-Israel organizations around the world.”
Fighting back against the machine
Fighting this is an uphill battle, partly because these organizations are viewed internationally as the beacons of justice and paragons of morality. It is not easy to convince skeptics that their findings and public statements should be subjected to the same scrutiny as those of governments and other parties.
“It’s hard, but we need to be constantly putting out facts,” Hoffman continued. “We know how many tons of aid we’re giving to Gaza. We know what everything Israel did unprecedentedly to help an enemy combatant in the time of war. We know how much effort Israel made to minimize civilian casualties. Little by little, we can chisel away at this false narrative that has been hoisted upon the world.”
Hoffman’s determination to remain optimistic is a recurring theme throughout both the book and the interview, even as he describes the scale of the challenge facing Israel.
“I didn’t want to write a book of gloom and doom. I wanted to write a book that would give people hope.
“That’s why the subtitle of the book is Exposing the anti-Israel Hate Network, and How to Fight Back. I give people 30 different tools they can use, whether it’s in mainstream media, social media, or AI platforms.”
Rather than leaving readers with a diagnosis of the problem, Hoffman devotes a substantial portion of the book to practical action. He does not believe it is too late for Israel to turn the tide.
“It’s not too late. Every day, every single person on social media and even people who aren’t on social media, in the checkout line of the grocery store, everybody can make an impact.
“I don’t view it as this mountain that’s insurmountable. I believe in celebrating incremental success. And we, every day, can change minds. Not of the most extreme people, but of the overwhelming majority.”
One way he suggests people take action is by engaging more critically with international media and holding them accountable when they find incorrect or biased reporting.
“People often ask me, should I cancel my subscription to The New York Times and other media outlets for being anti-Israel?
“I say absolutely not. You need to be reading it. If you want to hurt them, then read them more carefully. If you see something problematic, send it to the media watchdogs like HonestReporting or to journalists themselves, or send it to their local media and point out that their rival had made an error. And that’s all part of regaining deterrence on the media battlefield.”
This approach is shaped by his years in journalism and media monitoring. Rather than disengage from outlets they distrust, Hoffman argues, readers should become more informed, attentive consumers of their reporting.
He cited an example of when, during coverage of the release of the final 20 living hostages in October 2025, CNN reporter Christiane Amanpour claimed that Israeli hostages were treated “better than the average Gazan” because Hamas used them as bargaining chips.
Someone flagged the comment, and Hoffman himself then contacted Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, who contacted CNN and requested that she be held accountable.
Amanpour subsequently apologized, calling her comments insensitive and wrong.
“That came from ordinary people who were watching and made sure that we would realize this. And so people can have that role when they see things that are egregious.”
Social media also has the technology for users to critically engage. For example, users on X/Twitter can add community notes on posts that are incorrectly presented or are missing key information.
Looking to Israel’s next government
While Hoffman does believe responsibility can rest with individual news consumers, his criticism ultimately returns to Israel’s political leadership and its failure to treat public diplomacy as an essential element of national security.
While citizens may help challenge misleading narratives, only the government has the authority and tools to establish a coordinated, long-term communications strategy, one that anticipates the international consequences of its actions rather than responding after the damage has been done.
“They need to be taking this just as seriously as the nuclear threat from Iran, because it’s an existential threat to the future of the State of Israel and the Jewish people around the world.
“And they need to be caring about the way every decision they make is perceived abroad.”
With Israel’s October 27 elections approaching, the question is whether a new government, regardless of its political makeup, will be prepared to invest in the media battlefield as seriously as it invests in conventional security.
“It doesn’t matter who wins the election. They all need to make sure the next government allocates just as much, if not more, funding to media strategy and public diplomacy. They need to have people ready 24/7 to go on the media and explain what’s going on here, in every language imaginable.
“The embassies and consulates abroad are dreadfully underfunded. And that needs to be changed, because those are the people who are building the relationships with the people there on the ground and with the media.”
Hoffman makes the case that the fight over Israel’s international reputation will not end when the fighting on the ground does. It will continue in newsrooms, universities, online platforms, and in day-to-day communication.
And while governments bear the most responsibility for preparing Israel to confront that challenge, Hoffman’s resounding message is that the battlefield is no longer theirs alone. Its outcome will also depend on whether those watching from the sidelines are willing to take action.

Economy minister stresses accelerating finalization of projects supported by Islamic Development Ban
TEHRAN- The Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance emphasized the necessity of accelerating the finalization of approved projects, removing implementation obstacles, and using the Islamic Development Bank’s financing capacities to complete the country’s priority projects.
Seyyed Ali Madanizadeh, on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group in Bangkok, in a meeting with Muhammad Sulaiman Al Jasser, President of the Islamic Development Bank, added: “In this meeting, we exchanged views on the implementation process of projects supported by this bank and ways to strengthen financial and development cooperation.”
The Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance stated: “Following up on approved projects and removing obstacles to their implementation, especially in the environmental, urban wastewater, and educational infrastructure development sectors, were among the main axes of these negotiations.”
According to the report, the issue of extending the credit validity and re-approving some priority projects whose assessment stages had already been carried out was examined, and both sides emphasized the need to pursue the use of the remaining projected credits to complete projects under implementation.
Strengthening banking coordination, finalizing payments related to installments, and facilitating the repayment process of financial obligations were among other issues raised at this meeting; issues whose follow-up can help prevent interruptions in project implementation and ensure the continuation of joint cooperation.
In this meeting, emphasis was placed on continuing expert consultations, removing existing obstacles, and focusing on completing semi-finished projects with the aim of making more effective use of cooperation capacities with the Islamic Development Bank.
In mid-June, the Deputy Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance and Head of the Organization for Investment, Economic and Technical Assistance of Iran, as the alternate member of the Board of Executive Directors of the Islamic Development Bank, met and held talks with Muhammad Sulaiman Al Jasser, the President of the Islamic Development Bank.
The meeting was held on the sidelines of the 51st Annual Meeting of the Board of Executive Directors of the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) in Baku, the capital of the Republic of Azerbaijan.
Mehdi Heydari, Head of the Organization for Investment, Economic and Technical Assistance of Iran in this meeting, while once again congratulating Mr. Al-Jasser on his election and appointment as President of the Islamic Development Bank, emphasized the continued support of the Islamic Republic of Iran for the Bank and declared his country's expectations from the Islamic Development Bank to maintain and enhance interactions with Iran as a major shareholder.
Appreciating the Islamic Development Bank for its cooperation in financing the country's projects, he pointed to the position of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the Bank and its economic capacities for implementing various projects, and added that removing existing obstacles and challenges for advancing and increasing financial cooperation between the two sides is on the agenda as one of the main programs of the Investment Organization.
Heydari announced: A specific plan has been initiated to resolve financial issues between the two sides. Currently, part of the commitments has been fulfilled, and other commitments will be implemented within a short period of time.
He emphasized: In order to accelerate processes, it is necessary, within the framework of coordinated joint action, while fulfilling existing commitments, to also define a joint program for financing the introduced and finalized projects of our country.
In this meeting, a list of priority projects was presented to the President of the Islamic Development Bank, and the issue of capacity building and training, as well as holding bilateral or multilateral workshops focused on the Islamic Development Bank, was also emphasized.
Mohammed Al-Jasser, while welcoming the presence of the Iranian delegation at the meeting, emphasized that the Islamic Republic of Iran is one of the major shareholders and reliable partners of the Islamic Development Bank, and in the new circumstances that have emerged, suitable capacity and opportunity will be provided for further cooperation.
He added: The role and position of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the region is important, and the implementation of development projects in this country will not only help its economy but will also boost the regional economy and further progress of neighboring countries.
The President of the Islamic Development Bank, referring to the issues, requests, and proposals raised, expressed hope that we will soon witness the further expansion of cooperation between the Islamic Development Bank and the Islamic Republic of Iran.
The 51st Annual Meeting of the Board of Executive Directors of the Islamic Development Bank, under the slogan "Regional Convergence for Sustainable Prosperity," was held from June 16 to 19, 2026 in Baku.
The Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) is a multilateral development bank established in 1974 and headquartered in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. It began operations in October 1975 with a mandate to foster economic development and social progress in its member countries and Muslim communities worldwide, in accordance with the principles of Shariah (Islamic law). The Bank has 57 member countries across the West Asia, Africa, Asia, Europe, and South America, with membership open to states of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).

Russian forces are accused of executing Ukrainian prisoners of war (POWs) on the Huliaipole front in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, a Ukrainian military spokesperson told Ukrainska Pravda on Oct. 17.
Ukrainian forces intercepted radio communications between Russian soldiers as the alleged executions took place, according to Maksym Kravchuk, spokesperson for Ukraine's Southern Forces Group.
Kravchuk said Russian troops received orders to kill wounded Ukrainian soldiers, including instructions to "take them out immediately." The Russian soldiers reportedly carried out the orders, killing what Ukrainian officials believe were two unarmed POWs.
The incident occurred several days before the allegations were made public, although the exact date and location of the reported executions have not been disclosed.
The Russian soldiers are believed to belong to the 38th Separate Motorized Rifle Brigade, which is operating in the area. Kravchuk alleged that orders of this nature within the brigade are issued at the initiative of its commander, Colonel Valery Kazak.
The Ukrainian military said the intercepted communications and other relevant materials had been handed over to law enforcement authorities.
The execution of prisoners of war is prohibited under the Geneva Conventions and constitutes a war crime.
Russian forces have previously been accused of executing Ukrainian POWs in the Huliaipole sector. In November 2025, five Ukrainian soldiers were reportedly captured and executed near the village of Zelenyi Hai, according to the Ukrainian battlefield monitoring group DeepState. Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office subsequently confirmed that five POWs had been shot by Russian forces.
According to figures released by Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets in August 2026, Russian forces have executed at least 345 Ukrainian soldiers who surrendered since the beginning of the full-scale invasion.

Czech PM Babis suffers setback in Senate elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:30:36 UTC
01:30:36 KST

Czech PM Babis suffers setback in Senate elections
PRAGUE, Oct 17 - Leading Czech opposition parties won the most votes in Senate elections on Saturday, while Prime Minister Andrej Babis' party failed to secure any of the seats it contested in one of its first big electoral tests since taking power last year.
Babis' ANO party had hoped to make gains in the 81-seat upper house, where one-third of seats were up for election and opposition parties hold a majority.
Babis described the result as "catastrophic", but the outcome is unlikely to destabilise his eurosceptic coalition government, which includes right-wing and far-right parties.
Since taking office, the government has ended direct state military support for Ukraine in its war with Russia and challenged European Union climate policies.
The lower house remains the country's main legislative chamber and can override Senate vetoes, limiting the upper chamber's ability to block government legislation.
The Senate nevertheless plays an important role in approving constitutional changes, confirming presidential nominees to the Constitutional Court and electing its own speaker, the country's second-highest state official after the president.
Despite the setback, ANO continues to lead national opinion polls.
The government has loosened fiscal policy to boost wages, pensions and transport investment, drawing criticism in the traditionally frugal country of 10.9 million people.
Turnout in run-off voting for Senate seats on Friday and Saturday was low, following the first round last weekend. Under the electoral system, the top two candidates advance to a run-off unless one secures more than 50% of the vote in the first round.
The pro-European Mayors and Independents party emerged as the strongest performer, winning 10 of the 14 seats it contested, including two secured outright in the first round. The Civic Democrats won seven seats.
The vote followed municipal elections last weekend in which ANO won six of the country's 13 regional capitals, down from eight four years ago. REUTERS

Brazil: Historic Sister City Agreement Between the Colosseum and Christ the Redeemer in Rio
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
18:30:14 CEST
01:30:14 KST

The Colosseum and Christ the Redeemer in Rio de Janeiro are strengthening their bond and the collaboration between Italy and Brazil with the signing of the twinning agreement between the two monuments, which was initiated in Rome last May and ratified in Rio de Janeiro as part of the celebrations marking the 95th anniversary of the statue on Corcovado. The event took place at the Paineiras Visitor Center, within the “Christ the Redeemer – Toward 100 Years” exhibition, and concluded with a ceremony to illuminate the monument in the colors of the Italian flag. “It is deeply moving to attend such an important ceremony. This is not a one-off event, but the foundation for many future initiatives. I am certain of this,” said the Consul General of Italy in Rio, Minister Plenipotentiary Andreas Ferrarese, highlighting the presence of the high-level Italian delegation led by Dr. Alfonsina Russo, Head of the Department for the Promotion of Cultural Heritage at the Ministry of Culture. “I was impressed because there are so many projects and ideas, and I know that all our friends here will be allies of Italy in promoting culture and initiatives in both directions. I see many opportunities for collaboration in Rio de Janeiro,” the diplomat stated. The agreement provides for cooperation and the exchange of knowledge and experience in the fields of education, culture, tourism, sports, and the economy. Planned initiatives include conferences, workshops, reciprocal visit programs, and joint activities to promote the two monuments and increase their international visibility. “Today we are formalizing the twinning of two of the New Seven Wonders of the World, which, with their aura, attract millions of visitors every year from all over the globe—extraordinary monuments, each in its own way imbued with profound meaning and a supreme testament to human achievement,” said Simone Quilici, Director General of the Colosseum Archaeological Park. “The ruins of the Flavian Amphitheater are a powerful universal symbol, known and recognized everywhere, just like the statue atop Corcovado Mountain overlooking Rio de Janeiro. Through this twinning, they symbolically retrace a bond that has existed between Italy and Brazil since its inauguration, when the signal to illuminate the statue was transmitted from the Coltano radio station at the behest of Guglielmo Marconi.” The day traditionally dedicated to Italy—enriched this year by the signing of the twinning agreement—commemorates the Italian scientist’s contribution to the illumination of the Christ the Redeemer statue, which was inaugurated on October 12, 1931. At the end of the ceremony, Quilici activated the statue’s lighting display featuring the Italian tricolor, at the invitation of the sanctuary’s rector, Father Omar.

West Bank: Israeli settlers attack EU diplomats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:29:00 UTC
01:29:00 KST

West Bank: Israeli settlers attack EU diplomats, French mayor
October 17, 2026
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said on Saturday that masked settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank had attacked Palestinians, Catholic representatives, and Western diplomats and officials.
Prevot said the Belgian consul general and French and Polish diplomats, as well as a French mayor, were among those attacked.
In a post on X, he condemned "in the strongest terms" the attack in which a Belgian vehicle was also damaged.
Israeli police said they have opened an investigation into the alleged assault of diplomats in the occupied West Bank.
In a separate statement, the Israeli military said the visit was not coordinated with it and there were no soldiers present.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office reacted to the incident by criticizing an alleged "smear" campaign against settlers.
"These reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge," his office said in a statement, using the biblical name for the West Bank.
What do we know about the incident
According to witnesses, cars from the French, Belgian, and Polish embassies had brought diplomats to visit Taybeh, a predominantly Christian village in the occupied West Bank.
Settlers then descended on the area to prevent Palestinians from gathering olives.
Masked men reportedly surrounded a diplomatic vehicle with their off-road vehicles, then demanded identification and smashed a window.
A witness and two diplomats also told the AFP news agency that the settlers beat up Bernard Baudoux, the 78-year-old leftist mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, a town in northern France.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot called on Israeli authorities to arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux.
"They must urgently put an end to these criminal acts of violence and ensure the safety of civilian populations, as they are obligated to do under international law," he added.
French mayor says attackers were 'completely enraged'
Badoux told AFP that he was fine, having suffered minor injuries. He also expressed concern about the residents in the area.
"The whole world needs to know what's happening there," Badoux said.
Badoux said he was visiting Taybeh with the French consul general in Jerusalem, along with a priest from his home parish, to sign a goodwill cooperation agreement with his city, which has an olive emblem.
The mayor, who was wearing a sash in the French tricolor, said that the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground.
"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."
"It's absolutely incredible that settlers can behave like this," he said. "I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government."
Israel FM condemns 'rioters'
In a rare statement critical of settlers, which was released before Netanyahu's statement, Israel's foreign minister condemned the attack by Israeli "rioters" on the European diplomatic delegation in the West Bank.
"I strongly condemn the severe acts of violence by Israeli rioters in the area of Taybeh," said Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, who also faulted the diplomats for not coordinating with the Israeli military.
The West Bank has experienced an especially violent olive harvest season this year. Israeli settlers have tried to stop Palestinians from harvesting their crops by using physical force.
Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine was injured on Friday when she was attacked by a group of Israeli settlers while reporting in the occupied West Bank.
This violence is occurring during the final days of the election campaign. In hopes of gaining their support in the upcoming election, Netanyahu has championed the cause of the settlers.

Kenya confirms four new Ebola cases, bringing total number to seven
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:26:59 UTC
01:26:59 KST

Kenya has confirmed four new Ebola cases, bringing its total to seven, including the country’s first patient, who died earlier this month.
The health ministry said on Saturday that the new cases involved a close male relative of the first patient and three healthcare workers who treated him.
All four developed fevers while in quarantine and were immediately isolated before testing positive, the ministry said.
The relative had been quarantined since October 6. The healthcare workers, two men aged 29 and 35 and a 32-year-old woman, had been in quarantine since October 9.
The ministry said “the risk to the general public remains low”, adding that there was “no evidence of community transmission”.
Of 130 identified contacts, 128 had been traced and placed in quarantine, it added.
On Friday, authorities confirmed an infection in a 65-year-old female relative of the first patient. Another relative, a 39-year-old man, tested positive two days earlier.
First reported cases
Kenya had never recorded an Ebola case before October 6, when authorities reported the death of a Kenyan man who had returned from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
The patient, described as a 40-year-old businessman, fell ill around a month ago and received treatment in the DRC before travelling overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala.
He flew to Nairobi on October 3 and died on October 5 after receiving treatment.
Kenya has strengthened screening and established an emergency hotline for anyone who suspects they may have been in contact with an Ebola patient or develops symptoms.
The DRC declared its 17th Ebola outbreak in May. Congolese health authorities have since reported 9,066 infections and 4,381 deaths linked to the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no vaccine or specific treatment.
Neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 infections, almost all among people who had travelled from the DRC, and two deaths before being declared Ebola-free in August.
Ebola has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.

Ukraine cannot be forced to surrender, says commander whose brigade destroyed 57,000 Russian targets, as US pressure and Russian missiles test its will
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:24:08 UTC
01:24:08 KST

Ending the war by forcing Ukraine to capitulate is impossible, the commander of the 429th “Achilles” Unmanned Systems Brigade, Yurii Fedorenko, said in an interview with 24 Kanal.
His statements came as Ukraine absorbed the fallout from the US-Russia diesel deal that saw its Starlink throttled and US intelligence lapse, a gap tied to a strike that killed three in Kyiv.
Achilles is a volunteer unit formed in the first days of the full-scale invasion, built around aerial reconnaissance and drone strikes and credited with more than 57,000 strikes. Fedorenko, its commander, was named a Hero of Ukraine in January 2026.
Fedorenko says he believes that there would be no “miraculous de-escalation,” and now argues that neither pressure from Washington nor Russian missiles can break the country’s will to fight for its liberty.
Russia will keep terrorizing Ukrainians with ballistic missiles, jet drones and Shaheds, and no near-term shift in US policy will stop it, Fedorenko stresses, so Ukraine will keep defending itself and striking back. A lasting energy ceasefire, he added, will not hold.
“Ukrainian society is ready to defend itself and to uphold its right to life by force,” he says, arguing that the Kremlin’s mouthpieces, and those working for third countries, have misjudged the mood in Ukraine.
No measure, he insists, could force Ukraine to capitulate in the short term.
Why the US election could swing the pendulum back
Fedorenko sees the political balance shifting after the US vote. President Donald Trump will probably not hold the majority he once had, making it harder for him to take domestic decisions alone, he notes. Even foreign policy, a presidential prerogative, will have to reckon with that balance.
If Trump must bargain with Democrats to pass domestic measures, that will shape the wider picture, Fedorenko argues. He stopped short of predicting impeachment, calling that the wrong framing, but cautioned that decisions already taken could be reviewed, challenged and overturned in the courts.
“I am firmly convinced we will get through the difficulties dictated by circumstances, including those arising across the ocean,” he says.
A cold shower for Europe that could help Ukraine
The US turn toward Moscow has jolted Europe, in Fedorenko’s view. American threats to leave NATO or rewrite how it shares the burden landed on European leaders like a cold waterfall, he recounts, pushing each state to ask how it would stand if the US walked away and to treat the Russian threat as one standing at its own borders, no longer a problem confined to Ukraine.
That alarm can work in Kyiv’s favor, drawing more weapons, defense financing and economic support from European partners, Fedorenko argues.
The same logic drives the satellite question. Ukraine cannot build a Starlink alternative alone, lacking its own space program, so the answer is collective, with NATO states pooling launches into a shared network, he explains. Russia is taking the other path with its “Rassvet” system, much of it, in fact, built by China, and if Moscow and Beijing get there first, he warns, the fallout would reach far beyond Ukraine.

Kenya confirms 4 new Ebola cases, including 3 health workers, raising total to 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:19:13 UTC
01:19:13 KST

Andrew Wasike
17 October 2026•Update: 17 October 2026
Kenya confirmed four new Ebola cases Saturday, including three health workers who treated the country's first patient, bringing the total number of infections to seven, according to the Health Ministry.
"The Ministry of Health confirms four new cases of Ebola (Bundibugyo Virus Disease). This brings the total number of confirmed cases to seven including the deceased first case," Health Director General Patrick Amoth said in a statement.
The new infections involve three medical workers, two men aged 29 and 35 and a woman aged 32, who attended to the first patient between Oct. 3 and 4.
The fourth patient is a male relative of the first person to die from the disease. He had been quarantined since Oct. 6, according to the ministry.
Amoth said all four patients developed fever while under quarantine and were immediately isolated, with laboratory tests confirming they had contracted the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola.
The infections were confirmed by the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute.
The patients are receiving supportive treatment from trained health workers, with the ministry reporting that the second and third patients are stable and responding well to care.
Health authorities said detecting all four infections among people already in quarantine had helped reduce the risk of further transmission.
The ministry said 128 of the 130 identified contacts, representing 98.5%, had been traced and placed under quarantine, while efforts continued to locate the remaining two.
Amoth said there was no evidence of community transmission and maintained that the risk to the general public remained low.
The ministry is also monitoring four relatives who cared for the first patient during his hospital stay.
Despite the additional infections, Kenya has not imposed restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings, with authorities saying the country remains open for business.
The first confirmed patient had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo before traveling through Uganda and arriving in Nairobi on Oct. 3. He died two days later.
The infections have raised concerns about the potential spread of Ebola across East Africa, particularly given the movement of people between Kenya, Uganda and Congo.
Congo health authorities have reported more than 9,000 Ebola infections and over 4,000 deaths as of Oct. 14, making it the second-largest Ebola epidemic on record, according to figures attributed to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control.
Health authorities across the region continue to monitor the risk of cross-border transmission as Kenya intensifies contact tracing and surveillance to contain the latest infections.

Poland scrambled military aircraft on Saturday as Russia launched fresh strikes on western Ukraine.
Polish and allied aircraft were deployed to protect Polish airspace as Russian attacks targeted areas near the NATO member’s eastern border, according to Poland’s armed forces.
The precautionary move came as Washington and Warsaw increasingly appeared to be moving in different directions over Russia. Trump on Saturday waived key Russia-related sanctions and tariffs due to take effect under the recently adopted Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, saying the move was in US national interest. The law had been intended to increase economic pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The waiver followed a US-Russia diesel deal that has drawn criticism from Kyiv and some European leaders, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the agreement would provide Moscow with financial relief while Russia continues its attacks on Ukraine.
Warsaw has maintained a harder line. Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski this week criticized restrictions affecting Ukraine’s Starlink service and questioned whether Elon Musk was “playing politics” with a system that is crucial to Ukrainian defense. Poland pays for Starlink subscriptions used by Ukraine.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk has also repeatedly argued that continued pressure on Russia and support for Ukraine are central to Polish and European security.
Poland has adopted an increasingly active air-defense posture since a series of incidents linked to Russia’s war in Ukraine. In September 2025, Polish and allied aircraft were deployed during Russian strikes on western Ukraine, while Poland later became the first NATO member to shoot down Russian drones after incursions into its airspace.

Turkish Super Lig leaders Galatasaray snatched a 1-0 away victory over Genclerbirligi on Saturday after substitute Deniz Gul's late effort was deflected into the net by goalkeeper Irfan Can Egribayat.
The Istanbul side struggled to break down their opponents before Gul's 88th-minute effort from a tight angle on the right slipped past goalkeeper Irfan Can Egribayat, whose mistake handed the visitors all three points.
Both teams created chances late in the first half, with Genclerbirligi midfielder Salih Ucan coming closest in the 36th minute when his low shot was deflected onto the crossbar by goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir.

Galatasaray introduced Rafael Leao for Sane in the 61st minute, but the Portuguese winger was forced off through injury just 16 minutes later, making way for Gul.
The substitute proved decisive in the 88th minute, scoring from a difficult angle after Egribayat failed to keep out his effort.
The victory lifted Galatasaray to 19 points from eight matches, keeping them at the top of the Super Lig standings.
Genclerbirligi, playing their second match under new head coach Bernd Storck, remained on eight points and extended their winless run to six league games.
Galatasaray will host archrivals Fenerbahce in their next league match, while Genclerbirligi will travel to Konyaspor.

US Rep. Ilhan Omar challenges legality of FBI home search: WSJ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:12:20 UTC
01:12:20 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
17 October 2026•Update: 17 October 2026
The defense of US Congresswoman Ilhan Omar have challenged the legality of a search of her Washington home, demanding that federal prosecutors immediately return all seized property and provide recordings made during the operation, The Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday.
In a letter sent late Friday, the Minnesota Democrat’s legal team argued that the search, conducted by Homeland Security Investigations agents early Monday under a federal judge-approved warrant, was “neither justified nor lawful.”
According to the Journal, the investigation focuses partly on how Omar, 44, obtained US citizenship after arriving from Somalia decades ago.
“There is no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status,” the letter said.
Her lawyers alleged that agents failed to follow the judge’s instructions, including a requirement to notify the US House general counsel before executing the warrant. They also said Omar and her attorneys were not given a copy of the warrant beforehand, as ordered by the judge.
The letter claimed agents prevented Omar from contacting her lawyers for more than an hour after the search began.
A Justice Department spokeswoman rejected the allegations, describing the letter as “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies. Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do.”
Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for Washington, defended the operation earlier this week, saying it had been approved by a federal judge mindful of constitutional protections.
“That judge would not have signed that warrant unless there was probable cause,” Pirro said on Fox News.
Omar’s lawyers also accused prosecutors of abusing the grand jury process through subpoenas issued in Washington and Minnesota.
“This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the president’s chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar’s constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers,” the letter said.
The search came three weeks before November’s midterm elections, in which Omar is seeking a fifth term.
The letter also accused the Justice Department of violating its longstanding practice of avoiding public investigative actions involving political candidates within 60 days of an election, a measure intended to prevent the appearance of partisan interference. Department officials have denied violating any policy.
“This search—which arose from a years-old, tired conspiracy theory concerning conduct stretching back decades—violated longstanding Justice Department policy concerning interference in elections,” the letter said.
Omar has long been targeted by President Donald Trump and conservatives, as well as GOP-led congressional investigations.

Vietnam embassy, Iran–Vietnam chamber of commerce chart a path for bilateral trade, investment co-op
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:10:56 UTC
01:10:56 KST

Vietnam embassy, Iran–Vietnam chamber of commerce chart a path for bilateral trade, investment co-op
TEHRAN- Vietnamese Ambassador to Iran Nguyen Luong Ngoc and Mr. Seyed Mostafa Mousavi, President of the Iran–Vietnam Joint Chamber of Commerce, met at the Chamber’s headquarters in Tehran on Saturday, together with members of the visiting Vietnamese trade delegation and representatives of Iranian business associations and enterprises, to discuss ways to strengthen bilateral economic, trade and investment cooperation.
During the meeting, Mr. Mousavi highlighted Vietnam’s strong economic potential and expressed interest in expanding cooperation in agriculture, industry, oil and gas, logistics and tourism. He also emphasized the importance of strengthening business ties, promoting investment opportunities and facilitating exchanges of business delegations between the two countries.
Ambassador Nguyen Luong Ngoc underscored the need to enhance the exchange of market information, establish connections between reliable business partners and address challenges related to international payments and goods transportation. He stressed the importance of translating cooperation proposals into concrete and practical initiatives.
The Ambassador reaffirmed the Embassy of Vietnam’s commitment to working closely with the Iran–Vietnam Joint Chamber of Commerce, business associations and enterprises from both countries to promote substantive, effective and mutually beneficial economic, trade and investment cooperation.
A Vietnamese trade delegation arrived in Tehran on October 6 and stayed until October 18, led by Mr. Nguyen Dang Dinh. The mission aimed to expand Vietnam’s commercial reach in the Middle East and engage directly with Iran’s market.
The delegation visited Bandar Abbas, where it assessed Shahid Rajaee Port, including container operations, bonded storage facilities, and possible land leasing for agricultural commodities and re-export goods. It also visited Petro Pasargad’s bitumen refinery and obtained samples of 60/70 penetration-grade bitumen exported to Vietnam.
In Shiraz, the delegation attended Expo Shiraz International Exhibition and explored agriculture, petrochemicals, construction, tourism, healthcare, and handicrafts.
In Tehran, it met Petro Pasargad’s CEO and signed an MoU on bitumen cooperation; the company produces about 300–400 tonnes per day and currently offers products mainly FOB due to port and export difficulties. The delegation also visited the MED 26/Iran Med 2026 medical equipment exhibition, met Ohad Group—a manufacturer of oxygen generators and ventilators used in about 80% of Iranian hospitals—and discussed a possible joint-venture manufacturing facility in Vietnam with phased technology transfer.
On October 16, DHT Mining Joint Stock Company and Petro Pasargad Hormozgan Company signed an MoU covering provision and distribution of POH-origin bitumen in Vietnam.
Dinh identified banking restrictions as the main operational concern and called for flexible settlement frameworks such as bilateral barter trade or compliant local-currency clearing. Official Vietnam–Iran trade is around $170 million, but actual potential is significantly higher because the economies are complementary.
Priority sectors for immediate cooperation include agriculture and food processing; industrial raw materials such as specialty chemicals, construction supplies, and polymers; and healthcare and pharmaceuticals, including medical equipment, active ingredients, and biotechnology.
Key bottlenecks include long transit times, high freight costs, and differing quality-compliance frameworks such as Halal certification. The delegation recommended direct links with regional logistics providers and mutual recognition between regulators to standardize inspections and expedite customs clearance.
Vietnam’s 17 free trade agreements and access to 60 economies offer a platform for joint ventures or Vietnam-based production, enabling Iranian firms to add value inside Vietnam and jointly access ASEAN and wider international markets under compliant arrangements. Follow-up should focus on clarifying commercial terms, logistics arrangements, and specific cooperation mechanisms while assessing legal, financial, and technological feasibility.

Students, farmers and the Yellow Jacket movement are taking to the street in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:05:23 UTC
01:05:23 KST

Students, farmers and the Yellow Jacket movement are taking to the street in France
A wave of mass protests swept across France Saturday, with dozens of peaceful marches taking place alongside scenes of violent clashes between demonstrators and police forces, Politico reported.
The demonstrations were also a battleground for candidates ahead of next year’s high-stakes presidential election: The far-right’s Marine Le Pen sided with law enforcement while the far-left’s Jean-Luc Mélenchon backed protesters.
Throughout the day, media reported incidents in the country’s largest cities including Lyon, Bordeaux, Marseille and Paris. Dozens of rioters clashed with law enforcement on the capital’s Place de la République, next to a much larger number of demonstrators gathered for an authorized march that started from Paris’s central square.
“A very large majority of people are protesting without violence,” Paris’s police prefecture said on Saturday afternoon.
Students, farmers and members of the Yellow Jacket movement, among others, took to the streets on Saturday in a “convergence of struggles” to protest rising living costs, sluggish wages and deep disagreements with the government.
About 500,000 protestors took to the streets across the country, according to the CGT union. France’s interior ministry has yet to release its figures, which are usually lower than counts issued by unions.
Saturday’s demonstrations grew out of the student protests that began last month with school blockades and calls for better study conditions, more teachers and more funding. The movement has since spread nationwide — and become a political issue as the campaign for next year’s presidential election heats up.
In recent weeks, the government has struggled to deal with the crisis — which Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu described as “urban violence” — and is hoping the student movement will now fade because of a two-week school holiday that started Friday evening.
“The mobilization is marked by a very strong involvement of the ultra-left movement, which is only looking to cause disorder,” Nuñez’s office said Saturday, adding that the minister reiterated his “instructions of utmost firmness” to local prefects and police forces.
Footage showed Lyon’s tourist board office engulfed in flames on the city’s Place Bellecour. A police station was vandalized in Marseille, where a group of “rioters” also entered city hall, Mayor Benoît Payan said. He told BFMTV that “damage was objectively fairly limited,” although the act of vandalism was “unacceptable.” The headquarters of right-wing TV channel CNews in Paris was also targeted, authorities said.
The government has defended the law enforcement response to the student protests despite numerous allegations of police brutality, including incidents that left one teenager with a severed hand and another blind in one eye. Nuñez said the use of “stun grenades” was authorized on Saturday, after a temporary ban on their use against students.
About 163 people had already been arrested in Paris by mid-afternoon, authorities said.
The far-left France Unbowed slammed the police response to the protests.
The party’s presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon participated in the demonstrations in Paris and backed protesters. He also criticized the media for only showing violent clashes while “everything is proceeding peacefully, with tens of thousands of people calmly taking part.”
On the other side of the political spectrum, far-right leaders Jordan Bardella and Marine Le Pen pledged support for the police. “Legitimate social demands have once again been hijacked by the far left,” Le Pen said, as an increasing number of polls show she could end up in the second round against Mélenchon.
Bardella said on Saturday that protests were made up entirely of “chaos professionals,” adding: “As we said, working France, which is taking the full brunt of inflation and cost-of-living struggles, did not take to the streets today.”
The police and protesters clashed in other European countries on Saturday, too. A student-led protest against corruption and unemployment in Albania’s capital Tirana reportedly turned violent, as did another one in Brussels.

“This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the president’s chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar’s constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers,” the letter said.
The search came three weeks before November’s midterm elections, in which Omar is seeking a fifth term.
The letter also accused the Justice Department of violating its longstanding practice of avoiding public investigative actions involving political candidates within 60 days of an election, a measure intended to prevent the appearance of partisan interference. Department officials have denied violating any policy.
“This search—which arose from a years-old, tired conspiracy theory concerning conduct stretching back decades—violated longstanding Justice Department policy concerning interference in elections,” the letter said.
