Revealed: French police used UK-funded 4x4 vehicles to charge student protesters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:00:34 UTC
01:00:34 KST

French police have used 4x4 vehicles paid for by British taxpayers to charge at student protesters during the school protests that have swept the country.
The French government has confirmed that an investigation has been launched into why the cars, funded by the UK government specifically to prevent asylum seekers crossing the Channel, were used during a protest involving school students in Dunkirk.
School protests have been taking place across France for a third week with an estimated 160,000 people involved, with protesters raising concerns about crumbling schools and teacher shortages. Demonstrators have criticised policing tactics after teargas was fired at protesters in two areas.
The incident involving the UK-funded 4x4, a land cruiser known as Masstech VEZI (Vehicule d’Eclairage de Zone d’Intervention), was reported by French media outlet BFM TV on 10 October. The report included footage of the VEZI driving at speed, reversing backwards then driving forwards again with a bin caught under the vehicle’s front wheel and dragged along. Students can be heard screaming and scattering from the path of the vehicle.
According to reports, a 14-year-old girl was injured by the vehicle and was taken to hospital, sustaining a haematoma. She was later discharged from hospital. She is now recovering, but she told reporters that what happened to her was “unacceptable”.
The VEZI was earmarked for UK-funded operations on French beaches to stop asylum seekers boarding dinghies, part of an Anglo-French border agreement signed in January 2018 and known as the Sandhurst treaty.
This treaty specifies cooperation between France and the UK in combating irregular immigration and secures UK financial support for French efforts through the “Sandhurst funds”. These funds enable France’s National Gendarmerie (police service) to acquire additional resources such as all-terrain vehicles suited to dunes and beaches, including the VEZIs, which are reinforced with grilles.
According to a recent French parliamentary cross-party inquiry into Anglo-French border agreements known as Le Touquet, nine of these specialised VEZI vehicles have been bought under the terms of the Sandhurst treaty. The inquiry report states that to be eligible for Sandhurst funding the equipment must contribute directly to combatting illegal migration in the UK.
A spokesperson from the office of Laurent Nuñez, France’s minister of the interior, when asked why a vehicle funded by the UK and specifically earmarked for border control was used to counter a schools protest, said: “We can confirm the opening of an investigation into this.”
Sources close to the investigation said: “I don’t think the British are aware that their money is being used to beat French kids.”
Another expressed concern about the expanding militarisation of French policing to support authoritarian policies.
A spokesperson for Utopia 56, a French association that provides support to asylum seekers in northern France, said: “In Dunkirk, the 4x4 that ploughed into high school students during the protests is a vehicle funded by the British Sandhurst fund – money earmarked for combating Channel crossings. The practice of using 4x4s to chase people in the student protest is the same one used on the beaches.
“Disproportionate force is employed to silence, intimidate, and deter. The repressive tactics being tested at the border to prevent crossings should serve as a warning to everyone. These are surveillance, control and repression methods that will be replicated in other contexts. The incident involving the vehicle in the student protest is proof of this.”
The UK Home Office declined to comment.

Russia views idea of shortcut to ‘nuclear zero’ as counterproductive — diplomat Postnikov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:00:22 UTC
01:00:22 KST

MOSCOW, October 17. /TASS/. Russia believes that ideas of a shortcut to a "nuclear zero," which implies an immediate abandonment of nuclear weapons and declaring them illegal, are counterproductive, Director of the Department for Non-Proliferation and Arms Control of the Russian Foreign Ministry Oleg Postnikov said.
"Russia remains committed to the ideals of nuclear disarmament in the comprehensive manner, as envisaged by provisions of the NPT [Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty]. It unconditionally remains our key legal benchmark and foundation for implementing efforts in this domain," he said in his October 16 address to the First Committee of the 81st UN General Assembly, published by the Russian foreign ministry.
"Real progress on this path may be achieved only through carefully balanced, step-by-step measures that do not jeopardize anyone’s security and help reinforce global stability," the Russian diplomat continued. "Ideas of a shortcut to ‘nuclear zero,’ which imply an immediate and unconditional abandonment of nuclear weapons along with arbitrarily outlawing them, we view as unrealistic and counterproductive."
"Attempts to artificially establish disarmament deadlines, especially in the current turbulent and unpredictable international situation, are equally unfeasible. We are firmly convinced that disarmament initiatives should correspond to the military, political and strategic context," Postnikov added.
In his words, a serious obstacle to further reductions of nuclear arsenals are doctrinal positions and military programs of Western powers and their allies. They are aimed at "gaining overwhelming military superiority" and are therefore deeply destabilizing.
"Russia is open to seeking mutually acceptable dialogue solutions aimed at comprehensive stabilization of the strategic situation, provided that appropriate prerequisites are established for a truly equal interaction among nuclear powers, based on mutual respect to each other’s core security interests," Postnikov said.

Unhealthy daily habits cluster together to predict adolescent anxiety and depression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:00:15 UTC
01:00:15 KST

A large study of teenagers reveals that specific patterns of unhealthy daily habits predict a higher risk of developing both anxiety and depression simultaneously. The findings highlight how different lifestyle risks group together to influence adolescent mental health over time. The study was published in the journal BMC Psychiatry.
Adolescents are in a sensitive period for physical and mental development. During these years, teenagers often pick up habits that can harm their well-being, such as skipping meals, spending hours on screens, or staying up late. These actions rarely happen in isolation. Instead, they tend to group together within the same individuals.
When a person experiences two mental health conditions at the same time, professionals refer to this as a comorbidity. Anxiety and depression share many behavioral and environmental risk factors, making them a common comorbid pair. Adolescents facing both conditions often experience more severe symptoms, a higher risk of relapse, and more suicidal behavior than those dealing with just one.
Researchers Wanyu Che, Ziyan Ruan, and Xiaoyan Wu of Anhui Medical University led a team to investigate how clustered lifestyle habits relate to these combined mental health challenges. They wanted to see if identifying specific groupings of behaviors could help predict the future onset of combined anxiety and depression. Understanding the behavioral roots of these conditions could aid in early prevention efforts.
The researchers conducted a large study tracking 6,656 adolescents across eight regions in China. The participants lived in a mix of first-tier and second-tier cities, encompassing both urban and rural areas. The average age of the students was about 14 years old, evenly split between middle school and high school grades.
The team surveyed the participants twice, with the baseline assessment in late 2021 and a follow-up a year later. Students completed electronic questionnaires on their smartphones during class time. The researchers asked about 15 specific unhealthy behaviors to build a comprehensive picture of their daily routines.
These behaviors included smoking, alcohol consumption, physical inactivity, poor sleep duration, late bedtimes, and excessive screen time on weekdays and weekends. The survey also tracked dietary habits like insufficient fruit or vegetable intake, frequent fast food consumption, skipping breakfast, and drinking sugary beverages. Finally, the questionnaire asked about suicide-related thoughts, plans, and actions.
The team also evaluated the participants for anxiety and depression using standard self-report scales. They identified students who scored above the symptom screening cutoffs for both conditions simultaneously at the one-year follow-up.
Before looking at the behavior clusters, the researchers noted demographic differences in mental health outcomes. At the one-year mark, 13.6 percent of the participants experienced comorbid anxiety and depression. The rates were notably higher among girls than boys. Students who reported a heavy learning burden, those from poorer families, and teenagers with two or fewer friends also showed elevated rates of both conditions.
Using statistical modeling, the researchers grouped the students based on their behavioral patterns. They identified four distinct categories. The first category was a low-risk group, making up 24 percent of the sample. These teenagers consistently reported very few of the 15 unhealthy behaviors.
The second category, encompassing roughly 40 percent of the students, was defined by poor dietary habits. These individuals frequently skipped breakfast, ate fast food, and consumed too few fruits and vegetables. The third category was a sedentary and screen-time group, representing 22 percent of the teenagers. This group exhibited low physical activity combined with heavy device usage.
The final category was a multiple unhealthy behaviors group, which made up almost 14 percent of the sample. Teenagers in this group showed high rates of almost all 15 behaviors. This included a higher likelihood of reporting suicidal thoughts and actions alongside poor diet and sleep habits.
The researchers also looked at the sheer volume of unhealthy habits per student. They found that more than half of the participants engaged in four to six of the listed behaviors. About a quarter of the teenagers reported having seven or more of these habits.
To understand the impact on mental health, the researchers adjusted their analysis to account for outside factors that might skew the results, such as family income, number of friends, academic pressure, and family history of depression. After these adjustments, the data showed that students in the sedentary and multiple unhealthy behavior groups faced a substantially higher risk of developing combined anxiety and depression than those in the low-risk group.
The risk also climbed as the total number of unhealthy habits increased. Teenagers with seven or more poor habits had nearly triple the odds of experiencing both mental health conditions compared to those with three or fewer habits.
The researchers anticipated that including suicide-related items in the behavior list might artificially inflate the connection to depression. To test the strength of their findings, they ran a second analysis that removed the three suicide-related questions.
This secondary analysis focused entirely on the remaining 12 lifestyle factors, such as diet, sleep, and exercise. The results held steady. The grouping of poor physical habits still predicted a substantially higher risk of future anxiety and depression, showing that the lifestyle factors independently contribute to mental health vulnerability.
The study authors suggest that these clustered behaviors likely represent a shared foundation that contributes to internalizing problems during adolescence. Rather than acting as specific triggers for either anxiety or depression alone, these habit profiles might act as common risk factors that elevate a teenager’s overall psychological vulnerability.
The study relies on self-reported questionnaires, which can introduce bias. Teenagers might not remember their daily routines perfectly or might be reluctant to report certain actions honestly.
The sample only included adolescents currently enrolled in middle or high schools. Teenagers who drop out of school might experience different environments and higher rates of risk behaviors, meaning these findings might not perfectly reflect the broader youth population.
The study is observational and cannot prove that these habits directly cause mental health conditions. Unmeasured variables, such as early childhood trauma or neighborhood environments, could independently influence both a teenager’s daily habits and their psychological well-being.
Future research could explore whether community or school programs designed to change these clustered behaviors actually prevent mental health conditions. By addressing groups of habits together, health professionals might offer better support for adolescent development.
The study, “Associations of clustered unhealthy lifestyle behaviors with comorbidity of anxiety and depression among adolescents,” was authored by Wanyu Che, Ziyan Ruan, Shuman Tao, Meng Wang, Yuxuan Cao, Yaqian Niu, Yuming Chen, Tangjun Jiang, Tingting Li, Liwei Zou, Fangbiao Tao, and Xiaoyan Wu.

Croatian PM meets Chinese FM, voices willingness to expand bilateral cooperation
China

2026-10-17
23:49:40 CST
00:49:40 KST

Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic meets with visiting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, in Zagreb, Croatia, Oct. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Peng Ziyang)
ZAGREB, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic met with visiting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi here on Saturday, expressing Croatia's willingness to further expand cooperation with China.
During the meeting, Plenkovic asked Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, to convey his sincere greetings to the Chinese leadership, saying that he looks forward to visiting China at an early date and meeting with the leadership.
Relations between Croatia and China have continued to improve, underpinned by mutual respect and sincere cooperation, Plenkovic said. Chinese enterprises have participated in infrastructure projects in Croatia, including roads, bridges and tunnels, he said, noting that the Peljesac Bridge has played a significant role in improving connectivity between different parts of the country.
The Croatian side highly appreciates these contributions and welcomes continued participation of Chinese enterprises in the country's development, he said. Croatia is willing to further expand cooperation with China in such areas as tourism, photovoltaics and wind power, he added.
The prime minister also welcomes the launch of direct flights between Croatia and China, looking forward to closer exchanges between their peoples.
Stressing that Croatia attaches great importance to cooperation with China under the China-Central and Eastern European Countries (CEECs) framework and the Belt and Road Initiative, Plenkovic said Croatia is willing to continue contributing to these efforts and looks forward to the early resumption of CEEC-China leaders' meeting mechanism to create new opportunities for closer high-level exchanges between the two sides.
For his part, Wang conveyed the Chinese leadership's good wishes to Plenkovic and welcomed him to visit China at a mutually convenient time.
Wang said China was among the first major countries to establish diplomatic relations with Croatia, adding that bilateral relations have enjoyed healthy, steady and sustainable development under the strategic guidance of the two countries' leaders.
China and Croatia treat each other with sincerity and mutual respect and have established a mature, long-term comprehensive cooperative partnership, Wang said, noting that this has been the right choice made by both sides. China is willing to further elevate bilateral relations on this foundation, he added.
Moreover, Wang said China cherishes its traditional friendship with Croatia and is willing to translate it into a strong driving force for bilateral relations in the new era.
Wang also said China respects the choices of the Croatian people and Croatia's governance model, and is willing to deepen mutually beneficial cooperation to support each other's development and revitalization.
China values people-to-people and cultural exchanges with Croatia and has introduced measures, including unilateral visa-free access and direct flights, to facilitate travel and enhance mutual understanding between the two peoples, Wang stressed.
In addition, Wang noted that China firmly believes that China and the European Union (EU) are partners, not rivals. China supports European integration and Croatia's efforts to achieve faster development through this process, and hopes Croatia will play a constructive role in deepening China-EU cooperation, Wang added.
Meanwhile, Wang stressed that China and CEECs share a practical need to strengthen exchanges and cooperation. Such cooperation is entirely open and transparent and contributes to European integration, he said.
China is willing to strengthen cooperation with interested countries in the region through established mechanisms, Wang said, noting that China appreciates Croatia's positive attitude in this regard and is ready to use the 15th anniversary of the China-CEEC cooperation mechanism next year as an opportunity to reinvigorate mutually beneficial cooperation between the two sides.
The two sides also exchanged views on China-EU economic and trade relations. Plenkovic said that EU countries, including Croatia, have concerns about trade imbalances. Participants at the recent EU summit spoke positively of the consensus reached through the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism and expressed hope that the two sides would continue to strengthen communication and dialogue to properly address their differences, he said.
Wang said that trade issues between China and the EU stem from the international division of labor and market demand. Imports of high-quality, competitively priced Chinese goods benefit European consumers and help curb inflation, reflecting demand in the European market, and there is no so-called "overcapacity" problem, he noted.
China is willing to import more high-value-added products from Europe and hopes the EU will ease restrictions on exports to China, Wang said. China is committed to promoting balanced growth in bilateral trade, with both sides moving forward rather than backward and expanding shared benefits rather than diminishing them, he added.
He also said China is ready to strengthen dialogue with the EU on the basis of equality and mutual benefit, jointly uphold free trade and advance open and inclusive economic globalization.
Meanwhile, Plenkovic briefed Wang on the situation in the Western Balkans. Wang said that China does not interfere in the internal affairs of countries in the region and hopes that all countries will enhance understanding, rebuild mutual trust and coexist in harmony through dialogue. China is willing to play a constructive role in line with the needs of countries in the region, he added.

Feature: Uzbek girl connects to China through Tai Chi
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
23:48:50 CST
00:48:50 KST

TIANJIN, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- On a Chinese university campus, 22-year-old Uzbek student Ibrohimkhonova Ezozaxon practices Tai Chi in the dawn light, moving slowly and steadily through the routine.
Ezozaxon won first place in Tai Chi at Uzbekistan's national youth competition. Today, she is studying at Tianjin Normal University in north China's Tianjin Municipality. For her, Tai Chi has become more than a sport.
"Tai Chi connects me with China and helps me understand Chinese culture and Chinese people," she said.
Tai Chi is a traditional physical practice characterized by relaxed, circular movements that work in concert with breath regulation and the cultivation of a righteous and neutral mind. UNESCO inscribed it on its Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2020.
In China, about 78.6 million people practice Tai Chi, including 35.1 million regular practitioners, according to an official national survey released in late 2025.
Ezozaxon's connection with the sport began when she was three. Then, her father returned from China, where he had studied Chinese and Tai Chi. She still remembers seeing her father practicing in their yard wearing a white Tai Chi suit. Later, watching films starring Bruce Lee, Jackie Chan and Jet Li with her family deepened her interest in Chinese martial arts.
In high school, Ezozaxon took up Tai Chi to improve her health. At first, she found the movements "too slow, only for the elderly," and nearly gave up. Her coach helped her see that Tai Chi was about more than slowness: it is performed by controlling breath, strength and movement in slow motion, combining softness with firmness.
The competition victory that followed changed how she saw the practice. "As I delved deeper, I found Tai Chi looks gentle but holds power. It helps me cultivate my character," she said.
Driven by her interest in Tai Chi and Chinese culture, she chose to study in China, where she found martial arts far more diverse than she had imagined.
In the early mornings in Tianjin, many older people practice Tai Chi in public squares, and she joins them. "I see a sense of ease and calm in them, and I read the Chinese way of cultivating body and mind," she said.
The philosophy embodied by Tai Chi also touched her. "No coach taught me to attack others. They always say: first protect yourself, then protect others," Ezozaxon said.
To her, Tai Chi reflects the Chinese temperament -- gentle and calm, embodying the Chinese concepts of peace, harmony and friendliness.
"It helped me understand the Chinese philosophical idea that harmony is precious," she said.
Chinese martial arts, or Wushu, is stepping onto a broader global stage. With the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games approaching, Wushu Taolu (choreographed sequences) will make its debut as an official sport on the Olympic stage. In Tianjin, Ezozaxon has seen athletes from Senegal's national youth Wushu team training in China ahead of the event.
"Wushu originated in China but belongs to the world," said Zhao Qingjian, a coach for the youth team and an associate professor at Capital University of Physical Education and Sports. "We want to further improve their skills and performance."
Through training and competition, Ezozaxon has experienced the exchange and integration brought by Wushu's growing internationalization. She has competed in Wushu events across China against athletes from around the world.
"On the field we are rivals; off it, we become friends," Ezozaxon said. Now she rehearses Wushu routines with Chinese classmates and students from other countries and regions. Wushu has given young people worldwide a new common language.
"Tai Chi has taught me to slow down, to feel strength within softness, and to appreciate the Chinese cultural wisdom in it. I will keep practicing, strive to be an envoy of cultural exchange, and pass on this beauty of harmony rooted in China to more friends," Ezozaxon said. ■

How one invented claim becomes a chatbot’s confident answer in cognitive warfare: Ukraine’s drone chief maps Russia’s AI attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:46:52 UTC
00:46:52 KST

Ask a chatbot why something happened in the war, and the answer may be written by Russia. Russia is poisoning AI chatbots with millions of fake articles so they repeat Kremlin narratives as fact, a cognitive weapon with strategic impact, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert “Madiar” Brovdi warns on Telegram.
Russia has waged a cognitive war against Ukraine for years, and it intensified sharply with the full-scale invasion. This war goes beyond fake news and disinformation: it aims to shape the deeply ingrained beliefs that drive people’s attitudes, decisions and behavior, and its newest weapon is artificial intelligence.
Brovdi calls it a cognitive operation with strategic impact, one his forces studied among the technological risks of 2027. People increasingly ask a chatbot “why did X happen?” and take the instant answer, he explains, without asking where it comes from.
“Artificial intelligence does not know the truth. It retells the internet, literally,” Brovdi claims.
How the strategy works, step by step
Brovdi lays out a chain that turns a single lie into something a machine will repeat as fact:
- The enemy invents a lie. For example, that Ukrainian soldiers did something terrible, when nothing of the sort happened.
- It is copied across thousands of sites. The same fabrication is published again and again, in many languages, until it looks like everyone is reporting it.
- It fakes a crowd of independent sources. The sites cross-link to one another, but ten sites copying one lie are not ten independent confirmations.
- A person asks the AI. They type “why did Ukrainian soldiers do X?”, though X may never have happened, so the lie is already smuggled into the question as fact.
- The AI may repeat the lie. If the system ingests unreliable material and checks facts poorly, it echoes the fabrication in a calm, confident tone.
- The person trusts it. “The AI said so,” they think, so the answer feels objective, and they believe it, retell it, or share it online.
- The lie shapes decisions and trust. People start to distrust the army, the state, or one another, and even an unproven fabrication has already changed how they feel.
The machines already repeat the lie
The attack runs on volume. Russia floods the web through the “Pravda” network, close to 200 sites in dozens of languages posting 4 to 6 million near-identical articles a year, Brovdi claims, written for machines, not people.
It works, by his account. Of the ten most popular chatbots studied, about a third of the time they reproduce Russian fakes, he noted, and four of ten in a 2024 test affirmed that Azov fighters had burned an effigy of Trump, a fabrication, and cited sources for it.
A war Ukraine admits it is losing
Brovdi is blunt about the balance. Ukraine is losing this fight to Russia’s troll farms, he concedes, even as a layer of homegrown trolls has sprung up too.
His closing advice was aimed at readers.
“Critical thinking should not be delegated. Not even to the smartest machine. Switch on your own judgment and always check the source and the information,” Brovdi states.

Wired for War: Israeli firm ran global surveillance operation through online ads, investigation finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:45:53 UTC
00:45:53 KST

Wired for War: Israeli firm ran global surveillance operation through online ads, investigation finds
Israeli ad tech company Discover-Tech exploited online advertising infrastructure to track targets and help deliver spyware to dozens of devices belonging to Al Jazeera staff and members of other entities, according to investigations by the Canadian cybersecurity watchdog Citizen Lab and New York-based ad security firm Confiant.
The researchers said Discover-Tech used a sprawling network of online ads to identify potential targets, monitor their activity and facilitate the compromise of their devices.
“The core finding is the weaponization of ad infrastructure for advanced staging, preliminary targeting, and payload delivery, characterized by exceptional technical sophistication, robust anti-interception measures, and surgical micro-targeting,” Confiant said in its findings.
Devices belonging to staff at the international news network Al Jazeera were among those infected through malicious ad placements, which operated silently, without visible pop-ups or suspicious links. The Qatar-based media network condemned “the spyware attacks targeting a number of its staff,” describing them as an “assault on press freedom,” and called for those responsible to be held accountable.
The investigation also linked the malicious activity to Israeli spyware developer Candiru, which has been blacklisted by the US and rebranded as Integrity Labs, and Israeli surveillance technology provider Intelos. The companies allegedly exploited ad inventory on major platforms, including Google, Russia’s Yandex and US ad tech platform Beeswax to track targets and compromise consumer devices.
Discover-Tech used a system called Controlium to turn routine ad auctions into a surveillance tool. Over four months, it served ads across nearly 200,000 websites and mobile apps on Android and iOS devices in dozens of countries. According to Confiant, the company generated about 10 million ad impressions daily, harvesting device fingerprints, IP addresses, authentication tokens, cookies and other personal data, including without consent where required under EU privacy rules. Citizen Lab also identified a group linked to Discover-Tech, dubbed Dark Cartographer, which allegedly exploited vulnerabilities at mobile carriers and matched advertising IDs with phone numbers to track subscribers on a large scale.
Geographic data revealed sharp spikes in traffic that researchers said pointed to targeted intelligence-gathering operations rather than routine commercial advertising. Palestine was the most heavily targeted territory, where Discover-Tech accounted for nearly 2% of all digital ad impressions, peaking at around 10% on April 7. The activity also reached sensitive networks, including the Armenian prime minister’s office, international organizations, courts, universities and defense institutions. Investigators detected targeted connections to Candiru servers in nine countries, with Belgium accounting for 56% of recorded activity, followed by the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Mexico and Spain.
Confiant described the campaign as highly sophisticated, citing its anti-interception measures and precise targeting capabilities. Citizen Lab said the findings provided the first public technical evidence that spyware could be delivered through online ads without users clicking on anything, a technique researchers dubbed “AdFection.”

“But friends, in the long arc of history, nothing is static. And those that try to hold on to the past fail to grasp the opportunities of the future.

“We all have common demands, whether it’s students, high schoolers, the 'Yellow Vests,' or the trade unions — we are fighting for better public services, more resources, a better quality of life, better wages, and so on,” said Karl speaking to Euronews’ correspondent in Paris.

Protesters accuse the government of not doing enough to intervene in the ongoing crises and of mismanaging public funds. They have vowed to continue protesting until their demands are met.

Erez Halevi, Israeli pop pioneer and voice of self-acceptance, dies at 71
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:37:39 UTC
00:37:39 KST

Erez Halevi, one of the most original and intriguing figures in Israeli pop music during the 1980s, died on Saturday at the age of 71.
Halevi will be remembered above all for Kach Bara Otcha Hateva ("That's How Nature Made You"), a gentle, beautiful song that, over the years, became much more than a hit. It evolved into something of an anthem of self-acceptance and the freedom to be who you are.
The song appeared on Halevi's debut album, Halayla ("The Night"), released in 1984. Halevi wrote the lyrics and composed the music for every song on that enchanting album, which was produced by Matti Caspi, who also played nearly all the instruments.
Alongside the title track and Hadayagim ("The Fishermen"), Kach Bara Otcha Hateva was one of the highlights of a highly unusual album that brought together soft pop, melancholic melodies, intimate vocals, and Halevi's distinctive high-pitched voice.
Over the years, the song took on new meaning. The LGBTQ community embraced it as a symbol of acceptance of others and resistance to attempts to impose identities on people that are not their own.
A song that became an anthem of self-acceptance
Halevi himself recounted that he wrote the song in response to expectations placed upon him as a musician of Yemenite descent, who was supposedly expected to create Mizrahi music. According to Halevi, the song was written in opposition to any establishment that seeks to dictate how an individual should be.
The song went on to take on a life of its own, with interpretations by other artists, including Dudu Tassa and Ivri Lider.
Halevi's career did not follow the conventional trajectory of a pop star. He released additional albums over the years, including Matzav Beinaim ("Intermediate State") and Hasha'ar Niftach ("The Gate Opens"), but largely withdrew from the Israeli music spotlight.
Halevi is gone, but Kach Bara Otcha Hateva, alongside Hadayagim and Halayla, will remain among the most wonderful moments in Israeli music for generations to come.

Several hundred mostly young people protested in Brussels on Saturday, with rioters clashing with police in unrest partly inspired by demonstrations in neighboring France.
Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible.

Unrest sparked by protests across France
The unrest in France began last month as protests over education funding and school conditions before broadening into a wider movement centered on inequality, public spending and living standards. Similar protests also spread to Albania.
On Saturday, French authorities said 140 protests involving 32,800 people had been recorded outside Paris by midday and blamed the unrest on what they described as the "ultra-left".
Violent incidents were reported in several cities, including vandalism in Marseille and attacks targeting police, media, and public buildings, the Interior Ministry said.

Washington Post photojournalist undergoes surgery after settler attack, demands arrests - interview

Israel-based Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine underwent surgery at Beilinson Hospital on Saturday after being attacked by Jewish rioters during an olive harvest in the Binyamin region of the West Bank on Friday, Walla reported on Saturday.
Levine, whose condition was described as moderate, sustained injuries to her limbs, according to medical information provided. Speaking to Walla, she said she had also suffered injuries to her back and a rib, describing a prolonged assault during which her cameras and personal belongings were stolen.
She alleged that IDF soldiers witnessed the attack but did not intervene to protect her.
Days before the assault, Levine had returned from covering the war in Ukraine. On her way back to Israel, she traveled through Poland, where she met her son. She recalled that even then, he had told her he was more concerned about her work in the West Bank than her coverage of the war in Ukraine.
That fear manifested on Friday during the olive harvest in Binyamin.
'They slammed me to the ground and kicked me again and again'
According to Levine, the two sides had been relatively evenly matched before the soldiers arrived. She alleged that when the soldiers reached the scene, they fired tear gas toward the journalists and Palestinians, causing those present to disperse.
Levine said she was then left alone.
"At that point, they realized I was alone and decided to attack me," she recounted.
According to Levine, approximately 15 rioters ran toward her, assaulted her, and stole her cameras, photography equipment, identification documents, and jewelry.
"They slammed me to the ground and kicked me again and again and again, while stealing everything from me," she said.
Levine alleged that the soldiers witnessed the assault but did nothing to stop it or separate her from her attackers.
"Fifteen people are beating a woman. Why didn't they help me? Do they care where the woman is from? Whether she's from Poland? Or American? To understand that they need to save her?" she said.
Following the attack, Levine received treatment at a hospital in Ramallah. She was subsequently transported in a Palestinian ambulance to a checkpoint, where she was transferred to an Israeli ambulance for the journey to Beilinson Hospital.
She said military personnel questioned her during the transfer, describing the treatment she received there as "pretty disgusting."
Levine underwent surgery on her left hand on Saturday morning. According to her account, doctors had to stitch numerous deep cuts.
She also said four vertebrae in her back and a posterior rib had been fractured, despite her wearing a protective vest and helmet during the assault.
Her son, Michael, told Walla, "My mother went through a very frightening lynching as a woman, regardless of politics."
He said her back was expected to take weeks to heal.
Michael added that this was not the first time his mother had been attacked while working as a journalist.
According to him, her vehicle had previously been set on fire, overturned in another incident, and, on a separate occasion, a settler punched her.
He alleged that none of those incidents had received an adequate response.
Netanyahu calls for investigation as Levine demands arrests
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the incident on Friday, saying that "those responsible will be brought to justice."
However, in a post on X/Twitter, Netanyahu wrote that many facts surrounding the incident had yet to be established.
He cited a report claiming that approximately 200 Arabs and left-wing activists had confronted 40 young Israelis, saying the investigation should determine who initiated the violence.
Levine expressed disappointment with his response, saying she felt Netanyahu was casting doubt on the credibility of her account.
She called for a thorough investigation and arrests, demanding that authorities stop allowing lawbreakers to operate without interference.
Levine also categorically rejected a claim by the Yesha Council that a young Israeli had helped her during the incident.
"That is a blatant lie," she told Walla.
According to Levine, the video presented to support the council's account had been edited in a way intended to reinforce its version of events and did not reflect the assault she described.
On Saturday, hundreds of former senior defense, police, and judicial officials, along with academics and business leaders, published a letter supporting Levine.
Among the signatories were former IDF chief of staff and defense minister Moshe Ya'alon, former Mossad director Tamir Pardo, former Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) chief Ami Ayalon, and former Israel Police commissioner Moshe Karadi.
The signatories expressed solidarity with Levine, concern for her well-being, and wishes for a speedy recovery.
According to Levine, her son spoke with the US deputy secretary of state, who told him the United States would keep pressing for a thorough investigation and expected arrests.
Now, from her hospital bed, Levine is making the same demand: that the attack not end with another condemnation, but with an investigation that results in those responsible being brought to justice.

For Israel, Greece is more than a friend - it is a strategic partner - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:37:05 UTC
00:37:05 KST

In the Middle East, where alliances are repeatedly tested by crises, Greece is a partner Israel should value.
Beyond the blue sea, the islands, and the beloved music stands a country that understands the importance of its relationship with Israel and gives it diplomatic, security, and economic depth.
Relations between Jerusalem and Athens show how geographic proximity can become a strategic partnership when political leaders invest in it over time.
Relations between countries also have a personal dimension, expressed through diplomatic encounters.
One such occasion was a dinner hosted by Ami H Orkaby, dean of the Israeli Consular Corps and honorary consul general of South Korea, and his wife, Shirley.
Gil Haskel, Israel’s chief of protocol, attended the dinner, which was held in honor of Nikolaos Margaropoulos of Greece, president of the World Federation of Consuls (FICAC).
Such gatherings illustrate the importance of diplomacy in connecting people and countries, building relationships, and cultivating trust.
The organization president’s Greek background also gives the occasion a personal connection to relations with Greece. Honorary consuls, who operate at the intersection of diplomacy and business, can help expand relationships and advance new initiatives.
Alongside formal agreements, hospitality, conversation, and a willingness to listen and help create the foundation for future partnerships, Orkaby’s contribution to cultivating these encounters and strengthening Israel’s international relationships deserves recognition.
What makes Greek-Israeli ties so significant
Greece’s approach toward Israel is especially worthy of appreciation because it exists within a complex political reality. Friendship does not require agreement on every issue.
Athens maintains independent positions and has criticized Israel on diplomatic matters, but disagreements do not erase the relationship’s importance.
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis’s visit to Israel in October 2023, following the Hamas attack, expressed solidarity during an exceptionally difficult period and demonstrated the human significance of the partnership.
Greece’s ambassador to Israel, Maya Solomou, also deserves recognition for her contribution to this continuing effort. She presented her credentials to President Isaac Herzog in February 2025.
Her work demonstrates the value of diplomacy that connects governments, business communities, and professionals.
Her presence in economic and security forums provides an active point of contact and helps turn goodwill into meetings, new relationships, and the exploration of practical opportunities for cooperation.
In January 2026, Solomou was the guest of honor at a meeting of the Israel Greece Chamber of Commerce’s security, policing and cybersecurity forum. She emphasized the trust between the countries and the importance of expanding their economic and technological ties.
The chamber also published an invitation to a business meeting at her residence in June.
These are examples of diplomacy’s practical contribution: opening doors, bringing entrepreneurs together, and strengthening mutual familiarity. Her investment in making this friendship part of everyday life deserves appreciation.
The security partnership offers particularly impressive examples.
The international flight training center in Kalamata, established and operated by Elbit Systems under an agreement between the two countries’ defense ministries, combines Israeli experience with the needs of the Hellenic Air Force.
Training aircraft, instructional systems, and simulators create professional infrastructure for the long term.
The project’s significance extends beyond a commercial transaction: it reflects Greece’s willingness to entrust a central component of its pilot training program to a reliable partner.
JOINT MILITARY exercises provide another important dimension.
In September 2023, the IDF described an aerial exercise with Greece that included long-range flights, aerial refueling, low-altitude flying, and deploying munitions at Greek training ranges.
Exercises of this kind allow both sides to learn from each other and become familiar with diverse operational conditions.
The 2026 military cooperation program among Israel, Greece, and Cyprus demonstrates that the relationship is also expanding into an organized regional framework based on planning and coordination.
Alongside aircraft and military exercises, the friendship also has a distinctly civilian dimension. In the summer of 2023, Israel sent firefighting aircraft and crews to help Greece confront severe wildfires.
When communities, forests, and human lives are in danger, cooperation gains tangible meaning. Operational expertise and the ability to mobilize quickly demonstrate how a relationship between countries can provide direct assistance to people in need.
Tourism is another central pillar of the relationship. Proximity, culture, and Greek hospitality create a natural foundation for encounters between the two peoples, along with economic opportunities in hospitality, aviation, and related services.
In September 2026, the Greek tourism minister and Israel’s ambassador in Athens discussed expanding tourism cooperation. This continued engagement has considerable value. Every successful personal encounter can strengthen familiarity, reduce suspicion, and generate mutual interest.
Energy, water, and innovation offer more opportunities for progress. Joint business forums are exploring ways to connect Israeli technological capabilities with opportunities in Greece and Cyprus.
Energy connectivity projects still require economic evaluation, financing, and solutions to diplomatic challenges, but the coordination itself is important.
It allows the countries to think regionally about energy security, supply diversification, and stronger links between the Eastern Mediterranean and Europe.
This is also where the significance of the trilateral partnership with Cyprus and the cooperative framework with the United States becomes clear. These relationships can serve as a counterweight to exert pressure in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Amid disputes with Turkey over maritime boundaries and energy resources, coordination strengthens the negotiating position of the participating countries.
In the face of the Iranian threat and regional attacks on trade routes, stable security relationships become even more important.
Greece pursues an independent foreign policy, and the trilateral relationship should not be interpreted as a threat to other countries.
Its strength lies in responsible deterrence: protecting sovereignty, infrastructure, and freedom of navigation while leaving the door open to dialogue.
Successful cooperation increases the prospects for regional stability.
Greece deserves a central place in Israel’s foreign policy and treatment that recognizes both its contribution and its needs.
The work of Solomou, the efforts of professional officials, and the political commitment in both capitals give the partnership an opportunity to continue deepening.
In an era of uncertainty, knowing that a country across the sea stands ready to train, trade, innovate, and exchange assistance is a genuine strategic asset.
That asset should be cultivated wisely, with mutual respect and gratitude. It is an investment in our security, our economy, and the ability of future generations to live in a stable and prosperous region.
The writer is the CEO of Radios 100FM, an Honorary Consul and vice dean of the Consular Diplomatic Corps, president of the Israel Amateur Radio Club, and previously served as a monitor for Israel Army Radio and as a television correspondent for NBC News.

Tajikistan celebrates ancient Mehrgon Harvest Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:36:04 UTC
00:36:04 KST

Tajikistan celebrates ancient Mehrgon Harvest Festival
Festivities marking Mehrgon, the ancient festival of harvest and gratitude for the earth's bounty, are taking place in Firdawsi Park in Dushanbe, a Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
Mehrgon's origins date back thousands of years. Historically, it was celebrated after the completion of agricultural work, when communities gave thanks for a successful harvest. The choice of venue is symbolic: the park is named after the great Persian poet Firdawsi, author of the Shahnameh, where Mehrgon is also celebrated. In modern Tajikistan, the festival continues to be observed with great enthusiasm and scale.
At the center of the festivities stood a large floral and fruit installation bearing the inscription "Jashni Mehrgon" ("Mehrgon Festival"), where residents and visitors gathered throughout the day for photographs. Guests were welcomed by performers dressed in striped chapans tied with colorful sashes, as well as an actor portraying the "King of Mehregan" in golden robes and a crown.
Each region of the country presented its own exhibition. The Khatlon region, one of Tajikistan's main agricultural areas, greeted visitors with a long dastarkhan featuring hot traditional flatbread, layered fatir, sambusa, black and white grapes, pomegranates, quinces, peaches, dried fruits, and sweets. Around the table stood young women dressed in atlas and adras, traditional Tajik fabrics known for their distinctive patterns.
An equally impressive display of vegetables included a wooden cart filled with cabbages, eggplants, sweet peppers, radishes, beets, pumpkins, and yellow carrots, an essential ingredient in traditional Tajik plov.
The highlight of the celebration was a theatrical performance. Folk ensembles presented dances dedicated to the harvest season, with young women carrying baskets of persimmons and pomegranates, while young men in striped chapans reenacted scenes from the lives of farmers. The performances took place against a backdrop of decorative mountains made from pumpkins, watermelons, and melons.
In modern Tajikistan, Mehrgon was revived in 2009 at the initiative of President Emomali Rahmon. In 2017, it was added to the country's national list of intangible cultural heritage. Alongside Nowruz and Sada, Mehrgon is considered one of the principal ancient celebrations of Persian-speaking peoples.
It should be noted, “Ceremony of Mehrgon” officially inscribed in Representative Register of UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2024.

Azerbaijan reignites debate over secularism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:32:32 UTC
00:32:32 KST

Azerbaijan reignites debate over secularism
MADRID - A decision by the Azerbaijani government that effectively bans students and teachers from wearing the hijab in educational institutions has sparked a wave of protests.
The amendment, approved last month, does not directly ban the Islamic veil. Instead, it prohibits clothing that the government considers to violate the “principle of secularity.”
From a Western perspective, secularism is often used to judge the hijab in a way that excludes certain views while supporting others. The hijab is often presented as a sign that women lack freedom and control over their own decisions. Women who wear it are sometimes portrayed as lacking independence and the ability to make their own choices. However, this view does not necessarily reflect the experiences of women who choose to wear the hijab. Instead, it follows a way of thinking that gives priority to values such as visibility and individual freedom as understood within a Western framework.
By placing a barrier between the body of an Oriental woman and the Western gaze, the veil appears to put her beyond Western observation and desire. Its covering makes the woman seem mysterious and inaccessible, frustrating the desire to see and understand her. When a veiled woman refuses to be observed, the Western gaze may respond with disappointment and subject her to even greater scrutiny.
The portrayal of the Orient and its women as an “enigma” that must be uncovered turns the veil into a central part of this process. The veil becomes a symbol through which Western fantasies about discovering the secrets of the Orient and understanding the inner lives of its people are expressed. The desire to unveil the Oriental woman is not simply about removing what covers her. It also creates a power relationship in which the Western observer gains access to knowledge that was previously beyond their reach.
One might expect Azerbaijan, a country with a Shia Muslim majority, to be protected from this kind of thinking. However, the facts show the opposite.
Azerbaijan's Shia majority has undeniable cultural importance. Yet the way the government in Baku presents Islam reduces it to what could be called “Islamization.” In this context, Islam is allowed a certain degree of visibility in cultural life, but it is not treated as a framework that can shape international relations or public policy.
Moreover, Islamization must be understood within a broader political approach to modernity. This approach treats public expressions of Islam as remnants of a tradition that must be removed or, where possible, confined to specific spaces. Outside those spaces, the hijab is portrayed as a sign of oppression and backwardness. In many European countries, support for banning the veil has been based on the belief that it is the “definitive symbol of Islam's resistance to modernity” and a challenge to secular democracy. Similar attitudes toward visible signs of Islam can also be found in Westernized parts of Muslim-majority countries, as seen in Azerbaijan today and in Turkey several decades ago.
The distinction between modern citizens and those who publicly resist this process creates a division within the nation itself. This division can serve as a racial marker. In this view, the nation is treated as an unchanging political community with a stable past, an identity passed down through generations, a relatively fixed territory, and a shared destiny that connects the present with the future. Although nation-states emerged relatively recently and have constantly changed, they often present themselves as if they had existed forever.
This idea assumes that a particular people forms the core of the nation. That people is seen as a “natural community” with its own origins, culture, and interests, an identity that exists beyond individual differences and changing social conditions. In other words, the nation-state is assumed to be based on what is commonly called “ethnic unity.”
However, no nation-state truly has a fully formed ethnic identity that existed before the state itself. As a result, nationalism must constantly create and reproduce what is known as fictive ethnicity. This process gives the nation what appears to be a natural origin and creates the myth that its population has always been culturally and ethnically homogeneous.
This imagined homogeneity creates racial divisions within the nation. It becomes a means of excluding people who do not fit the dominant idea of modernity. The official discourse presents some citizens as representatives of progress while treating others as obstacles to the nation's unity and transformation. Those who do not fit the preferred national identity are therefore viewed with suspicion. They become reminders of a past that the nation claims to have left behind, as well as a threat that could bring that past back.
The situation in Azerbaijan, where protests against the hijab ban have brought students and teachers into the streets, reflects an attempt to use secularism as a means of social control. In this case, secularism becomes a political tool that recognizes some beliefs and ways of life as legitimate while portraying others as threats. Rather than simply separating religion from the state, this approach can be used to regulate public life, restrict individual choices, and determine which forms of identity are accepted within the nation.

Ukraine Hunts Down Second Russian Mi-28NM Attack Helicopter in One Week With Interceptor Drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

15:28:40 UTC
00:28:40 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hunts Down Second Russian Mi-28NM Attack Helicopter in One Week With Interceptor Drone
Ukrainian forces have targeted a second Russian Mi-28NM attack helicopter in less than a week, using a domestically developed interceptor drone to pursue the aircraft over Russia’s Belgorod region. The latest strike follows a similar attack on the same helicopter model just days earlier.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s 115th Separate Mechanized Brigade announced the operation on October 16, releasing footage showing operators from its air defense unit, known as “Aliens,” pursuing the Russian helicopter.
The Ukrainian troops deployed a VB140 Flamingo fixed-wing interceptor drone manufactured by the Ukrainian company Vinnytsia Bees.
Video released by the brigade shows the drone closing in on the Mi-28NM from behind, apparently aiming for the helicopter’s engine compartment. The footage cuts off just before a possible collision with the rotor blades, leaving the extent of any damage unconfirmed.
Open-source intelligence researcher Bendik geolocated the attack near Yasnozorenskoye in Russia’s Belgorod region, approximately 16 kilometers (10 miles) from the front line.
The location is roughly four kilometers (2.5 miles) north of the site of an earlier Ukrainian drone attack against another Russian Mi-28NM helicopter. On October 14, the same brigade reported striking a Mi-28NM using an FPV drone, marking the first of two reported engagements against Russian attack helicopters within a single week.
The Mi-28NM is one of Russia’s modernized attack helicopters, designed to engage armored vehicles, fortified positions, and other ground targets in both daytime and nighttime operations.
It is equipped with an N025 mast-mounted radar, advanced targeting systems, a 30mm 2A42 cannon, and guided missiles, including the LMUR, also known as the Izdeliye 305.
Russian forces have also employed Mi-28NM helicopters to intercept Ukrainian long-range drones and reportedly adapted the aircraft to launch smaller cruise missiles, including the S8000 Banderol and Dan-T.

Cosmic Breath: Global calls to prayer answer rising Islamophobia in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:24:08 UTC
00:24:08 KST

Tucked away just a stone's throw from the relentless hum of Oxford Street, a new sonic sanctuary has taken root in central London. Joe Namy, an American-born Lebanese artist and composer whose practice encompasses sound, its history, and its physical impact on the built environment, has brought his multi-channel sound installation, Cosmic Breath, to the UK capital.
The work is reimagined for Ibraaz’s Musalla, a space dedicated to spiritual practice as both lived experience and creative expression.
Composed of recordings of the adhan—the Islamic call to prayer—the installation brings together historical and contemporary calls from different geographies, amplified through horn speakers like those mounted on mosque minarets.
Played simultaneously, each speaker softly emits a different adhan recording, inviting the audience to lean in and listen closely. At prayer times, the volume increases, making the calls clearly audible throughout the room, creating a congregation of calls to prayer.
The work forms part of Namy's wider exploration of sound systems, community, and spirituality.
First commissioned for the Islamic Arts Biennale in Jeddah in 2023 by its artistic director and architect, Sumayya Vally, the installation explores collective auditory experiences and public sound landmarks.
"A lot of my work deals with the politics of sound, and deals with the spirituality of sound as well, how it affects us in different ways," Namy explains. "So, I'm interested in sound system cultures (and) collective sound experiences as well, and how they impact our lives."
Developed in close collaboration with Vally, who designed the installation’s spatial scenography, the artwork grew out of a poetic reflection on time and geography.
Namy was moved by the idea that "at any moment in time on Earth, there is an adhan happening somewhere on this planet, which I think is such a really powerful and beautiful gesture."
Approaching the adhan through a sociological lens, Namy examines how an ancient oral tradition has transformed alongside modern technology, amplification, and recordings.
Bringing the piece from Saudi Arabia to London reshapes its meaning dramatically, particularly given the current social atmosphere in the UK.
"Showing it for the first time in Jeddah was a very different experience than showing it here in London, which ... situates the work very differently than how it was situated there," Namy underlined.
He pointed directly to the heightened hostility surrounding the current political landscape: "Especially now today in the current kind of political climate here in London... there's just a more heightened kind of Islamophobia, xenophobia, prejudice... all these things that we've been experiencing and has been increasing."
For Namy, installing the piece in the heart of London serves as a sanctuary and an antidote to that hostility.
"I feel like it's a more powerful gesture to be able to show it here in the center of London, you know, just off of Oxford Street, and to be able to have this space for people to be able to come, relax," he said.
He notes how rare it is in contemporary art spaces to engage with faith so openly: "I think, what I really enjoy is the fact that it's thinking about the spirituality in relation to art, which you don't always get a chance to explore, but also providing a kind of third space for people to explore more.”
To ground the exhibition in its current environment, this iteration at Ibraaz features a local recording. "So, this recording is from London," Namy notes.
"Actually, it was important to bring in something that was local as well, and so this was actually one of the first recordings of a public adhan in London that happened in Walthamstow during COVID. It was again a time (when) everyone was social distancing, and so it was a way for the community to be able to kind of -- although they were distant -- to feel closer together, so it was important to bring in a local element into the setting as well, so that we have some a more closer connection to where we are here in London."
The recording captures the historic call performed by the Waltham Forest Islamic Association in 2020, offering a sonic expression of shared experience when physical gathering was impossible.
The audio selections in Cosmic Breath span more than a century and cross vast physical and acoustic terrains, revealing how each call carries a unique character shaped by local traditions, acoustic environments, and regional histories.
"The selections that we included within this installation each represent a certain aspect, or have a unique aspect for the adhan," Namy says. "Part of it is thinking about spaces (where) you normally wouldn't encounter the adhan, spaces in which recordings of the adhan are kind of historically significant as well."
Among the archival highlights is what is considered the first recording of the adhan at the Haram Mosque in Mecca, dating back to the late 19th century. "I think this one is the first recording that was ever done of the adhan from the late 1800s in Mecca. You can kind of hear the grain of the recording. It's not a really great recording, but it's interesting to hear it in context of all the other ones," Namy reflects.
From Asia, the piece gathers landmark history and geography.
"From the Philippines, (there is) an archival recording from the 1950s. It was one of the first recordings of the adhan in the Philippines," Namy points out.
Contemporary and historical selections also feature the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem and Singapore's Sultan Mosque, thought to be the first mosque to adopt loudspeakers in the 1930s.
"This one is from Singapore, and this was recorded at the first mosque that actually used speakers to amplify the call to prayer. The mosque is still there, and that was important," he adds.
Other field recordings offer stark contrasts in style and setting—from the ornate to the stripped-back.
"This one is Georgia Tbilisi, and this one is probably the most flowery, I think. You really hear the improvisation and the embellishments and how the voice gets extended in the recitation," Namy says.
In contrast, "one is from the Sahrawi refugee camp in Algeria, and it's one of the only ones that's not recorded, that's not amplified," Namy explains saying, "It's somebody who is old school-style, kind of just reciting it without any speakers or anything like that, just their voice."
The installation captures deeply intimate acts of faith as well as distinct colloquial traditions.
"I think this one is from Japan," Namy shares, explaining that similar to the recording mentioned before, it was "somebody just kind of reciting it into the forest for themselves, basically, which I thought was a really beautiful gesture. So, it's a very personal personal recording reflection."
A call to prayer from Khartoum highlights regional identity: "This one is Khartoum. It's recorded in Sudan, and again, you hear the colloquial differences and how the adhan is recited. It's very different in the recitation. It's very Sudani in its style, which I really love."
Not every place could be captured on audio.
Namy recalls attempting to record the first mosque built in South America, located in Brazil. Because the building is reserved for special occasions, "you don't hear the adhan there, so we recorded just kind of like the empty space from that room, just to have that kind of gesture," though it ultimately remained unreleased alongside seaside field recordings from Egypt.
The initial impulse for Cosmic Breath traces back to a pivotal moment of civic resistance in South Africa. During the COVID-19 lockdowns in 2020, rising social tension, Islamophobia, and xenophobia in Durban led to a local ban on publicly broadcasting the adhan.
In response, an act of interfaith solidarity emerged. "This protest was actually organized by a Hindu community member. He wasn't Muslim, but he organized this protest in solidarity with the Muslim community there," Namy recalls.
Sumayya Vally shared the link to the event with him, sparking the broader concept.
Restricted by social distancing rules, residents adapted: "How do you protest at a time when you can't congregate and gather together? And so they asked everybody to bring their cars and made this huge parade. Everybody tuned their car stereo systems to one of the channels that was broadcasting the adhan."
The resulting soundscape of hundreds of car speakers reverberating through the streets of Durban provided the foundation for the entire project. "This is the recording from that experience as well," Namy reflects.
"And that was kind of the first recordings that really made me think about the piece... and bring everything together."

Florida fisher dragged into water and killed by 12ft alligator
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:23:32 UTC
00:23:32 KST

A man fishing at a pond in Florida was killed on Friday by an alligator that was almost 12ft long in a rare kind of animal attack, according to authorities and media reports.
Steve Hamilton, 71, was on the shoreline in the community of Winter Garden when the animal dragged him into the water, the Florida news outlet WOFL reported, citing local police and the state’s fish and wildlife conservation commission.
Emergency crews responded to the park where Hamilton was fishing at about 5.20pm on Friday after receiving a 911 call and attempted to rescue him – but they had difficulty doing so because of nearby alligators, the outlet reported.
Hamilton’s body was recovered from the water a couple of hours later.
Capt Michael Mason of the Winter Garden police department told news media that the alligator had been killed after the fatal attack on Hamilton.
Authorities were not alerted of a gator sighting on Friday at the pond, which is connected to Lake Apopka, Mason said.
The body of water has “tons of alligators in it. That is not uncommon to see alligators in this part of town,” Mason said.
The chief encouraged people to “be aware of your surroundings”.
The gator “looks like it’s docile. It looks like your Florida emblem, but it can be dangerous,” Mason said.
Alligator attacks are statistically rare. Nonetheless, at least 34 people have been killed by them in Florida since 1948, according to the Florida fish and wildlife conservation commission, which compiles reports of encounters with the state’s estimated 1.3 million gators.
Hamilton’s death came less than four months after a woman named Brittany Clark was attacked and killed by a 13ft alligator while swimming with her boyfriend in the Econlockhatchee River in Florida’s Seminole county.
Autopsy results released in July showed Clark, 31, struggled for her life before dying from the wounds inflicted on her by the alligator, which was removed from the river and euthanized.
After Clark’s death, the Republican US House member Greg Steube of Florida introduced a resolution calling for the federal comptroller general and the US Department of the Interior to study how American alligators’ being listed as “threatened due to similarity of appearance” to crocodiles affects his state’s ability to remove nuisance gators from residential and commercial waterways.
Steube said the species has been fully recovered since 1987, but it remains protected to prevent the trafficking and hunting of the similar-looking American crocodile.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el Sisi has said Egypt is ready to defend Saudi Arabia “if requested”, as fighting intensifies between the kingdom and Yemen’s Houthi militia.
Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian military academy on Saturday, Sisi said it was “inconceivable” for Cairo to stand by while Saudi Arabia was “harmed or its security and stability threatened”.
“Egypt, of course, with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, will carry out any measure to protect you or defend you,” he said.
Sisi stressed that Egypt was “not looking for a role to play” in regional conflicts and that any deployment would require parliamentary approval.
He said he hoped lawmakers would convene an emergency session to grant authorisation “if it is requested of us”.
“I’m not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone,” he said. “We are speaking only about defence.”
Since Yemen’s war reignited in July, the Houthi militia has repeatedly attacked Saudi targets, including energy facilities and Riyadh’s international airport, where 13 people were killed in a single attack last week.
The Houthi militia has also blockaded the Bab al-Mandab Strait, adding pressure on energy exports as Iran maintains its own blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Red Sea shipping concerns
During a visit to Egypt last month, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Sisi called for free and secure navigation in the Red Sea, a vital trade route.
The conflict threatens both Saudi Arabia’s security and energy exports and Egypt’s revenues from the Suez Canal, a key source of foreign currency.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said last month that disruptions had cost the canal about $11 billion in revenue since the Houthi militia began attacking commercial vessels since 2023, when Israel began its war on Gaza.
Despite its longstanding military ties with Gulf states, Egypt has not joined the Mecca agreement, a mutual defence pact signed by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan in August.

How big is Russia's threat against Germany?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:23:00 UTC
00:23:00 KST

How great is the Russian threat against Germany?
October 17, 2026
Warnings keep mounting about Russia's threat to Germany. On October 12, Sinan Selen, president of Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, said that Russia's covert attacks and destabilization efforts against Germany and other European countries are "not a temporary development but a long-term hybrid attack."
Even if the war in Ukraine were to end, said Selen, the Russian threat would not disappear. "For Russia, this is about completely redrawing the map of Europe and redefining its own role within Europe and in global politics."
He added that Russia's aggression would continue to be felt not only in Ukraine, but also in the Baltic states, in Poland and in Germany.
Russia is tied down in Ukraine — for now
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has described the threat situation as one in which "our country is not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare." Russia's goal, he said, is not to defeat Germany militarily "but to subdue us politically and socially."
Security experts, however, are not so sure that Russia is only interested in exercising political and social influence. Last year, political scientist Carlo Masala told the political talk show Maischberger that "Russia is preparing for a major war." And he didn't mean just a cyberwar. Inspector General Carsten Breuer, the Bundeswehr's highest-ranking officer, agreed.
For now, though, Russia remains tied up in its war against Ukraine. According to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, there is no immediate military threat to NATO territory. But according to military experts, European intelligence agencies, and the German Defense Ministry, Russia will have the personnel and equipment to wage a conventional war against NATO by 2029. The Russian defense industry is running at full speed, and Moscow plans to expand its armed forces to 1.5 million soldiers.
At the moment, Russia has other objectives, believes Stefan Meister, an expert on Eastern Europe at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP): "I don't think Russia has any interest in a direct military conflict with NATO right now. It wants to test NATO and also display its capabilities," he tells DW.
An accidental military confrontation?
An example of Russia's hybrid war might be the failed attack with an explosive-laden drone against a Ukrainian transport aircraft at Leipzig-Halle Airport in August. Soon after, the German government stated that it was certain Russia was behind the attack.
Security expert Nico Lange told DW at the time that Germany was very lucky the explosives did not detonate: "Honestly, it was pure coincidence and not the result of German defensive measures."
As for why Germany was targeted specifically, Lange said: "I believe that Germany has always been a primary target of Russian influence and hybrid warfare. Russia believes that Germany is the key to European decision-making. Germany is now leading the way in supporting Ukraine."
Moscow swiftly responded to the German government's accusation with an angry denial. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said it was "the beginning of a real war," though there was no immediate further escalation.
Nevertheless, there is always the risk that things could spiral out of control following a Russian provocation and subsequent response, according to Stefan Meister: "Accidentally shooting down an aircraft that they were trying to intimidate would trigger a counter-reaction. But I don't believe that Russia is currently aiming for a direct war but rather for provocations, polarization, and sowing uncertainty among the population."
AfD says less money for Ukraine means more for Germany
Not everyone shares the assessment that Russia poses a threat to Germany — some believe that the threat can be averted.
Despite the war in Ukraine, politicians from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the populist left-wing Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) want to improve relations with Russia, resume Russian energy supplies and end support for Ukraine.
AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said in early September, "People are fed up with this escalation against Russia, with the billions being squandered there on a system that is actually funded by German taxpayers' money."
The message appears to have resonated among the population, especially in eastern Germany. The AfD saw strong gains in all three state elections in September. In Saxony-Anhalt, it became the strongest party by far and may even run the government there soon, which would be the first time that a far-right party has held power in Germany since the end of WWII.
The CDU's security policy expert Roderich Kiesewetter disputed the claim made by the AfD and BSW that ending aid to Ukraine would mean greater security and more money for German schools and infrastructure: "Spending on education, social policy, and infrastructure is only possible if we live in freedom and democracy — and, above all, in peace and security. Anyone who believes that we'll have more money for social programs if we stop supporting Ukraine and let Russia have its way is either gravely mistaken or is making themselves a tool of Russian propaganda."
A decades-long pacifist mindset
The perceived security threat has led the German military, the Bundeswehr, to fast-track significant modernization through substantial investment. But it is struggling to find enough recruits for its planned expansion. Many young Germans have taken to the streets to protest against plans to reintroduce conscription. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius faced criticism from inside his own party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), for saying that Germany must become "capable of waging war." Many found the statement to be too militaristic.
Is Germany prepared for a military threat? "Not at all. Germany is not well prepared militarily or in the civilian sector, and the population isn't mentally prepared for it either," said Meister. "Just look at the demonstrations against conscription and the military that continue to take place, even though Germany needs a draft. For decades, we've grown up in this culture of pacifism, in a comfort zone. I believe there is very limited societal resilience, but above all, we are not at all mentally prepared for war."
Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) are under increasing political pressure — especially from the far right — to scale back support for Ukraine. But Merz never tires of emphasizing that Ukraine will continue to receive support under his chancellorship, calling it a matter of Germany's security. He recently visited Kyiv once again and, together with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, surveyed the destruction caused by Russia.
But this also means that the threat from Russia will continue and even intensify, says Stefan Meister: "I believe we will see a massive increase in attacks such as the one in Leipzig, of provocations involving drones. We will see attacks on infrastructures and possibly also on specific individuals within the military-industrial complex. I believe this is the real, concrete danger facing Germany in the coming months."
This article was translated from German.
