Ilhan Omar’s lawyers demand the return of property seized in house raid
Omar’s legal team says the search violated safeguards designed to protect constitutional rights of members of Congress.
Lawyers for Democratic United States Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota have demanded the return of property seized in a federal raid of her Washington, DC home, accusing the US Department of Justice of conducting a politically motivated investigation and failing to follow judicial instructions during the search.
“The political motivations behind this pre-election investigation and search are clear as day,” Omar’s lawyers wrote in a letter sent to federal prosecutors on Friday and obtained by The Associated Press news agency. “This search was neither justified nor lawful.”
In the letter, Omar’s lawyers, Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, challenged an investigation into her immigration history, saying there was “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”.
The letter accuses federal agents of threatening the separation of powers and failing to comply with a magistrate judge’s instructions for the search of Omar’s northeast Washington home on Monday.
Federal agents searched Omar’s home on Monday as part of an investigation into alleged immigration fraud. Authorities seized her phone and passport, and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to The Washington Post. Her lawyers also asked authorities to preserve audio and video recordings from the search.
Omar’s lawyers claim that investigators did not provide a copy of the warrant to them in advance, nor did they contact the House of Representatives’ Office of General Counsel, which disregarded the magistrate judge’s orders. The notice would have allowed Omar to seek legal counsel and potentially leverage legislation that could have challenged the warrant.
Her lawyers said the procedures outlined by the judge are intended to protect Omar’s constitutional rights as a sitting member of Congress, and safeguard against the seizure of materials related to her legislative work.
Her lawyers also argued that the investigation was politically motivated due to its proximity to the November midterm elections.
“Historically, the Department has refrained from this type of investigative activity so close to an election, so as to avoid even the appearance of politically motivated law enforcement actions,” they wrote.
The Justice Department rejected the accusations, describing the letter as “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies”.
“Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” Justice Department spokesperson Emily Covington said.
Omar became a naturalised US citizen in 2000 after fleeing Somalia with her family as a child, according to her House biography. She has repeatedly rejected allegations by conservative critics about her immigration status, which was also probed in 2019 during Trump’s first administration.
Omar’s lawyers have requested records relating to the 2019 inquiry into her immigration history. The former investigation found insufficient evidence of wrongdoing to warrant a full investigation, according to The Washington Post.
The scope of the current investigation remains unclear.
The search took place days after Trump attacked Omar at a rally in Tennessee, describing her home country as a place of “crime and squalor” and suggesting that Vice President JD Vance and others were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump denied any involvement, telling reporters the matter was “really up to the DOJ”.

As the assault on Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine continues to draw widespread condemnation, Jewish extremists on Saturday attacked diplomats from France, Belgium and Poland who were visiting an olive harvest near the Palestinian village of Taybeh, considered the last entirely Christian village in the West Bank.
Videos from the scene show a group of masked men approaching a vehicle carrying diplomats with clubs and stones and pursuing them on all-terrain vehicles. In subsequent footage, Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, is seen sitting on the ground with his back against a vehicle, wearing an armband displaying the French flag for identification. A separate image shows a shattered window in a vehicle belonging to the Belgian consulate.
The mayor of Taybeh said in a statement that settlers had attacked foreign diplomatic delegations visiting the village during the olive harvest season.
Approximately seven rioters are believed to have taken part in the attack, which also targeted Palestinian olive pickers in Taybeh, an area designated as Area B under the Oslo Accords, where the Palestinian Authority exercises civil control and Israel retains overriding security responsibility.
"We notified the army in real time, but they didn't come or respond," said Amit Orpeli, one of the activists at the scene. "They threatened to kill us."
Orpeli, an activist with the Torat Tzedek organization, arrived with fellow activist Roni Federman. The two told ynet that they had received reports of a major settler attack in a larger nearby olive grove.
"We drove there, and seven masked settlers armed with clubs immediately came toward us," they said. "We didn't recognize them. They weren't people from the nearby settlement whom we know."
According to Orpeli, the attackers were particularly violent and arrived on ATVs. Palestinian landowners who fled the scene also reported that the settlers had stolen olives they had already harvested.
Belgian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot strongly condemned the attack, saying masked settlers in Taybeh had targeted Palestinians, Belgium's consul general, French and Polish diplomats and Catholic representatives. He said a French mayor had been assaulted and a Belgian diplomatic vehicle damaged, but confirmed that Belgian personnel were safe.
Prévot noted that Palestinians face such violence daily and that settlers have also targeted journalists documenting the attacks and diplomats carrying out their duties. Harvesting olives, reporting the news and conducting diplomatic work, he said, should never expose anyone to such attacks.
The Belgian foreign minister linked the violence to Israel's settlement policies, which he condemned as illegal, and to what he described as attempts to forcibly remove Palestinians from their land. He called for an end to the occupation and to impunity for violent settlers, saying Belgium would continue pressing for European Union sanctions against those responsible for the attacks and those supporting them.

The IDF strongly condemned the violence near Taybeh, saying Israeli rioters had attacked diplomatic representatives in the area under the responsibility of its Binyamin Regional Brigade.
The military said police officers and forensic investigators from the Israel Police's West Bank district were entering the area under IDF protection to collect evidence, document the scene and take witness statements as part of an investigation.
However, the IDF also said the consular visit had not been coordinated with the military in advance, stressing that such coordination was important in preventing incidents of this kind.
According to the military's preliminary inquiry, no troops were present at the location when the attack occurred. The IDF said a report about the incident had been sent to an account belonging to the brigade's operations center, which is intended to receive reports from security personnel rather than civilians.
The operations center receives dozens of operational reports each day, the military explained, and responds only to authorized security officials. Other channels are available for complaints and reports from civilians. The IDF said the entire incident would be examined.
Israel Police said the Binyamin station in its West Bank district had opened an investigation after footage circulated online showing an attack on several diplomats near Taybeh.
Police said the Foreign Ministry had been notified to help locate the victims, obtain their statements and identify the suspects so they could be prosecuted. The police condemned violence of any kind and pledged to pursue those responsible. 
Democrats Party chairman Yair Golan condemned the incident, describing the reported attack on foreign diplomats by Jewish rioters in the West Bank as a serious and dangerous development requiring an immediate and decisive response.
Golan accused the Netanyahu-Smotrich coalition of allowing nationalist violence to escalate, warning that Jewish terrorism in the West Bank threatened the rule of law, Israel's security, IDF soldiers and the country's international standing.
He called for Jewish terrorism to be fought with the same determination as Palestinian terrorism, including restoring the use of administrative detention against dangerous Jewish extremists in accordance with the law, dismantling centers of extremist violence, evacuating illegal outposts and arresting and prosecuting those responsible.
Golan said that if his party returned to power, the IDF, Shin Bet security agency and Israel Police would receive full backing to enforce the law and restore security and order in the West Bank. He insisted that Jewish terrorists should enjoy no immunity and that Israeli law must apply to everyone.
Meanwhile, Palestinians reported another incident in which settlers allegedly blocked a vehicle carrying foreign activists on the Khallet al-Homs road, south of Yatta in the southern Hebron Hills.
Earlier Saturday afternoon, IDF and Border Police forces were dispatched to the Shirat Zion outpost near Beit Lid in the northern West Bank following clashes between Israelis and Palestinians. Settlers were suspected of arriving to disrupt Palestinian olive harvesting, with initial reports indicating that both sides had thrown stones and several Palestinians had been injured.
Hours later, conflicting accounts emerged about the circumstances in which an Israeli civilian was injured. Settlers initially reported a vehicle-ramming attack, but a subsequent account suggested that Israelis had stolen a Palestinian vehicle and crashed it. Another version claimed that the vehicle belonged to Arab Israelis who were attempting to flee the area and struck a settler. The circumstances remained disputed.
Hundreds of former security officials apologize to injured photographer
In recent days, the IDF and police have failed to prevent several serious attacks on Palestinians harvesting olives in different parts of the West Bank. Among those assaulted was Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who underwent surgery Saturday on a finger of her left hand that was nearly severed during the attack, according to her daughter, Ashley Milner. 
Hundreds of former senior Israeli security officials sent Levine a letter of apology Saturday. The signatories described what they said was the daily targeting of innocent people in the West Bank and warned that such violence was damaging Israel's security and international standing.
They also criticized senior government officials and lawmakers who, they said, encourage violence, and called for a fundamental change in government policy.
The letter was signed by members of Commanders for Israel's Security, a movement comprising approximately 600 former senior officials from the IDF, Mossad, Shin Bet, police and diplomatic service, as well as members of a forum representing about 200 former police commissioners and senior police officers.
Among the signatories were former IDF chief of staff and defense minister Moshe "Bogie" Ya'alon; former Mossad director Tamir Pardo; former Shin Bet director Ami Ayalon; former police commissioner Moshe Karadi; former deputy IDF chief of staff and deputy defense minister Matan Vilnai; former heads of the IDF Central Command; Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities President Prof. David Harel; and legal expert Talia Sasson.
Back in Taybeh, residents have long warned about the growing pressure on their community. During a previous visit to the village for Ynet's filmed series In No Man's Land, Rabbi Benny Lau spoke with Father Jacques, one of the local church leaders, who described the despair spreading among residents.
Father Jacques recalled with longing the days before the Second Intifada and the Oslo Accords, which he remembered as simpler and more peaceful times. Back then, he said, he could get into his car and drive to Jaffa, while Israeli settlers would stop in the village to buy popsicles and ice cream for their children.
According to residents, 15 families have left Taybeh since the October 7 massacre, moving to various countries around the world.

Peace with Israel: A Lebanese illusion?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:14:47 UTC
00:14:47 KST

Peace with Israel: A Lebanese illusion?
TEHRAN – The occupying Israeli regime continues to wage almost daily aggression against towns and villages in southern Lebanon.
Israeli Occupation Forces (IOF) fired artillery shells in at least eight areas of southern Lebanon. In the town of Bayada, an IOF tank reportedly shelled Al-Mansouri in Tyre district with several rounds.
IOF aggression was also reported in Zawtar al-Sharqiyah, which the regime has been trying to occupy over the past week. The developments have raised questions about the intentions behind the “framework agreement” signed between the Israeli and Lebanese governments on June 26.
The Lebanese government has also faced criticism for reaching a direct agreement with Tel Aviv while southern Lebanon remains under the regime’s occupation forces.
A recent study published by the Israeli Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) outlines a new security doctrine. While the doctrine has yet to be officially announced, it is already being put into practice, reflecting a broader shift in how the regime views its security mechanisms.
The study argues that this new doctrine changes how Israelis understand the relationship between security, war, and peace. The regime no longer sees peace as a lasting strategic goal, but rather as a temporary arrangement. Conflict, by contrast, is increasingly viewed as a permanent condition to be managed rather than brought to an end.
At the heart of this new doctrine is a shift in how the Zionist regime views war: no longer as an exceptional situation, but as a permanent feature of its security.
The study describes this principle of war as a foundational condition, arguing that war is becoming essential to the regime’s security and that peace cannot take its place.
From this perspective, peace is not a goal in its own right, but a temporary means of serving the regime’s interests. The study also links this shift to the belief that the prolonged pursuit of political agreements and peace was part of the “conceptual failure” that led to the October 7 attack.
As a result, the regime’s new security doctrine places greater emphasis on preemptive war and sustained military action.
This raises questions about the assumptions underlying the positions of certain Lebanese groups that advocate “peace with Israel.” Their argument rests on the assumption that the regime seeks to protect its security rather than occupy Lebanon indefinitely, and that it would therefore be willing to withdraw in exchange for a peace agreement that serves its interests.
These changes in Israeli thinking also call into question Lebanese assumptions based on the regime’s peace agreements inked with Egypt and Jordan. The crucial difference is that, when Egypt signed the Camp David Accords, the Israeli political leadership, on both the right and the left, regarded peace with the largest Arab country as a strategic goal in its own right.
The same was true of the treaty with Jordan. Both agreements reflected a broader period in the regime’s thinking when peace, regional integration, and political compromise were seen as essential to its national security.
At the time, the prevailing view among Israelis was that peace produced security. Today, however, a very different view is gaining ground: security is achieved through aggression and a volatile region, while peace is a temporary instrument to be used when it serves the regime’s interests.
The problem with some Lebanese debates is not whether they support or oppose peace, but the assumption that the Israelis still view peace as they did when Tel Aviv signed the Camp David Accords and the Wadi Araba Treaty.
Before considering what Lebanon might offer or gain, the more fundamental question is whether the occupying regime still regards peace as a strategic goal worth making concessions to secure.
More importantly, opinion polls conducted within Israel in recent years have revealed a striking pattern: a majority of Israelis support continuing the pattern of war, even though they do not believe it will bring lasting peace or long-term stability.
This points to an important distinction: a society that supports war without expecting a political settlement does not see war as a path to peace, but as a means of managing a conflict it considers impossible to resolve.
This stands in sharp contrast to the political climate that produced the Camp David Accords and the Wadi Araba Treaty, when peace was viewed as a natural extension of military success rather than an alternative to it.
From this perspective, peace with Lebanon is unlikely to hold the same strategic value for the Israelis that peace with Egypt did in the aftermath of the 1973 war. For a regime that views conflict as a permanent condition, a historic peace agreement holds little appeal.
Instead, it may favor security arrangements that preserve its military superiority and freedom of action while allowing it to maintain its occupation of territory under the pretext of “forward defense.”
This is where the Lebanese and Israeli approaches to the “framework agreement” diverge most sharply. Some Lebanese advocates of peace assume that the occupying regime shares their interest in ending the war and regards doing so as a major strategic priority.
The debate within the Zionist regime today, however, focuses on how to manage a long-term conflict, not how to bring it to an end.
Ultimately, the emerging doctrine points to a view of security in which conflict is permanent, peace is temporary, and war is treated as the norm.
Critics of the Lebanese authorities argue that they should therefore recognize that the strategic conditions, which made the Egyptian and Jordanian agreements with the Zionist regime possible, no longer exist. Trying to replicate those agreements would mean relying on a model of Israeli strategic thinking that no longer exists.

Ukraine still can't intercept drones due to Starlink issues, Zelenskyy says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:14:16 UTC
00:14:16 KST

Ukraine still unable to intercept Russian drones due to Starlink restrictions, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine is still unable to use its interceptor systems against Russian drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday, because of speed restrictions imposed on Starshield, an upgraded military version of Elon Musk's Starlink, amid an ongoing row with President Trump.
"Unfortunately, we can't use Starlink or Starshield technology on our territory today to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds," Zelenskyy said in an online group chat with reporters at the EU Summit. "They fly, and we can stop them with aircraft and other air defense, but we don't use Starlink for that, unfortunately. God willing, this will be restored."
Zelenskyy said Kyiv was discussing the issue with U.S. officials, and he was told the restrictions were linked to technical issues. The Ukrainian president added, however, that Starlink appears to be operating at higher speeds on European Union territory.
"Yes, we are in dialogue at the level of the military, the Ministry of Defense and diplomats, in touch with everyone including SpaceX. Nobody there is answering our military or the Ministry of Defense now," Zelenskyy said. "At various levels they say these are technical problems."
"Here (in Ukraine) Starlink works up to a speed of 161 km/h, then shuts off," he continued. "In the EU it works at 180-plus and works constantly. Here it shuts off in the second minute after 161 km/h and stops working. We lose both drones and connectivity."
Denys Sienik, the chargé d'affaires of Ukraine to the U.S., told CBS News in a statement later Saturday that Ukraine had still not received a response from the Pentagon or SpaceX regarding its inquiries about Starlink or Starshield service, "including confirmation that unlimited speeds have been restored and that Starshield is operating as it did previously."
Sienik said "based on the data currently available to us, we cannot confirm that these capabilities have been fully restored."
Mr. Trump told reporters on Friday he had not limited Ukraine's access to Starlink, adding he didn't believe Musk, SpaceX's CEO, was responsible either.
"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Mr. Trump said while leaving the White House to travel for a rally in Georgia. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."
Musk said Wednesday he isn't responsible for deciding how Starshield is used, writing on X: "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia carried out a large attack on Ukraine's energy sector, targeting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities across the country. A day earlier, the president said the current restrictions on Starshield had left people vulnerable to Russian drones, which was "very painful and frustrating"
Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including speed limits that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions.
Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent days, blaming the war between Russia and Ukraine for high global energy prices. The Trump administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel last week in an effort to ease pressure, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.
In a social media post on Saturday, Zelenskyy called the move "unfortunate," adding the act, championed by late Sen. Lindsey Graham, "could have helped enormously." Later, he told journalists he believed the Trump administration will lift more sanctions on Russia.
"Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the 'diesel deal' is just the first step," Zelenskyy told reporters.
"President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end. As talks continue, this Act provides the President with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CBS News on Saturday in response to a question about lifting the sanctions. "Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests."
Mr. Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire" over the weekend. Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Russian government never confirmed it had agreed to a ceasefire.
In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," urged both sides to make a deal and said the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin.
"I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said.
On Wednesday, Musk had tweeted: "Time for Zelensky to go."

Illegal Israeli settlers attack European delegation in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:06:00 UTC
00:06:00 KST

Illegal Israeli settlers attacked a European diplomatic delegation visiting the occupied West Bank on Saturday, injuring several people as representatives from France, Belgium and Poland toured the Palestinian town of Taybeh.
The attack took place after an official ceremony marking the signing of a twinning agreement between the Palestinian town of Taybeh and the French town of Saint-Pierre, Taybeh Mayor Suleiman Khourieh told Anadolu Agency (AA).
The ceremony was attended by the French and Belgian consuls, a Polish representative whose name was not disclosed, and Saint-Pierre Mayor Christian Ravain.
The attack targeted the delegation in the western part of the town, as well as Palestinians who were picking olives.
It left several town residents injured and shattered the window of a vehicle belonging to the Belgian delegation, Khourieh added.
The 78-year-old French mayor said masked settlers yelled defamatory comments about France, kicked him and hit him with iron bars as he joined Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank alongside the top French and Belgian representatives in Jerusalem and Polish diplomats.
"I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government," Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, told AFP after he was attacked.
"The whole world needs to know what's happening," he said. "For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here."
Baudoux, who was wearing a sash with the French tricolour, was seen collapsed on the side of the car after the attack, but he did not need hospital care.
He, said he had come to the town of Taybeh, a Christian stronghold, along with his local pastor from France to sign a goodwill agreement.
He was attacked just as he joined the harvest as a symbolic gesture with the Palestinians, for whom olives are an important cultural symbol.
Extremist Israelis have issued calls to stop the Palestinians' annual harvest after months of escalating attacks in which settlers have stolen land and property.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said in a statement that Israel must "urgently halt criminal violence" and arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux, with his Belgian counterpart issuing a similar call.
Israeli Army Radio, citing witnesses and footage, also said that the occupiers hurled stones at one of the diplomatic vehicles, smashing its window.
Footage showed a member of the delegation lying on the ground after the attack. The person shown lying on the ground beside the diplomatic vehicle was Bernard Boudot, a French politician and mayor of Aulnoy-lez-Valenciennes in northern France, the broadcaster said.
Israel’s Channel 12, citing the Israeli military, reported that the incident was "under review” and none had been arrested immediately.
Khourieh described the attack as "a flagrant violation of the sanctity of diplomatic and humanitarian work” and part of ongoing restrictions imposed on Palestinian farmers.
Attacks by Israeli occupiers against Palestinians and their land have intensified during the olive harvest season, which began in early October and provides a key source of income for thousands of Palestinian families.
Israel's foreign ministry condemned the attack on the diplomats and Israeli police promised to open an investigation.
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is seeking to shore up support from the fiercely pro-settlement far-right in the October 27 election, instead alleged a "smear" campaign against settlers.
Netanyahu said the diplomats should have coordinated their movements with the Israeli military and pointed out that Baudoux is a communist known for supporting the Palestinian cause.
"We urge caution before drawing conclusions" about the attacks, Netanyahu's office said in a statement.
His main rival in the elections, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, strongly criticised Netanyahu over the violence, saying it was "burning away the little legitimacy the State of Israel still possesses".
The attacks are "Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government", Eisenkot said.

Russia is trying to make Ukraine’s major cities uninhabitable - The Guardian
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
18:01:40 EEST
00:01:40 KST

Russia is trying to make Ukraine’s major cities uninhabitable - The Guardian
Kyiv • UNN
An intercepted document describes strikes on energy infrastructure to worsen living conditions in cities and drive an exodus of the population. The attacks have already hit facilities in the Kyiv region.
Russian strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure may be part of a plan aimed at worsening living conditions in major cities and forcing the country to capitulate. The Guardian writes about this, citing a document that, according to Ukrainian intelligence, was intercepted in Russia, reports UNN.
Details
The attacks on power plants reflect a Russian plan to make Ukrainian cities uninhabitable. The Kremlin is resorting to punishing the population of Ukraine in major cities, as the front lines remain frozen
According to the publication, the document titled "Analysis of Ukraine’s Energy and Housing and Utilities Sectors" contains an assessment of vulnerable facilities in Ukraine’s energy system and even anticipates strikes on high-risk facilities, in particular distribution substations at several nuclear power plants. It describes the possible consequences of the strikes—from a "deterioration in the quality of life" of Ukrainians due to power outages to a complete cessation of water supplies, which, as coldly predicted in the document, would cause "a deterioration in sanitary conditions and the forced departure of residents from cities."
According to the publication, the document does not specify which Russian agency prepared it; however, according to several European officials interviewed by the publication, the authors may have been connected to Russian military or intelligence services.
As Russian missiles and drones systematically struck power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the ongoing outages of electricity and water increasingly resemble an alleged Russian plan to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities, which the Guardian newspaper has seen. Even when Donald Trump unilaterally announced an "energy ceasefire" between Moscow and Kyiv last week, Russia continued its methodical and destructive strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, including in Kyiv, as part of a strategy aimed at punishing Ukraine’s population and driving the country to capitulation
According to the publication, this year "Russia appears to be putting these plans into practice."
In particular, on Tuesday evening, Russian strikes hit three major power plants in the Kyiv region—CHP-4 and CHP-5, and the Trypilska Thermal Power Plant in the Kyiv region—as well as a major electrical substation that transmits electricity from the country’s two main nuclear power plants to the capital.
These, together with other substations forming the "Kyiv energy ring," which helps supply electricity from across the country to the capital, became targets of a Russian barrage that, if successful, could threaten a humanitarian catastrophe in the city of 3 million people
It should be recalled
Russia attacked Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in 10 regions overnight and in the morning of October 17, leaving some residents without electricity. Electricity outage schedules are in effect in a number of regions.

====================================================================================================

Why Britain should reject the lure of cheap – and  scary – Chinese AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:00:33 UTC
00:00:33 KST

There is much to fear from artificial intelligence developed in China and handed to businesses and governments in the west almost free of charge.
Every month Chinese AI developers such as DeepSeek and Xiaomi dispatch the latest versions of their “open-weight” models that allow users to take the core software and use it without paying an expensive ongoing licence.
In Britain, we love cheap Chinese kit, usually setting aside any concerns about how it was made and who by.
The row over whether to allow Chinese electric cars unfettered access to British retail forecourts is a case in point. They are cheaper than other EVs sold in the UK and, consumers ask: What is not to like? These same consumers might consider how Chinese EVs are subsidised by Beijing deliberately to boost exports and, in so doing, undermine foreign domestic car industries.
Cheap AI takes this export threat to a higher level.
It’s scary because Beijing is entering a new phase in the long march of economic development, taking the world’s second largest economy closer to making China great again.
Go back 10 years and Xi Jinping’s close supporters were alert to the internal contradictions of a totalitarian, command and control state apparatus and how it could trigger social unrest, much as it did in the last century in Tiananmen Square.
A property crash that still acts as a drag on the economy, rising unemployment, poor health services in many regions, a mismatch of men and women, an ageing population – they could all be the spark that threatens Communist party rule.
Then came AI and the state discovered complete control.
Now Beijing has huge surveillance capabilities, using AI to capture images of its citizens and monitor their activities if they need to.
Don’t think it means Chinese people are under virtual house arrest. They can go about their daily lives, gathering in the street for an impromptu dance or to discuss how their local region might be better run. But serious dissidents? They are rooted out and sidelined, re-educated or punished.
For the central committee, AI is a blessing. While the financial constraints from having to please a domestic audience have not entirely disappeared, Beijing’s leaders can concentrate on the threats they face from the rest of the world.
Not that it wants to invade countries in the same manner as Russia. China’s reinvigorated belt and road initiative creates permanent channels for trade less obviously than the previous iteration, allowing Beijing to turn states into clients who depend for the basics of life on Chinese technology.
Where Russia is using AI to enhance cyber-attacks on European government agencies and businesses to create chaos, China wants merely to widen the circle of friends that consume its goods without asking awkward questions.
Military force is also being contemplated. Now that Beijing can redirect precious resources previously needed to subsidise Chinese consumers, it is building a fleet of warships to challenge the US in the Pacific, much as Japan did in the 1930s. Taiwan, the engine of semiconductor development, is in its sights.
Meanwhile, Chinese developers are launching AI models by the dozen each month at a fraction of the cost of US equivalents.
There are tech analysts who say Chinese models add to the rich tapestry of AI, supplementing the closed, proprietary models of OpenAI and Anthropic. And they say there are European and Indian versions in development. Adding to that tapestry, Meta is fast developing open AI models, but like the other challengers, lags in the race to win over customers.
In practice, an AI user has the choice between a cheap Chinese open system they can tweak for their own ends or expensive US software that comes with bells and whistles they probably don’t need.
Both types have the potential to destroy humanity, as many AI experts have documented. But on a more mundane level, in day-to-day use, only one comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent, and it’s not the Chinese option.
As Ross Burley says, Chinese AI comes with extra baggage. Burley is director of the Centre for Information Resilience (CIR), an independent, non-profit group dedicated to, among other things, exposing human rights abuses and countering disinformation.
He says DeepSeek cannot access the properly isolated use of its software, “but that addresses just part of the risk. Running a model on your own servers doesn’t automatically remove any political censorship. Or indeed repair weaknesses in any security defences.”
An evaluation report by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (Nist) found political censorship in downloaded DeepSeek models running on its own infrastructure, which means that hosting those models in the UK wouldn’t, by itself, remove censorship.
“We should be deeply concerned about embedding Beijing’s political restrictions into systems that businesses and public services rely on for information and decisions,” he says.
The policy governing DeepSeek’s online chatbot says it collects prompts and uploaded material, processes and stores personal data in China, and permits disclosure to Chinese authorities.
Michael Wooldridge, a professor of AI at the University of Oxford, says it is not unreasonable to assume data inputted into the chatbot could be shared with the Chinese state.
The consequences for policymaking are profound. The UK should reject the lure of cheap Chinese AI and seek to better tame US AI while supporting domestic and EU suppliers.
Relying on Chinese tech, from cars to AI, is going to hollow out industry and undermine the security of our data.

Zelensky: U.S. working to arrange possible meeting with Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17

King's Colour Squadron Concludes Public Duties at the Tower of London
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:00:00 BST
00:00:00 KST

For the King’s Colour Squadron (KCS), another period of Public Duties at the Tower of London has drawn to a close.
Throughout the deployment, RAF Regiment personnel from the RAF's dedicated state and ceremonial unit carried out a series of historic duties at one of the nation's most iconic landmarks. Through rehearsals, Officers' Rounds, the Ceremony of the Word and the world-famous Ceremony of the Keys, the Squadron represented the RAF in front of thousands of visitors from across the UK and overseas.
The King’s Colour Squadron is made up exclusively of RAF Regiment personnel who balance ceremonial responsibilities with operational military roles. During their careers, members of the Squadron move seamlessly between operational deployments and ceremonial commitments, demonstrating the agility expected of today's RAF personnel.
Whether contributing to force protection and airfield security operations or representing the Royal Air Force on ceremonial duties, Squadron personnel apply the same discipline, professionalism and attention to detail in every role they undertake.
For Air Specialist (Class 1) Joshua, the Tower deployment provided another memorable chapter in a varied military career.
"I joined KCS in March 2024 and have already experienced a diverse range of opportunities. Most recently, I deployed on Operation Shader and, following my return, took part in Public Duties at the Tower of London. It is a privilege to serve in both operational and ceremonial roles, representing the RAF at home and overseas."
Reflecting on the experience, he described it as:
"An unforgettable experience guarding one of Britain's most historic landmarks. A proud moment, a unique responsibility, and a memory that will stay with me for life."
Throughout the deployment, every ceremonial movement was underpinned by extensive preparation, rehearsals and attention to detail. While visitors witnessed the finished product, considerable effort behind the scenes ensured each duty was carried out to the highest standard.
For AS1 Harvey, the duties highlighted the contrast between operational service overseas and ceremonial service at home.
“During my deployment, I served in a Base Defence team as part of ORCUS Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems which allowed me to develop these essential skills on operations for use back in the UK as part of the RAF Regiment’s airfield defence capability. Following my tour, I went on to serve on Guard at the Tower of London. Transitioning from an operational environment in the Middle East to guarding one of Britain’s most historic and iconic landmarks was a unique experience.”
Despite the difference between the roles, the standards remained the same.
While this period of Public Duties has now concluded, the King’s Colour Squadron continues to represent the Royal Air Force at major ceremonial events across the UK and overseas.
The uniforms may be ceremonial, but behind them are serving RAF Regiment personnel whose professionalism, discipline and commitment ensure that some of the nation's most enduring military traditions continue to be upheld for future generations.

🔴 Israeli settlers beat French mayor, attack European diplomatic cars in West Bank

Israeli settlers attack European delegation convoy in West Bank, beat French mayor
Israeli settlers on Saturday attacked a convoy carrying a European delegation in the occupied West Bank, beating up a 78-year-old French mayor. While Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – who is just days from a crucial election – described the incident as a "smear" campaign against Israeli settlers, France's top diplomat urged Israel to "urgently halt criminal violence".
Israeli settlers on Saturday attacked a convoy of European diplomats and beat up a visiting French mayor, in a new escalation of violence during the Palestinian olive harvest, witnesses and diplomats said.
The 78-year-old mayor said masked settlers yelled defamatory comments about France, kicked him and hit him with iron bars as he joined Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank alongside the top French and Belgian representatives in Jerusalem and Polish diplomats.
“I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government,” Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, told AFP after he was attacked.
“The whole world needs to know what’s happening,” he said. “For me, I’ll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here.”
Baudoux, who was wearing a sash with the French tricolour, was seen collapsed on the side of the car after the attack but did not need hospital care.
Read moreUS journalist injured during Israeli settler attack on West Bank olive harvest
The attack came just one day after settlers beat an American photographer for The Washington Post, who was in moderate condition with broken vertebrae on Saturday.
In a post on X, France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, describing the attack as “appalling”.
“The Israeli authorities must arrest those responsable for these appalling acts and take them to justice. They must urgently halt this criminal violence and guarantee the safety of civilian populations, as they are compelled to do under international law.”
Israel’s foreign ministry also condemned the incident and Israeli police promised to open an investigation.
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, days away from an election in which he is seeking to shore up support from the far-right, instead alleged a “smear” campaign against settlers.
Netanyahu said the diplomats should have coordinated their movements with the Israeli military and pointed out that Baudoux is a communist known for supporting the Palestinian cause.
“We urge caution before drawing conclusions” about the attacks, Netanyahu’s office said in a statement.
His main rival in October 27 elections, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, strongly criticised Netanyahu over the violence, saying it was “burning away the little legitimacy the State of Israel still possesses”.
The attacks are “Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government”, Eisenkot said.
Belgium called for an end to “impunity for violent settlers” after the latest attack.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Attacks on cultural symbol
Baudoux, the mayor, said he had come to the town of Taybeh, a Christian stronghold, along with his local pastor from France to sign a goodwill agreement.
He was attacked just as he joined the harvest as a symbolic gesture with the Palestinians, for whom olives are an important cultural symbol.
Extremist Israelis have issued calls to stop the Palestinians’ harvest after months of growing attacks in which settlers have stolen land and property. There has also been violence against Israelis, with a Palestinian shooting dead a settler last month.
Bashar Fawadleh, a priest in Taybeh, said settlers had already attacked the harvest and snatched olives before beating the mayor.
“One person was hit in the head and needed stitches. They also beat up an older lady in her 70s after insulting her with very bad words,” the pastor said.
The West Bank violence has shocked much of the world, with Britain leading economic sanctions that in turn caused Netanyahu to voice outrage.
Netanyahu had also sought to throw doubt on the circumstances behind the beating Friday of the photographer, Heidi Levine, suggesting that Palestinians and “far-left” activists caused trouble.
But President Isaac Herzog, who holds a mostly symbolic role, took the initiative Saturday to call Levine in the hospital, calling the attack “outrageous and shocking” and saying it weighed on his conscience.
Israel Gantz, head of an umbrella settler group, blamed the recent incidents on “groups of provocateurs and terrorists” and implicitly acknowledged some Israelis’ responsibility, saying that they caused harm to the settlers’ cause.
Settlers earlier this month also beat up AFP photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh as he covered the olive harvest tensions, fracturing several of his ribs.
Netanyahu’s government has ramped up approval of West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law.
Some 500,000 Israelis live in the West Bank, which Israel seized in 1967, alongside three million Palestinians.

China braces for heavy rain, flood risks as cold air brings sharp cooling
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
22:58:41 CST
23:58:41 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- China's national flood control authorities on Saturday stepped up preparations for heavy rain across wide areas of the country, as 15 provincial-level regions were forecast to see heavy to torrential rainfall and some areas faced risks of flash floods and geological disasters.
The State Flood Control and Drought Relief Headquarters and the Ministry of Emergency Management convened a multi-agency meeting on Saturday to assess the evolving weather and coordinate flood control measures in key areas, the ministry said.
The rainfall would affect a broad area, with persistent rain in parts of southern China and significant precipitation expected in northern regions that have received relatively little rain in recent months.
Authorities were urged to strengthen weather and hydrological monitoring, issue timely warnings and inspect vulnerable areas for potential hazards.
The National Meteorological Center forecast that a strong cold air mass would bring widespread rain and snow, strong winds and falling temperatures. Saturday was expected to mark the peak of the rainfall, with hourly precipitation exceeding 50 millimeters in parts of Liaoning, Shandong, Hubei, Hunan and Chongqing.
Temperatures across northern China were also expected to fall to their lowest levels since the second half of the year began.
From Saturday to Sunday, temperatures in parts of the northwest, Inner Mongolia, north China, northeast China and other regions were forecast to drop by 4 to 8 degrees Celsius, with some areas seeing declines of more than 10 degrees, Fang Chong, chief forecaster of the National Meteorological Center, said.
The weather could disrupt autumn harvesting and planting, while the rainfall would also help replenish soil moisture in northern China and support the sowing and seedling emergence of winter wheat, Fang added. ■

SANAA, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group on Saturday released 159 prisoners whom it described as having surrendered during recent fighting, under an amnesty issued by the group's leadership.
Abdul Qader al-Murtada, head of the Houthis' prisoner affairs committee, announced the release at a press conference in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.
Al-Murtada described the prisoners as fighters who had "voluntarily surrendered without fighting" during recent combats, without identifying the forces to which they belonged or specifying where they were captured.
He said the release was carried out under a general amnesty issued on Sept. 10 by Mahdi al-Mashat, head of the Houthi Supreme Political Council.
According to al-Murtada, Saturday's release was the second batch carried out under the amnesty, following the release of 323 prisoners in the Red Sea province of Hodeidah on Sept. 15. He said dozens of others had also been released in separate operations in Taiz province.
The released prisoners would be returned to their home areas and families in coordination with local authorities in their respective provinces, which would handle arrangements concerning their status, al-Murtada said.
The release comes amid renewed fighting between the Houthis and forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government, which is backed by the Saudi-led coalition.
The warring sides have conducted several prisoner exchanges under UN-mediated agreements in recent years.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, forcing the internationally recognized government out of the capital. ■

News Analysis: China-EU auto trade consensus eases uncertainty, delivers mutual benefits
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
22:58:27 CST
23:58:27 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- The latest consensus reached between China and the European Union (EU) on hybrid vehicle trade is expected to reduce policy uncertainty, stabilize market expectations and safeguard the interests of businesses and consumers on both sides, paving the way for more predictable and mutually beneficial cooperation in the sector, analysts and industry representatives said.
Guided by the principles of mutual respect and equal consultation, the two sides, in the consensus reached during the latest meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism in Beijing, emphasized and confirmed three basic principles regarding hybrid vehicles: compliance with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules, non-discrimination and respect for facts.
Under the arrangement, China retains all its rights under the WTO framework, including the right to seek dispute settlement and trade compensation, while Chinese products will not be subject to discriminatory treatment. The arrangement also uses the trade volume recorded in 2025 as a baseline, allowing room for continued growth in Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to Europe.
The consensus comes against the backdrop of rapidly expanding Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the European market. In 2024, the EU imposed additional countervailing duties of up to 35.3 percent on Chinese-made battery electric vehicles, while hybrid vehicles were not subject to the additional tariffs.
Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to Europe subsequently surged. According to Eurostat, the EU imported 107,000 hybrid vehicles from China in 2024, with the figure rising to 302,000 in 2025.
Fu Xin, a senior partner at Jincheng Tongda & Neal Law Firm in Beijing, described the outcome as a breakthrough, noting that using the 2025 volume as the baseline accommodates the reasonable concerns of the Chinese automotive industry and its expectations for stable growth.
"Admittedly, quota restrictions will constrain excessively rapid growth by Chinese automakers, but they will encourage companies to compete on quality and pursue higher profit margins through higher-value-added products, in line with China's broader goal of promoting high-quality foreign trade development," noted Shi Xiaoli, director of the WTO Law Research Center at the China University of Political Science and Law.
For Chinese automakers, one of the most immediate benefits of the consensus is a substantial reduction in policy uncertainty surrounding exports to Europe.
Fu noted that growing uncertainty in trade and investment policies in recent years has made it increasingly difficult for Chinese automakers to formulate long-term business strategies.
The latest consensus, he said, will give Chinese companies operating in Europe a more stable framework of rules for the foreseeable future, allowing them to plan exports, investment and production with greater confidence.
Chinese automaker BYD said the consensus has effectively managed trade differences, prevented further escalation and taken into account the realities and legitimate concerns of industries on both sides, creating favorable conditions for sustainable cooperation.
At the 2026 Paris Motor Show, BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li disclosed the company's plans to expand its manufacturing presence in Europe. BYD's plant in Hungary is scheduled to begin large-scale production in the fourth quarter of this year. The company is also planning to establish its second and third manufacturing facilities in Europe, with France among the potential locations.
European automakers have extensive experience in automotive hardware, design and vehicle lifecycle management, while Chinese companies have competitive strengths in battery supply chains, intelligent driving and software technologies. These complementary advantages offer considerable scope for technological cooperation between the two sides, analysts noted.
Highlighting the strong complementarity between the two industries, Chinese carmaker Chery Group said closer cooperation would benefit businesses and consumers on both sides while contributing to the stability of global automotive supply chains.
Cooperation between Chinese and European companies could combine their respective strengths to improve vehicle quality, noted Andrea Levy, president of the Turin Motor Show.
Beyond the immediate benefits for trade, experts said that against the backdrop of rising trade protectionism and growing uncertainty across the global economy, the choice by the two major economies of dialogue over confrontation to resolve differences sends a positive signal in itself.
The China Association of Automobile Manufacturers said managing differences through institutionalized consultations and resolving disputes through cooperation rather than confrontation represented a rational choice that served the fundamental interests of both sides.
Responding to claims that the consensus was the result of EU pressure, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce stressed Friday that the understanding on hybrid vehicle trade is reciprocal and mutually beneficial, dismissing such claims as entirely unfounded.
The purpose of China-EU economic and trade consultations is to properly manage differences and address each other's concerns through dialogue and consultation, the spokesperson said, calling on both sides to demonstrate sincerity in resolving problems.
The spokesperson also stressed that the EU should not expect to gain benefits by exerting pressure, nor should it underestimate China's determination and ability to safeguard its own interests. ■

====================================================================================================

American Jews face a bitter dilemma as Israel's election approaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:57:45 UTC
23:57:45 KST

Israel's October 27 election is generating intense interest and growing concern among American Jews, as three years of war in the Middle East have deepened divisions over Israel within American society. Those disagreements are increasingly visible in street demonstrations and in the campaign for the U.S. congressional midterm elections in early November.
American Jews remain sharply divided along political, religious and often generational lines over the outcome they hope to see in Israel's election, widely regarded as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The vote is also taking place against the backdrop of the continuing trauma of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, which triggered the war in Gaza.
Netanyahu's supporters, particularly among Orthodox Jews, believe he is defending a country they love and regard as central to their identity. Many liberal and younger American Jews, however, believe his policies have damaged Israel's international standing and generated widespread hostility that threatens to affect them in the United States as well.
The situation is especially sensitive amid rising antisemitism and antisemitic violence. Even some of Netanyahu's harshest critics, whether over the war in Gaza or Israeli settler violence in the West Bank, acknowledge that responsibility for attacks against Jews cannot be placed entirely on the Israeli prime minister.
Rabbi Dan Levin of Temple Beth El, a Reform synagogue in Boca Raton, Florida, said many American Jews feel caught between competing concerns. They want an end to attacks on Palestinians by Israeli settlers in the West Bank, while also rejecting accusations of genocide against Israel and what they regard as double standards applied to the Jewish state.
Israel remains central to many American Jews' identity
Levin's large Reform synagogue is among numerous congregations across the United States holding educational programs this fall about the Israeli election. Although most members are not Israeli citizens and cannot vote, Levin said they feel a profound emotional investment in the outcome.
Israel's complex multiparty electoral system makes the October 27 result difficult to predict. Polls suggest a close contest between the political bloc led by Netanyahu and an alliance of his opponents, with neither side assured of forming the next government.
Many American Jews have friends and relatives living in Israel. Beyond those personal ties, supporting Israel remains an important part of Jewish identity for many older Americans, particularly religiously affiliated Jews aged 45 and above, according to a recent poll conducted by The Associated Press and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research.
Reform Judaism, the largest Jewish denomination in the United States, places considerable emphasis on progressive values. Many Reform Jews see no conflict between their liberal beliefs and Zionism, which they understand as the Jewish people's aspiration to live freely and independently in their homeland, according to Rabbi Josh Weinberg of the Union for Reform Judaism, an umbrella organization representing more than 800 Reform synagogues across North America.
But Weinberg said many Reform Jews are concerned about the growing influence of ultra-Orthodox parties over Israel's political and religious life, as well as government settlement policies and the treatment of Palestinians in the West Bank. They regard those policies as fundamentally inconsistent with their values.
Weinberg warned that another Netanyahu victory could deepen the disillusionment of younger American Jews, some of whom may ultimately decide they have had enough and say, "I'm giving up on Israel."
The generational divide is reflected in the AP-NORC survey. Only about four in 10 religiously affiliated Jewish adults under 45 said supporting Israel was extremely or very important to their Jewish identity. Younger respondents were more likely to place greater importance on other expressions of Jewish identity, including observing Jewish holidays.
Antisemitism remains a central concern
The same survey found that most Jewish American adults consider prejudice against Jews an extremely or very serious problem in the United States today.
With Israel's election approaching, many Jewish communities are concerned that its outcome could affect attitudes toward Jews in the United States. Jonathan Sarna, professor emeritus of American Jewish history at Brandeis University, said some American Jews believe a different kind of Israeli prime minister, one more like previous leaders who frequently spoke about their desire for peace, could change how Jews themselves are perceived in America.
Even Netanyahu's critics, however, do not expect antisemitic attacks to disappear simply because Israel elects a different government. Their concern is particularly acute when anger over Israeli policies toward Palestinians is used to justify violence against Jews regardless of their nationality, political beliefs or connection to Israel.
Weinberg pointed to a protest slogan calling for an intifada and revolution, which he and others interpret as encouraging violence against Jews. He argued that the meaning of such rhetoric changes depending on where it is heard. A slogan shouted in the Palestinian city of Ramallah, he said, carries a different implication when repeated on the streets of Minneapolis. For him, the latter raises an unmistakable concern about antisemitism.
Others believe changes in Israeli policy could nevertheless help reduce hostility. Rabbi Jill Jacobs, CEO of T'ruah, a rabbinic human rights organization, said people who attack Jews in the street or deliberately drive vehicles into synagogues bear full responsibility for their own actions. Such violence cannot be blamed on the Israeli government's conduct.
At the same time, Jacobs warned that the election of another Netanyahu government, particularly one continuing policies she described as expanding the occupation, ethnic cleansing and an endless war, would create a deeply frightening environment for Jews around the world.
Stanley Weinstein, an Orthodox Jew from Florida, rejects much of the criticism directed at the Israeli military and the country's political leadership, particularly given the threats posed by Hamas terrorists in Gaza and other continuing confrontations. These include tensions with Hezbollah in Lebanon and Iran, even as fragile ceasefires remain in place.
Weinstein considers Israel's security essential, especially as he sees increasingly hostile rhetoric toward Israel and Jews among American political figures on both the right and the left. He has observed those trends even from his home in Miami Beach, which has a large and diverse Jewish community.
He said he was appalled by the growing hostility, both as an American and as a Jew, but added that it only reinforced his gratitude for Israel's existence, declaring, "thank God there is an Israel."
Netanyahu, Trump and elections that could deepen divisions
For American Jews, Israel is also becoming an increasingly important issue in the U.S. midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress for the next two years. American voters will go to the polls on November 3, exactly one week after Israelis cast their ballots.
From New York to Michigan and elsewhere, support for Palestinians and demands to end American military assistance to Israel have become more prominent issues among Democratic voters.
Both elections could influence the longstanding alliance between Israel and the United States. Relations have been particularly close under the Trump and Netanyahu administrations, although tensions have emerged in recent months, especially over the war the two countries jointly launched against Iran.
Despite growing controversy over some Israeli government policies in the United States, support for Israel itself remains substantial among American Jews, according to Jason Isaacson, chief policy officer of the American Jewish Committee, a prominent advocacy organization seeking to represent a broad spectrum of Jewish communities in the United States and internationally.
Isaacson said there is continued strong backing among American Jews for maintaining the U.S.-Israel relationship, as well as broad agreement on the importance of Israel's continued existence and security.
Yet regardless of political affiliation or religious outlook, some American Jews are most troubled by the possibility that Israel's election will produce even deeper divisions within the country and across Jewish communities abroad.
Levin, the Reform rabbi from Boca Raton, said the upcoming vote could prove one of the most consequential elections in modern Israeli history. He argued that the Netanyahu government's deeply divisive character has created tensions severe enough to threaten the cohesion of Israeli society itself.
Weinstein, the Orthodox Jewish resident of Miami Beach, believes Netanyahu has performed extremely well as prime minister. Nevertheless, he shares Levin's anxiety about Israel's future. For him, the greatest challenge facing the country is the lack of national unity, a problem he considers more important than the outcome of any individual political contest.
His central question is whether Israel can overcome those differences: "Is there a way to unify the country, unify the people?"

Thousands rally for biggest protest in years against Tunisia’s Saied

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17

Thousands rally for biggest protest in years against Tunisia’s Saied
Unions and opposition groups unite to demonstrate against worsening living conditions and restrictions on political freedoms.
Thousands of Tunisians have marched through the capital to protest against President Kais Saied, worsening living conditions and restrictions on political freedoms.
The latest demonstration in Tunis on Saturday was led by the Tunisian General Labour Union (UGTT), an influential trade union federation, alongside opposition parties and civil society organisations.
It was the largest protest against Saied in years, bringing together political opponents whose longstanding divisions have weakened their ability to challenge his rule.
The AFP news agency reported that more than 3,000 people were on the march, but the total could not be independently confirmed.
Protesters gathered along Habib Bourguiba Avenue, a major street in central Tunis, as hundreds of police deployed across the capital. Several surrounding roads were closed.
The crowd included lawyers, doctors, journalists and the unemployed, as well as activists and members of parties from across the political spectrum. They demanded the release of detained government critics and an end to restrictions on trade union rights.
Placards reading “No democracy without freedoms” and “No dignity with poverty” reflected the political and economic grievances driving the demonstration.
Protesters also revived a slogan demanding the government’s removal, widely heard during Tunisia’s 2011 uprising.
Addressing the rally on Saturday, UGTT leader Salah Eddine Salmi criticised the concentration of political power in the presidency and said “silence will no longer be acceptable”.
The political demands came alongside mounting frustration over the cost of basic goods and declining purchasing power.
Prolonged difficulties
Tunisia has struggled with prolonged economic difficulties, deteriorating public services, recurring water and electricity cuts, as well as shortages of medicines and other essentials.
Demonstrator Yassine Gharseli, who travelled from Sfax, about 250km south of Tunis, said repeated disruptions to basic services had deepened his frustration with the authorities.
“I came from Sfax to stand up for my freedom,” he told the Reuters news agency at the demo, expressing his determination to continue speaking out.
Saturday’s march followed other demonstrations over similar grievances.
On August 20 , protesters in Tunis rallied against rising prices and shortages of basic goods.
Last month, fuel transport workers went on a two-day strike over wages and working conditions, led by a union federation affiliated with the UGTT.
The demands recall the uprising that ousted longtime President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali in 2011, which helped ignite protests across the Arab world.
Tunisia subsequently held competitive elections and expanded political freedoms, but unemployment and struggling public services remain persistent sources of anger.
Saied came to power promising an alternative to that political system; however, in 2021, he suspended parliament and dismissed the government, saying he was confronting corruption and political deadlock.
He later dissolved parliament and a new constitution increased presidential powers in 2022.

Trump waves Russia sanctions passed by Congress amid deepening row with Ukraine
Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest, the Guardian reported.
In an executive order on Friday, the president said he was waiving many sanctions, restrictions and duties on Russia, in a move that comes as he has been publicly criticizing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including suggesting that Ukraine needs a new leader.
The move was greeted by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who wrote on social media: “The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment.”
Trump signed the legislation last month, after Congress passed the measure in an act of rare bipartisan agreement. It sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling Russia’s war in Ukraine.
The legislation – whose primary backer in Congress was the late senator Lindsey Graham – sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving and was due to be implemented in two days.
It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Friday’s announcement comes a week after Trump said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of U.S. and Western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.
Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1m tons “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional 3m tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
Under the legislation he signed into law, Trump had until October 18 to impose the sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy, or waive them. The administration had not told lawmakers whether it would impose the sanctions or issue a waiver.
Facing midterm elections on November 3, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing up energy prices that could cost his Republican party its thin majorities in the US Senate and House of Representatives.

Singularities: von Neumann, Good, Vinge, …
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:48:26 UTC
23:48:26 KST

Singularities: von Neumann, Good, Vinge, …
« previous post |
The OED gives citations for singularity going back to the 14th century, e.g. this example from 1398 in the sense "The fact or condition of being alone or apart from others; solitariness":
Men vsyd to ete togyders in open place, leest syngularite schuld brede lechery.
A mathematical singularity, as Wikipedia tells us,"is a point at which a given mathematical object is not defined, or a point where the mathematical object ceases to be well-behaved in some particular way, such as by lacking differentiability or analyticity", with an obvious example being what happens to the reciprocal function 1/x at the point x=0. I'm not sure when that usage began, but it's easy to find references back to the 19th century, e.g. Charlotte Angas Scott, "On the higher singularities of plane curves", American Journal of Mathematics 1892.
Most uses of the term these days involve a metaphorical extension of the mathematical concept to the idea of a technological singularity, which Wikipedia describes as "a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization."
The first documented use of this metaphor is attributed to John von Neumann in a 1958 posthumous tribute by Stanislaw Ulam:
Quite aware that the criteria of value in mathematical work are, to some extent, purely aesthetic, he once expressed an apprehension that the values put on abstract scientific achievement in our present civilization might diminish: "The interests of humanity may change, the present curiosities in science may cease, and entirely different things may occupy the human mind in the future." One conversation centered on the ever accelerating progress of technology and changes in the mode of human life, which gives the appearance of approaching some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue.
Then in the early 1960s, I.J. Good presented "Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine". Good doesn't use the term singularity, but he clearly expresses (a version of) the idea. From his Introduction:
Let an ultraintelligent machine be defined as a machine that can far surpass all the intellectual activities of any man however clever. Since the design of machines is one of these intellectual activities, an ultraintelligent machine could design even better machines; there would then unquestionably be an 'intelligence explosion', and the intelligence of man would be left far behind. Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.
And from his Conclusion:
It is more probable than not that, within the twentieth century, an ultraintelligent machine will be built and that it will be the last invention that man need make, since it will lead to an "intelligence explosion." This will transform society in an unimaginable way. The first ultraintelligent machine will need to be ultraparallel, and is likely to be achieved with the help of a very large artificial neural net. […] The machine will have a multimillion dollar computer and information-retrieval system under its direct control. The design of the machine will be partly suggested by analogy with several aspects of the human brain and intellect. In particular, the machine will have high linguistic ability and will be able to operate with the meanings of propositions, because to do so will lead to a necessary economy, just as it does in man.
The whole article is well worth reading carefully, and it's a scandal that the only available (and somewhat corrupted) version is on the Wayback Machine. For more on I.J. Good, see my 2009 post "Good is dead", which sketches his contributions (with Alan Turing) to the world's first Language Model, as part of the Enigma decryption effort more than 80 years ago.
The next step (that I know of) was taken by Vernor Vinge, in a 1983 op-ed in Omni Magazine (I've typed out the contents because the original, black type on a dark grey background, is hard to read):
A favorite game of futurists is to plot technological performance – computer speed, say – against time. Such trend curves climb ever more steeply. Extrapolated 30 or 40 years, they are so high and steep that even the most naive futurist discounts their accuracy. Some who talk about that era predict a leveling off of progress. After all, saturation effects are observed in other growth processes.
There is an important reason why this process won’t level off. We are at the point of accelerating the evolution of intelligence itself. The exact means of accomplishing this phenomenon cannot yet be predicted – and is not important. Whether our work is case in silicon or DNA will have little effect on the ultimate results. The evolution of human intelligence took millions of years. We will devise an equivalent advance in a fraction of that time. We will soon create intelligences greater than our own.
When this happens, human history will have reached a kind of singularity, an intellectual transition as impenetrable as the knotted space-time at the center of a black hole, and the world will pass far beyond our understanding. This singularity, I believe, already haunts a number of science-fiction writers. It makes realistic extrapolations to an interstellar future impossible. To write a story set more than a century hence, one needs a nuclear war in between – to retard progress enough so that the world remains intelligible.
In a 1993 article "Technological Singularity", still (for now) available on the web, Vinge elevates singularity into the title. He quotes Ulam/von Neumann and Good, and concludes by speculating about "the Best We Can Ask For". The whole thing is worth reading.
It's striking how accurately some recent developments were foreseen by von Neumann and Good and Vinge 30-70 years ago — but what strikes me most about the current situation is how much of it was not predicted. None of those seers told us about Data Center politics; AI hallucinations; the socio-political and cybersecurity effects of AI bots and agentic AI; the economics of a possible AI bubble; and so on.
Maybe this is just temporary turbulence as a smoothly-flowing post-singularity future is forming, whether utopian or dystopian or both. But from where I sit, the foreseeable future of (things called) "AI" looks even more chaotic, which is one more reason to doubt that the concept of a singularity is really helpful.
A different metaphor is implied by Richard Dooling's 2009 book Rapture for the Geeks , as well as a 2012 work the rapture of the nerds by Cory Doctorow and Charles Stross. Both allude to the (religious) Rapture, which is conceived in many different ways by different individuals and groups, but is generally seen as an abrupt event that's positioned in the middle of other variously defined and described times, and affects different groups of people in very different ways.
