Meta on Friday denied politically favoring Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro after a court ordered the company to treat him and incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva equally ahead of their Oct. 25 runoff.
Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported, citing internal messages it reviewed, that Meta employees acknowledged restrictions had hindered Lula's Instagram accounts and that the platform recommended Bolsonaro's profile and WhatsApp channel.
Lula's campaign alleged that some of his posts lacked sharing options, received reduced reach and had technical issues affecting audio and user interactions.
His camp also said it would file a complaint with the Organization of American States, accusing Meta of manipulating social media during the election.
Meta said the technical issues were already public and that the internal conversations concerned their severity, not political interference.
"Any suggestion that Meta favors one side is false," the company said, adding that its rules apply equally to all candidates.
 
Irregular political ads
On Thursday, a justice at Brazil's top electoral court ordered Meta not to unjustifiably restrict the reach of political content related to either candidate during the runoff campaign.
The ruling also required Meta AI, the company's chatbot, not to favor either candidate in election-related content.
The dispute comes after a stronger-than-expected first-round performance by Bolsonaro, who will face Lula in the second round.
Lula's administration has pursued tighter regulation of technology platforms, including measures targeting illegal content and misinformation.
Separately, a study by researchers at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro found Meta allowed at least 1,613 irregular political ads between July and September, generating 171 million views and approximately 2 million reais ($400,000) in revenue.
Meta said it would continue to defend itself against the lawsuit.

On Saturday, police fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at crowds of young Albanians who gathered outside the Education Ministry in the center of Tirana on the fifth day of a growing student-led movement to force Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
Reuters video footage showed police firing a shotgun towards crowds outside the education ministry during clashes with protesters. Reuters reporters found rubber pellets on the ground, and pellets hit two Reuters journalists and several protesters, leaving round marks.
The incident marks an escalation in a confrontation between police and protesters that has engulfed central Tirana in recent days. Demonstrators have burned government buildings and banks and hurled rocks at police, who have responded with tear gas and water cannon.
Albania's police chief Skender Hita did not deny the use of rubber bullets when asked about it at a news conference on Saturday.
"All means that were used were employed in a limited manner, including the most recent ones," he said.
Hita said seven police officers have been suspended and are facing disciplinary investigations for "exceeding their authority" and "failure to respect the principle of proportionality" in dealing with protesters. He did not specify the incidents that led to the suspensions.
Kushner-backed resort triggered summer protests
The demonstrations have been fueled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs, and poor education standards. They have also drawn support from people who felt ignored during a summer of largely peaceful protest against a luxury coastal development backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.
The unrest poses the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who last year won a fourth term in office.
"It's been 13 years of corruption and 13 years of doing nothing and empty promises. So the jar is filled, and we are here for our rights," said Juri Taullahu, a 22-year-old medical student, on Saturday.
Police and the government condemned the unrest and called for calm.
Hita said that 1,067 people had been arrested and 388 criminally prosecuted. Scores of police officers and protesters have been injured.
Rama administration plagued with scandal
Rama's administration has been dogged by corruption scandals, while analysts say Albania has become a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drug and weapons trafficking, complicating the country's efforts to join the European Union.
Villagers told Reuters in July that their land had been wrongfully sold for the Kushner-backed development on a pristine stretch of coast in southern Albania. Reuters later reported that the man who sold the land was wanted by prosecutors on suspicion of drug trafficking, accusations his lawyer denied.
Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who is not directly involved in the villagers' dispute.
Rama, who denies wrongdoing and told Reuters this week that he would not step down, said on Saturday that his government respected the students and their right to protest.
"My responsibility is even clearer during these difficult times ... to protect our citizens, guarantee justice, and move Albania forward — together with this governing majority, which holds a very clear mandate: to see Albania in the European Union by 2030," he said on Facebook.
Along with Montenegro, Albania is leading the EU accession process among Balkan countries.

Mushrooms and the Autumn Moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:41:00 UTC
23:41:00 KST

This autumn, thousands upon thousands of Ukraine’s inveterate mushroom pickers have headed into forests where the harvest is unusually abundant.
For many “mushroomers,” this pleasant activity is no longer just a hobby but a vital part of preparations for winter – one predicted to be even more difficult than the last, with potential food supply issues on top of a lack of heating and electricity.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Gathering and preserving mushrooms has become not only a means of self-sufficiency but also a small-scale business. On online forums and classified ad sites, hundreds of Ukrainians are selling preserved mushrooms to those unable to venture into the forest themselves.
In the Poltava region, mushroom pickers can safely forage only five days a week. Regional authorities strongly advise against going into the forest on weekends as local officials have opened the wildlife hunting season. Mushroom picking is not banned on weekends, but it carries the obvious risk of becoming an accidental casualty of someone else’s hunt.
In areas where local authorities have authorized hunting, police patrols are expected to be present in the forests to check the legality of hunters’ guns. These checks may enable the police to recover some of the weapons that have made their way from the front lines to the rear, but it is a risky business. Hunters carrying unregistered weapons pose a danger not only to wildlife but also to the police.
Ukraine Rebuts Russian Claims of Major Autumn Land Gains
The most notorious “hunting accident” was the 2007 killing of Yevhen Kushnariov, an influential politician who served as mayor of Kharkiv, head of the Kharkiv Regional Administration, and head of the Presidential Administration of Ukraine.
Although also considered a pro-Russian politician, Kushnariov was a potential rival to the pro-Russian governor of the Donetsk region, Viktor Yanukovych, in the 2010 presidential election.
Incidentally, the hunter who killed Kushnariov was never convicted. The court ruled that the incident was an accident and granted amnesty to the person responsible.
While Ukrainians are preparing stocks of mushrooms for the harsh winter ahead, Russia has turned its expansionist gaze toward space. Alexander Prokhanov, a conservative writer and chairman of the so-called “Izborsk Club,” joined forces with the Kremlin-aligned “Night Wolves” biker club to hold a “Baptism of the Moon” ceremony near the Estonian border.
Prokhanov explained the move to the Russian journalists present: “Just as Rus’ was baptized and Russia became Orthodox, we have decided to baptize the Moon, to make it Orthodox, and unite it with Russia.”
The Izborsk Club, founded in 2012 by Prokhanov and Alexander Dugin, the chief ideologue of the “Russian World” concept, continues to enjoy Putin’s support.
Funded by the Kremlin, the club develops “educational materials” for schools in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories. It has also been active in “cultural-patriotic” projects in annexed Crimea, where, with the club’s backing, a rock opera titled “Journey into the Fire” was staged. Based on Prokhanov’s own poetry, this production celebrates the heroes of the war against Ukraine.
The Russian Orthodox Church has not yet officially commented or formally ratified the introduction of the Moon into the Moscow Patriarchate. That does not mean the Moon won’t be recognized as Orthodox at some point in the future. After all, Alexander Dugin has been calling for war with the West and the elimination of the Ukrainian state for nearly 30 years. As early as 1997, he published “The Foundations of Geopolitics,” describing Ukraine as a “state with no geopolitical significance” – a “territory that must be subordinated to Russia.”
In today’s Russia, almost any delusional idea stands a chance of becoming part of actual policy. In the Pskov region, where the “christening” of the Moon took place, an unprecedented mushroom harvest is being observed. Russia has not seen a mushroom harvest like this in years. Thousands of mushroom pickers are gathering, drying, and preserving wild mushrooms in the area, and the regional Russian press is filled with articles about the harvest. Indeed, there is currently more talk of mushrooms than of Russia’s war against Ukraine. This is understandable. Mushrooms provide a far more pleasant topic of conversation.
Incidentally, neither Dugin nor Prokhanov are known for a love of the “silent hunt.” However, in one of his essays, Prokhanov wrote that in the event of a nuclear war, “it [the Russian people] will leave the cities for the fields and forests. It will gather mushrooms, berries, and nuts. In times of great sorrow, the Russian people are ready to transform into a nation of chipmunks and hamsters – stocking up on all manner of roots and bulbs.”

Why adults are going back to summer camp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:36:25 UTC
23:36:25 KST

After dinner, the marshmallows came out. A group of nurses and support staff from a New York City clinic gathered around the campfire, sharing stories about childhood and how they got into the field. Above them, the upstate New York sky was full of stars. For a few hours in July 2026, the clinical titles and workplace hierarchies that normally defined this group of US health professionals disappeared.
Aleksey Aronov, CEO of VIP's IV, had brought his team to Camp No Counselors for a four-day weekend to unwind and bond.
“A lot of my staff members were new, and some were quite shy,” Aronov said. “But after the camp experience, everyone felt comfortable around one another, got to know each other better and bonded seamlessly.”
His team had arrived together. Other campers go looking for a group to belong to.
For adults heading to summer camp, the draw goes beyond childhood memories. Some are turning to camp experiences to network or mitigate burnout, while others are seeking a way to make new friends. Whatever their reason, an increasing number of people around the world are finding that the summer camps of their youth are the perfect antidote to the pressures of modern adult life.
Mia Morin, 29, of Toronto and her husband attended YMCA Camp Queen Elizabeth on Beausoleil Island in Ontario, Canada in May 2025 to meet new people.
“We wanted to gather around interesting people, exchange ideas and do things together,” Morin says. “Going to YMCA Camp Queen Elizabeth was easy because nobody there was random. Since everyone has already selected the same thing, you have a starting point with something in common.”
Once a niche getaway for nostalgic campers, adult camps have exploded in popularity, offering weekend and weeklong retreats where grown-ups trade screen time and their comfy beds for campfires, sports, arts and crafts, and bunk beds. Unlike the children’s day and overnight camps, however, today’s adult versions often include grown-up perks, such as open bars, wine tastings, chef-prepared meals and wellness programming.
Yelp’s 2025 Trend Forecast showed searches for “adult camps” were up 347 percent from September 2023 through August 2024, compared with the previous 12-month period. The online directory of the American Camp Association (ACA) lists 85 adult camp programmes in the United States, and while the ACA does not track the number of adult camps year-over-year, it confirms that there has been positive growth in adult camp programming over the last decade.
As of 2026, the concept has expanded well beyond the US and Canada, with camps launching in destinations ranging from the Swiss Alps to the United Arab Emirates.
“The rising popularity of adult camps reflects a larger movement toward meaningful, in-person experiences we’ve been seeing through Yelp,” said Yelp’s trend expert, Tara Lewis.
“People are looking to unplug and foster connections in shared physical spaces. These camps give adults the chance to go analog, rediscover favourite activities, focus on wellness and make genuine connections," she added.
Just how much has the concept grown? When founder Adam Tichauer pitched Camp No Counselors to the reality TV contest Shark Tank in 2016, the sharks didn’t bite. Fast forward 10 years, and all the Camp No Counselors dates through 2027 have waitlists.
Remedy for loneliness and burnout?
Adults across generations — from Gen X to Millennials to Gen Z — are embracing camp life as a remedy for two major ills of modern life: loneliness and burnout.
“Hundreds of millions of people every day feel a gap between their level of connection and where they want it to be, for a variety of reasons: social media and AI leading to feeling disconnected, not going into the office, living far away from their families, not having connected neighbourhoods,” said Adam “Smiley” Poswolsky, a keynote speaker and author who specialises in human connection and workplace culture.
Poswolsky’s career naturally grew out of his experience as an adult camp counselor at Camp Grounded from 2013 to 2017.
“I think the idea of adult camp might initially produce an eyeroll. ‘Why would an adult need camp? It’s childlike; we’re too old.’ But it’s the exact opposite,” said Poswolsky, who met his now-wife, Ali, at Camp Grounded.
“It’s the very thing many adults are missing the most — this chance to play and opportunity to connect with people that’s not related to networking, your career, your title.”
In 2023, Melanie Kelly, 44, felt burnt out from her work running marketing and communications for a solar company. A former painting major, she signed up for a weeklong art-making camp at Anderson Ranch Arts Center in Snowmass Village, Colorado in the US, to see if she could rediscover the “flow state” she remembered from painting that she rarely experienced at work.
Overnight, Kelly’s days went from being spent answering emails and staring at her computer screen to creating tangible art and sharing workshop space with like-minded campers.
“I was always trying to be more productive in a work sense or seeking professional development aligned with my work,” said Kelly. Art camp was the antidote to that tendency.
“It feels like there’s a bit of release in these types of moments or activities because you’re allowing yourself to rest,” she said. “Rest isn’t sleep. The opposite of work isn’t sleep; it’s play.”
Outside of workshop time, the art programme at Anderson Ranch also organised meals and activities for attendees to make socialising as frictionless as possible. While many of these camps are attended by couples, groups of girlfriends or, in Aronov’s company’s case, coworkers, they also cater to solo campers looking to meet new people.
At Michigan’s Camp Forever Fun, founder Joel Reisig actively encourages single attendees with the promise of a safe, fun and connected experience.
Reisig, a movie producer, had the idea to open an adult camp about a decade ago, after filming a movie about a group of girls attending horse camp. After shooting wrapped each day, the cast and crew relaxed by stargazing, petting horses and having dance parties.
“I thought to myself, adults need a summer camp break every bit as much as kids do,” Reisig said.
“It is very hard to make new friends after college. You are generally interacting with a few neighbours and a couple of people you work with. A weekend at Camp Forever Fun is a time to relax, climb the rock wall, sit in a kayak, ride a horse and actually have real conversations and possibly friendships with other stressed-out adults.”
At Camp Forever Fun, it’s 100 percent socially acceptable to introduce yourself to every single person at camp with zero fear of rejection. That’s not something most adults are able to find at a bar or coffee shop — and certainly not from the comfort of their couch, where people are increasingly spending their time. (According to a 2024 study, from 2003 to 2022, the average time Americans spend at home on a typical day has risen by one hour and 39 minutes.)
Alyx van der Vorm, 25, is a John Harvard Scholar who studied neuroscience and is the founder of social connection platform Clyx. She attributes rising rates of loneliness in part to how easy it’s become to get what we need without ever leaving home.
“So many things have been made frictionless, from laundry to ordering food, that when it actually comes to making plans, it seems like a bit of a mountain,” she says. “Add the fact that not everyone wants to be reaching out and initiating, and you suddenly have people spending a lot less time in person.”
That erosion of boundaries extends beyond social life: home, work and leisure are increasingly bleeding into one another. Since 2020, work increasingly follows people home, a recipe for burnout. According to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, in March 2026, 22.6 percent of American workers teleworked, compared to just 17.9 percent in 2022. Telework was so rare before the coronavirus pandemic that the agency did not even measure rates prior to that.
“Many adults are now working in environments that constantly ask them to produce, multitask and stay connected,” said Matthew Leahy, a licensed clinical psychologist who has spent years designing and running camp programmes. “AI has only increased this. Even our downtime often becomes another form of consumption through our devices.”
Camp programmes and spending time in nature interrupt that cycle, Leahy said.
“Instead of focusing on productivity, at camp we encourage presence. People spend time outdoors, try new things, laugh, play and engage with others simply because it’s enjoyable.”
Adult camps “offer a container”, explained Sarah Boss, psychiatrist and clinical director of The Balance clinic, in Mallorca, Spain. “In that container, normal rules are suspended. Permission is given to be silly, to be bad at things and to talk to strangers. And that permission does a lot of the therapeutic work.”
Leahy believes that people aren’t necessarily looking to escape adulthood so much as environments where every hour feels like it has to be productive or plugged in.
“I don’t think adults are trying to relive childhood so much as recover some of the emotional experiences that childhood offered — wonder, awe, playfulness and genuine connection,” he said.
Loneliness and burnout aren’t just affecting people in the United States; the adult camp trend is growing globally as well.
Sarah El Nabulsi, a licensed clinical psychologist based in Dubai, is seeing this same burnout among her patients. Adult camps are also on the rise in the UAE, like the Bear Grylls Explorers Camp in Jebel Jais, Ras Al Khaimah, which opened in 2021 as a collection of nine recycled shipping container cabins and has since expanded to 16.
Meanwhile, the broader outdoor adventure market is also attracting visitors. Hatta Resorts and Wadi Hub, a glamping and outdoor-adventure destination in Dubai’s Hajar Mountains, welcomed more than 351,000 visitors between September 2023 and April 2024 — a 40.4 percent increase over the previous season, according to Dubail Holding.
“What I see in session, repeatedly, is that adults aren’t burned out from work alone; they’re burned out from the absence of unstructured, low-stakes social contact,” El Nabulsi said.
“Adult life strips out almost every context where people used to make friends without trying: no assigned seating, no shared schedule, no built-in repetition of seeing the same faces. Camp reintroduces exactly that structure, low-pressure, physical, screen-free and bounded in time.”
A camp for everyone
Some adults choose to go to camp to satisfy an interest or hobby they have harboured since childhood but were not able to pursue at the time, often due to financial constraints.
Stephanie Hamilton, 38, is an elementary school librarian in Tuscaloosa, Alabama in the US. The self-described “absolute science nerd” wanted to attend Space Camp as a child, but it was too expensive for her family. Through her school —where she designs many space- and weather-related modules for her students — Hamilton learned about an Alabama state programme that funds Space Camp attendance for librarians. She applied and was selected to attend in 2022.
The experience changed the course of Hamilton’s life. After meeting an archivist at camp who works in curation at the US Space & Rocket Center, Hamilton was inspired to start a museum studies certification programme and hopes to ultimately work in space archives or curation one day.
“I learned there are still opportunities for me as a librarian to entertain that science passion that I’ve always had,” said Hamilton, who still keeps in touch with her fellow campers.
Robin Soprano, VP of Space Camp, said that many adult campers are “almost brought to tears at the end of the weekend,” because they challenged themselves and stepped outside their comfort zone.
Some adult camps are geared toward particular demographics. Divya Vaid, founder of Catskills Camp, has built a camp experience in the US Catskill Mountains specifically for adult women. Rather than a traditional wellness retreat packed with self-improvement programming, the concept returns women to the simplicity of summer camp: shared meals, outdoor activities, crafts, games, exploring the area and enjoying unstructured time together.
“I’ve been particularly interested in creating an experience that feels welcoming to women traveling solo who want connection and adventure without having to plan an entire trip themselves,” said Vaid. For women accustomed to managing every moment of their family’s lives, it’s a reprieve to simply show up.
There are no clocks in Vaid’s camp, and that’s by design. Instead, the house is stocked with games, puzzles and activities, as well as outdoor games and spaces that encourage guests to use the full property.
While not every camp is right for everyone, everyone can find a camp that caters to them. Club Getaway in Kent, Connecticut in the US offers themed camps for everyone from Generation X to Jewish professionals. Peace activist and entertainer Wavy Gravy runs a weeklong circus arts camp, Camp Winnarainbow, in Northern California every summer, where attendees can learn trapeze, clowning, juggling and more. At Central New Jersey’s Zombie Survival Camp, campers can learn specialised skills ranging from crossbow to advanced first aid.
“People often think camp is magical, and maybe it is, but in reality it’s also incredibly intentional,” said Leahy. “The strongest camps are designed to create belonging and small moments of awe. Shared meals, cabins, traditions, campfires, group challenges and repeated interactions all create opportunities for people to connect over time.”
Costly getaways?
Adult summer camp is a remedy for many of the issues that ail people in 2026 — but it also comes with an adult price tag.
Some of the more affordable camps include overnights or quick two- or three-night stays. Big Cedar Lodge, located on nearly 2,025 hectares (5,000 acres) in the US's Ozark Mountains, for example, offers a wilderness getaway for around $280 per night. Connecticut’s Club Getaway offers three-day all-inclusive getaways from $459 per person.
The $950-plus price tag for three nights at Camp No Counselors, which currently offers camps in California, Michigan, New York and Texas, is also for an all-inclusive experience, including alcohol.
The high end of the spectrum sees two trends collide: adult summer camp and glamping. The Green O in Montana features 12 luxury “hauses” that go for around $3,900 per night. Add-ons include horseback riding and fly-fishing excursions.
Brady Gill, Camp Grounded co-creator and the founder of Custom Camps, which hosts play-based corporate retreats and events, says camps are most often funded one of three ways: attendees pay for themselves, their companies pay for it, or they win a contest or receive a grant, like Hamilton did with Space Camp.
“Accessibility is a big deal,” said Gill. And when a company is paying for camp, it allows people to access the benefits without having to spend money. On the other hand, “people are more bought in when they’re paying for it themselves”, he said.
Gill is running a revived iteration of Camp Grounded in October 2026 called The Reunion, and he and his team have been “hyperconscious” of keeping costs reasonable. Early bird tickets went for $400, and the top-ceiling ticket is $500. “You can’t do a weekend away with friends anywhere for under $400,” Gill said.
Because his camp work is not a full-time job, Reisig does not need to focus so much on profits. This helps Camp Forever Fun run with very small margins, making it half the price of some competitors.
“I truly want adult summer camp to be a joyous experience that is available to everyone,” Reisig said.
There are camps at every price point, much like hotels, but the all-inclusive camps are naturally more expensive, ranging from $400 to $1,200 per weekend.
Whether they’re all-inclusive or a la carte, many adult camps have one thing in common: they are heavy on alcohol.
On one hand, it makes sense; the ability to attend a whisky tasting or sip craft beer by the bonfire is probably the element that most distinguishes the adult camp experience from childhood. On the other hand, with the percentage of Americans who drink alcohol hitting historic lows in Gallup’s nearly 90 years of tracking, a camp experience that revolves around drinking may ironically leave attendees feeling more isolated.
Though late founder Levi Felix founded Camp Grounded as a digital detox camp, it was also completely substance-free. Gill and his fellow organisers are keeping that commitment with The Reunion.
“I’m personally not a fully sober person, but I love throwing fully sober events,” Gill said. “There is an unending amount of opportunities to socialise with alcohol … but shockingly few opportunities without it.”
Adult camp may come with a decidedly grown-up price tag, but its growing popularity suggests people are willing to pay for something modern adulthood has made increasingly scarce: unscheduled time and space to simply be with other people.
“There’s a quote attributed to Plato that says, ‘You can learn more about a person in an hour of play than in a year of conversation,’” Gill said.
That sentiment is at the heart of what adult camps are trying to accomplish.

Yemen’s Houthis release 159 detainees in Sanaa: ICRC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:34:37 UTC
23:34:37 KST

Mohammed Al-Samei and Sahin Demir
17 October 2026•Update: 17 October 2026
Yemen’s Houthi group released 159 people it recently detained, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said on Saturday.
The ICRC said the unilateral release was carried out by authorities in Sanaa with its support.
Its delegates interviewed the detainees before their release, informed their families and provided assistance for their return home.
Medical teams also assessed their health and fitness for road travel and arranged additional travel support for those who needed it.
The release was initiated by the Houthi-affiliated National Committee for Prisoners Affairs and does not fall under the Stockholm Agreement, the ICRC said, stressing that it played no role in determining who or how many people would be released.
The Stockholm Agreement was reached in Sweden in December 2018 under UN auspices between Yemen’s internationally recognized government and the Houthis.
The Houthis said on Friday the detainees were prisoners who “voluntarily surrendered without fighting during the recent events.”
The group said they were being released under an amnesty issued by Mahdi al-Mashat, head of its Supreme Political Council, and that local authorities would coordinate their return to their families and home areas.
The release comes amid renewed fighting between the Houthis and forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, backed by a Saudi-led coalition.
The Houthis have controlled the capital Sanaa and large parts of northern and western Yemen since 2014, while the Saudi-led coalition intervened in the conflict in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Breadcrumb
Egypt's Sisi seeks parliamentary approval for military support for Saudi Arabia
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Saturday called for an emergency session of the House of Representatives to grant him authorisation to intervene in Saudi Arabia’s defence, should Riyadh request it.
Speaking at a graduation ceremony for new classes at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital, Sisi explained that such a move would require parliamentary approval.
"I call on parliament to convene an emergency session to grant us authorisation to take action to intervene in defense of Saudi Arabia if we are asked to do so," the president said.
Sisi stressed that Cairo was not seeking to attack anyone or enter a war, but rather to defend Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states, without disclosing details about the nature, scope, or timing of any potential intervention.
The move comes as Yemen's Houthis have ramped up their attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, including the targeting of an Aramco building, airports, and other key infrastructure.
Article 152 of the Egyptian Constitution stipulates that the president, as Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces, may neither declare war nor dispatch the armed forces on a combat mission outside the country’s borders without first consulting the National Defence Council and obtaining approval from the House of Representatives by a two-thirds majority of its members.
His statements come two days after he said, during a meeting with officials and media figures following a graduation ceremony at the Police Academy on Thursday, that Saudi Arabia’s security was directly linked to Egyptian and Arab national security. He stressed that Cairo rejected any threat to the kingdom’s security or borders, as well as any threat to maritime navigation in the Red Sea.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty previously said in an interview with Bloomberg on the sidelines of International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok that Egypt would respond to any Saudi request and was prepared to provide various forms of support, including military assistance.
He also noted that Cairo was seriously considering joining the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
At the same time, Cairo has maintained its diplomatic approach. During a phone call with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, last Tuesday, Abdelatty stressed the need for an immediate halt to attacks targeting Saudi territory, describing them as unjustified and unacceptable. He called for de-escalation and for political and diplomatic solutions to take precedence.
Sisi's latest remarks on the conflict between the Houthis and Riyadh come amid an escalation in attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, including missile and drone strikes that hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and resulted in fatalities and hundreds of injuries.

Belgium Confirms Delivery of 10 F-16 Fighter Jets to Ukraine by End of 2026

- Category

Belgium Confirms Delivery of 10 F-16 Fighter Jets to Ukraine by End of 2026
As Russia increasingly deploys faster jet-powered attack drones against Ukraine, Belgium is preparing to strengthen Kyiv’s air defenses with additional F-16 fighter jets, whose 20mm cannons could provide a new advantage in intercepting aerial threats.
Belgium has confirmed plans to deliver 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2026, despite earlier delays caused by the slower-than-expected arrival of US-made F-35 fighters intended to replace its existing fleet.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Brussels Times on October 16, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever confirmed the timeline following talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the sidelines of an EU summit in Brussels.
De Wever explained that Belgium’s ability to transfer the aircraft depends on receiving new F-35 fighters, which are gradually replacing the country’s aging F-16 fleet.
The deliveries have fallen behind schedule because of delays in the F-35 program. However, with replacement aircraft now arriving, Belgium expects to proceed with the transfers while maintaining its commitments to NATO.
The Belgian prime minister emphasized that Ukraine urgently needs additional combat aircraft, particularly to counter Russia’s growing use of jet-powered attack drones.
He identified the F-16's 20mm cannon as a potentially effective weapon against these threats, allowing Ukrainian pilots to engage incoming drones without relying exclusively on air-to-air missiles.
Beyond intercepting Russian drones, the aircraft could strengthen Ukraine’s ability to protect its cities, energy infrastructure, and Black Sea grain export routes.
During their meeting, De Wever and Zelenskyy also discussed accelerating military assistance and supplying additional ammunition for the aircraft.
Belgian defense manufacturer FN Herstal produces 20mm ammunition compatible with the F-16's cannon, making the country a potential supplier of munitions needed for Ukraine’s air defense operations.
De Wever did not specify whether all 10 aircraft in the revised delivery plan would be combat-ready or whether some would be designated for maintenance and spare parts.
Belgium initially committed in May 2024 to supplying Ukraine with 30 F-16 fighters by 2028. The delivery schedule subsequently faced setbacks as the Belgian Air Component awaited replacement F-35 aircraft.
Ukraine’s combined fleet of Western-made F-16 and Mirage 2000 fighter jets now outnumbers its remaining Soviet-era MiG-29s and Su-27s. F-16s are playing an increasingly important role in intercepting Russian jet-powered drones as Ukraine expands its Western fighter fleet and strengthens its air defenses.

Quote: "The operation of the plant has been suspended! Our absolute priority is the safety, life and health of every employee.
We are assessing the current situation and coordinating further action."

"We started with a small team of 300 people in 2005, and now we have around 5,500 employees. Importantly, our workforce has continued to grow since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion," the website says.
The production department employs 4,300 workers.

Tensions within Azerbaijan erupted last month after the government in Baku introduced new regulations prohibiting students from attending school in clothing that violates official uniform requirements or is deemed incompatible with the secular character of public education. The regulations did not explicitly mention the hijab, but reports subsequently emerged that students and teachers wearing Islamic headscarves were being denied entry to schools.
Although the controversy over the hijab restrictions is primarily a domestic Azerbaijani issue, conspiracy theories have begun circulating online in recent days claiming that Azerbaijan's close relationship with Israel was among the reasons authorities introduced the measures.
Alongside these claims, cartoons mocking Aliyev have spread across social media, employing classic antisemitic stereotypes, including an exaggerated long nose. The illustrations depict the Azerbaijani president as doing Netanyahu's bidding and seeking to undermine Islam. In one cartoon, Aliyev is shown kneeling on the ground, attached to a leash held by the Israeli prime minister.
According to the assessments cited in the report, Turkish, Iranian and Russian actors are suspected of involvement in the campaign. Turkey is widely regarded as Azerbaijan's most important ally, but figures within President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) have criticized the school dress-code restrictions. 
Officials in Baku were also displeased by remarks Erdogan made at the United Nations General Assembly last month, when he condemned school headscarf bans as violations of women's fundamental rights. Although Erdogan did not name any particular country, his remarks were interpreted in Azerbaijan as a criticism of Baku's policies.
Relations between Iran and Azerbaijan have been strained for decades, partly because of the close ties between Jerusalem and Baku. Iranian officials have repeatedly alleged that Israel uses Azerbaijani territory to conduct operations against Iran. Sources familiar with the issue said the hijab controversy presents another opportunity for Iranian actors to criticize Azerbaijan's relationship with Israel and portray it as hostile to Islam.
Russia is the third country whose actors are suspected of involvement in the online campaign. Relations between Moscow and Baku have been strained by Azerbaijan's ambitions to become a regional power in the Caucasus and by its neutral position on the war in Ukraine. According to the assessments, Russia has an interest in weakening Aliyev's domestic standing, partly to limit his room for maneuver on the international stage.

Hurricane Trudy makes its way towards Mexico, threatening heavy rain
Trudy is the latest in successive storms that have hit Mexico’s Pacific coast this year.
Hurricane Trudy maintained its strength as it moved towards Mexico’s western coast on Saturday, with forecasters warning it could strengthen further before beginning to weaken on Sunday.
A hurricane warning was in effect from Manzanillo in Colima state to Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco.
The United States National Hurricane Center said Trudy was about 305km (190 miles) south-southeast of Manzanillo early on Saturday, with maximum sustained winds of 150 km/h (90mph).
The hurricane was moving at about 13km/h (8mph) and was forecast to approach southwestern and west-central Mexico later on Saturday before passing near the coast overnight into Sunday.
Hurricane conditions are expected in the warning area on Saturday night, while tropical storm conditions are expected to spread across the region during the day, the NHC said. Hurricane conditions are also possible in areas under a hurricane watch.
Trudy is forecast to bring 10 to 20cm (four to eight inches) of rain, with isolated totals of about 38cm (15 inches), across parts of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco through the weekend, raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and landslides, especially in steep terrain, according to the NHC.
Outer rain bands could produce two to four inches of rain, with isolated totals of approximately 15cm (six inches), in Guerrero and Nayarit, where localised flash flooding is possible, the centre said.
The NHC also warned of possible coastal flooding from storm surge in areas exposed to onshore winds, accompanied by large and destructive waves.
Swells generated by Trudy were already affecting parts of Mexico’s southwestern coast and are expected to spread northward towards the country’s west-central coast through the weekend, creating life-threatening surf and rip current conditions, the NHC said.
The Mexican navy urged the maritime community and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution due to high waves, heavy rains and the risk of rising river levels, flooding and landslides in vulnerable areas.
The state of Colima has said that risks are currently low, but the storm could bring significant rainfall that could have damaging effects due to the saturated ground following the successive storms that have hit the Pacific coast.

2026-10-17
14:27:47 UTC
23:27:47 KST

What if NATO’s ‘Theory of Victory’ is a recipe for disaster?
On October 5, 2026, at the Warsaw Security Forum, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR) Alexus Grynkewich unveiled a military strategy titled ‘Theory of Victory’.
The strategy covers the next few years and outlines NATO’s preparations to counter a potential “Russian attack.” While the details are likely classified, the main points have been made public. Here are the key publicly disclosed aspects of NATO’s ‘victory’ plan:
- Economic exhaustion of the adversary: The development of military and industrial capabilities that would make continued hostilities costly and futile for the aggressor. Here, NATO is positioning itself as the defending party.
- Destruction of support infrastructure: Strikes against the enemy’s infrastructure, targeting not only the attacking forces but also the entire system sustaining the armed forces – logistics, command centers, supply lines, and reserves.
- 2029 as the operational readiness benchmark: By 2029, the US Armed Forces and NATO’s European allies must complete the main preparations for countering potential global threats and must be ready to address any external challenge.
- NATO’s technological superiority: This point emphasizes achieving comprehensive technological dominance through the widespread use of drones and AI-driven combat management systems.
That’s the ‘theory of victory’; now, it has to be put into practice. Certain types of political documents don’t present any interest as long as they’re stored in bureaucratic folders – no one cares about numbers, timelines, logistics, and readiness levels. But once they enter the public domain, they quickly acquire symbolic meaning. A “defense plan” becomes a “war plan,” “deterrence” turns into “targeting,” and a simple date on a calendar becomes a prophecy. This is precisely the case with this strategy. Formally, NATO’s plan doesn’t contain anything sensational: it talks about strengthening the eastern flank, preparing equipment and resources, expanding exercises, aligning industrial capabilities with evolving needs, setting readiness targets, integrating air and missile defense systems, creating logistical routes, and developing crisis response scenarios. All of this has been part of NATO’s alarmist yet necessary routine for decades. However, this time, something new has been added: a deadline!
And the deadline – 2029 – resonates not just as an administrative milestone but as a psychological turning point.
The question that comes to mind is both simple and unsettling: how dangerous is it to prepare society, the military, and politics for a threat that may be driven by fear rather than grounded in reality? ‘Being prepared’ is one thing; but can it lead to the idea that ‘since we’re prepared, we can be the first to act’? 
Let’s talk about the potential threat. The rhetoric, plans, and timelines all point to a specific year: 2030. Various Western ‘seers’ suggest that this is when ‘Eastern hordes’ will charge westward. In other words, Western analysts anticipate a Russian assault on NATO countries around this time. At the same time, NATO leadership candidly states that currently, the threat from Russia is assessed as minimal. But by 2030, Russia will be ready!
It’s tempting to call this the “mythical Russian threat,” but the term “mythical” has been used so often that it has lost its meaning. It seems to create a divide between those who “believe in the threat” and those who “perceive reality.” However, geopolitics rarely fits neatly into black-and-white categories. A threat can be simultaneously real, exaggerated, distorted, and dangerous, precisely because it contains a kernel of truth.
In reality, Russia doesn’t even have the personnel and resources to attack NATO – unless one assumes such an attack would be suicidal in nature. Nevertheless, the existence of an external enemy provides excellent justification for any political initiatives, and this concept seems to have been embraced by NATO as the primary driver for development.
According to NATO’s charter, it is strictly a defensive alliance. Article 5 discusses collective defense, not preemptive strikes. Regional plans, exercises, troop movements, and forward basing are designed as deterrents: to demonstrate to potential adversaries that aggression would come at too great a cost. However, active preparation for defense and the resulting substantial military buildup could offer politicians new options that might tempt them to act.
Finally, measures that one state views as protective can be perceived by another as a threat to its security. This sets off a spiral of escalation and mutual intimidation, pushing both sides into a standoff where they’re heavily armed for ‘deterrence’ yet unable to pass each other without starting a conflict. Although NATO’s plans may appear defensive on paper, they trigger this very mechanism – especially when accompanied by public rhetoric like “Russia could attack in a few years,” “Europe must be prepared by 2030,” or “the window of opportunity is closing.” While these statements may reflect genuine concerns, they also create a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Of course, in defense planning, timelines are essential. Without them, the military risks becoming a bureaucratic museum, while the defense industry could turn into a shop selling antique rifles. However, deadlines have a downside; they turn preparedness into a race. In public discourse, 2029 begins to sound less like a guideline and more like a deadline. By 2029, forces, equipment, munitions, logistical routes, command structures, trained reserves, integrated air defense systems, intelligence networks, and industrial capacities should be in place. This goal is quite reasonable for a military document.
But it raises a key question: what happens if someone in NATO eventually says, “We’re ready!”? This may first emerge as a report or assessment and may then be proclaimed as a political achievement; next, it may be used as an argument, and in times of crisis it may very well become a temptation to act.
The logic of preemptive action always appeals to those who fear they might miss the boat. ‘If we wait, our adversary will grow stronger. If we strike now, we can avert a major war’ – this reasoning is as old as time and often deeply manipulative; it appears rational until it leads to death and destruction.
Preemptive “threat prevention” is an oxymoron. According to this logic, to prevent a war, one must start a war; to avoid a strike, one must strike first; to protect the status quo, one must disrupt it. Most importantly, no one can guarantee that retaliation will be limited, that escalation will stop at the desired threshold, that nuclear weapons will not be used, that allies will remain loyal, or that the public will bear the costs of the war.
The temptation exists. But can we halt escalation before it spirals into a full-blown crisis? There may still be a chance.
Firstly, transparency is crucial. We’re not talking about the disclosure of combat plans, but about clear signals regarding the kinds of actions that are considered defensive; limitations on certain military exercises; the types of forces that are not intended for a first strike; and the types of communication channels that will remain open even during crises.
Secondly, rules for de-escalation are necessary. These could include notifications about military activities, major exercises, limitations on movements near borders, incident verification mechanisms, military hotlines, and agreements on the actions of drones, aircraft, and vessels in contested areas.
Thirdly, political leaders must consistently distinguish readiness from resolve. There is a difference between being prepared to defend oneself and launching a preemptive strike. This distinction needs to be emphasized not just in official documents but also in public statements.
Fourthly, we need responsible journalism and analytical insight. What’s required is neither naive reassurance – claiming there’s no threat – nor panic-driven claims that war is imminent. The goal should be to reflect the complexity of the world. A threat can be considered significant, but it may not necessitate war; and deterrence can be firm without leading to aggression.
And lastly, we must work to restore at least minimal arms control frameworks. Without them, each side will feel compelled to run faster, even if the race leads both to jump off a cliff.
The year 2029 could be when Europe becomes stronger and more resilient. Or, it might be the year when someone declares, ‘We’re ready, and we can do anything!’ The former concept is about deterrence; the latter is deterrence in its perverted form. It’s crucial for all parties in this race to understand this clearly.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

Iran rejects pressure, remains open to dialogue: Araghchi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17

23:27:05 KST

Addressing the 52nd Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in Baghdad, Araghchi said Iran did not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation, stressing that any dialogue must be grounded in mutual respect and backed by credible guarantees.
The full text of his speech is as follows:
In the Name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful
Excellency, Mr. Fuad Mohammed Hussein, Deputy Prime Minister, and Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Iraq,
Mr. Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed, Secretary-General of the OIC,
Excellencies,
Ladies and Gentlemen,
I begin by thanking the Government and people of the Republic of Iraq, our neighbor and brother, for hosting this meeting of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation and for their warm hospitality. I congratulate Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed for his appointment as the new Secretary-General, and wish him full success. I also thank the Republic of Tyrkiya for all its efforts during its successful chairmanship of the OIC CFM. Moreover, I should thank the Secretary-General and the General Secretariat for their efforts in preparing this meeting.
It is fitting that we gather in a land that has long been a meeting place of civilizations, at a time when unity and dialogue within the Islamic world are needed more than ever.
The OIC was founded to give the Islamic Ummah a common voice and to promote solidarity, cooperation and the defense of our shared interests. Keeping the path of dialogue open among us is not weakness. It is a responsibility. The Charter of our Organization rests on principles that reflect those contained in the UN Charter: sovereign equality, territorial integrity, non-interference in internal affairs, peaceful settlement of disputes, and refraining from the threat or use of force. These principles belong to no single country or group of countries. They protect all of us, and when they are applied selectively, they lose their value.
Dear Brothers and Sisters,
Iran has been steadfast in its commitment to international law, the UN Charter and diplomacy. Over the past two years we continued to pursue diplomacy. The United States chose the opposite path: aggression, threats, assassination and economic warfare, with a blatant disregard for international law and the UN Charter. About five thousand people were killed as martyrs, including hundreds of women and children. The United States and the Israeli regime assassinated Iran's Supreme Leader and other senior political and military officials, a grave violation of international law. The killing of more than 160 students and teachers in Minab, the cluster-munition attack on the Lamerd stadium, the bombing of a desalination unit in Qeshm and the attack on a wedding ceremony in Kuhestak, Sirik, are only some of the documented examples. The United States and the Israeli regime cannot whitewash these crimes by reversing the roles of victim and aggressor. I thank those member states that have expressed solidarity with the Iranian people in these difficult times, and I call on the Organization as a whole to stand firmly against attacks on the sovereignty and territorial integrity of its founding member.
Iran defended its people, its sovereignty and its legitimate interests, and will continue to do so by any means. We never attacked our neighbors, but we did attack and destroyed the US military bases and military installations, which are unfortunately, located in our neighborhood. But there is no contradiction between defending our rights and pursuing peace. We know the cost of war, and that is precisely why we value peace.
Iran asks for no special treatment, only the equal application of rights and responsibilities to all. This issue will not be resolved on the battlefield. Peace cannot be built through threats of annihilation.
Iran also remains committed to safe and secure navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway vital to the energy and trade of many of our member states. Until 28 February 2026, the Strait was open. The insecurity and disruption of maritime navigation since then are the direct result of the aggressive actions of the United States and the Israeli regime, and of the blockade and coercive measures imposed by the United States. Security cannot be restored by more of the same. One cannot bomb a country, threaten its annihilation and impose a blockade, and then expect the security of navigation return to normal.
Diplomacy was in fact working. Through the good offices of Pakistan, with the support of Qatar, both members of this Organization, Iran and the United States signed the Islamabad MoU on 17 June. Under paragraph 5, Iran undertook to make the necessary arrangements to facilitate the safe movement of vessels, and we immediately began technical discussions with the Sultanate of Oman to implement that commitment. Within two weeks, maritime traffic had recovered to approximately 60 percent of its pre-war level. Subsequent unilateral US measures and military action then blocked implementation of the Memorandum, and the dispute-resolution mechanisms it envisaged were bypassed.
Over the past two years, Iran has negotiated in good faith, and repeatedly, it was met with military action rather than diplomacy. This has created deep distrust about renewed negotiations without credible assurances against a repetition. Even so, Iran has kept the door open. Through Qatar, we have conveyed a concrete seven-day plan: if the necessary conditions are met, the Strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days. The choice now rests with the United States.
Excellencies,
The Palestinian cause remains the central cause of the Islamic world, and we cannot speak of peace while ignoring it. Palestine remains a wound on the conscience of the international community, and Gaza, a victim of genocide, has become a symbol of the failure of international mechanisms to protect civilians. Dozens of resolutions have not ended occupation and violence. The continuing suffering of the Palestinian people, the killing of innocent civilians by the Israeli regime and the threats to Al-Quds Al-Sharif and its holy sites should concern everyone. Iran stands with the Palestinian people, and we call on the OIC and all its members to do whatever it takes to put an end to the killing and the blockade and to make the protection of civilians and the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people a shared priority, backed by practical and coordinated action. And finally, I would like to endorse the proposal made by my brother, Hakan Fidan, the distinguished Foreign Minister of the Republic of Turkiya, to assign a day as Gaza Genocide Memorial Day.
On Yemen, for almost a decade, the people of Yemen have endured a devastating conflict, a prolonged blockade, and severe restrictions on vital civilian infrastructure. The role of the US and Israeli regime in inflicting suffering on Yemenis is undeniable. The resulting humanitarian catastrophe remains one of the gravest in the world, with serious violations of international humanitarian law continuing with impunity.
Iran's position is clear and unchanged. We support the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of Yemen, and those of the Saudi Arabia. We support a peaceful, inclusive and comprehensive political process as the only viable and sustainable means of resolving the conflict. Sustainable peace cannot be achieved through military escalation or coercion. There is no military solution.
The region's crises have no military solutions, and insisting on a military approach while disregarding a political solution only further complicates the situation. Iran is deeply concerned by developments in the Arabian Peninsula and remains ready to provide every assistance to facilitate dialogue between the parties, on the basis of the peace roadmap they previously agreed. The people of Yemen have the right to live with dignity, free from pressure, sanctions and blockade.
Dear Colleagues,
No state can build lasting security at the expense of the security of others. We believe the problems of our region are best resolved within the region, by its own states, before they become a pretext for the wars of distant powers. In that spirit, we believe the territory, airspace and infrastructure of every regional state should be used only to serve regional security and never become a platform for staging attacks on a neighbor. We say this in a spirit of brotherhood and good-neighborliness. Our peoples share one region and one future, and the choice before us is a simple one: either we build security together, or we will endure insecurity together. Iran stands ready to work with all its brothers and neighbors toward the former.
Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure. But we remain ready for dialogue based on mutual respect and credible guarantees.
I renew my thanks to our Iraqi hosts, and I wish this meeting success in serving the unity, peace, security and prosperity of the Islamic Ummah.
I thank you.
MNA

Zelenskyy says Russia sanctions relief could continue, diesel deal ‘first step’

Kanyshai Butun
17 October 2026•Update: 17 October 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday that easing of US sanctions against Russia could continue, describing the recent diesel deal as only the “first step,” the Interfax-Ukraine news agency reported.
Speaking to journalists, Zelenskyy said sanctions relief would give Russian President Vladimir Putin a sense of support rather than persuade him to end the war.
His comment came after US President Donald Trump signed an executive order suspending certain sanctions, restrictions and tariffs on Russia provided for under the Graham Act.
Zelenskyy, however, expressed hope that Trump "will do everything in his power" to halt attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and end the war.
He said Ukrainian and US negotiators could meet as early as this week, stressing that Kyiv remained committed to negotiations.
He said Washington was working on a proposal for a trilateral meeting involving Ukraine, the US and Russia.
Possible venues included the US at the Group of 20 summit, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia or a European country. No confirmation had yet been received from Moscow or Washington, he said.
On alleged Starlink restrictions, Zelenskyy said terminals in Ukraine disconnect at speeds above about 161 kph, affecting interceptor drones targeting Russian jet-powered Shahed drones and food deliveries to isolated Ukrainian positions. He said tests in some European countries showed connections remained active at speeds exceeding 180 kph.
He said military officials, the Defense Ministry and diplomats were involved in ongoing discussions, but SpaceX had not been engaging with the military.
“At various levels, it is being claimed that these are technical issues. However, these technical issues exist in Ukraine, while they do not occur within the territory of the EU,” Zelenskyy said.
He added that European countries were exploring alternatives to Starlink after recognizing that US-based access could be restricted.
On frozen Russian assets, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had information that Moscow could seek to recover some of them through partner countries. He said he had discussed the risk with Belgium and EU leaders, adding that the assets remained under European control and were secure.
European partners opposed the US-Russian diesel deal and agreed that sanctions should remain in place while Russia continued its attacks, Zelenskyy said, adding that work on another sanctions package was also underway.

Protesters clash with police in Brussels
BRUSSELS, Belgium - Several hundred mostly young people protested in Brussels on Oct 17, with rioters clashing with police in unrest partly inspired by demonstrations in neighbouring France.
Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible.
Demonstrators gathered in central Brussels, many wearing masks and chanting anti-fascist slogans. Police used tear gas and water cannon, while some protesters overturned a car, according to a Reuters witness.
Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin said in a post on X that “what is unfolding in Brussels is no longer mere protest” and “all necessary means will be used to restore order in the face of the rioters”.
A protest also took place in the eastern city of Liège, where students earlier in October demonstrated over the French-language education system, citing rising education costs and difficulties accessing study materials.
The unrest in France began in September as protests over education funding and school conditions before broadening into a wider movement centred on inequality, public spending and living standards. REUTERS

Egypt's Sisi seeks parliament's backing to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked
CAIRO, Oct 17 - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday Egypt would take any measures necessary to defend Saudi Arabia if asked, amid escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom, and parliament announced an emergency session on Sunday.
"It is inconceivable that we would allow Saudi Arabia, its security or stability to be harmed," Sisi said at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy. He said Egypt was not seeking to attack anyone, but was prepared to act in defence.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have in recent days attacked Riyadh's international airport and the state oil giant Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting with the Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government following the collapse of a truce.
Sisi said Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited, to discuss issues including security and navigation in the Red Sea.
"I know this requires the approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I ask that an emergency session be held so that it can give us that authorisation if we are asked," Sisi said.
Shortly after he spoke, parliament said it would hold a plenary session at 1 p.m. (1000 GMT) on Sunday in response to the request, though it did not disclose the agenda.
Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich Gulf states provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of Islamist president Mohamed Morsi in 2013.
Egypt also joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in 2015 to support the Yemeni government against the Houthis. REUTERS

The Italian Ambassador to Poland, Luca Franchetti Pardo, participated yesterday, along with the Defense Attaché, Col. Sandro Iervolino, in the burial ceremony at the Italian Military Cemetery in Bielany, Warsaw, for Sergeant Biagio Avolio, who fell in 1942. Two of the soldier’s grandchildren were present at the ceremony. After a moment of prayer and the blessing, as well as the recitation of the Soldier’s Prayer, those present paid tribute to the memory of the soldier who fell during World War II and to the sacrifice of all those who lost their lives in the service of their country. In an atmosphere of solemn reflection and emotion, the casket was escorted to its final resting place. At the conclusion of the ceremony, the ambassador presented the family with the Italian tricolor that had draped the coffin, in a solemn and deeply meaningful gesture, symbolizing the bond that unites the country with its fallen heroes and preserves their memory.” Born in Naples on April 2, 1919, Sergeant Biagio Avolio served in the 2nd Company of the 156th Machine-Gun Battalion of the “Vicenza” Division. Killed in action on October 4, 1942, at the age of 23, his remains were found and identified in Poland following a lengthy search conducted by his family in close collaboration with Italian authorities, making today’s burial possible. “At last you have a place to honor the memory of your uncle; at last he can rest on Italian soil alongside so many of his fellow soldiers,” said the ambassador. Franchetti Pardo then concluded by emphasizing: “The Italian Embassy and our institutions remain committed to the search for all the fallen soldiers still missing in Poland.”

A Paid Community is Coming to AIs without Minds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:21:09 UTC
23:21:09 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
This post is about my upcoming paid community tier, a post I’ll pin for future paid subs to read, and where I am laying out what I want the community space at AIs without minds to be. Get comfy and dig in! If you’re interested in an intentionally built intellectual community, on questions of minds and all things AI, this might just be the perfect space for you. ✨
Why a Community?
I’ve talked to my paid subscribers, and others who closely engage with my work and what I have heard most consistently is that folks want a space to think with others, a space to talk to others about all things AIs and minds. So that’s what’s happening.
I am launching a community space as part of the paid tier. I am thinking of this as a broader project, one that I’ll continue working on.
So this is just the first instalment, and I would love to receive feedback and other suggestions from folks who have ideas about what else they would like to see as part of a paid AIs Without Minds community.
The first instalment is a chat for paid subscribers and monthly zooms where we can discuss whatever ideas, thoughts, or arguments are on peoples minds.
Members will be able to start their own conversations/threads about questions related to all things AIs, minds, and everything in between; reply to each other in substantive, respectful, and genuinely curious ways; meet others, and hopefully, through the chat and monthly lives, form substantive friendships around intellectual issues that deeply matter today.
The monthly zooms are deliberately not Substack lives, where only I am visible. They will be held on zoom so folks have the opportunity to talk to not just me, but to engage with and meet others who are interested in similar issues.
What Kind of Community Space Will This Be?
There is a reason I did not open my chat from day one when I started this newsletter. It’s because I knew that if I did ever build a community space here, I would want to do it intentionally, and in a way that would actually be valuable to my subscribers.
As someone who works in academia, I am deeply aware of how important the shared spaces we have to talk about issues are, and I also know that such spaces are rarely accessible to those who do not have the privilege of pursuing higher education or working at universities and similar institutions.
With that in mind, as I choose to build this community, I want to lay some ground rules for how the space operates. Here they are, and I am always happy to update them and welcome feedback:
(1) this is a space for human thinkers: by this, of course I don’t mean that I am here to police your writing style or AI use, rather that AI slop being copy and pasted into a chat won’t be tolerated. We want to learn from fellow humans in this space, and hear what you think, so your thinking can develop. That’s the point of the community.
(2) if you start a thread about a particular idea/argument/question be sure to stick around to engage with those that respond to your thread. This sets up mutual trust and respect that’s needed in engaging in learning together. Please don’t start several threads at once that you cannot / are not willing to consistently return to and engage with. if the chat is flooded with unfinished threads, it wont be a fun space to engage and learn in.
(3) if you link things to the chat, they need to be explained. No linking your own pieces for self-promotion (sorry, but this is not what this chat is about), and no dumping in memes etc, that are not about generating real conversation and learning.
note: the exception of course, is if you’re working on something and want to share it because you’re stuck on an idea, an argument, etc and would appreciate feedback. But even then, do be mindful of giving as much to the community as you receive in terms of time commitment and effort.
(4) be respectful of peoples contributions and don’t screenshot and share things from that chats. I want this to be a welcoming and good-faith space for people to learn, ask questions, and engage. The chat is restricted to paid members partly because I want this to be a smaller, more intentional space for learning than a public feed.
(5) you do not have to agree with my views in the chat, or with anyone else’s. Disagreement is encouraged, so long as it’s respectful and what is being challenged are ideas and arguments, not people.
(6) its okay to come with half formed thoughts and ideas, but don’t dump into the chat incredibly long chunks of writing without yourself first making sure you have been as succinct as you reasonably can.
(7) Please don’t expect this space to be somewhere where I respond to questions on demand. This is somewhere I will occasionally participate and start threads, but the primary benefit is not access to me, its access to a community of thinkers. If you have specific questions for me, the better place for those is in monthly zooms.
If these rules are consistently violated, I may reach out to you and remove you from the chat. this is in the interest of making sure this space is a place where intentional learning happens. For that to happen, we need community cooperation.
The goal of this space is to allow people to learn to how think better, together, and in community. These rules exist to maintain that, and ill update them accordingly if something isnt working.
We launch today! For paid subscribers, you’re already in. If you’d like to upgrade to the paid tier, now’s an excellent time to do that.
Become a part of the community

Ukraine did not receive any warnings about the suspension of U.S. sanctions. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this while speaking with journalists. He also reported that Ukraine continues negotiations concerning the operation of Starlink and Starshield, UNN reports.
Details
No, we did not receive any warning that the sanctions would be suspended overnight. Just as we knew nothing about the Diesel Deal, and just as we learned about the possibility of an energy truce from the media. So, as of today, that is the situation. As for Starlink and Starshield: yes, we are engaged in dialogue, at the military level, at the level of the Ministry of Defense, and at the diplomatic level; we are contacting everyone, including SpaceX. Our Starlink works at speeds of up to 161 km/h, and then it shuts down. In the EU, it works at 180-plus and operates continuously. Here, it shuts down after 161 km/h for the second minute, switches off, and stops working. We are undoubtedly losing both drones and communications. Unfortunately, today we cannot use Starlink or Starshield technology in our country to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds. The President said this while speaking with journalists in a chat, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“Is there a threat of strikes and an increase in attacks on the western part of our country? Absolutely. Is Russia preparing for this? I think so. Why, in my view, are they constantly involving Belarus? Because we know that they are deploying signal repeaters in Belarus to use this corridor for drones and intensify the relevant attacks. But that is not enough for them. They need Lukashenko’s support to have other types of weapons deployed in Belarus, including ballistic weapons,” Zelensky said.

projection mapping and performances make the night come alive at signal festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:15:19 UTC
23:15:19 KST

projection mapping and performances make the night come alive at signal festival
co-founder martin pošta reflects on the origins of the digital art festival that transforms prague’s streets, landmarks, and historic buildings with light, sound, and performance.
prefer designboom on google
Signal Festival co-founder in conversation with designboom
Signal Festival reemerges for a weekend of immersive digital art installations that light up the corners and monuments of Prague. Founded by Martin Pošta, alongside producer and curator Jan Rolník and artist Amar Mulabegovič from the art group The Macula, nearly fourteen years ago, the event has grown from a yearly festival to also include a permanent space, open year-round in the Czech capital. Following the opening night of the event’s fourteenth edition, Dream On!, Pošta catches up with designboom in the recently opened Signal Space in Prague’s city center to chat about the event’s history.
The projection-mapping project that started it all
From the beginning of his career, even before Signal Festival, Pošta was interested in creating things people would love to watch. He started out producing films and documentaries, eventually attending film school in Prague and going on to organize a film festival in the Czech Republic. After leaving the television industry, he was asking himself what he would do next when he met up with some friends in a bar. As they were chatting, they got the idea to transform a local church with projection mapping. This was 2010, the nascent days of the technology, which had even Pošta himself asking, ‘what is video-mapping?’
After discussing the project with the deputy mayor at the time, he suggested that they instead work with the Prague Astronomical Clock (Orloj), which at the time was about to celebrate its 600th anniversary. ‘I went to roam around and to check out what’s the vibe amongst the people,’ remembers Pošta of the crowds that gathered for this first project. He recounts seeing an older gentleman looking up at the clock tower in awe, telling his wife that she ‘must come and see the installation.’ ‘And I literally got tears in my eyes,’ Pošta admits. ‘I was touched… it was the moment when I kind of knew that I found my next calling.’ It was from this first project that he’d go on to champion new media projects.
Bringing light art to Prague with Signal Festival
After that event in 2010, Pošta and his team at The Macula created and produced these types of installations around the world. Seeing all the emerging talents in the sector spread across the world, he began to work on an event that would bring them all to one place. ‘I was lucky enough that the guy who was deputy mayor for culture, was still there. He knew what we were doing, so it was easier to explain to where we were heading towards,’ Pošta reflects on the early days of organizing what would become Signal Festival. ‘And then I was lucky to get introduced to the Ministry of Regional Development. And I got the first funding for the festival… honestly, we hardly knew what we were doing, but that’s how it happened. We had the list of the artists that we really wanted. There was no curation back then – we were just like, OK, we love this guy, this guy, that guy.’
Creating art, community, and performance
‘It’s a huge matrix of the stuff that you have to combine,’ says Pošta of bringing the festival to fruition each year. Not only do they invite artists from around the world, but they also commission new, site-specific works. ‘Some of them are super ephemeral, like with the video mapping projections, there are four nights and that’s gone,’ he says of the installations. Nevertheless, with the newly opened Signal Space, a permanent mainstay in the heart of Prague, some of the works can be seen year-round under Old Town Market Hall. Inside the space, the ceilings open up to reveal some of the turquoise metal supports that hold up the historic building.
Over fourteen years, Pošta has built up a team of what he affectionately calls ‘like-minded lunatics,’ who have come together to create ‘a lot of things that would be deemed impossible.’ These are the coordinators, administrative staff, and tech teams that pull together the festival. They also include the artists who realize the installations, some of whom return for subsequent editions.
Laterna Magika at the 14th Signal Festival
One group that reappears in the dark evenings of Signal is Laterna Magika. Pošta shares a bit about the group’s history in the Czech Republic, saying that ‘they are a faction of the Czech National Theater.’ He describes their technique as one where, ‘They play with the fact that you cannot see people dressed in black against a black stage. You can just see what is lit up, so they created first illusions,’ with this particular technique and projected light and video. He goes on to say, ‘about six years ago, we introduced performative aspect to the festival, and it’s always super interesting to explore with [Laterna Magika] the possibilities of performance, dance, body and visuals.’ This year, they create a live, site-specific performance at the Old Wastewater Treatment Plant in Bubeneč, working from a poem by the Czech author František Vinant.
project info:
name: Signal Festival
theme: Dream On!
date: October 15–18, 2026
location: Prague, Czech Republic
in conversation with: Martin Pošta | @_martinposta_
founders: Producer Martin Pošta, curator Jan Rolník, and artist Amar Mulabegovič from the art group The Macula
founding date: 2013
