Putin’s Nightmare: The Coming Congressional Realignment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:14:00 UTC
23:14:00 KST

During his six years in office, President Trump dominated the Federal government and global relations because the Republicans controlled Congress and he controlled the Republican Party.
However, the nation, including non-MAGA Republicans and many independents, has moved past its early fascination and patience with Trump and is now looking to the Democratic Party as an antidote to MAGA. If these trends continue and the forecasting polls and historical precedents hold up, the Democratic Party is very likely to win control of the House of Representatives and has a better-than-even chance of winning the Senate in early November.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Of the two parties, the Republican Party has traditionally taken stronger positions in support of democracies and in constraining authoritarian regimes – as exemplified by Republican Reagan’s unswerving pressure on the USSR and Democrat Obama’s flaccid response to Putin’s invasion of Crimea.
However, after the invasion, polls show striking partisan reversals. Democrats have increasingly viewed Russia as a “major threat” from 2014 to the present, while Republican perception of Russia as an existential threat has declined sharply after Trump took office in 2016, increased briefly in 2022, and then continued to decline.
According to the Pew Research Center, between 2022 and August 2026, Democratic Party members’ support for “aid to Ukraine” has risen and held steady at close to 80% since Russia’s full-scale invasion. Conversely, Republican members’ support dropped from 68% to 38/42%. These partisan differences inevitably show up in congressional voting patterns.
Midterms 2026: What Comes Next for the US and Europe?
With one exception, House and Senate Democrats voted more consistently and nearly unanimously on every major aid package for Ukraine, while Republicans were deeply fractured, with a large and growing anti-Ukraine faction. (The one exception was the recent vote on the 2026 Russia Sanctions Expansion Act, which House Republicans watered down and altered so much that many Democrats mistrusted Trump’s intentions and use of the act’s tariff authority.)
If Democrats win one or both chambers of Congress, President Trump will face an intensely adversarial Congress with enormous power to oversee the executive branch as a coequal.
Trump may become a virtual lame-duck president, his every move scrutinized, and his time preoccupied with Democrat-led investigations into his and his family’s dealings and the efficacy of his policies. Many of his “loyal” appointees will likely resign before the new Congress takes office on Jan. 3, while others will be forced out for cause.
In Washington, when a polarizing officeholder loses power, phones stop ringing, dinner invitations get red-lined, damning accusations appear in the media, and the succession guessing game starts all over again. Democratic Congressman Raskin of the House Judiciary Committee described his investigative agenda as “gargantuan.”
Across the Atlantic, Kyiv and Europe’s other capitals will collectively sigh with relief that so many strong Democratic supporters of NATO, the EU, and Ukraine now have real power. Influential figures and leaders such as Hakeem Jeffries, Gregory Meeks, Chuck Schumer, Steny Hoyer, Mark Kelly, and perhaps even Eugene Vindman will emerge to redirect Trump’s trans-Atlantic policies towards more predictable, constructive, and traditional ends.
In distant Moscow, Putin’s hopes and expectations will be shattered when he realizes that it won’t get any better for Russia, so he’d better take his lumps and start thinking seriously about peace.
The first impact of the realignment (even before the end of the year) may be the enactment of the Ukraine Support Act (H.R. 2913), which the House passed on June 4, 2026, and the Senate put on the calendar in July but has not submitted to a full vote. While all attention has been focused on the “Russia Sanctions” bill, the “Ukraine Support Act” is a true “dream” bill with far weightier implications for Ukraine and Europe in securing an early, lasting peace. This is the one “omnibus” bill that merits full, coordinated support by the Ukrainian-American diaspora.
Although Trump will retain much of his constitutional authority over national security and foreign policy, Congress, through its power of the purse, senior appointments, oversight, legislation, treaties, legally binding frameworks, public hearings, and investigations, could reinvigorate US support for Ukraine and NATO and restore predictability.
By assembling veto-proof majorities with pro-Ukrainian Republicans, Democrats could force robust military and direct budgetary assistance packages such as the “Ukraine Support Act” even without the president’s approval. Putin’s worst nightmare – a militarily strong Ukraine supported by Congress and increasing sanctions on his economy – could well result in a secure and just peace.
Democratic control of Congress is likely to produce other, more subtle but very serious implications. Trump’s alignment with Russia’s efforts to break up European unity by encouraging “populist”/nativist movements should be defunded so that fringe, extremist, pro-Russian groups would lose two of their three biggest boosters – Trump, Vance and Putin.
Although every effort should be made to push Europe to develop its own security and reimburse the US for all expenditures incurred on Europe’s behalf, a strong Congressional recommitment to NATO would let NATO members systematically build up their forces without fearing Russia. Congress should also repudiate any territorial claims against NATO members or the Western Hemisphere.
A Democratic victory in the mid-term elections would bring welcome relief to both Ukraine and Europe and restore stability and normality to the US as long as the Party can keep its own fringe elements in check. Future historians, commenting on this period, may define it as the Fall of the House of Trump.

Britain puts stealth fighters to sea in the High North
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:10:57 BST
23:10:57 KST

British F-35 jets will fly from HMS Prince of Wales in the Arctic and North Atlantic when the carrier sails from Portsmouth on Sunday, returning fifth-generation airpower to the skies of the High North as part of the second phase of Operation Firecrest, according to the Royal Navy.
The carrier deploys with an air group comprising F-35 jets, Merlin Mk4 Commando and Mk2 anti-submarine helicopters, Wildcat helicopters and Malloy drones, accompanied by the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless and more than 1,200 British personnel.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, placed the air wing at the centre of the message: “The deployment of the HMS Prince of Wales and her air wing to the High North and the North Atlantic, operating under NATO leadership, is a clear demonstration of the UK’s commitment to the Alliance and contribution to the enduring security and stability of the North Atlantic.”
Commodore Richard Hewitt, who commands the UK Carrier Strike Group staff, said the group would work with allies throughout: “Led by the UK Flagship HMS Prince of Wales, the Strike Group will bring together a range of assets and capabilities, while taking every opportunity to train, operate and integrate with our NATO allies and partners.”
They are flown by a joint Royal Navy and Royal Air Force force based at Marham.
Operating them in the Arctic brings problems the Indo-Pacific deployment did not. Deck icing, salt spray freezing on surfaces, low cloud, short daylight and a sea state that moves the landing spot all bear on an aircraft that lands vertically onto a moving deck, and the maintainers work on an exposed flight deck in conditions that degrade both people and equipment faster than warm water does. Running a fifth-generation aircraft in that environment, and proving the stealth coatings, the sensors and the logistics chain can take it, is a large part of why the deployment is worth doing.
Russia’s Northern Fleet operates from the Kola Peninsula and the government’s Arctic Policy Framework, published this week, described it as capable of threatening Britain, Western Europe and North America, with expanded patrols and new capabilities across multiple domains. The same document committed Britain to stepping up its defence contribution in the region, including doubling the number of troops deployed to Norway to two thousand over the next three years and taking on a role in NATO air policing from Iceland.
The strike group will operate under NATO command and contribute to the alliance’s Neptune Strike series of exercises, working with Norway, Denmark and Germany. The Royal Navy said the focus of the phase is operational readiness, interoperability and preparedness to respond in a region it calls increasingly important.
Prince of Wales will also host the Atlantic Future Forum and the International Sea Power Conference in Oslo during the deployment, bringing defence leaders, industry and policymakers aboard to discuss Euro-Atlantic security.
The ship is due to leave Portsmouth Naval Base at 1700 on Sunday 18 October, weather permitting.

BANGKOK, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Thailand cast itself as a "trusted connector" in a fragmented global economy on Saturday as it began wrapping up its hosting of the 2026 annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group.
During a concluding press conference on Thailand's hosting of the meetings, Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance Ekniti Nitithanprapas said the event had demonstrated the country's capacity to help set the global agenda together with the IMF and the World Bank.
Ekniti emphasized that resilience in a fragmented world must be built both across borders and within countries, by bringing small businesses and local communities into global supply chains.
The Thai government said the week-long meetings drew more than 19,000 registered participants, citing official IMF and World Bank registration data.
The "Bangkok Dialogue Notes" were unveiled at the press briefing. Officials noted that they are not a negotiated international outcome or formal policy recommendations but rather a distillation of themes raised in discussions among policymakers, international institutions, businesses, and other participants.
The document argues that economic fragmentation is happening within countries as well as between them. It says leading firms may gain access to new technologies and markets faster than small- and medium-sized enterprises, while some communities still lack the tools to seize new opportunities. ■

Yin, the 2024 champion, made five birdies to climb to third place at 7-under 209, while Choi maintained her lead for the third consecutive day with a 69 that left her at 9-under 207.
Choi holds a one-shot advantage over compatriot Amy Yang, who sits second at 8-under 208.
Choi made four birdies on the front nine but struggled with her driving after the turn, dropping a shot at the 15th hole.
"My approach shots were good on the front nine, and I took advantage of many opportunities. But on the back nine, my tee shots kept finding the rough," Choi said.
"There will be a lot of spectators tomorrow, and I'll keep working hard to try to win my first LPGA Tour title."
Yin credited an adjustment to her putter for her improved performance after struggling on the greens during the opening two rounds.
"My putting wasn't in good shape over the first two rounds, and I missed a lot of short putts," she said. "After finishing yesterday's round, I realized there was an issue with the angle of my putter, so I went to the club-fitting workshop to have it adjusted. Things felt much smoother today."
Yin won the FM Championship earlier this season for her sixth LPGA Tour title, ending a title drought of nearly two years.
She also enjoyed success at the Asian Games in Nagoya earlier this month, taking silver in the women's individual event and helping China claim its first Asian Games golf gold in the women's team competition.
The 2024 Shanghai champion said she would focus on her own performance rather than the prospect of another home victory.
"Of course, it would be great if I could win the title. But if I play to my ability and don't end up winning, I won't have any regrets," Yin said.
Yin will play alongside Choi and Yang in Sunday's final group, setting up a three-way battle for the title.

Ukraine Dismisses Russia’s Latest Claimed Territorial Advances as ‘An Illusion’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17

23:07:24 KST

Ukraine on Saturday rejected Russia's claim to have captured more than 1,800 square kilometers (695 square miles) of Ukrainian territory and nearly 100 settlements, including the eastern town of Dobropillia, since the beginning of September.
On Friday, the chief of Russia's General Staff, Valery Gerasimov, told President Vladimir Putin that Russian forces had captured 92 Ukrainian settlements and made significant territorial gains since last month.
Ukraine's General Staff spokesman, Andriy Kovaliov, dismissed the claims.
"In fact, through their active operations, the Ukrainian Defense Forces have liberated more territory since the beginning of the fall than the enemy has managed to capture," he said in an emailed statement.
"The Russian military leadership continues to create an illusion of major victories for its political leadership and domestic audience," Kovaliov added.
Russia's advances along the front line have slowed this year. Still, its forces have been bearing down on the so-called "fortress belt" cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, the capture of which would bring Russia closer to its goal of seizing the entire Donetsk region.
Kovaliov also rejected Gerasimov's claims that Russian troops had reached the outskirts of Kramatorsk and were advancing in the suburbs of Sloviansk.
He said Dobropillia, southwest of the two cities, remained under Ukrainian control despite sustained Russian attacks.
Reuters could not independently verify the battlefield claims.
With many front lines largely static across a deadly "kill zone," both sides have intensified their air campaigns in recent months.
Russia fired hundreds of ballistic missiles over the summer and early fall, and it is widely expected to target critical infrastructure, including heating and power sites, into the winter.
Ukraine, which has a far smaller missile arsenal, has launched hundreds of long-range drone attacks on Russian oil refineries, ships and commercial sites.

Gallery: Public bomb shelter in Tallinn hidden behind woodland mural
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:06:00 UTC
23:06:00 KST

Gallery: Public bomb shelter in Tallinn hidden behind woodland mural
A street-level public civil defense shelter in the heart of downtown Tallinn has been transformed with a mural featuring Estonian trees and wildlife.
Located next to Kalev Sports Hall in Tiigiveski Park, the modular concrete shelter cannot withstand a direct missile hit, but it can protect around 20 people from blast waves, shrapnel and debris from an explosion as close as 50 meters away.
Similar shelters are already widely used in Ukraine, including in Kramatorsk.
The concrete module, donated by security company Citysec, is also now fully wrapped in a woodland mural by Colorees Art's Helena Hanni and Vahur Agar, featuring a wild hare, a bear family, an owl in flight and a wolf.
While usually kept closed in peacetime, the shelter was open to visitors on Friday, when officials were on hand to explain its features to the public.
City weighs dozens more shelters
Citysec CEO Eduard Rikkas said the module was developed on a 50-50 basis with partners in Ukraine, where the design has already been in use for years.
Deputy Mayor Tiit Terik (Center) said the shelter door can be opened remotely during an emergency, and will unlock automatically if power or communications fail.
The shelter door, he added, will be kept locked in peacetime.
Tallinn has mapped 40 to 50 potential sites for similar shelters, with public procurement to follow if the city decides to order more.
According to the manufacturer, the shelter model installed on Juhkentali tänav costs up to €70,000.

Hurricane Trudy threatens western Mexico with heavy rain, coastal flooding
Oct 17 - Hurricane Trudy maintained its strength as it moved toward Mexico's western coast on Saturday, with forecasters warning it could strengthen further before beginning to weaken on Sunday.
The US National Hurricane Center said Trudy was about 190 miles (305 km) south-southeast of Manzanillo early on Saturday, with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph (150 kph).
The hurricane was moving at about 8 mph (13 kph) and was forecast to approach southwestern and west-central Mexico later on Saturday before passing near the coast overnight into Sunday.
Hurricane conditions are expected in the warning area on Saturday night, while tropical storm conditions are expected to spread across the region during the day, the NHC said. Hurricane conditions are also possible in areas under a hurricane watch.
Trudy is forecast to bring four to eight inches (10 to 20 cm) of rain, with isolated totals of around 15 inches, across parts of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco through the weekend, raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and landslides, especially in steep terrain, according to the NHC.
Outer rain bands could produce two to four inches of rain, with isolated totals of around six inches, in Guerrero and Nayarit, where localized flash flooding is possible, the center said.
The NHC also warned of possible coastal flooding from storm surge in areas exposed to onshore winds, accompanied by large and destructive waves.
Swells generated by Trudy were already affecting parts of Mexico's southwestern coast and are expected to spread northward toward the country's west-central coast through the weekend, creating life-threatening surf and rip current conditions, the NHC said. REUTERS

According to local media, the party has challenged both the legitimacy of the appointment process and the new leadership's authority.

The party also warned institutions against cooperating with the new leadership, saying those that did so would be considered affiliated with the ruling Prosperity Party and held accountable.
The rejection came hours after Abiy's government dissolved Tigray's previous interim administration and appointed a new leadership team to govern the conflict-hit region for six months.
The government named Asefa Abrahaga Hagos as chief administrator, with other officials assigned responsibility for security, reconstruction and political affairs. The government appointed Shishay Amare mayor of Mekelle, Tigray's regional capital.

"The people of Tigray must emerge from the agony of conflict to reclaim their distant peace, reaffirm their right to self-administration, and be able to heal the developmental setbacks they have suffered over the many past years," the prime minister's office said on Friday.
The TPLF, however, maintained that the appointees lacked the authority to govern the region and challenged the legitimacy of decisions made under federal supervision.
The party accused the federal government of using airports in Tigray for military purposes, and warned residents to stay away from the facilities.

Federal troops and allied Tigray Peace Force (TPF) fighters have expanded their control across northern Tigray, including Mekelle and several strategic towns near the Eritrean border.
The renewed conflict threatens the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement, which ended a devastating two-year war between Ethiopia's federal government and Tigrayan forces.
The fighting has also heightened tensions between Ethiopia and neighboring Eritrea, with both governments exchanging accusations of military aggression amid growing international calls for de-escalation.

Egypt’s Sisi seeks authorisation for defence assistance to Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:00:24 UTC
23:00:24 KST

Egypt’s Sisi seeks authorisation for defence assistance to Saudi Arabia
Egyptian president pledges ‘any measure’ to help defend Saudi Arabia ‘if it is requested of us’.
Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has called for an emergency parliamentary session to authorise him to approve any requests from Saudi Arabia for defence assistance, if Riyadh were to ask.
Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy on Saturday, el-Sisi emphasised Cairo’s readiness to back the kingdom.
Egypt will “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia “in accordance with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and the directives of the Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman”, he said.
“I know that this matter requires the approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I hope that parliament will convene in an emergency session to give us this authorisation, if it is requested of us,” he said.
“I am not speaking in order for us to fight anyone or attack anyone. I am speaking only for defence.”
Attacks on Saudi Arabia
The request follows a barrage of attacks on the kingdom from Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, including airports and oil facilities.
Recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have mainly targeted key infrastructure on the outskirts of the capital, Riyadh, but they appear to be edging closer to the city centre.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport earlier this month killed 14 people and wounded more than 300. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including Dammam, Abha, Jazan and Najran.
Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government launched a full-scale military campaign against the Houthis this month to recapture territory seized by them.
El-Sisi had backed Saudi calls for secure and unhindered navigation in the Red Sea in a meeting with the Saudi Crown Prince, known as MBS, in Cairo last month.
A statement from the Egyptian presidency then said that “the security of Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states is an integral part of Egypt’s national security”.
Red Sea security
That meeting came just days after the Houthis seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, gaining significant control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal.
Saudi Arabia already has a defence pact with Pakistan and Turkiye, known as the Mecca Alliance for Defence, which was signed in August.
Earlier this month, the three countries agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under the pact and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.
Analysts say Riyadh is looking for help to protect the kingdom and Red Sea shipping and that Egypt, whose Suez Canal revenue depends on the same traffic, is an obvious partner.
They say Egypt is eager to prevent Iran and its allies from imposing control over the region, especially over maritime traffic in the Red Sea, given the direct repercussions for the Suez Canal.
Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging Houthi attacks against the kingdom, a claim Tehran rejects. Iran has offered assistance to halt the conflict between the two sides.
Sisi’s future
Speaking to recruits at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital on Saturday, el-Sisi also confirmed that he would not seek to extend his presidency beyond 2030, in line with the Egyptian constitution.
“The period leading up to 2030 will be the end of my term as president of the state, if I am still alive,” he said.
He added that his decision is “completely settled” and there will be “no discussion” about it.
Egypt’s constitution was updated in 2019 to increase term length to six years from four, and to allow el-Sisi to run for another six-year term in 2023. That means his term is due to expire in 2030, and he is not allowed to run again.
He said the Egyptian constitution “would not be touched”.

Ending wars, establishing lasting peace remain essential conditions for sustainable global growth – IMFC statement
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:00:16 EEST
23:00:16 KST

Wars and conflicts continue to cause severe humanitarian suffering, accompanied by significant economic costs and tangible negative side effects, which hit the poorest and most vulnerable segments of the population the hardest, according to a statement from the 54th meeting of the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC) in Bangkok on Saturday.
"Ending wars and conflicts and securing lasting peace around the world remains essential for sustainable growth and long-term stability," the statement's introduction notes, without specifying particular conflicts, according to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
The IMFC, which is the key advisory body of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), noted that the global economy weathered the latest shock better than expected, but such resilience should not be taken for granted.
"Disruptions to supply chains are adding to uncertainty and price pressures. Major structural transformations are underway. In this more complex environment, which brings opportunities but also risks, our priority remains to promote macroeconomic and financial stability while enabling broad-based, private sector-led growth, and strengthening resilience through credible policies and international cooperation," the document states.
The committee pins its hopes for growth on the rapid development of cutting-edge intellectual technologies, which stimulate investment and trade and can help boost productivity, but notes that low-income countries and fragile states risk falling even further behind in development.
"Risks remain tilted to the downside: escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food insecurity," the statement reads.
The IMFC also draws attention to rising yields on sovereign bonds in major economies, which are negatively affecting global financial conditions against the backdrop of high public debt and refinancing needs in many countries.
"Rapid technological change, demographic shifts, more frequent extreme weather events and natural disasters, and geoeconomic fragmentation are compounding policy tradeoffs," the committee adds, painting a bleak picture.
It calls for sound and consistent macroeconomic policies and multilateral cooperation, as well as fiscal consolidation efforts to ensure debt sustainability, while protecting the most vulnerable and prioritizing investments that stimulate productivity and growth.
The statement also emphasizes the importance of preserving central bank independence to maintain confidence in policy and keep inflation expectations stable, and advises banks to remain firmly committed to ensuring price stability in accordance with their mandates.
"We underscore the importance of secure and resilient energy flows and of upholding the principle of freedom of navigation as essential to global economic stability," the IMFC also stated.
Regarding artificial intelligence – whose positive impacts and risks to global and national economies were one of the main topics at the annual meeting in Bangkok – the committee looks forward to further analysis of the situation by the IMF and its recommendations.
The next IMFC meeting will take place in April 2027 in Washington.

Learning to read may shape how adults reason about what others believe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:00:13 UTC
23:00:13 KST

A study of literate and illiterate women in Turkey found that reading fluency was strongly linked to performance on a test of reasoning about what one person thinks another believes. The findings, published in PLoS One, suggest that literacy and the schooling that typically comes with it may shape this kind of advanced social reasoning in adulthood.
A central concept in social psychology is “Theory of Mind,” which refers to the ability to recognize that other people have their own thoughts, desires, and intentions. One way to measure this is through a false-belief task. This test assesses whether an individual understands that someone else can hold a belief that contradicts reality.
A more advanced version of this test is the second-order false-belief task. Rather than just asking what one person believes, this task requires reasoning about what one person thinks another person believes. This level of social reasoning typically matures between ages 8 and 10, around the time many children are becoming fluent readers.
Past research suggests that language acquisition and impulse control both help people reason about others’ perspectives. For example, a 2009 study of deaf adults using a newly emerging sign language in Nicaragua found that those whose signing improved over two years also improved on false-belief tests, which the authors took as evidence that language drives this ability. Similarly, a 2001 study of preschoolers found that children better at holding back automatic responses tended to do better at tracking others’ beliefs, though evidence in adults has been mixed.
Other research has shown that reading stories relates to social understanding. For instance, a 2018 meta-analysis found that reading fiction produced a small improvement in social understanding compared with reading nonfiction or nothing.
Tan Arda Gedik of Bilkent University and Friedrich Alexander Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg and his colleagues set out to test whether differences in false-belief reasoning between literate and illiterate adults could be explained by reading fluency or related factors like intelligence and impulse control.
“Most theory of mind (ToM) studies have focused on children or highly educated neurotypical adults, leaving a gap regarding the roughly 700 million illiterate neurotypical adults worldwide, at least according to UNESCO,” Gedik, a cognitive scientist and instructor in the Department of Psychology at Bilkent University and the Department of Foreign Language Teaching at Middle East Technical University, told PsyPost. “Since literacy acquisition significantly alters brain structures that also support ToM, we wanted to investigate this overlooked population and see what differences (if any at all) we might observe.”
For their experiment, the researchers recruited 76 female native Turkish speakers. The sample included 41 illiterate women with an average age of about 49, and 35 literate women with an average age of about 46. The illiterate participants had recently started attending an adult education center and had received only a few months of formal schooling on average. The literate group, by contrast, had an average of over 17 years of formal education.
“I would like the readers to take a moment to appreciate the great lengths these women went to emancipate themselves from some awful sociocultural practices they were subjected to by attending literacy classes (sometimes in secret from their family members, sometimes with bruises on their arms), learning one letter at a time,” Gedik said. “We hope that each and every one of our participants will make their wishes come true (i.e., finding a job, getting a driver’s license or just being able to help their children with their homework).”
Participants completed several tests designed to measure their cognitive and academic abilities. To assess reading fluency, the researchers timed the participants for one minute as they read lists of real Turkish words and made-up words. They measured inhibitory control, which is the mental ability to override an automatic response, using an emotional Stroop task. In this task, participants looked at happy and sad face emojis on a screen and had to state the opposite emotion out loud.
The researchers also measured nonverbal intelligence using Raven’s Colored Progressive Matrices. This task requires participants to look at a series of visual patterns with a missing piece and select the correct option to complete the design. By using visual puzzles, the task assesses reasoning abilities without relying on spoken or written language.
The illiterate group averaged about 12 out of 36 on this test, versus about 30 for the literate group. The authors note that the illiterate group’s scores match those of other adults with very little schooling and reflect limited education rather than cognitive impairment.
Finally, the authors tested false-belief understanding using two short stories, presented orally with the help of artificial intelligence-enhanced images. In one story, a boy hides a chocolate bar in a drawer, and his sister moves it to a toy box while he is away. However, the boy secretly watches her move it through a window.
The participants were asked where the sister thinks the boy will look for the chocolate. Answering correctly requires understanding the sister’s mistaken belief about the boy’s knowledge.
Under the stricter of two scoring methods, literate participants answered the belief questions correctly about 80 percent of the time, compared with about 20 percent for the illiterate participants. The illiterate group still answered a basic comprehension question about the stories correctly 87 percent of the time, suggesting they followed the narratives.
“We expected to see large individual differences (within and between groups) in false-belief understanding but the gap in understanding between the two groups was the most striking,” Gedik noted.
When looking at the cognitive predictors, reading fluency emerged as the strongest factor in explaining these differences. Reading scores alone accounted for 49 percent of the variance, or statistical variation, in the participants’ false-belief performance. Age accounted for an additional 6 percent of the variation, with older adults tending to score slightly lower.
Reading fluency, however, was almost perfectly tied to which group a participant was in and to years of schooling, and the results looked nearly identical when the researchers used education instead. As a result, the authors treat reading fluency as a stand-in for literacy and the education that typically accompanies it, rather than reading alone.
The illiterate adults also scored lower on the measure of inhibitory control, averaging about 6 out of 10 compared with about 9 for the literate adults. However, once the researchers factored in reading fluency, individual differences in intelligence and impulse control did not add any predictive power. The authors suggest that literacy, and the language and thinking skills that come with it, may account for much of the gap. They caution, though, that with 76 participants these null results should not be taken to mean intelligence and impulse control are unimportant for this kind of reasoning.
“The take home message is that literacy is not as simple as it seems and has consequences that go well beyond being able to decode written words,” Gedik explained.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that lifetime exposure to fiction is linked to better theory of mind and perspective-taking. Both studies connect reading to improved social understanding. This new study measured reading at a much more fundamental level, though, focusing on basic literacy and word-reading fluency in adults rather than engagement with fictional narratives.
There are a few things to keep in mind about these findings. The study is correlational, meaning it cannot confirm that learning to read directly causes improvements in social reasoning. The sample was small, and the literate group was unusually highly educated, averaging 17 years of schooling with many graduate degrees, which widens the gap between the groups.
“The biggest misconception would be to interpret the study as saying that illiterate people don’t understand other people’s minds or that they fail to take perspectives of others,” Gedik clarified. “Our task measures one relatively specific form of perspective-taking. So we should not equate performance on this task with someone’s general capacity for empathy and social understanding, broadly speaking.”
Earlier accounts show that illiterate women understand basic deception, though standard false-belief tasks assess more advanced reasoning that the authors suggest may be strengthened by the kind of practice reading provides.
“As discussed in the paper, similar demographics have been documented to make references to perspective-taking or other forms of theory of mind,” Gedik added. “The question is: to what extent is this automatized/mastered?”
The sample was entirely female and specific to Turkish speakers, so the results might differ for men or for people from other cultural and linguistic backgrounds. Because illiterate women in this demographic often experience highly restricted social environments, their lower performance might also reflect a lack of diverse social interaction rather than reading itself.
“Next on the list is testing ideally the same participants (or participants similar to this demographic) on a nonverbal ToM (theory of mind) task to rule out language related limitations,” Gedik noted. “The other (perhaps obvious) next step would be longitudinal research following people as they acquire literacy and documenting changes in their ToM performance.”
“While we feel that these findings are significant and important, we are at the beginning of a long journey,” he said of the research’s practical impact. “We will need many more studies (ideally longitudinal and cross-cultural) to more confidently propose the effects of these findings.”
“Readers who are broadly interested in this line of work and population can find further literature and experimental studies in Gedik (2026): Literacy at Work: Ultimate Native Language Attainment, published by De Gruyter,” he concluded.
The study, “Literacy predicts performance on a second-order false-belief task,” was authored by Tan Arda Gedik, Vania De la Garza, and Ewa Dabrowska.

How Taiwan’s new AI satellite system aims to speed up early warning against PLA moves

Moscow warns of ‘hunt for Russians’

Moscow warns of ‘hunt for Russians’
Russia’s Foreign Ministry has warned citizens to exercise caution when traveling abroad “amid a worldwide hunt for Russians.”
The statement follows the detention of Russian military blogger Mikhail Zvinchuk in Montenegro, a NATO member state in the Balkans, on October 9.
After nine hours in custody, Zvinchuk, founder of the Rybar Telegram channel, his wife and three associates were expelled from the country on the grounds of what Montenegro’s leading daily, Vijesti, described as “criminal, operational and intelligence processing.”
“We are compelled to once again remind people of the need to remain vigilant when traveling abroad, even if there is the slightest suspicion of any kind of claims by US law enforcement agencies, amid a worldwide hunt for Russians,” Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said on Friday.
Montenegro, where the blogger was detained, is not on Russia’s list of unfriendly states, Zakharova said, adding that similar situations were unfolding in countries not considered unfriendly to Russia.
The arrest was described as targeting alleged “hybrid activity” by the Rybar network, but no specific evidence supporting the accusation has been presented.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declined to comment on the details of the arrest but warned Russian citizens that visiting Europe is “currently dangerous.”
The Rybar channel, which has around 1.3 million subscribers, had previously also faced US and British accusations of spreading Russian propaganda and conducting information operations abroad. The US State Department had even issued a $10 million bounty in 2024 for any information about the individuals behind the channel.
Russians who have been targeted include basketball player Daniil Kasatkin, a point guard playing for the national team, who was arrested at Paris airport in June 2025 at the behest of the US, which accused him of being a member of a ransomware gang. He denied the allegations and was released in January 2026 as part of a Russia-France prisoner exchange.

Pope Leo discharged from hospital four days after lung surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:59:00 UTC
22:59:00 KST

Pope Leo leaves hospital after cancer surgery
October 17, 2026
Pope Leo XIV left the Gemelli hospital in Rome on Saturday afternoon. He returned to the Vatican four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.
The 71-year-old pope walked unaided to his car and stopped to speak with well-wishers outside the hospital.
"I am better, thank you," Leo XIV said as he was driven away in a black SUV. Leo XIV entered the Vatican ten minutes after leaving the hospital.
After conducting blood tests and imaging scans of his chest, the pope's doctors said he was well enough to return home.
Currently, Leo is undergoing physiotherapy to help him breathe more easily.
What do we know about the Pope's health?
On Tuesday, Leo XIV had the lower lobe of his right lung removed after doctors identified a nodule suspected to be cancerous. The surgery confirmed that he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
The doctors said his surgery was successful and complication-free. However, they have not yet disclosed the size of the tumor or if the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes. These factors are key in determining the prognosis.
The diagnosis of the relatively young and energetic pontiff, elected in May 2025, came as a shock. It raised questions about the future of his papacy as he deals with the illness.
On Sunday, Leo is expected to lead weekly prayers with pilgrims in St. Peter's Square at noon (10:00 a.m. GMT), which will be his first public engagement since his surgery.

California Gov Newsom boosts AI regulation as he eyes 2028 presidential run
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:56:29 UTC
22:56:29 KST

California Gov Newsom boosts AI regulation as he eyes 2028 presidential run
Newsom signed an executive order to examine kill switches for AI models and other measures he had earlier vetoed.
San Francisco, United States – In his last few executive orders signed as California governor, Gavin Newsom, whose final term ends in January, issued one asking for independent verification of artificial intelligence models and set up an expert committee to create kill switches for AI agents that could go rogue and cause harm.
In 2024, Newsom vetoed a bill, passed in the state assembly, asking for similar requirements that the governor has now called for in his executive order. Newsom said at the time that it would amount to “thwarting the promise of this technology”.
Now eyeing a 2028 United States presidential run, he wants to expand the definition of safety incidents, potentially to include the recent series of safety breaches, explore a kill switch and include other measures that were in the vetoed bill.
“He is in a lame duck period here,” says Alex Hanna, director of research at the Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR), unsure that the measures will pass in the remainder of his term. “He is setting up his next thing.”
US voters are increasingly concerned about AI safety, data centres and job losses, and this could show Newsom is acting to address this, Hanna says.
After vetoing the 2024 bill, Newsom had asked Scott Wiener, the state senator who drafted the bill, to redraft it in consultation with an expert committee. He signed that frontier AI bill, the nation’s first, into law in October 2025. It asks large developers to disclose certain safety incidents, including the deaths of 50 or more people, large-scale cyberattacks or monetary theft.
Christabel Randolph, associate director at the Center for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP), says, “It seems the governor operated from the premise that a slower pace of regulation would be sufficient because the companies would pace their investments, and did not anticipate that the companies would be accelerating the risks.”
AI companies have reportedly had thousands of safety incidents in internal and real-world tests in the last few months. These include efforts by agents to get information from the US Securities and Exchange Commission and Census Bureau, as well as confidential information from Australian and Canadian government sites. AI startup Hugging Face had earlier revealed that OpenAI agents had infiltrated its systems, one among a spate of such incidents.
“No governor has been more out-front on addressing the risks of AI than Governor Newsom,” Tara Gallegos, the governor’s director of communications, told Al Jazeera.
Monopoly of big AI companies
In his message vetoing the bill in September 2024, Newsom had said “the bill applies stringent standards to even the most basic functions” and noted that 32 of the world’s 50 leading AI companies are in California.
Industry representatives, too, had rallied against the bill.
“In essence, the bill is creating this disastrous regressive tax on AI innovation,” Anjney Midha, general partner at the Bay Area-based venture capital firm Andresen Horowitz, had said at the time. If enacted, it would force AI founders to move elsewhere, Midha warned.
“The bill was unworkable when it reached his desk,” Newsom’s spokesperson Gallegos told Al Jazeera.
But Hamid Ekbia, professor at Syracuse University and founding director of the Academic Alliance for AI Policy, says industry cannot be relied on to regulate itself.
“There is a need to break down the monopoly of the big AI companies,” Ekbia told Al Jazeera.
“Their financial stakes are too high,” to self-regulate, he said, referring to Open AI and Anthropic’s upcoming public offerings and tax breaks that some companies are reportedly taking advantage of to build data centres.
Newsom has now set up an expert committee to examine setting up a kill switch, which had been proposed in a more comprehensive manner in the original bill.
“SB 1047 [the bill that was vetoed] had a concrete architecture; the EO [executive order] only includes one aspect – the Kill Switch or shutdown/stoppage mechanisms, which is quite different and weaker than the ex ante termination obligation of SB 1047,” which required stronger safety measures even before training runs of the AI models could start, CAIDP’s Randolph said.
DAIR’s Hanna says that with the order, Newsom “is showing he is attentive without planning anything drastic”.
Building AI safety in real time
“We are building the field of AI safety in real time,” says Rebecca Finlay, chief executive officer of Partnership for AI, a nonprofit that works on technology governance, underscoring the challenges of regulating an industry growing at a meteoric pace.
Newsom has asked the California Emergency Services Office to send recommendations on AI regulation by November 15 and could convene a special legislative session to discuss how to implement these, possibly before his term ends.
This would be in contrast to the federal government, which has pushed for self-regulation by industry. CAIDP’s Randolph says California could play an important role in setting the floor for AI regulation given that much of the global AI industry is based there.
DAIR’s Hanna says Newsom is not only looking to show a contrast with US President Donald Trump, who believes in self-regulation by firms and last month signed a voluntary accord with several AI leaders, but also with possible Democratic contenders.
“With this, Newsom can look good on the primary debate stage,” she said.
Gallegos, the governor’s spokesperson, told Al Jazeera that “Governor Newsom isn’t interested in virtue-signalling or chasing headlines — he is leading the nation by taking a smarter, strategic, and effective approach to addressing frontier technology”.
Experts say that along with Newsom’s order setting up a committee to examine a kill switch, there is a need for measures for controls across the life cycle to reinforce safety.
“Safety needs to be built in. We issued 12 guidances across the lifecycle when the last ChatGPT model was released. There is a need for safety features throughout the life cycle,” of an AI model, Partnership for AI’s Finlay said.
As Newsom considers such recommendations from California agencies and the expert committee, Ekbia says governments “should take a lesson from what happened with social media. A handful of companies having control were able to do a lot of harm,” and regulate with an anticipatory approach and take on corporate monopolies.

Bringing HMS Bangor home cost more than four million
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:56:13 BST
22:56:13 KST

The heavy lift contract that carried the minehunter HMS Bangor back to Britain from Bahrain cost £4.13million, and the ship arrived on 29 November last year, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for the date of the return and the cost of the replacement heavy lift contract, following an answer of 8 September.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “HMS Bangor returned to the UK on 29 November 2025 via heavy lift. The cost of the heavy lift contract to bring her back to the UK was £4.13 million.”
Heavy lift means the ship was carried home aboard a semi-submersible transport vessel instead of sailing under her own power, an arrangement the Royal Navy uses for its mine countermeasures vessels on long passages.
Obese-Jecty had asked about a replacement heavy lift contract, and the £4.13 million figure covers the contract used; no explanation was given for why the original arrangement fell away.
HMS Bangor is a Sandown class single role minehunter, one of a class built with glass reinforced plastic hulls to keep their magnetic signature low enough to work safely in a minefield. The ships displace around 600 tonnes, carry a crew of roughly forty, and hunt mines with sonar, remotely operated vehicles and clearance divers. Several of the class spent years forward deployed to Bahrain as part of the Royal Navy mine countermeasures force in the Gulf, and the class is being paid off as the role moves to uncrewed systems operated from motherships.

‘I quit my tax office job to run my husband's TikTok’: Meet Israel's Korean food star Yong Park
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:54:28 UTC
22:54:28 KST

If you spend any time on TikTok, chances are you've come across Yong Park, one of Israel's hottest social media personalities. A Korean architect who now lives in Israel, Yong has become an online sensation thanks to his entertaining videos documenting life in his adopted country from his own perspective, with a particular focus on food. In just a year and a half, he has gained hundreds of thousands of followers and millions of views, becoming so popular that ahead of Rosh Hashanah, Israel's Channel 13 News even aired a video of him tasting gefilte fish.
Yong's following and view counts soared when he began posting videos teaching viewers how to prepare Korean dishes. His recipes include kimchi, fermented vegetables seasoned with chili and considered Korea's national dish; gimbap, rice and vegetable rolls; tteokbokki, rice cakes cooked in a sweet and spicy chili sauce; and the country's famous Korean fried chicken. When he samples Israeli food for his reviews, Yong rarely delivers a harsh verdict. Negative criticism is simply not part of his cultural approach, so his ratings range from "very good" for shawarma in pita bread to "so-so" for amba, the tangy mango condiment. The latter, pronounced in his accent, comes out sounding like "kaka kaka," much to his followers' amusement.
The person managing Yong's TikTok account is his Israeli wife, Zlata, who runs the operation from the couple's home in Ashkelon. It all began when they started posting videos about their lives as an intercultural couple. "We uploaded things we enjoy doing together and memories from Korea, and people started taking an interest," Zlata says. "One day, Yong was eating shawarma and wanted to share his opinion. We said, 'Let's just upload a video,' and it blew up, getting more than a million views. We never imagined it would go this far. People really love Yong. They tell us, 'You two are so adorable.'"
Which of Yong's videos has been the biggest hit so far?
Yong: "I showed people how to make a Korean sausage with vegetables, and it got 1.3 million views, along with tens of thousands of shares and saves. The video where I tried halva also got more than a million views."
Did you like it?
"Not really. Kaka kaka," he says, laughing.
Zlata: "Koreans have trouble pronouncing the Hebrew 'kh' sound. He calls matbucha 'matbuka,' and instead of calling me 'chaim sheli' [my life, a Hebrew term of affection], he says 'kayim sheli.' For some reason, people find that hilarious."
Yong, how did you get into cooking?
Yong: "I learned to cook because I don't like eating out. When Zlata and I used to have video calls while I was still in Korea, I'd cook while we talked and show her what I was making. She loved it. We started getting lots of comments from people asking for Korean recipes, so I began sharing them. So many people make the dishes, post their results and tag us."
‘You will be my wife’
Yong, 34, who speaks a mixture of English and Hebrew during the interview, was born and raised in Koya, near Seoul. He studied architecture for four years at a university in Seoul and spent two years serving in the South Korean military during his studies. "Military service is mandatory in Korea, just like in Israel," he explains. He went on to work for six years at an architecture and interior design firm before moving to Israel to reunite with Zlata.
Zlata, 33, was born and raised in Ashkelon to parents who immigrated from Uzbekistan. Her parents divorced when she was five, and she grew up as an only child with her mother, who works at an electronics factory in Ofakim. Zlata served in the Israeli Air Force and later began studying business administration at Ashkelon College. She dropped out midway through her studies to help support her mother financially. 
She subsequently began working at the Israel Tax Authority's offices in Ashkelon, a job she eventually left as the TikTok venture she had built with Yong took off. "My life changed within a year," she explains. "Suddenly, brands started approaching us for collaborations, and I needed to devote my time to it."
The couple met on Instagram, just as Zlata was becoming interested in Korean culture after watching the television series Squid Game and Yong was developing an interest in Israel, which he had already visited. "After watching 'Squid Game' sometime in late 2021, I thought, how cool, I'd love to go to Korea," Zlata recalls. 
"Everyone said, 'Are you crazy? Who goes there?' But I was already completely into it. I started looking at websites and joining Facebook groups about Korea. Yong happened to be in Israel at the time and noticed my interest. He sent me a message on Instagram saying, 'Hey, how are you? What's up?' I replied, and we started chatting. The next day, he flew back to Korea, so we never actually met. We moved on to video calls, and that's how things continued for a long time. Right from the beginning, he told me, 'You're going to be my wife.'"
How did you react?
"Come on, I was an Israeli girl who had never had anything to do with Korea. It was a little overwhelming. I remember thinking, Zlata, what are you doing with a Korean guy all of a sudden? But something inside me felt that this was right."
Yong: "I think it was love at first sight. I realized where things were heading before she did."
Zlata: "I couldn't quite process it. How was I supposed to have a relationship with someone who lived a 12-hour flight away? My friends said, 'Zlata, couldn't you have found someone from Europe?'"
Tell us about the first time you met in person.
Zlata: "He came to visit me in Israel a few months after everything started. I admit I had mixed feelings. We'd only just gotten to know each other, and suddenly I was supposed to host him around the clock. On one hand, it was stressful, but on the other, I was incredibly excited. I was still living with my mother, and she was so thrilled. Everyone fell in love with him as soon as they met him. They saw how happy he made me, and they appreciated that."
And how did the relationship develop from there?
"It was tough. Yong came to Israel every few months, but it felt strange being in a relationship with someone you only saw two or three times a year. Once we realized things were getting serious, the long-distance relationship became unbearable. Suddenly, celebrating holidays and birthdays without him became really difficult."
Yong: "It developed gradually. All those conversations, all the talking and planning, made us look forward to building a life together."
Zlata arrived in Korea for the first time on October 7, 2023, the day of the Hamas massacre in Israel. "I thought it was going to be the trip of a lifetime, but as soon as I landed, I started hearing what was happening back home, and I almost lost my mind," she recalls. 
"The day before I left, on October 5, I'd invited all my friends to a restaurant to say goodbye. One of them was Eden Gaz, who was murdered two days later at the Nova music festival along with her friend Stav Geta. Just two days earlier, Eden had given me a big hug and told me, 'Enjoy your trip and your time with Yong,' because she knew him and loved him. I couldn't believe any of it was happening. I stayed at Yong's parents' house and barely went outside. It took a month before flights resumed and I was able to return home."
How did Yong's family welcome you in Korea?
"Wow, I was so lucky. I got an amazing family. They're such wonderful, loving people."
During one of Zlata's visits to Korea, Yong got down on one knee and pulled out an engagement ring. "I was very emotional, but we both knew that was where things were heading," she says.
Why did you decide that Yong would move to Israel rather than you moving to Korea?
"He really loved Israel. He'd already been here twice before he even met me. The first time, he came with his parents on a trip. The second time, he was traveling around Europe with friends and decided to leave them and come back to Israel because he'd fallen in love with the country and the people. As for me, I can't leave Israel because I'm an only child and I don't want to leave my parents here alone."
Was it difficult to get permission from the Israeli authorities for Yong to live here?
"Generally speaking, South Koreans don't have many problems with the authorities. But after we submitted the application, Yong had to leave Israel for six months because he wasn't allowed to stay here before receiving approval. 
"I had a very difficult year. On January 9, 2025, I was celebrating my birthday at a restaurant with friends when I received the approval allowing him to enter Israel and get an Israeli ID card. You should have heard us screaming. It was unbelievable. He still has to choose between permanent residency and citizenship, and he'll probably choose residency because Korea doesn't generally allow dual citizenship. The difference, as we understand it, is that he won't be able to vote in Knesset elections."
Yong moved to Israel in January 2025, and the couple married on June 5, just one week before the outbreak of the first war between Israel and Iran. "We got married at Makom Bayam, a venue in Ashkelon, and had a beautiful sunset wedding. It was amazing," Zlata says excitedly. "Yong's parents couldn't come because traveling for so many hours is difficult for them, but we're going to Korea this month and they're planning to throw us a second wedding."
‘From here, we're only going up’
Two months ago, Yong took another significant step in his new career when he was cast in a children's and teenagers' drama series called Evacuees on Nickelodeon. The series follows teenagers who were evacuated from their homes in northern Israel because of the latest war. Yong plays Sian, an Asian chef who worked at a restaurant in Kiryat Shmona before being evacuated to a kibbutz himself. "Acting was another pleasant surprise that I never planned," he says. "I've never done anything like it before. It's a completely new experience for me."
How did you get the role?
"It turns out that the daughter of someone involved in the production knew me from TikTok. When they were looking for an Asian actor to play Sian, she told him about me."
So you didn't plan on becoming a TikTok star or an actor. What did you originally plan to do in Israel?
"I wanted to open a Korean restaurant, but shortly after I arrived in Israel, the war with Iran began."
How did you feel being caught up in a war that wasn't really yours?
"My family is Zlata, and Zlata's family is here, so it is my war too, in a way. I'd rather stay here with them. We have a strong army and people we can rely on. My parents were very worried. They were in touch with us every day. After all, war isn't something they're used to dealing with."
How did your parents react when you told them you were moving to Israel?
"My parents have always trusted me to know what I'm doing. They always said, 'If you fall in love, it doesn't matter what country she's from or what religion she belongs to. We trust your choices.' The only thing they care about is my happiness."
What do you think of Israel?
"Wow, I love Israel, but it's really expensive. The first time I went to a supermarket, I was shocked. I bought a bottle of Coke at a convenience store and couldn't believe they wanted 10 or 12 shekels for it. In Seoul, you can buy three bottles for that price. On the other hand, if I get lost, someone will always come over and offer to help. People here are very warm, whereas Koreans tend to be a little colder and more reserved."
Is there anything about Israeli culture you find difficult?
"Look, in Korea, a line is a line. People stand in a perfectly straight queue, like a ruler. Here, everyone pushes in, and nobody seems to care who got there first. Everything is 'yalla, yalla' [come on, hurry up]. Everyone is so intense, for better and worse. Public services are also incredibly slow and complicated. In Korea, service providers are very helpful and efficient, whereas here it seems to be the opposite. For example, the checkout lines at supermarkets barely move. They're so slow it drives me crazy."
Do you feel the cultural differences in your relationship?
Zlata: "There was a communication gap in the beginning. I'm Israeli. I say exactly what I think, very directly. In Korean culture, that kind of directness isn't considered acceptable."
Not everyone is enthusiastic about your relationship.
"That's true. We've received nasty and racist comments because Yong isn't Jewish. People ask me why I'm with him and say it's assimilation. They don't understand that what matters isn't someone's religion, but the person themselves. And I was lucky enough to find a perfect person. Even when I explain that our children will be Jewish, they refuse to accept it. We believe everyone should do what's right for them and mind their own business. 
"There's a Jewish saying that basic decency comes before religious observance, and there's also a proper way to speak to people. We don't let those comments bother us. The love we receive is truly incredible, and most importantly, Yong and I have found the kind of love most people can only dream of. I wouldn't give that up for anything in the world."
Do people already recognize you on the street?
"Of course. So many people ask for selfies, from five-year-olds to people in their 60s. I don't know if you ever really get used to it. Not long ago, we were in Ashdod, and there were some Israelis who live in Canada and were visiting Israel. I could already see them looking at us, so I said, 'Yes, yes, it's Yong.' They came over and said, 'We're crazy about you two! All our friends in Canada watch Yong.'"
Do people in Korea know Yong is famous in Israel?
Yong: "My parents aren't on social media at all, and my friends aren't really the TikTok generation anymore. Besides, they don't understand Hebrew. When we go to Korea, we'll show them all the videos."
Zlata: "I want to surprise them. When we get there and I show his mother what a star he is here, she's going to be in shock."
Can you make a good living from TikTok alone?
"Yes, it's a good income. We have quite a few commercial partnerships, including with Rami Levy, Of Tov, Beit Hashita, the Super Fly credit card, Tali Grapes and others. Sometimes we can earn 10,000 shekels for a video, sometimes even more. So thank God, we're doing well."
What's your role in the business?
"I manage the whole operation. I handle inquiries, speak with clients, negotiate prices and what each deal includes, and sign contracts. Sometimes I also appear in the videos alongside Yong. We want to keep growing and expand into other lifestyle areas, such as travel and flights. We've signed with Roberto's agency, so we now have professional representation. I really believe the only way from here is up."
What do you think is the secret behind your popularity?
Yong: "People like authenticity. They're also curious about our relationship."
Who does the cooking at home?
Zlata: "Usually Yong. I only cook on Fridays, when I make matbucha and fish, and sometimes bake challah. Since I met Yong and discovered his delicious cooking, I honestly have no reason to go into the kitchen. I love everything he makes, especially tteokbokki, japchae and mandu."
Are you already thinking about starting a family?
Yong: "We're ready and we want to. We're waiting for God. He decides."
Zlata: "Of course we want children. God willing, we'll come back from Korea and start working on it."

North Korea tests new AI-powered precision-guided torpedo: KCNA
North Korea said Saturday it has conducted an underwater test of a new AI-powered high-speed precision-guided torpedo weapon system, Yonhap reported.
North Korea test-fired the Zam-2.0 super-speed precision-guided torpedo weapon system Thursday to confirm the successful technical upgrade of the weapon, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). It did not disclose further details of the weapon.
North Korea said AI technology was applied to the target detection and the guidance function of the torpedo.
"The test proved the core technology for raising the efficiency of propulsion and the performance of rocket propulsion devices," the KCNA said, adding more than 180 rounds of related tests have been conducted over the past five years.
Experts said the newly disclosed weapon system could be a "supercavitating torpedo" given the North's claims that rocket propulsion devices were fitted on the torpedo, and the term "super-speed" used to describe the new torpedo.
A supercavitating torpedo is an ultra-high-speed torpedo that creates an air bubble in the nose to overcome water resistance and travel at higher speeds than conventional torpedoes.

Antarctica’s Thwaites Glacier melting faster than thought, could double sea-level contribution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:47:06 UTC
22:47:06 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
17 October 2026•Update: 17 October 2026
One of the world’s largest glaciers is melting much faster than previously understood and could contribute about twice as much to global sea-level rise by the end of the century as earlier projections suggested.
New research published this week in Nature Communications found that Antarctica’s Thwaites Glacier is rapidly losing mass as warm ocean water pushes several kilometers beneath it and melts the ice from below.
Researchers estimate the process could cause Thwaites to contribute up to 30 millimeters (1.2 inches) to global sea-level rise by 2100, even without additional warming beyond recent conditions.
In previous conventional ice-sheet models, scientists estimated that the Thwaites Glacier would contribute roughly 15 millimeters (about 0.6 inches) to global sea-level rise by the year 2100.
Nicknamed the Doomsday Glacier because of the potentially severe consequences of its collapse, Thwaites covers around 192,000 square kilometers (74,000 square miles) in West Antarctica — roughly the size of Senegal and larger than the US state of Florida.
It forms part of the much larger West Antarctic Ice Sheet and, together with glaciers including Pine Island, acts as a barrier holding back vast quantities of inland ice.
Thwaites currently accounts for around 4% of global sea-level rise and has lost more than 1 trillion tons of ice since 2000, with losses continuing at roughly 50 billion tons annually.
Scientists have closely monitored the glacier since discovering in the 1980s that it was retreating rapidly.
Warm ocean water driven beneath the ice is considered a key factor. Human-caused climate change, particularly warming linked to fossil fuel emissions, is raising ocean temperatures and increasing pressure on glaciers worldwide.
The latest study focused on Thwaites’ “grounding zone,” where ice resting on bedrock begins to float on the sea.
Previous models often treated the grounding line as a fixed boundary. Researchers instead modeled a broader zone where tides repeatedly lift and lower the ice, allowing warm seawater to penetrate farther underneath.
Lead author Mattia Poinelli, a project scientist at UCLA, said this “tidal pumping” enables warm water to reach deep beneath the ice and cause vigorous melting.
The new modeling also raises concerns that Thwaites could lose contact with the underwater Mouginot Ridge, which currently helps restrain its movement.
Simulations consistent with recent observations indicated around a 60% chance of the glacier becoming detached from the ridge by 2100, potentially as early as the late 2030s.
Researchers warned that such a shift could accelerate the glacier's retreat and expose coastal communities worldwide to greater sea-level rise and flooding risks than previously projected.

Olesia Avramenko: ‘Ukrainian Art Preserves What the World Is Gradually Losing’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:47:00 UTC
22:47:00 KST

Olesia Avramenko has spent more than four decades researching Ukrainian art. Every project she undertakes – whether an article, a book, a solo exhibition, or a group plein-air painting session in Crimea or Kaniv – it always begins with a fascination of the person whose work she sets out to explore with such care and passion.
Her new monographs on Ukrainian artists are always major events in the art world.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
This year, Avramenko received the Taras Shevchenko National Prize of Ukraine. In an interview with Kyiv Post, the acclaimed Ukrainian art historian recalls her father’s final advice, reflects on the artists who have become the subjects of her monographs, and discusses the Ukrainian art school, the war, and how Ukrainian art is perceived internationally. She also speaks about beauty – something she says she has come to feel with particular intensity during Russia’s full-scale invasion.
                                                                                                                                                                         Olesia Avramenko at the presentation of her book about Viktor Zaretsky at the exhibition commemorating the 100th anniversary of his birth. 2025. (Photo by Serhii Mazurash)                             
Kyiv Post: You were born into a family of a journalist and writer, and a philologist and educator. What first drew you to art history?
Russian Glide Bombs Strike Kherson, Killing 1, Injuring 33
Olesia Avramenko: It is an almost mystical story. My father, Oleksandr Avramenko, was a journalist and writer. I was 14 when, one February evening, we were alone together. He called me over, asked me to sit beside him, and wanted to know what profession I was planning to choose.
“A journalist, like you,” I replied confidently, expecting his support.
Instead, my father looked surprised. “Why?”
“I want to see the world and travel,” I answered naively.
But he objected anxiously. He said journalism was not a suitable profession for a girl, that I might end up as a reporter for a district newspaper in the USSR, writing about harvests, milk yields, and socialist competitions between collective farm brigades. It was hard, thankless work, he said.
“Then what should I become?” I asked, confused.
“An art historian! You will work in a museum, in a quiet environment, and write about paintings and artists.”
I disagreed and went to bed. The next morning, my father’s heart stopped. And at the very moment he was dying, my alarm clock rang.
For many years afterward, I woke up at precisely that time. I came to understand that my father had left me a final wish. I decided I would become an art historian and never change my surname. And that is exactly what I did.
I fall in love with the talent of the people I write about, and that helps me create, too. I rarely accept commissions. I do so only when a subject, a personality, or a body of work genuinely captures my interest.
This is both my strength and my vulnerability. It is a strength because my writing is passionate and leans toward literature. Perhaps this is where I most closely follow in my father’s footsteps.
Your books appeal to a wide readership and explore artists as different as Kateryna Bilokur, Ivan Prykhodko, Oleh Tistol, Anatoly Kryvolap, and Hanna Kryvolap. What connects them?
I would not try to group them together. They are like trees standing in a vast field: each is magnificent in its own right and knows how to withstand a storm. This is neither a grove nor a forest. Still, perhaps they are united by the same soil in which they grow. (Smiles.)
One way or another, Ukrainian artists share powerful cultural roots. They are sensitive, yet they have great confidence in themselves and their choices, and the strength to defend them. They are educated, have broad horizons, and possess a powerful sense of national identity. They also often have a distinctive character and a Baroque temperament shaped by Ukraine’s dramatic history.
                                                                                                                                                                         At the opening of the art exhibition Ukrainian Identification. Anatoly Kryvolap, Ihor Stupachenko. Murals of the Church of the Protection of the Holy Mother of God. Curated by Olesia Avramenko, 2019. (Image courtesy of Olesia Avramenko’s personal archive)                             
The war has radically changed international attention to Ukrainian culture. Is there a risk that the world will come to see Ukrainian art primarily through the lens of war?
We must emerge from this terrible ordeal imposed on us with dignity, defeat the invasion, and save Ukraine. For now, the lens of war is unavoidable when the world looks at our country. The international community must not close its eyes to the scale and horror of the tragedy unfolding on our soil. When your neighbor’s house is on fire, the flames can spread to other rooftops.
The artists who have left Ukraine but are doing more than simply trying to survive. Through their work, they are raising a powerful outcry about the bloody war in their homeland. They also use the proceeds from their art to support Ukraine’s Armed Forces.
I am really proud of those who have stayed in Ukraine and continue working with determination. It is important for the international community to look inside Ukraine, into artists’ studios and exhibitions, and see what they are creating.
Consider Oleksandr Dubovyk, who is 95, or the 80-year-old Anatoly Kryvolap and Anatoly Kushch, alongside their colleagues Viktor Sydorenko, Oleh Tistol, Mykola Matsenko, Matviy Vaisberg, Hanna Kryvolap, and Nikita Titov. There are also artists working in Uzhhorod, Ivano-Frankivsk, Kryvyi Rih, Lviv, and elsewhere.
It is here, in Ukraine, that extraordinary ideas with significance for the entire world are emerging, even at this deeply traumatic moment. Artists of immense power and talent continue to create.
What does the world still fail to understand about Ukrainian art?
Its humanity. Ukrainian art is deeply heartfelt, profound, and penetrating. It stirs emotions without manipulation, doing so with nobility.
To a considerable extent, it grows out of an academic tradition. Ukrainian artists know how to draw, understand composition, and know how to present their work. With this foundation, they can move forward and explore themselves through other materials and forms.
It is like singing, music, or ballet: you have to know the fundamentals. At a certain point, the international art world decided that a gesture alone was enough – without skill, articulation, or command of the language.
But can you write poetry without knowing the language?
I believe craftsmanship and taste will always remain valuable, alongside profound ideas and a contemporary artistic language.
                                                                                                                                                                         Against the background of a portrait by Matviy Vaisberg, 2024. (Image courtesy of Olesia Avramenko’s personal archive)                             
What sustains you during the war? What are your main sources of strength today?
I have become acutely sensitive to the beauty around me and to the flow of life itself – so much so that it can be painful. There is death all around, and yet you are still alive…
Yet sometimes you can look at a work of art, and it brings you back to life.
My work sustains me. When I am writing a book, I live inside it. I fall asleep thinking about how to structure a chapter and what to change when a new idea emerges.
At the same time, I am not simply working on a book. I work at the Modern Art Research Institute, where my texts are reviewed by doctors of science and approved by the academic council. It is serious scholarly work.
You have inspired artists, and many have painted your portrait. How many portraits do you have, and is there one that holds a special place in your collection?
I have never counted them. There are probably about ten. (Smiles.)
Over time, Viktor Zaretsky’s portrait “A Cup of Coffee” has become the most important to me.
                                                                                                                                                                         Portrait by Viktor Zaretsky, A Cup of Coffee. Olesia, 1990.                             
And this year, another portrait appeared in my life – one I had not even known existed. Some time ago, the painter Viktor Hryhorov, an artist known for his monumental painting, invited me to his studio to sit for a portrait. I never went.
This year, I published a book about him. In response, an acquaintance who is a collector gave me a large drawing and said, “This is your portrait.”
Everything came together – the timing, the feeling, and the way I looked at that time. For me, it was a special sign, arriving years later.
All these portraits bear witness to relationships: those that happened and those that never came to be. Today, they offer me another way to leaf through the pages of my own life and often to discover the artist anew.
