Coordinated campaign against Russian logistics
The strikes on Roboavia and the missile brigade depot arrive as Ukrainian forces intensify deep interdiction against transport bottlenecks, industrial suppliers, and unmanned aviation installations within the Russian Federation and occupied territories.
Throughout Friday, Oct. 16, and early Saturday morning, Ukrainian precision units struck a strategic railway bridge spanning the Unecha River near Sloboda-Seletska in the Bryansk region, complicating the movement of heavy armor, ammunition, and petroleum products by rail toward frontline sectors.
Concurrently across Russian-occupied territory in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, Ukrainian fire struck Russian military material-technical supply warehouses in Novoandriivka, Mykilske, and the port city of Mariupol, alongside an active Russian UAV command and control post near Malynivka.

Tunisians stage biggest protest in years against President Saied
Thousands of Tunisians joined the largest protest in years against President Kais Saied in the capital on Saturday, accusing him of undermining democracy and mishandling the economy in a growing challenge to his rule.
The demonstration, led by the major UGTT labour union and civil society groups, comes as Tunisia grapples with an economic crisis, worsening public services, recurring water and power cuts, and shortages of medicines and essential goods.
Saied seized broad powers in 2021 and 2022, dissolving parliament, dismissing dozens of judges and ruling by decree, moves that opponents described as a coup.
Rights groups say he has intensified a crackdown on civil society, journalists and opposition figures. Saied rejects those allegations, saying he is not a dictator, and has accused his opponents of engineering economic crises to fuel social unrest.
In a rare show of unity, opposition parties from across the political spectrum joined lawyers, doctors, journalists, unemployed people and civil society groups in marching along Habib Bourguiba Avenue, a focal point of the 2011 protests that helped trigger the Arab Spring uprisings.
The protest poses a significant challenge to Saied after years of divisions weakened the opposition's ability to mobilise large crowds.
"Silence will no longer be acceptable...the state cannot built by concentrating all powers in the hand of one person", Slah Eddine Salmi, head of the UGTT, told the rally.
Hundreds of police were deployed across the capital.
Protesters chanted: "No fear, power belongs to the people!" and "The prisons are full, people are hungry!" They also revived the iconic slogan of the 2011 uprising, which was notably peaceful in Tunisia: "The people want the fall of the regime!"
They called for the release of Saied's critics and demanded an end to what they described as attacks on trade union rights. Some carried banners expressing frustration over unemployment and pollution.
"Enough is enough! The country is collapsing. We suffer from power and water cuts, and one crisis after another," said Yassine Gharseli, a protester from Sfax, about 250 km (155 miles) south of Tunis.
"I came from Sfax to stand up for my freedom, and I'm not about to give up, even if I become the last voice in the country."

Protesters clash with police during nationwide demonstrations in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:44:42 UTC
22:44:42 KST

Tear gas and unrest as hundreds of thousands protest for reforms in France
More than 500,000 gather in Paris and other cities for protests uniting students, teachers, unions and ‘yellow vests’.
Paris, France – Marianne, the statue personifying the French Republic, towers over Place de la Republique in Paris, wearing a yellow vest.
At the base of the monument, the faces of the three allegorical figures representing Liberty, Equality and Fraternity are streaked with black tears. Above them, tear gas canisters arc through the air, filling the square with smoke.
This was the scene as tens of thousands of protesters, mostly young people, rallied at the heart of the French capital on Saturday in the latest act of a movement that has been rocking France to the core for more than a month now.
The demonstrations were spearheaded by students demanding education reforms but quickly swelled to channel mounting anger over failing public services, rising living costs and a future that feels increasingly out of reach.
“Everybody has come together asking the government for a final time to hear us loud and clear because it is not OK what is happening,” said a high school student who asked not to be identified, her fist raised in the air.
“We are here because we want to take back our rights,” she said.
The social movement, hailed by some as historical, has gained cross-class, cross-working sector support, uniting groups including remnants of the “yellow vests” – the grassroots cost-of-living protests that shook France in 2018.
The presence of nurses, human rights lawyers, firefighters, parents, teachers and some remnants of the “yellow vests” on Saturday was a testament to how pupils have catalysed a social discontent running deep across French society.
The CGT, one of France’s major labour unions, also backed the protests, calling for “higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people’s needs”.
Authorities said 550,000 people protested across the country on Saturday, including 110,000 in the capital.
‘Young people are anxious’
A recurring theme among protesters interviewed by Al Jazeera was that the system has failed them, violence is used too casually, and that any prospect of a better future looks bleak.
Anxiety was a recurring word.
“Young people are anxious about their futures and their failing schools; the yellow vests are distressed by the cost of living, which is literally exploding; and there are existential anxieties regarding the geopolitical situation,” said Jean Pierre, a member of the French Human Rights League. “That is why there are so many people out there; it is the result of a whole host of anxieties that people are feeling today,”
Parents were also present. Amelie, a mother of three, did not want to provide her last name. With eyes tickling over the smell of tear gas, she said it was important for her to support them.
“We will keep up the pressure to make sure someone is taking care of our children’s future,” she said, while standing next to her teen daughter.
At each corner of the square, there was a heavy police presence of large numbers of riot police officers dressed in full gear.
Gas canisters were launched in the early hours of the protest at noon despite a scarce presence of people. Yet, from 2pm onwards (12:00 GMT), the square was packed, and it became tense.
Clashes broke out between the police and some of the protesters, who threw firework mortars at officers and set one car and a newspaper stand on fire, sending a thick cloud of black smoke up into the sky.
The smell of tear gas could be felt from streets away, as well as the sound of what seemed like stun grenades that became more frequent as the day progressed.
Coffee shops and boutiques closed for the day as firefighters’ sirens crossed the city. Still, the vast majority of the protesters peacefully joined the march that started moving towards northwestern Paris.
Elsewhere in France, in the southern city of Marseille, demonstrators breached the town hall and looted shops; in Lyon media reports said a tourism office was set ablaze.
France’s Ministry of the Interior said that at least 400 people had been arrested after violent incidents involving hooded individuals, including in Paris, Marseille in the south, Rennes in the northwest, Toulouse in the southwest and Angers in the west.
“Such actions include attempted looting, confrontations with law enforcement, the setting of fires to street furniture and the targeting of seats of power and media outlets,” it said, blaming the unrest on what it described as the “ultra-left”.
Bruno Cautres, a researcher at the Paris-based Center for Political Research, told Al Jazeera that Saturday’s events are the “culmination of different mobilisations” that emerged out of frustrations about high taxes combined with a significant national debt and deficit that is preventing the government from satisfying public demands.
“The French are asking themselves where are we going as a country? How are we going to get out of this budget crisis?” Cautres said.
No easy way out
The protests began in mid-September at a high school in the Paris suburb of Creteil, where students took to the streets over dilapidated buildings, overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and what they see as a deeply unequal education system.
Saturday’s mobilisation followed calls on social media to revive the “yellow vests” movement, which emerged in 2018 against diesel prices but quickly morphed into a movement against President Emmanuel Macron’s perceived bias in favour of the elite.
It is also taking place in the last stretch of Macron’s presidency amid a highly polarising political landscape before crucial elections next year, which could pave the way for Europe’s second-largest economy to be led by a far-right party, the National Rally.
Macron appealed for calm on Friday, the eve of the protests. “There is a constitutional right to protest and to express oneself. But this right comes with the need to respect. Respect for people, respect for property, and therefore a commitment not to insult or destroy,” he said in Brussels.
But the government has no easy way out. France has been trying to reduce its ballooning public debt but has failed so far to reassure investors, pushing the government borrowing costs to their highest levels in more than 20 years.

Will Paramount’s creation of Skydance test France’s cultural exception?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:43:00 UTC
22:43:00 KST

Will Paramount’s creation of Skydance test France’s cultural exception?
Skydance’s $110 billion creation tests whether France’s cultural exception can still compel a leveraged global media giant to fund, protect and prioritise French creativity, or merely treat it as a compliance cost.
The completion this month of Paramount’s $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery has created Skydance: a media behemoth that, as a result of the transaction, comprises some of Hollywood’s most recognisable studios, including Warner Brothers, Paramount Pictures, HBO, Paramount +, a vast television portfolio, as well as news platforms, CNN and CBS.
The takeover was months in the making and garnered much public attention. What started as a tête-à-tête bidding war at the end of 2025 against Netflix culminated in a federal ruling against the 12 US states that tried to block the transaction on antitrust grounds at the end of September – just a week before final approval.
Read moreParamount completes takeover of Warner Bros, creating media behemoth Skydance
As film industry opponents feared job cuts, media groups worried about the editorial independence of a news platform under David Ellison, whose family has close ties to Republican US President Donald Trump. But from a French perspective, the development may cultivate a narrative that is less a question of whether yet another media giant can succeed in presenting true competition against the likes of Netflix or Canal+, and more about how a heavily indebted, consolidated global studio can operate profitably inside of one of the world’s most protected audiovisual markets.
Creative works and cultural products are required to be handled differently when it comes to international trade laws, according to France’s “cultural exception” policy. It hinges on a unique arrangement: international films and platforms may sell to French audiences, but they must actively contribute to preserve, invest in and stimulate France’s creative economy. Ellison’s deal therefore interrogates whether this principle can remain viable when the counterparty becomes larger, more leveraged and more focused on global scale.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Can Skydance afford French content?
Skydance began life with nearly $80 billion in debt, though it aims to reduce company costs by $6 billion in “structural and tech-stack cost savings” over the next three years, according to the Financial Times. One of its first post-merger moves has included price increases on Discovery+, while reports indicate the firm’s plans to combine the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services into a single platform or bundle.
This doesn’t make French investment impossible. Indeed, consolidation may benefit French cinema by increasing the amount the company is required to invest locally under France’s SMAD regime.
Introduced in 2021 and enforced by France’s multimedia regulator, Arcom, the SMAD regime requires any foreign on-demand audiovisual service provider targeting France to contribute 20-25 percent of its French revenue towards European and French-language productions. A subsequent Paramount-HBO operation would aggregate subscription revenue, increasing the firm’s local content obligations.
Read moreParamount CEO says politics fueling Warner Bros. merger battle
In the streaming universe, a related battle is underway among Netflix, Prime Video and Disney+. In July, the platforms filed appeals with France’s highest administrative court – the Conseil d’ État – to contest an amendment to the rule introduced in January this year that requires them to dedicate 20 percent of their investment requirement in French content specifically to animation, documentaries and live performance programming. The streamers argue that this “over-regulation” infringes on creative freedom and creates an unsustainable financial burden. But the court has not yet issued a final ruling on the legal challenges.
"These new rules suddenly double our obligation to invest in these genres, target streaming services exclusively and end up dictating our content offerings without taking audience expectations into account," Pauline Dauvin, vice president of Netflix France, said in an opinion column.
Pledging plurality
But scale does not guarantee cultural diversity.
Considering that the deal would enable Skydance to wield significant purchase power alongside other Hollywood heavyweights Sony, Disney and Universal, the transaction was submitted to the European Commission (EC) for regional approval, which it passed in July, subject to specific conditions.
At film production level, the EC found the conglomerate’s studios to be suitably competitive. But at a distribution level, it stipulated that the company would need to unravel its ties from its Universal-Paramount joint venture, United International Pictures, within thirteen months of financial close, noting a “high concentration” in European Economic Area markets.
The transaction would have meant Skydance had advantageous distribution channels leading to “worse rental and distribution terms for cinema operators, ultimately disadvantaging consumers”, the EC wrote. It added that the conglomerate would also need to refrain from entering joint distribution arrangements for ten years and to avoid sharing releases with those also handling Universal or Disney rights in relevant markets.
Such redress is important for French exhibitors and distributors. While it does not prevent Skydance from fulfilling its role as a formidable supplier of content – indeed, as part of the firm’s legally binding antitrust settlements with the 12 US states and the US Department of Justice, Skydance is required to produce at least 30 films per year for its first two years; rising to 32 films for the subsequent three, with penalties for shortfalls – it at least preserves a measure of plurality in how its films reach French cinemas.
Bloody broadcast
The key question perhaps is what type of content receives the funds?
In a joint statement titled “Bleeding public broadcasting: the shame of the Republic” and published last month via the Civil Society of Authors, Directors and Producers, France’s leading film production and director unions, including the Trade Union for independent film, animation and audiovisual production (SPI), expressed fear that a merged giant is likely to favour global franchises, English-language formats and algorithm-friendly brands over smaller French films and original dramas.
Watch moreCannes, Canal+, Bolloré, blacklists: Is France's cultural diversity under threat?
In the context of bargaining asymmetry, it is possible that independent French producers – already navigating funding pressures and platform concentration – could come face-to-face with a single transatlantic buyer with the capacity to demand self-serving favourable rights and production models. And with every euro of compliance likely to be contested, there is potential for the long-term value of French intellectual property to erode, even where headline investment obligations are formally met.
On home turf, there is ongoing contention surrounding Canal+’s announcement last month that it is entering exclusive negotiations to acquire a minority stake in French cinema group UGC.
“Since its creation in 1984, Canal+ has been the number one partner and supporter of French and European cinema,” CEO of Canal+ Maxime Saada said in the group’s statement.
“This transaction demonstrates the group’s commitment to Cinema and theatrical exhibition, which play a vital role in showcasing and enhancing the value of films,” he added.
Subject to agreement by shareholders, the deal offers Canal+ the option to take full control of the UGC Group from 2028.
The news followed the production house’s announced commitment at the end of July to invest “€980 million over five years in support of French and European cinema, starting in 2028”.
‘Chronologie des médias’ under strain?
France’s chronologie des médias constitutes a pillar of its system. It is a framework that sees box office features wait around 15-17 months before moving from screen to subscription platforms. The delay serves to protect cinema owners and ticket sales while channelling levies into the state-managed National Centre for Cinema and Moving Image’s financial ecosystem.
And so Skydance’s creation sharpens this tension. If the group wants its blockbusters to reach French viewers quickly, it must either respect the long release date windows or limit its cinema-wide releases (and box office turnover). But with a leveraged deal that puts the firm under pressure to monetise its strongest franchises across as many territories and platforms as possible – leaning on speed and scale, either option is likely to cost.
The danger is perhaps less that Skydance will bypass France, and more that the country may concede to the pressures of international dominance, resulting in fewer, safer, more commercial films. The firm could balance French release windows and funding local content if it treats the market as strategic ground rather than a regulatory obstacle course. But debt service, revenue targets and shareholder pressure risk rendering French-language content as compliance costs over creative priority. A possible outcome is selective investment: visible flagship French productions alongside reduced appetite for mid-budget and independent work.

Pope Leo discharged from hospital after cancer operation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

13:41:49 UTC

Pope Leo has been discharged from hospital in Rome after undergoing an operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung.
Leo, 71, was deemed “fit for discharge”, his doctors, Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement published by the Vatican.
He walked unaided from the hospital on Saturday afternoon, to cheers from well-wishers.
Leo, who in May last year became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church, has been in the Gemelli hospital since Tuesday, when doctors removed part of his right lung in order to extract the tumour.
“Considering the blood tests, the chest X-ray done this morning, and evaluating the clinical picture, the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge,” the statement said.
Doctors said on Wednesday that Leo’s recovery from the operation was progressing normally. They are waiting for the results of tests to determine whether the cancer has spread and if more treatment will be needed.
Leo was diagnosed with the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma.
The pontiff celebrated mass in his room on the 10th-floor of the Gemelli hospital in the north-west of the Italian capital before being discharged.
The Vatican said he would recite the Angelus prayer on Sunday “from the window of the papal apartment”. It was during his angelus last week, in a rare moment of Vatican transparency, that Leo made the shock announcement to the crowd gathered in St Peter’s Square that a small nodule on his lung had been detected during a check-up.
The pope has worked from hospital, including making a phone call on Friday to Vladimir Putin, during which he urged the Russian president to call a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
The Vatican had originally estimated a week-long stay in hospital. The pope’s appointments had been cancelled until 20 October.
However, the pope’s surgeon told Vatican media on Saturday that there were “no clinical reasons” to prevent him from traveling to Latin America as scheduled from 6 to 17 November.
Dr Stefano Margaritora said that “the Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery” and that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery “in another 10 days or so”.
“As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place,” he told Vatican News.
Before the cancer diagnosis, Leo, who enjoys sports, especially playing tennis, was generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.
The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish a high-security papal suite.

Why Trump’s latest White House press secretary lasted just five days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:41:49 UTC
22:41:49 KST

Why Trump’s latest White House press secretary lasted just five days
Katie Zacharia is the shortest-serving White House press secretary after a rocky tenure, but she’s not the first to go.
United States President Donald Trump’s latest press secretary has been let go after just five days on the job, following a widely criticised first – and only – White House news conference and amid scrutiny of her credentials.
Trump told reporters on Friday that he believed the press had been harsh towards his new top spokesperson, Katie Zacharia, but that he had advised her to “reconsider” the role.
Shortly after, Al Jazeera and other media confirmed that Zacharia would be “transitioning out” of the position.
That made her the shortest-serving press secretary in US history – even shorter than the tenure of Anthony Scaramucci, the former White House communications director who was fired after 10 days on the job during Trump’s first term in office in 2017.
His sacking gave rise to the term “one Scaramucci” – or “a Mooch” – which journalists and White House observers use jokingly as a measure of time to predict how long Trump officials would last in their jobs. Now, a new unit of time – “one Zacharia” – is only half as long.
Recalling his own White House stint this week, Scaramucci wrote on X: “Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.”
Here’s what we know about Zacharia’s brief tenure:
Why was Katie Zacharia removed as White House press secretary?
The White House has not given an official reason for Zacharia’s departure, but it came amid mounting concerns about her competency and professional background.
During her first and only news conference on Tuesday, Zacharia appeared uneasy at the podium and struggled at times to get through her sentences. She fumbled her words while looking down at her notes, once confused the words “husband” and “president” and ended the briefing after 14 minutes, taking only three questions from reporters.
Scrutiny intensified after it emerged that Zacharia, who has a law degree and described herself as “an attorney”, had studied law at university but never passed the bar exam required to practice law in the US. She later claimed she had worked as a lawyer in China.
Conservative Fox News host Sean Hannity asked Zacharia during an awkward interview on Thursday: “Why didn’t you just say: ‘I never practised law’?”
Following news of her departure, Zacharia wrote on X that it had been “an honour” to work for Trump, calling him a “kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man”.
How was her one White House briefing received?
Zacharia, who took over from former press secretary Karoline Leavitt, was widely criticised as unpolished and unprepared during her appearance before the White House press corps on Tuesday this week, even by many of Trump’s allies.
During Hannity’s interview with Zacharia, he noted that she had been “widely panned” for her performance.
Conservative journalist and commentator Megyn Kelly said Zacharia needed “to present as a serious person”.
Jen Psaki, a former White House press secretary who worked under Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, compared Zacharia’s troubled briefing to a comedy skit. “Maybe this whole White House press secretary thing isn’t really for Katie,” she said. “It’s not for everybody.”
As a fellow White House deportee, Scaramucci gave Zacharia some advice. “Speaking as the world’s leading expert on short White House tenures: turn off the news and go enjoy your family. In time you’ll realize that the Universe did you a major favor,” he wrote on X.
Who will take over White House press briefings now?
That remains to be seen.
The White House has not announced a permanent replacement, and Trump told Fox News he is “not in a hurry” to fill the role.
The vacancy leaves Trump without a top spokesperson as the US remains mired in a conflict with Iran and heads into crucial midterm elections next month.
How many press secretaries has Trump gone through?
Zacharia was the sixth person to serve as White House press secretary under Trump. He went through four of the officials during his first term and, so far, two in his second.
Zacharia’s predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, had held the position since the start of Trump’s second term in January 2025. She resigned in August to spend more time with her children.
Trump’s first-term press secretaries were Kayleigh McEnany, Stephanie Grisham, Sarah Huckabee Sanders and Sean Spicer.
McEnany and Spicer now work in media. McEnany hosts several shows on Fox News, while Spicer contributing to NewsNation and has launched his own podcast.
Huckabee Sanders currently serves as the governor of her home state of Arkansas, where she is seeking re-election on November 3.
Grisham left the press secretary position after less than a year in 2020 and became First Lady Melania Trump’s chief of staff. She resigned that role after the January 6, 2021 insurrection and has since become a major critic of the US president.
Which other Trump-appointed officials have been fired?
Zacharia joins a roll call of Trump administration officials to be pushed out during his second term.

The incidents occurred days apart during an air-to-air refueling exercise and simulated aerial combat training, with both objects spotted above 10,000 feet.
In the first incident, an RAF Airbus Voyager tanker was refueling a Typhoon fighter near Cromer, Norfolk, when an unidentified object passed so close that the tanker pilot reflexively ducked.
The commander reported the encounter to military controllers, according to the newspaper.
On Feb. 23, a Typhoon pilot practicing aerial combat with another fighter near Humberside spotted a black circular object passing approximately 300 feet above the aircraft.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said enhanced vigilance and improved detection capabilities had strengthened its ability to identify, record and assess potential drone activity.
The spokesperson said Britain was investing more than £2 billion ($2.67 billion) in broader air defense and counter-drone capabilities, including upgrades and maintenance for the Typhoon fleet.
The ministry added that reported drone sightings were not necessarily hostile and that it had measures available to respond if the activity was assessed as posing a credible threat.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Times on October 17, the exercises will focus on preparing European forces for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine as part of security arrangements intended to deter renewed Russian aggression.
The drills will test the movement of military personnel, coordination between national armed forces, and the delivery of essential supplies, including fuel and food. These logistical preparations are considered necessary for any future deployment of European troops to Ukrainian territory.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting confirmed that thousands of military personnel would take part in the exercises next month. Streeting said the training would help participating countries prepare to support Ukraine’s military training requirements and post-war reconstruction.
The planned exercises form part of the Coalition of the Willing initiative, which brings together countries working on potential security guarantees for Ukraine following a cessation of hostilities.
According to The Times, the training will bring multinational units together to practice operating alongside one another, with particular attention to the practical requirements of moving and sustaining troops across borders.
The coalition’s plans have developed through a series of discussions between Ukraine and its European partners over the possible deployment of an international security contingent.
In January 2026, Ukraine, the United Kingdom, and France signed a declaration of intent concerning the potential deployment of multinational forces following a peace agreement. The proposed mission would support Ukraine’s defense capabilities, military training, and long-term security.

Gaza shelter crisis deepens as millions face winter rains, floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:39:00 UTC
22:39:00 KST

Repeated displacement during three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has left shelters across the enclave increasingly damaged, while restrictions and funding shortages are undermining efforts to prepare for winter, a senior U.N. migration official said late Friday.
Karl Baker, the International Organization for Migration’s (IOM) regional crisis coordinator for the Gaza response, said some Palestinians have been displaced as many as eight times, with each forced move further damaging or destroying tents and other makeshift shelters.
“When they move, all those goods that they currently have or did have either get destroyed, or they have to seek new shelter,” Baker told U.N. News.
Even basic materials such as tarpaulins need to be replaced roughly every six months, but humanitarian agencies have been unable to bring replacements into Gaza at the required scale, he said.
Baker said agencies now need to move beyond temporary solutions toward more durable transitional shelters.
Materials needed for stronger roofing, concrete floors and more substantial walls, however, are subject to Israel’s “dual-use” restrictions, which are imposed over security concerns.
“After three years of war, we do need to improve the level of shelter which is inside, and move further away from temporary and more toward transitional type of shelter,” he said.
Baker said IOM remains in constant contact with Israeli authorities, but some durable materials continue to be denied entry over security concerns.
He also cited funding shortages and disruptions to international shipping as obstacles, saying IOM relies on suppliers in countries including China, India and Pakistan.
Although funding has begun to arrive, it remains insufficient to meet the needs of an estimated 1.8 million to 1.9 million people requiring shelter assistance, he added.
Baker said only around 30% of Gaza is currently accessible to most of the population, forcing displaced Palestinians into increasingly crowded and often flood-prone areas.
“The 30% in which they currently live is a very large displacement camp,” he said.
With winter rains already beginning, humanitarian organizations are working to address flood-prone areas and deploy water pumps. Baker warned, however, that getting displaced Palestinians through the winter would be the biggest challenge.
Earlier this month, IOM said available and incoming shelter supplies covered only 17% of Gaza’s winter needs, while more than half of tents and makeshift shelters were in poor condition.
A cease-fire has been in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, but Israeli attacks and restrictions on the entry of humanitarian aid and shelter supplies have continued.

'Nine murders' claim, then a clarification: How 'Chote Sarkar' has put Nitish, JD(U) on the spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:36:18 UTC
22:36:18 KST

Anant Singh is no ordinary legislator as locals rarely use his given name. They call him 'Chhote Sarkar'.
NEW DELHI: Anant Singh, Bihar's bahubali MLA, who is intensely popular on social media reels for his impromptu one liners in local Magahi dialect, made a jittering claim to prove his loyality and sacrifice for JD(U) chief Nitish Kumar."I got nine people murdered," he said on camera, reviving the distressing memory of Jungle Raj that once besieged Bihar. The statement also had a dramatic irony as he was mentioning the man who ruled Bihar as 'Sushasan Babu', Nitish Kumar.Speaking to reporters about his years of loyalty with Bihar's former chief minister Nitish Kumar, the six-time legislator said: “Who has made so many sacrifices as I have? Nitish Kumar was nothing back then; he used to roam around here and there. At that time, while being with Nitish Kumar, I got nine people murdered.”However, maybe after releasing the political gravity of his remark, the Mokama MLA backtracked and pinned the blame on Lalu Yadav, who was once an ally of Nitish Kumar.
In 2004, Anant Singh weighed Nitish Kumar against silver coins during a public rally in the Barh parliamentary constituency to show his support.
The video went viral and the timing was fatal, because Singh, popular as 'Chhote Sarkar', is already at odds with his party over the Patna Graduates’ MLC election.He is backing the candidate fielded by Prashant Kishor against JD(U)’s Neeraj Kumar, the very man he defeated in the 2015 assembly election.
As criticism came crashing in from the party and the opposition, Singh sensed the backlash and tweaked his remark, saying: “During the Lalu Prasad regime, nine of my associates were killed, and I myself was shot. It was because we aligned ourselves with Nitish Kumar that Lalu had them killed. We have suffered such immense losses. My father also passed away due to a heart attack.”However, the RJD held back the attack as Lalu's party spokesperson Shakti Singh Yadav, said: “Anant has publicly confessed to killing nine persons during the NDA regime. Now Nitish will have to offer explanations.”He went further: “Although he (Anant) has confessed to his involvement in nine murders, the responsibility straightaway goes to Nitish regime...Is paap se chhutkara nahin milekga (There will be no escape from this sin).”
Fate tied to bahubali brother
Anant Singh is no ordinary legislator as locals rarely use his given name. They call him 'Chhote Sarkar', or little lord, because in the Barh and Mokama belt his word has often counted for more than the government’s.His story begins with his elder brother, Dilip Singh. Dilip won as an independent and became a minister in Lalu Prasad’s cabinet during its first term, from 1990 to 1995. Dilip Singh is remembered as the first of the so-called bahubalis, or musclemen politicians, to reach such a post.Anant Singh, who first handled his brother’s election campaigns, took over the family's political reins following Dilip Singh's electoral defeat to rival strongman Surajbhan Singh in 2000.In the next election cycle in 2005, Nitish Kumar, who came to power that year promising to clean up one of India’s poorest and most fractured states, brought Anant Singh into the JD(U). Anant Singh's backing could help the party among upper castes, who did not naturally support Nitish Kumar.However, his allegiance to Nitish began a year before. In 2004, Anant Singh weighed Nitish Kumar against silver coins during a public rally in the Barh parliamentary constituency to show his support.Anant Singh successfully contested the Mokama assembly seat in 2005 on a JD(U) ticket.Once asked why he had embraced a man with such a reputation, Nitish Kumar replied, “There are certain compulsions of politics.”Anant Singh then again contested as a JD(U) candidate in 2010, and the relationship lasted until he quit the party before the 2015 polls.
Pet lover who loves python
Anant Singh keeps a python as a pet, owns an elephant trained to shake hands and rides an antique buggy pulled by expensive horses.Residents describe him holding a durbar where he settles disputes, hears complaints against the police and acts against “miscreants”. Admirers credit him with safer streets and quicker access to services. Critics see a parallel government.
Anant Singh with his horses
Jail, raids and remarkable run at the polls
Aanant Singh has faced around two dozen serious cases, ranging from murder and kidnapping to conspiracy to kill and the possession of illegal arms. But for years none ended in a conviction, as judges died, officers were transferred and evidence went missing.In his last affidavit he filed in 2025 Bihar elections, he mentioned 28 criminal cases involving undue influence or personation at an election, making preparation to commit dacoity, insult intended to provoke breach of the peace, rioting and armed with a deadly weapon, dishonest misappropriation of property possessed by deceased person.In 2015, after he was arrested on murder and kidnapping charges, Nitish Kumar cut him loose. The move was widely read as a gesture to Lalu Prasad Yadav, his old rival turned new partner. Nitish JD(U) had snapped ties with the BJP-led NDA over Narendra Modi being chosen as the PM face.Anant Singh, however, fought the election from jail as an independent. His wife, Neelam, campaigned in his name and called him a “rare diamond”. Interestingly, he won comfortably without stepping onto the campaign trail.The pressure returned in 2019 after police arrested three suspected sharpshooters on 15 July, who allegedly planned to kill a contractor, Bhola Singh, and his brother Mukesh Singh.They reportedly told investigators that Anant Singh had given them the contract. He gave a voice sample to the state forensic science laboratory.Soon afterwards, an AK-47 and hand grenades were recovered from his ancestral house, and he was booked under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, or UAPA. Anant Singh disappeared for nearly a week.“The man, whose name once spelt terror, is now running for cover,” a senior IPS officer said at the time. He eventually surrendered in a Delhi court and alleged a “conspiracy by political forces”, an apparent dig at the JD(U).Nonetheless, Bihar politics is never bereft of bahubalis. And 2020 was different from 2015. Nitish was back with NDA with ever-dominant BJP under Prime Minister Narendra Modi. And RJD, which was by then handled actively by Lalu's son Tejashwi Yadav, forged an alliance with the Congress.This dynamic also shifted the allegiance of Anant Singh, who fought on RJD's ticket and Nitish Kumar's party. Still in jail in 2020, he won with 78,721 votes, about 53 per cent of valid votes cast, by a margin of more than 65,000.In 2021, a special court in Patna sentenced him to 10 years in the arms case, which cost him his seat. Neelam Devi then won the by-election for the RJD, showing that the family’s hold on Mokama had not loosened.Nitish again dumped the BJP in 2022 and returned to the RJD's Mahagathbandhan fold. But nothing much changed for Anant Singh.
The fluid loyalty
In February 2024, Nitish Kumar flipped again, leaving the RJD-led alliance for the BJP-led NDA. He won the floor test comfortably with 129 votes, as the opposition walked out. Anant Singh’s wife, Neelam Devi, was one of three RJD MLAs who cross-voted in his favour, a pointed gesture even though the numbers did not depend on it.Months later, Anant Singh stepped out of Patna jail on 15 days of parole in the middle of the Lok Sabha elections. He backed Lalan Singh of the JD(U) in Munger, a sworn enemy whom his wife had challenged on a Congress ticket in 2019. Munger has roughly 3.5 lakh Bhumihar voters, the community to which Singh belongs. The RJD questioned the timing of his release.
A fragile equilibrium
The most dramatic chapter came during the Mokama assembly contest in 2025. Dularchand Yadav, 76, was murdered while campaigning for a Jan Suraaj candidate. Police arrested Singh, then the JD(U) nominee, in connection with the killing. The NDA responded that, unlike under the Lalu regime, no leader enjoys immunity from legal action.The case revived an old rivalry with Surajbhan Singh, another Bhumihar strongman. Surajbhan began in the LJP, later moved close to the RJD, and saw his own electoral influence shrink after criminal convictions. His wife, Veena Devi, kept the family relevant in nearby seats. The two men have long competed for land, contracts and political dominance.The arithmetic made the stakes plain. Mokama has about 2.9 lakh voters. Bhumihars number roughly 55,000 to 60,000, Dhanuks about 45,000 and Yadavs about 40,000.Muslims and Dalits together make up roughly 30 per cent. A shift of 5 to 10 per cent could move 15,000 to 25,000 votes. The killing of a Yadav campaigner threatened to unsettle backward caste voters, while the Bhumihar vote risked splitting between two powerful figures.
Net-net, contrary to Anant Singh' remark, "Chhote Sarkar" has been an ally, an outcast, a prisoner, a convict and a kingmaker, often within a few years. And this time again, he has been vocal against his party's MLC candidate Neeraj Kumar and backing Jan Suraaj's Anuj Kumar Singh.“Nishant (Nitish Kumar's son) should not have campaigned for Neeraj Kumar. Sometimes he is taken to Barh, sometimes some other places, but there are few people to support him,” Anant Singh said, claiming he would “medically treat” Neeraj in the election.

====================================================================================================

Predictions of Gaza’s death toll were wrong - why is no one being held accountable? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:34:30 UTC
22:34:30 KST

In late September, Gaza’s Hamas-run Health Ministry published its 2025 mortality report, the first since the war began to purport to count every death in Gaza.
Of 24,650 deaths, it attributed 17,286 to “war operations,” without separating combatants from civilians, and 1,584 to accidents. Independent analyst Eirik Schrøder-Bråtane calculated that the remaining 5,780 nonviolent deaths roughly matched Gaza’s prewar annual nonviolent toll. The ministry also recorded 50,227 births.
This was 2025: the year Israel halted aid for 11 weeks after Hamas refused to extend the truce and release more hostages, following a six-week ceasefire during which 25,200 trucks delivered nearly 450,000 tons of aid. Israel said Hamas was seizing and selling supplies to finance its war. By September, Israel counted over two million tons delivered during the war.
It was also the year UN officials warned of babies dying by the thousands and the IPC, the UN-backed hunger monitor, declared famine in Gaza City.
Yet the ministry’s own figures show nothing resembling the mass-mortality footprint those warnings suggested: no surge in nonviolent deaths from hunger, disease, or other indirect causes.
Andrew Fox, a former British Army officer and senior fellow at the Henry Jackson Society, argued in 2024 that Gaza’s war toll was being padded with natural deaths. Now, he wrote, the famine allegations and other claims had been “debunked by Hamas’s own numbers.” The modelers who predicted hundreds of thousands of deaths, he added, “should lose their careers.”
Then he said: “They won’t. They’ll get a free pass.”
That may be the safest prediction anyone has made about this war.
For years, Israel’s accusers have issued confident predictions of mass death and confident counts of massacres. The headlines circle the globe. When the predictions fail, or the numbers collapse, the correction barely travels at all.
On May 20, 2025, the UN’s humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, told BBC Radio 4 that 14,000 babies in Gaza “will die in the next 48 hours” unless aid reached them. Within a day, the UN clarified that the figure meant roughly 14,100 projected cases of severe acute malnutrition among young children under age 5.
Not deaths. Not babies. Not 48 hours.
The report does show deterioration: infant mortality of 15.8 per 1,000 live births and under-five mortality of 33.4, both worse than before the war. But in the year of the UN’s warnings, Gaza’s infant mortality roughly matched Egypt’s peacetime rate of 16.1, and both its rates sat below the global average. Worse, yes. Mass death, no.
In February 2024, researchers at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine and Johns Hopkins projected as many as 85,750 excess deaths in Gaza over six months in a worst-case scenario of escalating war and epidemic disease. Activist outlets ran headlines like “Israel Could Kill 85,000 More Gazans in 6 Months,” and a lead author told US news program Democracy Now! that the escalation scenario was “currently what’s happening in Rafah.” That epidemic never came.
In Sudan’s largely forgotten war, the same London School found the dead going uncounted: some 26,000 violent deaths in Khartoum State alone in the first 14 months, more than monitors had recorded for the entire country, and over 61,000 deaths from all causes.
In Gaza, the alarm far outran the dead. In Sudan, the dead outran the alarm.
In March 2024, the IPC projected famine in northern Gaza by the end of May if fighting and severe aid restrictions continued. By June, its own Famine Review Committee found the evidence did not indicate famine.
The IPC declared famine in the Gaza Governorate in August 2025, over Israel’s objections to its methodology. Somalia’s 2010-2012 famine killed an estimated 258,000 people, including 133,000 children under five. At its peak, it killed about 30,000 people a month.
Incentive to inflate numbers
Gaza’s Health Ministry, an arm of Hamas with every incentive to inflate, reported 455 malnutrition deaths across nearly two years of war, fewer than Somalia’s famine killed in half a day at its height.
By the IPC’s own threshold, two deaths per 10,000 people a day, the declared famine should have killed about 9,000. Hamas’s own ministry counted fewer than 200, across all of Gaza, fewer than the US records in four days.
Rafah followed a familiar pattern. Before Israel entered the city in May 2024, the Palestinian Authority’s Foreign Ministry warned an assault would bring “the annihilation of about 1.5 million Palestinians.” The EU’s then-foreign-policy chief, Josep Borrell, scoffed at evacuating civilians: “Where? To the moon?” Within three weeks, about a million people had evacuated Rafah. There was no annihilation and no apology.
The pattern is older than this war, and it only ever runs in one direction.
In April 2002, during Israel’s operation in Jenin, PA negotiator Saeb Erekat told CNN that Israeli troops had killed more than 500 people. The UN secretary-general’s own report later counted 52 Palestinians dead, at least half of them terrorists, along with 23 Israeli soldiers, and found the 500 figure unsubstantiated. By then, the “Jenin massacre” had entered the world’s vocabulary.
Operation Cast Lead followed the same arc. Hamas initially acknowledged fewer than 50 dead combatants. The since-discredited 2009 Goldstone Report cited a Palestinian Centre for Human Rights tally identifying just 236 of the dead as combatants. Then, in November 2010, Hamas interior minister Fathi Hammad acknowledged that up to 700 men from Hamas’s military wing and security forces had been killed, close to Israel’s count of 709.
Abroad, the dead were nearly all civilians. At home, they were Hamas martyrs.
On October 17, 2023, Hamas’s health authorities instantly blamed Israel for the Ahli hospital explosion and reported nearly 500 dead. American, British, French, and Canadian intelligence assessments concluded that a misfired Palestinian rocket was the likely cause; US intelligence put the toll at a fraction of the ministry’s tally. The New York Times later conceded that its early coverage had relied too heavily on Hamas’s claims.
The progressive Left, which prides itself on following the science, rarely asks why so many catastrophic predictions and claims about Israel fail. A growing faction of the populist Right, the so-called “woke Right,” recycles Hamas figures and UN forecasts it would ridicule on any other subject.
The method works because the claims and predictions do their work before they can be tested. Put Israel in the dock. Push for sanctions or an arms embargo. Pressure Israel, but not those sworn to its destruction. By the time the evidence arrives, the damage is done.
Tom Fletcher still runs the UN’s humanitarian office. The IPC has not retracted its 2025 famine declaration. Newsrooms still headline the forecasts and bury the accounting.
In most fields, predictions this consequential would at least produce an audit. When the subject is Israel, they produce the next failed prediction.
The writer is an attorney, former IDF soldier, and former NYPD officer. He writes widely on Israel, Zionism, antisemitism, and Jewish history. He serves on the board of Herut North America.

In Pittsburgh, campus antisemitism report’s authors neglected to speak with Jewish students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:34:21 UTC
22:34:21 KST

Can a college campus accurately assess its antisemitism problem without talking to Jews?
That’s the question facing the University of Pittsburgh, where an internal working group on campus antisemitism recently published a report that did not include, and did not appear to solicit, the perspectives of the school’s estimated 1,400 Jewish students, or any other members of the campus Jewish community beyond the group itself.
The July report by Pitt’s working group on campus antisemitism, which is made up of Jews, has divided the campus, drawing criticism from the left for what they perceive as recommendations that would limit speech, and from within the campus Jewish community for not adequately consulting with Jewish students and faculty. Before it was even published, one author of the report said her home was targeted after she was named to join the working group.
Addressing campus antisemitism after Oct. 7
The report has also resurfaced questions about the most effective methods for universities to address antisemitism for Jewish students three years on from the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks that prompted so much uproar across campuses.
The report’s omission of any research on its Jewish community was by design, the working group’s chair recently told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
“Our charge from the chancellor and provost was not to provide data as part of our report,” Katherine Blee, a sociologist and the faculty chair of the Pitt working group, said in an interview.
Instead, she said, the recommendations came out of discussions between the group members, whom she characterized as “a very diverse group with a very diverse set of opinions, which is representative of the university.”
The school immediately agreed to take action on the group’s recommendations, which include strengthening its Title VI civil rights law compliance; giving “clear guidance” on free speech and protest policies; reviewing its bias training; and committing to new “Dialogue and Discourse” programming to facilitate constructive conversations around Jews and Israel.
The issue of antisemitism at Pitt became particularly urgent after two Jewish students wearing kippahs were wounded in a violent off-campus attack in 2024 in an incident that preceded the announcement of the working group. The perpetrator, who wore a keffiyeh and had no apparent university affiliation, attacked the students with a bottle as they were on their way to a Hillel Shabbat dinner.
“We recognize that members of our Jewish community have experienced harm, and we take that seriously,” the university said in its press release following the report. The school’s statement went on to quote the Mishnah-era rabbinic sage Rabbi Tarfon: “It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you at liberty to neglect it.”
This was a heartening development for some of the committee members. But the finished report, along with a strict confidentiality agreement the authors agreed to, has sparked local controversy.
Non-Jewish faculty criticized report's recommendations
The university’s Jewish Studies program director, initially a member of the working group, didn’t sign the final document.
And some non-Jewish campus faculty writ large have criticized the report’s recommendations for, they claim, potentially threatening shared governance principles at the university. The university’s chapter of the American Association of University Professors, the national faculty union that in 2024 ended its longstanding opposition to academic boycotts to allow members to boycott Israel, called for the report to be withdrawn.
Blowback among a more progressive contingent of Jewish personnel at Pitt has led to the proposal of an alternative set of recommendations for tackling antisemitism, including creating a joint Kosher/Halal dining area and emphasizing teshuvah, or the Jewish tradition of repentance, “when a member of the university community does harm.”
This cohort has stronger, more ideological concerns with the report than whether it surveyed Jewish students. “We refuse to let anyone use the pain of antisemitism to dismantle academic freedom, free speech, and open engagement within our university community,” an open letter proposing the new plan reads.
Proponents of the second plan stressed the importance of soliciting perspectives from the broader Jewish community.
“If you’re going to really talk about this, you need to be really thinking more broadly about what the rest of the community thinks,” Harry Hochheiser, a Jewish biomedical professor at Pitt and critic of the report who has helped push the alternative set of recommendations to the university, told JTA.
Pitt’s report, and the response to it, comes as the question of how to respond to campus antisemitism feels less settled than ever. Some campuses are continuing to see fresh threats to Jewish safety: Recent flyers at the University of Oregon targeted that school’s Hillel director, by name, as an “enemy of the people.”
At the same time, the Trump administration’s aggressive response to the issue is starting to see pushback. A recent bipartisan report from the federally mandated US Commission on Civil Rights criticizes the administration’s handling of campus antisemitism cases, as well as its withholding of documents related to the investigations.
In response to a series of emailed questions from JTA, a Pitt spokesperson said the working group “drew on perspectives from across the University community rather than establishing a faculty-only process,” and that the school is “taking next steps on a number of the Working Group’s recommendations.”
The working group includes administrators, a student Hillel president, the lone student named in the final report, and a former director of Pittsburgh’s Jewish Community Relations Council.
The Pitt spokesperson, Jared Stonesifer, also said the school “is in frequent and ongoing discussions with Jewish students about their experiences and their views on the campus environment, and student input was included on the Working Group that produced the report.”
Both Blee and Stonesifer framed the report as the first of many future steps to help Pitt confront campus antisemitism, and expressed hope that future steps would involve talking to Jewish students. One of the report’s recommendations is to “survey antisemitism in the campus environment regularly.”
Pitt’s undergraduate student body is home to around 1,400 Jews, just under 7% of the 21,000 total students, according to Hillel International estimates. The school is served by Hillel Jewish University Center, a local Hillel that also tends to Jewish students at other Pittsburgh colleges, as well as a dedicated Chabad house and a Jewish Studies program that grants an undergraduate certificate.
Julia Jassey, co-founder and CEO of the national Jewish student advocacy group Jewish on Campus, offered a mixed assessment of the Pitt report and of the school’s promise to include students in future decision-making.
“Students should be a part of the process in the implementation, not looking at it as a postmortem,” Jassey told JTA, noting that student input is valuable because “no two campuses are exactly the same.”
Yet, Jassey added, “That doesn’t mean that the report itself is inherently not helpful.”
Tree of Life Synagogue, the site of the 2018 mass killing that was the deadliest act of antisemitism in U.S. history, seen on April 21, 2023, in Pittsburgh, PA. (Jahi Chikwendiu/The Washington Post via Getty Images)
A sensitive climate
That Pitt would commission a campus antisemitism report was, on its own, not unusual.
In addition to the attack on the two Jewish students in 2024, Pitt’s Jewish community also continues to live in the shadow of the 2018 shooting at the Tree of Life worship center, two miles from campus. Many of the university’s Jewish students and faculty have personal connections to it; Pitt has also hosted exhibits about the attack. A local memorial and museum commemorating the attack, now under construction, is scheduled to open to the public in 2028.
Both the 2024 attack and the Tree of Life massacre were part of “the context in which we were writing,” Blee said.
Blee is a longtime member and past president of Congregation Dor Hadash, the Reconstructionist synagogue located inside the Tree of Life building. One Dor Hadash congregant was among the 11 killed in the attack.
In addition, her research specialty is white nationalism and far-right antisemitism: When the perpetrators of the deadly 2017 “Unite the Right” rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, were charged with violations of federal law, Blee was called to the stand as an expert witness.
So when her synagogue became the site of the deadliest antisemitic attack in US history, Blee recalled, “my work and my Jewish life intersected in a really terrible way.”
Blee’s 2025 appointment to chair the antisemitism working group, the Pittsburgh Jewish Chronicle reported, marked the moment the working group “begins to take shape.”
The final report recommends the university form an “advisory group” on Jewish issues and suggests that the local Hillel and Chabad-Lubavitch house, as well as the Pittsburgh Jewish federation, be represented, a recommendation that spurred criticism from pro-Palestinian groups on campus who objected to the federation’s presence.
Additional members of the working group contacted by JTA for this story, including the former JCRC staffer, directed requests for comment to Blee or declined to comment. The director of the Hillel serving Pitt’s campus, after requesting questions from JTA by email, did not respond by press time.
In a statement accompanying the report’s publication, the working group’s vice chair, Jennifer Murshatashvili, wrote, “My goal was to contribute to outcomes that would improve life for everyone at Pitt, not only Jewish and Israeli members of our community.”
Murshatashvili, a professor of Eurasian studies at Pitt, also told the university community that after she was named to the working group, “my home was targeted, and I was subjected to extensive online hatred and harassment.”
Even though the working group was not charged with gathering data, Blee told JTA that one of its instructions was to investigate “how effective” the university’s existing policies on antisemitism were after the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks in Israel strained relationships on the campus. There was disagreement among the group about how seriously to take the encampments mounted by pro-Palestinian groups at Pitt, she said.
“Some people were more concerned about the encampments than others,” she told JTA. Drawing on her own research into the far right, she explained, “Everybody would agree that a Nazi rally is antisemitic. Not everyone on the committee, and not everyone at the university, and not everyone in the United States Jewish community, would agree that the totality of the protests after October 7 were antisemitic.”
Blee declined to elaborate on how the working group determined policy effectiveness without gathering data. The confidentiality agreement brokered by the group members also prevented her from sharing more detail on their internal deliberations, she said.
“I can tell you that the committee gathered information that was needed,” she said. “But under that confidentiality agreement, I don’t want to go into exactly how that was done.”
Rachel Kranson, the director of Pitt’s Jewish Studies program, was announced as a member of the working group in 2025 but does not appear on its final report. Kranson declined to comment to JTA.
A flood of reports
Internal reports chaired by Jewish university faculty, officials and students have become part and parcel of the standard university response to campus antisemitism since October 7.
At public and elite private schools alike, the formation and release of an internal antisemitism report has been greeted with considerable fanfare, and no small amount of controversy, directed at everything from the political makeup of committee members to the data-gathering process and final recommendations.
Yet one consistency among such reports has been the presence of at least some polling of the experiences of that school’s Jewish students, which many Jewish groups and Jewish leaders have agreed is a crucial component of any successful campus antisemitism response.
Committees at Harvard and Columbia, two schools figuring prominently into the national conversation on campus antisemitism, each conducted surveys with more than 500 Jews on campus to inform their findings. Harvard’s final report runs 311 pages, while Columbia released multiple reports on the subject.
Stanford’s antisemitism committee report, released in 2024, runs nearly 150 pages and draws on listening sessions with more than 300 people, plus one-on-one interviews with students, administrators, and representatives of national Jewish groups.
The University of Washington and the University of California, Los Angeles, both public universities like Pitt, also surveyed and interviewed Jewish students to inform their own reports. The data itself can sometimes lead to controversy: A contingent of progressive Jews at UW criticized that school’s report for conducting focus groups with only a few dozen Jewish students, among other objections.
Pitt’s report, published two years after the administration committed to forming the working group, runs eight pages and includes no references to interviews or focus groups. It largely praised the university for, its authors said, already taking meaningful steps to combat antisemitism.
“I was surprised at the brevity of the report as the culmination of 1.5 years of work,” Andrea Goldschmidt, a psychiatry professor at Pitt and member of the Pitt Jewish Community affinity group, wrote in an open letter. “This stands in sharp contrast to the very lengthy and thorough reports I have seen come out of other universities.”
Goldschmidt also criticized the lack of “listening sessions or focus groups with the Jewish community during the course of the task force’s work.” She suggested that the lack of such conversations “reflects either that there was so much internal disagreement on the task force that the short report reflects the only areas of confluence among its members, or that the task force was somehow hobbled in its work before it even began.”
The Pitt Jewish Community affinity group’s president, Vicky Davide, echoed those concerns in comments to the student newspaper, telling the Pitt News that she and her colleagues had trouble accessing information about the group’s inner deliberations. They were “really disappointed” by the finished report, Davide, who leads engagement programs at Pitt, said.
Some suggested that, despite the lack of input from Jewish students, the recommendations themselves could still be useful. Jassey claimed that Pitt’s recommendations generally enjoy a “consensus” among Jewish students more broadly, and expressed hope that students would be included in the implementation step.
“I guess the question now is, what’s next,” she said.

Tear gas, clashes between protesters and police hit French cities in cost-of-living demonstrations

Police fired tear gas and clashed with protesters in several French cities on Saturday as some of the most violent protests in years over living costs and public services drew thousands onto the streets.
French authorities said 140 protests involving 32,800 people had been recorded outside Paris by midday and blamed the unrest on what they described as the "ultra-left".
The protests began last month at high schools in Paris' poor northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards.
Violent incidents were reported in several cities, including vandalism in Marseille and attacks targeting police, media and public buildings, the Interior Ministry said.
Police were visible in central Paris, especially near landmarks such as the Champs-Élysées and the Arc de Triomphe, which were excluded from the routes of two authorized demonstrations.
Protest echoes Yellow Vest movement
Protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, echoing the Yellow Vest movement that marked President Emmanuel Macron's previous term.
In Marseille, the mayor said the town hall had been vandalized, and that additional police were being sent to the city following talks with the prime minister and interior minister.
"We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris.
About 100 people walked towards the start of the protests shouting "All cops are bastards", according to a Reuters witness.
The tourist office of the French city of Lyon was also set on fire amid the protests, French broadcasting network BFMTV said.
Police fired tear gas and clashed with protesters in several cities across France on one of the most violent days of protest in years in the country, as demonstrations against rising costs and declining public services drew thousands onto the streets.
Macron, who urged calm on Friday, is entering the final stretch of his presidency amid a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy.
France's efforts to reduce public debt have failed to reassure investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in more than two decades.
Police response under scrutiny
Police tactics have drawn criticism following a series of injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up a stun grenade. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said more than 900 police officers had also been injured.
The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence. France suspended the use of stun grenades during the student demonstrations, but Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said they could be used on Saturday.
Calls on social media for veterans of previous protest movements to join the demonstrations appeared to have broadened participation, raising the prospect of larger.
The Yellow Vest movement emerged in 2018 in opposition to diesel taxes before expanding into a wider protest against living costs and inequality. The movement subsided after Macron announced billions of euros in tax cuts.
Yannick Maillou, a teacher from La Crèche in western France who participated in the Yellow Vest movement, said local organizers had set up several gathering points for Saturday's protests, and labor unions were also encouraging participation.
