====================================================================================================

The Christian progressive who could flip Texas: James Talarico on Trump, Gaza and a rabbi's lessons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:31:44 UTC
22:31:44 KST

Last weekend, a man called Lindner Center of Hope, a mental health treatment facility in Mason, Ohio. Claiming to be a relative of James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for a U.S. Senate seat in Texas, he asked whether Talarico had been discharged. Shortly afterward, on Sunday, two influencers from the MAGA movement, which supports President Donald Trump, published what they claimed was a recording of the conversation, suggesting that Talarico had indeed been hospitalized at the psychiatric facility and subsequently released. 
Given that Talarico had been absent from public appearances for nine days because of what his campaign described as a severe case of the flu, this appeared to be the kind of revelation that could destroy the campaign of the first Democrat in decades with a realistic chance of winning in the vast conservative stronghold.
But the Lindner Center of Hope quickly issued an official statement confirming that Talarico had never been treated there. The New York Times reviewed time-stamped images from security cameras at his home showing that he was there between October 1 and October 8. Talarico himself declared, "I've never even been to Ohio." 
Finally, the complete recording of the phone call revealed that the version circulated by the two influencers, Nick Sortor and Rhein Amacher, had been selectively edited. The full conversation showed that the caller, who lacked the required patient access code, supplied a made-up code, while the staff member repeatedly said she could find no record of anyone named James Talarico. The recording provided no evidence that he had ever been admitted to the facility.
By now, of course, none of that seems to matter. Elon Musk has amplified the conspiracy theory, as has Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff and one of Trump's most influential advisers. The vast MAGA media machine is demanding that Talarico produce geographical proof that he was not in Ohio during his absence. 
This entire manufactured drama is unfolding because Talarico, 37, is leading Republican candidate Ken Paxton in the polls and has a genuine chance of winning one of the key races in the November 3 midterm elections. Polling suggests that Democrats could capture not only the House of Representatives but also the Senate, severely complicating Trump's final two years in office.
Midterm elections have historically been viewed as a referendum on the sitting president. His party generally suffers losses and sees its congressional strength diminished. But with polls showing Trump's popularity at a low point, and Republican and independent voters increasingly frustrated by the cost of living and price increases following the war with Iran, Democrats now hope to win even in traditionally conservative strongholds. 
Texas is the most striking example. America's second-most populous state, with approximately 32 million residents, has been considered reliably Republican for decades. Trump defeated Kamala Harris there by 14 percentage points in 2024. The last time Texas elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate was in 1988, a year before Talarico was even born.
Democrats have suffered repeated disappointments in Texas. In 2018, they placed enormous hopes in Beto O'Rourke, whose campaign against Republican Senator Ted Cruz generated tremendous enthusiasm. O'Rourke ultimately lost, although by just 2.6 percentage points, a historically narrow margin in Texas. 
Unlike Talarico, however, O'Rourke had not established a sustained polling lead before the election. That is why Democrats are more optimistic this time, while Republicans are increasingly alarmed, as reflected in the extraordinary sums they are pouring into efforts to rescue Paxton.
The intensity of the contest is reflected in its cost. It has become one of the most expensive nonpresidential races in American history, with spending surpassing half a billion dollars. Republican groups alone have committed enormous sums to defending the Senate seat being vacated by veteran Republican John Cornyn, with approximately $232 million earmarked for the final stretch between early September and Election Day. 
Cornyn lost the Republican primary to Paxton after Trump backed the challenger, regarding the longtime senator as insufficiently loyal. Polling had suggested Cornyn would have been a much stronger candidate against Talarico, and analysts believe the race would not have been nearly as competitive had the incumbent won the Republican nomination. Paxton, by contrast, carries considerable political baggage, including corruption allegations and an impeachment attempt led by fellow Republicans in Texas.
Trump and conservative billionaires are now mobilizing behind Paxton with an aggressive campaign designed to portray Talarico as far too liberal for Texas. They have seized on statements from his past that he has since sought to clarify or distance himself from, including his assertion that God is nonbinary. 
Trump has given him the mocking nickname "TalaFREAKO," while the campaign has been accompanied by false allegations, including the debunked psychiatric hospitalization claim and Trump's repeated assertion that Talarico is a vegan, despite the Democrat explicitly saying he eats meat. 
The attacks may nevertheless be succeeding in bringing moderate and undecided Republican voters back into the party's camp. Recent polls indicate that Talarico's lead has narrowed. A New York Times/Siena poll conducted in late September put him six points ahead, but a Marist poll conducted October 8-11 found his advantage had shrunk to just two points, within the margin of error.
‘We have lost the South for a generation’
It is difficult to remember, or even believe, today, but Texas was once a Democratic stronghold. For nearly a century after the American Civil War, Texas was a cornerstone of the Democratic-dominated South. Republicans, the party of Abraham Lincoln, were deeply unpopular across the former Confederate states. 
Then came Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal, which helped pull the United States out of the Great Depression, won enormous popularity in impoverished, agricultural Texas and further strengthened the Democrats. Democratic politicians from Texas, including Roosevelt's vice president John Nance Garner and later President Lyndon B. Johnson, emerged from that political system.
The transformation began as conservative white Texans grew increasingly resentful of the Democrats' movement to the left on civil rights for Black Americans and the expansion of the economic safety net. The turning point came after President Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964. 
According to a widely repeated account associated with his close aide Bill Moyers, Johnson feared that the legislation would cost Democrats the South for a generation. The remark, commonly rendered as "We have lost the South for a generation," became almost mythical in explanations of the seismic political shift that turned Texas and other Southern states from Democratic territory into firmly Republican strongholds, although historians have questioned whether Johnson actually used those precise words.
In 1961, John Tower became the first Republican senator from Texas since the 19th century. Bill Clements became the state's first Republican governor in more than a century in 1978. During the 1980s and 1990s, the suburbs of Dallas, Houston and Austin experienced enormous population growth. Many of these new residents were affluent white, religious, middle-class business owners and people employed in the oil industry. Attracted by the Republicans' low-tax policies, they shifted their political allegiance.
Democrats managed to hold on for a while, thanks in part to popular figures such as charismatic Governor Ann Richards. But in 1994, Richards lost the governorship to George W. Bush, and four years later Republicans had secured control of every statewide executive office, including governor, lieutenant governor and attorney general, as well as the Texas Supreme Court. 
No Democrat has won a statewide office in Texas since 1994, and the state has not elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1988. Over the past decade, however, the growth of Texas's Hispanic population, whose voters historically leaned Democratic, revived hopes of another political transformation. Those hopes have not materialized. 
Now, though, polls suggest Hispanic voters are abandoning Trump amid frustration over the cost of living and his administration's mass deportation campaign against undocumented immigrants. Democrats are dreaming of Texas once again.
Christianity takes center stage: ‘Economic justice appears 3,000 times in Scripture’
Until a year ago, anyone who was not a political obsessive had probably never heard of Talarico. Born in Austin, he is an eighth-generation Texan. His grandfather was a popular pastor in South Texas, and his grandson grew up to become a devout Christian, a Harvard-educated former teacher who continues to study Christian theology at Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary alongside his political career. 
Since November 2018, Talarico has served in the Texas House of Representatives, representing districts in the Austin area, the state capital and a Democratic island in an overwhelmingly Republican state.
The first time Talarico's name reached an audience well beyond Texas politics was during an interview former President Barack Obama gave a year ago on comedian Marc Maron's podcast. Maron expressed his frustration with Democratic candidates who, he felt, were unable to connect authentically with voters, relying instead on talking points prepared by political consultants. Obama acknowledged the problem but pointed to a young Texas politician who stood out. He mentioned Talarico, describing him as "terrific" and a "really talented young man."
Since then, Talarico has become a rising star in the Democratic Party. He comfortably defeated his much better-known rival in the Democratic primary, outspoken progressive Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, while building a grassroots campaign that made highly effective use of social media. 
Talarico has carved out an unusual political identity within the party: a progressive candidate who is also a devout Christian and places Christianity at the center of his political work. His message emphasizes social justice, loving one's neighbor, caring for the poor and immigrants, defending the separation of church and state, and opposing Christian nationalism. 
"Economic justice is mentioned 3,000 times in our Scriptures," Talarico has said, arguing that concern for the poor and oppressed is central to the biblical tradition but largely absent from modern Christian nationalism and the religious right. In deeply religious Texas, that message is finding an audience.
Like many Democratic candidates, Talarico has pledged not to accept money from corporate political action committees. Nevertheless, large sums have flowed into his campaign, both through individual contributions and from billionaires supporting outside groups. He has explained that he cannot afford to disarm unilaterally while Republicans benefit from hundreds of millions of dollars in billionaire-funded spending. 
He has also managed to capitalize on attempts by the Trump administration and federal regulators to restrict his access to late-night television programs, whose networks depend on federal broadcasting licenses. Two planned television interviews, with Stephen Colbert and Jimmy Kimmel, were kept off their respective CBS and ABC broadcasts amid legal concerns and pressure from the Federal Communications Commission. Both were instead made available online, where they attracted tens of millions of views and helped Talarico raise millions of dollars.
Since Cornyn's defeat in the Republican primary, Talarico has sought to court moderate conservative voters who are disappointed by Paxton's nomination and troubled by the corruption allegations surrounding him. He has repeatedly made clear that such voters are welcome in his campaign. 
According to the New York Times poll from late September, 60% of voters identifying as independents supported him, along with 7% of self-identified Republicans. One of them, Pete Nodecker, an 81-year-old retired restaurant industry supplier who voted for Trump twice, told CNN that he intended to vote for a Democrat for the first time. "I'm rather disillusioned with the Republican Party," he said. "The Republican Party has been hijacked. They're not the Republican Party that I was a member of for all my life."
Netanyahu, AIPAC and ‘the moral test of our time’
Although Talarico is considered a progressive, with a campaign focused on fighting the cost of living, raising taxes on the wealthy, combating corruption and expanding access to health insurance, he has adopted more moderate positions than some of his ideological allies, including on Israel. He emphasizes his support for Israel's right to exist and defend itself, but has sharply criticized the war in Gaza. 
He has said that, if elected to the Senate, he would vote to halt sales of offensive weapons to Israel and oppose the use of American taxpayer money to finance actions that harm civilians. At the same time, in communications with Texas's Jewish community, he has made clear that he supports continued funding for defensive systems such as Iron Dome.
Talarico has described the war in Gaza as "the moral test of our time," accused Netanyahu's government of war crimes and collective punishment, and strongly criticized what he describes as the use of starvation and restrictions on humanitarian assistance. Nevertheless, he has repeatedly declined to characterize Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide, saying the legal question is being considered by the International Court of Justice. 
He has also said Hamas is a terrorist organization that must be removed from power. During a CNN town hall on Wednesday, he was questioned by a Jewish voter about rising antisemitism in the United States. Talarico responded that he had deep love and respect for the Jewish people and Jewish scripture, explaining that he had studied the Hebrew Bible under a local rabbi rather than from a Christian perspective. 
He named Rabbi Neil Blumofe of Congregation Agudas Achim in Austin, crediting him with helping shape his understanding of Judaism. Talarico also said he had stood alongside Jewish leaders in Central Texas in confronting antisemitism and had consistently opposed hatred in all its forms, believing that Texans should feel welcome regardless of their religious beliefs.
When the woman questioning him, Rabbi Holly Levin Cohn of Congregation Beth El Binah in Dallas, asked about the relationship between criticism of Israel and antisemitism, Talarico stressed that his criticism was directed at Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, not the Israeli people. Speaking as a former teacher, he said that watching the devastation in Gaza, particularly the suffering of children, "makes me sick to my stomach." 
He also acknowledged that the October 7 massacre was the deadliest day for the Jewish people since the Holocaust. Talarico reiterated his belief that Israel, like any other country, has the right to defend its citizens, but argued that this right did not give Netanyahu permission to wage war against civilians, impose collective punishment or restrict humanitarian aid. That, he explained, was the conduct he had spoken out against.
Talarico, who supports a two-state solution and calls for a halt to Israeli settlement expansion in the West Bank, has taken an aggressive stance toward the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC. He has accused the organization of discouraging legitimate criticism of Netanyahu by threatening political candidates with massive spending against them, a practice he argues damages the prospects for reconciliation and peace in the Middle East. 
At the same time, he has drawn clear lines against antisemitic rhetoric, more forcefully than some of his progressive colleagues. Among other things, he refused to campaign alongside Maureen Galindo, an extremist Democratic candidate seeking a Texas seat in the U.S. House of Representatives who pledged to turn an immigration detention facility into a prison for American Zionists if elected. Talarico condemned her statements as antisemitic, and Galindo ultimately lost her primary runoff. In any case, Jewish voters account for less than 1% of Texas's population, making their direct electoral influence relatively limited.
Another thing Talarico and a new generation of Democratic candidates are doing is taking their message directly to conservative media audiences. Talarico has appeared repeatedly on Fox News and sat down for a two-and-a-half-hour interview with Joe Rogan, the enormously popular podcaster whose audience is heavily male. 
During their conversation, Rogan told him, "You need to run for president," adding that the country needed someone who was genuinely a good person. All of this has helped put Talarico in a position where he leads by margins generally ranging from one to four percentage points in the polls. It is an advantage no Democrat running for the Senate in Texas has enjoyed in more than 30 years. 
But it is also an extraordinarily fragile lead, underscoring just how conservative Texas remains. That reality becomes even more striking when considering the identity of Talarico's opponent, a politician weighed down by scandals and opposed by many within his own party, yet one who still has a very real chance of winning.
Affairs, a confrontation, impeachment and loyalty to Trump
Paxton, 63, was born in North Dakota to a U.S. Air Force officer. He holds a bachelor's degree in psychology, a master's degree in business administration and a law degree. He married Angela Allen, now a member of the Texas Senate, and the couple have four children. Their marriage has become the subject of highly publicized divorce proceedings, which we will return to later. 
Paxton began his political career in Texas state government. He was among the politicians who rose to prominence through the Tea Party movement, which emerged in response to Barack Obama's election and laid much of the ideological groundwork for Trumpism. Between 2003 and 2014, Paxton served in the Texas House and Senate before being elected the state's attorney general.
He quickly became a Republican star who waged an aggressive legal campaign against Democratic administrations. He filed dozens of lawsuits against the Obama and Biden administrations, particularly over immigration, environmental regulations and the Affordable Care Act, commonly known as Obamacare. He took an uncompromising position against abortion rights and strongly supported gun ownership. 
After the 2020 presidential election, Paxton led a legal challenge seeking to overturn Joe Biden's victory. He also spoke at the January 6, 2021 rally in Washington where Trump addressed supporters before a mob stormed the U.S. Capitol. All of this made Paxton extremely popular with Trump, who has repeatedly praised his loyalty and recently said that Paxton had stood by him more than almost anyone else. That loyalty paid off in this year's Republican primary, when Trump endorsed him against incumbent Senator John Cornyn.
Throughout his tenure as attorney general, Paxton has been dogged by scandals. As early as 2015, his first year in office, he faced securities fraud charges stemming from allegations that he misled investors. The criminal case dragged on for nearly a decade. In 2024, he reached a pretrial agreement requiring community service, legal ethics training and nearly $300,000 in restitution, without admitting wrongdoing. 
The criminal charges were formally dismissed in 2025 after prosecutors said he had fulfilled the agreement's terms. The most sensational scandal surrounding Paxton involved an extramarital relationship with a woman named Laura Olson. What began as a private marital matter developed into a major legal and political controversy. 
According to testimony from former senior officials in his office, Paxton allegedly arranged for a political donor, real estate developer Nate Paul, to employ Olson and, in return, used his public office to help Paul with legal matters. In May 2023, the Republican-controlled Texas House voted to impeach Paxton on allegations including abuse of office and bribery. He was temporarily suspended, but in September of that year the state Senate acquitted him, allowing him to return to office.
Last year, reports emerged that Paxton had been involved in another relationship, this time with Christian influencer Tracy Duhon. An American tourist reported an encounter in London, alleging that Paxton physically confronted him and attempted to seize his phone after the tourist photographed him walking with Duhon. 
Paxton's wife, Angela, had publicly stood by him throughout years of criminal investigations and even sat in the chamber during his impeachment trial, when details of his infidelity were revealed. But last year, after 38 years of marriage, she formally filed for divorce. Nevertheless, this month she appeared in a campaign advertisement urging voters to support the entire Republican ticket, without directly mentioning her estranged husband's name.
No-meat campaigning and a nonbinary God: ‘California doesn't need a third senator’
Paxton is popular with relatively few figures in the Republican establishment, and resentment over his victory against Cornyn, who is also well-liked by many Democrats in Congress, has produced a steady stream of leaks from private conversations, revelations about past romantic relationships and even mockery of his physical appearance. 
An injury he suffered as a child left his right eyelid permanently drooping. Yet the Republican Party is still investing everything it can to save him. Trump has already visited Texas three times in recent weeks, and there is every reason to believe he will return before Election Day. Republicans might be able to live with losing ground in the midterms, as virtually every governing party does. But losing Texas is something they cannot afford.
The Republican campaign has already shown early signs of success. Throughout the race, Talarico has found himself defending statements from his past that Paxton's campaign has repeatedly highlighted as evidence that he is concealing his true political views. Among them are remarks he made in 2021, when he said that God was masculine, feminine and everything in between, describing God as nonbinary. 
In another exchange, he argued that modern science recognized six biological sexes rather than simply male and female, referring to chromosomal variations. Paxton has seized on the remarks, dubbing him "Six-Gender Jimmy." At one rally, Paxton declared, "California already has two senators. It doesn't need a third," suggesting that Talarico would represent the values of California's liberal left rather than conservative Texas.
The false claim that Talarico is a vegan also stems from remarks he made in 2022, when he argued that Americans should reduce their meat consumption and described his campaign for reelection to the Texas House as a "non-meat" campaign. In an interview with CBS News earlier this year, Talarico sought to distance himself from some of the statements he made just a few years ago, acknowledging that he regretted certain remarks and that others had "missed the mark." 
He accused Paxton of deliberately circulating embarrassing clips taken out of context to distract voters from his record of corruption. Asked whether he still believed there were six biological sexes, Talarico replied, "I know there are two sexes, men and women." He added that a small percentage of people have chromosomal variations and emphasized that they deserve dignity and respect.
And yet, as the campaign enters its final stretch, Trump already sounds as though he is preparing to shift the blame if Paxton loses. In a lengthy post on Truth Social on Thursday, he accused Republican Senator Cornyn, whom Trump himself helped defeat in the primary, and veteran Republican strategist Karl Rove, one of Trump's most prominent critics within the party, of doing everything they could to prevent Paxton's victory. 
Trump described Talarico as a radical left-wing lunatic, calling him "James TalaFREAKO" and "the ANTITHESIS of Texas Values." He went on to argue that any Paxton defeat would be the fault of Cornyn, Rove and other weak, ineffective Republican political operatives who had opposed him throughout his career.

Israel’s election: The Arab vote and Netanyahu’s politics of exclusion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:28:45 UTC
22:28:45 KST

Mansour Abbas is offering Israel a practical demonstration that Arabs and Jews can share responsibility for their country. Benjamin Netanyahu presents that possibility as a threat. Too many of his opponents still behave as though he is right.
That contradiction could determine whether Israel’s election on 27 October produces a change of government.
At a recent Economist conference in Thessaloniki, where I was also a speaker, former Israeli foreign minister Shlomo Ben-Ami highlighted the dilemma: Netanyahu’s opponents may need Arab parliamentary support to govern, yet remain reluctant to accept that partnership.
Netanyahu does not necessarily need his opponents to lose. He needs them to remain unable to govern together.
The New York Times’ 16 October profile describes Abbas’s partnership with Yoav Segalovitz, a Jewish former senior police officer and centre-left legislator who is second on Ra’am’s electoral list. Their cooperation centres on fighting violent crime in Arab communities: a concrete test of whether shared government can deliver public safety.
The report also recalls Netanyahu’s own negotiations with Abbas in 2021, before Ra’am joined the coalition that removed him from power. Today, his campaign portrays Arab participation as a danger. Partnership apparently becomes intolerable when it threatens his position.
READ: Secret meeting held between US ambassador, opposition leader ahead of Israeli elections: Report
Yet Associated Press reporting on 16 October describes Gadi Eisenkot’s and Yair Lapid’s public rejection of coalitions with Arab-led parties. Outside parliamentary support remains possible, but requires negotiated commitments.
A Maariv poll published that day, reported by The Jerusalem Post, gave each principal bloc 51 seats, Arab parties 14 and the Reservists-Economic Party four outside either bloc. Ra’am’s six seats plus the opposition’s 51 would produce only 57; adding the four-seat party would reach 61. That is a mathematical possibility, not an agreed coalition or an election forecast.
Arab parties have distinct programmes. Their seats cannot simply be assigned to an opposition majority, nor their representatives dismissed as illegitimate because their voters are Arab. An opposition promising democratic renewal must challenge that exclusion.
Abbas’s compromises also deserve scrutiny. The Times reports criticism within Arab communities of his restraint over Gaza. Equal citizenship cannot depend on a minority politician proving endlessly agreeable to the majority. Public safety, housing, education and fair access to resources are obligations of government, not rewards for political silence.
Accountability is equally central. Before the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, mass demonstrations challenged Netanyahu’s judicial overhaul. He was already on trial for bribery, fraud and breach of trust—charges he denies—with imprisonment possible if convicted.
Israel’s Channel 12 television news reported repeated strategic warnings about weakening deterrence before 7 October, rather than specific predictions of the attack. Netanyahu disputes the reports. They demand an independent investigation into what he knew, when he knew it and how he responded. His resistance to such an inquiry is indefensible.
In my view, he has turned prolonged emergency into an argument for his own indispensability. A catastrophe occurring on a leader’s watch cannot entitle him to indefinite political protection. Electoral victory cannot substitute for an inquiry or a court judgment.
The Hamas attack was indefensible. So too is the denial of Palestinian rights. Palestinian medical sources report more than 74,000 deaths in Gaza since 7 October 2023.
More than 20,000 children have been killed, according to Palestinian Health Ministry figures cited by the United Nations. Behind those numbers are lives cut short, bereaved families and futures destroyed. No claim of military success can make this devastation a foundation for lasting security.
READ: Netanyahu, opposition blocs tied as 55% back unity government if election inconclusive: Poll
The diplomatic costs are substantial. Pew’s 2026 survey found that 60 per cent of Americans viewed Israel negatively, up from 53 per cent in 2025. Its international findings showed increases from 64 to 73 per cent in Germany and from 66 to 75 per cent in Italy. These surveys do not establish a single cause; my judgment is that Netanyahu’s conduct in Gaza and support for settlement expansion have deepened the damage.
Even President Donald Trump’s personal backing cannot be taken for granted. In his TIME interview published on 1 October, he repeatedly avoided endorsing Netanyahu’s re-election. This does not establish a rupture between them. It does weaken Netanyahu’s claim that keeping him in office is essential to Israel’s relationship with Washington. American support for Israel is not a personal mandate for Netanyahu.
In the region, his continuation in office also risks raising the political cost of engagement. Security contacts may persist, but they cannot replace the public trust needed for deeper cooperation.
The Holocaust’s historical truth and Jewish suffering are immutable. What a government can squander is present-day moral credibility. Criticism of Netanyahu must never become antisemitism or collective blame.
Removing him, however, would only begin the reckoning. Opposition to Palestinian statehood extends beyond his coalition. His successors must be judged by their willingness to protect civilians, restrain settlement expansion and settler violence, uphold judicial independence and restore a credible Palestinian political horizon.
Arab participation in Israeli government cannot substitute for Palestinian self-determination. Both Israel and Palestine need internationally recognised, secure borders and the sovereignty and viability necessary for sustainable peace. Equal citizenship inside Israel and Palestinian statehood must advance together.
Israel needs a government capable of restoring trust. Keeping one man in office is not a national strategy.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has described Donald Trump’s decision to roll back sanctions on Russia as a “reward” for Vladimir Putin and warned it will embolden the Russian leader and intensify the Kremlin’s war, as Moscow launched one of its worst strikes yet on Ukraine’s power plants in an attempt to black out the country’s cities before winter.
The Ukrainian president also said he expected the Trump administration to lift more sanctions against Russia in the future and called for Europe to establish its own negotiations with Moscow as the US has sought better ties and business deals with the Kremlin.
“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the ‘diesel deal’ is the first step,” said Zelenskyy on Saturday. “Unfortunately, it seems to me that this cannot stop Putin; on the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that he has such support.”
In a social media message earlier, Zelenskyy wrote: “A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground.
“We must keep trying to end the war. To end it, not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely.”
In the Trump administration’s latest effort to reduce tensions with Russia, the US president announced on Friday that he would put a hold on a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.
The act, named after the late senator Lindsey Graham, who championed the legislation, would have introduced tough new sanctions on Russia including a 100% tariff on major importers of Russian oil such as China and India, as well as sanctions on Russia’s energy sector, financial institutions and shadow fleet of oil tankers.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said the decision to waive the sanctions would encourage Vladimir Putin to intensify the war in Ukraine and called for support in the US to resurrect the bill.
“At the time when the Russians launched such a massive strike against our energy sector, in America, regrettably, a decision was made to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war,” he wrote in a statement. “This law could have – and still can! – help a great deal. But the law needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters.”
The move was greeted by the Russian presidential envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, who wrote on social media: “The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment.”
The legislation, which sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps the country’s energy supplies moving, was due to be implemented in two days.
It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Zelenskyy also said the military-grade Starlink terminals used by Ukrainian forces still had limited functionality, and would disconnect from the network when travelling at more than 161km/h (100mph), interfering with drone operations.
The service was throttled inside Ukraine without warning on Tuesday, and Zelenskyy said his government had determined that the restrictions were a “deliberate operation … to prevent us from defending ourselves”.
 
By sending vehicles with the terminals into EU countries, the Ukrainians found they operated at speeds of more than 180km/h, in effect proving that the terminals were only experiencing restrictions in Ukraine.
 
“The conclusion is clear: the restrictions are in effect within Ukraine but do not apply within the European Union,” he said. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”
Trump’s announcement that he would pause US sanctions came a week after he said Washington had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.
Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1m tonnes “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional 3m tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
The Trump administration’s decision to waive the sanctions is the latest consequence of a brutal quarrel between Trump and Zelenskyy. Several times this week, the US did not provide intelligence of impending ballistic missile attacks to Ukraine, in addition to the White House reportedly ordering the Pentagon to throttle the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet network used by Ukraine’s armed forces.
“We very much hope – and I personally hope – that the president of the United States of America will do everything so that Putin stops the killings, stops the strikes on our energy infrastructure, and stops this war,” Zelenskyy said. “But once again, you cannot achieve this by restricting Ukraine’s responses to Russia for killing our people. And even less so by lifting sanctions.”
Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries, as he has blamed the war in Ukraine, rather than the closure of the strait of Hormuz, for the worldwide spike in diesel prices. Ukraine unilaterally halted the strikes after Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, but resumed them when it became clear that Russia was stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian power plants and substations.
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia had launched one of its worst strikes yet against the country’s energy infrastructure, hitting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities and causing “severe consequences”.
He also indicated that Ukraine’s dwindling stock of anti-air weapons made it difficult to shoot down many of the loitering munitions, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles being launched each night at Ukraine.
“Although our warriors are shooting down a significant number of them,” he said, the “sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia’s strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences.”

NASA’s Roman Space Telescope exceeds expectations by nearly 30%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:28:13 UTC
22:28:13 KST

NASA’s Roman Space Telescope exceeds expectations by nearly 30%
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has exceeded expectations after engineers made incredibly tiny adjustments to sharpen its view of the universe. By moving a mirror just one-sixteenth the width of a human hair, the team helped bring its powerful instruments into near-perfect alignment. Roman’s Wide Field Instrument now produces image quality nearly 30% better than predicted, promising exceptionally sharp cosmic surveys.
- Share:
NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is performing even better than scientists anticipated after engineers completed an extensive series of tests and precision adjustments. The work has brought the observatory's powerful instruments into exceptionally sharp focus, with its main camera system now delivering image quality nearly 30% better than predicted.
The achievement marks an important step toward the telescope's ambitious mission to investigate dark matter, dark energy, and other mysteries of the universe. Even the smallest improvements in optical precision could help Roman capture clearer images during its sweeping surveys of the cosmos.
"All of Roman's sweeping surveys will rely on the Wide Field Instrument," said Dave Hickey, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "Many of the mission's primary goals, like studying dark matter and dark energy, wouldn't be possible without it, so it's both exciting and a huge relief to see that it's working well!"
NASA Puts Roman's Powerful Camera System to the Test
Following the activation of the Wide Field Instrument in September, engineers began a comprehensive testing campaign to confirm that each component worked properly on its own and as part of the complete system.
Their first priority was examining the instrument's 18 detectors, each roughly the size of a sticky note, along with the electronics that operate them. The team then evaluated the element wheel, a rotating mechanism equipped with filters and other optical components. These allow selected wavelengths of light to reach the detectors and can separate incoming light into its individual colors.
Next came the instrument's internal calibration system. Engineers activated its light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, which function as adjustable light sources that can produce different colors and brightness levels under commands from Earth. By measuring how the detectors respond to these controlled signals, scientists can identify differences in sensitivity and make the corrections needed for accurate observations.
Engineers also tested the instrument's alignment mechanism and moved it from the deliberately unfocused position used during launch to the position expected to provide the sharpest images. They finished by checking the thermal control system, which maintains the temperatures required for the instrument's various components to function correctly.
"Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," said Maxime Rizzo, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA Goddard. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."
A Space Telescope Already Close to Perfect Alignment
While one group concentrated on preparing the Wide Field Instrument, another worked to refine the telescope's overall optical alignment.
The results were encouraging from the beginning. Roman's mirrors and other optical components were already positioned with remarkable accuracy, meaning engineers needed to make only minor corrections.
"The telescope's performance was excellent even before we began adjusting the alignment of all the mirrors and other optics, thanks to exceptional preparatory work done on the ground prior to launch," said Matthew Bolcar, Roman's optical systems lead at NASA Goddard. "All of the testing and modeling work done at Goddard and by contractors at L3Harris and BAE Space and Mission Systems left only small corrections for us to make to bring everything into near-perfect alignment."
Achieving that level of precision is especially challenging for a spacecraft. The forces experienced during launch can cause tiny shifts in sensitive equipment, and conditions in orbit differ significantly from those on Earth. Roman launched on August 30, carrying optical systems that had been meticulously tested before leaving the ground.
"Our ground testing couldn't exactly reproduce the environment Roman would experience in space, such as the absence of gravity," Bolcar said. "And there are also slight differences in temperature variations and moisture content. Despite those challenges, the recent assessments showed that our ground testing was excellent, with both instruments either matching or exceeding the performance we had predicted."
A Mirror Adjustment Smaller Than a Human Hair
Roman relies on an intricate arrangement of mirrors and optical components to collect light from distant cosmic objects and direct it toward its two scientific instruments. For the resulting images to remain sharp, the light must follow an extremely precise path.
Even a microscopic misalignment can affect how accurately the telescope brings light into focus.
Fortunately, Roman's optical system was already so well aligned that only incredibly small movements were necessary to improve its performance.
"We moved the secondary mirror by about one-sixteenth of the diameter of a human hair," said Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer working on Roman at NASA Goddard. "This adjustment nudged the height of the secondary mirror above the primary. If we scale that height up to the height of the Empire State Building, the change in height is a little bit less than you would get by stacking a single U.S. penny on top of the tip of the tower."
Although nearly impossible to appreciate at a human scale, such a small adjustment can make an important difference when a telescope is designed to study objects across vast cosmic distances.
The team initially concentrated on Roman's Coronagraph Instrument, which had been producing images that were slightly out of focus. The problem was less severe than engineers had anticipated, making it relatively straightforward to correct.
The coronagraph now meets the team's demanding performance expectations. Engineers will continue refining its camera settings and determining the optimal configurations for its deformable mirrors, which can change shape to make extremely precise corrections to incoming light.
In the coming weeks, the team plans to test the coronagraph's ability to block unwanted light, an essential capability for observing faint objects near much brighter ones.
Once the coronagraph's focus had been optimized, engineers returned to the Wide Field Instrument for another round of adjustments.
Roman's Image Quality Exceeds Expectations by Nearly 30%
The final measurements revealed an especially impressive result. Roman's Wide Field Instrument achieved optical performance nearly 30% better than the team had predicted.
Before launch, engineers established an image quality requirement of approximately 90 nanometers RMS (Root Mean Square). This measurement describes the amount of optical error in the system, or how far the incoming light deviates from an ideal, perfectly focused wavefront.
To put that scale into perspective, 90 nanometers is roughly 1,000 times thinner than a human hair. At these tiny dimensions, even seemingly insignificant imperfections can influence the sharpness of astronomical images.
After the latest corrections, however, engineers measured an optical error of just 63 nanometers RMS, substantially better than the original requirement.
That improvement means Roman should be capable of producing even sharper images than its designers initially expected, strengthening its ability to carry out detailed observations across enormous regions of the sky.
"All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Jurling said. "It's a great outcome from years of careful modeling, precision metrology, and testing."
With both scientific instruments meeting or surpassing their expected performance, Roman has cleared another important milestone in its preparation for routine observations. The results highlight the extraordinary precision of the telescope's design and offer a promising outlook for its upcoming investigations into the hidden structure and evolution of the universe.

Zelenskiy asked neighbours to let grain cargoes through, Hungary PM Magyar says

Zelenskiy asked neighbours to let grain cargoes through, Hungary PM Magyar says
BUDAPEST, Oct 17 - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has asked neighbours Poland, Romania, Slovakia and Hungary to allow the transit of Ukrainian grain cargoes because of a Black Sea blockade, Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Saturday.
Magyar, who agreed with Zelenskiy to reset Ukraine-Hungary ties at talks on Friday, said he would have no objections to the measure if the Ukrainian grain cargoes only passed through Hungary to other destinations, private broadcaster RTL reported.
Ukraine is among the world's top producers of wheat, corn and sunflower seeds and around 90% of its exports of such crops go through the Black Sea, where a Russian campaign of attacks has almost halted agricultural exports from its Black Sea ports.
The grain transit would be modelled on a solution proposed shortly after Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Magyar said.
"(Zelenskiy) asked Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Hungary and all neighbouring countries to allow transit, as they had three or four years ago at the start of the war," Magyar told RTL in an interview.
Magyar has taken a less confrontational stance towards Kyiv than Viktor Orban, whom he succeeded as Hungary's prime minister. Magyar had repeatedly said, however, that Hungary would not send arms to Ukraine and demanded progress on the rights of its ethnic Hungarian minority.
Magyar also assured Zelenskiy of his full solidarity over the "inhuman Russian aggression" against Ukraine.
"He mentioned to me during our one-on-one meeting that it would help them a lot if they could transport maize in sealed trains to Western Europe," Magyar said.
"I said as long as it merely transits the country, there would be no obstacle."
In late August the European Commission forecast the European Union's maize harvest, typically its second-largest cereals crop, would be 50.1 million metric tons this year, a near two-decade low and about a fifth below the average of the past three years.
Farmers in France and Hungary were hit especially hard as record heat and drought had decimated maize plantings. REUTERS

The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has refuted claims by the Russian military command alleging that Russian forces captured over 1,800 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory and 92 settlements since Sept. 1, military spokesperson Major Andrii Kovalov announced on Saturday, Oct. 17.
Speaking in an official dispatch, according to Ukrinform, Kovalov characterized the claims – delivered in a recent briefing by the Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, Valery Gerasimov – as deliberate disinformation engineered to project battlefield progress for domestic audiences and Kremlin leadership amid a lack of operational breakthroughs.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Due to the absence of significant successes on the battlefield, the leadership of the Russian army continues to create an illusion of large-scale victories for its own political leadership and domestic audience,” Kovalov stated.
“The report of the Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, Valery Gerasimov, is built on outright falsehoods, manipulations, and exaggerations.”
Kovalov asserted that Ukrainian Defense Forces have liberated more total territory through active counter-offensive and stabilization operations since early autumn than Russian forces managed to seize over the same timeframe.
Rebuttal of claims across Donbas and Zaporizhzhia fronts
The General Staff systematically contested Russian assertions regarding specific towns and frontline axes across eastern and southern Ukraine.
Zelensky Calls Trump’s Sanctions Waiver a Mistake
Addressing claims surrounding Dobropillia in the Donetsk region, Kovalov affirmed that the city remains firmly under Ukrainian control.
The spokesperson compared Gerasimov’s statements to previous unverified claims made by Russian President Vladimir Putin on Sept. 1, when the Russian leader announced the capture of Sviatohirsk, a town that has remained under continuous Ukrainian administration.
Kovalov also rejected Russian reports claiming the capture of Kostiantynivka and Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka, alongside assertions that Russian forward elements reached the municipal outskirts of Kramatorsk.
As of Saturday morning, Oct. 17, Ukrainian forces maintain established defensive positions inside Kostiantynivka where active fighting continues, while Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka remains uncontested by occupying forces.
In the Sloviansk sector, the General Staff denied reports of Russian advances into municipal suburbs and claims of Russian control over more than 50 percent of Mykolaivka.
Kovalov explained that a small Russian reconnaissance team infiltrated the southern periphery of Mykolaivka, adding that Ukrainian forces are conducting search-and-strike sweeps to neutralize the pocket.
In the southern Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian military authorities dismissed Russian claims alleging active battles inside Orikhiv and the capture of Novopavlivka and Novoandriivka, confirming all three settlements remain under Ukrainian control.
Furthermore, Kovalov refuted statements that Russian forces had advanced to within five kilometers of Zaporizhzhia’s southern perimeter, stating the line of contact has remained stabilized roughly 22 kilometers from the regional center.
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, Kovalov rejected recurring Russian reports alleging the seizure of Velykomykhailivka, confirming the settlement remains under Ukrainian administration with the frontline situated eight kilometers to the east.
Sustained combat tempo across Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka sectors
The Ukrainian rebuttal arrives amid persistent high-intensity ground combat along the eastern theater.
Earlier in the week on Oct. 14, the General Staff logged 222 combat engagements across the frontline within a 24-hour cycle, identifying the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka axes as the focal points of Russian offensive operations.
During that daily window, Russian forces launched 29 assaults on the Pokrovsk axis, attempting to advance near Bilytske, Novyi Donbas, Chernihivka, Svitle, Dobropillia, and Novopavlivka, alongside 19 assaults repelled around Kostiantynivka.
Ukrainian defense analysts have observed that Russian informational messaging often anticipates tactical objectives rather than reflecting actual operational control, utilizing premature announcements of territorial captures to influence Western political debates and mask high attrition rates ahead of the winter season.

Ukraine loses ability to use Starlink to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds – Zelensky
President Volodymyr Zelensky said this while speaking with journalists in a chat, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
He noted that Starlink is important for maintaining communications both at the front and for civilians. In particular, the system is used to deliver food and water to troops at forward positions that other vehicles cannot reach.
Starlink is also used on some interceptor drones to destroy jet-powered Shaheds. “Today, our interceptors are not working because of the speed restriction. The maximum speed today is 161 km/h; once that speed is exceeded, Starlink shuts down, and we lose the drone,” Zelensky said.
According to him, Ukraine sent several vehicles equipped with Starlink to European countries for testing, and they traveled at a speed of 180 km/h while the system continued to operate.
“The conclusion is as follows: the restrictions apply in Ukraine and do not apply in EU countries. In other words, this is a planned operation,” Zelensky stressed.
He said that negotiations are currently being held at the military, Defense Ministry and diplomatic levels, while SpaceX is not engaging with the military.
“At various levels, they say these are technical problems. But these technical problems exist in Ukraine; they do not exist in the EU,” Zelensky added.
As reported, Ukraine is awaiting an official response from the Pentagon and SpaceX on the full restoration of the Starshield satellite system, while its operating speed remains unstable.
According to The Telegraph, U.S. billionaire Elon Musk approached U.S. President Donald Trump with a proposal to limit the operating speed of the Starlink satellite system in Ukraine. The Pentagon has not publicly explained the reasons for imposing the restrictions.

Protests erupt in France against living costs, support of students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17

22:13:51 KST

Protests erupt across France against rising living costs and in support of students
Cars were set on fire and shops were looted in Paris on Saturday as police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse violent protesters who joined nationwide demonstrations against rising living costs and in support of high school students' grievances.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez's office reported "a growing number of violent incidents" across the country, including assaults on officers, looting and damage to public buildings. Police made at least 272 arrests across the country, including in Paris.
Protesters across France responded to calls on social media to revive the "yellow vest" movement, which emerged in 2018 against social injustice. Demonstrators expressed widespread frustration and anger at the government as gasoline, energy and food prices have spiked in recent months.
Police fired tear gas and water cannons to push back people wearing hoods and masks and throwing fireworks, paving stones and other objects at officers in the Place de la République, northeast of the Paris city center.
Associated Press reporters saw thick black smoke rising from cars, bicycles and other vehicles, and trash bins on fire. A kiosk was also burning, while several shops have been looted. Several people have been injured in the clashes.
Police tried to prevent other small groups of protesters from converging on government buildings, Nuñez's office said.
Many metro stations were closed Saturday at police request, including those around the Champs-Elysées and near the presidential palace, parliament and government offices.
Meanwhile, the majority of peaceful protesters joined a march that moved toward northwestern Paris. The crowd chanted France's national anthem and waved flags, and some people played trumpets and violins.
Violence hit Lyon, Marseille and other cities
In Lyon, France's third-largest city, where about 20,000 protesters joined the march, a fire broke out inside a tourist office.
In the southern port city of Marseille, some shops and a municipal police station were damaged, while protesters briefly forced their way into the lobby of City Hall.
"This is unacceptable," Marseille Mayor Benoît Payan told BFM TV, describing the damage in City Hall as "limited."
Nuñez's office also reported violence by masked groups in Rennes, Toulouse, Montpellier and Grenoble, among other cities.
Sonia Mabrouk, 40, said she came from a suburb west of Paris with her daughter, a high school student, to protest "everything that's going wrong," particularly the neglect of public services. Mabrouk, who took part in the yellow vest protests, criticized "policies that favor the rich and always hit the poorest people in their wallets."
Many protesters could be seen wearing the fluorescent yellow vests that became a symbol of the 2018 rallies. "There's a general sense of frustration and anger," Mabrouk said, as she marched alongside peaceful demonstrators of all ages.
Saturday's protests follow weeks of school blockades
Student groups protesting since mid-September through school blockades have urged supporters to join them.
The CGT, one of France's major labor unions, also backed the protests, calling for "higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people's needs."
It said that over 500,000 protesters joined the rallies Saturday.
In recent weeks, France has seen thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries and schools set on fire as the new school year descended into nationwide student protests that are influencing the country's presidential election campaign and drawing international attention.
Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who backed the high school students' movement, also took part in the Paris protest Saturday.
Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons. Nuñez suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against the young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand.

Wang, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), made the remarks during an inspection tour in Chengdu, Deyang and the Garze Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture in southwest China's Sichuan Province from Oct. 13 to 16.

The front changes faster than any headquarters, so Ukraine’s war chief went to the people who fight on it. On 16 October, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara met commanders and soldiers from front-line units to discuss the needs of the front, command practices that save lives, and ways to raise combat effectiveness, the Defense Ministry reported.
The front keeps changing, with technology, tactics and weapons shifting constantly, so decisions made far from it risk arriving late and costing lives. Khmara’s answer is to anchor ministry policy in the experience of the soldiers who fight, a continuation of the “machines over men” program.
"The front does not stand still. But the key thing is people. People will always be the foundation and the main value of the Defense Forces,” Khmara said.

Ukraine's most battle-hardened brigades say their word
The meeting drew commanders from across the force, including the Airborne Assault Forces, the Marine Corps, the 93rd, 100th, 28th and 155th mechanized brigades, the 1st, 425th and 475th assault regiments, the 3rd and 59th assault brigades, and Azov.

Command tricks that keep soldiers alive
The talk turned on how good commanders cut their own losses. Participants discussed command approaches that help save soldiers’ lives, use resources efficiently, and achieve combat results.
The ministry wants those methods studied and spread to other units, treating commanders' hard-won judgment as something to scale rather than leave in one brigade.
One goal: fewer Ukrainian losses, more Russian ones
Khmara framed the task in plain terms.
“We must adapt faster and give our warriors modern and effective tools,” he stressed, calling it the shared job of the Defense Ministry, the commander-in-chief and the General Staff.

FSSAI proposed to "prohibit the addition of sucrose and fructose in food products intended for infants up to six months of age." (Representative image: Baby food).
NEW DELHI: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India on Saturday proposed a ban on adding fructose and sucrose in food products for infants up to six months of age.The food regulator published a draft amendment called 'The draft Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Amendment Regulations 2026' over the previous 2020 regulations, for public consultation.FSSAI proposed to "prohibit the addition of sucrose and fructose in food products intended for infants up to six months of age," the draft said.According to the proposal, Stakeholders can submit objections and suggestions within 60 days.The objective is to strengthen nutritional safeguards for infants, according to a statement from the ministry of health and family welfare, cited by PTI.
"The first six months of life represent a critical period for healthy growth and development, making appropriate nutrition particularly important. The proposed restriction seeks to ensure that infant nutrition products meet the nutritional needs of this age group without unnecessary addition of sucrose and fructose," the ministry said.The existing regulations set nutritional composition, quality and safety standards for infant nutrition products designed for children from birth to 24 months. They identify lactose and glucose polymers as the preferred carbohydrate sources, while allowing sucrose and fructose to be added, within prescribed limits, when needed to provide carbohydrates.The proposed amendment seeks to tighten these provisions by barring the addition of sucrose and fructose to products intended for infants up to six months of age.

Alana Hadid, Jenan Matari drop Random House Palestine book deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:08:38 UTC
22:08:38 KST

Breadcrumb
Alana Hadid, Jenan Matari walk away from Random House book deal after publisher ‘sanitises’ views on Palestine
Alana Hadid and Jenan Matari have pulled a children’s book they co-authored on the Palestinian experience from Penguin Random House publishers, after they said their account on history was “sanitised and misrepresented”.
Random House Children’s Books, a division of Penguin Random House, signed the book deal in November 2024, and it was set for release last month.
However, the authors, who have both been outspoken about the plight of Palestinians in the face of Israeli occupation and abuses, included the history of Palestine in the book, with the manuscript also including elements of their own families’ stories.
It touched on the Palestinian resistance, the forced exile of Palestinian civilians and the Palestinian diaspora around the world as a result.
It also centred on how the Palestinian story has long been erased and ignored, as well as the rise of Zionism, the Nakba (Catastrophe of 1948), the relationship between the US and Israel, and how life feels under a military occupation.
It described Israel as a settler colony, and Hadid documented her personal family history, mentioning how her real-estate mogul father Mohammed Hadid and his parents were expelled from Safed, and forced to live as refugees in Syria.
Matari explained in the book how her relatives were expelled from Deir Yassin and Ein Karem after the Israeli massacre in 1948, where over 100 Palestinians were killed.
However, the writers said they withdrew the book after Random House requested changes, after they had submitted a final copy.
Random House told reporters that the process was normal and had “followed our standard bookmaking procedures”.
In excerpts of communications between the authors and Random House shared with The Guardian, the writers and activists engaged in disagreements over language in the book over the course of several months.
One particular sticking point was the 7 October attack on southern Israel, and the writers stating that people under “colonial domination” have the “right to resist”. The book also cited a UN general assembly resolution that says people under colonial domination are entitled to “the right to self-determination” and to restore that right “by any means at their disposal”.
Random House demanded that a disclaimer, or counter-narrative be added to say that the attack on Israel was in violation of international law.
A failure to agree on the details resulted in the authors walking away from the deal, choosing to instead release it through Palestinian-owned US publisher Interlink Books.
“They continued to try to sanitize our history because they didn’t want to make certain communities uncomfortable. But decolonial history is supposed to make you uncomfortable,” Matari said.
“I believe it was a revolutionary book, which is why it was under so much scrutiny,” she continued.

Britain deploys carrier to Arctic and North Atlantic
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:07:53 BST
22:07:53 KST

HMS Prince of Wales sails from Portsmouth on Sunday for the Arctic and North Atlantic, leading the UK Carrier Strike Group into the second phase of Operation Firecrest under NATO command, according to the Royal Navy.
The carrier is accompanied by the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless and carries an air group of F-35 jets, Merlin Mk4 Commando and Mk2 anti-submarine helicopters, Wildcat helicopters and Malloy drones. More than 1,200 British personnel are deployed with the group, working alongside allies including Norway, Denmark and Germany.
The Royal Navy said the deployment of Britain’s flagship aircraft carrier alongside NATO allies is “a powerful shield for the nation, ensuring that the critical energy, trade, and communication links we all rely on everyday in the region remain secure.”
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The deployment of the HMS Prince of Wales and her air wing to the High North and the North Atlantic, operating under NATO leadership, is a clear demonstration of the UK’s commitment to the Alliance and contribution to the enduring security and stability of the North Atlantic.”
Commodore Richard Hewitt, who commands the UK Carrier Strike Group staff, said he was pleased to be going back: “I am delighted to return to the Arctic and North Atlantic as we build on the successes of the first phase of Operation Firecrest.
“Led by the UK Flagship HMS Prince of Wales, the Strike Group will bring together a range of assets and capabilities, while taking every opportunity to train, operate and integrate with our NATO allies and partners.”
The Royal Navy said the focus of the second phase is maintaining operational readiness, strengthening interoperability and ensuring the group is prepared to respond to the challenges of a region it describes as increasingly important. The strike group will contribute to enhanced vigilance activity including the latest in NATO’s Neptune Strike series of exercises, which runs across swathes of Europe and the North Atlantic in a test of allied land, sea and air forces.
While deployed, the carrier will host gatherings of military and political leaders in Oslo. The Atlantic Future Forum and the International Sea Power Conference will bring together defence leaders, industry and policymakers to discuss the future of Euro-Atlantic security, and holding both aboard a British carrier alongside in the Norwegian capital puts the ship itself at the centre of the diplomacy.
Prince of Wales is due to leave Portsmouth Naval Base at 1700 on Sunday 18 October, weather permitting.

How to pack your hand luggage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:06:20 UTC
22:06:20 KST

How to pack your hand luggage
A power bank, a laptop and a bottle of shampoo may all be travel essentials, but they do not follow the same baggage rules. Knowing what belongs in the cabin, what can go in the hold and what needs approval can help passengers avoid problems at the airport. Qazinform News Agency explains how to pack hand luggage, check power bank restrictions and prepare everyday items for a flight.
Before packing, check the rules of the airline operating each flight and the security requirements at departure and transfer airports. Permission to carry an item does not necessarily mean permission to use it on board.
Keep power banks in the cabin
Power banks and spare lithium batteries must be carried in hand luggage, not checked baggage.
Lithium batteries can overheat or catch fire if damaged or short-circuited. Keeping them in the cabin allows crew members to respond if something goes wrong.
This rule also matters at the boarding gate. If staff take your cabin bag to place it in the aircraft’s hold, remove your power bank and spare batteries before handing it over.
Check the capacity before travelling
The key figure on a power bank is its energy rating in watt-hours, written as Wh.
Power banks rated at up to 100 Wh are generally permitted in cabin baggage without prior airline approval, subject to the carrier’s other restrictions.
For devices above 100 Wh and up to 160 Wh, do not assume that carriage is allowed. IATA’s guidance for 2026 explains that ICAO provisions allow these power banks with airline approval, but a carrier can apply stricter limits. Contact the operating airline before travelling.
If the label shows only milliampere-hours, or mAh, the battery voltage is also needed to calculate its energy capacity:
For example, a 20,000 mAh battery rated at 3.7 volts has an energy capacity of 74 Wh. A 30,000 mAh battery at the same voltage has a capacity of 111 Wh.
Do not assume you can charge devices during the flight
Carrying a power bank and using it on board are separate matters.
ICAO introduced new specifications effective March 27, 2026, limiting power banks to two per passenger and prohibiting passengers from recharging them during flights. This includes plugging a power bank into an aircraft’s charging outlet.
IATA’s implementation guidance also recommends against using power banks to recharge phones or other portable electronics on board. Some airlines make this a firm prohibition. FlyArystan, for example, states that passengers must not use power banks to charge other devices during the flight.
Charge your devices before boarding and follow the crew’s instructions on using and storing electronics.
Protect batteries from damage
Keep each power bank or spare battery protected against short circuits. Original packaging, a suitable protective pouch or insulation over exposed battery terminals can help prevent contact with metal objects.
Do not travel with a swollen or damaged battery. Check whether the manufacturer has recalled your device because of a fire risk.
If a battery becomes unusually hot, expands or starts smoking during the flight, alert the cabin crew immediately.
Keep phones and laptops with you
IATA recommends carrying phones, laptops, cameras and other lithium-powered devices in hand luggage. Its passenger guidance also advises removing lithium batteries and electronic devices if a cabin bag is taken at the gate for transport in the hold.
Where an airline permits a device with an installed battery in checked baggage, the FAA says it must be completely switched off and protected against damage and accidental activation. Sleep or hibernation mode is not sufficient.
This does not create an exception for power banks or spare batteries, which must remain in the cabin.
Check the container, not just the liquid inside
Liquids must be carried in containers of no more than 100 millilitres each, with a combined volume of no more than one litre per passenger.
The container’s capacity matters. A half-full 200 ml bottle still exceeds a 100 ml container limit.
Liquids include more than drinks. Creams, gels, toothpaste and other pastes may also fall under security restrictions.
Requirements can differ between airports. While many retain the 100 ml container limit, some allow larger containers. Exceptions may apply to essential medicines, baby food and special dietary requirements.
What cannot go in checked baggage
Not everything prohibited in hand luggage can be transported in checked baggage.
Explosives, fireworks, flammable liquids such as gasoline and acetone, toxic substances, corrosive chemicals and radioactive materials are prohibited in both checked and carry-on baggage. Restrictions also apply to compressed gases and other hazardous materials.
Some items, however, are allowed only in the cabin. Power banks, spare lithium batteries and electronic cigarettes must not be placed in checked baggage because of fire safety risks.
Knives, sharp objects and certain tools should generally be packed in checked baggage, subject to airline regulations. Some toiletries and medical items are permitted under specific conditions.
Earlier, on October 11, an IndiGo flight from Delhi to Chennai was forced to divert to Hyderabad after a passenger’s power bank caught fire in an overhead luggage compartment. The cabin crew managed to extinguish the fire, and the aircraft landed safely. No injuries were reported. The incident once again raised concerns about the safety of lithium-ion batteries on board aircraft.

This bird flies thousands of miles, but its wings have a catch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:05:02 UTC
22:05:02 KST

This bird flies thousands of miles, but its wings have a catch
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- Lund University
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered an unexpected trade-off in the wings of the European nightjar, a bird that migrates thousands of kilometers but sacrifices high-speed flight efficiency to hunt insects with remarkable agility. Even more surprisingly, it generates thrust on the upward wingbeat, a technique that could inspire new flying technologies.
- Share:
A bird that migrates thousands of miles has revealed a surprising secret about how wings work. Scientists have discovered that European nightjars sacrifice flight efficiency for agility and use an unexpected wingbeat technique previously associated mainly with bats and insects.
The European nightjar (Caprimulgus europaeus) is a nighttime hunter that makes an extraordinary annual migration between Europe and southern Africa. Yet the wings that carry it across vast distances must also perform a very different task: helping the bird catch insects while flying slowly and making sharp turns.
Scientists at Lund University have discovered that these competing demands come with a surprising trade-off. Although the nightjar is built to handle long migrations, its wings are not perfectly optimized for efficient flight at higher speeds.
Why Nightjar Wings Sacrifice Efficiency for Agility
To investigate how nightjars fly, researchers studied the birds in a wind tunnel, recording their movements at different speeds and measuring the patterns of airflow left behind their wings.
The experiments revealed that the nightjar's broad wing tips, which likely help it maneuver during slow flight, become a disadvantage as the bird flies faster. At higher speeds, its wings generate lift less efficiently. Lift is the aerodynamic force that helps keep a bird airborne.
The findings challenge the assumption that birds traveling enormous distances must have wings optimized primarily for efficient long-distance flight.
"This runs counter to the intuitive image of a long-distance migrant as a perfectly optimized flying machine. Instead, the nightjar's wings appear to be a compromise between several different demands. The bird can fly slowly and maneuver while hunting, but the trade-off is reduced efficiency in lift generation at higher speeds," says Christoffer Johansson, associate professor at Lund University.
Scientists Discover an Unexpected Wingbeat Trick
The researchers also uncovered another surprising feature of the nightjar's flight. Even as the bird raises its wings during the upward portion of each wingbeat, it continues to generate thrust, the force that helps propel it forward.
This is unusual because such an active upward wing movement, known as an upstroke, has previously been linked mainly to the flight mechanics of bats and insects rather than birds.
The discovery suggests that animals with very different evolutionary histories may have developed similar aerodynamic solutions to the challenges of flying.
"What's interesting is that the same type of aerodynamic solution seems to appear in quite different animals. This suggests that the upstroke does not have to be merely a passive or lift generating part of the wingbeat. It can be actively used to generate thrust when the wings cannot be folded very much," says Christoffer Johansson.
What Bird Flight Reveals About Evolution and Flying Robots
The results offer a broader lesson about how evolution shapes animals that depend on the same body structures for different activities.
Rather than producing wings perfectly suited to one purpose, evolution can favor designs that balance several competing needs. For the nightjar, that means combining the ability to migrate across continents with the agility required to hunt insects at low speeds.
Understanding these compromises could also lead to improvements in aviation technology, particularly drones and other robotic aircraft that use flapping wings.
Like birds, these machines may face mechanical restrictions on how much their wings can fold during each wingbeat. Learning how nightjars generate thrust during the upstroke could help engineers develop more effective ways to move through the air.
Researchers now hope to determine whether this unusual flight mechanism is widespread among other birds and flying animals or whether it represents a more specialized adaptation.
"We now want to investigate how common this way of generating force is among other birds and flying animals. It could help us understand which aerodynamic principles are specific to the nightjar and which are more general. This knowledge may also inspire the development of new types of flapping aircraft," Christoffer Johansson concludes.
