Shadow fleet now a third of Northern Sea Route traffic
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:03:49 BST
22:03:49 KST

Sanctioned vessels sailing in and out of the Russian Arctic now account for nearly a third of all cargo traffic along the Northern Sea Route, and pose what the government describes as a potentially serious threat to British interests, according to the updated Arctic Policy Framework.
The document, published by the government and signed by Uma Kumaran, the Minister for the Polar Regions, sets out the first full revision of British Arctic policy since 2023.
On the shipping route itself, the framework said: “The commercial use of the Northern Sea Route (NSR) between Asia and Europe has slowly been developing, notwithstanding that many operators judge this sea route to be operationally risky and environmentally precarious. We have also seen the growth of the shadow fleet, with sanctioned vessels sailing in and out of the Russian Arctic now accounting for nearly a third of all cargo traffic along the NSR and posing a potentially serious threat to UK interests.”
It set out the wider risk the fleet carries. “Russia has also dramatically expanded its use of shadow fleet vessels in an attempt to circumvent sanctions on its energy exports. The use of these vessels poses a systemic risk to international maritime safety and standards, in addition to increasing the potential for serious environmental damage in a highly sensitive region.”
Deterring and disrupting the shadow fleet is named in the framework as a British priority, pursued through the Nordic Baltic 8++ partnership. The document also records that Britain took command of NATO’s Joint Force Command Norfolk in September, and names the Lunna House Agreement with Norway, under which the two navies will operate side by side in the North Atlantic protecting critical national infrastructure from malign activity.
The shadow fleet is the collection of ageing tankers, typically operating under flags of convenience with opaque ownership and uncertain insurance, that Russia has assembled to keep its oil moving past the price cap imposed after the invasion of Ukraine. Hundreds have been designated by Britain, the European Union and the United States, and the vessels have been linked to dark fleet transfers, falsified tracking data and a string of incidents involving undersea cables in the Baltic.

China urges Israel to rethink its policies
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has urged Israel to halt and reverse the establishment of settlements in the occupied West Bank, describing the Palestinian issue as the “greatest historical injustice of this century,” according to a statement released by Beijing following his meeting with Israeli President Isaac Herzog.
The two officials met on Thursday on the sidelines of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) summit in Baku, Azerbaijan.
Wang said achieving peace and reconciliation in the Middle East remained a cornerstone of Chinese foreign policy, stressing that a two-state solution was the only viable path toward resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
The Chinese diplomat also warned that the humanitarian situation in Gaza remained critical despite the ceasefire reached a year ago.
“The immediate priority is to fully open access to Gaza,” Wang said, arguing that two million civilians must not be left struggling to survive or exposed to a worsening humanitarian catastrophe.
He added that Israel should “stop and reverse” its efforts to forcibly establish settlements in the West Bank.
Herzog, meanwhile, said Israel wanted peace but continued to face “security threats.” In a post on X, he claimed Iran and its regional allies were the primary dangers.
The meeting comes amid continued Israeli settlement expansion in the West Bank, which Israel occupied during the 1967 Six-Day War. Most countries consider the settlements illegal under international law, a position Israel disputes, citing historical claims and security concerns. Settlement construction has long been a major obstacle in negotiations over a Palestinian state.
According to figures compiled by UN agencies and settlement monitors, more than 750,000 Israeli settlers lived in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, in 2025. The same year, the Israeli authorities approved 54 new settlements and established 86 additional outposts.
Settlement expansion has also coincided with rising violence against Palestinians. The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs documented 1,828 settler attacks causing casualties or property damage in 2025, up from 1,420 in 2024 and 1,189 in 2023 – the highest annual total since monitoring began in 2006. 
China has repeatedly backed Palestinian statehood and sought a greater diplomatic role in the Middle East. Beijing brokered the restoration of diplomatic relations between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023 and hosted talks between rival Palestinian factions in 2024, although the resulting reconciliation agreement has yet to be implemented.

Nearly third of teachers at schools transitioning to Estonian unqualified

Unknown Publisher

Nearly third of teachers at schools transitioning to Estonian unqualified
Nearly a third of teachers at schools transitioning to Estonian lack the required qualifications, as heavy workloads and limited pay make recruitment and retention harder.
When Tallinn's Ehte High School of Humanities switched to Estonian-language instruction in 2024, it hired 17 new teachers. One in three has since left, and the school continues to hire 10–15 more a year to replace both retiring teachers and those who leave due to burnout.
Principal Marika Kranisver said teaching students whose first language is Russian can require more work, as teachers have to adapt materials and bridge students' language gaps. Some end up leaving for schools with more native Estonian-speaking kids.
"I have tremendous respect for the teachers who have taken on this challenge and come to a transitioning school," Kranisver said, acknowledging how much more work it involves than teaching at schools where Estonian is already the main language.
Higher pay has helped attract teachers, but increasing funding constraints are making this harder for schools.
Tartu Jogentaga School principal Alina Braziulene said their school has had to cut the bonus pay for qualified teachers from 20 percent to just 3 percent as state support for Ukrainian students has ended and enrollment is down.
"A third of our students came from Ukraine, and the state used to provide substantial funding to support them," Braziulene explained. "That support is gone now."
When schools could no longer offer higher pay, some teachers quit. Meanwhile, the number of teachers required to teach in Estonian has grown, but funding has not, further squeezing budgets for bonus pay.
'The workload is killing them'
At Tallinn's Läänemere High School, principal Deniss Presnetsov said bonus pay is important, but the school can't offer it to everyone, especially as some applicants lack the required qualifications.
He said workloads are also taking a toll on teaching staff, who juggle heavy administrative demands, lesson planning and consultations on top of the teaching itself.
"That kind of constant workload is killing them," Presnetsov stressed, adding that it quickly drives young teachers away. "They end up leaving the school after a couple of years. Some leave after just one."
The Ministry of Education and Research recommends training to help teachers work with students with non-Estonian language backgrounds, adding that with the right methods, teaching Russian-speaking students isn't necessarily harder.

Ukraine says Russia's claimed territorial advances are 'an illusion'

Reuters could not independently verify the battlefield claims.

‘We’re not playing games’: Parents launch playground protests to fight school field sell-off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:00:31 UTC
22:00:31 KST

On Saturdays throughout autumn, residents of Totnes have met at a field on the banks of the River Dart to play ballgames, fly kites or simply sit on the grass and chat.
But it hasn’t just been about having fun – this has been a “play protest” aimed at trying to save a beloved piece of open land in the historic Devon market town.
The local comprehensive, King Edward VI Community College (KEVICC), has been given the go-ahead by the UK government to sell the 1.5-hectare plot – Lower Field – and it is likely houses will be built on it.
School leaders say they desperately need funds to revamp neglected buildings but campaigners claim the sell-off is an example of land that has been used by communities for decades being whisked away – a modern “enclosure” of public space.
“It’s devastating,” said Becca Robinson, who uses the field for women’s and girls’ fitness classes. “I’m trying to get women and girls to be more active and to get outdoors. The great thing about the field is it’s an open space, so it feels safe. It really worries me that, if we lost it, fewer women and girls will exercise.
“It’s also a spot people go just to do their own thing rather than take part in structured sport. You can just make an ad hoc decision to go and play a game or just to sit and read.”
Earlier this year, the anti-poverty charity Trussell published research revealing almost half of UK residents (45%) had lost access to at least one community space – such as a park, social club, library or post office – since 2023.
Danielle McIlven, who has been organising games of rounders on the field, attended the school and said Lower Field had been part of her life for years. “It’s about the unstructured play that can take place there. In the summer you see swarms of teenagers playing there or heading down to the river.”
Anna Ali, the organiser of a women’s football “kickabout” and a member of the campaign group Friends of Lower Field, said the town had a reputation for being middle class and affluent. “But there is quite a lot of hidden impoverishment. Public green spaces are vital. I was speaking to a woman who brings her grandchildren here. They can’t afford to join sports clubs, so kicking a ball around on the field is a lifeline.”
Lewis Winks, a leading member of the Right to Roam group, said Lower Field had been shared by the school and the wider Totnes community since it was gifted by the Elmhirst family, known for progressive farming, forestry and educational projects on the nearby Dartington Estate, about a century ago.
A key issue the Friends group is digging into is the details of the Elmhirst gift – and whether it may have been legally given to the community or permanently protected for community use.
Winks said: “Lower Field is a vital place for young people and families to play, exercise and spend time together. Losing it would undermine the town’s vitality and wellbeing.”
The Friends group wants Education South West, the trust the school is part of, to explore whether the field could be sold to the community. Winks said: “We are asking for a realistic window to raise the money. A community purchase could help fund improvements at KEVICC while safeguarding the field for its pupils and the wider community.”
But it is a race against time. The land is expected to be put on the market in January, giving little time to raise funds. Campaigners also highlight that measures under the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 aimed at giving communities greater influence over the places and assets that matter to them are unlikely to come into force in time. “We’re falling through the gap regarding a right to buy,” Winks said.
Matthew Shanks, chief executive of Education South West, said it understood how important the site was to the Totnes community and wanted to have an open and constructive conversation with people.
He said money raised would support significant refurbishment and modernisation across the school estate, including improvements to buildings and facilities. Shanks said the school would retain playing fields which would remain available for public use.
School principal Alan Salt said he understood the future of the field mattered hugely to the community. “We want to be open and transparent about what is proposed.” The trust and school have organised an open meeting to discuss the field.
Salt argued that selling it made sound financial sense. There had been little capital investment in the school for six years and it had “temporary” classrooms more than half a century old.
“So we’ve got a really acute set of challenges within a very difficult national context,” he said. “At the end of the day, we are a comprehensive school trying to get the best for the students in a really difficult national picture.”

Inside the long, bitter fight over one man’s quest to build the biggest AI datacenter in California
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:00:31 UTC
22:00:31 KST

Sebastian Rucci zoomed in on a map in late 2024, looking closely at a large block of brown earth. The barren plot sandwiched between sprawling alfalfa fields and sleepy desert suburbs was exactly what he’d been searching for – the perfect place to realize his dream of building the largest artificial intelligence datacenter in California.
The dusty expanse wasn’t an obvious location. It was in the Sonoran desert, just north of the Mexican border, where temperatures regularly rose past 100F (37.8C). Water was scarce in the once-booming agricultural area, which gets its supply from the beleaguered Colorado River. And then, there was the city of Imperial – population 22,000 – to win over. As controversial datacenter projects have sprung up across the US, residents were naturally skeptical of a new, energy-guzzling neighbor.
But for Rucci, a 66-year-old lawyer with a complicated past, none of these obstacles seemed insurmountable.
Rucci is among the new class of middlemen who inhabit the burgeoning world of datacenter development. The rapid rise of artificial intelligence – galvanized by Silicon Valley companies worth trillions of dollars – has fueled one of the biggest industrial construction booms in history. The technology requires far more computing power than traditional internet services, and that means building enormous new structures to house millions of servers.
This proliferation of datacenters is now attracting modern-day prospectors seeking land in hopes of cashing in on one of the fastest-growing and most lucrative industries on Earth. Set in their sights are areas like Imperial county: rural, underdeveloped and desperate for an economic boost.
“I didn’t know much about datacenters,” Rucci said, recalling a couple of years back. “I made calls to people I knew in Silicon Valley. And within a short period, I realized: holy shit, this stuff is huge.”
Rucci, a self-described expert at doing the tedious legwork of packaging permits and plans, proved adept at selling a bright future of economic development to county lawmakers. He said his sales skills also nabbed him a direct line to Google, which floated interest in being the tenant of the datacenter, according to emails between Rucci and county agencies.
With the promise of these potential partnerships and support from construction unions, Rucci moved into high gear last year and began plotting his nearly 1m-square-foot datacenter – a facility the size of 16 football fields combined. He said he had invested about $5m already, and, if it gets approved and passed off to a builder, he expects “big multipliers of that” in return.
What Rucci didn’t expect, however, was the firestorm of resistance his project set off in the community.
Over the past year, more than half a dozen lawsuits have been filed, along with recall efforts for local officials who supported the project. Even a temporary 45-day datacenter moratorium was approved. Echoing similar battles against such development across the US, Imperial county residents told the Guardian they fear increased emissions, harm to the region’s rare desert wildlife, constraints on the power grid and rapidly dwindling water supply, along with noise issues. Rucci denies the project will have such effects.
It seems the backlash succeeded – for now. Rucci’s developments are on pause after a county judge ruled last month that his project cannot move forward until it clears an extensive environmental review. Despite a bold start, Rucci could end up a cautionary tale of what can go wrong when a businessman moves too fast without community buy-in.
“This project was presented as a Noah’s Ark that’s going to come save everybody,” said Francisco Leal, who lives in a residential neighborhood across the street from Rucci’s proposed datacenter. “But the community sees this project as a Trojan horse.”
From strip club owner to datacenter developer
When Rucci landed on that vast plot of land in Imperial county in late 2024, only two things really mattered: finding a location that could be exempted from California’s strict environmental building requirements, and getting his hands on a lot of electricity. In unincorporated Imperial county, he had both.
Because the land was zoned for industrial use, he was able to apply for an exemption from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), which would fast-track the project by avoiding the environmental permitting process. And for electricity, Rucci was able to work with the local energy provider to eventually get 330 megawatts of electricity – enough to power a city the size of Tallahassee.
Rucci is based in Huntington Beach, but has started several businesses throughout southern California, St Louis and Ohio. In early 2025, he said one of his connections introduced him to a longtime Google employee who helped guide him through the process. In a July email to Imperial county’s planning and development services, Rucci wrote that the datacenter would “enable Google to conduct artificial intelligence and large language model training for its Gemini system”, Google’s suite of AI models.
“We have secured interest from Google for this project, which we are confident will transform the area through increased tax revenues, new employment opportunities, and expanded energy production,” Rucci wrote in another email in August to the county’s air pollution control district.
“We are not involved in a datacenter project in Imperial county,” said a Google spokesperson. She did not respond to questions about the company’s relationship with Rucci. He said Google’s response made sense considering they do not have a formal agreement.
While California has dozens of datacenters capable of cloud computing, streaming and internet searches, the state has scant facilities dedicated to AI. That’s because California is one of the most rigorous states when it comes to environmental permitting for energy and water-intensive facilities such as AI datacenters.
Major projects in California take an average of seven years to get completed, said Michael Thomas, the founder of Cleanview, which tracks datacenter development. For comparison, the average in Texas is about three years. Thomas said he had seen a surge of new players, like Rucci, get into AI datacenter development nationwide. These people, he said, were willing to take on the risk and find ways to speed up the process.
“Land and power have become so scarce at the scale that these big tech companies need,” Thomas said. So, if a developer can shorten the timeline, “a company like Google or Microsoft or Meta may be willing to pay you a huge premium … It’s potentially a way to make millions of dollars very quickly.”
Rucci is no stranger to taking on risk. He has owned a strip club, addiction treatment centers and dozens of accounting and real estate endeavors. In 2010, while operating the strip club, Go Go Cabaret, he was convicted on four counts of illegal liquor sales for which he had to serve a 30-day jail sentence. He was also charged with engaging in a pattern of corrupt activity, money laundering and promoting prostitution, but those charges were later dismissed. In 2019, California suspended his license to practice law for nearly three years.
He has also filed for corporate bankruptcy at least twice. The most recent time, in 2023, took place after the Department of Justice investigated one of his addiction treatment centers for alleged fraud, ending with a government seizure of $600,000 of assets. No criminal charges were filed, however, and that money was later returned with interest after Rucci sued the government to reclaim the seized funds.
Since zeroing in on Imperial county in 2024, Rucci has registered several new businesses related to the vast datacenter campus, from construction and energy supply to ongoing operations. The umbrella company for his project is an LLC called Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing (IVCM). Rucci says the facility will bring in more than 1,600 construction jobs and nearly $30m in annual tax revenue. It will also include an electrical substation, on-site battery energy storage and more than 130 methane-gas-fueled generators, according to an application submitted to the county planning department.
Rucci said his diverse experience was well-suited for such a complicated project. “That doesn’t mean that my background isn’t colorful,” he said. “I’ve challenged cities. I fought the federal government. I’ve done a lot of stuff. But that doesn’t mean that I don’t know how to process this and get it through.”
Battle lines
At first, Leal had no clue that the dusty 75 acres of land across the street from his house had been bought by a developer. It wasn’t until the day before Thanksgiving last year when he found a colorful flyer hanging from his door that his world began to swirl around him. The flyer mapped out the huge project and warned that construction was moving forward without requiring the state’s usual environmental review.
Leal began scanning the internet, and what he found shocked him. His back fence was all that separated his home from Rucci’s property. While Leal lived in Imperial city, the datacenter would fall just outside city limits on unincorporated county land. It was clear that living next to this facility would permanently change the quiet life he and his wife had envisioned when they moved there some 20 years earlier.
“When we bought that house, we planned for it to be the house where we would retire, where our kids would grow up and return when they visit,” Leal said. “The quality of life of anybody living half a mile from the datacenter will be affected.”
He started texting his neighbors that same day. As word spread, people began to organize, holding meetings and rallies against the datacenter proposal. Within months, close to 3,500 people would sign a petition opposing the facility, and state senator Steve Padilla, who represents the district, would sound the alarm, introducing a series of bills aimed at datacenters.
As AI datacenters have popped up around the world, they’ve come under scrutiny for being extremely resource-intensive. A query through chatbots such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini needs nearly 10 times as much electricity as a typical internet search, and that number can increase for more complicated prompts. Because supercomputers run hot, they typically need extensive water-cooling systems.
Imperial county is a critical habitat for wildlife like the desert pupfish, which is listed as an endangered species under the California Endangered Species Act and swims through agricultural drains and canals, much like one that crosses Rucci’s property. Other desert animals of concern include the flat-tailed horned lizard, yellow-breasted chat and burrowing owls.
As Leal got more involved in the datacenter fight, he met other concerned residents, like Christopher Scurries. Scurries lives nearby and is a music teacher at Imperial high school. He said he was worried about datacenter noise, what’s known as a constant low hum. “I’ll definitely hear when I’m here in my house,” he said. Scurries and his wife moved to the area in 2017 so they could afford a home. Now with a two-year-old daughter, his previously pleasant life feels uncertain in the shadow of the datacenter.
It’s testament to a long-simmering sentiment in this corner of the Sonoran desert, where pollutants from agriculture and industry, along with poverty, have long taken an undue toll. One in five adults is unemployed in the region and the poverty rate, at close to 20%, is the highest in California.
“The benefits these structures may bring into a community – the jobs, tax revenue, even the infrastructure improvements – may feel uncertain or uneven compared to the scale of the impact,” said Carla Walker, the US director of environmental justice and equity at the research organization World Resources Institute. “Communities are asking these questions of who benefits and who pays the price.”
For Jacob Rodriguez, who was born and raised in the area, who pays the price has been top of mind. “It’s an existential threat,” he said of the datacenter project, noting that residents had long dealt with pollution and dwindling water supplies. “The respiratory problems and the air quality here are already abysmal … eventually, indirectly, this will cost lives.”
‘I’m not here to run for Miss America’
By March, tensions between Rucci and the community had reached a boiling point. At an Imperial county board of supervisors meeting, dozens of residents, including Leal and Scurries, packed into the chambers for a public feedback session. As Rucci stood at the lectern, trying to present his more than 100 slides on the project, the crowd steadily chanted “no datacenters” and waved “not in my backyard” signs. It got so raucous that Rucci, the main speaker on the schedule, left the meeting early.
As he walked out of the building, protesters yelled “Fuera, Rucci, fuera” (“leave” in Spanish). Visibly fed up, Rucci unexpectedly approached a person screaming through a bullhorn and roared in their face.
By this point, the project was at the center of a heated legal battle. The city of Imperial had sued the county for bypassing public input and environmental reviews when it approved the datacenter (the environmental nonprofit Sierra Club later joined on). Rucci, in turn, counter-sued in federal court on behalf of his company IVCM, alleging the city carried out a “bad-faith campaign of administrative obstruction and targeted retaliation”.
He then went on to sue an anti-datacenter activist named Jake Tison, the Comité Cívico del Valle non-profit, and its executive director, Luis Olmedo, and the local public-media news station KPBS and one of its reporters, Kori Suzuki, for defamation. Those three defamation suits were dismissed. Rucci has appealed in the cases against KPBS and Comité Cívico del Valle and is working to reverse the ruling on Tison.
“Look, I’m not here to run for Miss America or Mr America,” Rucci said. “I’m here to do a datacenter.”
Rucci, on behalf of IVCM, also sued the local utility, the Imperial irrigation district, for rejecting an application for water to cool the datacenter. The utility’s sole source of water is the drought-stricken Colorado River. The AI facility would need about 750,000 gallons of water a day, according to Rucci.
He says the water the datacenter would use is equivalent to a 160-acre farm, of which there are several in the area. The utility’s officials, however, voiced concerns about how the project would affect residents. Karin Euenio, one of the utility’s directors, wrote in an op-ed: “I believe it is my duty to speak up when a proposal raises serious concerns about ratepayers, reliability, and community wellbeing.”
The tumult continued through the spring and summer, with Rucci’s IVCM spending $30,000 in a campaign to back his company spokesperson, Carlos Duran, to fill the seat of one of the utility district’s directors. He lost.
For its part, the community instigated its own political organizing efforts with a recall campaign of Peggy Price, the chair of Imperial county’s board of supervisors who has been supportive of the datacenter. That campaign is ongoing.
While things had been looking good for Rucci after he got county approval for the project in April, it took a drastic turn over the last month. The judge presiding over the city’s lawsuit ruled Rucci must go back to square one for the entire approval process. That means before breaking ground, the datacenter must clear lengthy environmental reviews to assess its impact on the power grid, water supply and emissions.
Alene Taber, a lawyer representing Imperial, said these reviews could take a year or more and that alternative locations for the datacenter would have to be taken into consideration. She said it was meaningful “that there [will be] a transparent, public, environmental process”.
Rucci, however, said he was not deterred and is going to challenge the judge’s ruling. “It’ll be just a matter of time,” he said. “I’m not going away.”

Weak handgrip strength linked to higher risk of depression over time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:00:08 UTC
22:00:08 KST

New research indicates that people with lower handgrip strength have a higher likelihood of developing depressive symptoms over time. The findings position muscular strength as a potential indicator of general health and vulnerability to depression rather than a direct protective factor. These conclusions come from a massive study published in the Journal of Psychiatric Research.
Depression is a widespread mental health condition affecting almost four percent of the global population. Rates are even higher among middle-aged and older adults. The condition frequently co-occurs with physical ailments and can reduce overall life expectancy. Because of the heavy personal and societal toll, health experts are continuously searching for markers that might help identify those at risk before symptoms appear.
Handgrip strength, measured by a device called a dynamometer, is a standard tool used by health professionals to assess a person’s physical capabilities. A patient simply squeezes the device to record the maximum force they can exert. Because muscle mass naturally declines with age, a person’s grip strength acts as a convenient proxy for their general physical functioning and overall muscular capacity. People with stronger grips tend to have better cardiovascular health, a lower risk of falls, and greater mobility.
Past research has also linked physical strength to brain health, including improved cognitive performance and larger brain volumes in specific regions. Several cross-sectional studies have noted that individuals with weaker hand grips often experience higher rates of depression. A cross-sectional study looks at data from a single point in time, meaning researchers cannot tell which came first between a physical trait and a mental health outcome.
To better understand the timeline of this relationship, a team of researchers led by Jênifer de Oliveira from the Federal University of Santa Maria in Brazil conducted a new review. The research team focused entirely on prospective cohort studies. This type of research follows a group of people over an extended period to see how specific traits or behaviors relate to future health events. By combining multiple studies of this kind, the researchers hoped to clarify whether weak grip strength precedes the onset of new depressive symptoms.
De Oliveira and her colleagues performed a meta-analysis, a statistical method that combines data from many independent studies to identify overarching trends. They searched five major scientific databases for research published up until early 2025. To ensure they were only looking at new cases of depression, they excluded any studies that included participants who already had depressive symptoms at the start of the tracking period.
The team selected sixteen articles to include in their analysis. These articles contained data from fourteen distinct groups of participants across multiple countries, including China, the United Kingdom, Italy, Japan, and the United States. In total, the massive study encompassed 497,336 participants, with an average age near sixty-one years. The researchers extracted data about the participants’ grip strength at the beginning of each study and their depression status at follow-up assessments, which occurred anywhere from one to ten years later.
Because the selected studies reported their data using two different statistical frameworks, the researchers divided their analysis into two parts. First, they looked at eleven studies that calculated the odds of developing depression. Odds represent the probability of an event happening compared to the probability of it not happening.
In this first analysis, the researchers found that individuals categorized as having lower handgrip strength at the start of the study had forty-two percent higher odds of developing depressive symptoms later on. This comparison was made against participants who started with higher handgrip strength. The data showed high variability among the studies, meaning the exact size of the effect varied depending on the specific study population and methods, but the overall trend remained consistent.
Next, the researchers conducted a second analysis using five studies that reported relative risks and hazard ratios. These metrics express how the risk of an event in one group compares to the risk in another group over a specific time frame. This second analysis served to verify the trends seen in the first group of studies.
The findings from this second group aligned with the initial results. Participants with lower handgrip strength faced a twenty-six percent higher risk of incident depression compared to their stronger counterparts. Once again, the results showed substantial variation between the individual studies, but the directional trend remained the same.
To understand why the results varied so much from one study to the next, the researchers looked at various moderating factors. They tested whether the age of the participants, the proportion of women, smoking habits, or the size of the study influenced the strength of the relationship. The results for these personal characteristics were not statistically significant, meaning they did not meaningfully alter the relationship between grip strength and depression.
However, the length of the study did play a minor role. The researchers observed that studies tracking participants for a longer duration reported a slightly stronger relationship between low grip strength and future depression. While the mathematical difference was small, it suggested that the link between physical capacity and mental health might become slightly more apparent over extended periods.
While the data show a consistent pattern, the relationship between handgrip strength and the onset of depression is relatively small in magnitude. Handgrip strength should be viewed as a general indicator of overall health and functional resilience rather than a direct cause of mental well-being. A weaker grip might simply reflect lower physical activity levels, a higher burden of other medical conditions, or a less robust health profile, all of which can increase a person’s vulnerability to depressive symptoms.
Because the researchers relied entirely on observational data, the results cannot prove that building muscle will directly prevent depression. Improving strength through exercise is highly beneficial for physical and mental health, but this specific analysis does not test whether strength training interventions lower depression risk. Handgrip measurements in a doctor’s office should not be interpreted as a standalone diagnostic tool for mental health screening.
Additionally, the individual studies included in the review used different numerical cut-offs to define what constituted low versus high handgrip strength. This variation makes it impossible to identify a universal target weight or specific strength threshold that corresponds to a lower risk of depression. The definition of a weak grip depended entirely on the average strength of the participants in each specific group.
Future investigations will need to explore the underlying behavioral and biological mechanisms that connect physical strength with mental health outcomes. Researchers also aim to see if these patterns hold true for younger populations, as the current data heavily features middle-aged and older adults. Randomized controlled trials, where participants are specifically assigned to strength-building programs, will be required to determine if improving muscular capacity has any direct effect on preventing depression.
The study, “Association between handgrip strength and incident depression: a meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies,” was authored by Jênifer de Oliveira, Ismael Mignoni, Davy Vancampfort, Liye Zou, Brendon Stubbs, Aline Josiane Waclawovsky, and Felipe Barreto Schuch.

Participation in EU security architecture also guarantees Ukraine’s security – Mathernová
EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“To quote President Costa, who said it repeatedly, one of the best anchoring of security guarantees is to be part of the European Union, be integrated in the EU structures, and be a key part of the future European security architecture,” Mathernová said.

Commenting on the continued full-fledged presence of the EU diplomatic mission in Ukraine, as well as the diplomatic corps of EU member states, Mathernová recalled that the European Union and its member states are “the strongest and most reliable allies of Ukraine” and therefore should demonstrate this through their physical presence in Kyiv.
“I think it would be inconsistent if we are not physically present while Ukrainians are, right? So, it's very simple: we have work to do, and we are doing it from Kyiv and traveling around Ukraine,” Mathernová stressed.
She also welcomed the Verkhovna Rada’s progress over the past week in advancing reforms important for European integration and called on lawmakers to remain on this productive path.
“I think that this week was an important step, there were some very sensitive pieces of legislation that got adopted, so my message is: let's keep up the good work,” the diplomat stressed.

India news: CJP founder released a day after detention

Unknown Publisher

India news: CJP founder released a day after detention
Published October 17, 2026last updated October 17, 2026
What you need to know
- India's 'Cockroach' movement founder Abhijeet Dipke was released a day after his detention over a fresh protest call in the capital
- Student leader Neha Bora has been released from detention
- Six US lawmakers have urged Marco Rubio to bring up India protest crackdown during his upcoming visit
Here is our rolling coverage from India on Saturday, October 17:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Many killed in stampede at religious festival in Kolkata
At least 17 people, including 13 women and a child, were killed in a stampede at the Durga Puja religious festival in North Kolkata that was likely caused by sudden rainfall.
"Today (17/10/26), at around 19:40 hrs, a stampede occurred at the exit gate of the Sarada Park (Chor Bagan) Puja Pandal in the Girish Park Police Station area due to heavy crowds of pandal visitors amid rain," the Kolkata Police said in a statement, adding that the injured were taken to the hospital.
West Bengal's Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari told reporters that the fatalities included a seven-year-old girl and that 25 others were injured in a stampede.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi called the incident "extremely distressing" and announced interim compensation for the families of those who died.
The largest annual Hindu festival in India's eastern state of West Bengal, Durga Puja attracts thousands of devotees to temporary structures called pandals that house idols of the goddess Durga.
Poor management and safety lapses at large events in India, such as religious festivals, often result in deadly crowd incidents. A stampede at last year's Kumbh Mela religious fair killed 30 people and injured several others.
CJP founder released a day after detention
Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), was released by an Indian court on Saturday, one day after his detention for attempting to lead a protest rally in New Delhi.
The movement published a photo of him on X in which it referred to Dipke as "a free man."
The CJP's head of legal affairs, Ratna Singh, said Dipke was released after agreeing to certain conditions. She did not provide details about the terms.
Neha Bora, a prominent student activist and the face of the protests, was also detained on Friday while attempting to reach central Delhi with dozens of supporters. She was released earlier on Saturday.
Dipke called Friday's protest a show of support for the two CJP leaders detained and jailed for five days this week for demonstrating at an unauthorized protest site.
Opposition parties and CJP activists defied a security crackdown and rallied to demand the resignation of India's chief election commissioner.
They accuse the election commission of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party.
WATCH — Indians in Germany protest as voter roll controversy goes global
India's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party is challenging the Indian Election Commission over alleged electoral irregularities.
The controversy is spilling beyond India's borders. Indians in Berlin are joining calls for accountability over controversial voter list revisions.
Supreme Court says access to internet fundamental right for children, calls blanket bans 'disproportionate'
India's top court declared that access to and use of the internet is a fundamental right of every individual, including children, legal news outlet LiveLaw reported Saturday.
It said that a blanket ban on children's internet activity could make them vulnerable to greater risks rather than protect them from online abuse and exploitation.
The Supreme Court also issued directions to bolster the processes for detecting and removing child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) from social media and other online platforms, the report said.
The court stressed that the right to freedom of speech and expression also incorporates the right to know, receive and impart information and ideas, LiveLaw reported.
The two-judge bench described the internet as a "marketplace of ideas, creative expression and information" and said that its value went beyond the material it contains, as it provides opportunities for children in remote areas and those with disabilities.
"For many children, particularly in remote areas, it is often the only source of learning and information," the court said, according to LiveLaw.
For children with special needs, the internet is often the only platform where they can find company with others like them, the court said.
The court acknowledged that the internet, in its current form, poses safety risks to children. But it said that keeping children away from the internet because of failures by platforms and the relevant authorities to detect and remove harmful content would amount to mistaking the victim for the problem, LiveLaw reported.
What did the court say on blanket restrictions on internet use for children?
The Supreme Court said that a legal ban would not stop children from using the internet, and that they could move to other unregulated platforms.
"Any blanket restriction on the access of internet by children is nothing more than unproven measures of proven disproportionality," LiveLaw cited the court as saying.
The Supreme Court called for safeguards to ensure online child safety and the regulation of content accessible to children.
It suggested measures such as a "child mode" for social media accounts, LiveLaw said.
Saturday's Supreme Court judgement comes amid a global debate on the ban of social media for children over risks from harmful content. Australia declared the world's first social media ban for under-16s last year.
France followed suit this summer, before its Constitutional Court blocked the move.
US lawmakers urge Marco Rubio to bring up India protest crackdown
Six lawmakers from the United States' Democratic Party have called on US Secretary of State Marco Rubioto raise India's handling of the youth protests during his visit next week.
The US representatives include Pramila Jayapal, Ilhan Omar, Jim McGovern, Rashida Tlaib, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Jesus Garcia.
"As the world's largest democracies, the US and India have an obligation to promote and defend the rights to freedom of assembly and expression," Jayapal wrote on X, sharing a letter addressed to Rubio.
The letter alleges a "pattern of repression, wrongful detention, and excessive use of force by security forces" during the student protests in Delhi and other parts of the country.
The lawmakers also highlight incidents of "apparent surveillance," saying that they had received reports that the Indian diplomatic missions in the US "hired photographers to surveil protesters on American soil."
"These incidents raise particular alarm in light of India's documented pattern of engaging in transnational repression, including through the weaponization of consular services, harassment, intimidation, and physical violence," the letter said.
The group urged Rubio to prioritize the issues in his discussion with Indian officials.
The US Secretary of State is visiting India early next week, after traveling to Uzbekistan.
He is slated to meet Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar in Mumbai. His agenda also shows a trip to Jamnagar in the western state of Gujarat.
Student leader Neha Bora released from detention
All India Students' Association (AISA) President Neha Bora, who was also detained during the latest protest in New Delhi on Friday was released later in the night.
Bora has emerged as a prominent face in the protests against India's top poll official.
Speaking to the media after her release, Bora called for Dipke and other protesters to be released, saying that they had been "illegally detained".
"They are ordinary citizens demanding accountability and their right to vote. Carrying out such illegal detentions and keeping people at the police station overnight makes no sense at all," Bora said.
A widespread review exercise — called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — has struck off over 130 million names from India's electoral rolls since it began last year.
Opposition leaders and critics say that those removed from the voter lists include a large proportion of minority voters. They accuse Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains.
The neutrality of the Election Commission of India (ECI) is being questioned.
The ECI denies favoring any party. It says the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also helps in preventing the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
Youth being made 'pawns' — BJP
Modi's party has slammed its opponents for undermining democracy and has denounced the protests as attempts to create "anarchy".
BJP's Rajnath Singh — who is also India's defense minister — addressed the protests at a press conference on Friday.
Singh accused the opposition, led by the Congress party, of wanting to bring a "regime change along the lines of Bangladesh" and using Indian youth as "pawns in the politics of disorder."
"It appears that the Congress and its political allies, both directly and through their affiliated organisations, are attempting to channel the energy of young people not into constructive activities and nation-building, but into instruments of political confrontation and the spread of chaos," he said.
CJP's Dipke arrested after detention — reports
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Founder Abhijeet Dipke has been arrested, following his detention on Friday when he stepped out to participate in a rally he had called in New Delhi, media reports said.
Dipke was arrested to prevent a breach of the peace and will be taken before a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court later today, news agencies ANI and PTI reported.
CJP legal affairs head Ratna Singh also said that Dipke had been arrested, adding that he would appear before the SEM court in central Delhi's Mandir Marg at 12 p.m. (630 UTC).
Singh claimed that Dipke's lawyers had not met him.
The 'Cockroach' movement said early on Saturday that they did not know where their founder had been detained, calling his detention a "kidnapping."
"Until now, neither his parents nor his lawyers and not the CJP team have been given any updates about his location," the CJP said on X, as it published a video of CJP leader Ajinkya Shinde asking about Dipke's whereabouts.
Dipke was detained publicly on Friday as he left the house in Jhandewalan where he was staying to take part in CJP's 'Lehra Do Tiranga' (Wave the tricolor) protest rally in Connaught Place.
Videos of his detention showed the CJP founder being told by a police official that he was being placed under "preventive detention" before he was taken to a police car.
Dipke was seen displaying India's flag as police and media personnel surrounded him. Some supporters were seen trying to block the police vehicle from driving away with Dipke.
Just hours earlier, a group of Delhi Police officials had visited the 31-year-old at the Jhandewalan residence and served him a notice barring the Friday protest.
The Delhi Police had previously reiterated that Section 163 of India's criminal procedure law, which prohibits any form of assembly or protest, was in force in the Connaught Place area.
"The manner in which he was picked up from right outside his residence, no information about his whereabouts, and the fact that even his lawyers have been unable to meet him raise serious concerns about due process and fundamental rights," Singh wrote on X.
Even after Dipke's detention, hundreds of protesters turned up in Connaught Place defying the heavy security deployment. The protesters were seen waving the Indian national flag as part of the CJP's 'Tricolor' rally. According to police, some 150 protesters were detained during the demonstrations.
The fresh protests came after CJP co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were sent to a five-day detention in jail on Wednesday for alleged violation of prohibitory orders and breach of a peace bond after they attempted a demonstration. They too were carrying the Indian tricolor and the flag has since been at the center of CJP's campaign.
The Indian flag "belongs to the 1.3 billion people of this country and not the Delhi police. We will wave it where we want!" the movement has said.
Dipke, Das and Ranka were earlier detained on October 10 from a plane as they arrived in the capital for a protest march calling for the resignation of India's Chief Election Commionser Gyanesh Kumar over alleged manipulation of voter lists.
They were released after nearly 24 hours.
Welcome to our coverage
This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you the weekend edition of the India blog, where we break down all the biggest headlines that are creating a buzz in the country.
The world's largest democracy has seen almost daily protests since the start of October. The youth-led 'Cockroach' movement, opposition parties, student organizations and civil society members are calling for India's election chief to step down over a sweeping revision of voter rolls that they say benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
On Friday, another protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) at a key business district in the heart of Delhi culminated in detentions.
CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke was taken away in a police car even before he could get to the protest location. It was the second time that Dipke was detained in less than a week.
Reports now say that the 'Cockroach' founder has been arrested following his detention, and is due to appear before a Special Executive Magistrate court today.
With protests being prohibited and demonstrations ending in detentions, the stir over accountability and electoral reform has also sparked a debate over the public's right to protest.
Meanwhile, a group of Democratic lawmakers in the US have called on Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is visiting India next week, to raise with Indian officials the alleged wrongful detentions and excessive use of force during the student protests in New Delhi and other parts of the country.

Zelenskyy warns US’ Russia sanctions relief could reward Putin and fuel more attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:59:27 UTC
21:59:27 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that US President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russia could encourage the Kremlin to continue its war against Ukraine, saying he fears further concessions to Moscow.
Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving sweeping US sanctions targeting Russian energy revenues, prompting concern in Kiev as Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure continue.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said he feared the move was only the beginning of a broader relaxation of restrictions.
“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the ‘diesel deal’ is just the first step,” Zelenskyy told reporters.
He said he still personally hoped Trump would do everything in his power to persuade Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war, but argued that limiting Ukraine’s ability to respond to Russian attacks while easing pressure on Moscow would not achieve that goal.
At least two people were reported killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine on Saturday, according to Ukrainian officials.
Russian strikes hit Ukraine’s energy infrastructure
Zelenskyy said the US sanctions decision came on the same day Russia attacked 15 critical power-generation facilities across Ukraine in what he described as one of the largest assaults on the country’s energy grid.
Officials said a Russian attack in the southern city of Kherson killed one person and wounded 22 others, including two children. Another person was killed in the northeastern city of Sumy.
Zelenskyy warned that Russia was seeking to leave millions of Ukrainians without electricity and heating ahead of winter, when damage to energy infrastructure could have severe consequences for civilians.
Last winter, hundreds of thousands of people in Ukraine experienced prolonged interruptions to heating and electricity during freezing temperatures.
The Ukrainian president called on Kiev’s allies to increase pressure on Moscow and argued that sanctions were intended to raise the cost of continuing the war.
Kiev urges Washington to maintain pressure on Moscow
Zelenskyy also appealed to the United States to reconsider its approach to sanctions, highlighting the Lindsey Graham Act, which targets Russia’s energy and defence sectors, Putin and the so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western restrictions.
The legislation, named after the late US senator who sponsored it, was intended to increase economic pressure on Moscow.
“It is important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening,” Zelenskyy said on social media, arguing that the sanctions framework could still help bring the conflict to an end.
He warned that easing restrictions while Russia continued attacking Ukraine risked rewarding the aggressor and encouraging further military action.
Trump’s sanctions waiver followed his announcement of a deal with Putin allowing Russian diesel exports in exchange for sanctions relief.
The US president’s move came shortly after Putin, appearing in military uniform, said Moscow aimed to capture the remaining parts of eastern Ukraine.
Moscow welcomes Trump’s decision as talks stall
Russian officials welcomed the sanctions relief, although the Kremlin and Putin had not issued a direct response to Trump’s announcement at the time of the report.
Kirill Dmitriev, a Putin envoy, described the suspension of the Graham Act as an “important and truly historic moment”. He argued that the legislation would have caused serious damage to the US economy and global markets.
Zelenskyy met European leaders in Brussels on Friday, urging the European Union to continue financing Ukraine’s defence. He said he was standing up for his country amid the dispute with Washington.
As Russian strikes continue and winter approaches, Kiev is pressing its allies to sustain economic and military support while diplomatic efforts to end the conflict remain uncertain.

France rocked by protests over rising prices as Yellow Vests return
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:56:00 UTC
21:56:00 KST

Police clashed with protesters in Paris and other French cities Saturday as thousands demonstrated against rising living costs, stagnant wages and alleged police brutality, reviving the Yellow Vest movement and increasing pressure on President Emmanuel Macron’s government ahead of the presidential election.
Officers fired tear gas and used water cannons in Paris to disperse groups of demonstrators wearing hoods and face masks who threw fireworks and other objects at police.
Riot police were deployed around Place de la Republique, while authorities closed metro stations and banned some gatherings near government buildings.
Windows at the Paris offices of French broadcasters CNews and Europe 1 were broken after protesters threw projectiles at the buildings, according to reports from the scene.
The Interior Ministry said authorities had recorded about 140 protest actions outside the Paris region by shortly after midday, involving more than 32,000 people. Police had detained at least 166 people nationwide.
The demonstrations followed weeks of student-led protests over education funding and police conduct, with labor unions and supporters of the Yellow Vest movement joining calls for higher wages, lower prices and better public services.
The unrest has intensified scrutiny of the government’s response to demonstrations, particularly after several teenagers suffered serious injuries during confrontations with riot police.
In Marseille, France’s second-largest city, masked demonstrators forced their way into the lobby of City Hall after striking the entrance with security barriers.
Some entered the building, and one spray-painted an anarchist symbol on an interior wall before police moved in to disperse them.
Shops and a municipal police station were also damaged. Mayor Benoit Payan described the damage inside City Hall as limited in an interview with French broadcaster BFM TV.
“We’re taking the Bastille,” one demonstrator shouted, invoking the 1789 storming of the Paris fortress that became a defining moment of the French Revolution.
An Agence France-Presse (AFP) photographer also witnessed protesters attacking a police building in Marseille.
“We’re here to protest the deplorable resources allocated to education and against police brutality,” said Aude, a masked student who declined to give her surname.
In the western city of Rennes, about 20 people erected a barricade using trash bins and large wooden pallets near a shopping mall.
Christophe, a 47-year-old carpenter and former Yellow Vest protester, said he was angered by what he considered excessive police force against teenagers during recent demonstrations.
“We’ve reached the point where the repression is targeting our own children,” he told AFP.
In central France, about 300 people, including high school students, gathered in Gueret to protest rising prices and stagnant wages.
“At the end of the month, I have nothing left. Prices are going up but wages aren’t,” said Franck, a civil servant in his 40s who declined to give his surname.
“We can’t take it anymore, we’re suffocating,” he added.
Authorities also reported violence in Paris, Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers, including attempted looting, attacks on police officers, fires involving street furniture and damage to government institutions and media offices.
The demonstrations were organized partly through social media, with supporters seeking to revive the Yellow Vest movement, which emerged in 2018 in opposition to planned fuel tax increases and broader concerns about economic inequality.
Named after the high-visibility vests worn by protesters, the movement organized months of demonstrations against Macron’s government, drawing support from workers and rural communities who felt the cost of living was rising faster than their incomes.
Organizers called for renewed protests under the slogan “yellow and youth,” urging teachers, students, workers, pensioners and farmers to participate. More than 600 demonstrations were planned across France, according to a website established by organizers.
The mobilization coincided with the start of school half-term holidays, as student groups sought to broaden support for protests that began in mid-September. School blockades and demonstrations have focused on education funding and allegations of excessive police force.
The CGT, one of France’s largest labor unions, also backed the protests, calling for higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services.
Authorities imposed restrictions on demonstrations in central Paris, including near the Champs-Elysees, major railway stations and government buildings. Police detained about 60 people in the capital on Saturday morning, according to AFP.
Macron appealed for calm Friday in Brussels, emphasizing that the right to demonstrate did not justify violence or property damage.
“There is a constitutional right to protest and to express oneself,” he said. “But this right comes with the need to respect. Respect for people, respect for property, and therefore a commitment not to insult or destroy.”
The demonstrations have unfolded amid growing criticism of police tactics during student protests. Thousands of people have been arrested in recent weeks, while hundreds have been injured and some schools have been set on fire during the unrest.
Some of the most serious injuries have involved teenagers struck by police crowd-control weapons. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez suspended the use of a type of stun grenade against young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand.
The incidents have become a rallying point for protesters who accuse authorities of using disproportionate force to control demonstrations.
Climate activist Greta Thunberg joined students at a high school in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis on Tuesday, bringing further international attention to the student movement.
The government faces the challenge of addressing public anger over household costs while preventing further violence. The demonstrations have also become a political issue as France approaches a presidential election campaign in which purchasing power, public services and law enforcement are prominent concerns.
A survey of 2,000 people published earlier this month found that about 45% of French people were concerned about the cost of living and inflation.
Purchasing power has come under pressure, while fuel prices have climbed since the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war earlier this year, adding costs for motorists and businesses.
France is also struggling with mounting public debt, which is projected to exceed 120% of gross domestic product next year, roughly double the European Union’s 60% benchmark.
Economists say significantly reducing the debt will require major reforms, potentially including changes to France’s costly pension system. Such proposals have long been politically sensitive, particularly among workers and retirees concerned about their incomes and benefits.
The unrest has given political parties on both the far left and far right an opportunity to position themselves ahead of the presidential race.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the left-wing France Unbowed party, has backed the student protests and joined a demonstration earlier in the week. Marine Le Pen, whose National Rally party has led opinion polls in the presidential race, has positioned herself in support of the police.
The competing responses reflect the political divisions surrounding the demonstrations, as protesters demand relief from rising prices and improvements to public services while the government faces calls to restore order.

Trump weighs in on Ukraine’s Starlink access
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:55:41 UTC
21:55:41 KST

Trump weighs in on Ukraine’s Starlink access
US President Donald Trump claimed on Friday that he did not order restrictions on Ukraine’s military access to Starlink satellite services, adding that he did not believe SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had done so either.
Ukrainian state and military officials earlier this week accused SpaceX of abruptly restricting access to Starlink satellite communications services and Starshield, its military-grade version, which Kiev relies on for frontline drone operations. Musk responded that Starshield is owned and controlled by the US government. The billionaire stressed that Starlink should be used only for civilian and defensive purposes, arguing that employing its systems for offensive operations would be “inappropriate for a commercial company.”
The development followed US President Donald Trump stepping up pressure on Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he blames for surging global energy prices. Trump has also repeatedly urged the Ukrainian leader to hold a long-overdue presidential election.
At the same time, Washington lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports following talks with the Kremlin, prompting criticism from Zelensky. On Friday, the US President stated that he waived penalties aimed to target Moscow’s economy and countries purchasing Russian energy, which had been signed into law just a month ago.
“Well, I don’t know if it was anybody because it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said when asked who had been behind the alleged suspension of the Starlink systems. “And from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”
Reuters reported on Thursday, citing officials briefed on the matter, that people “inside the White House” had instructed the Pentagon to impose speed restrictions on Starshield terminals. The report did not name the people who allegedly issued the directive, while a senior US official told Bloomberg at the time that Trump had not personally ordered restrictions on Ukraine’s use of Starshield.
On Friday, The Telegraph cited four sources familiar with the discussions as saying that Musk had approached Trump with the proposal to introduce speed limits on the system. One of the sources told the newspaper that Trump “agreed” with the suggestion, paving the way for the Pentagon to execute the slowdown.
The reports came as Washington continued to ramp up pressure on Kiev to accelerate efforts to reach a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine. Earlier this week, Zelensky claimed that the US had threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Kiev if it continued to ignore Trump’s demands to halt strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Ukrainian officials have also complained about receiving no advance warning from the Americans before Russian missile strikes. The White House has not confirmed the claims.
Media reports emerged earlier this month that the US had also threatened to halt the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons to press authorities in Kiev to stop attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said earlier this week that Russia was unaware either of the Starlink slowdown for the Ukrainians or that intelligence sharing had been cut off. Peskov noted that “overall, of course, it would be better if such amazing technology… was not used for military purposes at all.” Moscow has persistently condemned Western military aid to Ukraine, arguing that it only serves to prolong the conflict without changing the outcome.

Taiwan top security official speaks at Berlin forum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:54:11 UTC
21:54:11 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) told a forum in Berlin that peace in the Taiwan Strait also affects Europe’s security and economy, reports said Saturday.
Wu was speaking at the Taiwan Forum Thursday organized by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, a thinktank allied with Germany’s Free Democratic Party. He compared Taiwan’s situation with Ukraine facing the Russian invasion, per CNA.
Conflict in the Taiwan Strait will impact European industry and disrupt global supply chains, the former foreign minister said. He also called for closer Taiwan-EU cooperation in the fields of cyber security, AI, and semiconductors.
European Parliament Committee on Security and Defense Chair Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann said most European countries supported Taiwan, but in different ways. Germany’s problem was that its economy was too reliant on China, she said, adding that Beijing was watching how the EU responded to the war in Ukraine.
Wu said that Taiwan was facing a difficult choice in how to react to China’s actions in the region, including its repeated military drills and incursions into Taiwanese restricted waters and Air Defense Identification Zone, CNA reported. A response might raise regional tension, but not responding would lead China to increase the pressure, he said.
Wu said Taiwan will not rely on other countries, but shoulder its responsibility to defend its freedom, sovereignty, and democratic system. The country will continue to improve its defense capabilities and deter regional conflict with its democratic partners, the top national security official said.

The governor of Syria’s southern Quneitra province on Saturday called on the UN Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF) to monitor and document Israeli violations in the area, Anadolu reports.
Ghassan al-Sayyed Ahmad made the call during talks with UN Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations Jean-Pierre Lacroix, according to the Quneitra Governorate.
The two discussed the situation in the province, UNDOF’s responsibilities, and the impact of Israeli violations on local residents.
Ahmad said documenting the violations in line with UNDOF’s mandate could help protect residents and mitigate the effects on local population.

READ: Israeli army enters Syria’s Quneitra countryside, blocks construction work
A UN report issued on Sept. 23 documented continued violations of the 1974 Disengagement Agreement, including Israeli military presence and activities in the area of separation.
Israeli forces remained at 11 positions on the Syrian side of the area of separation as of Aug. 12, according to the report.
Established in 1974, UNDOF monitors the ceasefire and disengagement between Syrian and Israeli forces. Its mandate was extended in June through Dec. 31, 2026.
Damascus has demanded that Israel withdraw from Syrian territory and respect the 1974 agreement and Syria’s sovereignty.

Trump Blocks Lindsey Graham’s Russia Sanctions Just Weeks After Signing Them Into Law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:53:39 UTC
21:53:39 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Trump Blocks Lindsey Graham’s Russia Sanctions Just Weeks After Signing Them Into Law
US President Donald Trump has blocked the implementation of sweeping sanctions and tariffs against Russia and buyers of Russian energy under a law championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, just weeks after signing the legislation himself.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a White House executive order published on October 16 and reported by Bloomberg on October 17, Trump waived measures under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which was designed to increase economic pressure on Moscow over its ongoing war against Ukraine.
The legislation, passed in September, authorized tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the five largest buyers of Russian oil, alongside additional restrictions targeting Russian financial institutions, government officials, and companies supporting Moscow’s war effort.
In the executive order, Trump stated that waiving the measures at this stage was consistent with US national interests. The administration also submitted the required justification to Congress.
The decision came shortly before an October 18 deadline for implementing key provisions of the legislation.
Under the law, the president was also authorized to impose 500% tariffs on Russian energy imports into the United States and expand sanctions against Russian entities, financial networks, and individuals involved in circumventing existing restrictions.
Bloomberg reported that the executive order formally establishes certain tariffs while simultaneously suspending their enforcement. This leaves the administration with the option of introducing the measures at a later date without requiring new legislation.
The waiver does not repeal the law or automatically remove sanctions imposed under earlier authorities.
The legislation was originally introduced in April 2025 by Republican Senator Lindsey Graham and Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal. Following Graham’s death in July 2026, lawmakers presented a revised version that also incorporated measures targeting Iran.
The suspension has prompted criticism from lawmakers who supported the legislation. Blumenthal condemned Trump’s decision, arguing that it undermined congressional efforts to restrict Russia’s ability to finance its war against Ukraine.
According to Bloomberg, a bipartisan group of senators had already urged the administration to enforce the legislation and reverse a separate arrangement involving Russian diesel exports.
The waiver also reduces the immediate risk of additional US trade restrictions affecting major purchasers of Russian energy, including China, India, and Turkey.
The decision follows Trump’s October 9 announcement of an agreement with Russian leader Vladimir Putin concerning the supply of Russian diesel fuel to international markets. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized that arrangement, warning that easing pressure on Russian energy exports would benefit Moscow.
