The Russian Milblogger Arrested in Montenegro Is a Kremlin Stalking Horse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:53:00 UTC
21:53:00 KST

For years, Russia has treated the Balkans as a battleground for its geopolitical ambitions, exploiting ethnic divisions, fueling tensions, and challenging Western influence. Now, Montenegro is pushing back.
The arrest in Montenegro of Mikhail Zvinchuk, founder of the influential pro-Kremlin military blog channel Rybar, signals a potential turning point in the country’s confrontation with Moscow. Detained on Oct. 9 alongside his wife and three other Russian nationals before being expelled from Montenegro and flying to Russia. Prime Minister Milojko Spajić confirmed Zvinchuk’s detention on X, citing warnings that Montenegro could face destabilization efforts and hybrid warfare.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zvinchuk is now back in Moscow, but what does his expulsion reveal about Montenegro’s evolving relationship with the Kremlin?
Zvinchuk has been part of the Russian military and he founded Rybar with Denis Shchukin, a Moscow-based programmer in 2018 focusing mostly on the Middle East. Its audience remained modest until Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 transformed it into a major information warfare platform as it has over 1.5 million subscribers.
According to the State Department, Rybar was initially funded by the late Wagner Group founder Yevgeny Prigozhin and later was funded by Rostec, the Russian state defense conglomerate that the US Treasury Department sanctioned in June 2022.
Ukraine Hits Russian Rail Bridge, Ammunition Warehouses
Beyond its commentary, the channel is a direct participant in the war. It has published the positions of Ukrainian forces and boasted that the Russian army uses its data for missile strikes, and Zvinchuk has claimed to supply target coordinates to the Defense Ministry and Wagner. In December 2022, Putin appointed him to a working group coordinating Russia’s mobilization effort, and the EU sanctioned him over that role in 2023.
Its work also extends well beyond Ukraine as the channel promotes pro-Kremlin narratives in Africa and the Middle East.
Montenegro is not the only Balkan country where Moscow has sought to expand its influence. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, Russia has exploited deep ethnic divisions, cultivating close ties with pro-Putin Bosnian Serb politician Milorad Dodik, who has repeatedly threatened Republika Srpska’s secession. Thirty years after the Dayton Peace Accords ended the war, the country’s fragile political system remains vulnerable to Russia’s interference.
During a June 2024 visit to Republika Srpska, the majority-Serb territory within Bosnia and Herzegovina, Zvinchuk discussed plans to launch a Rybar “media school.” In an interview that year, Zvinchuk warned the Balkans “will catch on fire” as other conflicts subside. In November 2025, he traveled to Bosnia and Herzegovina entering on the day of Republika Srpska’s presidential election and reportedly filming election commentary outside the entity’s government building.
At an RT-organized festival in Serbia in 2025 and Zvinchuk called Kosovo and Republika Srpska “very sensitive points of pressure on Russia” and claimed the West wanted to build an American base in Republika Srpska.
Rybar’s expansion into the Balkans is part of a broader international influence operation that has drawn growing scrutiny from Western governments.
The EU sanctioned Zvinchuk in 2023, followed by London, putting Rybar’s Kremlin ties under mounting Western scrutiny. In 2024, the State Department accused Zvinchuk of trying to interfere in the US presidential election and offered up to $10 million for information on those involved. The UK sanctioned 10 individuals behind Rybar in 2026 for “for spreading false narratives about Ukraine and interfering in European elections, including in Moldova and Armenia.”
For Moscow, Montenegro represents a potential weak link in NATO’s southeastern flank and a strategic gateway to the Adriatic Sea. Since joining NATO in 2017, the country has faced Russian efforts to undermine its Western alignment and EU ambitions. Tensions date back to 2016, when Montenegro accused Russian operatives of plotting a coup to overthrow the government and prevent its accession to NATO.
The stakes are now even higher. The EU has reaffirmed its support for Montenegro’s ambition to join by 2028, making it the leading EU accession candidate in the Western Balkans. However, as Podgorica approaches this milestone, Russian interference threatens to complicate its path. The arrest of Rybar founder Mikhail Zvinchuk signals a tougher stance against Russian influence operations. But Montenegro is far from out of the woods. With its European ambitions on the line, Moscow still has plenty of opportunities to exploit the country’s vulnerabilities.
NATO should renew its support, building on its 2019 deployment of a Counter-Hybrid Support Team to Montenegro, while the EU should send hybrid response teams, following its model in Moldova.
For Moscow, Montenegro’s Western ambitions are a threat to its influence in the Balkans. Rybar is one tool in that fight, and Zvinchuk’s arrest is a warning shot. The question is whether NATO and the EU will step up before the Kremlin strikes back.

Pope Leo XIV celebrated Mass at Gemelli Hospital in Rome just three days after undergoing surgery to remove a lung tumor. Bild reports this, UNN reports.
Details
Earlier, Reuters reported that the Pope was due to leave the hospital on Saturday afternoon after surgery for lung cancer. The results of his blood tests and a chest X-ray confirmed that he could return home.
On Sunday, he will lead prayers from his apartment in the Vatican for pilgrims in St. Peter’s Square, marking his first public appearance since being admitted to hospital
The 71-year-old Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma—the most common form of cancer affecting this organ. On Tuesday, doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung at Gemelli Hospital in Rome.

The cancer diagnosis of the Pope, known for his relative youth and energy and elected only in May 2025, came as a shock and raised questions about the future of his papacy as he battles the disease
To remind you
The recovery of 71-year-old Pope Leo after the removal of the lower lobe of his right lung is proceeding as planned. The Pontiff is carrying out daily activities independently and undergoing physical therapy.

Intl. Archaeology Day: A glimpse of Iran’s Paleolithic heritage and museums
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:51:12 UTC
21:51:12 KST

Intl. Archaeology Day: A glimpse of Iran’s Paleolithic heritage and museums
TEHRAN - On 17 October, archaeologists and cultural institutions worldwide mark International Archaeology Day, highlighting archaeology’s contribution to our understanding of the human past. The occasion also invites reflection on the broader role of archaeology in reconstructing human history, investigating changing relationships between people and their environments, and communicating scientific knowledge to the public through museums and other cultural institutions.
In Iran, this day offers a valuable occasion to recognize a heritage that extends far beyond monumental architecture and written records. Long before the emergence of urban centers, human groups inhabited the Iranian Plateau and its mountain ranges, developed stone-tool technologies and other early technologies, adapted to changing climatic conditions, and exploited a wide range of environments. The Paleolithic represents the longest period of this history, and it places Iran at the center of important debates concerning human evolution, hominin dispersals across Eurasia, and adaptation during the Pleistocene.
Situated between Southwest Asia, the Caucasus, Central Asia, and the Indian subcontinent, Iran encompasses a remarkable diversity of landscapes and ecological settings. These environments formed part of the geographical context in which prehistoric populations moved, settled, and adapted to changing conditions. Iran should therefore be understood not just as a corridor between better-known prehistoric regions, but as a distinct archaeological landscape with real potential to contribute to future research on the early human occupation, Neanderthal behavior, and the dispersal of Homo sapiens.
The earliest chapters of Iran’s Paleolithic record are documented primarily through stone-tool assemblages recovered from open-air sites and sedimentary contexts. Sites such as Kashafrud in northeastern Iran and Dehtal, north of the Persian Gulf, have contributed to discussions of Lower Paleolithic occupation. Nevertheless, questions concerning chronology, stratigraphic integrity, and the relationship between artifacts and their depositional contexts remain important. Addressing these issues requires carefully designed field investigations, critical reassessment of existing collections, and reliable dating wherever suitable materials and archaeological contexts are available. Darband Rashi Cave is a key example, where modern dating methods and lithics associated with faunal remains in stratigraphic context help advance understanding of Iran’s Lower Paleolithic.
The Zagros Mountains are particularly important for understanding the Middle and Upper Paleolithic in Iran. Caves, rockshelters, and highland valleys preserve archaeological sequences that provide evidence of Neanderthal technology, subsistence strategies, and responses to environmental change. These records are also essential for investigating the arrival and subsequent expansion of modern humans, as well as the cultural and demographic processes associated with the Middle-to-Upper Paleolithic transition. Together, they offer a valuable basis for examining how human populations occupied and adapted to the varied environments of the Iranian highlands.
Over recent decades, Iranian archaeologists have advanced Paleolithic research through independent projects as well as, in some cases, collaboration with international colleagues. Their work has expanded field investigations, strengthened analytical capabilities, and brought Iran’s prehistoric record to greater attention within the international archaeological community.
The contributions of Iranian women archaeologists have been particularly significant, advancing scientific knowledge, broadening research perspectives, and strengthening the foundations of the discipline. Dr Marjan Mashkour has made major contributions to zooarchaeological research, deepening our understanding of past subsistence strategies, human–animal relationships, and interactions between human populations and their environments. Through her teaching and mentorship, she has also trained and helped shape a new generation of Iranian zooarchaeologists, many of whom are now conducting research at institutions across Iran, contributing to the development of the field nationally. Her work illustrates how specialist research can enrich museum collections and exhibitions, helping visitors understand how animal remains recovered from archaeological sites provide evidence of past diets, economies, and relationships between people and animals. Dr Sonia Shidrang has also made important contributions to Paleolithic research and to the international recognition of Iran’s prehistoric heritage, notably through her involvement in the UNESCO nomination of the Prehistoric Sites of the Khorramabad Valley, which were inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2025. Beyond research and heritage management, her commitment to teaching and organizing workshops at Shahid Beheshti University and other institutions has helped transmit specialized knowledge and practical skills to a new generation of archaeology students. Their work illustrates how Iranian women archaeologists contribute not only to scientific research and international collaboration, but also to the development of national research capacity and the future of the discipline.
Field archaeology matters just as much for heritage management, particularly when development projects threaten archaeological sites and landscapes. The Darian Dam Archaeological Salvage Programme in the Sirwan Valley, conducted in 2015–2016, demonstrated the importance of archaeological investigation in a landscape undergoing substantial transformation. Although salvage archaeology cannot replace the preservation of sites in situ, it can document threatened remains and recover information that would otherwise be lost. The project also underscores why prehistoric landscapes, even when they lack monumental structures or visible architectural remains, must be recognized as integral components of Iran’s cultural heritage.
The Khorramabad Valley occupies an exceptional place within this broader archaeological landscape. Its caves, including Kunji, Yafteh, and Ghamari, preserve important evidence for reconstructing Paleolithic lifeways and investigating the long-term human occupation of the Zagros. In 2025, the inscription of the Prehistoric Sites of the Khorramabad Valley on the UNESCO World Heritage List marked a major achievement for Iranian archaeology. As a member of the nomination team, I witnessed firsthand the importance of a rigorous scientific foundation in securing international recognition for archaeological heritage. This inscription provides an important opportunity to advance archaeological research, strengthen site management and conservation, and communicate the valley’s significance to local communities and international audiences.
My work in Gilan Province similarly brought prehistoric research into dialogue with broader questions of cultural heritage through my involvement in the UNESCO nomination of the Cultural Landscape of Masouleh. This experience highlighted the value of examining cultural landscapes across different timescales, taking into account the environmental and historical processes that have shaped them. Archaeological research can extend this perspective beyond standing architecture and documented history to explore the deeper relationships between people and their environments.
Museums play an essential role in connecting archaeological research with public understanding. In 2001, I led the establishment of the Paleolithic Gallery at the National Museum of Iran to present archaeological evidence in a form accessible to a wider audience. Stone tools may appear simple at first glance, but their technological characteristics, raw materials, and archaeological contexts can reveal important aspects of past human behavior when interpreted carefully. The challenge for museums is to communicate these findings clearly while preserving the scientific context essential to their interpretation.
The establishment of the Zagros Paleolithic Museum in Kermanshah extended this work into the region whose archaeological record constitutes a major part of Iran’s Paleolithic heritage. Regional museums are particularly valuable because they connect archaeological discoveries with the landscapes and communities from which the evidence originates. More recently, Paleolithic displays developed at the Archaeological Museum of Lorestan in 2024 have further strengthened the presentation of western Iran’s prehistoric heritage within its regional context. Together, national and regional institutions can help audiences appreciate the diversity of Iran’s archaeological record and its contribution to our understanding of the human past.
Museums also play a central role in the responsible management of archaeological collections. An artifact’s scientific value depends not only on its physical characteristics, but also on its provenance, stratigraphic position, and association with other evidence. When these relationships are lost, important opportunities for interpretation and future research are diminished or disappear altogether. Documentation, conservation, and responsible curation must therefore remain integral to archaeological practice.
International Archaeology Day provides a moment to recognize the scientific and public value of Iran’s Paleolithic heritage. Advancing research requires sustained fieldwork, renewed investigation of existing collections, interdisciplinary collaboration, and stronger connections between research institutions and the public. Such efforts can integrate Iran’s archaeological record more fully into international scholarly debates while ensuring that future generations of researchers have the evidence, expertise, and institutional resources needed to investigate it.
As head of the Paleolithic Department at the National Museum of Iran, my experience in field research, museum development, and UNESCO nominations has reinforced the importance of connecting scientific investigation with public interpretation and long-term heritage management. Archaeology achieves its greatest value when discoveries contribute not only to scholarly understanding but also to a broader appreciation of humanity’s shared past. Iran’s Paleolithic record offers an exceptional foundation for advancing that understanding, connecting the history of human adaptation across deep time with the responsibilities of scientific research and cultural stewardship today.

Israeli settlers attack European diplomats during West Bank olive harvest
Four Palestinian women and a child are among those injured in separate ongoing Israeli assaults and pogroms.
Israeli settlers have attacked European diplomats, including a French mayor, near the Palestinian village of Taybeh in the occupied West Bank.
The delegation was visiting Palestinian olive harvesters on Saturday when the Israeli attackers confronted the group. The attack comes a day after settlers assaulted a US journalist north of Ramallah.
In Saturday’s incident, the settlers targeted Belgium’s consul general, French and Polish diplomats and Catholic representatives, Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said.
“A French mayor was assaulted and a Belgian vehicle damaged,” Prevot said, linking the attack to what he called Israel’s “illegal settlement policy” and pledging to push for further European Union sanctions.
Bernard Baudoux, the French mayor who was assaulted, told the AFP news agency that the attack suggests that “there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government” towards settler violence.
France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noel Barrot, called on Israel to arrest the “extremist settlers” who “violently assaulted” Baudoux, and bring them to justice. “They must urgently halt this criminal violence and guarantee the safety of civilian populations, as they are compelled to do under international law,” he said in a post on X.
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah, said the settlers had surrounded the diplomats’ vehicles, before pelting them with stones and smashing their windows.
The assault has prompted an Israeli police investigation and condemnation from Belgium as settler pogroms disrupt the harvest across the occupied territory.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office, however, appeared to question the reports of the attack on the Europeans, saying on X that they are “alleged” and require “compelling evidence”, despite acknowledging that published footage of the incident exists.
Settler attacks continue
Earlier on Saturday, several Palestinians were injured by Israeli settlers, as Israeli forces arrested farmers during pogroms across the occupied West Bank.
Four women and a child were among six people injured when Israeli settlers attacked residents in Ma’in village in the Masafer Yatta area, south of Hebron, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS).
In the town of Deir Ammar, west of Ramallah, Israeli forces opened fire on farmers picking olives, forcing them to leave their land, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa. In the same area, Israeli settlers shot and injured two Palestinians.
In the village of Tuqu, southeast of Bethlehem, Israeli forces fired on a Palestinian civilian vehicle.
In the village of Kafr Malek, northeast of Ramallah, settlers raided a farm at dawn and killed about 20 sheep, Mayor Najeh Rustum told Al Jazeera.
Al Jazeera’s Odeh said settlers also destroyed olive trees across the Beit Furik plain, east of Nablus, in the northern West Bank while Israeli forces arrested landowners and olive pickers.
In the village of Deir Jarir, east of Ramallah, she said, settlers under army protection fired live ammunition at farmers in the al-Hariq area to prevent them from completing the harvest and forced them off their land.
Settlers also smashed the vehicle of international activist Jonathan Budlak in the village and threw stones at a farmer’s vehicle.
In the village of Burqa near Ramallah, Israeli forces and settlers prevented farmers from picking olives, Odeh said, adding that settlers attacked farmers in the Wadi al-Sha’er area, southeast of Salfit.
“What we see, whether it’s in Beit Furik, Kafr Malek, Deir Jarir or elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, is part of a campaign,” Odeh said.
She said settlers have become increasingly emboldened, publicly advertising attack campaigns on social media platforms.
“There have been 300 documented attacks since the beginning of October, and that has had a devastating impact on a very important season for Palestinian farmers,” she said, adding that danger comes from soldiers and settlers alike as military forces routinely intervene to protect settlers and attack Palestinians defending their land.
Prominent rabbi justifies attacks
The attacks follow a religious edict issued by Rabbi Dov Lior, a prominent rabbi for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party and a leading authority among the Hilltop Youth, which is a religious Zionist group devoted to seizing Palestinian land in the West Bank.
In the edict, Lior stated that harvesting olives in the Holy Land is entirely permitted and carries an added virtue, given security dangers.
He wrote that Jews are permitted to harvest olives even in areas far from Jewish communities to publicly display ownership of the land and fulfil God’s commandment of conquering it. He claimed the land belongs to the Jewish people and Palestinians did not buy or rent it.

Iran proposes joint tourism packages, measurable targets to boost Chinese arrivals
TEHRAN – Iran has proposed five practical measures to increase Chinese tourist arrivals, including joint travel packages, familiarization tours and direct cooperation between travel agencies, as it seeks to turn longstanding cultural ties with China into tangible tourism business.
The proposals were outlined in a message from Iran’s Minister of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts, Seyyed Reza Salehi-Amiri, read at a specialized meeting on strengthening Iran-China tourism cooperation in Beijing on Friday.
Salehi-Amiri said that Iran eyes China to be become one of its most important tourism partners, stressing that the success of bilateral cooperation would depend on moving beyond discussions to concrete agreements and actual tourist exchanges.
The meeting, hosted by Iran’s embassy in Beijing, brought together officials and representatives of tourism companies from both countries to discuss barriers to bilateral travel, develop joint tourism products and expand cooperation between tour operators.
Marking the 55th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Iran and China, Salehi-Amiri described the occasion as an opportunity to advance cooperation from dialogue to implementation.
He proposed establishing a joint working group of Iranian and Chinese travel agencies and tour operators, developing at least three travel packages specifically tailored to the Chinese market, and organizing familiarization tours in Iran for Chinese travel agency executives and journalists.
The other proposals focused on providing services suited to Chinese visitors, including Chinese-speaking guides and easier payment arrangements, as well as setting measurable targets and clear timelines for tourist exchanges.
“The outcome of this meeting should not be limited to discussions and exchanging business cards,” Salehi-Amiri said in his message. He called for an action plan, travel packages, contracts and the actual dispatch of tourists.
Referring to the historic Silk Road, which connected the two countries through trade and cultural exchange, he said tourism could give the ancient route renewed life.
“The Silk Road was once kept alive by caravans, and today it will be kept alive by the movement of tourists,” he said.
Iranian Ambassador to China Abdolreza Rahmani Fazli also emphasized the need to remove obstacles, reorganize cooperation mechanisms and increase China’s share of Iran’s tourism market.
He described the Silk Road as more than a commercial route, saying it had historically facilitated exchanges in culture, art, music and traditions. Modern technology, he added, offered new opportunities to strengthen people-to-people ties.
Rahmani Fazli also highlighted China’s potential role in Iran’s postwar reconstruction, following the recent war against the country, and said both nations sought peace and security in West Asia.
Chinese tourism representatives described Iran as a destination with considerable cultural appeal and economic potential, expressing interest in expanding travel between the countries. They also identified several obstacles, including the absence of an Iranian tourism promotion office in Beijing, flight disruptions following the war and limited opportunities for familiarization tours.
Their recommendations included establishing an Iranian tourism representation office in Beijing, organizing promotional events for Chinese media and travel bloggers, arranging familiarization trips, developing tailored travel packages and ensuring more stable air connections.
Participants also suggested using shared cultural interests, including tea culture, to promote tourism cooperation.
During the meeting, Roozbeh Kardooni, an adviser to the minister and director general of the ministry’s ministerial office, said Iran could host a group of Chinese tourism industry representatives in the near future. Such a visit could help Chinese tour operators assess Iran’s attractions firsthand and explore opportunities to develop joint travel products.

Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:44:22 UTC
21:44:22 KST

Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- University of Edinburgh
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising cause of age-related cognitive decline involving brain cells previously thought to be entirely beneficial. As these cells become dysfunctional, they can produce abnormal amounts of myelin, disrupting nerve fibers and potentially contributing to worsening memory and thinking skills.
- Share:
Brain cells that normally help protect the brain may play an unexpected role in cognitive decline as we grow older. Scientists have discovered that cells responsible for maintaining the protective coating around nerve fibers can become dysfunctional with age, potentially contributing to the gradual loss of memory and thinking abilities.
The research, published in Nature Medicine, challenges the long-held belief that these cells are always beneficial. By examining human brain tissue and conducting experiments in mice, researchers found evidence that problems with these normally supportive cells can damage nerve fibers and interfere with cognitive function.
The discovery also points to a possible new approach for protecting the aging brain. Drugs that act on the biological pathway involved are already being used to treat other neurological conditions, raising hopes that existing treatments could eventually be adapted to combat age-related cognitive decline.
Scientists Discover Changes in the Aging Brain
The study was led by researchers from the University of Edinburgh and the UK Dementia Research Institute, who investigated how changes in the brain relate to declining cognitive abilities later in life.
Their research focused on the Lothian Birth Cohort 1936, a group of people whose cognitive abilities have been tracked from childhood into old age. This unusually extensive record allowed scientists to investigate how thinking and memory changed over decades.
Between ages 70 and 82, participants underwent assessments measuring memory, the speed at which they processed information, and their ability to understand spatial relationships.
Of the 1,091 people enrolled in the cohort, 866 completed additional cognitive testing after age 70. Nearly everyone experienced at least some decline, but the rate varied considerably. These differences gave researchers an opportunity to investigate what might distinguish brains experiencing faster deterioration from those aging more gradually.
When scientists examined brain tissue collected after death from a subset of participants, they discovered a striking pattern. Individuals who had experienced greater cognitive decline tended to have fewer large nerve fibers, along with an abnormal buildup of unhealthy myelin.
Myelin is the protective coating that surrounds nerve fibers, helping electrical signals travel efficiently through the brain. Although this insulation is essential for normal brain function, the findings suggest that excessive or abnormal myelin may become part of the problem.
The changes were especially pronounced around the large nerve fibers that remained. Importantly, these abnormalities were associated with how quickly cognitive abilities declined, rather than how well someone performed on cognitive tests at a particular age.
A Protective Brain Cell May Have a Hidden Weakness
To understand what might be causing these changes, the researchers turned their attention to oligodendrocytes, specialized brain cells responsible for producing and maintaining myelin.
Oligodendrocytes have traditionally been regarded as beneficial because they help keep nerve fibers insulated and functioning properly. However, the new findings suggest that these cells can become dysfunctional during aging and may contribute to the very problems they normally help prevent.
The researchers discovered that people with more severe cognitive decline had lower levels of a protein called NRF2 inside their oligodendrocytes.
NRF2 plays an important protective role in cells by regulating hundreds of genes involved in defending against damage and maintaining normal cellular function. When its activity decreases, cells may become less capable of protecting themselves and performing their usual jobs.
To investigate whether this protein was directly involved in the brain changes, the team conducted experiments in mice.
When researchers specifically reduced NRF2 in oligodendrocytes, the animals developed excessive myelin and lost large nerve fibers, closely resembling the abnormalities observed in human brain tissue. The mice also showed reduced improvements in cognitive performance as they aged.
These experiments provided evidence that declining NRF2 activity can directly disrupt oligodendrocyte function, potentially triggering changes in myelin and nerve fibers that contribute to cognitive decline.
Existing Drugs Could Offer a New Treatment Strategy
The findings may have important implications for developing treatments that help preserve cognitive abilities in older adults.
One particularly promising aspect is that the NRF2 pathway is already a target of medications used for other conditions, including a drug prescribed to treat multiple sclerosis (MS).
Previous studies have found that increasing NRF2 activity can improve cognitive function in people with MS. That raises the possibility that medications acting on the same pathway might eventually be repurposed to address oligodendrocyte dysfunction and age-related cognitive decline.
Although further research is needed to determine whether such treatments would benefit older adults experiencing cognitive decline, the discovery identifies a potentially valuable therapeutic target.
Veronique Miron, MRC Senior Non-Clinical Fellow and UK Dementia Research Institute Group Leader at the University of Edinburgh and St. Michael's Hospital, part of Unity Health Toronto, said:
"As the prevalence of cognitive decline is rising with an aging population and no current treatments exist, we are excited about this work as it points to a potential strategy for new therapeutic strategies to preserve cognitive ability in aging."
A New Understanding of Cognitive Decline
Beyond its potential medical applications, the research changes how scientists understand the role of oligodendrocytes in the aging brain.
Rather than simply providing support for healthy nerve function throughout life, these cells appear capable of becoming dysfunctional and contributing to cognitive problems.
Georgina Craig, the study's first author and a Postdoctoral Fellow at St Michael's Hospital in Toronto and the UK Dementia Research Institute, said:
"This study has fundamentally shifted how we think about these brain cells in aging. We have always considered oligodendrocytes as purely beneficial, yet here we surprisingly find that they can become dysfunctional and contribute to cognitive impairment in aging."
The findings suggest that maintaining healthy oligodendrocyte function could become an important strategy for protecting memory and thinking abilities as people grow older.
Published in Nature Medicine, the study was funded by the UKRI Medical Research Council (MRC) and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR). The research also involved scientists from the University of Edinburgh's Lothian Birth Cohort studies and Northwestern University.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Edinburgh. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Georgina A. Craig, Emeric Merour, Luise A. Seeker, Annette J. Haughian, Keon Arbabi, Jamie Rose, Alana Hoffmann, Jessica Thapar, Andrea Corsinotti, Stephen Mitchell, Janie Corley, Susan D. Shenkin, Colin Smith, Tara L. Spires-Jones, Lu O. Sun, Simon R. Cox, Anna Williams, Shreejoy J. Tripathy, Brian Popko, Véronique E. Miron. Oligodendrocyte dysfunction in human age-related cognitive decline. Nature Medicine, 2026; 32 (10): 3661 DOI: 10.1038/s41591-026-04608-y

Everyone has received my message that sanctions must not be lifted, and everyone agrees that no sanctions can be lifted from Russia until Putin stops the killings. On the contrary, everyone is working on the next sanctions package," Zelenskyy said, responding to questions from journalists on Saturday.
He also said he had discussed with Belgian officials and EU leaders the U.S. proposal to unfreeze a portion of Russian assets in an effort to resume peace talks.
"Everyone understands that there is a risk that Russia will do everything it can to try to seize some of the frozen assets through one partner or another. Yes, that's true. We have such information. But again, we've gone over the details with the Europeans. This is currently under control – fully under Europe's control. And that means it's safe for now. Thank you to all our partners," the President of Ukraine said.
According to him, he discussed with European partners the issue of strengthening air defense and the need for budgetary support amounting to EUR 70 billion. "I know this isn't easy, and I'm grateful to the Europeans that no one said "no,"" Zelenskyy said.
As previously reported, Zelenskyy called on Europe to ensure the protection of the entire amount of frozen Russian assets and to find a mechanism for using them to support Ukraine, warning that otherwise Russia could gain access to them and use the funds to finance the war.

Chile’s Lawyers for Palestine call for investigation into country’s ambassador to Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:40:01 UTC
21:40:01 KST

Lawyers for Palestine in Chile have issued a press statement confirming that they have filed a formal petition with the Office of the Comptroller General of the Republic. The petition is requesting an investigation into Chile’s Ambassador to Israel, Gabriel Zaliasnik, over an interview broadcast on 26th August by the US program “Defending Israel” on the Jewish Broadcasting Service (JBS).
Introduced as Chile’s Ambassador, Zaliasnik accused Chile’s Palestinian community of manipulating its numbers: “They play with the number because that’s politics.” In the same interview he conceded that, as to the figure, “we can speculate only.” He was asked only about the community’s size, yet he went on to refer to the “radicalizing” of “some small sectors” of it, without identifying any person, organisation or event.
The entire interview took place in front of a map showing the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza as part of Israel. The Ambassador raised no objection about the map, although Chile has recognised the State of Palestine since 2011. He remained silent precisely where he was obliged to represent Chile.
The press release said that according to Chilean law, the Civil Service Statute prohibits all public officials from engaging in arbitrary discrimination as defined in Law No. 20,609. That law protects, among other grounds, ethnicity, nationality and political opinion.
READ: Thousands rally for Palestine in Chile as activists pursue UN action against Israel
The Lawyers for Palestine statement recalled that in 2025 the Ministry of Foreign Affairs terminated the posting of Chile’s Ambassador to New Zealand over her public statements. In this light, their petition seeks the application of the same standards with regard to Zaliasnik.
On his part, the Ambassador has, thus far, expressed regret for terms that “may be offensive.” While the Government has acknowledged that the ambassador “made a mistake,” it has until now not opened any disciplinary proceeding.
The Lawyers for Palestine are calling on the Comptroller General to:
- Thoroughly investigate whether the Ambassador acted with authorisation and in accordance with his duties of probity, impartiality and non-discrimination;
- Order the corresponding disciplinary proceeding; and
- Issue general rules governing ambassadors’ public statements.
“This is not about the Ambassador’s beliefs, but about the use of his office. If this ends with a call to order, the message to the entire Foreign Service is that probity, and the honour of Chilean citizens, are negotiable. They are not,” said Paula Abugattas Nazal, attorney for Lawyers for Palestine.

Pope discharged from hospital days after lung cancer surgery
- Published
Pope Leo XIV has been discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung.
The 71-year-old walked unaided to his waiting car, stopping to speak to well-wishers.
The Vatican said the Pope will give the traditional Angelus prayer and blessing to a crowd in St Peter's Square on Sunday, as he did last week when he surprised the world by announcing the surgery.
On Friday, photographs were released of the Pope celebrating Mass and distributing communion in hospital for staff.
A statement from his doctors said blood tests and a chest X-ray showed "steady improvement" following his operation.
The surgery on Tuesday, which lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung. The results of further tests to check for any sign that the cancer has spread have not yet been announced.
The Pope also spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, in their first call since June 2025. The Vatican said the call was to urge "dialogue and peace".
It came as Russia's bombardment of cities across Ukraine intensifies, with a growing number of civilian casualties and no sign of Putin being ready to halt the invasion.
The Pope also called for a humanitarian ceasefire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshkiy, occupied by Russia and under constant shelling, to allow people to be evacuated and for the urgent delivery of food and medicine. The BBC recently reported on residents there being forced to eat garden weeds to survive.
The Pope's schedule has been cleared completely until 20 October, so his reappearance in public so soon is a surprise and will be some relief for Catholics around the world.
Those close to the Pope said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America, planned for early November and which includes a visit to Peru, where he was a missionary for many years.
It is not yet clear whether he might be fit to travel or require further treatment.

F-16s Down Majority of Jet Drones Amid Munition Build-Up, Zelensky Says

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:37:00 UTC
21:37:00 KST

Combat aviation, primarily Western-supplied F-16 multirole fighter jets, accounts for 55 to 60 percent of all intercepts against Russian turbojet-powered Shahed strike drones as Ukraine scales up stockpiles of 20mm aircraft ammunition, President Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists.
He explained that Ukraine has expanded procurement contracts to supply F-16 squadrons with the 20mm cannon rounds required to engage high-speed aerial threats, noting that deliveries have reached stable volumes.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Regarding the interception of jet-powered Shaheds, we are using our aviation very successfully,” Zelensky stated. “Today there is a build-up of ammunition for F-16s with 20mm shells. Both I and our Ministry of Defense had agreements. Right now we are receiving an appropriate quantity, and it is very good. That is, right now we have this.”
The Ukrainian head of state emphasized that combat aviation represents one pillar of a multi-tiered counter-unmanned aerial vehicle (C-UAV) posture, designed to mitigate disruptions caused by bandwidth restrictions on satellite-guided drone platforms.
“Next, we have several other solutions. Inexpensive missiles that are beginning to work,” Zelensky said.
“Several new solutions that will arrive in Ukraine from partners shortly, alongside domestic production that is already functional. Furthermore, we have turrets, and as you know, we began manufacturing them – not in isolated units, but in dozens. We will continue to scale them up.”
Major Russian Strike on Vinnytsia Region Injures 6
European Patriot packages and the FREYJA anti-ballistic initiative
Addressing the defense against Russian ballistic missiles, Zelensky stated that Ukraine requires an immediate transitional package of Patriot PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors from European partner nations to safeguard critical municipal infrastructure ahead of winter.
The president outlined a sequential air defense roadmap under which European transfers will bridge the gap until bilateral procurement contracts with Germany and the multilateral FREYJA anti-ballistic missile project become fully operational.
“Right now a package is needed from Europe and from certain other nations,” Zelensky explained.
“Next, our contracts with Germany and FREYJA should begin operating in parallel. This is the plan, these are my calculations.”
Zelensky observed that Ukrainian defense planners have identified European partner countries that maintain sufficient interceptor inventories, noting that deliveries through the NATO-coordinated PURL program have been constrained because the majority of US-manufactured PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors have been redirected to combat operations in the Middle East.
“Partners heard all our concerns,” Zelensky said.
“They know the quantities we receive through the PURL program and understand that the majority of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles from the United States went to the Middle East. They know that I need their support right now.”
Zelensky confirmed that development work is progressing on the FREYJA anti-ballistic system, a 10-nation cooperative initiative involving key partners such as France and Norway.
While acknowledging that sovereign ballistic missile defense systems historically require decades to formulate, Zelensky emphasized that the strategic timetable requires accelerated engineering schedules.
“Regarding the FREYJA anti-ballistic project, Ukraine has done what it needed to do. What the partners need to do – 10 countries are participating – is in progress,” Zelensky noted, adding that he reviewed the program during bilateral consultations with French President Emmanuel Macron.
“Systems like this are worked on for decades. We want this very quickly, because there is no time.”
Push for European satellite autonomy following Starlink speed caps
The technical adjustments across Ukrainian air defenses unfold following disclosures earlier on Saturday that Starlink satellite terminals operating inside Ukraine have been subjected to an artificial velocity cap of 161 km/h (100 mph), disabling domestic unmanned interceptors designed to pursue turbojet loitering munitions.
Zelensky revealed that comparative trials conducted by Ukrainian specialists confirmed that Starlink-equipped vehicles operated normally at speeds of 180 km/h (112 mph) within EU borders, demonstrating that the operational constraints were geographically confined to Ukrainian territory.
The unilateral throttling has prompted European governments to examine sovereign alternatives to commercial American satellite communications networks, Zelensky observed.
“All of Europe saw that it is possible to regulate Starlink from the United States, regardless of agreements and contracts, and to limit speeds,” Zelensky said. “Therefore, Europeans themselves are now raising the issue of analogues. And they are already working on this.”
Ukrainian defense officials have stressed that diversifying air defense munitions, scaling domestic automated gun turrets, and establishing independent European satellite communications frameworks remain vital to preserving municipal utility grids and civilian population centers ahead of freezing winter conditions.

Protesters briefly broke into the town hall in Marseille, France’s second-largest city, on Saturday as demonstrations against the rising cost of living spread across the country, according to an AFP reporter at the scene.

One sprayed an anarchist “A” symbol on a wall before police intervened, the reporter said. “We’re taking the Bastille,” one protester shouted, invoking the 1789 storming of the Paris fortress that became a landmark of the French Revolution.
The incident came as former members of the Yellow Vest movement joined high school students, university students, farmers, climate activists and trade unionists in protests over living costs, public services and education.
French authorities expected up to 170,000 people to take part nationwide, with around 500 actions and more than 90 demonstrations planned, according to sources close to the Interior Ministry.
Clashes and arrests reported in several cities
In Lyon, police used tear gas to disperse around 100 demonstrators. Authorities in Rennes said protesters had erected burning barricades to block a road.
In Marseille, rubbish bins and scooters briefly obstructed Boulevard du Prado before riot police cleared the route.
The Paris police prefecture said 40 people had been arrested in the metropolitan area by 9.30 am, mainly for carrying prohibited protective equipment or weapons.
Police also reported 21 arrests after around 100 people targeted broadcaster CNews’ headquarters in Paris, blocking access to a car park, throwing projectiles and smashing windows.
Demonstrations were prohibited around several key locations in the capital, including the Élysée Palace, the prime minister’s office and the Champs-Élysées.
Yellow Vests return as discontent widens
The Yellow Vest movement emerged in 2018, initially protesting fuel taxes and the rising cost of living before developing into a broader challenge to government policies and economic inequality.
Saturday’s mobilisation brought together groups with different grievances, including students demanding more education funding and improved study conditions, as well as criticism of police interventions during protests.
In Lille, around 20 demonstrators, including Yellow Vest protesters, gathered outside the Hauts-de-France Regional Council behind a banner declaring that their struggle was continuing.
In Paris, authorities anticipated between 30,000 and 60,000 protesters. The main march was scheduled to leave Place de la République at 2 pm local time and proceed towards Place de Clichy.
Macron urges calm as tensions rise
President Emmanuel Macron called on Friday for calm and respect for people and property during the demonstrations.
The nationwide protests followed weeks of student-led actions and brought together a wider coalition of groups expressing concerns about living costs, public spending and social conditions.
The scale of the planned mobilisation and incidents reported in several cities placed renewed focus on the government’s response to public discontent, while authorities sought to maintain order and prevent further disruption.

Fires and clashes rock France amid massive nationwide protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:31:24 UTC
21:31:24 KST

Fires and clashes rock France amid massive nationwide protests
Protesters clashed with police in Paris and other French cities on Saturday as hundreds of thousands took to the streets to protest higher living costs and the declining conditions in schools and other public services. Several town halls were broken into – and in at least one instance set on fire – and many shops were vandalised and ransacked. One protester had his hand torn off by what appeared to be a crowd-control grenade used by police.
Police and protesters clashed violently in Paris and other French cities Saturday on the sidelines of nationwide marches against soaring inflation, with one demonstrator's hand blown off, multiple blazes set and looters breaking into dozens of stores to strip them bare.
The widespread unrest follows weeks of student protests and deepens political uncertainty in France as it readies for elections in six months' time to replace President Emmanuel Macron.
Macron and his government were criticised by many of the demonstrators, who numbered 500,000 across the country, according to the CGT union. Authorities did not immediately give their estimate of numbers.
Police used tear gas and water cannon against masked protesters in Paris and other cities who were throwing projectiles and aiming fireworks. Several parked cars were torched in the capital, and more than 130 arrests made.
Read more'Finish what we started': After student protests, France braces for return of the Yellow Vests
In the southern city of Saint-Etienne, a male protester had his hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, a police source told AFP. His maiming came after a 15-year-old lost his hand October 5 to a police stun grenade during another protest in the city of Lens.
In Lyon, protesters set ablaze a tourist office in the city centre, and smashed their way into town halls in the cities of Marseille and Lille, where they vandalised the premises before leaving.
Dozens of shops were looted, including many in Marseille, among them a Hermes boutique, an Apple store in Lille, several shops in Nice and at least one mobile phone outlet in Paris, AFP journalists saw.
A crowd of more than 300 protesters tried to move up Paris's Champs-Elysees, home to flagship luxury stores. As police firing tear gas blocked their way, they yelled "All cops are bastards".
'Macron, resign'
The looting and confrontations with police were being carried out by masked youths on the sidelines of marches that were largely peaceful and which attracted people of all ages, including families with children.
Paris mayor Emmanuel Gregoire stressed that "the overwhelming majority of demonstrators" wanted to "march calmly", but "acts of vandalism" were tarnishing their protest.
In Paris, tens of thousands marched across the east and north of the city in one major march, some shouting "Everyone hates the police" and "Macron, resign".
One demonstrator, Jules Petrichor, 47, who had brought his son, said: "There was a good atmosphere and then suddenly they (the police) started gassing us, even though nothing was happening. Naturally that worsened things and the hot-heads got hot-headed."
Another protester who gave his first name as Louis, 19, complained that police were trigger-happy any time there was a demonstration.
"We can't protest any more, it's frightening," he said.
Demonstrators' hostility towards the police had sharpened over the course of the preceding student protests, when several teens were maimed and thousands were arrested.
France's Yellow Vest movement, which eight years ago staged street protests against Macron's government over planned fuel tax hikes, had called for the Saturday's "yellow and youth" demonstrations.
The principal grievance was the cost of living -- pushed up in part by the war in the Middle East -- that has helped send inflation soaring in Europe as elsewhere.
But there were other issues too.
High school student Kamil Alahyan, 18, said he was protesting "for so many reasons -- the elections coming up in 2027, politicians who lie, the ultra-rich who've been taking more and more wealth over the past 10 years".
"For years we've had climate, economy and equality problems but the government is not doing anything about it," said Agnes, a 50-year-old actor who did not give her second name.
Anae, a 24-year-old student who did not give her surname, said she was protesting because she did not have a "sustainable future".
"Our planet's burning. And we've got a government that doesn't give a toss," she said.
Le Pen blames 'rioters'
Opposition politicians vying to succeed Macron have seized upon the protests.
Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, who has sided with the police, said on X: "Looting, pillaging, attacking police -- rioters have once again sullied the October 17 demonstrations over the cost of living."
She claimed that the protesters' demands had been "hijacked by the far left".
Her far-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon, insisted early Saturday that "everything is passing off peacefully", while accusing television news of "flooding us with images of violence in dozens of cities".
Several protesters sought to draw parallels with the French Revolution of 1789.
"It's the Revolution -- we're taking the Bastille!" some shouted in Marseille during the forced entry of the mayor's offices.
In the western city of La Rochelle, marchers streamed behind a placard reading: "Revolution or death."
"The government is trembling and it's right to tremble because when the French people are angry, they never let up," Ryad Rani, the head of the LSU high school student representative body, told journalists in Paris.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

After the unimaginable happens, an Oregon town mourns: ‘You can’t stop thinking about the kids’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:30:30 UTC
21:30:30 KST

For three long hours on Thursday afternoon, Joe Camarlinghi waited at a Bend, Oregon, church for word about his daughter.
Camarlinghi had received an alert about a shooting at Silver Rail elementary, heard sirens and quickly headed to campus, where he was directed to the church along with other parents. Parents and teachers cried and hugged, and waited.
“The gravity of that room was like nothing else I’ve ever felt before,” he said while standing not far from a memorial outside the school on Friday. “Every parent [there was] in the same boat of, is my child OK, and not knowing for hours.”
Camarlinghi and his wife soon had a tearful reunion with their third grade daughter. Other parents would not.
On Thursday afternoon, Griffin J John II, a 16-year-old former Silver Rail student, climbed over a school fence, fired a gun through a set of locked doors and headed toward a special education classroom. He shot six people, killing a teacher and three children, before a parent fatally shot him, according to police.
The students killed were aged five, eight and 11, and were all in the same classroom. Officials identified the teacher as Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old whose family said she loved her students, and “fought for the underdog” and “those with special needs”.
The violence has devastated the tight-knit central Oregon city of 100,000 people, an area well-known for its outdoor recreation and craft breweries.
Though the school was closed and patrolled by police officers, a make-shift memorial of flowers in front of the campus sign quickly formed. It grew larger by the minute as a steady stream of people arrived all day long, delivering bouquets, balloons, teddy bears, Minnie Mouse stuffed animals and a pumpkin. They wrote messages in chalk: “love always wins” and “fly high Megan”.
Some stopped by for just a moment, while others sat, and parents held their children and cried together. “It’s hard to leave,” one woman remarked as she took in the scene.
Kacy McCarney and her daughter Bayleigh brought half a dozen bouquets of roses and daisies to pay their respects at the school the 12-year-old attended for years. Bayleigh drew hearts in chalk on the sidewalk.
It still feels like Bayleigh’s home, McCarney said, as the family know all the teachers and many students.
“She still has us drive by every time we’re in the area,” McCarney added. Bayleigh, now a middle schooler, learned about what occurred when a classmate received a text message and screamed. She immediately called her mom, asking her about friend after friend she knew at the school. One of them was injured and hospitalized, Kacy McCarney said.
“You see the horrific things that happen outside of your town and it’s horrific and terrifying and so sad. You never think it’s going to happen on the home front to our community, to our babies,” she said.
The steady volume of visitors to the memorial showed the impact the violence has had in the area, but also the deep appreciation people have for Silver Rail. More than one person described the school as a “blessing”, including Camarlinghi, who volunteered at Silver Rail for seven years.
“The teachers, we know them. They’re amazing,” Camarlinghi said, adding that even former educators showed up at the reunification center on Thursday to offer their support. “It’s a tight-knit community, and I just want to say thank you to all of them.”
The memorial was solemn and largely silent with the exception of the sounds of Adagio in G Minor on the cello. David Chinburg drove from a nearby town to play the instrument at the memorial to bring comfort to people. It’s a tradition that originated during the siege of Sarajevo when a cellist played the instrument at a marketplace where 22 people had died.
Chinburg has been playing for more than 60 years, but his bow arm was shaking as he sat in front of the elementary school, he said.
“I just hope it helps to cleanse the grounds, the space, so that people can feel safe going back,” he said. He planned to come back three more days to honor each of the victims.
All around the city, the sadness is palpable, said Fabiola Caseres, who runs a local preschool and came to the memorial to deliver flowers. Many of her former students attend Silver Rail.
“It just feels so heavy,” she said. “Everybody is looking like deer in the headlights. It’s so sad, and you can’t stop thinking about the kids. They’re supposed to come home.”
She’s been comforted by the way people have come together with fundraisers and meal trains. “I’m not surprised. I’m just proud to come from here,” she said.
On Friday evening, people came together again for the second vigil in as many days. Volunteers offered candles, tissues, soup and cookies.
In the downtown space known as Peace Corner, not far from passing tourists and bar goers, hundreds of people stood in silence as they grieved all that had been lost.

Zelenskyy notes improvement in Ukrainian-Polish relations
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes Ukraine's relations with neighbouring Poland have improved recently, noting that the two countries share a common enemy: Russia.
Source: Zelenskyy answering questions from journalists online, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy was asked whether his resumption of trips abroad via Rzeszów Airport reflects an improvement in relations with Poland and whether further signs of closer ties could be expected.
In response, he noted that "our relations with Poland have indeed improved".
Quote from Zelenskyy: "I'm very grateful for this to both Poland and our teams, and I'm grateful to the Prime Minister [Donald Tusk – ed.]. I'm grateful to the people of Poland for supporting Ukraine. It's very important for us to be together right now. There is only one enemy – Russia, which is deeply concerned about a strong alliance between Ukraine and Poland."
Details: Zelenskyy stated that both countries simply need to strengthen their relations and resolve any problematic issues more calmly.
"Even very difficult things, we'll resolve them, I'm sure of it... These will be mutually beneficial relations, out of respect, because of the importance of security in Europe," he added.
Background:
- On 14 October, for the first time since the start of the scandal over the Order of the White Eagle, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy departed for an overseas trip from the airport in Rzeszów.
- Relations between Ukraine and Poland seriously deteriorated in late May and early June when Polish President Karol Nawrocki decided to strip Zelenskyy of the Order of the White Eagle due to the naming of a military unit in honour of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) heroes.
- On 7 June, Zelenskyy flew to the UK via Chişinău Airport in Moldova, having previously used Rzeszów Airport in Poland regularly for trips abroad.
- All of the president's subsequent overseas trips departed from Moldova or Romania. It was not until late July that Zelenskyy flew into Lublin on his return from the United States, as he had a meeting with Donald Tusk scheduled there.

Persian Gulf Internet, AI Infrastructures within Iran’s reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:29:27 UTC
21:29:27 KST

The threat of expanding the scope of a potential conflict between Iran and the United States to include the region’s digital infrastructure introduces new dimensions to the security equations in the Persian Gulf.
These infrastructures, which may appear unrelated to the military sphere, actually underpin significant portions of the economies, commerce, communications, and technological activities of nations in the region. Submarine internet cables, data centers, and facilities associated with artificial intelligence have now become strategic assets for these countries; assets whose damage could trigger consequences extending well beyond national borders.
In an interview with Press TV, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) Mohsen Rezaei discussed the possibility that regional communication and technology infrastructure could be targeted in the event of a renewed conflict with the United States. These remarks, viewed alongside the extensive investments made by the Persian Gulf Arab states in the digital economy and artificial intelligence, draw attention to the vulnerability of infrastructure that relies on high-speed connectivity, a stable and sustainable power supply, and expansive data transmission networks to function.
Submarine Cables: The Hidden Arteries of the Internet
A significant portion of international internet communications takes place via submarine fiber-optic cables. These cables are laid on the seabed and ocean floors, transmitting data over long distances using light pulses. Messaging, video calls, data exchange between companies, cloud services, and many international financial transactions all rely, directly or indirectly, on the capacity of these networks.
The significance of this infrastructure lies in the fact that a large portion of global digital communication relies on pathways that often remain hidden from users. Contrary to popular belief, the Internet is not merely a collection of wireless or satellite networks; the major portion of the global data transmission depends on terrestrial networks and fiber-optic cables. Submarine cables, in particular, play a fundamental role in intercontinental connectivity due to their high capacity and ability to transmit massive volumes of data.
The Persian Gulf and its associated communication routes are also part of this extensive network. The region’s geographical position, linking Asia, Europe, and other global economic hubs—lends particular significance to its data transmission routes. In the meantime, the Strait of Hormuz is crucial to security and economic calculations, given its strategic role in maritime transport and its proximity to regional infrastructure. However, the precise routing of cables and the degree of dependency vary from country to country. Therefore, it should not be assumed that all communication networks in the region rely on a single, unified path.
What are the consequences of damage to the cables?
Damage to a submarine cable does not necessarily mean a complete loss of internet access within a country or globally. Communication networks typically consist of multiple paths; if alternative capacity is available, some traffic can be rerouted. However, such rerouting often comes at a cost. If multiple paths are damaged simultaneously, or if the capacity of alternative routes is insufficient, there is an increased likelihood of slower speeds, higher latency, and disruptions to certain services.
The consequences depend on the location of the damage, the number of affected cables, the volume of traffic, and the capacity of alternative networks. Telecommunications companies, internet service providers (ISPs), financial institutions, and businesses that rely on the rapid exchange of information may face increased costs or a decline in service quality. Given that digital communications play a vital role in economic activities, such a disruption can escalate from a mere technical issue into a source of economic loss.
Repairing submarine cables is neither a quick nor a simple process. Locating the damage, deploying specialized vessels, and carrying out repairs depend on various technical and environmental conditions. Consequently, in the event of extensive damage or damage occurring simultaneously across multiple routes, restoring the network to its normal state can be time-consuming. The very characteristic has made the protection of such infrastructure a critical issue for communications security.
Data Centers and Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Critical Point for the Digital Economy
The significance of potential threats becomes even greater when data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure are taken into account. In recent years, the Persian Gulf Arab states, most notably Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, have made extensive investments in the development of their digital economies, cloud services, and artificial intelligence. These investments are aimed at diversifying their economies, reducing reliance on traditional energy revenues, and transforming the region into a global technology hub.
Data centers serve as hubs for storing and processing vast amounts of information, supporting services ranging from website and financial system hosting to complex artificial intelligence computations. The stable operation of these centers relies on several fundamental factors: reliable power, cooling systems, high-speed connectivity, and specialized equipment. A serious disruption in any of these areas can impair a data center's performance or, in extreme cases, bring its operations to a complete halt.
With regards to the artificial intelligence, the issue extends beyond the mere existence of powerful computers. Training and running advanced models require substantial computing power, as well as energy and data transmission infrastructure. Furthermore, the connectivity between data centers, cloud networks, and users constitutes an integral part of the service delivery chain. Consequently, any disruption to communication infrastructure or energy supply can drive up operational costs for technology companies and lead to delays in their development plans.
Of course, any disruption to internet cables should not be interpreted as a cessation of operations for artificial intelligence centers. Data centers may utilize diverse communication routes, redundant systems, and emergency power sources. The vulnerability of any given facility depends on its technical design, geographical distribution, level of protection, and capacity to shift processing workloads to other locations. Nevertheless, the interdependence of these infrastructures demonstrates that digital security is no longer merely a technical matter; rather, it is inextricably linked to the economic resilience and national security of nations.
Regional Consequences of a Costly Scenario
Should the conflict extend to digital infrastructure, its potential impact could spread to sectors such as financial services, e-commerce, transportation, corporate communications, and public services. Companies that rely on cloud computing or cross-border communications may face operational disruptions and increased costs. This situation is of particular significance for countries striving to attract foreign investment and enhance their standing within the digital economy.
Ultimately, concerns regarding the potential targeting of the region’s communication and technology infrastructure underscore that rivalry and tension in the Persian Gulf extend well beyond military capabilities or energy exports. Subsea cables, data centers, and artificial intelligence infrastructure have emerged as strategic regional assets, and any security crisis could jeopardize their functionality. For nations investing billions of dollars in their digital future, the critical question is whether this technological expansion is accompanied by a commensurate strategy for infrastructure protection, the establishment of redundant pathways, and the enhancement of resilience against crises.

Defence technologies, smart mobilisation can help Europe amid shortage of mobilisation resources – Zaluzhny
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:27:49 EEST
21:27:49 KST

Ukraine's Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021-2024) Valeriy Zaluzhny discussed challenges to international security with officers from the Netherlands who are participating in the Higher Defense Education program.
"Europe needs new doctrines and a new security system that take into account the realities of modern warfare. This is not just about technology and drones, but about the tactics for their use, their integration into the organizational structure of the armed forces, and the establishment of new production facilities. Old systems operate by inertia – the same arms manufacturers have multimillion-dollar contracts scheduled for decades to come. Are they interested in seeing their niche taken over by new, cheap drones? The answer is obvious," Zaluzhny said on Facebook on Saturday following the meeting.
According to him, the issue of personnel is another challenge that is particularly acute for small European countries that cannot rely on large mobilization resources. "The only way out here is the implementation of defense technologies and smart mobilization," the former commander-in-chief noted.
The diplomat also emphasized the need for political will to bring about change, clear goals, a strategy for achieving them, and a willingness to make decisions that are not always popular.
"Europe has the resources, it has the technology, and it has among its allies one of only two countries in the world with real experience in modern warfare – Ukraine. With Ukraine's experience, we have every opportunity to build a common European security system that is effective in a world of new threats," Zaluzhny said.

Hardline Israeli rabbi ruling on stolen Palestinian olives prompts uproar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17

Hardline Israeli rabbi ruling on stolen Palestinian olives prompts uproar
A hardline religious ruling justifying the theft of Palestinian olive harvests escalates violence and political tensions before Israeli elections.
Prominent Israeli Rabbi Dov Lior issued a Jewish religious ruling on Friday permitting settlers to steal olives from Palestinian orchards in the occupied West Bank.
Lior’s ruling claims that Palestinian landowners who could not access their olives during the harvest season due to Israeli restrictions have been sufficiently compensated in the years they had access to the fruit. According to the ruling, Jews are permitted to pick these olives to claim ownership of the Palestinian land.
Lior, born in Poland in 1933, went as far as classifying the theft of olives from Palestinian farms as an “additional virtue”, as settler pogroms and Israeli occupation continue in the West Bank.
He added that settlers should “conquer the land” far from Jewish communities in order to publicly “demonstrate our ownership” and follow biblical commandment.
“The Jewish people have never given up on the Land of Israel, as we express in our prayers every single day,” the ruling continues. “The Arabs never purchased the land from the Jewish people or from any individual Jew, and therefore it is stolen land in their hands… They never bought it in any way and it remained under the ownership of the Jewish people.”
Harvest violence
The ruling coincides with another wave of settler pogroms against Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest season. On Friday. at least 19 people were injured in 34 attacks by the Israeli military and settlers on Palestinians harvesting their crops across the West Bank.
An American photojournalist working for The Washington Post was assaulted by settlers while covering the daily violence, and five vehicles were torched.
Many Palestinian farmers have been unable to access their crops due to Israeli restrictions and the dangers from the settlers.
While settler pogroms are not exceptional, they come weeks before Israeli elections, with a push by far-right parties to gain the support of settlers and their supporters. But not all Jewish religious leaders backed the call to steal Palestinian olives.
Religious backlash
Rabbis from the religious council of the Gush Etzion settlements published a letter calling the illegal harvesting of Palestinian crops theft, blasphemy, and a moral defect.
Tzohar, an organisation of 800 orthodox rabbis, said in a statement that only the state has the authority to confiscate property. As long as the state recognises Arab ownership of the olives, they belong to them, it added.
Mamoun Abu Amer, an analyst on Israeli politics, told Al Jazeera that there could be political reasons behind the religious groups’ rejection of Rabbi Dov Lior’s comments.
“The position of the other rabbis who rejected this call might be a move driven by political motive and pressure from entities within the government to give the impression that these are anomalous voices that do not represent the general opinion of the settlers.
“The Israeli government is trying to portray that those who carry out these riots are a limited-number group that does not represent public opinion in the settlements, and that the settlers are peaceful, good, and law-abiding, and that the issue is confined to the ‘Hilltop Youth‘ boys who commit these crimes,” he explained.
Rabbi Dov Lior holds immense influence among hardline settler groups, such as the Hilltop Youth, who fiercely back his hardline religious decrees that oppose any territorial compromise with Palestinians.
He is also a prominent figure within Israel’s Religious Zionist movement and serves as the spiritual guide for the far-right Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
“Ben-Gvir relies on the religious rulings of Rabbi Dov Lior, which rely on biblical texts and the Book of Deuteronomy,” Abu Amer noted. He claimed that Rabbi Lior adopts the most extreme interpretations in the Jewish religion.
“There is an important matter, which is that Ben-Gvir competes via the TikTok platform, propaganda, and populist rhetoric, and this is a rhetoric that serves him and brings him votes, given the environment and general atmosphere in Israel after the events of October 7, as there is a ‘market for extremism’ in the Israeli society,” Abu Amer added.
Knesset member Gilad Kariv of the left-wing Democrats Party criticised Lior, accusing him and his followers of dragging Israel into a flood of moral vice.
“Whoever stands on the sidelines in this issue joins the camp of Rabbi Dov Lior and his criminals,” Kariv said.
