NASA’s Webb reveals the wild weather of a mysterious world 20 light-years away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:26:49 UTC
21:26:49 KST

NASA’s Webb reveals the wild weather of a mysterious world 20 light-years away
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- Trinity College Dublin
- Summary:
- NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has revealed that a turbulent world 20 light-years away has a surprisingly orderly weather system, with three recurring atmospheric states driven by temperature changes and shifting clouds. The breakthrough gives scientists a powerful new tool for uncovering weather patterns on distant worlds and understanding the conditions that shape their atmospheres.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a powerful new way to decode the weather on distant worlds, revealing surprisingly organized patterns hidden within the turbulent atmosphere of a mysterious object 20 light-years from Earth.
Researchers at Trinity College Dublin used observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope to investigate SIMP 0136, a brown dwarf previously associated with phenomena resembling the northern lights. They found that its complex weather is largely governed by just two factors: changes in temperature and the vertical structure of its clouds.
The discovery offers a new way to understand the atmospheric conditions of distant worlds and could help astronomers investigate planets far beyond our Solar System.
How NASA's Webb Telescope Decoded Alien Weather
To investigate SIMP 0136, the researchers analyzed observations collected by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) using a mathematical technique called Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
This technique helps scientists make sense of large, complicated datasets by identifying the strongest patterns within them. In this case, the team examined how the brown dwarf's light changed as it rotated, looking for subtle variations that could reveal what was happening in its atmosphere.
Rather than beginning with detailed assumptions about how the atmosphere should behave, the researchers allowed the observations to reveal the most important processes. The method also helped separate genuine atmospheric changes from minor fluctuations and random noise in the measurements.
Webb's exceptionally sensitive instruments made this possible by detecting extremely small changes in the object's brightness as different parts of its atmosphere rotated into view.
Scientists Discover Hidden Order in Chaotic Alien Weather
The results revealed something unexpected. Although SIMP 0136 appears to have a highly complicated atmosphere, nearly all of its observed atmospheric variability could be explained by just two dominant components, consistent with temperature fluctuations and changes in the vertical arrangement of clouds.
Even more remarkably, the researchers identified three recurring weather states that appear and disappear from view as the brown dwarf rotates.
Together, these states create a shifting atmospheric patchwork. Some regions are hotter and have thinner clouds, while others are cooler and contain thicker cloud layers that extend farther vertically through the atmosphere.
Instead of constantly changing in an unpredictable way, these weather patterns appear to follow an underlying structure.
The findings, published in Astronomy & Astrophysics, suggest that the seemingly chaotic atmosphere of SIMP 0136 is actually governed by a remarkably consistent set of processes.
Brown dwarfs occupy an unusual place between planets and stars. SIMP 0136 is larger and hotter than a typical gas giant planet, but it lacks the mass needed to shine like a star. Its atmosphere contains enormous cloud systems that evolve rapidly, making its weather more comparable to an extreme version of Jupiter's than anything experienced on Earth.
These immense weather systems can span planetary scales, continually changing the appearance of the distant world.
"We also discovered that these drivers of the weather patterns on SIMP-0136 persist over time, even as the detailed appearance of the atmosphere evolves over more than a dozen rotations," said first author Merle Schrader, a PhD candidate in Trinity's School of Physics.
"In relative terms, SIMP 0136 is one of the easier brown dwarfs for us to capture high-quality data from. These data have been studied before by established methods, allowing us to compare some of the results from this new technique to what we already know about this object. The technique has also helped us develop a better understanding of what drives the weather on this faraway world and how these weather patterns interact and co-exist, but perhaps even more importantly, it shows how this approach can be further refined and applied to other, less well-known brown dwarfs in different parts of space."
A Remarkable Connection Across 20 Light Years
For Schrader, the research also revealed an extraordinary personal connection to the distant object.
SIMP 0136 is located approximately 20 light years from Earth, meaning its light takes about two decades to reach us. The light captured by Webb in 2023, which provided the observations used in the study, had actually left the brown dwarf during the year Schrader was born.
"Light travels at around 300,000 km/s but, even at that speed, it took two decades to reach us, peering through the JWST lenses," she said.
"When you consider light takes just over a second to reach the Moon after leaving Earth, that gives a sense of how far away SIMP 0136 is, and how incredible astrophysical progress has been. I think it's amazing that we have been able to discern the intimate weather patterns of a distant world and map their interactions from our cozy little corner of the universe, when all we observe directly of these objects is a single pixel spread across the light spectrum."
The achievement highlights how much information astronomers can extract from seemingly tiny amounts of light. Even though SIMP 0136 appears as little more than a single point in telescope observations, changes in its brightness at different wavelengths can reveal detailed information about its atmosphere.
What This Discovery Means for Distant Planets
The new technique could have implications far beyond SIMP 0136.
Brown dwarfs are particularly valuable for investigating the atmospheres of giant exoplanets, which are planets orbiting stars outside our Solar System. Because brown dwarfs can often be observed directly, they give scientists an opportunity to study atmospheric processes that are much harder to investigate on most exoplanets.
By examining these objects, researchers can test how clouds form, how heat moves through an atmosphere, and how atmospheric circulation behaves under extreme conditions.
The technique developed by the Trinity team could make those investigations considerably more efficient. By quickly identifying the processes responsible for most of the observed atmospheric changes, astronomers can better determine which features deserve closer examination using more complicated computer models.
Professor Johanna Vos, Associate Professor in Trinity School of Physics, explained the potential significance of the findings.
"Our findings will transform how astronomers analyze future JWST observations. Since our approach rapidly identifies the dominant components of the atmosphere it offers an efficient first step before we begin computationally intensive modeling.
"Applying this technique to a wide range of brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets will help us better understand the diverse weather systems that shape worlds far beyond our Solar System."
Ultimately, understanding weather on distant worlds is about more than identifying clouds and temperature changes. Atmospheric behavior can provide important clues about a planet's chemical composition, physical conditions, and overall environment.
Those insights are also relevant to one of astronomy's biggest questions: which planets beyond our Solar System might have conditions capable of supporting life?
By revealing how complex alien atmospheres can be understood from faint changes in light, this new approach could help scientists take another step toward answering that question.

Europe Readies Post-Truce Ukraine Deployment Drill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:26:00 UTC
21:26:00 KST

At least 1,500 military personnel from the UK, France, and Germany will deploy to Poland in November to conduct specialized joint exercises simulating troop deployment and stabilization procedures in Ukraine in the event of a negotiated ceasefire, The Times reported.
The multinational maneuvers were formally announced by UK Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting following bilateral consultations with US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Thursday, Oct. 15.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Streeting confirmed that “hundreds” of British soldiers will participate in the deployment exercise alongside European counterparts.
“Next month, thousands of military personnel will take part in major exercises in Poland to ensure that we are ready to support the military training and post-war reconstruction that Ukraine will need,” Streeting stated.
According to defense sources cited by The Times, the exercise marks the first dedicated allied simulation designed specifically to prepare for a post-conflict phase in Ukraine, where the physical presence of European forces would serve as a conventional deterrent against renewed aggression.
Logistics, training, and deterrence protocols
Participating formations will rehearse cross-border transit logistics, rapid re-supply chains, and baseline sustainment operations – including forward food and fuel pipelines – under the framework of a prospective multinational peacekeeping or training commitment.
EU Tasks Commission to Bridge Ukraine’s €70B Funding Gap
Defense officials emphasized that the maneuvers do not indicate an imminent deployment of NATO troops into Ukrainian sovereign territory.
Instead, the exercise is engineered to validate technical protocols and joint command interoperability should a durable armistice or cessation of hostilities materialize.
The initiative highlights expanding coordination among European defense ministries to assume greater responsibility for continental security frameworks and wartime transition contingencies, ensuring rapid response capabilities if a ceasefire is formalized between Kyiv and Moscow.
Black Sea security requests and maritime friction
The planning for post-conflict deployment rehearsals in Poland arrives as NATO’s eastern and southeastern frontiers confront mounting operational challenges and maritime security friction.
Meanwhile, Bulgaria requested expanded defensive assistance from NATO on Oct. 16, asking the alliance to supply combat aircraft, air defense missile batteries, counter-unmanned aerial vehicle (C-UAV) systems, and regular air patrols following repeated drone attacks against merchant shipping transiting its Black Sea exclusive economic zone.
Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov confirmed that Sofia requested “the entire spectrum of available assets” to reinforce deterrence in the region, noting that regional partners Romania and the Baltic states confront comparable aerial and maritime vulnerabilities.
The security appeals followed consecutive drone strikes targeting civilian commercial shipping off the Bulgarian coastline throughout October.
On Oct. 6, strikes hit the commercial vessels Alfa Watan and Able within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, causing the Alfa Watan to sink and marking the first hostile kinetic attack inside the maritime economic perimeter of a NATO member state.
Subsequent strikes on Oct. 13 damaged the Maltese-flagged cargo vessel Chelsea 3 roughly 18 nautical miles off Byala and sank a second vessel near Krapets, prompting Bulgarian authorities to deploy additional missile batteries and drone-tracking systems along the coastline.

80 pct of ancient laterite wall restoration completed at Cambodia's Angkor Thom
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
20:25:33 CST
21:25:33 KST

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- An archaeological team has completed 80 percent of the restoration of Angkor Thom's centuries-old laterite wall within the UNESCO-listed Angkor Archaeological Park in Cambodia's Siem Reap province, an APSARA National Authority (ANA) news release said on Saturday.
The project, which began in April, focuses on the southwest section of the ancient wall near the prominent Tonle Om Gate.
Mao Sokny, a technical officer with the ANA's Department of Conservation of Monuments and Preventive Archaeology, said the reinforcement of the wall and its internal staircase is progressing smoothly.
"The reinforcement of the 15-meter-long wall is now finished," he said. "The team is currently backfilling the surrounding area with soil and applying mortar between the stones to secure its long-term structural stability."
Additionally, a 23-step internal staircase has been reassembled and reconnected to the wall, he added.
Built in the late 12th century by King Jayavarman VII, Angkor Thom was the grand capital of the ancient Khmer Empire, according to the ANA.
Its enclosure wall extends about 3 kilometers on each side, stands approximately 8 meters high, and is surrounded by a moat. The ancient city is accessed through five monumental gates. ■

Asia-Pacific Community: How Chinese TCM training hones Indonesian medical skills
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
20:25:25 CST
21:25:25 KST

by Zhang Yisheng, Nurul Fitri Ramadhani
JAKARTA, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- For three grueling months, even simple movements brought pain to Dr. Hetty Helen's hand. As a physician at Indonesia's Rumah Sakit Pusat Pertahanan Negara (RSPPN) Soedirman, her relief finally came from an unexpected source: the hands of a Chinese traditional medicine practitioner.
"The hand feels lighter and better," Helen said, visibly relieved. Having tried acupuncture before, she noted the technique used by the Chinese medical team was noticeably more precise, targeting the exact source of her pain.
Helen's experience underscores the unique value of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) and the vital role of medical exchanges in enhancing Indonesia's healthcare capabilities.
Under the "Belt and Road Acupuncture Station" initiative launched at RSPPN Soedirman, Chinese specialists worked shoulder-to-shoulder with Indonesian medical staff from Oct. 13 to 15. The program featured clinical training, free community consultations, and practical workshops on cutting-edge, AI-assisted TCM diagnostics.
Organized by the Shenzhen Shouzheng Innovative TCM Development Foundation, the training went beyond theory, guiding participants through needle safety, emergency protocols, and precise acupoint location. Doctors and students rolled up their sleeves to practice targeted techniques for shoulder and knee conditions, as well as specialized scalp and abdominal acupuncture.
For the Indonesian medical trainees, the program bridged the gap between textbooks and clinical reality, giving them rare, hands-on confidence under expert mentorship.
Natalia Santoso, a student of acupuncture and herbal medicine in Jakarta, felt a lightbulb moment during the workshops. She said learning directly from Chinese masters helped deconstruct techniques that had long puzzled her.
"Learning TCM, which we thought was difficult, turns out not to be so difficult once you understand the key points or acupuncture points," she said.
Santoso added that hearing the concepts explained straight from native Mandarin speakers gave her a far richer insight than reading translated Indonesian textbooks.
Beyond traditional techniques, the program introduced participants to AI-powered TCM diagnostic tools, offering them a firsthand look at the future of digital healthcare.
Hetty Helen Yanti, head of the hospital's TCM department, noted that such cross-border collaborations allow local doctors to refine their skill sets, particularly in mastering high-precision acupoint targeting.
Hafna Rosita of Indonesia's Traditional Health Council viewed the exchange as a dual opportunity: upgrading local practitioner skills while fueling the development of Indonesia's homegrown traditional medicine.
"TCM has advanced considerably, with extensive documentation, analysis and research," Rosita said, pointing out that Indonesia's traditional medicine similarly holds vast untapped potential.
The two systems could complement each other, for instance, by integrating precision acupuncture techniques with rich Indonesian herbal remedies, Rosita said.
Dr. David Song, a physician at the hospital's Traditional Indonesian and Chinese Medicine (TICM) division, emphasized that the initiative ultimately aims to fuse local Indonesian remedies with time-tested Chinese practices.
Through the TICM division at RSPPN Soedirman, "we are seeking to integrate Indonesia's local herbal remedies, known as jamu, with thousands of years of TCM wisdom to better serve our community's healthcare needs," Song said.
Looking ahead, Song said he believes partnership with Chinese institutions will drive deeper exchanges in medical technology, research, and clinical training.
Chen Zhigeng, director of the medical department at Wenzhi Traditional Chinese Medicine, a TCM-focused AI digital healthcare company, said the program's outcomes far exceeded expectations, voicing strong hopes for sustained partnership.
The event serves as a bridge for both medical and cultural exchange, enabling the Chinese side and its Indonesian counterpart to learn from one another and deepen long-term cooperation in traditional healthcare, he said. ■

South Africa's IEC extends candidate-list relief to 32 political parties
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
20:24:43 CST
21:24:43 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- South Africa's Electoral Commission (IEC) will recognize the candidate nominations of 32 political parties that failed to complete the final online submission step, extending relief following a Constitutional Court ruling in favor of the African National Congress (ANC) ahead of the upcoming local government elections.
IEC Chairperson Mosotho Moepya said at a media briefing in Pretoria on Friday that the decision was made to ensure fair treatment of political parties and uphold the constitutional requirement for free and fair elections.
"It would be irrational and offensive to the principle of parity of treatment to exclude parties similarly situated to the ANC," Moepya said.
The 32 parties had nominated eligible candidates and paid the required election deposits but, like the ANC, had failed to submit their final candidate lists through the commission's online system. They had intended to contest in 121 municipalities across the country, covering metropolitan, local and district council ballots.
The decision follows Thursday's Constitutional Court order requiring the IEC to include 181 ANC candidates across six municipalities. The commission said its decision to extend the relief to similarly affected parties was intended to ensure equal treatment in the electoral process.
Moepya said the developments were not expected to affect the election date on Nov. 4, although they had significantly compressed the time available for logistical preparations. ■

Japan-U.S. large-scale joint drills draw widespread concern, opposition
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
20:24:42 CST
21:24:42 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Japan and the United States will conduct large-scale joint military exercises at multiple locations across Japan from Oct. 19 to 29, involving nearly 60,000 personnel and drawing widespread concern and opposition in Japan, Kyodo News reported Saturday.
The drills, dubbed "Keen Sword 27," will involve comprehensive training by ground, maritime and air forces. The Japan Self-Defense Forces and the U.S. military will deploy about 45,000 and 12,000 personnel, respectively. Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines will also participate, with the latter five countries taking part for the first time, the report said.
Notably, the Type-25 surface-to-ship missile system, deployed in Kumamoto Prefecture in March despite local opposition, will take part in the exercises. The system will be moved to the Ohnobaru training area from its base in Kumamoto. The missile has a range of about 1,000 km, extending well beyond Japan's territory.
The U.S. military will also deploy advanced military equipment, including the Naval and Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System and the Marine Air Defense Integrated System, to Yonaguni Island in Okinawa Prefecture for the first time, according to the report.
The two militaries will conduct drills to counter ballistic missiles and military aircraft in waters off Hokkaido and northeastern Japan. Other exercises across the country will include parachute drops, amphibious vehicle landings, and casualty care and evacuation. Training will also cover support for ground, maritime and air operations in space and cyberspace.
The exercises have triggered widespread concern and opposition across Japan. Japanese media have reported protests in Okinawa, Nagasaki and Oita prefectures since the beginning of October, with demonstrators calling for the cancellation of the drills and an end to military training at civilian facilities.
Civic groups have warned that the joint exercises will only heighten regional tensions and put local residents at risk. ■

Kenya steps up Ebola containment as cases reach three
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
20:24:39 CST
21:24:39 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Kenya has intensified contact tracing, quarantine measures, screening at airports and border crossings, and infection prevention efforts as the number of Ebola cases in the country rises to three.
On Friday, Kenya confirmed its third case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease.
Patrick Amoth, director-general for health in Kenya's Ministry of Health, said the patient, a 65-year-old woman, was a close relative of the first and second cases.
She had been in quarantine since Oct. 6 and had developed a fever, sore throat and malaise.
"Having been in quarantine, she was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care, improving her chances of recovery while limiting the risk of further spread of the disease," Amoth said.
To prevent further spread of the disease, Amoth said Kenya had significantly scaled up its surveillance operations, successfully tracing and quarantining 127 of the 130 identified contacts.
"Of the 130 listed contacts, 127 (97.7 percent) have been traced and placed in quarantine, exceeding the global benchmark of 85 percent required to break the chain of transmission, while active efforts continue to locate and quarantine the remaining three," he said.
Amoth said the overall risk in the country remained low, as there was no evidence of community transmission. Contacts in quarantine were being closely monitored to ensure that any new cases could be detected and treated promptly.
On Oct. 12, Kenya declared Ebola a formidable epidemic disease under the Public Health Act, with the government introducing new regulations governing disease surveillance, screening, isolation, quarantine and the management of suspected infections.
Under the regulations, public health screening must be conducted at major points of entry, suspected cases must undergo medical assessment, and patients must be isolated and referred for treatment. Individuals who may have been exposed to the virus must also be monitored and quarantined.
The regulations also require the designation of health facilities responsible for managing Ebola cases and the establishment of procedures for inspecting and decontaminating premises where infections may have occurred.
Kenya notified the World Health Organization (WHO) after reporting its first Ebola case, in accordance with the International Health Regulations (2005).
"The two new cases have been detected early because they were already in quarantine and were being checked every day," said Neema Kimambo, WHO representative to Kenya, on Friday.
She commended the Ministry of Health, the Kenya National Public Health Institute, and national and county health teams for their swift response.
"We thank the health workers, response teams and families in quarantine for their commitment," she added.
Kenya is the fourth country in the world to confirm Ebola virus disease in the current context, following the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Uganda and France.
Most Ebola cases in Kenya and Uganda were imported from the DRC, while the case in France was travel-related and reported in June.
According to WHO, the early symptoms of Bundibugyo Ebola can resemble those of malaria and other common illnesses. They include fever, fatigue, muscle or joint pain, headache and sore throat.
There is currently no licensed vaccine or specific treatment for Bundibugyo Ebola, although clinical trials are underway in the DRC, according to WHO.
Kenya's borders remain open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings. ■

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy waits for Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson ahead of their bilateral meeting on the sidelines of a European Union summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels on October 16, 2026. | Olivier Hoslet/ AFP via Getty Images
Starlink restrictions hampering Ukraine’s war effort are “a planned operation,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday.
The satellite service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX is still deactivated in Ukraine at speeds over 160 km/h, which prevents some of its drones to intercept high-speed Shahed drones used by Russia, Zelenskyy told reporters in a WhatsApp chat.
He added that Ukraine conducted a test by sending Starlink-equipped vehicules to European Union countries, at speeds over 180 km/h. “Starlink kept working … The conclusion is this: the restrictions are in effect in Ukraine, but they are not in effect in European Union countries. So, this is a planned operation,” Zelenskyy said.
Advertisement
The restrictions have revived questions on Ukraine’s reliance on the satellite system operated by a U.S. company amid escalating tensions between Kyiv and the White House. “This will cost many of us our lives,” an experienced Ukrainian officer told POLITICO and the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network earlier this week.
“We’re reaching out to everyone at the military level, at the Ministry of Defense level, and at the diplomatic level, including to SpaceX. Right now, no one is responding to our military or the Ministry of Defense,” Zelenskyy told reporters.
The European Union is under increasing pressure to provide Ukraine with an alternative to Starlink. But negotiations between Brussels and Kyiv over access to the bloc’s Govsatcom program — which gives participating governments secure communications capabilities— have been stalling. And IRIS², the EU’s in-house planned network to match Starlink, is only expected to come online in 2030.
“The Europeans are now raising the question of alternatives themselves. And they’re already working on them. They’re already making progress, and they’ll succeed in this area. I can already see that,” Zelenskyy said.
SpaceX did not immediately responded to a request for comment.
Earlier on Saturday, Zelenskyy accused Russia of looking to create a blackout across Ukraine, amid attacks on energy infrastructure and the waiver of U.S. sanctions on Moscow.
Advertisement
“Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating. Pressure is needed to stop this,” he said on Telegram.
“An American sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, monetary rewards for [Russian President Vladimir] Putin: all of this only encourages him to keep striking,” he added.
The Ukrainian leader’s comments come after Russia carried out strikes on the war-torn country’s energy sector, including power generation and transmission facilities, with more than 320 jet-powered Shahed drones, loitering munitions, cruise and ballistic missiles. Power was reportedly cut for about 1 million people.
They also come as U.S. President Donald Trump signed on Friday an executive order that waived key sanctions on Russia — a decision that Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special envoy for investment and economic cooperation, described as “an important and truly historic moment.” Trump’s move comes only a few days after he made a deal with Putin over supplying barrels of diesel, leaving European countries and Ukraine stunned.
“A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely ignore Lindsey Graham’s bill, which was supposed to introduce truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war,” Zelenskyy said. “This bill could have helped a great deal, and it still can! But the law needs to actually work, and every vote for it matters.”

Protests sweep France as riots erupt in Marseille, police fire tear gas in Paris | Live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:22:22 UTC
21:22:22 KST

France is bracing for mass demonstrations Saturday as several protest movements join forces against the high cost of living, deteriorating public services and rising fuel prices. Tens of thousands of people are expected to take to the streets in demonstrations bringing together members of the Yellow Vests movement and student protesters, among others.
The student protest movement in France began Sept. 17 and has gained momentum in recent weeks, with students at hundreds of schools, particularly in impoverished, working-class suburbs such as Saint-Denis outside Paris, blocking school entrances, taking over roads, setting trash cans on fire and attacking police officers and passersby. The students say they are protesting neglected school infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages. The demonstrations erupted as the French government seeks to pass its 2027 budget, which aims to reduce the deficit.
In central Paris, large numbers of police officers gathered, particularly near the Champs-Élysées and the Arc de Triomphe. Police also fired tear gas canisters at demonstrators in Place de la République. Some protesters wore masks and black clothing and launched fireworks.
But the more dramatic scenes, even before the demonstrations officially began, came from Marseille. In the southern city, protesters were filmed smashing windows at a local police station and spray-painting graffiti, including on police flags. Fires were set in the streets, with mannequins apparently looted from stores thrown into the flames.
Dozens of protesters also briefly stormed City Hall, shouting, "This is the revolution — we're storming the Bastille!" Police removed the demonstrators from the building and deployed officers at the entrance to prevent them from returning. Officers in the streets of Marseille also used tear gas, while some images showed arrests taking place.
By midday, French authorities had recorded approximately 140 protest actions involving tens of thousands of people. A total of 166 people had been arrested across France, including dozens in Paris. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said he feared that "far-left elements" could inflame the demonstrations and turn them violent during the afternoon.
In a post on X, Paris police said, "We will not back down in the face of rioters and those who come to attack law enforcement officers," accusing "hostile individuals" of carrying out attacks against police.
"We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," a 19-year-old protester who identified herself as Lola told Reuters.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said Thursday that authorities were concerned about possible riots during the protests. President Emmanuel Macron, for his part, called for "calm" ahead of Saturday's demonstrations but stressed that he believed in the right to protest. He urged demonstrators to respect people and property.
Opponents of the protests accused the France Unbowed party, led by radical left-wing leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a staunchly anti-Israel politician, of inciting violence and fueling the unrest. They also emphasized the involvement of immigrants and their descendants in the street violence. The party categorically denied the allegations.
Palestinian keffiyehs and flags were seen at many of the demonstrations. About a week and a half ago, U.S. President Donald Trump weighed in on the issue in a social media post, alleging that the protests were not really about conditions in schools but rather reflected immigration spiraling out of control and an attempt by Islam to take over France.
Police could resume use of stun grenades
Last week, France announced it was suspending the use of stun grenades following an incident in which a 15-year-old boy lost his hand. Police said they had faced more than 200 students throwing stones and launching fireworks, and that the boy had picked up a grenade that exploded in his hand. Students, however, claimed he was struck directly after a police officer fired the grenade at him.
In another incident last week, a 14-year-old boy named Eden was struck in the face by a tear gas canister near Paris. According to his lawyer, he lost several teeth and suffered a fractured jaw.
On Friday evening, however, Interior Minister Nuñez announced that the use of stun grenades could resume.
"If there are clashes, all types of equipment may be used," he said in a television interview Friday.
The wave of unrest in France has erupted just six months before the presidential election, against an already tense social and political backdrop, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen leading in the polls and fuel prices soaring.
Current polls suggest that Le Pen will not win outright in the first round and that she will face radical left-wing leader Mélenchon in the decisive runoff — and defeat him.
Either way, such a showdown would signal that France is abandoning the political center and finding itself forced to choose between two parties widely regarded as extreme.

Israeli rabbi rules settlers can steal Palestinian olive harvest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:20:13 UTC
21:20:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli rabbi issues ruling permitting settlers to steal Palestinian olive harvests
A prominent Israeli rabbi on Friday issued a religious ruling that would allow Israeli Jews to steal olives from Palestinian land in the occupied West Bank, with several Israeli media outlets affiliated with the religious Zionist movement, including Channel 7, publishing the religious edict.
The ruling, issued by prominent religious Zionist rabbi Dov Lior, said that the olives belong to the Jewish people, and that taking the crops represents the implementation of what he described as the "commandment to occupy the land".
The ruling, titled “In response to numerous enquiries regarding olive harvesting in the groves throughout Judea, Samaria and Binyamin” — biblical names used by Israelis to refer to areas of the occupied West Bank — states that “the people of Israel have never relinquished the Land of Israel, as we express in our daily prayers".
This comes amid escalating Israeli settler violence and terrorism targeting Palestinian farmers in the occupied West Bank, with mobs stealing tractors, setting alight olive trees, and damaging cars.
Lior further claims that "the Arabs never purchased the land from the people of Israel or from any Jew, and therefore it is usurped in their hands".According to his assertion, Palestinians “did not acquire ownership of it by any means, and it has remained the property of the people of Israel".
The rabbi further states that if Palestinian farmers cannot reach their crops for security reasons, it can be assumed that they have abandoned the crops.
“If they planted trees that bear fruit, such as olives, the principle of despairing of recovering them applies to them. Therefore, if they are unable to harvest them for security reasons, it should be assumed that they have given up on them — and all the more so that they have given up on olives that have already been picked," the rabbi said.
He adds that even if the owners of the trees were entitled to compensation for cultivating them, they had already received sufficient produce from them over previous years. He maintains that the land and its fruits should ultimately return to what he describes as the ownership of the Jewish people.
Lior goes so far as to declare that settlers harvesting olives from Palestinian land is “entirely permissible". He adds that this act contains an “additional virtue”, given the security risks supposedly posed by Palestinians approaching settlements and settlement outposts.
His position is not limited to olive harvesting on land adjacent to settlements. He extends the ruling to groves farther away, stating: “Jews are permitted to harvest olives even in areas far from Jewish settlements, in order to publicly demonstrate our ownership of the land, and thereby fulfil the commandment to conquer the land.”
Dov Lior is one of the most prominent rabbis associated with Israel’s religious-nationalist movement. He previously served as the chief rabbi of the Kiryat Arba settlement near Hebron. Lior is known for his hard-line religious and political positions towards Palestinians and his support for expanding settlements in the West Bank. He wields influence among settlers and religious movements associated with the settlement movement.
Israeli media reported that Lior’s ruling came in response to a religious ruling issued last Tuesday by seven rabbis from settlements in the Gush Etzion bloc, south of Bethlehem. Those rabbis prohibited settlers from stealing olives from Palestinian land, even when Israeli forces prevent the owners from accessing their property for security reasons.
The rabbis, including Ze’ev Whitman, Uri Lifshitz, Avi Bliedstein and Moshe Shifter, argued that preventing Palestinians from reaching their groves does not mean they have relinquished ownership of the harvest. They stressed that seizing the olives constitutes "theft forbidden by religious law and a desecration of God’s name".
The seven rabbis based their position on provisions of Jewish religious law prohibiting the theft of property belonging to non-Jews. They emphasised that even if the landowners were assumed to have abandoned their fruit, this would not make it permissible for others to take it.
The Tzohar movement, which includes prominent rabbis, also joined the opponents of Lior’s ruling on Friday. It stated that “theft is forbidden from any person, whether Jewish or non-Jewish”, and that individuals do not have the authority to confiscate property.
The circulation of the ruling comes amid escalating attacks by Israeli forces and settlers against Palestinian farmers during the current olive harvest season. These attacks have included beatings, gunfire, the theft of crops, the burning of trees and vehicles, and preventing farmers from accessing their land.
Several areas of the Ramallah and al-Bireh governorate witnessed widespread settler attacks on olive pickers on Friday. The attacks targeted the villages of Abu Falah, Turmus Ayya, Burqa and Deir Jarir, causing injuries among Palestinians and resulting in olive trees and vehicles being set on fire.
Israeli settlements built on occupied Palestinian land are considered illegal under international law.

Mathernová outlines how EU is helping Ukraine prepare for winter
EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“We have a whole series of interventions on energy. Our Energy preparedness package is worth close to a billion euros, and it's a combination of support to energy equipment repairs, the entire logistics and transport chain,” Mathernová said.
She explained that all the equipment provided to Ukraine by most donors is delivered through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism. “We support the key state-owned enterprises, whether on electricity or on gas,” the diplomat said.
In addition, she said, the EU provides guarantees for loans and investments by international financial institutions aimed at developing renewable energy. A comprehensive “winter package” of humanitarian assistance has also been prepared for vulnerable households, including the provision of generators.
“And my colleagues are actively working with the ministry, the regional authorities, city authorities in many different places, and also with the energy companies, also going on the ground, monitoring, and trying to make sure that the assistance we bring is used efficiently,” the EU Ambassador to Ukraine said.
She added that the EU is also supporting measures to actively protect key energy facilities.
“And last, but not least, is the import of electricity that Ukraine can do because it's connected to the European continental grid,” Mathernová said, noting that the arrangement was introduced in the first days of the full-scale invasion and assuring that sufficient capacity is available for this purpose.
As reported by Ukrinform, international partners have provided Ukrainian energy workers with 4,807 pieces of energy equipment since the beginning of 2026.

>ANSA-LA-STORIA/ A “digital fortress” from Italy for the memory of Lebanon
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:20:00 CEST
21:20:00 KST

Italy is taking custody of Lebanon’s memory and safeguarding it from war: through the “Archiving Lebanon’s Heritage” platform, launched at the National Library of Beirut, family photos, letters, maps, songs, and videos preserved by Lebanese people at home and by millions in the diaspora, as well as by travelers, collectors, and scholars from every country—can now be collected, screened, and transferred to the CNR’s servers, thousands of kilometers away from the hottest Mediterranean front of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.
                                    
As Israeli bombings continue near archaeological sites in southern Lebanon and the Bekaa Valley, this marks the first time the protection of the country’s heritage has been entrusted to a participatory archive open to the entire world and hosted on European infrastructure. Meanwhile, over the weekend, an Italian-Lebanese mission traveled to Faqra, in the mountains north of Beirut, to begin a comprehensive 3D mapping of the Roman site.
                                    
The initiative stems from scientific cooperation agreements signed in Parma between the Heritage International Institute (HII), the Italian institute for the protection of cultural heritage worldwide, founded in 2024 under the auspices of the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the General Directorate of Antiquities (DGA) of the Lebanese Ministry of Culture.
                                    
At the launch, alongside Italian Ambassador Fabrizio Marcelli, were Minister of Culture Ghassan Salame, DGA Director Sarkis Khuri, and HII President Sergio Iovino. Conflicts, said Iovino, “may damage the stone of monuments, but they cannot erase the identity of a people if that people decides to preserve it.”
Anyone who uploads a document will retain ownership of it, decide whether to keep it private or make it public, and choose how to sign it—including the option to remain anonymous. Files approved by a joint DGA-HII scientific committee will be stored in the federated “Dariah-It” infrastructure, coordinated by the CNR, with security protocols and long-term preservation measures. 
In Faqra, the Italian organizers plan to develop two protocols to be applied to other locations across the country: how to digitize a monument to prevent its loss and protect it permanently, and how to virtually reconstruct what has already been destroyed.
                                    
The war and the Israeli occupation have caused damage in the Tyre region and the Baalbek area, both of which are World Heritage sites. The Beirut authorities have not yet completed their assessment of the damage, partly because the IDF maintains positions well beyond the border—occupying about 6% of Lebanese territory—and the raids on the south have never stopped.
                                    
A request is also coming from the Lebanese project site, one that Beirut’s institutions are repeatedly emphasizing to their Italian counterparts: to open museums and cultural sites to people with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities. The same authorities report a sharp increase in autism diagnoses and are asking the HII—which has long been working on accessible museum experiences in Italy—to extend this initiative to Lebanon.
                                    
The immediate next step will be the creation of the archive, month by month. The scientific committee will select the materials to be made publicly available and notify the donors; in twelve months, a group of “custodians” will be guests at an international gala in Rome, featuring three awards for the pillars of the project—tangible, intangible, and natural—from the cedar forests to the Qadisha Valley.

Trump feud with Zelenskyy raises fears over Ukraine aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:20:00 UTC
21:20:00 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump’s growing dispute with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is raising concerns that Kyiv could lose critical American military and intelligence support as Russia continues its war, with Washington’s efforts to curb fuel prices adding to tensions between the allies.
From threats to restrict intelligence sharing to a potential deal to import Russian diesel, a series of developments has exposed the fragility of the relationship between Kyiv and its most important ally.
Trump has repeatedly criticized Zelenskyy over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he partly blames for rising energy costs.
The U.S. president has pushed Ukraine to stop targeting Russian energy infrastructure, but Zelenskyy has rejected the demand, arguing that Kyiv cannot halt its attacks while Moscow continues striking Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
The dispute intensified after disruptions to U.S.-controlled satellite internet services raised concerns about Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian missile and drone attacks, particularly as it prepares for another winter of assaults on its energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy has responded to Trump with unusually direct public criticism, accusing Washington of increasingly favoring Moscow.
His remarks have fueled fears that the deteriorating relationship could lead to further restrictions on U.S. weapons deliveries, a suspension of battlefield intelligence sharing or additional economic agreements that benefit Russia.
Despite the public confrontation, Kyiv wants to maintain contact with Trump's envoys, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president's son-in-law, two Ukrainian officials familiar with the discussions said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Ukraine is also seeking to preserve its diplomatic relationship with Washington.
Denys Sienik, charge d'affaires at Ukraine's embassy in Washington, said Friday that Kyiv appreciated Trump's efforts to end the war and remained willing to engage in negotiations with Russia.
Trump, meanwhile, said he would continue dealing with both Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"I want that war to end," Trump told reporters Friday.
Daniel Fried, a former senior State Department official responsible for European affairs from 2005 to 2009, said it remained unclear whether Washington was making a lasting shift away from Ukraine.
He warned, however, that the fallout was undermining prospects for ending the war, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
"It's not only a missed opportunity, it causes genuine suffering in Ukraine and encourages Putin to continue the war, so it's not cost-free," said Fried, who is now with the Atlantic Council, a Washington-based think tank.
Trump's relationship with Zelenskyy has been strained for much of his presidency. In February 2025, Trump and Vice President JD Vance publicly reprimanded the Ukrainian leader during a contentious meeting in the Oval Office.
Since returning to the White House, Trump has paused or slowed military assistance to Ukraine at various points, while allowing European allies to purchase American weapons for Kyiv.
Relations had shown signs of stabilizing before Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities became a fresh source of friction this year.
Rising fuel prices have added urgency to the dispute for Trump, whose Republican Party faces a difficult battle to retain its majorities in Congress in November's midterm elections. High gasoline and diesel costs remain a political liability for the administration, analysts say.
But experts attribute much of the increase in energy prices to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, which prompted Iranian attacks on energy infrastructure and largely shut the strategically important Strait of Hormuz.
Frustrated with Zelenskyy, Trump turned to Moscow in an effort to increase fuel supplies and contain prices, according to a person familiar with the internal discussions who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Trump said Oct. 9 that he had reached an agreement with Putin to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel.
The move raised concerns that Washington could ease economic pressure on Moscow while demanding concessions from Ukraine, potentially giving the Kremlin additional revenue to sustain its war effort.
For Kyiv, the consequences of a breakdown in relations with Washington could be immediate.
Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Ukraine had received no advance warning from Western partners before a deadly Russian attack on the capital, underscoring concerns about the reliability of intelligence support.
American intelligence has been central to Ukraine's ability to detect incoming Russian missiles and drones, assess battlefield developments and plan military operations. A reduction in that assistance could leave Ukrainian forces less prepared to counter attacks, particularly against power plants and other critical infrastructure.
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's energy system during previous winters, seeking to disrupt electricity and heating supplies as temperatures fall.
Trump has said Washington continues to share intelligence with Kyiv. Zelenskyy, however, told NPR that U.S. officials had warned Ukrainian commanders that intelligence support could be reduced or cut off.
Concerns deepened after Ukraine's Starshield service, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet system, was disrupted. Two U.S. officials and a Western official briefed on the matter said the disruption followed an order originating from the White House, Reuters reported Thursday.
The service has since been partially restored, but the episode highlighted Ukraine's dependence on technology controlled by American companies and potentially affected by decisions made by the Trump administration.
Satellite communications are crucial to Ukrainian military coordination, particularly on the front lines. Any prolonged interruption could complicate communications between units and undermine operational effectiveness.
That dependence also gives Trump leverage as he presses Kyiv to pursue negotiations with Moscow.
Trump's approach could face resistance from Republicans in Congress who remain supportive of Ukraine and oppose pressuring Kyiv into a settlement that favors Russia.
Some lawmakers have argued that Washington should maintain support for Ukraine rather than allow Moscow to benefit from a weakening of Western assistance.
Zelenskyy's increasingly forceful responses to Trump carry risks, particularly given Washington's influence over Ukraine's military capabilities. But he may be betting that the balance of power in Congress could shift after the November midterm elections, making it more difficult for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia or further reduce assistance to Kyiv.
That is the assessment of Brett Bruen, a former foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration who heads the Global Situation Room consultancy.
Bruen said Zelenskyy understood the risks of confronting Trump but appeared less intimidated by the president's threats than during earlier clashes.
"Zelenskyy knows who he's dealing with," he said. "Trump's threats don't have the same kind of effect as they did when JD Vance tried to shame him in the Oval Office."

India’s top court says children’s right to internet access 'fundamental'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:16:47 UTC
21:16:47 KST

Ahmad Adil
17 October 2026•Update: 17 October 2026
India’s top court has said children, like all other individuals, have a fundamental right to access and use the internet.
“We have no hesitation in saying that the right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right of every individual under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the constitution,” a Supreme Court bench of Justices Jamshed Burjor Pardiwala and Vinod K. Chandran said in an order.
The Supreme Court stated that “children, irrespective of their age, enjoy the same rights,” adding that, “deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a conscience worth protecting or a freedom of speech worth expressing.”
“The safety of our children and their freedom are not at odds with each other. Our children are entitled to both,” the order said.
The court was hearing a plea filed by a nongovernmental organization alleging “serious lapses” by intermediaries in tackling child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) online.
The top court also sought details from the government about the tools and technological measures that intermediaries have put in place to detect and remove CSEAM.
Among its several directions, the court ordered the federal government to create a “national hash and URL list” database solely to detect and remove CSEAM.
“Digital safety and age-appropriate sex education must form a part of the core curriculum,” it said.
The Indian court’s order comes as some countries have banned or restricted children’s access to social media platforms.
India's chief economic advisor proposed age-based policies on access to digital platforms this year, saying that “younger users are more vulnerable to compulsive use and harmful content.”
The South Asian nation has been rapidly expanding its digital footprint in recent years. According to the online statistics portal Statista, as of last October, India had the largest Facebook audience worldwide, with more than 403 million users. It said India also has the largest YouTube audience.

US and Iran both claim control of Strait of Hormuz amid attacks on vessels
Two vessels have been struck with naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz this week.
Tehran, Iran – Dozens of ships were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz in October as Iran and the United States compete to assert their authority over the waterway.
At least 12 ships were attacked in the week ending on October 16, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported late Friday, with one important caveat.
“UKMTO is struggling to accurately report true number of attacks with majority of vessels attacked refusing to report to UKMTO,” the maritime security organisation stated. It said it was aware of more incidents in the waterway via other sources but could not verify them due to a lack of information.
The same pattern has been true for the first half of October. The month has seen the highest number of ship attacks since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28.
Of the 12 vessels that were confirmed attacked, the organisation said half continued to their destination or reached port. One sank, two were disabled, and three were either damaged or had an unconfirmed outcome.
The UKMTO also reported a new type of attack on Saturday. The master of a tanker said their vessel was hit by a rocket-propelled grenade (RPG) fired from a small boat 78 nautical miles (equivalent to about 144km) northeast of Saudi Arabia’s city of Jubail, Eastern province, resulting in damage to the aft port quarter.
In recent months, the US has managed to increase energy transits through the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways through a shuttle system coordinated with Arab powers. But volumes have oscillated weekly due to rising Iranian attacks.
Oil flows through Hormuz were at 11.6 million barrels per day (bpd) over the seven days to October 13. This was about 68 percent of the 17.1 million bpd pre-war baseline, according to Kpler figures.
On Friday, Brent crude also touched $110 a barrel for the first time since May in light of ongoing attacks. The situation has been exacerbated by the Iran-aligned Houthis’ attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and their capture of the Bab al-Mandeb strait. Expectations that the conflict between the US and Iran was escalating have also impacted prices.
The US military has provided a starkly different outlook on the situation in and around the Strait of Hormuz, which accounted for roughly a fifth of global oil and natural gas flows before the war began.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) chief Brad Cooper claimed in a video message late Friday that despite the Iranian attacks, 400 ships and 100 million barrels of oil moved through the Strait of Hormuz over the past week.
“Let me be clear: The Strait of Hormuz is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran,” he said, attributing the greatly increased ship attacks to “desperation” by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The US military also claimed that it continues to prevent Iranian exports and imports via its southern ports through an “ironclad” naval blockade. It claims the blockade has cost Iran $25bn in oil export income, and that the US has recently seized $350m in Iranian cryptocurrency financing.
The UKMTO report said total outbound transit over the last seven days was 125 ships, with total inbound transits standing at 129. Over the week, most transits by the Western security agency were for dry bulk cargo, followed by tanker products and general cargo.
Tehran has not provided exact figures on how many vessels have been attacked, or how many are passing through the Hormuz, although it has said Washington is exaggerating numbers to project success of its naval campaign.
It comes as two vessels were reportedly hit by naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz this week, with the US and Iran offering contradictory claims about the situation.
The IRGC has increasingly reported that vessels are hitting mines across the strategic waterway, which it says remains unsafe for vessels which do not coordinate with Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority, an entity set up during the war to manage passage through the Hormuz.
The latest claim came on Saturday, when the IRGC said a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil caught fire after striking a mine while moving through an “unauthorised” route.
Iran’s state-run Press TV shared footage it says showed the tanker on fire. But CENTCOM said it had cleared the strait of naval mines, and that vessels are being struck by projectiles.
The latest incident “fact-checked” by the US military was on Thursday, when it said a civilian container ship, the M/V GFS Pride, was hit by an IRGC projectile, not by a mine as the Iranians had claimed. The vessel sank as it was being towed to shore.
The US has refrained from responding to any of the recent vessel attacks, but there are concerns that Washington could escalate the war after the November 3 midterm elections.
Diplomacy has not fully halted, with messages continuing to be relayed between the two parties by regional mediators like Pakistan, Qatar and others. But no breakthrough in talks is expected any time soon.
President Donald Trump has reportedly ordered the US military to remain prepared for launching bigger attacks after the elections. Those attacks could potentially include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, nicknamed the “mother of all bombs”, according to US media.
But Tehran has signalled that it intends to continue the attacks, with acting Defence Minister Majid Ibn Reza saying on Saturday that it will be Iranian missiles, not US bombs, that determine the future of the war.
“Your bombs will explode elsewhere; in your global reputation, the US economy, and even your electoral calculations,” he was quoted as saying by state media.

Killers of U.S., Australian surf trio sentenced to 158 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:08:49 UTC
21:08:49 KST

Mexican killers of U.S., Australian surfers sentenced to 158 years in prison
A Mexican judge on Friday sentenced three men to more than 158 years of imprisonment for the murder of two Australian surfers and their American friend during an attempted robbery in 2024.
Brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico's Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California during an attempted robbery.
They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked on April 27, 2024.
Their bodies were found days later, dumped in a cliff-top well, with gunshot wounds to their heads. A 9mm and a .45 caliber pistol were used in the attack.
Judge Raul Hernandez ruled that the three Mexican defendants, identified only by their first names — Jesus Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus — acted with premeditation. Jesus Gerardo, known as "el Kekas," had a criminal record before the attacks.
On Friday, the court sentenced the three to 158 years and nine months each. Prosecutors had sought more than $100,000 in damages, but the judge rejected it and said any compensation would have to be pursued through civil proceedings.
"There can never be justice for the loss of a son, but we are grateful that these men will never hurt anyone else," Rhoad's mother Page said after learning the verdict.
Killers wanted to steal truck tires
The trio was attacked on April 28 or 29. Police found bloodstains and drag marks at their last known campsite, according to the Baja California state prosecutor's office.
Chief state prosecutor María Elena Andrade Ramírez theorized that the killers drove by and saw the group's pickup truck and tents and wanted to steal the vehicle's tires and other parts. Andrade Ramírez said it was unlikely that the trio was targeted because they were tourists.
Jesus Gerardo's former girlfriend, Ary Gisell Silva, admitted to goading him into stealing the tires from the vehicle. She was sentenced to 20 years in prison in November. She said Jesus Gerardo sneered at the trio's plea for their lives and bragged about the items he stole from them.
Prosecutors said the attack was followed by a hurried attempt to destroy evidence. The tents and truck were burned, and the bodies were dumped in a well at "a site that is extremely hard to get to" about 4 miles away, investigators said.
The well had been covered with boards and was "literally almost impossible to find," Andrade Ramírez said. It took two hours to remove the bodies, she said.
Investigators also found a fourth body, which had been there much longer. Andrade Ramírez said the men who killed the surfers may have been behind the previous killing, but they have not been charged in relation to it.
"Such cruelty"
The Robinsons' parents had traveled to Mexico from Australia for the month-long trial and left after the verdict. They had spoken movingly in court about their loss.
"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," Martin Robinson said.
Debra Robinson said what hurt the most was that her sons "were treated with such cruelty" in their final hours.
The families of the victims followed the sentencing hearing via video link.
Rhoad's mother and his fiancée, Natalie Weirtz, addressed the court by video link. Weirtz called for the accused to "be punished so that no other family suffers the same pain." Rhoad and Weirtz had been set to marry just a few months after he was killed.
Baja California is one of Mexico's most violent states, plagued by organized crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Still, the callousness of the surfers' killings shocked Ensenada, a surfing mecca that attracts visitors from around the world.
Other foreign visitors have been targeted in attacks on Mexico's Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were murdered in 2015 while traveling through the northwestern state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

‘The army told us we were on our own’: Oct. 7 survivors return to Gaza border kibbutz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:06:32 UTC
21:06:32 KST

How do they deal with overdrafts, how much do they pay for housing and what dream did they fulfill amid the war? People from across Israel speak candidly about everyday life, both before and during the war. This time: The Weintraub family from Kibbutz Holit.
How did you meet?
Alex: "We both immigrated to Israel. I'm from Ukraine and Yulia is from Uzbekistan. We met at Gadna [a pre-military training program for Israeli teenagers] when we were in 11th grade. We've been together ever since."
Why Holit?
Yulia: "We've been here for 13 years. We moved from Beersheba after deciding we wanted our children to have a kibbutz education."
Alex: "We were looking for a sense of purpose. I wanted to make a meaningful change in my life and was looking for a place with a community we could become part of. We ended up here because of the late Ofir Libstein, who was killed on October 7. At the time, he was the head of the kibbutz, before becoming head of the Sha'ar HaNegev Regional Council."
What was it like in the beginning?
Yulia: "There were 21 members and seven children at the time. It was a tiny place. Once you're accepted as a member, you can buy a home. Today, houses here range from 1 million to 1.7 million shekels. We're starting new construction here."
Alex: "Surprisingly, demand for housing in the Gaza border communities now exceeds supply. There are no vacant homes. Even though we're in the southern part of the Gaza border region, which makes it challenging to attract new families because we're far from central Israel, there are still almost no available homes. It's true that if you walk around here, the place looks empty, but that's because we're still recovering from October 7 and most members haven't returned yet."
When did you return?
Yulia: "We came back just two and a half months ago, exactly 1,000 days after we were evacuated. We hadn't been here for three years. After October 7, the entire kibbutz was evacuated to Ein Gedi for a year. We didn't stay the whole time because Alex was serving in the reserves, so I moved to Ofakim to be closer to my family and the base where he was stationed. After a year, we settled in Revivim, where we spent two years."
What happened on October 7?
Alex: "Sixteen members of our community were murdered, along with four soldiers. This is a small community of just 200 residents, so it was devastating. As a family, we spent 14 hours in our safe room. I was outside during the first few minutes and immediately realized this was no ordinary attack..
"Unfortunately, we're familiar with the sounds in this area and the different types of gunfire. You develop a sharp ear for these things. I had complete faith in the military and was certain the incident would be over within 10 minutes, so the shock was enormous. We were fighting to survive."
Fighting to survive?
Alex: "While we were in the safe room, we were reading the messages and witnessing the murders of our friends unfold. At the same time, I was trying to contact people I knew in the military, but none of them could tell me what was happening. One of them told me, 'Alex, you're on your own. Nobody is coming. You need to take care of yourselves.'"
Yulia: "Our youngest was hiding in a closet the entire time, and I tried to distract the older girls. The house across the street burned to the ground. We were probably supposed to be next, but somehow we were spared."
What happened to your house?
Yulia: "The house sustained bullet damage, but most of the destruction came from the years we were away. There was moisture damage, roots, overgrown vegetation and cracks. We had to completely renovate the house before we could move back in."
Alex: "There are emotional and physical aspects to the recovery. Emotionally, it's a very long process, and I know some people will decide not to return.
"Then there's the physical reconstruction. We're classified as a 'red kibbutz,' like Be'eri and Kfar Aza, because of the high number of people killed and the extensive damage to the community. Tanks drove through the kibbutz, many homes were burned down and need to be rebuilt, and all the infrastructure has to be replaced. It's a massive project."
Yulia: "There was never any question about whether we'd return. Even if it means living amid excavations, dust and holes in the ground, this is home."
"Emotionally, recovery is a very long process, and I know some people will decide not to return. Then there's the physical reconstruction. We're classified as a 'red kibbutz,' like Be'eri and Kfar Aza, because of the high number of people killed and the extensive damage to the community."
What's it like living on a construction site?
Yulia: "What bothers me most is that our friends' homes are empty. We're almost alone on the kibbutz, and it's frustrating. I hope that by next summer, we'll finally know who's coming back."
What do you do?
Yulia: "I'm the head of the kibbutz's new-member admissions committee. I'm working to bring families here and breathe new life into the community. I have eight families going through the admissions process, and we're building another 15 homes."
And you, Alex?
Alex: "I own an organizational development company. I work in strategy and management development, specializing in emergency preparedness, resilience and welfare. I work mainly with government ministries and local authorities.
"Over the past three years, I've spent a lot of time on reserve duty. I went from being a company commander in a battalion to serving as an organizational consultant in the reserves as well."
How has reserve duty affected your work?
Alex: "For the first two years after October 7, my business practically came to a standstill. Clients left, and I was focused entirely on reserve duty. Over the past year, I've slowly been getting back to work.
"Beyond that, I'm socially active and involved in various initiatives in the south. I was among the founders of the 'Future for the OTEF' movement, which focuses on rehabilitating the region. I'm also a member of the regional council. I try to find time for everything."
What's life like in the Gaza border region?
Yulia: "The nearest cities are Ofakim, which is 25 minutes away, and Beersheba."
Alex: "Life here is good. We have a strong sense of community, plenty of social activities and a good quality of life. We have a swimming pool and plenty of open space."
Yulia: "There's a lot of potential here, and when a place is small, everyone has a much more meaningful role to play. It might not look particularly beautiful or thriving right now. We're going through a difficult period, but it's also an opportunity."
How are you doing financially?
Alex: "We're doing OK. There's a myth that residents of the Gaza border communities received a lot of money. That's partly true, but the expenses we faced as a family during this period were enormous. There was the home renovation, the treatments and other costs."
What do you do for fun?
Yulia: "We like sitting on the porch. There's an excellent Thai restaurant in a neighboring kibbutz, and we also have a cultural committee here that organizes events."

Albanian police fire rubber bullets as student protests rage
TIRANA, Oct 17 - Police in Albania fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters on Saturday, the fifth day of mass student demonstrations demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama step down.
Reuters video footage showed police firing a shotgun towards crowds outside the education ministry during clashes with protesters. Reuters reporters found rubber pellets on the ground and pellets hit two Reuters journalists and several protesters, leaving round marks.
The incident marks an escalation in a confrontation between police and protesters that has engulfed central Tirana in recent days. Demonstrators have burned government buildings and banks and hurled rocks at police, who have responded with tear gas and water cannon.
Albania's police chief Skender Hita did not deny the use of rubber bullets when asked about it at a news conference on Saturday.
"All means that were used were employed in a limited manner, including the most recent ones," he said.
Hita said seven police officers have been suspended and were facing disciplinary investigations for "exceeding their authority" and "failure to respect the principle of proportionality" in dealing with protesters. He did not specify the incidents that led to the suspensions.
The demonstrations have been fuelled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards. They have also drawn support from people who felt ignored during a summer of largely peaceful protest against a luxury coastal development backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.
The unrest poses the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who last year won a fourth term in office.
"It's been 13 years of corruption and 13 years of doing nothing and empty promises. So the jar is filled and we are here for our rights," said Juri Taullahu, a 22-year-old medical student, on Saturday.
Police and the government condemned the unrest and called for calm.
Hita said that 1,067 people had been arrested and 388 criminally prosecuted. Scores of police officers and protesters have been injured.
KUSHNER-BACKED RESORT TRIGGERED SUMMER PROTESTS
Rama's administration has been dogged by corruption scandals, while analysts say Albania has become a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drug and weapons trafficking, complicating the country's efforts to join the European Union.
Villagers told Reuters in July that their land had been wrongfully sold for the Kushner-backed development on a pristine stretch of coast in southern Albania. Reuters later reported that the man who sold the land was wanted by prosecutors on suspicion of drug trafficking, accusations his lawyer denied.
Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who is not directly involved in the villagers' dispute.
Rama, who denies wrongdoing and told Reuters this week that he would not step down, said on Saturday that his government respected the students and their right to protest.
"My responsibility is even clearer during these difficult times ... to protect our citizens, guarantee justice, and move Albania forward — together with this governing majority, which holds a very clear mandate: to see Albania in the European Union by 2030," he said on Facebook.
Along with Montenegro, Albania is leading the EU accession process among Balkan countries.
Albania's unrest coincides with growing street protests elsewhere in Europe.
In France, student protests demanding more teachers and better facilities have spread into a broader wave of unrest.
Spain has seen protests against high rents and a lack of housing, prompting the government to call a snap election. REUTERS
