Britain’s lesson for Israel: The West Bank settlement policy has consequences - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:03:38 UTC
21:03:38 KST

The saga of the closure of the British Consulate in Jerusalem reached its end last week, at least temporarily, with both governments able to claim victory.
Israel can boast that, as per its instruction a month ago, there is no longer a British consulate in its capital city, and most of Britain’s diplomats have departed. On the other hand, the British government has stated that the building will not be closing. It will be known as the “UK Mission, Jerusalem,” and will continue its work with the Palestinian people.
Israel’s decision to close the consulate followed a British decision to impose a ban on imports from the settlements. There had previously been certain restrictions, but this time, His Majesty’s government took a significant step further.
There is no doubt that the British move was driven in part by political pressure from Labour supporters, and that such pressure is not unrelated to what is happening in the West Bank and Gaza. Israel’s retaliatory measure is also political.
All this is natural and understandable. But what, exactly, was all the fuss about?
The principle of the matter: Issues with Israeli settlements in the West Bank
For the purposes of this discussion, it is irrelevant that exports from the settlements account for roughly 1% of Israeli exports; it is the principle that matters. There is broad international agreement that the territories are not part of Israel. This is not news to Israel and its officials.
In fact, over the years, successive Israeli governments have signed agreements that excluded the territories from various benefits. That is why Ariel University cannot participate in European Union research programs, and why a bottle of wine exported from Gush Etzion cannot be labeled “Made in Israel.” If Israel chose to compensate Israelis in the territories for their losses, that was a domestic decision.
Israel is not merely aware of the aforementioned international position and, to some extent, cooperates with it; as a general rule, it acts accordingly. From Israel’s perspective, there are two exceptions – east Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, which it has annexed.
As for the rest, despite deepening Israeli civilian presence in the West Bank, the territories’ formal status remains as it was on June 11, 1967, the day after the Six Day War: occupied territory, which is subject to international law.
INTERNATIONAL LAW stipulates that territory cannot be acquired through conquest, and that occupation is, by definition, temporary. It sets out what an occupying power may and may not do, including restrictions on transferring its population into occupied territory, and vice versa.
It also defines the occupier’s obligations toward the local population, like protecting their security and property. With limited exceptions, such as the taxes paid by Israelis who live there, the law applied in the territories is military law.
Until now, Britain and other countries have, at least in part, turned a blind eye to the contradiction between the reality on the ground and international law, which Israel ostensibly claims to follow. This appears to be changing. So, what is Israel to do?
Israel can continue along its current path and ignore moves like the recent British step, which will likely not be the last or the harshest. But there is another option, which takes us back to the diplomatic compromise and what preceded it.
Before it was reached, there were hints that Britain could retaliate by expelling 27 Israeli diplomats from London, matching the number of British diplomats who were told to pack their bags.
The fact that such a possibility was raised over a political disagreement is inconceivable. Diplomats are generally expelled over suspicions of espionage, and Israeli ambassadors have been expelled in the aftermath of wars. The thought of so many Israeli representatives being told to leave Israel’s second-largest export market (after the United States), to depart the country which is home to the Diaspora’s fourth-largest Jewish community, is hard to contain.
Israel can choose to continue to ignore every criticism or regard it as antisemitic. But it also has the option to view the British move as a warning: a signal of what may happen in its relations with other countries if it continues to treat the territories – and their inhabitants – as though it is free to do whatever it pleases, as though no constraints apply to it.
The writer was Israel’s first ambassador to the Baltic states after the disintegration of the Soviet Union, ambassador to South Africa, and the congressional liaison officer at the Israeli embassy in Washington. She is a graduate of Israel’s National Defense College.

Swiss bakery makes world’s largest pink Carac for breast cancer awareness
The world’s largest pink Carac was made by a Neuchâtel-based confectioner as part of the Pink October campaign to raise awareness of breast cancer. Around 200 people, most of them dressed in pink, turned out on Saturday in Neuchâtel to enjoy a slice.
In 2025, it was the Ackermann Artisan bakery in Yverdon-les-Bains in canton Vaud that had baked a pink carac measuring 80 centimetres in diameter. The one made in Neuchâtel measures 82.5 centimetres in diameter and weighs an estimated 17–18 kilos, as noted by a photographer from Keystone-ATS news agency.
For the fifth year running, the traditional green caracs have turned pink in participating shops. The slightly higher price helps to fund prevention campaigns. More than 300 bakeries and partners are taking part in the campaign, which is now also running in German-speaking Switzerland.
+ Swiss researchers reveal mechanism behind breast cancer metastases
On Saturday morning, the people of Neuchâtel were also able to take part in activities and visit stands dedicated in particular to breast cancer prevention and self-examination.
The charity Le Carac rose was founded in Lausanne by Mélanie Tanner. Having been diagnosed with breast cancer in 2020 at the age of 38, she chose to put her marketing skills to work in the cause of prevention, particularly amongst young women.

Zelenskyy: Relations with Poland indeed improved; grateful to Polish people for their support

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that relations with Poland have improved recently.
"I want to say quite frankly that our relations with Poland have indeed improved," Zelenskyy said on Saturday, responding to a question about whether his resumption of international travel via the airport in Rzeszów, Poland – after a long hiatus – was linked to this improvement.
He thanked both the Polish and Ukrainian teams, as well as Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, for this. "And I am grateful to the people of Poland for supporting Ukraine. It is very important for us right now to stand together against a single enemy – Russia. And Russia is very concerned that Ukraine and Poland have a strong alliance. We just need to strengthen our relations and resolve any problematic issues," Zelenskyy said.
He expressed his conviction that "we will resolve even the most complex issues." "This will be a mutually beneficial relationship based on respect and the importance of security in Europe," Zelenskyy said.

snøhetta unveils completed shanghai grand opera house with spiraling public rooftop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:00:34 UTC
21:00:34 KST

snøhetta unveils completed shanghai grand opera house with spiraling public rooftop
the norwegian architecture studio completes the 146,786-square-meter shanghai grand opera house with three auditoriums and a rooftop open to the public.
prefer designboom on google
SNØHETTA’S SHANGHAI GRAND OPERA HOUSE OPENS ON HUANGPU RIVER
After nearly a decade in the making, Snøhetta’s Shanghai Grand Opera House officially opens on October 17, 2026, bringing a new cultural landmark to the banks of the Huangpu River. Spanning 146,786 square meters, the completed building houses three auditoriums with a combined capacity of 4,200 seats, alongside rehearsal, production, education, exhibition, and hospitality facilities. Yet the Norwegian architecture studio’s ambitions extend beyond creating a world-class performance venue. Conceived as an accessible public destination, the Opera House invites residents and visitors to experience its architecture and surrounding landscape, whether or not they have a ticket.
The project follows Snøhetta’s winning proposal in the 2016 international competition and was developed in collaboration with East China Architectural Design & Research Institute (ECADI), Theatre Projects, and Nagata Acoustics, formally commissioned as a consortium in 2019. Designed to accommodate everything from traditional opera and classical music to experimental productions, the venue brings together the technical demands of a major cultural institution with a decidedly more open approach to public space. Its inaugural season, running through February 20, 2027, will feature 82 performances across 47 productions.
A SPIRALING ROOFTOP CONNECTS THE OPERA HOUSE TO SHANGHAI
The building’s defining architectural gesture is Snøhetta’s sweeping white roof, which rises from the surrounding landscape in a continuous spiral. Inspired by the movement of the Huangpu River and the unfolding geometry of a traditional Chinese fan, the structure creates a fluid connection between the waterfront, the city, and the Opera House itself. A spiraling staircase leads visitors from ground level to the elevated roof, transforming it into an observation deck, informal stage, and year-round gathering space. With panoramic views of Shanghai’s skyline, the rooftop offers perhaps the building’s most democratic feature: an architectural experience that requires no admission ticket.
This sense of continuity extends throughout the exterior, where a geometric facade connects different public levels while balancing transparency and enclosure. Expansive glass surfaces introduce natural light into the shared interiors, while exterior lighting transforms the stage towers into luminous volumes after dark. At ground level, the surrounding landscape follows a radial arrangement that extends the building’s geometry into the Expo Houtan district, strengthening connections with the neighboring park and waterfront. Restaurants, exhibition spaces, and educational facilities further integrate the complex into everyday urban life, ensuring that the building remains active beyond its scheduled performances.
THREE AUDITORIUMS BRING 4,200 SEATS TO THE SHANGHAI GRAND OPERA HOUSE
Inside, the architectural language shifts from the predominantly white exterior to a series of richly textured performance spaces. The centerpiece is Harmony Hall, a 2,000-seat auditorium arranged across five levels, with a dramatic dark-red interior conceived to enhance the acoustics of the human voice. Carefully positioned balconies and smaller side boxes help establish a closer relationship between audiences and performers. The 1,200-seat Soar Theatre offers a more intimate setting for classical opera, operetta, regional productions, and theater, while the 1,000-seat Open Stage introduces adaptable seating and stage configurations for experimental performances, complemented by panoramic views toward the surrounding park.
Although the three auditoriums differ in scale, atmosphere, and technical requirements, they share a cohesive architectural identity beneath the spiraling roof. Carefully selected materials, contrasting color palettes, and fluid circulation routes guide visitors through the building, making movement itself part of the experience. Passive design strategies, natural daylight, and landscape integration also contribute to its environmental approach. Ultimately, Snøhetta’s Shanghai Grand Opera House proposes a cultural institution whose public role extends well beyond the performances it hosts. The curtain may rise inside, but the architects have made sure there is plenty happening outside, too.

From little acorns … to his 1,000th article for the Guardian country diary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:00:30 UTC
21:00:30 KST

In the autumn of 1987, Mark Cocker sat in a field near Norwich and watched a jay burying acorns for the long winter ahead. He described the scene in his first country diary for the Guardian. Thirty-nine years on, some of those jay-planted acorns will be mature oaks now, and Cocker is completing his 1,000th diary for the world’s oldest column in an English-language newspaper.
In his next diary, he will reflect on the changing birdlife around Flint Clough, in the Peak District, where he first marvelled at rare birds aged 12 after devouring bird books in his bedroom. As a boy, he would find cuckoo, golden plover, ring ouzel and twite, a once-common bird which is now virtually extinct in England.
On his latest visit a few weeks ago, he saw raptors he would have only dreamed of as a boy, “a whole slew of buzzards, two peregrines, two marsh harriers – the first I’ve ever seen in Derbyshire – and several red kites”.
The Guardian country diary began in 1904 with the nature-loving dispatches of Thomas Coward, a retired textile bleacher from Cheshire. Today there is a diverse roster of about 30 diarists spread from Cornwall to the Cairngorms who include farmers, scientists, conservationists, a vicar, a thatcher and a forager, as well as writer-naturalists such as Cocker, who pens a fortnightly dispatch, usually from his local patch in Derbyshire.
Despite honing his skills by working as a warden at Holkham national nature reserve in north Norfolk, while also becoming the first member of his family to attend university, where he studied English, Cocker says it took him 10 years to master the deceptively difficult craft of the diary – a compelling story about rural life in just 360 words.
“You need quite a long apprenticeship to get it right because it’s so short,” he said. “It’s like a haiku. You’ve got to awaken the subject from its dormancy and get straight into the theme. And then the best diaries link it to something else.
“You have a single shaft of light and, if you can, you excavate its relationship to the other parts. You have to often imply or adumbrate rather than specify. And it’s that connection between the part and the whole, the moment and the universal, which is the trick of the diary.”
For Cocker, who earlier this month published The Nature of Seeing, a collection of recent diaries alongside new essays exploring how we might experience nature more fully, the close observation required for appreciating nature is a discipline that benefits all writing. He points to the surprising number of literary greats who have also kindled a passion for wildlife, from Margaret Atwood to Vladimir Nabokov.
Before he began writing, Cocker worked as a refuse collector, a road sweeper, a potato picker and, as a penniless student, posed nude for the local art college.
His big break came after a conservationist friend wrote to the Guardian to complain about the surfeit of inconsequential diaries about cricket matches. “She said: ‘The Guardian needs to get its boots and hat and coat on, and get out into the wild,’” remembered Cocker.
Cocker did that, writing early columns on chiffchaffs, silver-studded blue butterflies and sparrowhawks, before becoming a regular when the legendary Lakeland diarist Enid Wilson fell ill. Between them, Wilson and Cocker have covered a span of 76 years.
Cocker shrugs off his own skills as a naturalist, which he says would be completely normal in another culture or era. In The Nature of Seeing, he writes about Inuit fishers who navigated home through the fog by recognising the subtly different patterns of snow bunting songs which corresponded to particular sections of the (invisible) coastline. “That is the level of attention to the living world which we’ve lost and need to recapture,” he said.
He never steps outside with a preordained list of subjects to write about but seeks powerful encounters. “I have to feel the article viscerally. I have to feel that it moved me. That’s really where the experience begins and ends. If it doesn’t engage you personally, if you aren’t affected by it, the diary is a cheat.”
After Phil Gates retired recently following nearly 40 years on the diary, Cocker is now the longest-serving diarist.
The country diary editor, Paul Fleckney, said: “Mark is a gift to the diary. What you get from him is hyper-detailed knowledge with one eye on the bigger picture, and all written with such persuasion. Beneath it is a deep, deep love for the natural world, but also a rare kind of indefatigability. It’s as if all he wants to do is open people’s eyes and ears to the wonders around us, and it is infectious.”
In a time of climate and biodiversity crises, as overconsumption imperils humanity, Cocker is convinced that, for all its modesty, the country diary’s time has come.
“Meaning has been poured on to the diary because it is a repository now for a sense of the impending crisis which assails all life,” he said. “We’re now recognising that the intensifying nature of capitalism, the rise of the right, migration, climate change, drought, starvation, overpopulation – everything is to do with one meta-story, and that is our relationship with the rest of life. The diary’s become a valuable philosophical place for big ideas to be shared.”

From 3,000 feathers to pet portraits, Rolls-Royce rides high on custom craze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:00:29 UTC
21:00:29 KST

They are the plaything of kings, presidents and A-listers, with Rolls-Royce enthusiasts ranging from the Sultan of Brunei to Rowan Atkinson, from King Charles III to Kermit the frog.
And at the carmaker’s factory in Goodwood, West Sussex, special requests from customers get more indulgent every year. An interior lined with 3,000 iridescent feathers, or a built-in champagne cooler, or a car built in homage to its owners’ dog, have all become part of the job.
Even with a fast-growing team of artisans and engineers, the company is stretched, and soon it will nearly double the size of its factory as part of a £300m investment by its owner, BMW, which it said at the time of the announcement was part of “securing our future here in the UK”.
Behind much of the demand is a new kind of client, who is younger than ever and with a fortune built in technology, says Julian Jenkins, Rolls-Royce’s director of sales and brand. The average buyer is now just 43 – down from 56 in 2010. “Never has there been so much wealth created so quickly at such a young age,” he says.
Bespoke, high-value customisation is becoming an increasingly valuable pillar of UK manufacturing, which still makes up about 9% of the UK economy despite the years of deindustrialisation that Andy Burnham has vowed to reverse. This week, the wider sector helped drive a surprise expansion of GDP in August, after growing 0.8% month on month.
On a tour of the Goodwood factory, an inner door panel is emblazoned with a bitcoin symbol, hinting at changing tastes. “The industries – cryptocurrency, AI and tech – are where we see some of these young entrepreneurs finding their way very quickly to Rolls-Royce,” Jenkins says. “They are very specific about what they want.”
Another car, built for a wealthy American couple, was devoted to their Labrador, Bailey. The dog’s face was pieced together on a rear panel using more than 180 individual slivers of wood, which was a four-month project, with paw prints engraved in the doors for good measure. Clients nowadays, Jenkins says, “are creating something in their image”.
Four models make up the current Rolls-Royce range: the Phantom, starting at £441,000, the nearly three-tonne Cullinan SUV, from £345,000, the Spectre electric car, from £333,000, and the cheaper Ghost, from £290,000.
But the average Rolls-Royce sells for about £500,000, up from about £300,000 a decade ago, driven largely by customisation work. A heavily personalised car can cost 25% more than the standard price, and seven-figure sums are “not unusual”, a spokesperson says.
“The limits are set by the client,” Jenkins says. “We’ve seen some extremely complex and intricate commissions, and some of those can take multiple years. With that, there is value that comes as a consequence.”
It is a vision Rolls-Royce’s founders could scarcely have imagined for a company that staked its early reputation on reliability. The business dates back to 1904, when Charles Rolls, an aristocrat and racing driver, met Henry Royce, an engineer, at the Midland Hotel in Manchester, and agreed to sell every car the latter could build.
By 1907, Autocar magazine called the Silver Ghost, an early model, the “best car in the world” after completing the gruelling Scottish Reliability Trial without a single mechanical fault. Now, Rolls-Royce has its own entry in the Collins dictionary, as a byword for “anything considered to be the very best of its kind”. Its longest-running model, the Phantom, celebrated its centenary last year.
An expansion into aero engines during the world wars made it a manufacturing powerhouse, but later financial collapse forced the government of the time to nationalise the company in 1971. The car business was split off and sold to the engineering firm Vickers. Rolls-Royce, the FTSE 100 aerospace giant, still shares the same logo.
In 1998, BMW bought the right to put the Rolls-Royce name on cars, and in 2003 opened the Goodwood factory, promising to triple annual production from about 2,000 cars a year. Two decades later it succeeded, when output peaked at 6,032 cars, falling back to 5,664 last year.
Would the Rolls-Royce engineers whose Merlin engines powered the second world war Spitfire have guessed the company name would end up in German hands?
“Rolls-Royce motorcars is very much a British company at heart,” says Chris Brownridge, its chief executive. However, he admits it benefits from “synergies” with BMW, such as “battery technology research and development, access to wind-tunnels and other major facilities”.
The expansion at Goodwood comes as carmakers are under significant strain from Chinese competition, soaring industrial energy costs and US tariffs. Jaguar Land Rover recently said it would cut 4,000 jobs, while Volkswagen, which owns Rolls-Royce’s arch rival Bentley, is cutting 100,000 jobs by 2030.
Shrinking demand in China, a key export market for luxury goods, has “obviously been significant”, Jenkins admits, pointing to Rolls-Royce clients “who made their wealth through the [Chinese] property market … which has been adversely affected.”
Electrification has been part of that story, too. Rolls-Royce’s first electric vehicle, the Spectre, launched in 2022, alongside a pledge from the company to sell only EVs by the end of the decade. The model sold briskly at first but deliveries nearly halved in 2025, and earlier this year Rolls-Royce scrapped its 2030 target.
Jenkins says the company is “not immune to the shifts that have happened, and some of the resistance that we’ve seen [to EVs]”. A revamped version, the Spectre Series Two, recently launched with a longer range and more power.
The latest factory upgrade, Jenkins says, is less about pumping out more cars, but rather about meeting the “ever more complex” demands of clients. Every car is made to order and assembled at Goodwood, where 2,500 people work across a production line with 45 stations. A single car can take up to 600 hours to build, passing through more than 100 pairs of hands.
Those include 14 artisans finishing personalised vehicles. Artists hand-paint designs on bodywork and inner panels, while embroiderers are on hand to make the ceilings of cars look like the night sky. A standard sky contains up to 1,600 fibre-optic stars and takes around nine hours to thread by hand, while the most elaborate commissions can take two full days.
A trio of innovation specialists work on novel techniques. One dragon design used a method borrowed from fine furniture called sand shading, in which each individual scale is burned at the edges in a hot pan to create a shadow effect across the creature’s body.
Andrew Hopkins, a lead craftsperson, studied furniture making before joining Goodwood when it opened in 2003. Does he ever think a request is a bit much? “Whether you like it personally, you don’t really take it into account,” he says. “You learn quite fast not to be the taste police.”
But who is paying for it? Well-documented owners include Tyson Fury, David Beckham and members of the Kardashian family. Kylie Jenner had her Rolls-Royce Cullinan finished with a pink interior and a plaque reading “Stormi’s Mom” in honour of her daughter.
Despite its slowdown, many of the youngest, tech-rich buyers are still coming from China. Jenkins was recently in Beijing, opening a new dealership and presenting a car to a 26-year-old woman who had “fallen in love” with a custom design.
“They are individuals that are very much on the way up in terms of their wealth creation,” he says, “but doing so at an incredible pace.”
Is the growing concentration of wealth among fewer and younger people a good thing for society? Whatever the answer, it has certainly helped Rolls-Royce. “It’s a fact, isn’t it?” says Jenkins.

Scientists identify DNA regions tied to binge eating, including one near a well-known obesity gene
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

A large genetic analysis has identified DNA regions linked to binge-eating behavior and anorexia nervosa, suggesting that the two share genetic ties to other psychiatric conditions but run in opposite directions when it comes to body weight. The findings, published in Nature Mental Health, extend eating disorder genetics beyond its long focus on anorexia.
Anorexia nervosa is a condition where individuals experience an intense fear of gaining weight, leading them to severely restrict their food intake to maintain a dangerously low body weight. Binge-eating behavior involves episodes of eating unusually large amounts of food while feeling a loss of control.
Eating disorders also overlap, and people often move from one diagnosis to another over time. A 2010 twin study found that anorexia and bulimia nervosa, a condition in which people of normal or higher weight binge eat and then try to compensate through behaviors such as vomiting or fasting, share a moderate portion of their genetic risk. Large-scale gene-mapping studies, however, have centered on anorexia: a 2019 study by the same research consortium identified the first eight genetic regions linked to the disorder, and its authors argued that anorexia has both psychiatric and metabolic roots.
Binge eating has received far less genetic attention, even though it appears across several eating disorders. A 2021 study by members of the same network found that people with binge-type eating disorders tended to carry more genetic variants linked to higher body mass index (BMI), a measure of weight relative to height, pointing to the need to map binge eating’s genetics directly.
The new study was led by Jet D. Termorshuizen of Karolinska Institutet and Helena L. Davies and Sang-Hyuck Lee of King’s College London, who contributed equally, with Jonathan Coleman, a senior lecturer in statistical genetics at King’s College London, among its senior authors. The work was carried out by the Eating Disorders Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, an international research collaboration.
“We had previously carried out a large genetic study of anorexia nervosa and we wanted to expand this and implicate more regions of the genome as associated with this disorder,” Coleman told PsyPost. “This is valuable because it provides useful genetic information that others can use to study anorexia nervosa more deeply. However, we also wanted to extend beyond anorexia nervosa and also beyond diagnoses (which are based on grouping observed symptoms rather than being based in biology).”
“For that reason, we wanted to carry out a large genetic study of binge eating, as this is a key, under-studied symptom that is present across different eating disorders (anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge-eating disorder) in different contexts (notably, the relationship with BMI is different across these disorders),” he added. “Having a large genetic study of binge eating would allow us to understand how the genetics of an eating behavior (binge eating) related to those of an eating disorder (anorexia nervosa), as well as how a common eating symptom (binge eating) related to other common symptoms and conditions such as body composition measures.”
The researchers conducted a genome-wide association meta-analysis, which pools results from many studies that each scanned the genomes of many people for genetic variations associated with a trait. They analyzed 27 studies, 14 of which had been part of the consortium’s 2019 analysis, comparing the DNA of people who had a history of binge-eating behavior or anorexia to the DNA of people without these conditions.
The sample sizes were vast, with the binge-eating analysis including 39,279 cases and 1,227,436 controls, and the anorexia nervosa analysis including 24,223 cases and 1,243,971 controls. All participants in the primary analyses were of European ancestry.
Binge eating was defined broadly: people counted as cases if they described eating unusually large amounts of food with a sense of lost control, answered yes to a single question about binge eating, or reported a diagnosis of bulimia or binge-eating disorder, even without confirmation from a health professional. Most cases were women, making up 96 percent of the binge-eating group and 94 percent of the anorexia group.
The researchers analyzed millions of genetic markers to see if certain variations appeared more often in people with these eating behaviors. They also calculated genetic correlations, comparing the genetic patterns of the eating disorders with those of other traits like psychiatric conditions and BMI. To see if the genetic risk for eating disorders was just a side effect of genes that control weight, they mathematically separated out the genetic influence of BMI.
The analysis identified six independent genetic regions associated with binge-eating behavior. Some had previously been tied to smoking, risk-taking, and the age at which girls have their first period. One lies near FTO, a gene region well known for its links to obesity; it was associated with binge eating but not with anorexia, and the authors suggest that FTO’s connection to higher BMI may run partly through binge eating.
For anorexia, the researchers identified eight genetic regions: six that had appeared in the 2019 study and two new ones. Because the new analysis reused much of the same data, the repeat findings are not fully independent confirmation, and two regions from the earlier study no longer reached the threshold for significance. The team also found one region specifically tied to the restricting subtype of anorexia, in which people limit food intake without regular binge eating or purging.
When comparing the conditions, binge eating and anorexia shared some genetic influences. They showed a genetic correlation of 0.46, a measure of the extent to which the same genetic variants influence two traits, on a scale where 0 means no shared genetic influence and 1 means complete overlap. Both conditions shared positive genetic correlations with psychiatric issues like major depressive disorder, anxiety, and schizophrenia.
The findings are broadly in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that people with major depression reported more disordered eating behaviors than healthy volunteers. That study measured symptoms directly in patients, whereas the new study examined overlap at the level of genetic variants.
However, the two conditions also differed psychiatrically. Anorexia, but not binge eating, was genetically linked to obsessive-compulsive disorder. Binge eating had a stronger link to ADHD and, unlike anorexia, was genetically linked to smoking, problem drinking, and general risk tolerance.
Despite their shared psychiatric links, binge eating and anorexia displayed opposing genetic correlations with body measurements. The genetic markers for binge eating tended to align with a higher BMI and higher body fat percentage. In contrast, the genetic markers for anorexia were associated with a lower BMI and lower body fat percentage, though anorexia showed no genetic overlap with naturally being very thin, suggesting its genetics reflect more than just low body weight.
The researchers also found that these eating disorder traits are largely distinct from simple weight regulation. Using a statistical technique to separate out genetic influences shared with BMI, they found that this shared component accounted for only about 12 percent of the genetic signal for binge eating and 10 percent for anorexia, leaving the large majority independent of body weight genetics.
“Anorexia nervosa is not just a consequence of a genetic predisposition to low body weight, and similarly binge eating is not just a response to a genetic predisposition to high body weight,” Coleman explained. “Each has genetic links to the other, and to other psychiatric disorders and traits, but each has unique genetic features too.”
Finally, the team generated polygenic risk scores, which summarize a person’s overall genetic risk based on many small genetic variations. When the researchers applied anorexia risk scores built from the European data to two small studies from Japan and Korea, with about 150 anorexia cases combined, higher scores were linked to higher odds of anorexia, though they explained only about 1.3 percent of the variation in risk. This suggests that some genetic factors for anorexia are shared across ancestries.
“The effects of individual variants on psychiatric traits and disorders in general are very small, but there are a lot of them, and together their effects become similar in size to other risk factors like adverse life events,” Coleman noted. “That is also true for anorexia nervosa and for binge eating.”
“Speaking practically, those individual effects are not very important – most people with the risk version of any given variant won’t binge eat,” he said. “However, the combined set of variants (what we call a polygenic score) has a moderate effect, and we hope that further research can show that it can be useful in future alongside known non-genetic risk factors like family history and history of life events.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The primary limitation is the heavy reliance on participants of European ancestry. Applying these findings to other global populations requires caution, as differences in genetic background and environments could influence genetic risk.
Because the studies used different ways of identifying cases, and some comparison participants were never screened for eating disorders, the groups may be more mixed than in a clinic-based study. The mostly female sample also means the results may not apply equally to men.
Diagnostic crossover is another factor to keep in mind. People’s eating disorder symptoms can change over time, meaning someone with the restricting subtype of anorexia might develop binge-eating symptoms years later. Because the data relies on cross-sectional studies that take a snapshot in time, some people in one category might eventually migrate to another, though the authors note that diagnostic crossover more likely hides real genetic differences than creates false ones.
Although the combined scores carry real information about risk at the population level, the authors note they remain weak predictors for individuals: in the European data, anorexia scores accounted for about 2.3 percent of the variation in risk and binge-eating scores only about 0.3 percent. They still cannot tell whether a particular person will develop an eating disorder without looking at other risk factors. The authors hope to conduct even larger studies incorporating multiple eating disorder diagnoses and global ancestries to build a more complete biological map.
“It is also important that people understand that this is very much work in progress,” Coleman said. “We don’t fully understand the genetics of either anorexia nervosa or binge eating, and we are still a long way off being able to use genetics to help treat these conditions.”
“But our understanding is sufficient to say that, while genetics plays a role in these conditions, neither is genetically determined, and supportive treatment and supportive social environments can help both,” he concluded.
The study, “Genomic meta-analyses of binge-eating behavior and anorexia nervosa yield insights into the unique and shared biology of eating disorder phenotypes,” was authored by Jet D. Termorshuizen, Helena L. Davies, Sang-Hyuck Lee, Jessica K. Dennis, Christopher Hübel, Jessica S. Johnson, Yi Lu, Melissa A. Munn-Chernoff, Triinu Peters, Baiyu Qi, Katherine E. Schaumberg, Rebecca H. Signer, Karanvir Singh, Abigail R. ter Kuile, Laura M. Thornton, Jiayi Xu, Shuyang Yao, Zeynep Yilmaz, Ruyue Zhang, Johan Zvrskovec, Mohamed Abdulkadir, Ziada Ayorech, Elizabeth C. Corfield, Alexandra Havdahl, Kristi Krebs, Taralynn M. Mack, Maria Niarchou, Teemu Palviainen, Julia M. Sealock, Jessica H. Baker, Andrew W. Bergen, Andreas Birgegård, Vesna Boraska Perica, Katharina Bühren, Roland Burghardt, Matteo Cassina, Giovanni Castellini, Enrico Collantoni, James J. Crowley, Unna N. Encryption Is Getting Squeezed From All Sides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
Oh, Canada. The Great White North is the latest country to contemplate legislation that could essentially mandate backdoors and increase data retention in encrypted services. The proposed changes have prompted the Canadian anti-censorship company Psiphon VPN—which keeps millions of Iranians online during repressive internet shutdowns—to say it will leave the country if the bill passes. And Psiphon is not the only one.
Encrypted messaging app Signal has said it would exit the Canadian market because the legislation would require unacceptable changes to its open source projects. Apple and Meta have criticized the bill, and DuckDuckGo and NordVPN say they would consider pulling their services, too. But as countries around the world contemplate similar legislation, even larger questions begin to emerge about which states or regions could differentiate themselves as being safe havens for privacy services if global hostility to encryption continues to rise.
It’s been maddening and disturbing to see more and more democratic countries around the world propose changes to their surveillance and data collection laws, with the aim of giving cops and intelligence agencies greater powers to access people’s information. Governments already have broad digital surveillance powers and investigative tactics to solve crimes that involve encrypted data, but legislative proposals almost inevitably include provisions to expand this access even more—mandating additional logging and what amounts to backdoors or intentional flaws in encrypted products, which cryptographers and security engineers have consistently said cannot be built safely. Truly everyone who understands the issue has said it as much for decades. Yet policymakers return again and again to the idea, somehow expecting a different conclusion or a new breakthrough that will make it all possible.
“There have always been some officials within certain agencies that tend to view technology as a crime scene in and of itself, and it becomes a myopic point of fixation where access is desired,” says Kate Robertson, a senior research associate at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab. “But that type of siloed thinking forgets that technology needs to be the secure operating platform for hospitals, for banks, for national security agencies, for police services themselves to protect victims who report private information to them.”
In recent years, the UK and Australia have introduced sweeping surveillance reforms that can compel companies to break their encryption. Other encryption-threatening proposals have also emerged in the EU, France, India, Ireland, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and others. While not all measures have passed into law or been enacted, the hostility is clear.
First proposed in 2025, and partially revised due to blistering criticism from tech companies and civil society, Canada’s C-22 bill can broadly place requirements on tech companies, including those outside of Canada, to introduce “technical capabilities” that allow data to be accessed for law enforcement purposes. Like many such bills, C-22 says that companies will not have to introduce a “systemic vulnerability” into their systems. But opponents have pointed out that any capability to access end-to-end encrypted data amounts to a backdoor that could be discovered and abused by anyone. And this risk is only heightened even more by the ease with which anyone can now use AI tools for reverse engineering and system mapping.
“Companies could be asked to introduce vulnerabilities, build backdoors, bypass, weaken or otherwise defeat encryption,” members of the US House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committee said in a May letter to Canadian officials.
In addition to potential impacts on encryption, C-22 also includes provisions that could require companies to retain metadata about user activity, something that many privacy focused services (including VPN services from Psiphon and DuckDuckGo) intentionally avoid. As a result, these companies say, they would be forced to change their business models to collect data they do not need or want to collect about their users. And researchers say that such product changes would diminish user trust while increasing the potential for widespread surveillance.
“If you are asking and requiring for this infrastructural change—that they retain metadata by default—it is creating a surveillance capability within a tool that didn’t have it,” says Afsaneh Rigot, the founder of the De|Center, a research organization that aims to reduce the risk of technological harms. “There are contexts like Iran and other contexts globally, who all of this has a trickle effect on. It's not going to stay in Canada because these types of laws always get copy pasted around the world.”
As more countries contemplate such laws, developers focused on privacy and anti-censorship tools are increasingly casting around for safe jurisdictions to operate in. But this still doesn’t solve the problem of reaching users in all countries around the world and for now, there are no sure bets.
“Changing your headquarters isn’t much of a plan B when the law follows your users, as C-22 would,” says Joseph Lorenzo-Hall, security portfolio lead at the Internet Society. “The strongest protection is holding as little user data as possible, but ‘we don’t have it’ is no defense if governments can force you to start collecting it. A safe haven needs more than favorable winds in strong encryption. It needs laws that let companies keep their privacy promises and defend them against foreign threats to confidentiality and integrity.”
Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

Flour sacks turned flood barriers: Gaza faces another winter without safe shelter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Flour sacks turned flood barriers: Gaza faces another winter without safe shelter
Like many people in the war-ravaged Gaza Strip, Ahmed Al-Omari is preparing for another winter of bitter cold and rain that threatens to cause flooding as families struggle to survive in tattered tents and damaged buildings.
He is racing against time, working with other young men to fill sacks that once held World Food Programme (WFP) flour with sand to protect their makeshift shelters from the rain.
“These are flour sacks that we used to retrieve from the jaws of death, so that we could eat,” he told UN News, referring to the dangers of aid distribution in the Gaza Strip, where civilians have been killed while trying to obtain assistance.
“Now, they have become sacks that we fill with sand to act as barriers against rainwater,” he explained. “We flood every year and we have put these sacks in place in the hope that, somehow, rainwater will not get inside.”
Two million need better shelter
Around two million people in Gaza still need shelter assistance, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). Rain has already begun and an intensifying El Niño threatens more in the coming months.
Right now, agencies were working to get as much shelter material into the Strip as possible before winter, Karl Baker, IOM’s regional crisis coordinator for Gaza, said from Amman, Jordan.
“We know that the rains have already begun and that the volume of goods that we have to get into Gaza is not going to meet the demands of the population,” he said.
Funding shortages that began to decline in January have hampered preparations, Mr. Baker said.
“The funding has come a little later in the year. It is now arriving, but it’s not at the scale needed to support what we estimate is 1.8 to 1.9 million people needing some sort of shelter assistance,” he said.
Shipping routes disrupted
The continuing regional conflict is also disrupting supply chains. IOM relies on suppliers in countries including China, India and Pakistan, with goods routed through Jordan, Egypt and Israel before reaching Gaza.
“The other point, of course, is that the regional conflict seems to be only growing. That disrupts trade routes,” Mr. Baker said.
As long as the global shipping is disrupted, it will delay the volume or the timing for goods to reach Gaza, he added.
Tents that last six months
Quality is another concern. In other emergencies, Mr. Baker said, IOM could provide more durable transitional shelter, such as plywood and relief housing units.
In Gaza, tents typically last only about six months. With people constantly displaced, they are often destroyed or left behind when families flee at short notice.
“Constantly moving a tent or a temporary structure has caused, I would say, a lack of quality for what is currently inside of Gaza,” he said. “The quality needs to be enhanced with either more durable items or more goods, which currently help with temporary solutions.”
An impossible choice
More than 4,000 buildings, many of them home to thousands of residents, are reportedly at risk of collapse.
Briefing the UN Security Council, Ramiz Alakbarov, acting Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, said the UN was working with local communities to evacuate people from unsafe buildings. With no alternatives, many had little choice but to seek shelter in tents.
Recalling a recent visit to Gaza, he described the impossible decisions facing families: leave the homes they had returned to or stay in buildings at risk of collapse.
Living space is also shrinking. Only around 30 per cent of Gaza is now accessible to most people, IOM’s Mr. Baker said.
Conditions in displacement sites continue to deteriorate, humanitarian assessments show, with many exposed to flooding and few alternative places to go.
‘New experiment’
In Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, families are salvaging materials from the rubble. Displaced from Rafah, Mohammed Barhoum and his sons are using metal rods recovered from the wreckage to try to strengthen their shelter.
It is risky work amid unstable debris and explosive remnants of war.
“Every year during the winter, this area floods because of heavy rainfall,” Mr. Barhoum said. “This year, we decided to reinforce our tents using metal rods. It is a new experiment, and we will see how it goes. We hope the situation will be better than it was last time.”
Durable materials blocked
Most of the durable shelter materials IOM would normally use in emergencies fall under Israel’s dual-use restrictions, which date back to 2008.
They include roofing sheets, cement for floors and stronger walls to withstand the wind – items that could make shelters more resistant to winter, but are often deemed a security concern.
Mr. Baker said IOM was in repeated contact with the Israeli authorities to negotiate their entry.
“It is an everyday occurrence, five times per day, as we try to negotiate or we try to make sure that we have actually either understood what their concern is and trying to adjust whatever that might be,” he said.
“From our perspective, we must continue to advocate for more durable items to get in.”

IMF Warns Global Resilience at Risk as Fuel Reserves Dwindle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:59:00 UTC
20:59:00 KST

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned that the global economy risks rapidly exhausting its resilience as emergency fuel reserves dwindle and public debt burdens climb to record highs, according to the Fund’s updated World Economic Outlook (WEO) report.
While the IMF raised its 2026 global gross domestic product (GDP) growth projection slightly to 3.1 percent – up from 3.0 percent in its July update – analysts citing the report noted that risks to the macroeconomic baseline remain heavily tilted to the downside.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The forecast for global growth in 2027 was held unchanged at 3.4 percent.
The Fund identified a sequence of major macroeconomic shocks testing international economic durability over recent years, specifically citing Russia’s war against Ukraine, expanding armed conflict across the Middle East, the lingering aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, and recurrent commodity price volatility.
“The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience has limits,” IMF Chief Economist Silvana Tenreyro stated. “Without building supply capacity and replenishing buffers, the world could quickly reach the edge of its resilience.”
Depleted strategic fuel buffers
A central vulnerability highlighted in the WEO report is the exhaustion of sovereign emergency reserves that previously cushioned international markets from systemic supply shocks.
The coordinated release of strategic petroleum reserves by Western governments in the spring helped mitigate immediate price spikes triggered by the military conflict between the US and Iran. However, those emergency interventions have substantially reduced national stockpiles, leaving sovereign buffers depleted.
Russian Strikes Destroy Epicentr K’s Last Major Logistics Hub
Notably, the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) has declined to its lowest operating inventory level since 1982, limiting the capacity of policymakers to counteract future supply disruptions through reserve drawdowns.
The contraction of physical energy buffers coincides with rising fiscal vulnerabilities. With global sovereign debt levels approaching historical peaks, governments face constrained fiscal space to subsidize energy consumption or mount large-scale budgetary interventions without compounding inflationary pressures or sovereign borrowing costs.
European exposure
The IMF’s broader global assessment builds on regional projections released earlier in the week, which underscored the acute exposure of import-dependent economies to sustained energy market volatility.
According to the Fund’s regional modeling, economic growth in the eurozone is projected to slow to 1.1 percent in 2026 before edging up to 1.2 percent in 2027.
Persistent energy costs and underlying inflation—forecast at 3.1 percent this year and 2.8 percent in 2027 – continue to exceed the European Central Bank’s 2 percent target, with core inflation not anticipated to return to baseline until mid-2028.
Disparities across major European economies remain pronounced. While Germany is projected to expand by 1.3 percent in 2026 and Spain by 2.5 percent, France faces subdued growth of just 0.4 percent alongside rising unemployment, projected to reach 8.4 percent.
For the UK, the IMF revised its 2026 growth estimate up to 1.3 percent, though expansion is forecast to ease to 1.2 percent in 2027 as elevated borrowing costs and energy import bills constrain private domestic investment.
IMF officials emphasized that replenishing critical strategic reserves, stabilizing public debt trajectories, and expanding supply-side infrastructure remain imperative for governments to withstand prospective geopolitical and commodity shocks ahead of the winter season.

Zelensky: Starlink Capped at 161 km/h, Disabling Interceptors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:59:00 KST

A hard speed limitation of 161 km/h (100 mph) imposed on Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine has disabled domestic interceptor drones deployed against Russian jet-powered Shahed loitering munitions, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced.
Speaking with journalists, Zelensky disclosed that satellite terminals automatically disconnect whenever equipped platforms exceed the 161 km/h threshold, causing defenders to lose control of unmanned interceptors in mid-flight.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Today our interceptors are not working because there is a speed limit,” Zelensky stated. “The maximum speed today is 161 km/h; after exceeding it, Starlink shuts down and we lose the drone.”
The Ukrainian leader stressed that Starlink remains vital for military and civilian communications across the country, highlighting its role in guiding robotic and unmanned supply runs that deliver food and potable water to frontline infantry holding isolated positions inaccessible to conventional wheeled vehicles.
However, the operational impact on airspace defense has proven severe, rendering domestic interceptors unable to engage Russian turbine-propelled loitering munitions that cruise at several hundred kilometers per hour.
Cross-border testing confirms geographical restriction
Zelensky revealed that Ukrainian technical specialists conducted comparative trials to determine whether the velocity thresholds stemmed from global technical adjustments or deliberate geographical parameters.
Drone Attack Paralyzes Moscow Airports Again
To test the system, Ukrainian authorities dispatched vehicles equipped with Starlink terminals into EU territory, operating them at speeds of 180 km/h (112 mph). During the tests, the satellite links functioned normally without disconnections.
“The conclusion is as follows: the restrictions operate on the territory of Ukraine and do not operate on the territory of EU countries,” Zelensky emphasized. “That is, this is a planned operation.”
The president noted that while technical representatives across various channels describe the disconnections as engineering malfunctions, the issue remains strictly confined to Ukrainian airspace.
“At various levels they say these are technical problems,” Zelensky added. “But these technical problems exist in Ukraine; on the territory of the EU they do not exist.”
Blocked communications
Zelensky stated that Ukrainian military commanders, the Ministry of Defense, and foreign diplomats are conducting active negotiations to resolve the constraints. However, he noted that management at SpaceX has declined direct dialogue with Ukrainian military representatives.
Kyiv continues to await formal clarifications from both the Pentagon and SpaceX regarding the timeline for the restoration of unrestricted functionality across the military-grade Starshield variant, with data transfer rates remaining volatile.
The revelations follow statements delivered earlier on Saturday by US President Donald Trump, who denied involvement in service curbs, asserting that neither he nor SpaceX founder Elon Musk ordered operational limits. Trump claimed to reporters that “everything is the same as it’s always been.”
Trump’s statements contradict reporting published by The Telegraph, which cited four sources familiar with the matter stating that Musk proposed service caps directly to Trump, who approved the initiative, clearing the way for the Pentagon to restrict Starshield capabilities.
Sources indicated that Musk sought to deflect responsibility onto the White House amid concerns over consumer backlash across European markets following civilian casualties in Kyiv.
Ukrainian officials have underscored that restricting satellite connectivity compromises baseline defensive capabilities, preventing mobile air defense teams and unmanned aviation units from shielding urban settlements and municipal power infrastructure ahead of the winter heating season.

Estonia's Eneli Jefimova sweeps skins event, snags MVP at college swim meet

Estonia's Eneli Jefimova sweeps skins event, snags MVP at college swim meet
Estonian swim star Eneli Jefimova swept the breaststroke skins event at California college meet Friday, snagging MVP honors, a personal best and a win for alma mater NC State.
Jefimova clocked 2:06.19 in the 200-yard breaststroke at the College Swimming League (CSL) meet in Walnut, California, pulling away in the second half to beat Stanford University's Addie Robillard by 2.12 seconds — and shave 0.14 seconds off her previous personal best from February.
Robillard finished in 2:08.31, with teammate Lucy Thomas third in 2:09.67.
NC State's relay win gave the team the right to choose the stroke for the women's knockout skins competition, in which eight swimmers start and the two slowest are eliminated after each round until two remain.
The team picked breaststroke, and Jefimova won every 50-yard round despite having less than two minutes to complete all four, leaving little time to recover.
Jefimova swam the first three rounds in 26.71, 26.89 and 26.68 seconds before clocking her fastest time of 26.65 in the final. Italy's Anita Bottazzo, swimming for Indiana University, finished 0.42 seconds behind.
About 15 minutes later, the Estonian also took second in the 100-yard breaststroke, finishing 0.49 seconds behind Bottazzo with 58.74.
Another 15 minutes on, she helped NC State reach the final of the 4x50-yard medley relay skins event, where the team narrowly lost to Indiana, 1:36.95 to 1:36.18.
'It was so hard, I teared up'
"That was an insane meet!" acknowledged Jefimova, a two-time Olympian and four-time European champion. "I even teared up during the last 50 yards of the relay because it was so hard."
She was pleased with her new 200-yard personal best, saying it showed her endurance was improving. "I showed good speed in the skins," Jefimova said. "And the 100 breastroke? That was just hard!"
North Carolina State University (NC State) won the meet with 544.83 points, well ahead of Indiana's 469.83. Fellow Estonian swimmer Egle Salu's University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) team placed third with 394.33, followed by Stanford with 311.
The season's main event for both Estonians is the short-course world championships in Beijing on December 1–6. Jefimova won bronze in the 100-meter breaststroke at the previous championships.

UAE agrees with Saudi Arabia to re-enter Yemen conflict amid Houthi gains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:57:15 UTC
20:57:15 KST

The United Arab Emirates has agreed to re-enter the Yemen conflict by resuming payments to some government forces fighting Iran-aligned Houthis in the south, according to sources in Yemen. In return, Saudi Arabia has agreed to provide air cover for the anti-Houthi force.
The new cooperation agreement is the first tangible sign that the deep rift between the UAE and Saudi Arabia over Yemen’s future is starting to be healed – if only because the advance by Houthi forces across Yemen has alarmed all the rival Gulf state rulers.
Saudi Arabia is facing daily drone and missile attacks and is struggling to maintain an atmosphere of normality, as Houthi strikes immobilise its airports and some of its energy infrastructure.
Southern forces – mainly in the Giant Brigades – were previously trained and funded by the UAE, and are regarded as some of the most effective in the disjointed anti-Houthi military coalition. But the UAE quit operations inside Yemen in January, cutting off its funding supply line.
Neither Saudi Arabia nor the UAE have responded to a demand this week by southern Yemen separatists for a referendum on secession, a move that would restore the 1967-1990 borders, when Yemen was two separate states.
The separatist Southern Transition Council has also not yet agreed for its troops to fight outside the borders of the old Southern Yemen, but an explicit agreement by Saudi Arabia to allow a referendum would be likely to lead to the lifting of that restriction.
Yemen’s UN-recognised government, based in Aden, declared last week a counteroffensive to drive Houthi forces from the capital Sana’a, but so far the military drive has met with limited success around Majzar near Marib and the Bab al-Mandab strait.
There is also no direct contact between the STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, and Saudi officials. Zubaidi fled to Abu Dhabi in January after a failed STC attempt to take charge across the south and announce a referendum on separation in two years’ time. In response, the Saudis bombed UAE arms shipments for STC forces.
The UAE then announced it was quitting all involvement in Yemen, and the Saudi-backed government said it would seek to try Zubaidi for treason.
UAE officials are deeply concerned by the state of the conflict. Despite massive losses, the Houthis are determined eventually to capture Taiz and Marib, the two remaining cities outside the boundaries of the old Southern Yemen.
On Friday two missiles fired by the Houthis struck the airport of Aden while a passenger plane was preparing to take off. No casualties were reported.
The missiles landed about 500 metres from the Yemenia Airways aircraft, and approximately 100 metres from the midpoint of the runway, said Yemen’s information minister, Moammar Al-Eryani.
The strike came a day after at least five people were killed and 16 injured in a Houthi attack on a presidential palace in Aden.
Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said he was convening an emergency session of parliament to grant his country’s military the powers to take action in defence of Saudi Arabia. He stressed Egypt would not be taking any offensive action, and would only defend Saudi Arabia.
In the UK, discussions are continuing about a Saudi request for further military aid. The UK has sent an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft, but regional diplomats are pressing for the UK to do more. Some concern is being expressed over whether Riyadh should be engaging more closely with other Gulf States, including Oman and Qatar, on the issue.
The legal implications of a blanket UK backing for the largely Saudi air campaign is also being considered, since the court of appeal in 2019 found the UK had acted unlawfully in issuing arms export licences during a previous Saudi bombing campaign of Yemen in 2015-16. The Campaign Against Arms Trade said the UK had made no proper assessment of potential Saudi breaches of international humanitarian law, forcing the UK to revise its procedures.
Saudi Arabia claims to have revised its methods substantially since then, and certainly argues that it is acting in self-defence in line with the UN charter. The UN security council on 15 October adopted a UN presidential statement on 15 October asserting Saudi Arabia’s right to act in self-defence in line with international law.
No accurate death toll in the war since August is available, but more than 200,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN, which is placing increasing pressure on Aden-based humanitarian groups.

The president did not rule out that this meeting could also take place in one of the European countries. "I know that the Europeans are beginning to reach out regarding this. We'll see the outcome a little later," Zelenskyy added.

IRCS, ICRC hold workshops to strengthen readiness for CBRN incidents
TEHRAN – The Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) and the International Red Cross and Red Crescent (ICRC) have held the second and third training courses on Application of Personal Protective Equipment during Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) incidents.
The first round of the course was held in Tehran from June 7 to 21. The second and third courses were held from October 4-8 and 11-15, separately. The courses aimed to improve preparedness and the operational capacity of relief teams and has been attended by a total number of 150 members of rapid response teams from different provinces in the country, ICRC website announced in a press release on October 15.
During the closing ceremony, the attendees and instructors reviewed achievements, strengths, and ground for improvement. Stressing the need to repeat the exercises, organize the course in provincial levels, and to provide complementary equipment required, the attendees emphasized that the experience was different from previous maneuvers.
The instructors also expressed gratitude for the participants’ active involvement, reiterating their positive performance during practical simulation exercises in applying the learning points and following the decontamination process suited to each type of contamination.
Speaking on the sidelines of the ceremony, the head of ICRC’s Tehran Delegation, Marisela Silva Chau, highlighted the close collaboration between ICRC and the Iranian Red Crescent Society, citing the workshop a concrete example, putting together IRCS’ operational experience and ICRC’s academic expertise and technical, equipment support. She reiterated the ICRC’s readiness to throw support behind similar courses to be held at a provincial level, while stressing the importance of transferring learnings to operational teams and their application in daily activities.
The IRCS Deputy Director for Education, Research and Technology, Rouzbeh Rajaei, also stressed continued training, teacher training, and planning for similar course to be held for female participants, noting the participation of experts from different scientific institutions and centers.
 
The continued collaboration and transfer of knowledge and experience to operational teams is an important step in strengthening the incident preparedness and response capacity.
The first training course targeted basic health care unit (BHCU) team leaders from five high-risk provinces, namely Tehran, Qom, Markazi, Isfahan, and Bushehr, as well as passive defense trainers.
ICRC hails IRCS efforts, bravery during war
In April, the president of the ICRC, Mirjana Spoljaric Egger, commended the efforts, bravery, and accomplishments of the IRCS during the recent imposed war by the United States and the Zionist regime of Israel on Iran.

Highlighting the importance of respecting international humanitarian law (IHL), the official noted that the IHL is frequently violated in the region; the war impacts on civilians, particularly children, are unacceptable. There is no justified reason for depriving children of their rights.
The measures that lead to the breach of IHL, and the attacks that target civilians and humanitarian workers, have to be stopped and reversed, she added.
The official described the current situation as dangerous, saying that “We, and the Iranian Red Crescent Society’s staff, should use our capacity to reduce tensions, which is essential for the protection of civilians and children.
That is why we are here, staying here; we fulfil our responsibility inside and outside the country to change the situation, and offer assistance in any way that is possible.”
The IRCS is a leading, strong national society, equipped with good facilities. The ICRC representative in Iran will help meet the country’s medical needs to set up hospitals and facilitate the import of supplies that are not allowed under sanctions, she further noted.
The official went on to thank the head of the IRCS for his continuous follow-up on the issues and for providing the ICRC with information and reports.
Vincent Cassard, the representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), has highlighted the need to expand collaborations with the Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) in 2026.

Nationwide protests in France against high prices and fraying of social security system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:50:48 UTC
20:50:48 KST

More than 400 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protesters supporting high school student grievances clashed with police.
Police fired teargas in confrontations with protesters, as demonstrations across France were boosted by other groups angry over high prices and the fraying of a social welfare system.
Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets across the country, and tensions erupted on the fringes of the nationwide demonstrations over absent teachers, decrepit school buildings and police violence.
Late on Saturday, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said there had been 400 arrests and most were adults who were not part of the high school protests.
He said the official demonstration had been hijacked by casseurs – “opportunistic delinquents who had seen a chance to pillage and loot … we will find them and deal with them firmly”.
He said the state was not planning to declare a state of emergency but added: “I very strongly condemn the violence we have seen.”
In Marseille, protesters stormed the town hall, ramming the door with security barriers they removed from the street. They briefly managed to enter the municipal building, where a protester spray-painted an “A” for anarchy on a wall before the police removed them.
Around Place de la République in central Paris, a peaceful march turned violent, with police firing teargas at black-clad and masked rioters who threw fireworks and paving stones, attacked a bank and looted a sports shop.
 
“We’re taking the Bastille!” one demonstrator yelled.
Others set wheelie bins on fire and threw firecrackers inside or pushed over glass recycling bins and picked up the bottles inside to use as missiles. A lorry was set on fire and flames spread to a nearby building.
Along Boulevard Magenta, one of the main south-north axis north of Place de la République running through a mostly working-class area, dozens of shops were broken into and looted.
Residents in surrounding streets were forced to close windows and doors as huge clouds of teargas rose to roof level.
French authorities detained dozens of protesters across the country, with more arrests expected.
Saturday’s mobilisation followed calls on social media to revive the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) movement, which emerged in 2018 against social injustice.
The protests began last month at schools in the poor northern suburbs of Paris, where anger over teacher absences and shabby facilities quickly morphed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.
Saturday’s protests called for teachers and students, labourers, pensioners and farmers to join the protests and widen the movement.
French authorities said 140 protests involving 32,800 people had been recorded outside Paris by midday, blaming the unrest and violence on what they said was the “ultra-left”.
The CGT, one of France’s biggest labour unions, has also backed the protests, calling for “higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people’s needs”.
About 45% of French people are worried about the rising cost of living and inflation, according to a 2,000-person survey conducted in October.
Protesters in hi-vis vests blocked streets, an echo of the unrest that dogged President Emmanuel Macron’s previous term, and in Marseille rubbish bins were set alight.
Both the far left and far right in France sought to capitalise on the protest movement, with the left positioning itself on the side of the protesters and the right backing the police.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, marched in a demonstration on Tuesday and has expressed support for student protesters.
A large police presence was visible in central Paris, especially near landmarks such as the Avenue des Champs-Élysées and the Arc de Triomphe, which were excluded from the routes of the two official demonstrations.
About 100 people walked towards the police at the beginning protest yelling, “all cops are bastards!”.
“We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions,” said a 19-year-old protester in Paris who gave her name as Lola.
Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, leaving behind a polarised electorate and a badly fragmented political landscape.
On Friday, the president appealed for calm and respect for people and property as officials warned of possible violence.
“There is a constitutional right to protest and to express oneself, and I have always been vigilant and attentive that that right is fully respected,” he said. “But this right comes with the need to respect. Respect for people, respect for property, and therefore a commitment not to insult or destroy.”
Macron denounced as “unacceptable” the potential presence of people “solely to cause damage and create unrest”.
Nuñez said hundreds of protest actions and more than 80 marches were expected nationwide, including spontaneous gatherings, street demonstrations and blockades.
Police banned some other proposed gatherings in central Paris. Many Métro stations were closed on Saturday at the police’s request, including those around the Champs-Élysées and near the presidential palace, parliament and government offices.
In recent weeks, there have been thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries, and schools set on fire as the new school year descended into nationwide student protests that are influencing the country’s presidential election campaign and drawing international attention.
The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence, while the French prime minister said that more than 900 police officers had been injured.
Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons. Nuñez suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against the young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand, but said that they could be used on Saturday.
On Tuesday, the climate and social justice activist Greta Thunberg joined students at a school in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.
Agencies contributed reporting

Iran puts forward six proposals to boost SCO anti-drug cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
