Iran puts forward six proposals to boost SCO anti-drug cooperation
TEHRAN – Iran’s Drug Control Headquarters (DCHQ) has put forward six proposals to strengthen cooperation among Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) member states in combating illicit drugs and related crimes.
Mohammad Narimani, an official with the DCHQ, presented the proposals at the opening ceremony of the SCO International Conference of Member States, titled “For a Drug-Free World,” held on October 13–14 in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
The event was attended by representatives of the competent authorities of the SCO member states, the SCO Secretariat, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), the Central Asian Regional Information and Coordination Centre (CARICC) and other regional organizations, as well as government bodies, higher education institutions and civil society of the Kyrgyz Republic.
Iran’s six proposals included strengthening the regional early warning system on synthetic drugs and new psychoactive substances, promoting cooperation in countering chemical precursors used in illicit manufacturing of narcotic drugs, establishing a SCO specialized network in prevention, treatment, harm reduction, and rehabilitation fields, developing joint capacity-building and educational programs, fostering operational and intelligence collaboration in countering transnational drug trafficking networks, and protecting health and humanitarian services, ISNA reported.
Highlighting the need for strengthening regional and international collaborations to fight against illegal drugs, the official said, “Today, the issue of drugs has transcended beyond the law enforcement sector, as it is directly connected to public health, youths, families, sustainable development, organized financial crime, and the rule of law,” Narimani said.
International drug traffickers' use of online platforms, emerging technologies, artificial intelligence, and digital financial tools has worsened the situation. Hence, it is essential to adopt up-to-date, more coordinated, and forward-looking approaches at national, regional, and international levels to fight drug trafficking, he added.
Elaborating on the country’s achievements in addressing illicit drugs, the official voiced Iran’s readiness for the enhancement of ties with SCO member states through sharing expertise, as well as scientific and operational experiences.
The SCO International Anti-Drug Campaign “For a Drug-Free World” has been held since 2017. Its main goal is to foster in young people an intolerant attitude towards drug use and a commitment to a healthy lifestyle, as well as to establish contacts and exchange views between experts and representatives of the academic community in order to further deepen practical cooperation in countering illicit drug trafficking.
This year, during the two-day conference, participants discussed countering transnational drug trafficking, the spread of synthetic drugs and new psychoactive substances, the use of digital technologies in drug-related crime, as well as modern approaches to drug use prevention, treatment and rehabilitation of persons with drug dependence.
Following the event, the participants adopted recommendations aimed at strengthening interaction among the competent authorities of the SCO member states, improving the exchange of operational information, developing early warning mechanisms for new drug threats, conducting joint anti-drug activities and enhancing the effectiveness of preventive work.
Supporting Iran’s counter-narcotics work pays off beyond its borders: UNODC
In August, the UNODC released a report, emphasizing the need to support Iran in the battle against narcotics.
Supporting Iran’s counternarcotics work pays off beyond its borders, the report highlighted, saying it keeps drugs from reaching other regions, cuts into the money that funds organized crime, and supports public health by slowing the spread of addictive synthetic substances.
The main seizure of methamphetamine in and around the Middle East and South-East Asia over the past few years has been reported in Iran, according to the report, which was published on Thursday.
Iranian seizures of methamphetamine increased from 30,393 kilos in 2022 to 40,453 kilos in 2025, placing the country at the forefront of the fight against drug trafficking.
In the first quarter of 2026 alone, Iranian authorities have intercepted 3,663 kilograms of methamphetamine destined for Europe and the Persian Gulf.
These weren’t just street-level busts. These were five intelligence-led operations targeting industrial-scale shipments originating in Afghanistan, evidence that trafficking networks in the region are shifting toward synthetic drugs.
While international attention has primarily focused on the vast region’s declining opium production, advanced criminal drug trafficking networks have successfully shifted toward manufacturing and exporting synthetic drugs such as methamphetamine, commonly known as meth. West Asia is now the epicenter of a synthetic drug boom.
Iran is strategically positioned along the “Afghanistan-West Asia corridor,” which serves as the primary trafficking route for these illicit commodities. The clear signal from Tehran is that these substantial shipments are being intercepted before they can reach international markets. Yet, sustained success will require enhanced international cooperation and support.
Each interception reduces the illicit financial flows that fund organized crime and slows the spread of synthetic drugs into new markets. These shipments are not merely statistics. Each seizure disrupts a supply chain that would otherwise put methamphetamine on the streets of Europe and the Persian Gulf, while cutting into the earnings of organized criminal networks.
Through its Country Partnership Programme as well as the Cooperation Framework with the Islamic Republic of Iran, UNODC supports the country's efforts in advancing border technology with procurement of detection scanners, strengthening labs' forensic capabilities to identify new synthetic compounds, as well as regional intelligence sharing.
Sustained donor investment is critical to prevent this route from becoming a gateway for synthetic drugs. However, the scale of the challenge demands more than financial contributions—it requires a collective and sustainable approach by the international community. By supporting UNODC’s work in Iran, donor nations are investing in regional stability and international security, while also protecting their own borders from the flow of illicit substances.
Police seize over 250 tons of narcotics since March
The Iranian anti-narcotics police have seized more than 250 tons of narcotics in the first six months of the current Iranian year (started on March 21), indicating a 20 percent increase compared to the same period last year.
The anti-narcotics police have disbanded 780 drug trafficking gangs across the country, IRNA quoted Iraj Kakavand, the head of anti-narcotics police, as saying.
The official made the remarks at a press conference in Tehran on the occasion of the ‘national law enforcement week’, which is being held from October 2 to 8, under the theme ‘committed police, mobilized people, proud Iran’.
Over 7,000 smugglers were arrested, and six were killed; more than 330 weapons and 8,000 vehicles were confiscated, he added.
Monitoring social media, the police managed to arrest 196 individuals, seize over 460 kilograms of narcotics, more than 420,000 pills containing illicit drugs, and dismantle 14 gangs operating online, Kakavand further noted.

Biodiversity, peace and security are interconnected, DOE chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:47:46 UTC
20:47:46 KST

Biodiversity, peace and security are interconnected, DOE chief says
TEHRAN - Environmental diplomacy can become an instrument of peace diplomacy, while the relationship between biodiversity, peace, and security should be viewed as a two-way relationship, Shina Ansari, the head of the Department of Environment, has said.
Speaking on Friday at a specialized panel titled “Biodiversity and Peace: Protecting the Environment During Armed Conflicts” at the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, Ansari said the link between biodiversity and peace was not merely an ethical or political issue, but a fundamental concern in environmental governance, international law, and human security.
Under the Convention on Biological Diversity, she said, the main drivers of biodiversity loss are generally understood to include land-use change, habitat destruction, pollution, unsustainable exploitation of natural resources, and climate change.
“However, there is another factor that deserves far greater attention in this equation: the breakdown of peace and the outbreak of armed conflicts,” she said.
War can trigger several drivers of biodiversity loss simultaneously and with devastating intensity. Its consequences range from the direct destruction of habitats and widespread fires to soil and water contamination, the release of hazardous substances, human displacement, disruption of protected-area management, and the weakening of national capacities to monitor and protect nature.
Ansari said Iran was speaking about these realities not merely in theoretical terms, but on the basis of direct experience, having witnessed the consequences of such circumstances in recent years.
During the 12-day war in 2025, several protected areas in Iran were also affected by attacks and the consequences of the fighting. According to assessments, 13 protected areas and thousands of hectares of natural land, particularly across the Zagros Mountains, sustained damage and were affected by fires.
However, the actual scale of the damage goes far beyond the number of hectares burned or destroyed, she said.
The environmental vulnerability of the Persian Gulf was again exposed during what Ansari described as the recent war of aggression by the United States and Israel against Iran. Damage to oil and gas facilities, fires, and pollutant emissions raised concerns about the risks of pollution to the region’s ecosystems.
The Persian Gulf is a semi-enclosed, shallow, and highly environmentally sensitive body of water. Its coral reefs, mangrove forests, coastal habitats, and rich marine biodiversity are of considerable ecological value. These ecosystems are also directly linked to food security and the livelihoods of millions of people across the region.
Under such circumstances, no pollution incident can be regarded as merely a local problem, Ansari said. Pollutants can travel through marine currents, enter the food chain, and affect habitats far from the original source of contamination.
From this perspective, she said, condemning acts of aggression and holding those responsible accountable should extend beyond the traditional dimensions of international peace and security.
Assessments of the consequences of armed conflicts must therefore adopt an approach that examines environmental damage independently, scientifically, and over the long term. Such assessments should go beyond physical destruction to cover biodiversity loss, habitat degradation, damage to ecosystem services, soil and water pollution, and harm to genetic resources.
The international community must establish more effective mechanisms for monitoring, documenting, assessing, and compensating for environmental damage caused by armed conflicts, she added.
Countries across West Asia and Southwest Asia face mounting environmental pressures, including climate change, water scarcity, desertification, dwindling natural resources, and growing stress on ecosystems, while continuing to grapple with persistent security crises.
In these circumstances, war can intensify environmental crises and increase the vulnerability of both communities and ecosystems.
“The relationship between biodiversity, peace, and security should therefore be understood as a two-way relationship,” Ansari said. “Peace is essential for nature, while effective and responsible nature conservation can, in turn, contribute to strengthening peace.”
Cooperation on shared rivers, wetlands, seas, migratory species, and genetic resources can create valuable opportunities for dialogue, confidence-building, and closer collaboration among countries.
“I believe that it is precisely at this point that environmental diplomacy can become an instrument of peace diplomacy,” she said.
“Peace is more than the absence of war; it is an essential condition for protecting life. And protecting biodiversity means protecting life itself.”

Exotic species appear off California thanks to an unusually strong El Nino
- An unusually strong El Nino has brought tropical sea life to California, including longfin bigeye fish, whale sharks, hammerheads, flying fish and a yellow-bellied sea snake.
- The event has also caused harm, with stronger waves, sea level rise and beach erosion, and California has declared a state of emergency ahead of more winter effects.
- Some businesses are benefiting, with more tuna, wahoo and dorado catches, while experts warn kelp and less mobile species may suffer until conditions return to normal in 2027.
AI generated
DANA POINT, California – The longfin bigeye fish was spotted in California for the first time in September, and the first sea turtles of any kind nested on California beaches. Meanwhile, a venomous yellow-bellied sea snake swam ashore as whale sharks and hammerheads cruised just off the coast.
Exotic species have been visiting California’s shores since an unusually strong El Nino weather phenomenon arrived in 2026. Occurring naturally every few years, El Nino brings warm ocean water farther north, and tropical species with it, providing California with a stunning visual display that has become ever more evident with the advent of drone and video technology.
“There’s kind of a buzz. Fishermen are loving it for sure. I’m as interested as anybody else. It’s strange times,” said Nate Jaros, vice-president of animal care at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach.
Other visitors include flying fish and manta rays.
California had already experienced an unusual marine heat wave just before its arrival.
The phenomenon in 2026 coincided with a string of hurricanes in the eastern Pacific, fuelling sea level rise and large waves that have destroyed homes and denuded some Southern California beaches of sand. Preparing for more effects to come this winter, California has declared a state of emergency.
But it has provided a bounty for businesses like Dana Wharf Sportfishing & Whale Watching. Co-owner Donna Kalez said anglers have pulled in 5,000 yellowfin tuna in 2026, compared to two a year ago. They are also landing wahoo and dorado, also known as mahi-mahi, a green fish with a blunt head giving it the profile of a bulldozer.
“Dorado is very exciting because they’re very acrobatic, so they jump out of the water. We catch them off kelp paddies, and it’s a thrill,” Kalez said.
Experts expect conditions to mostly return to normal after El Nino, a natural phenomenon predating human-caused climate change, passes in 2027. The greatest short-term harm may be to kelp, which thrives in colder waters and provides habitat for multiple species, experts say.
“It’s good for some sharks and probably bad for others,” said Chris Lowe, director of the Shark Lab at California State University, Long Beach. “For animals that can’t move, that’s a bigger problem, right? Most sharks that are highly mobile. They can simply move.”
The yellow-bellied sea snake may have venomous fangs but cannot swim like a large shark. When an apparently sick one swam ashore in Orange County in September, a beachgoer used a palm frond to lift it off the sand and drop it in the sea. Jaros said that based on cellphone video he had little doubt it was the yellow-bellied sea snake, Hydrophis platurus.
There have only been six or seven confirmed sightings in California, said William Ludt, associate curator of ichthyology at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County. The last confirmed sighting came during the El Nino of 2015-2016, he said.
Exotic sharks such as the whale shark – a gentle giant and the largest fish on Earth – and the more menacing-looking hammerheads venture into California waters during El Nino. Both have been spotted recently. Lowe said a white shark nursery reappeared for the first time since 2011 in Santa Monica Bay, where juveniles frolic without bothering humans.
Ludt said the aptly named longfin bigeye fish species was recorded for the first time in California in 2026 when an angler caught one on the Venice Fishing Pier in Los Angeles.
When two olive ridley sea turtle nests were found on a pair of Orange County beaches in September, they marked the first-ever recorded nest for any sea turtle species on the US West Coast, according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
The first was discovered by a beachgoer in Seal Beach on Sept 16, the second by lifeguards in neighbouring Huntington Beach three days later, officials said.
And other new species may yet arrive.
“We still aren’t fully through it,” Ludt said. “It’s still very much ongoing.” REUTERS

US President Donald Trump’s decision to suspend statutory sanctions and trade tariffs targeting Russia is a grave error that encourages Russian President Vladimir Putin to prolong the war, President Volodymyr Zelensky stated on Saturday, Oct. 17.
Speaking with journalists, Zelensky characterized the executive waiver of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 as part of an expanding pattern of economic concessions to Moscow that risks emboldening the Kremlin.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue,” Zelensky stated.
“I consider the diesel deal to be the first step. It seems to me that it is impossible to stop Putin in this way. On the contrary, he feels joy, happiness that he has such support. And still, we strongly hope, and I personally do, that the President of the United States of America will do everything so that Putin stops the killings, stops strikes on our energy, and stops this war.”
Zelensky stressed that coercing Kyiv into limiting asymmetric responses while easing economic restrictions on Moscow will not bring an end to hostilities.
“This cannot be achieved by restricting Ukraine’s responses against Russia for killing people,” Zelensky emphasized. “And certainly not by lifting sanctions.”
Bipartisan congressional action

Midterms 2026: What Comes Next for the US and Europe?
“I am grateful to his [Lindsey Graham’s] friends in Congress who supported this law. It was a great victory – truly such bipartisan support for this law,” Zelensky said.
“And now the decision to cancel all of this, to block all of this, seems to me to be wrong. It definitely helps only the Russians. It definitely does not stop the war.”
The presidential remarks come 24 hours after Trump signed an executive order on Friday, Oct. 16, waiving sweeping trade duties and secondary sanctions enacted under the Graham Act just 48 hours before statutory enforcement was scheduled to commence on Sunday, Oct. 18.
The suspended provisions included an additional 500 percent tariff on all Russian-origin imports alongside mandatory 100 percent duties targeting the five largest global purchasers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, such as China and India.
The waiver also halted enforcement against third-party countries facilitating petroleum sanctions evasion and suspended actions aimed at dismantling Moscow’s maritime “shadow fleet” of oil tankers.
Section 115 waivers
In the executive order, Trump invoked Section 115 of the Graham Act, which authorizes the executive branch to waive statutory penalties upon certifying to Congress that such action serves US national interests. However, the administration did not provide public details regarding the strategic rationale for the determination.
The presidential waiver follows a bilateral commercial agreement unveiled on Oct. 9 between Trump and Putin, under which Moscow consented to export refined diesel fuel onto international markets through 2027 to ease consumer fuel costs ahead of the US midterm elections.
To enable the shipments, the US Treasury Department issued a general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 2027.
Ukrainian officials have warned that opening global markets to Russian refined hydrocarbons provides Moscow with vital hard-currency earnings that underwrite military operations and long-range bombardments against Ukraine’s municipal power grid.
Zelensky reiterated that durable de-escalation requires intensifying allied economic pressure and maintaining enforceable deterrence, cautioning that unilateral accommodations only incentivize further Russian aggression ahead of the winter season.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had received confirmation that the speed-based restrictions on Starlink satellite communication terminals apply only within Ukraine, and he views this as a planned operation.
"What is the current speed limit for Starlink? Today, the maximum speed is 161 kilometers per hour; after that, according to the reports I have seen, Starlink shuts down completely and we lose the drone. What have we done to determine whether these are truly technical issues at SpaceX, or whether this is some kind of operation or an agreement to restrict us, shut us down, and prevent us from defending ourselves and protecting our people – both on the front lines and among civilians? We sent a couple of vehicles equipped with Starlink into European Union countries, and they drove – where permitted – at speeds exceeding 180 kilometers per hour, and Starlink worked. We have the relevant records and evidence. The conclusion is this: the restrictions apply within Ukraine, but they do not apply within the European Union. In other words, this is a planned operation," Zelenskyy said, responding to journalists' questions on Saturday.
He said a dialogue is underway with SpaceX at various levels, "and at various levels, they say these are technical issues."
"But, as I've already said, these technical issues exist in Ukraine; there are no such issues within the European Union. We've verified this. Here, Starlink works up to a speed of 161 kilometers per hour, then it shuts off. Within the EU, it works at speeds of 180 kilometers per hour and above, and it works continuously," the president said.
Zelenskyy expressed regret that "we cannot currently use Starlink or StarShield technology within our country's borders to shoot down jet-powered suicide drones." "Unfortunately, they're flying, and we can stop them with our air force; we stop them using other means, but we don't use Starlink for this, unfortunately. God willing, this work will resume," the president added.
He said Starlink is crucial for Ukraine, both on the front lines and for civilians.
"We're helping and using Starlink for drones so that we can deliver food and water to our troops in combat positions. This is very important in places where military personnel or certain types of equipment cannot reach. In areas that are cut off due to enemy drone control. And right now, we simply don't have that capability," the head of state said.
The president also said Ukraine is using Starlink on some interceptor drones to intercept high-speed enemy kamikaze drones equipped with jet engines. "Of course, and thank God, thanks to our air defense systems, our engineers, and our partners' equipment as well, we're using not only interceptor drones against kamikaze drones, but also aircraft, missiles, and other air defense systems, and so on. But again, when it comes to intercepting high-speed jet-powered drones – such as the Shahed and other jet-powered drones – our interceptors are currently ineffective because of speed limitations," Zelenskyy said.

Longevity: In Tokyo, the Sardinian model meets the Okinawan model
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:40:53 CEST
20:40:53 KST

The fifth edition of MeDiet Japan 2026, the international symposium on longevity and well-being organized by the Italian Chamber of Commerce in Japan (ICCJ), took place at the United Nations University in Tokyo’s Shibuya district. The initiative, launched in 2021 to promote the Mediterranean diet in Japan and Asia, now serves as a platform for health and sustainable lifestyles, featuring a broad exchange of ideas among specialists in nutrition, lifestyle medicine, geroscience, genetics, sports science, and the social sciences. This year’s theme is “Longevity—The Italian and Sardinian Models in Global Dialogue”: the focus is on healthy aging, with a comparison between Sardinia and Okinawa, both considered “Blue Zones”—areas with a high concentration of centenarians. The topic takes on particular significance on the 160th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Italy and Japan, two countries that rank among those with the highest life expectancy in the world. Among the speakers was Valter Longo, director of the Longevity Institute at the University of Southern California and creator of the fasting-mimicking diet, who participated via video link. Also in attendance were María Blasco, a telomere researcher and former director of the CNIO in Madrid; Bradley Willcox, head of the Okinawa Centenarian Study; and Héctor García, co-author of the bestseller “Ikigai.” There were four panels, dedicated to genetics and neuroscience, nutrition and the microbiome, social connections, physical activity, and cell biology. Longo emphasized how the integration of scientific research, nutrition, and diverse cultural perspectives is essential for understanding healthy longevity, and how evidence-based dietary approaches can help people live longer and better lives. Alongside the scientific aspect is the economic one. The Region of Sardinia participated with a delegation of agri-food companies, which met with Japanese importers and industry professionals in B2B sessions, with the goal of translating the prestige of the Sardinian model into commercial opportunities. For ICCJ Secretary General Davide Fantoni, the initiative sought to bring the topic back to a “strictly scientific and social” framework. Sardinia and Okinawa, he noted, serve as reminders that a long and healthy life depends first and foremost on diet, exercise, and relationships—a message that the Chamber intends to promote as opportunities for growth for Italian businesses. The symposium was followed by a day open to the public, featuring seminars, extra virgin olive oil tastings, and cooking demonstrations. Among the participants were Katsuya Iijima, director of the Institute of Gerontology at the University of Tokyo and a leading expert in the prevention of frailty, Satoru Yamada, advocate of the “locabo” approach to moderate carbohydrate reduction, and Dr. Yoshinori Nagumo, author of best-selling books on anti-aging. Also in attendance was 90-year-old triathlete Hiromu Inada, a record-holder at the Ironman World Championship. The event is sponsored, among others, by the Italian Embassy in Japan and the city of Shibuya.

Egypt's Sisi pledges to leave office when term ends in 2030

Breadcrumb
Egypt's Sisi pledges to leave office when term ends in 2030
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that he would not seek to remain in office when his current term expires in 2030, describing the matter as "completely settled".
Sisi, 71, a former army general who became president in 2014, made the remarks at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital, one of his flagship megaprojects.
Speaking to graduates and state officials in the sprawling new city east of Cairo, Sisi said the Egyptian constitution "would not be touched".
"The period leading up to 2030 will be the end of my term as president of the state, if I am still alive. This is completely settled, and there will be no discussion about it," he said.
The Egyptian constitution, approved in 2014 following the 2013 military ouster of late president Mohamed Morsi, originally limited presidents to two four-year terms.
Constitutional amendments approved in a 2019 referendum extended presidential terms from four to six years and included transitional provisions that allowed Sisi to run for an additional term.
Under those amendments, Sisi was re-elected in 2023 for a six-year term that expires in 2030.
Critics and opposition figures have speculated about further constitutional changes that could allow him to remain in office beyond 2030.
Before running for president, Sisi denied having political ambitions, but he resigned as defence minister in 2014 and entered the race he went on to win.
On Saturday, he said the run-up to 2030 would groom a new generation of leaders, with the Military Academy training hundreds of prospective officials, ministers and presidential candidates in statecraft and leadership.
During his 12 years in power, Sisi has overseen an ambitious state-led development programme centred on megaprojects which critics say have relied heavily on borrowing and contributed to Egypt's mounting debt burden and economic pressures.
Sisi's presidency has also faced sustained criticism from international human rights organisations over restrictions on political opposition, civil society and freedom of expression, allegations the government rejects, saying its policies are necessary to preserve stability and security.

A protester lights smoke flares next to a fire during a demonstration to protest against the "high cost of living", Place de la Victoire in Bordeaux, southwestern France, on October 17, 2026. | Christophe Aarchambault/ AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — A wave of mass protests swept across France Saturday, with dozens of peaceful marches taking place alongside scenes of violent clashes between demonstrators and police forces.
The demonstrations were also a battleground for candidates ahead of next year’s high-stakes presidential election: The far-right’s Marine Le Pen sided with law enforcement while the far-left’s Jean-Luc Mélenchon backed protesters.
Throughout the day, media reported incidents in the country’s largest cities including Lyon, Bordeaux, Marseille and Paris. Dozens of rioters clashed with law enforcement on the capital’s Place de la République, next to a much larger number of demonstrators gathered for an authorized march that started from Paris’s central square.
Advertisement
Media also reported looting across multiple cities later in the day.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu posted a message on X backing police forces and slamming violent rioters. He accused “ultra-left groups” of “organizing violence” and said looters would be brought to justice. Lecornu is overseeing a crisis meeting on Saturday evening, AFP reported.
French President Emmanuel Macron echoed Lecornu’s comments on Saturday evening, although he didn’t mention “ultra-left groups.”
“No place for violence in our Republic,” he said. “We will stand together against those who seed chaos, who only seek to tear down our institutions and who prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing it.”
Students, farmers and members of the Yellow Jacket movement, among others, took to the streets on Saturday in a “convergence of struggles” to protest rising living costs, sluggish wages and deep disagreements with the government.
About 800,000 protestors took to the streets across the country, according to organizers. France’s interior ministry said 550,000 people took part in the protests.
Advertisement
“A very large majority of people are protesting without violence,” Paris’s police prefecture said on Saturday afternoon.
Around 4,500 secondary school pupils and university students involved in the Yellow Vests movement demonstrated side by side against the cost of living in Pau, south-west of France on 17 October 2026. | Jean-Christophe Chartre/AFP via Getty Images
Saturday’s demonstrations grew out of the student protests that began last month with school blockades and calls for better study conditions, more teachers and more funding. The movement has since spread nationwide — and become a political issue as the campaign for next year’s presidential election heats up.
In recent weeks, the government has struggled to deal with the crisis — which Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu described as “urban violence” — and is hoping the student movement will now fade because of a two-week school holiday that started Friday evening.
“The mobilization is marked by a very strong involvement of the ultra-left movement, which is only looking to cause disorder,” Nuñez’s office said Saturday, adding that the minister reiterated his “instructions of utmost firmness” to local prefects and police forces.
Footage showed Lyon’s tourist board office engulfed in flames on the city’s Place Bellecour. A police station was vandalized in Marseille, where a group of “rioters” also entered city hall, Mayor Benoît Payan said. He toldBFMTV that “damage was objectively fairly limited,” although the act of vandalism was “unacceptable.” The headquarters of right-wing TV channel CNews in Paris was also targeted, authorities said.
The government has defended the law enforcement response to the student protests despite numerous allegations of police brutality, including incidents that left one teenager with a severed hand and another blind in one eye. Nuñez said the use of “stun grenades” was authorized on Saturday, after a temporary ban on their use against students.
Advertisement
About 163 people had already been arrested in Paris by mid-afternoon, authorities said.
The far-left France Unbowed slammed the police response to the protests.
The party’s presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon participated in the demonstrations in Paris and backed protesters — he also criticized the media for only showing violent clashes while “everything is proceeding peacefully, with tens of thousands of people calmly taking part.”
On the other side of the political spectrum, far-right leaders Jordan Bardella and Marine Le Pen pledged support for the police. “Legitimate social demands have once again been hijacked by the far left,” Le Pen said, as an increasing number of polls show she could end up in the second round against Mélenchon.
Bardella said on Saturday that protests were made up entirely of “chaos professionals,” adding: “As we said, working France, which is taking the full brunt of inflation and cost-of-living struggles, did not take to the streets today.”

====================================================================================================

The power of AI is worrying senior Labour figures – as is the fear of ‘falling behind the public’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:33:20 UTC
20:33:20 KST

“I have this sense that, within a few months, AI is going to be all anyone is talking about,” said one cabinet minister, with an ominous stare.
It was Labour conference, with everyone from ministers to activists jubilant at Andy Burnham’s takeover and a bounce in the polls after the change of leader.
But a number of senior Labour figures were privately starting to name the power of AI as the thing worrying them most, alongside the immediate pressures on the cost of living and fragile economy.
One cabinet minister – with a brief unrelated to technology – told the Guardian that dangerous, out-of-control AI was the issue keeping them up at night, fretting about the threat to humanity. It was “not killer robots” causing the worry, they explained, but the idea of a huge amount of concentrated, super-intelligent power potentially ending up in the hands of bad actors.
Another expressed concern that the government was “falling behind the public” in terms of dealing with worries about AI safety – and that it needed to catch up fast.
In his conference speech, Ed Miliband was the most strident about the “daunting” dangers of AI, making the case that politicians could not and would not allow the profits of tech companies “to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity”.
And it has not taken long for these alarm bells to ring even louder, with the last seven days looking like the week Westminster fully woke up to the warnings.
A flurry of activity started on Monday with Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, stating it was “likely, if not inevitable” that rogue agents would hack the British state, and saying the UK was looking to strengthen its forthcoming cybersecurity legislation.
It was the main topic of discussion at cabinet on Tuesday, and that was followed by the MI5 chief Ken McCallum warning AI was “supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders”. He said the biggest threat was extremist groups using the technology to unleash bioweapons – toxins used to cause death and disease.
Liam Byrne, the chair of the business, innovation, science and trade committee, said the change of government from Keir Starmer to Burnham was partly behind the increased focus on protecting the UK from AI threats but more still had to be done. “The reality is that the Starmer administration was much too close to the big tech companies,” Byrne said. “And Burnham is not, frankly, so there has been a change of posture. Those things, plus the security services issuing their warning, that is what has changed the weather on this.”
One senior Labour government figure agreed that Burnham’s government was taking AI safety warnings more seriously. “I do feel there has been a shift. Under the last lot, too many of them had drunk the tech-bro Kool-Aid,” he said.
Byrne’s committee held an evidence session this week with civil service leaders in charge of AI security and executives from the key companies – Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind and Meta – with a split between them about whether government testing of new models should be mandatory.
He said his committee was “lighting up” the issue, particularly in terms of working with the US to regulate and monitor new models. It had been reported that Donald Trump’s administration had asked AI companies not to share their latest models with the UK’s cutting-edge AI Security Institute for testing, though Narayan confirmed this week that they had managed to retain cooperation.
But Byrne said the government now needed to seize the moment and take the lead on new regulation, particularly if Trump’s Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections to the Democrats.
“I think the government is still caught in a dilemma between how to keep model access, given a capricious US president, and the safeguards that the industry itself now says are essential. It’s make-your-mind-up time, I would say,” Byrne said.
“The companies want to cooperate … It’s not in their commercial interest to issue models which are lethal. Now they too have got to navigate the White House. So I just think this is a moment when the government has actually got to do what is right for the country because Congress is about to change the dynamics on this in the US.”
The UK’s upcoming G20 presidency will be the key moment to push for international action to rein in AI. Geoffrey Irving, the former chief scientist at AISI who spoke at this week’s parliamentary hearing, believes Whitehall concerns are justified. OpenAI and Anthropic’s technology has already shown its hacking capabilities but their models are released with safety guardrails in place that at least mitigate against the threat of malicious behaviour.
However, so-called open source AI models are freely available and can be adapted. Typically, they caught up with the paid-for models such as OpenAI’s within less than a year, said Irving, although they could cause disruption already.
“It’s very likely that open source models are already powerful enough to do serious damage,” Irving told the Guardian, adding that he expected open source technology to reach the capabilities of OpenAI and Anthropic products “soon”. Safety guardrails “either don’t exist or can be trivially removed” from open source models, he added.
The business committee heard this week that AI-enabled bioweapons could become the next serious threat to manifest itself, in the wake of cybersecurity, as models become more powerful and therefore capable of designing novel bio-harms – although experts suggest there is a gap between designing dangerous pathogens and weaponising them.
Concerns over cybersecurity and bioweapons can escalate rapidly to fears about AI wiping out humanity in a variety of scenarios – a concern that is widespread within the AI community, and is shared by Irving.
However, some experts argue that the government should focus on immediate risks from AI. Prof Elena Simperl, a co-director of the Institute for Artificial Intelligence at King’s College London, said the existential risk argument had “no evidence” and was a “theory” rather than a credible threat.
“There are bigger, more immediate risks that AI technology is posing now and are actually evidenced, like hacking and signs that AI can be as addictive as social media,” Simperl said.
In the absence of international AI regulation, there are some in Whitehall worried about whether the UK is doing enough preparation to defend against AI warfare and attacks.
Defence sources said there was concern about the cancellation last year of the AI programme at the government’s Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (Dstl), based at Porton Down, with worries that this was shortsighted given the need for cutting-edge research on advancing the nation’s capabilities and defending against its risks.
This was countered by an MoD spokesperson who said AI was “transforming defence from industry to the battlefield and will play a decisive role in how we fight and defend” and that it must be “integrated across all workstreams, rather than a standalone programme”. They pointed to a £400m investment in AI-focused capabilities over the next four years to “prepare the UK for the future of warfare”.
Others in Whitehall have the opposite concern: that worries about safety could become too dominant – and end up holding back the government’s adoption of tools that could be transformative for productivity and solving longstanding problems in public services, from medical care to reducing waiting lists.
The former cabinet secretary Gus O’Donnell told the Guardian that ministers needed to be as aware of “the risk of being left behind” when it came to AI as being aware of the need for guardrails.
Launching a Global Government Forum report on AI with the tech firm Cognizant, O’Donnell told the Guardian: “There is a big need to get it better and to really push on. I’m really optimistic, but the challenge for us, obviously, is managing the risks along the way, making sure that we don’t make mistakes, which reduce people’s trust, which means that that sets us back.”

Demand-side strategies could halve battery emissions by 2050: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
19:31:27 CST
20:31:27 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Demand-side strategies, including reducing battery sizes, extending battery lifetimes and promoting shared mobility, could cut global lithium-ion battery supply-chain emissions by around half by 2050, an Australian-led study finds.
The study found that demand for lithium-ion batteries used in electric vehicles and battery energy storage systems could increase twentyfold by 2050, driving a tenfold rise in related supply-chain greenhouse gas emissions, according to a statement released Saturday by Australia's University of Melbourne.
The study was one of the first detailed global assessments to examine both supply-side and demand-side factors, researchers said, adding that supply-side strategies reduce emissions from battery production through cleaner electricity, greener factories, switching battery chemistries and recycling.
While cleaner production remains essential, the findings suggest that reducing battery demand could offer a substantial additional opportunity to curb emissions, said University of Melbourne Associate Professor Li Wen, lead contact of the study published in One Earth.
Researchers from Australia, China and Britain estimated that without additional measures, the global battery supply chain could generate 19 billion to 23 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions through 2050.
Combining ambitious supply- and demand-side strategies could reduce the total to 9 billion to 12 billion tonnes, with demand-side measures accounting for 6 billion to 7 billion tonnes of the reduction, Li said.
The study assessed battery material and component production, manufacturing and end-of-life treatment from 2024 to 2050, with the researchers saying battery decarbonization policies should move beyond regulating production emissions to consider how much battery capacity is needed to provide transport and energy storage services. ■

====================================================================================================

World Insights: COP17 faces test of turning biodiversity pledges into action
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
19:31:06 CST
20:31:06 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Four years after the adoption of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, its first global progress report has found uneven progress toward the 2030 targets, with the biggest gaps in efforts to address the drivers of biodiversity loss.
The State of Biodiversity Action report, released by the United Nations on Thursday, will inform the first global review of collective progress under the framework at the upcoming 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP17) to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) in the Armenian capital.
With the conference opening on Oct. 19, the challenge is to turn the review's findings into concrete action.
UNEVEN PROGRESS
Countries have taken action across all 23 targets of the framework for 2030, but none presents an entirely positive picture, according to the report. Unless collective implementation accelerates, the 2030 targets and mission will not be achieved.
The report identifies two gaps: national targets do not fully reflect the scope and ambition of global commitments, and implementation falls short even of those less ambitious targets.
Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the CBD, said in August that fewer than half of the national targets assessed by parties and aligned with the framework were on track. The largest gaps concerned resource mobilization, harmful subsidy reform, business impacts and the transition to sustainable consumption.
Schomaker has noted promising conservation efforts, alongside slow progress on resource mobilization, harmful subsidy reform and inclusive governance.
The framework calls for reducing incentives harmful to biodiversity, including subsidies, by at least 500 billion U.S. dollars annually by 2030.
Yet an analysis by the Britain-based website Carbon Brief found that only about 5 percent of countries had set quantitative targets for subsidy reductions. Some countries reported that reform faced obstacles from vested interests and political resistance.
ECONOMIC OBSTACLES
A recent report by the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) points to tightening public finances and immediate pressures over food and energy security as reasons why some countries have shown insufficient political will for biodiversity protection.
The problem becomes more acute when reforms affect powerful interest groups or impose immediate costs on certain sectors, while conservation benefits are shared across society and take longer to emerge.
International financing presents another challenge. Under the framework, international biodiversity finance from developed countries and other contributors to developing countries was to reach at least 20 billion dollars annually by 2025, increasing to at least 30 billion dollars by 2030.
However, the State of Biodiversity Action report shows that reported international public finance totaled only 17.7 billion dollars between 2020 and 2023, averaging about 4.4 billion dollars a year.
An assessment by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services warns that delaying action could double the costs and increase the risk of irreversible losses, including species extinctions. Current economic models are also exacerbating biodiversity loss, climate change, water scarcity, food insecurity and health risks, with unaccounted-for costs estimated at 10 trillion to 25 trillion dollars annually.
Within and between countries, the central tension is who should bear the immediate costs of protecting nature and when. The longer action is delayed, the greater the overall costs.
TURNING REVIEW INTO ACTION
The key test for COP17 is whether the review can provide clear guidance for further action, according to the Institute for Sustainable Development and International Relations, a French think tank.
Under the convention's procedures, the global review materials will be submitted to COP17, where parties will examine implementation gaps and consider follow-up action.
Observers say three questions will be central to the conference.
First, what signals will its decisions send? Harmful subsidy reform and the integration of biodiversity into economic decision-making are among the areas lagging most. A general call to accelerate action would carry different weight from specific measures addressing these obstacles.
Second, how will funding be secured and managed? Financing is a major weakness identified by the review and an important measure by which developing countries will judge the conference's outcome. The WWF has called on COP17 to deliver results rather than further promises, including a credible path toward mobilizing at least 30 billion dollars annually in international biodiversity finance by 2030.
Third, how will supporting measures be implemented? At the Kunming Dialogue on the framework's implementation in September, participants broadly agreed that finance, capacity-building and technology were equally important. They also noted that support remained insufficient, while reliance on short-term funding hampered long-term planning and implementation.
Despite the gaps exposed by the report, Schomaker has stressed that the 2030 targets remain achievable, provided major changes are made.
COP17 will need to address who bears the costs of protecting nature and how to overcome resistance to reforms that bring short-term difficulties but long-term benefits. Its decisions will help determine whether the framework remains a set of commitments on paper or is translated into national budgets, subsidies and investment. ■

He warned that prolonged disruption to shipping could have wider consequences beyond the maritime sector.
"It may have an even bigger impact when it comes to the global economy and supplies of energy sources as well as food security," he said.
The IMO chief said the organization was continuing to support around 6,000 seafarers who had remained trapped in the region since the beginning of the conflict.
However, Dominguez stressed that protecting seafarers must remain a priority, even if avoiding high-risk waters leads to higher costs.
"Costs will increase globally; it's a reality, but we cannot put the lives of innocent seafarers at risk anymore," he said.
Asked whether the IMO had been in contact with the parties involved in the conflict, Dominguez said the organization was maintaining communications with all its member states, particularly those directly involved, as well as countries beyond the region and other United Nations agencies.
He acknowledged mediation efforts by several countries but said they had yet to produce the decisions needed to allow shipping operations to return to normal.
"The root causes are not being addressed," Dominguez said. "So from our side, we can only work on the operational aspects of shipping, but it's been very clear that until the parties in the conflict sit down and find a solution to why this crisis started, we will not be able to resume operations safely around the region."
On the protection of seafarers, Dominguez said the IMO was reviewing existing rules and guidance on risk assessments before vessels enter conflict zones or high-risk areas.
The organization was also engaging with shipowners, operators and seafarers' representatives to explore ways to help seafarers obtain necessary supplies and uphold their rights under the Maritime Labour Convention.
These include the right to refuse to transit dangerous areas without retaliation and the right to receive repatriation support.
He said the IMO was also examining how existing regulations could be better enforced, including the detention of non-compliant vessels until they demonstrate compliance with international requirements.
Dominguez noted that geopolitical conflicts were affecting shipping across several regions, including the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.
Until these areas become more peaceful and shipping is no longer used as leverage in conflicts, vessels should avoid operating in such high-risk waters, he said. ■

Snøhetta completes landmark opera house in Shanghai
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:30:27 UTC
20:30:27 KST

Snøhetta completes landmark opera house in Shanghai
A giant spiral staircase guides visitors to the roof of the Shanghai Grand Opera House, which international studio Snøhetta designed to be "as much a civic destination as a performance venue".
Located on the Huangpu River waterfront in Shanghai, China, the 146,786-square-metre opera house was conceived as a major cultural landmark that can accommodate a variety of musical performances.
While Snøhetta's design responds to a highly ambitious brief, the studio said it began the project as it always does, by taking time to examine and understand the specific site and its context, no matter the scale.
According to the studio, this helped it to create the desired landmark while ensuring it felt like an extension of the existing public realm, open and accessible to both ticket holders and passersby.
"We always begin the same way, regardless of scale: by understanding the context," Snøhetta co-founder Kjetil Thorsen told Dezeen.
"A cultural building, any building for that matter, must respond to its surroundings, the people who use it, the performers it serves, and the city it becomes part of," he reflected.
"When I last visited the site, I was asked by a Chinese architecture student how we managed to create a building that felt so Chinese despite not being from China. The answer lies in observation and understanding context."
Shanghai Grand Opera House's defining feature is its spiral staircase, which dramatically cantilevers at its peak and was intended to emulate everything from an unfolding fan to a dancer or a set of piano keys.
It leads directly to the publicly accessible rooftop, which doubles as a stage, an observation deck or simply a meeting point. According to Thorsen, it was integral to making the building feel part of the urban fabric.
He compared the design to the Oslo Opera House, which the studio completed in 2000, with both designs actively seeking to "reduce thresholds wherever possible".
"Buildings like opera houses inevitably create thresholds through walls, doors, and ticketed programs. We see it as our responsibility to challenge those thresholds and make the building as much a civic destination as a performance venue," Thorsen explained.
"People should be able to enjoy the building without attending a performance. It should become part of everyday life, a place to spend time, meet others, and experience the city," he added.
"A successful landmark is not only recognised by visitors, it is also embraced by the people who live around it and make it part of their everyday lives."
Shanghai Grand Opera House has a radial plan and contains a trio of auditoriums alongside exhibition and education spaces, restaurants and rehearsal and production areas.
The facade flits between transparent and opaque finishes, depending on where the studio wanted to provide privacy and openness. For example, expansive glass elements maximise natural light and views in the lobby.
Together, the three auditoriums can accommodate 4,200 people and host a range of performances. The main auditorium, called the Harmony Hall, contains 2,000 seats across its five levels, while the second hall, named the Soar Theatre, is more intimate, with space for 1,200 people.
The final auditorium contains 1,000 seats and was constructed as a highly flexible space with adaptive seating and staging, catering to more experimental performances. It is fronted with a large glass facade overlooking the river.
"For younger generations especially, that flexibility can help make cultural experiences feel more relevant, accessible, and connected to contemporary life," said Thorsen.
Shanghai Grand Opera House's material palette is a play of contrasts, with the light-coloured white stone, glass, and timber exterior having a more open feel than the darker, more intimate interiors.
Inside, the auditoriums each have a unique aesthetic. The main hall is filled with deep red tones and surfaces, intended to feel as though they are carved from a single block, while lighter wooden materials characterise the other two.
At night, the stage towers that project from the building are illuminated, shifting in colour to "animate the roof and the skyline".
Minimising the building's carbon footprint was a significant challenge due to the building's "scale and complexity", Thorsen said, but this was achieved through measures including passive design strategies.
The bright roof reflects sunlight and heat rather than absorbing it, and the public lobby opens towards both the river and the park, allowing for cross-ventilation.
A palette of durable materials and an adaptable interior will ensure a long lifespan for the building, while a close connection to public transport minimises dependence on private vehicles.
Shanghai Grand Opera House is complete with a landscape design that connects to existing parkland, wetlands and public spaces to support local biodiversity and provide ample public space.
Snøhetta was founded by Thorsen and Craig Dykers in 1989. It won an international competition to design the opera house in 2016 and developed it with the state-owned firm East China Architectural Design & Research Institute (ECADI) and consultants Theatre Projects and Nagata Acoustics.
Other major cultural projects by the studio include the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in North Dakota and the rippled Glasshouse Theatre in Queensland.
The photography is by Yumeng Zhu, Tian Fangfang, Chen Hao and StudioSZ.

The Best LED Grow Lights for Houseplants This Winter (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Summer is officially over, along with its allotment of free sunlight. You might be sad about this, but your indoor plants might be even sadder. A good LED grow light can replicate sunlight with full-spectrum light and day/night cycles, keeping plants lush and thriving even in a dark, windowless corner or basement.
I have no fewer than 40 houseplants in my home at any given time, as well as a fair number of grow lights, and what I've found to be important for a general consumer (i.e., someone not doing that kind of indoor grow) isn't necessarily certain colored light wavelengths but whether a grow light is easy to live with in your house.
Many grow lights are more or less going to serve the same purpose, so what you really need to know is this: Is the light so bright that it's disruptive? Does it require complicated installation? Is it easy for kids or pets to knock over? The grow lights recommended below are ones that WIRED staffers have lived with for months, if not years, and have found them both effective and easy to integrate into our lives.
Also be sure to check out our guides to the Best Indoor Gardening Systems, Best Gifts for Plant Lovers, and Best Kitchen Composters.
Featured Lights
What Is PPFD?
Photosynthetic photon flux Ddensity, or PPFD, expressed in micromoles per square meter per second (μmol/m²/s), is a measurement of how much light reaches your plant that's usable for photosynthesis. In general, the higher the plant's energy needs, such as producing a flower or a fruit, the higher the PPFD number you want. Though different lights have different height requirements given the plants they're made for, for standardization purposes, I measured the PPFD of each grow light at 18 inches with the Photone app and a light diffuser. Keep in mind these measurements are general and approximate.
How I Test Grow Lights
Some of these grow lights I bought myself, with my own money, before I even began working at WIRED. Others were owned by staffers and recommended to me. I also have press samples from other guides I worked on, which I liked so much I ended up keeping around.
For the traditional grow lights, I tested them at home under normal-life conditions. I put them where they'd fit, tested their timers, and noted whether or not they were dimmable. I also measured each light's PPFD (see above) and noted whether certain lights could be daisy-chained for more extensive coverage.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Best Grow Light for Small Plants and Seedlings
There are a lot of options out there for starting seeds and helping houseplants along in the winter, and many of them are bulky, fussy, or require elaborate hanging setups. This simple, 15-inch-long light from Vego sticks to its 3M adhesive mount with a magnet, so it's easy to take on and off and use with existing racks or, as I do, under a kitchen cabinet. Up to four Vego lights can be daisy-chained together, and the five preprogrammed modes (Seeds, Leafy, Fruits, Herbs, Microgreens) have varying intensities and automatic built-in off periods to simulate nighttime. I have not found this light especially disruptive, especially since it's easy to turn on and off with the button on the back.
WIRED commerce SEO director Stewart Savin used these lights to start her garden earlier this year and had 138 successful germinations across 144 seedling cells. ("The vast majority of those plants went on to have long lives in my garden after I hardened them off," she says.) Note that because this light can only go beneath a rack, shelf, or cabinet, it’s not inherently adjustable, and therefore is best for small plants (like seedlings) that aren’t going to grow especially tall.
Most Versatile Grow Light
This do-anything light, with a broad 2 x 3-foot head, can hang from the ceiling or swivel on its included stand where you need it. (Up to 20 of these lights can be daisy-chained.) Note that while the stand is useful, the 1-inch-diameter pole and offset base aren't the sturdiest, and it's easy to knock over, so I'd recommend hanging it if you have pets and small kids. I learned this the hard way while trying to revive a corn plant in a dark corner at the top of my stairs.
While this light is quite bright and potentially disruptive, it's easily dimmable via the remote, which hangs on a cord. At first I thought this was weird, but I found it extremely useful when the light was behind plants or in another hard-to-reach spot.
Also worth noting: While the stand height is supposed to be adjustable up to 72 inches, mine only goes up to about 64 inches, so it may not be the best option for extremely tall plants.
Best Grow Light for Serious Indoor Growers
Vivosun is a long-respected brand among indoor growers, and its LumaLight panels are sturdy and all business. In fact, you'll be hard-pressed to find a higher-quality grow light for the price. This is not necessarily a light for casual houseplant parents—the 100-watt, 12 x 12-inch model weighs 4.4 pounds and needs to be attached to the ceiling or inside one of Vivosun's grow tents using the included adjustable ropes and carabiners.
If you're growing fruiting or flowering plants, though, this is the grow light you want—none of the other lights I tested even came close to its level of brightness. That said, you probably won't want it in a main living area, though it is dimmable via a dial on top. The LumaLight is IP65-rated for water resistance, and up to seven units can be daisy-chained if you need.
Best Budget Grow Light
Former WIRED commerce director Martin Cizmar loved and recommended this grow light for his houseplants, which features three bendable heads on a clip you can attach to a table or shelf. It has a timer for three, nine, or twelve hours, plus a 10-foot cord if you need to place it away from an outlet. It also has warm and cool lighting options in addition to full spectrum, if you want to use it for ambiance (despite it looking, in my opinion, sort of like a creepy Freddy Krueger glove), plus 10 dimming modes. Right now, the base price on Amazon is for a two-pack.
Alternatives to Traditional Grow Lights
If you don’t have the space or desire for a classic grow light, I’ve used all three options below for at least a year, and all resulted in happy plants.
Other Grow Lights Tested
Sansi Pot Clip-On Plant Lights for $30: These Sansi grow lights came in handy when I was living in a dark basement with minimal light for plants and hardly any space to store them. They clip directly onto the pot, so you don't need a dedicated stand or extra space, and they run on a three-, six-, or twelve-hour timer. The long cord (just over 6 feet) also helps in awkward or tight spaces. These lights helped my Monstera stay alive over winter with almost no natural light. U.S. Army’s Arctic division gets its own supply brigade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:27:41 UTC
20:27:41 KST

- The U.S. Army activated the 11th Airborne Division Sustainment Brigade (Arctic) at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska, on Oct. 16, 2026.
- The brigade includes a reactivated intelligence and electronic warfare battalion, a renamed sustainment support battalion and a new troops battalion.
The U.S. Army has activated a new sustainment brigade for the 11th Airborne Division in Alaska, giving the Arctic-focused division its own formation to keep troops supplied and supported in some of the harshest conditions the U.S. military operates in.
The 11th Airborne Division Sustainment Brigade (Arctic) uncased its colors on Oct. 16, 2026, at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson near Anchorage, the division said. The ceremony also stood up the brigade’s subordinate battalions and companies: the 106th Intelligence and Electronic Warfare Battalion was reactivated, the 17th Combat Sustainment Support Battalion was renamed the 17th Division Sustainment Support Battalion, and a new 11th Airborne Division Sustainment Troops Battalion was activated.
“Today’s uncasing ceremony represents much more than the unfurling of our unit colors,” said Col. George Plys, the brigade’s commander. “It symbolizes the beginning of a new chapter, the commitment to a mission, and the readiness of our Soldiers to answer the call wherever and whenever our nation needs them.”
A division sustainment brigade handles the logistics that keep combat units moving, including fuel, ammunition, food, maintenance and transportation. In Alaska, where winter temperatures can fall far below freezing and distances between bases are vast, that support is central to whether troops can operate for long periods at all.
The U.S. Army reactivated the 11th Airborne Division in 2022, replacing the U.S. Army Alaska headquarters, and the division describes itself as both the youngest division in the active force and the fastest growing among comparable units. Until now, its main combat power has rested on two infantry brigade combat teams, one based at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson and one at Fort Wainwright near Fairbanks.
“Our ability to endure and sustain ourselves in the crucible of large-scale combat operations is impossible without the formations you see in front of you today,” said Maj. Gen. John Cogbill, the division’s commanding general.
The activation follows the U.S. Army’s release of new foundational doctrine, titled “How the Army Fights,” which names endurance as one of four linked operational elements alongside convergence, strike and close battle.
Plys said the brigade’s two main battalions do different but connected jobs, with the 17th sustaining the force and the 106th giving commanders intelligence and electronic warfare capabilities to understand the battlefield.
“While these two battalions have distinct missions, both are essential to our Army’s ability to fight and win,” said Plys. “One sustains the force; the other provides the intelligence and electronic warfare capabilities that help commanders understand the battlefield and make informed decisions.”

Moscow blasts UN for ignoring torture of Russian POWs
The UN should resist pressure from Kiev’s Western backers and finally address the issue of widespread abuse of captured Russian servicemen in Ukrainian secret prisons, Russian Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik has said.
During a conversation with the chairman of the UN Committee Against Torture Claude Heller on Thursday, Miroshnik said that Moscow is aware of a whole network of such detention facilities, operating in Ukraine’s Kharkov, Dnepropetrovsk, and Sumy Regions as well as in the country’s capital, Kiev.
The Russian servicemen are “going through hell” in so-called “transit prisons,” which are set up at deployment points of Ukrainian military units and nationalist battalions, he said.
“The thugs, who hide their faces behind masks... and address each other only by their call signs, subject the captured Russian troops to inhuman abuse. Waterboarding, electrocuting, baiting with dogs and amputations performed without anesthesia are just a few examples of the techniques systematically employed by the Ukrainian tormentors,” the envoy, who is charged with documenting Kiev’s war crimes, stressed.
According to Miroshnik, captured troops are usually sent to those facilities in the early stages of their imprisonment, where they are held in cages, pits, and stone dungeons.
The Kiev government does not allow ombudsmen and human rights activists into those “torture chambers,” but the Russian authorities have gathered hundreds of accounts of survivors detailing what has been happening there, he said.
“This information had been passed on to the UN Secretariat on more than one occasion,” but no action followed, Miroshnik added.
By ignoring the existence of the secret prisons and systematic torture of Russian troops, the global body “encourages the spread of such criminal practices and disregard for the relevant UN Convention,” he added.
“Many experts are aware of this disgraceful phenomenon, yet there is a lack of political will to overcome the pressure from the foreign accomplices to the conflict, who shield the Kiev regime from accountability and prevent a thorough investigation of its conduct,” the envoy said.
While turning a blind eye to the torture of Russian troops, the UN published several reports accusing Russia of mistreating Ukrainian prisoners, based on accounts by POWs returned by Moscow to Kiev. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has labeled those accusations of abuse “disinformation.”
Last month, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that the UN Secretariat was unable to properly perform its duties as most key positions are occupied by representatives of NATO countries.
The current team, led by [UN General-Secretary] Antonio Guterres, who is a Portuguese national, “promotes biased approaches and double standards, effectively serving the interests of a group of Western nations,” Lavrov insisted during a press conference on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

Russians attack Zaporizhstal for fifth time, firing six ballistic missiles – photo
Russia has attacked the Zaporizhstal steelworks with ballistic missiles. The plant has still not returned to normal production following a series of previous strikes.
Source: Metinvest
Details: On 17 October, Russia once again attacked the Zaporizhstal steelworks with ballistic missiles. Six ballistic missiles struck the plant's internal energy and logistics infrastructure at dawn and caused further damage to blast-furnace production facilities, the company reported.
Metinvest said there were no casualties this time, as employees had moved to shelters in time.
Zaporizhstal came under large-scale ballistic missile attacks on 11 and 27 August, 12 and 17 September, and again on 17 October. A total of 23 ballistic missiles have been launched at the plant during this period.
Eight employees have been killed in these attacks and another 31 workers have sustained injuries of varying severity.
Following the 11 August attack, the entire production site was shut down. Employees were involved in clearing rubble and dealing with the aftermath of the strike in order to assess the damage and determine whether production could be restored.
Some technological processes were quickly restarted to keep equipment in a safe condition and eliminate potential industrial hazards for employees and local residents. Metinvest said these processes have since been maintained at the minimum level necessary.
However, normal production has still not resumed.
Given the persistent security risks caused by systematic Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia, the plant has rapidly expanded its network of protective shelters.
Additional reinforced mobile shelters have also been installed in areas where employees are dealing with the aftermath of attacks and repairing damaged equipment.
This has significantly reduced the distance and time workers need to reach shelter, which is particularly important during ballistic missile attacks.
"I am grateful to our employees, to our team, who have proved stronger than the attacks and the immense pressure. Professionalism, competence and team spirit have always been our values. But in times like these, it is the strength of our people's spirit that comes to the fore," said Oleksandr Myronenko, Chief Operating Officer of Metinvest Group.
He stressed that Russia destroys and distorts, seeking to annihilate, while people continue to work.
"Metre by metre, people clear the rubble and come together to deal with the aftermath of the strikes. When they hear the air-raid warning, they head to the shelters together. And once the all-clear is given, they return to work at the damaged facilities," Myronenko said.
Background:
- Russian forces attacked an industrial facility in Kryvyi Rih on 17 October.
- Energy infrastructure in Zhytomyr Oblast came under Russian attack, causing widespread power outages.
- On the morning of 17 September, Russia struck the already-idled Zaporizhstal plant with two ballistic missiles. One employee was taken to hospital, while production equipment and railway infrastructure sustained significant damage.
- Zaporizhstal completely halted operations following a Russian ballistic missile strike on 11 August. In late August, Metinvest said it was not yet possible to determine when the plant could resume operations.

Bulgarian Power Exports Double as Battery Storage Expands
Bulgaria’s energy storage capacity has reached 6 gigawatts this year, approaching the country’s electricity demand of 7.4 GW and reshaping domestic and regional power markets
The crisis in the Black Sea has disrupted raw material supplies to Bulgaria’s ferrous metals industry, forcing a plant in Debelt to operate only two weeks a month, Nikola Rangelov, chairman of the Bulgarian Association of the Metallurgical Industry, told Bulgarian National Radio (BNR).
Rangelov described the situation in an interview with BNR’s program “Horizon until Noon” as a supply-chain shock that was gradually contracting the sector, with ferrous metal producers bearing the brunt of the difficulties.
The plant in Pernik is also struggling to obtain raw materials, although its situation is less severe than that of the facility in Debelt, he said.
The Debelt plant has received no billets, a semi-finished product used to manufacture rebar and other goods, since August. The billets are produced in Ukraine and normally reach the port of Burgas by sea.
“These billets are used to produce rebar and other products. The problem is that there haven't been any supplies since August,” Rangelov told BNR.
He said around 120 ships were waiting to be processed in the Izmail area, but shipping had effectively ground to a halt, with no movement.
The supply disruption is driving up the cost of finished products, but the more pressing concern is that production has largely stopped at the Debelt facility.
“To begin with, we won't even be able to manufacture anything, the plant simply isn't operating. It runs for only two weeks a month, provided raw materials can be secured at all; the rest of the time, it sits idle, yet wages still have to be paid... The management is facing significant difficulties due to this situation,” Rangelov said.
He added that 60,000 tons of billets had already been loaded, enough to cover approximately one month of the plant’s requirements, but the shipment could not reach its destination.
“These are the semi-finished products that could cover the month's needs, but they simply aren't arriving. The plant is not operating,” he said.
Rangelov noted that non-ferrous metals play a less prominent role in construction. The country’s largest metallurgical enterprise is not currently experiencing problems either with raw material supplies or with the dispatch of finished products, he said.
Aluminum supplies are also under pressure because of the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, Rangelov warned.
He said the Arabian Peninsula produces about 9% of the world’s aluminum and accounts for approximately 20% of the European Union’s aluminum imports. Bahrain is a major producer, but deliveries from the country have been severely restricted, as have supplies from Saudi Arabia.
Production across the region has fallen by between 40% and more than 60%, Rangelov said, affecting volumes needed by metallurgical plants in Bulgaria and Western Europe.
Aluminum prices have risen by 10% compared with previous months, he added, warning that the increase could complicate the fulfillment of existing contracts agreed at lower prices.
Bulgaria's government is moving away from trusting what companies report and towards watching what they do.
