France braces for nationwide protests as ‘yellow vests’ set to join
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:21:32 UTC
20:21:32 KST

Protests spread across France as ‘yellow vests’ set to join
Demonstrations began in mid-September at schools and have expanded, tapping into wider grievances.
Paris, France – Saturday is a day of many unknowns. That was how the French newspaper Le Monde described it as France braced for possible nationwide demonstrations bringing together high school students, trade unions and “yellow vest” activists.
The protests began in mid-September at a high school in the Paris suburb of Creteil, where students took to the streets over dilapidated buildings, overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and what they see as a deeply unequal education system.
Since then, the mobilisation has spread to thousands of “lycees”, or upper secondary schools, across the country. It is now beginning to reflect broader anxieties in a country grappling with a combination of fiscal pressures, economic stagnation and mounting social discontent.
Teachers, trade unions and university students have joined the movement.
On Saturday, some “yellow vest” activists – remnants of the participants in the grassroots cost-of-living protests that shook President Emmanuel Macron’s first term in 2018 – have also called on supporters to join the students.
“High school students are fighting for their future. Workers are fighting to earn a living from their labour. Retirees are fighting to preserve their dignity. Our paths may differ, but our concerns can converge,” Jerome Rodrigues, a prominent “yellow vest” activist, said in a video message released last week that called on people to join Saturday’s demonstrations.
Now France is waiting to see whether those calls will translate into a large, coordinated mobilisation.
Warlike injuries
Authorities have described the unrest as among the most violent in decades, saying more than 900 police have been injured since the start of the protests. But critics argued that although some demonstrators have engaged in violence, they represent a minority and the actions of a few risk overshadowing the grievances of the wider movement.
The government has also faced criticism over its response to the protests, including the detention of thousands of minors and the use of force against young demonstrators.
More than 6,700 children had been taken into police custody since mid-September, according to reports published this week.
Human rights lawyers said several teenage students have suffered warlike injuries.
Two cases have drawn particular attention: A 15-year-old lost his hand in the explosion of a stun grenade outside a school in the northern city of Lens, and a 16-year-old in western Tours lost his sight due to an injury caused by a rubber bullet.
There are fears of further clashes on Saturday.
“This is a moment of fatigue in the country,” Prime Minister Sebastian Lecornu said on Thursday. “We are in an atmosphere of perma-crisis: wars, inflation and issues surrounding purchasing power.”
The government has accused the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of inflaming the protests. The party has rejected the accusation.
While France suspended the use of stun grenades for the student demonstrations, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Friday that he authorised police to use them in the event of what he called “urban violence”.
Nunez also said he is expecting a “fairly significant” turnout on Saturday.
Hundreds of protest sites
Calls on social media for members of past protest movements to join the current one have been made for weeks. The website 17octobregiletjaune.net, which tracks “yellow vest” actions, listed more than 1,750 planned protest locations across the country.
The government has tried to quell student anger by scrapping plans to increase some higher education registration fees and promising to deploy 3,000 substitute teachers to high schools. This week, it set up a national online survey for pupils to hear their concerns.
But Mathieu Roger-Lacan, a French literature teacher in a disadvantaged area and author of A Language of One’s Own, a book about the growing language gap, argued that these measures fail to address the deeper problem: an education system that struggles to provide equal opportunities.
“If you have a pool that is leaking, the answer should not be to put more water into it but to work on its structure – and that costs money too,” he said.
For Roger-Lacan, the problem is not simply how much France spends on education but how it distributes those resources.
A government report published this week said that 32 percent of the French education ministry’s budget for next year will go towards funding the pensions of retired civil servants.
Students are not only complaining about deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms but also expressing a deeper anxiety about their future.
For many, a diploma no longer feels like a guarantee of stable employment or social mobility. That concern is compounded by questions about the quality of education itself amid evidence of persistent weaknesses in French students’ academic performance.
In September, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) said that French 15-year-olds’ results in mathematics and reading had fallen to among their lowest levels on record.
“There is a gap between the diploma we give at the end of school, which is given to a huge part of the population, and the reality around us, which is that many of these young students have great difficulties even in writing French,” Roger-Lacan said.
Competing demands
The protests come at a very difficult time for the government, which is caught between demands for better-funded public services and the need to rein in France’s debt.
The government recorded a deficit of 152.5 billion euros ($171.3bn) last year, equivalent to 5.1 percent of France’s gross domestic product (GDP). By contrast, the European Union average is 3.1 percent.
Meanwhile, public debt ballooned to 115.6 percent of GDP, the third highest in the EU after Greece and Italy.
Lecornu’s proposed 2027 budget seeks to reduce the deficit through spending restraint and tax measures, including a freeze on public sector pay and limits on pension increases.
Whether the government can make those savings without deepening public anger is another question.
The debate touches a nerve in France, where the welfare state and access to public services remain central political issues.
Macron’s decision to raise the retirement age from 62 to 64 triggered months of mass demonstrations in 2023, exposing deep opposition to reforms that many saw as unfairly burdening workers.
Now as the government prepares its next budget, it faces the challenge of persuading the public that spending cuts and other savings are necessary without further eroding confidence in public institutions.
The political stakes are high. The budget bill will be debated in a deeply divided parliament as parties position themselves before the 2027 presidential election, which will mark the end of Macron’s presidency.

Tunisians stage biggest protest in years against President Saied
TUNIS, Oct 17 - Thousands of Tunisians joined the largest protest against President Kais Saied in years on Saturday, accusing him of undermining democracy and mishandling the economy in a growing challenge to his rule.
The demonstration, led by the powerful UGTT labour union and civil society groups, comes as Tunisia grapples with an economic crisis, worsening public services, recurring water and power cuts, and shortages of medicines and essential goods.
In 2021, Saied seized broad powers, dissolved parliament, dismissed dozens of judges and began ruling by decree, moves opponents described as a coup.
Rights groups say he has intensified a crackdown on civil society, journalists and opposition figures. Saied rejects those allegations, saying he is not a dictator, and has accused his opponents of engineering economic crises to fuel social unrest.
In a rare show of unity, opposition parties from across the political spectrum joined lawyers, doctors, journalists, unemployed people and civil society groups in marching along Habib Bourguiba Avenue, a focal point of the 2011 protests that helped trigger the Arab Spring uprisings.
The protest poses a significant challenge to Saied after years of divisions weakened the opposition's ability to mobilise large crowds.
Hundreds of police were deployed across the capital.
Protesters chanted: "No fear, power belongs to the people" and "Prisons are full, people are hungry".
They called for the release of Saied's critics and demanded an end to what they described as attacks on trade union rights. Others carried banners expressing frustration over unemployment and pollution.
"Enough is enough! The country is collapsing. We suffer from power and water cuts, and one crisis after another", said Yassine Gharseli, a protester from Sfax, about 250 km (155 miles) south of Tunis.
"I came from Sfax to stand up for my freedom and I'm not ready to give up, even if I become the last voice in the country," he added. REUTERS

The initiative could strengthen transport links between Southeast and Central Asia and create additional opportunities for access to European markets.
Digitalization, artificial intelligence and tourism were also identified as promising areas for future cooperation.

"A prosecutor from the Office of the Prosecutor General has been detained on suspicion of violating traffic safety rules, resulting in a person's death. According to preliminary information, on the evening of October 15, 2026, near the settlement of Stavyshche in Kyiv region, the driver of a Renault struck a pedestrian and left the scene of the traffic accident. ====================================================================================================

Beyond oil: The Gulf crisis is becoming a food security crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:18:06 UTC
20:18:06 KST

Ask most people what the Gulf crisis will cost the world and they will say oil. Fair enough. Prices are the part we can watch every morning. But the bill that worries me more will arrive later and quietly: a farmer who buys less fertilizer than he needs, a thinner harvest, a family that can no longer afford a decent meal.
Two things are happening at once. The Gulf states import most of what they eat, so every delayed ship is a problem for their own tables. And the same region sells the raw materials that farmers elsewhere rely on to grow food. Block the sea lanes and you hurt the people eating in the Gulf and the people growing crops thousands of kilometres away.
On 14th October, UN Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva, who leads the UN task force on fertilizer shipments, warned that failure to reach an agreement could bring a food-security crisis to parts of Asia and Africa. His mechanism, he said, could start working within seven to ten days of a deal between Washington and Tehran. The scale of what he asked for is striking. Five vessels a day would be enough to keep fertilizer flowing to the countries most in need. Five ships, in a conflict that has put whole fleets at risk.
Why does this matter so much? Because of what the Gulf supplies. The FAO Director-General has said the region provides roughly 30–35 per cent of the world’s urea, about half of its sulphur exports and 20–30 per cent of its ammonia. FAO’s estimates, as reported by Fertilizer Daily, put the fertilizer trade delayed each month at between 1.5 and three million tonnes. Those are not cargoes sitting in a warehouse waiting for better days. They are next season’s wheat, rice and maize.
Farming does not negotiate. Fertilizer that arrives after the right weeks have passed cannot undo the damage, and no ceasefire can bring back a missed window.
Moreira da Silva made the same point in May, saying the planting season cannot wait. He also said that even if the strait reopened immediately, getting back to normal would take three to four months.
That gap between cause and effect is what makes this crisis easy to miss. Input prices jump at once. Smaller harvests show up in the statistics many months later, by which time the chance to prevent them is gone. Governments watching only the daily oil price are watching the wrong clock. They need to read this crisis against the planting and fertilizer calendar.
READ: Gulf countries seek alternative export routes amid Hormuz crisis
Freight adds another layer. Reuters reported on October 13 that oil shipping costs had hit new highs, with Hormuz risks among the causes. A few days earlier, the cost of hiring a supertanker to carry US oil to Asia had passed $77 million, over 700 per cent above its 2025 average. Dearer fuel raises the price of running a tractor, trucking inputs to a village and delivering food to a market. A country that buys little from the Gulf can still pay more for dinner.
The Gulf itself is hardly safe. Reuters has described the region as 80–90 per cent dependent on imported food, and Chatham House’s Neil Quilliam told the agency that over 70 per cent of GCC food comes in through Hormuz. He added that stockpiles and wider supplier networks could carry the region for only a few months. Money helps. It buys cargo and pays for air freight. It does not make a ship move through a closed passage.
There is a lesson here that goes beyond the Gulf. Buying from ten countries is not the same as having ten routes. If every shipment must pass through one strait, one port or one distribution hub, the diversity exists on paper only. Reserves give a government time, but only if they can be replaced and moved quickly.
Real food security means following a sack of grain from the foreign supplier to the local shop: the ship, the port, the warehouse, customs, the truck. If any one link fails, the rest count for little.
Nor will the pain be shared fairly. A large agribusiness can draw on stocks, credit and other suppliers. A small farmer facing a higher price simply buys less, or plants less. A well-off household grumbles about the grocery bill; a poor one skips meals. Hunger can grow even when shelves are full, because people can no longer afford what is on them.
Pakistan should not assume it is either safe or doomed. It should find out. How much fertilizer do we produce, how much do we import, what is in stock, when is the next delivery due, and can a farmer in a given district actually afford it? National totals can hide a great deal. A tonne in a warehouse in Karachi does nothing for a grower who needs it in the right district, at a price he can pay, in the right week of the crop cycle. Preparedness is measured at the farm gate, and the numbers should be published so that farmers, provinces and traders can plan. National totals can hide a great deal. A tonne in a warehouse in Karachi does nothing for a grower who needs it in the right district, at a price he can pay, in the right week of the crop cycle. Preparedness is measured at the farm gate, and the numbers should be published so that farmers, provinces and traders can plan.
The good news is that a diplomatic answer already exists. The UN task force has designed a mechanism built on registering vessels, keeping them out of each other’s way, monitoring, verifying and reporting, modelled on earlier UN-backed arrangements for grain. It covers fertilizer and related inputs only, and it is meant to be temporary. It does not claim to settle freedom of navigation. UN officials say it was developed in consultation with the parties and has drawn strong support from member states, especially the poorer countries that depend on fertilizer imports. The idea is to build a little trust while the larger talks go on.
Governments that care about food prices should say so loudly and put weight behind it. But a protected lane on paper is not a protected lane at sea. Crews, shipowners, insurers and port operators will use it only if they believe it is safe. The test is simple: how much fertilizer arrives, how predictable the sailing times are, and whether farmers get what they need before the window shuts.
READ: Iran’s navy reports oil tanker fire in Gulf of Oman
Looking further ahead, the crisis makes a strong case for routes that do not depend on one strait. Oman’s ports at Sohar, Duqm and Salalah sit outside Hormuz and connect to global shipping, so they are a natural place to start. But a port on the right side of the map is only the first step. Food landed there still has to travel on, by road or by sea, and that takes trucks, border clearances, cold storage and money. Moreira da Silva has also pointed to attacks in the Red Sea and on Black Sea cargo vessels as adding to the pressure on global food supplies. Escaping one chokepoint only to meet delay or cost at the next is not much of an escape.
One idea that deserves serious study is a corridor linking Central Asian producers through Afghanistan and Pakistan to Arabian Sea ports, and from there to Oman and the Gulf.
I would treat it as a long-term business proposition, tested against real demand, freight rates and reliability, and not as an answer to this season’s emergency. It would need far more than a road. Traders would want open borders they can count on, transit rules that are actually enforced, fast customs, warehouses and, for fresh produce, a cold chain that never breaks. The hardest question is political. Would Pakistan and Afghanistan keep transit open through a bad patch in their relations? A corridor that closes whenever tempers rise just swaps one risk for another. Shared profit may encourage both sides to keep it running, but encouragement is not a guarantee.
If Pakistan wants a role, reliability will earn it. Food traders care about clearance times, honest charges and cargo that arrives intact far more than they care about grand announcements. Gulf partners might back it through purchase commitments, logistics deals or investment in storage and distribution that makes commercial sense, with clear responsibilities and protection against disruption.
None of this replaces the urgent job of getting this season’s shipments through. Importing countries should say openly what stocks they hold and what is due to arrive, compare it with what their crops need, and buy together where that helps. Help should go first to the farmers whose harvests are most at risk, along with sensible advice on how to use less fertilizer well. Poor households need protection too. FAO has urged governments to keep trade open, be transparent about markets and target social support. Each government panicking alone only makes prices swing more.
A global food crisis is a risk, not a certainty. How bad it gets will depend on how long the disruption lasts, what other supplies appear, the weather, the size of stocks and the decisions governments make. Corridors will not rescue anyone this season, and nobody should pretend otherwise.
So the work divides into three. Diplomats must get the cargo moving. Governments at home must look after their farmers and their poorest families. And over the longer run, investors and planners must build supply lines that can lose one route and yet survive.
In the end, the people who will judge this crisis have no say in how it is fought. For them, security at sea means fertilizer in the shop, a harvest in the field and bread they can afford. Oil prices show one cost of this war within hours. A failed harvest shows another within months. The world should count both.

Congress gave Trump 30 days to hit Russia’s oil buyers with 100% tariffs. He waives them two days before deadline, citing US interests. Moscow calls it historic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:15:35 UTC
20:15:35 KST

US President Donald Trump has suspended the tariffs and sanctions on the biggest buyers of Russian oil set by the Lindsey Graham Act, the law he signed himself in September. He says the move serves US national interests, according to an executive order published on the White House site.
The act required the president, within 30 days, to impose 100% tariffs on all goods from the five biggest buyers of Russian oil, to sanction a range of Russian entities and to put 500% tariffs on all Russian energy imports to the US. The deadline for those measures fell on 18 October.
Trump has used the president’s power under Section 115 of the Graham Act, which allows him to waive sanctions, restrictions, and duties by certifying to Congress in writing that doing so serves US national interests and submitting a report explaining why. The act does not, however, allow him to cancel sanctions that have already been announced.
Moscow calls it historic, Kyiv calls it a gift to Putin
The two capitals read the same order in opposite ways. Kirill Dmitriev, an envoy for Russian leader Vladimir Putin, called it “an important and truly historic moment” on X, claiming the sanctions had mainly harmed the US economy and world markets.
“Economic cooperation between Russia and the US serves the interests of both nations, contributes to global economic stability and lays the foundation for building trust and achieving lasting peace,” Dmitriev writes.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy answered from under fire. Russia struck Ukraine’s energy system on 17 October, and at that very moment Washington chose “to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law, which was supposed to impose real, effective pressure on Russia to end this war,” he says.
A law its own backers say is being gutted
The waiver lands amid a bipartisan revolt in Congress. Seven Republican and Democratic senators had already warned on 11 October that Trump’s move to allow Russian diesel imports had broken the law Congress passed after the full-scale invasion, urging the administration to reverse it so US money would not help finance Russia’s war.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy argued the law can still work if Washington lets it.
“This law could, and still can, help a great deal. But the law has actually to work, and every vote for it matters,” he said, warning that the step only pushes Moscow to strike harder.
The world must not give up ground and must try to end the war, Zelenskyy added.
“To end it, and not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely,” he stressed, thanking everyone who “is truly fighting for peace and helping Ukraine," he stated.
The word from the Ukrainian opposition
The Ukrainian opposition also commented on Trump’s decision. Iryna Herashchenko, co-chair of the European Solidarity parliamentary faction, said that “the most cynical and stupid decisions are usually made by rulers on Saturday night,” when public attention is scattered, and people are preparing for the weekend.
“Rehabilitating Putin harms not only Ukraine but also the US itself, strengthens the axis of authoritarian regimes, and undermines international security,” she claimed.

Plants move to get away from their decaying brethren
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:11:26 UTC
20:11:26 KST

Plants seem stationary: they don’t skip, fly or walk around. But that doesn’t mean they don’t move. The organisms bend their roots and shoots in response to stimuli such as water, light, salt and gravity. These responsive movements, called tropisms, are crucial for plants’ survival.
Now researchers have discovered a new way plants move, which they call “saprotropism”: the bending of roots to avoid dead or rotting plant tissue. The results were published in Science.
The discovery began with a failed experiment and an unexpected observation. Yuzhou Zhang, a biologist at Northwest A&F University in China, was studying how plants move in response to gravity in a laboratory in Austria when one of his agar plates became contaminated with airborne microbes. Just before he threw it away, he noticed something striking: almost every single one of the plants’ roots in the plate was bent away from the spoilage. The consistency “immediately made me wonder whether this was more than a random response,” Zhang says.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
His team decided to investigate further. The researchers grew the common research plant Arabidopsis thaliana in containers, some of which were dotted with patches of rotting apple. The plants that encountered “decay zones” bent their roots to avoid the bad apple, whereas the ones in containers lacking decay grew straight through. Repeating the experiment with other plants, including tomatoes and wheat, yielded similar results—but an encounter with putrefying animal tissues had no effect. Zhang and his colleagues theorize that this reaction might help plants avoid pathogens, similar to the way unpleasant smells help animals steer clear of rotten food.
Saprotropism seems to operate differently than most other plant tropisms. “It does not follow the classical mechanism,” Zhang says. For example, gravitropism, or movement in response to gravity, and phototropism—in response to light—occur when plants redistribute the hormone auxin in their stems or roots, causing them to change their growth direction.
In contrast, saprotropism relies on a hormone called abscisic acid (ABA). When the plant roots encounter an area acidified by decaying plant matter—a chemical gradient distinct from that of animal matter—ABA builds up on the side facing the rot, encouraging growth in the other direction.
The work’s scope is impressive, says Chris Wolverton, a plant biologist at Ohio Wesleyan University, who was not involved in the study. He adds, however, that “there’s still a lot of open space in the signaling mechanism for more detail to get fleshed out.” At what point, for instance, does decaying plant tissue break down enough to become nutritious compost?
Zhang’s team hopes to fill those gaps in future studies. Ultimately the research could help illuminate how plants sense and interact with the world around them.

Trump eases Russia oil sanctions, but is Europe still buying Moscow’s gas?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:10:22 UTC
20:10:22 KST

Trump eases Russia oil sanctions, but is Europe still buying Moscow’s gas?
Analysts say Russia will benefit most from US sanctions waiver.
United States President Donald Trump has signed an executive order waiving newly-passed Russia sanctions, claiming the move is in the US’s “national interest”.
Earlier this month, Trump also announced a deal to bring stocks of Russian diesel into global markets, in a bid to drive down energy prices that have spiked during the US-Israel war on Iran. The US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel sales until April 2027.
Trump’s embrace of Russian energy has angered Ukraine, European partners and many US officials, who say the move rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war against its neighbour.
Ukraine’s President Volodmyr Zelenskyy slammed Trump’s diesel deal as “a gift” to Russia’s President Vladimir Putin that will help fund his war effort.
While European countries have also criticised Trump’s embrace of Russian energy, the US president has accused them of “hypocrisy”, as figures show that European Union countries continue to import Russian gas.
Here’s what we know:
Which sanctions has Trump waived?
In his executive order on Friday, Trump called off numerous planned Russia-related sanctions days before they were due to take effect, including duties on Russian goods and penalties for buying the country’s oil and gas.
The now-blocked measures were part of legislation passed in Congress with bipartisan support last month, named after the late US Senator Lindsay Graham, an outspoken critic of Russia.
They would have included up to 100 percent tariffs on all goods brought into the US from the five top importers of Russian crude oil or gas, including China and India. They could also have imposed equal penalties on countries deemed to have knowingly bought oil or gas from Russia 30 days after the law’s implementation, or to be among the top five countries helping Moscow circumvent sanctions on sales of its oil.
The waiver will hold until the Trump administration believes “further action is appropriate”, according to the executive order.
US Congressman Don Beyer, a Democrat from Virginia, said the sanctions waiver amounts to a “surrender to Putin” that “betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent”.
Who will benefit from this?
Vasily Astrov, an economist at the Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the Russian government will likely be the greatest beneficiary because the easing of sanctions means Russian oil will not have to be further discounted.
He estimated that about 60 cents of every extra dollar in the price of a barrel of Russian oil would “end up in state coffers”.
Russian official Kirill Dmitriev, an envoy for Putin, hailed the US decision to waive the sanctions as “an important and truly historic moment”.
Other beneficiaries include major importers of Russian oil and gas, such as China and India, who are now less exposed to the risk of secondary US penalties.
While Trump hopes the measures will also help bring down oil prices for US consumers before November mid-term elections, experts say that is less certain.
Addressing the US’s recent diesel deal with Russia, EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis said it is unlikely to have a significant impact on global prices.
According to Trump, that deal would bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel into US and global markets “immediately”, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November, and 1 million tonnes afterwards.
“If we look at the volumes, they are not of any macroeconomic significance, and frankly, there are strong doubts whether Russia is even able to supply those volumes, and according also to US quality standards, those are big question marks,” Dombrovskis told the AFP news agency.
Which countries still buy oil from Russia?
China and India are the largest buyers of Russian crude oil, purchasing 6 billion euros ($6.74bn) and 3.6 billion euros ($4.04bn) worth respectively in September, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a nonprofit think tank.
Hungary and Slovakia, the landlocked EU members that have exemptions to the bloc’s ban on Russian crude, also remain big customers, buying a combined 290 million euros ($326m) worth of the commodity in September, said CREA. Turkiye imported 172 million euros ($193m) worth of Russian crude oil the same month, the think tank added.
Since the end of 2022, the largest importers of Russian oil products, which include diesel, have been Turkiye, China, Saudi Arabia, Brazil and Singapore.
Saudi Arabia imported the most Russian oil products in September at 534 million euros ($600m), followed by Turkiye with 321 million euros ($361m), China with 304 million euros ($342m) and India with 161 million euros ($181m).
Is Europe buying increasing amounts of gas from Russia?
“The European Council regrets the United States’ decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel,” European leaders said in a joint statement adopted following a two-day European Council meeting in Brussels this week.
But despite its own near-blanket ban on Russian oil, the EU has continued to import large quantities of Russian gas, though it plans to phase out those imports next year.
Urgewald, a Germany-based group that researches coal companies, reported this week that more than 12 million tonnes of Russian Arctic LNG was transported into EU ports from January to September this year, a 9.5 percent jump from the same period last year.
In September, EU countries imported 817 million euros ($918m) of pipeline gas, and 615 million euros ($691m) of liquefied natural gas (LNG), according to CREA.
EU members France and the Netherlands were the largest LNG importers, bringing in 446 million euros ($501m) and 116 million euros ($130m) respectively, according to the think tank. France’s LNG imports represented a 103 percent increase from the previous month, it added.
France’s President Emmanuel Macron has been among the most outspoken about Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, saying on Friday that it “sends a negative message” and would have no impact on global prices.
Hungary imported the most Russian pipeline gas of any EU member by far during the month, with 414 million euros ($465m) worth. Slovakia and Bulgaria brought in 161 million euros ($181m) and 132 million euros ($148m), respectively, according to CREA data.

Syria’s Kurdish autonomy is fading as Arab unrest challenges Damascus’s control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:10:04 UTC
20:10:04 KST

Sunni Arab Syrians held large-scale demonstrations after Friday prayers in the northern Syrian city of Hasakah. The demonstrators, many of whom were members of Arab tribes, came from neighborhoods surrounding Hasakah, with some arriving from the adjoining Deir al-Zur province in Syria’s southeast.
Protesters assembled outside the Abu Bakr al-Siddiq Mosque in Ghweiran, where the protests began last week. After Friday prayers, they marched to the city’s main square, Liberation Square, carrying the flag of the new Syrian regime. The demonstrators were accompanied by members of the government’s internal security forces.
Regional outlets have given the unrest in Hasakah over the last week only minor attention, and almost none in the international media. The tensions in the city are noteworthy, however, because they attest to the ongoing instability bubbling beneath the surface in Syria, even as the new regime seeks to present an image of firm and exclusive authority.
Hasakah was the main city of the Kurdish-led Autonomous Administration of Northeast Syria, prior to the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. The Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), which partnered with the US-led coalition in the fight against Islamic State in the 2014-19 period, were the armed element of that administration.
However, after a swift military push by the Damascus government across the Euphrates in January, the SDF and the administration quickly agreed to dissolve. An agreement concluded on January 29 formally terminated the autonomous administration, and the SDF was formally dissolved on August 26.
But while the Kurdish-led authority was dissolved on paper, many of its institutions continued to function in reality. The SDF’s leaders deliberately sought to avoid confronting the new authorities. They understood that without external backing or protection, following the US abandonment of the Kurds and withdrawal, such a path would surely lead to bloodshed and their own forceful suppression.
Instead, they have sought to preserve as much autonomy as possible while remaining in formal cooperation with the central authorities. At the same time, semi-independent Kurdish political formations linked to the circles of the SDF remain.
This approach derives from a basic mistrust between the Kurdish structures and the new authorities, combined with the Kurds’ desire to make the best of the new situation and avoid the government-facilitated sectarian slaughters that have taken place in the Druze south and the Alawi western coastal area since the fall of the Assad regime.
The Syrian Kurds note the apparent reluctance of the Damascus authorities to punish those elements among its supporters who have engaged in violence against minorities. Only a tiny number of people have been tried, and only one or two convicted for involvement in the sectarian massacres in Sweida and Latakia.
Arab population appears determined to force the dissolution of Kurdish autonomous structures
THE LATEST incidents appear to derive from a determination by elements among the Arab population of Hasakah to force the pace of the dissolution of the Kurdish-led autonomous structures, and to demand the imposition by the central authorities in Damascus of speedy, full, and immediate control.
A source in the Kurdish authority in Hasakah told The Jerusalem Post: “The situation began approximately a week ago, when a coordinated campaign emerged on social media involving fake accounts and certain Syrians residing in Europe, particularly Germany.
“These accounts called upon Arab residents of the Ghweiran neighborhood in Hasakah to organize demonstrations and raise the Syrian national flag in the city center, under the pretext of ‘restoring state authority’ throughout Syrian territory.
“The Kurdish governor of Hasakah and the local authorities had already decided to raise the Syrian flag themselves during an official ceremony. But the social media campaign continued, calling on people from outside Hasakah city and the governorate to participate.
“It is particularly significant that the local Arab tribal leaders did not participate in these demonstrations. Instead, the gatherings consisted largely of groups of young agitators, including individuals reportedly associated with the former Islamic State and elements of the former Ba’athist establishment.
“During the demonstrations, participants raised portraits of Saddam Hussein, chanted inflammatory and explicitly sectarian slogans, including ‘Syria without minorities,’ and attacked Kurdish national symbols, flags, and banners. These actions appeared deliberately calculated to provoke a Kurdish reaction and potentially trigger wider ethnic confrontation.”
The source in Hasakah added: “These developments raise serious questions about the intentions of certain elements within Damascus. There are strong grounds to suspect that factions opposed to the integration process are actively seeking to undermine its implementation.
“These factions are believed to maintain close ties with Turkey, which may itself be encouraging such destabilizing activities, given Ankara’s apparent dissatisfaction with certain aspects of the integration agreement and its outcomes.”
'There is no deterrence or law to stop the tension in Hasakah by the government'
THE ROLE OF the Damascus authorities in the latest events remains open to question. A civilian source in Hasakah told the Post: “There is no deterrence or law to stop the tension in Hasakah by the government. Kurds and Arabs started to become afraid of moving inside the city. The risk of kidnapping has started to rise.”
The source from the Hasakah authority suspects that a broader political agenda may lie behind the latest events, namely “to exploit divisions between Arab and Kurdish communities, particularly through the mobilization of sections of the Arab tribal population, to create conditions conducive to sectarian or ethnic confrontation.
“Should such tensions escalate into widespread violence, the Kurdish authorities could find themselves under considerable pressure to request intervention by the central government to restore order.
“Damascus could then use such a request, or the wider deterioration of security, as justification for deploying additional government forces and progressively assuming direct security and administrative control over Hasakah.
“This would bear certain similarities to the approach initially envisaged toward Sweida and its Druze population, whereby internal instability could provide a political and security justification for expanding central government authority.”
A report on the Enab Baladi website, meanwhile, which is sympathetic to the Damascus authorities, blamed the Kurdish “Revolutionary Youth” for the tensions. This term is used to denote a Kurdish youth organization linked to the political organizations behind the Syrian Democratic Forces.
According to individuals quoted in the article, at Enab Baladi, the Revolutionary Youth established checkpoints in areas of the city, and “stopped passersby, searched their phones, and treated them in a humiliating manner.”
According to Abdulrahman al-Hassan, an Arab resident of Ghweiran, “The city was experiencing severe tensions because of the Revolutionary Youth’s conduct.” Al-Hassan said that in his assessment, “residents were not seeing sufficient intervention by government security forces to stop these practices or establish control throughout the city.”
In the period ahead, the stage appears to be set for further steps by the authorities in Damascus to terminate the remnants of Kurdish autonomy east of the Euphrates, and to extend the authority of the new Islamist regime to this area in its entirety.
Recent experience in southwest Syria indicates that such efforts have been conducted via a combination of local unrest, and then the entry of a combination of government-aligned “irregular” forces and official security forces into the area in question. The coming period will indicate whether such an effort is now beginning in northeast Syria.

Voices from the Arab press: Yemen’s fight to retake Sana'a mirrors Syria’s liberation of Damascus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:09:54 UTC
20:09:54 KST

Retaking Sanaa: Like Liberating Damascus
Asharq al-Awsat, London, October 10
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The current war in Yemen could bring about historic change, just as happened in Syria with the overthrow of another Iranian-backed regime.
Yemen’s internationally recognized government now controls more than two-thirds of the country and is fighting to reclaim the remainder. But that final third will be no walk in the park, given the terrain and military challenges involved. It may not be decided quickly, despite the gains achieved in the north and southwest.
This is a war against Iran’s Revolutionary Guard and Lebanon’s Hezbollah, whose operatives serve within the Houthi leadership and ranks.
This war differs in several important respects from the previous Yemen war, which began in 2015.
For years, the Houthi militia has operated under the supervision of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard. Its fighters are not the barefoot cave dwellers some portray them as. They have trained in Lebanon and Iraq and spent years preparing for this confrontation, making it another regional war with Tehran.
Reliable reports indicate that Abdul Reza Shahlai, a commander in Iran’s Quds Force, directed the Houthis’ latest offensive on the Tihama plain.
Several new factors distinguish today’s war from yesterday’s.
The international community, once divided, is now almost united against the Houthis and increasingly convinced that this is a just war on behalf of the Yemeni people. The conflict has also become a matter of regional security and international trade. There is now a desire to end Houthi control, as part of a broader effort to reduce Iranian influence in the region, an effort that reached a milestone with the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime nearly two years ago.
During the previous war, Britain and the US sought to prevent an advance toward Hodeidah and Sanaa, believing that a political settlement through the Stockholm negotiations would achieve the desired outcome.
After nearly a decade of Houthi rule, however, it has become clear that the movement differs little from terrorist organizations such as ISIS and Hezbollah. It is another branch of the Iranian regime’s network, notwithstanding certain differences.
The Houthis have become an even greater international threat this year, as the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has grown in strategic importance.
With the Strait of Hormuz nearly closed because of the war with Iran, the Red Sea has become an alternative outlet for energy exports.
In coordination with Tehran, the Houthis announced their intention to close the strait. Consistent with Iran’s attacks on oil shipments, they declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia and began targeting its tankers. It was for this purpose that they seized Perim island and the Mocha area last month, both of which have recently been liberated.
Previously, the international community showed little interest in correcting Yemen’s disastrous situation. That changed when the crisis ceased to concern only Yemenis and their neighbors and became a threat to international shipping. The European Union, Britain and the American administration quickly condemned the Houthis and offered logistical support for operations against them.
If the current war achieves its objectives, it will end Houthi domination of the Yemeni people and bring relief to millions. Some 22 million Yemenis living under Houthi control could be rescued from the brink of famine and epidemics. According to World Health Organization figures, cholera cases have tripled in just three weeks. Millions of children could return to school after years without education.
The extremist religious movement has also transformed Yemen into a transit route for people fleeing wars and famine in East Africa, a corridor for drug smugglers and a haven for al-Qaeda and ISIS, both of which operate there and maintain dealings with the Houthis. The movement also has an arms-smuggling relationship with the Somalia-based terrorist organization al-Shabaab.
Twelve years have passed since the Houthis forcibly seized Sanaa. Like Lebanon’s Hezbollah, they imposed their rule through coercion, adopted a similar name – Ansar Allah – and displayed portraits of their leaders.
This war is different from previous wars and skirmishes. For the first time, Yemen’s legitimate government is fighting as a unified force, bringing together diverse Yemeni factions under one banner. Earlier confrontations were largely fought by the Arab coalition alongside government forces with limited domestic reach.
The coming weeks and months could prove decisive. The chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council has clearly identified the objective: the liberation of Sanaa.
If Yemenis succeed in defeating Iran’s proxy, it will constitute a major regional victory, much like the achievement of Ahmed al-Sharaa’s forces when they advanced from Idlib province and liberated the Syrian capital from Assad’s regime. – Abdulrahman Al-Rashed
Iraq’s Kurds: Little Choice But To Work With Baghdad
An-Nahar, Lebanon, October 9
As Iraq celebrates the withdrawal of coalition forces from its territory, Iraqi Kurds are hardly in a celebratory mood. A Kurdish researcher at the London Dialogue research center believes the withdrawal calls for a funeral rather than a celebration.
“It is not good, but it is an Iraqi decision,” said Sirwan Barzani, a Kurdish military commander turned businessman. “They asked them to come to their country, and now they are telling them they are no longer needed.”
Barzani warned of renewed activity by ISIS terrorists. His forces and those of the Iraqi government have observed four or five Islamist cells operating near Makhmour in Nineveh province after months of inactivity. This is an alarming development.
“We know what happened in 2014. There will certainly be terrorist cell activity now, and we can already see it.”
Iraqi and Kurdish forces are nevertheless better trained and organized than they were in 2014, when ISIS captured a third of Iraq and extensive areas of Syria. The organization was eventually driven out of Iraq in 2017 and Syria in 2019 through counteroffensives by local forces supported by the international coalition.
In 2024, Iraqi and Iranian officials agreed that coalition forces would withdraw from Iraq by September 30, 2026.
Today, however, the greatest threat to Iraqi Kurds is not ISIS but continuing Iranian drone attacks, occurring amid the confrontation between Washington and Tehran and the possibility that Iraqi Kurds could help their Iranian counterparts conduct operations against the Islamic Republic.
On the very day coalition forces withdrew, an Iranian drone struck a civilian camp housing Iranian Kurds near Iraqi Kurdistan.
Since February 28, when the US and Israel launched their attack on Iran, the Kurdish Region of Iraq has faced approximately 1,000 drone and missile attacks from Iran and Iraqi armed groups loyal to it. These attacks have killed around 32 people, including 19 members of Iranian Kurdish parties.
In March, rumors circulated that Iranian Kurdish forces would launch a ground invasion of Iran with American and Israeli backing, but no such operation materialized.
On September 27, the Kurdistan Regional Government’s media office confirmed that Iranian Kurdish groups were aware of the 2023 security agreement between Erbil, Baghdad, and Tehran, intended to prevent armed Iranian Kurdish organizations from attacking neighboring countries.
Meanwhile, Iraq had set September 20 as the deadline for disarming Iraqi militias in response to American pressure, only to postpone it until June 30, 2027.
“The foremost internal Iraqi threat comes from pro-Iranian militias, which have attacked Iraqi Kurdistan and neighboring countries more than 100 times this year,” said retired US Army Col. Myles Caggins, a former coalition spokesman.
Baghdad faces a substantial challenge in confronting these illegal militias, which continue launching drones without serious consequences.
Barzani therefore believes the Kurds must be provided with air defenses. After all, this is Iraqi airspace. Even if Iraq itself lacks adequate defenses, it will remain vulnerable to these threats, and the hope is that any new air-defense systems supplied to Baghdad will also be extended to Kurdistan.
Joey Hood, a former senior State Department official for Near Eastern affairs who also served in Iraq, considers it unlikely that Iranian attacks across the Middle East, including Iraqi Kurdistan, will cease.
Iran has targeted not only American troops but also American interests, using that justification to strike a power station in Kurdistan and a water-analysis facility in Kuwait.
The federal government in Baghdad and the regional government in Erbil must work together, with partners such as the US, to acquire and deploy air-defense systems capable of countering these attacks.
Even before the American-Iranian war, Iran and its affiliated groups targeted positions belonging to Iranian opposition forces, Kurdish oil and gas facilities, and Kurdish businessmen.
On January 16, 2024, for example, Kurdish billionaire Peshraw Dizayee and his 11-year-old daughter were killed in a ballistic missile strike that Iran justified by claiming it had targeted an Israeli espionage headquarters.
On September 30, US Central Command chief Brad Cooper stated that Iraqi security forces, including the Kurdish Peshmerga, now possess the capabilities, leadership, and operational independence needed to confront threats to their territory. Yet another CENTCOM officer expressed concern that Baghdad would show little interest in protecting Kurdish areas, particularly amid fears of incursions across their boundaries.
The Kurds must therefore increasingly rely on themselves and on their relationship with Baghdad, according to a coalition official who previously advised the Peshmerga.
Unfortunately, the coalition is now leaving. Its continued presence would have been valuable both for confronting ISIS and for maintaining military assistance. Only time will tell whether these concerns prove justified.
At a farewell ceremony for American troops, Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani acknowledged one reality the Kurds cannot avoid: their growing dependence on Baghdad. This means entering a formative stage in which Iraq itself must assume an active and meaningful national role. – Sarkis Naoum
Resuming the Iran War: Congress vs Pentagon
Al-Ittihad, UAE, October 10
Developments within the Pentagon and Congress, alongside competing centers of influence in the American decision-making establishment, particularly the administration itself, reveal a growing dispute over how the war with Iran should be managed, how much should be spent on it, the mechanisms of oversight, and the limits of authority in conducting military operations.
Differences over the war have spread from Democratic leaders to figures within the Republican Party, many of them supporters of President Donald Trump. The debate also involves military and political leaders and reaches as far as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth himself.
At the heart of these disagreements are the war’s cost and the prospect of continued operations. Expenditure had already reached $43 billion by September, including additional costs and nearly $28b. for replenishing ammunition and other requested allocations.
This has prompted lawmakers from both parties to demand comprehensive accounting of operational costs, damage sustained by American bases, and the expense of repairing aircraft, ships, and other equipment.
The Congressional Budget Office has also presented estimates of the war’s costs and its impact on military stockpiles, further complicating the administration’s request for at least $67b. in additional funding. This comes alongside a proposed defense budget that could reach $1 trillion in 2027, with the possibility of still greater spending should full-scale war resume.
The central disagreement is that the Pentagon seeks additional resources, while Congress wants to define the objectives for which money may be allocated and restrict its use. Lawmakers from both parties may not fully appreciate the breadth of the military requirements involved.
The War Powers Resolution of 1973 will undoubtedly remain a source of contention if war with Iran resumes, particularly over whether Congress must approve a declaration of war or provide explicit authorization for military action.
There is also concern about the effects of renewed military operations on the armed forces themselves, the performance of the defense secretary and senior commanders, and the broader turmoil within the military establishment. Recent dismissals and resignations, together with delays in military appointments, point to the possibility of further confusion and even disorder within one of America’s most strategically important institutions.
Members of Congress are therefore pressing for serious consultations and a firm approach rather than direct confrontation, especially as the US faces challenges extending well beyond the Middle East. These include the Indo-Pacific, the growing demands posed by China and Russia, and security concerns closer to Europe.
Washington must consider its readiness to confront multiple contingencies, including the possibility of simultaneous military engagements in different regions.
Congress is consequently moving to rebuild a framework of understanding with the administration without waiting for the midterm elections. Several military priorities cannot be postponed, including investment in strategic programs such as missile defense, interception systems, early warning capabilities, and space technology.
Congress is also expected to examine the scale of American military deployments worldwide.
Virtually every major military issue may now be reopened as Congress moves urgently to reaffirm its political role in national decision-making, while the Pentagon continues operating with Trump’s direct support.
The consequences will be felt in both funding for military operations and the authority to wage war. Proposed increases in the 2027 defense budget, particularly for research, development, and procurement, underscore the scale of the decisions awaiting lawmakers.
The disputes between Congress, the Pentagon, the administration, and influential military institutions are unlikely to disappear. All sides may also be waiting for the midterm elections before reassessing their policies. Each has its own priorities, and reconciling them will require greater agreement, candor, and transparency, as American military involvement in the Middle East continues and the possibility of renewed war with Iran remains.
For now, the major policies under consideration will remain politically contested. – Tarek Fahmy
Hosni Mubarak, Military Commander
Al-Masry Al-Youm, Egypt, October 8
The anniversary of Egypt’s great October victory has arrived, and we have heard much said about it, yet almost nothing about Hosni Mubarak. I mean Mubarak the commander of the Egyptian Air Force during the October War, not Mubarak the politician, whose legacy remains controversial and always will.
It is the military commander who concerns me here, for one simple reason: we should imagine what might have happened had the airstrike he led at the opening moment of the crossing of the Suez Canal failed. Any ground forces fighting on the battlefield remain exposed to the enemy unless they have air cover protecting their positions.
The initial airstrike under Mubarak’s command provided that protection. Without it, our forces would have found it extremely difficult to cross the Suez Canal itself, let alone penetrate the earthen defenses of the Bar Lev Line. This was Mubarak’s contribution, alongside the airmen under his command, and it deserves to be remembered.
One of the principal reasons for the crushing defeat of June 5, 1967, was that the enemy struck our aircraft while they were still on the ground. Once our air force had been neutralized, the enemy knew our ground forces were completely exposed. What followed were horrors almost beyond belief, as anyone reading the political memoirs of those dark days can attest.
The heroic Anwar Sadat absorbed that lesson, as did the Egyptian Air Force. When our army went into battle and secured victory on October 6, 1973, every soldier knew that Egyptian aircraft were protecting him from above. Our ground forces advanced and kept advancing because Mubarak and his pilots provided a protective aerial umbrella.
Nor was that his only achievement. The Battle of Mansoura was also fought under his command, and anyone familiar with its details knows that it stands almost without parallel in the history of aerial warfare. Military academies continue devoting extensive attention to it when teaching the landmark battles of military history.
Israel launched 120 aircraft to destroy air bases in the Nile Delta, only to find our air force waiting for them. An extraordinary aerial battle followed, lasting a full 53 minutes. By its conclusion on October 14, 1973, the Israeli aircraft had been divided into two groups: those destroyed and those forced to flee. Mubarak led that effort.
The Koran teaches: “Do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just.” In other words, disliking someone must not keep us from giving them the credit they deserve. Another verse instructs us: “Do not deprive people of what is rightfully theirs.”
We have deprived Mubarak the military commander – not Mubarak the politician, I repeat – of the recognition he deserves in many respects.
– Soliman Gouda ■

How public opinion on transgender bathroom access shifted between 2016 and 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:59 UTC
20:00:59 KST

Public opinion in the United States has grown more conservative regarding restroom access for transgender individuals over the past several years, a shift the researchers link to changing beliefs about safety and discrimination. When people hold conflicting views about the rights and risks involved in this debate, they are now much more likely to side with restrictive policies than they were in the past. These shifts are detailed in a new study published in Politics, Groups, and Identities.
Over the last decade, lawmakers across multiple states have proposed and passed legislation regulating which public restrooms transgender people can use. These bills typically require individuals to use facilities that match the sex listed on their original birth certificates rather than their current gender identities.
Public restrooms have historically served as a political battleground regarding gender, space, and safety. As the study notes, the modern sex-segregated restroom emerged during the Industrial Revolution as women entered the paid workforce. At the time, separate facilities were framed as necessary safe spaces for women. Similar arguments about restroom safety appeared during the mid-twentieth century to police the behavior of gay men, and again in the 1970s by opponents of the Equal Rights Amendment.
Today, political rhetoric surrounding transgender bathroom policies tends to rely on three main arguments. Proponents of bathroom restrictions often argue that allowing transgender women into women’s restrooms poses a security risk to women and children. Opponents counter this by framing bathroom restrictions as a form of discrimination against transgender people. They also argue that forcing transgender individuals into facilities that do not match their outward appearance places those individuals at physical risk.
Patrick R. Miller, a political scientist at Kent State University, led a team of researchers to investigate how these three political arguments influence public opinion. The researchers wanted to understand which of these beliefs resonate most with the public. They also wanted to see how Americans formulate their policy preferences when they happen to agree with arguments from both sides of the political aisle.
The research team utilized data from two nationally representative online surveys. The first survey polled 1,291 adults in 2016, a year when national media coverage of bathroom legislation peaked. The second survey polled 1,618 adults in 2022, a period when media attention on this specific issue had cooled but conservative political focus on transgender policies remained high.
In both surveys, participants read three statements reflecting the main political arguments about bathroom access. They rated their level of agreement on a seven-point scale. The statements asked whether unrestricted restroom access poses a security risk to women and children, whether restroom restrictions discriminate against transgender individuals, and whether such restrictions endanger the safety of transgender people.
Participants also indicated their ultimate policy preferences. They were asked whether they agreed or disagreed with the statement that transgender people should only be allowed to use public restrooms consistent with the sex listed on their official state identification cards.
To ensure their findings isolated the impact of specific arguments, the researchers applied a robust statistical model to the survey responses. They accounted for a wide range of demographic and psychological variables known to influence political opinions. These included age, sex, income, religious attendance, and political partisanship.
The team also measured underlying psychological traits, such as moral traditionalism, egalitarianism, and a person’s baseline sensitivity to disgust. By accounting for these broad traits, the researchers could better isolate how the three specific bathroom-related arguments independently swayed policy preferences.
The researchers found that overall support for restrictive bathroom policies grew between the two survey periods. In 2016, about 54 percent of respondents supported laws restricting restroom access based on state identification. By 2022, support for these restrictions had risen to roughly 62 percent.
When examining the underlying beliefs, the researchers noticed shifting patterns. The belief that transgender restroom access poses a security risk to women and children grew stronger in the population by 2022. At the same time, the belief that bathroom restrictions discriminate against transgender individuals also grew slightly, while concerns about the physical safety of transgender people remained relatively stable.
Because people do not always hold perfectly aligned political views, the research team looked closely at respondents who agreed with conflicting statements. A substantial portion of participants believed both that open restroom policies pose a security risk to women and that restrictive policies discriminate against transgender people. The way these conflicted individuals resolved their internal tension changed dramatically over the six-year gap.
In 2016, conflicted respondents were highly likely to resolve their ambivalence in favor of transgender rights. A person who held both beliefs had about a 62 percent chance of opposing restrictive bathroom policies. They appeared to discount their own security concerns and elevate their concerns about discrimination when deciding on a final policy stance.
By 2022, this pattern flipped entirely. Conflicted respondents became much more likely to support restrictive bathroom laws. A person holding those same competing beliefs in 2022 had only about a 29 percent chance of opposing bathroom restrictions. They began weighing the perceived security risks much more heavily than their concerns about discrimination.
The researchers also observed changes in how education influenced attitudes among political liberals. In 2016, highly educated liberals held the most consistently pro-transgender beliefs about the bathroom issue, standing apart from less educated liberals. By 2022, this educational divide vanished, as highly educated liberals shifted toward a more neutral stance that matched the rest of their ideological cohort.
The study relies on observational survey data, which means it cannot establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship between political messaging and changing public opinion. The surveys capture snapshots in time, and the researchers note that self-reported attitudes do not entirely capture how these policies operate in reality.
Future research could rely on experimental designs to test how specific messages or news frames actively alter a person’s viewpoint. Researchers might also investigate why the argument regarding the security of women and children remains so persuasive to the public, as previous studies have not found empirical evidence of an actual security threat linked to inclusive bathroom policies.
The study, “Policing gender in the bathroom: attitudes toward the transgender bathroom issue,” was authored by Patrick R. Miller, Andrew R. Flores, Donald P. Haider-Markel, Daniel C. Lewis, and Jami K. Taylor.

Plaque telling story of African-Caribbean prisoners in Britain stolen within days

2026-10-17

20:00:58 KST

The theft of a plaque in Hampshire that told the little-known story of African-Caribbean prisoners in 18th-century Britain reflects the enduring racism that has fuelled centuries of atrocities against Black and Indigenous Caribbean people, their descendants say.
Ronald Raymond McDonald, a professional drummer, was part of a delegation that travelled from Belize and elsewhere to Portchester Castle near Portsmouth last week to honour their ancestors: 2,500 men, women and children transported to Britain as prisoners of war in 1796.
McDonald, whose Garifuna ancestors from St Vincent and the Grenadines were among the prisoners, said he was heartbroken to learn that the plaque had been stolen and a nearby bench vandalised with hateful graffiti.
“Why would somebody do something like that when people are simply honouring their ancestors … it’s very sad,” he said.
The plaque, installed at the castle, commemorated the more than 2,000 prisoners held there, marking an extraordinary chapter of Black British history: one of the largest known arrivals of African-Caribbean people in Britain before the Windrush era.
The unveiling was part of a ceremony organised by the St Vincent and the Grenadines 2nd Generation (SV2G), in partnership with the University of Warwick and English Heritage, and was attended by Caribbean communities, diplomats, researchers and heritage organisations.
But days later, English Heritage staff discovered the plaque was missing. They said a padlock to one of the castle gates had been removed and the incident had been reported to police.
Garifuna advocate Princess Eulogia Gorden said the theft reflected “a spirit of racism that haunts generation after generation and hides in plain sight”. It was time, she said, to recognise that “we are all connected” and to end the hate.
Queen Mother Chief Freda Paulino-Sideroff, who is Garifuna and had travelled to the UK for the ceremony, was returning home to the US when she learned of the theft.
“Hate will never define who we are as a people. We are resilient survivors of our ancestors who have endured,” she said.
In the 1700s, her Garifuna ancestors were expelled from St Vincent by British forces and left to perish on the barren island of Baliceaux as Britain sought to crush decades of resistance to colonisation.
Emilio “Sásamu” Thomas, a Garifuna cultural ambassador who also travelled from Belize for the ceremony, echoed Paulino-Sideroff’s sentiments, saying Garifuna people would not allow themselves to be victimised.
His message to the perpetrators, he said, was: “Whatever pain that they are experiencing, we’re here to help them to relieve that pain.”
The missing plaque was meant to honour the prisoners, whose story, researchers say, had been largely lost to history. They came from a coalition that included formerly enslaved Africans, Caribbean-born people, Indigenous people and French soldiers who fought against British control of St Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines and Grenada. Their defeat and removal helped strengthen British rule in the region.
It was unveiled on 9 October, exactly 230 years after one of the ships carrying the prisoners was wrecked at Rapparee Cove in Devon, with many of those onboard losing their lives.
Iona Keen of English Heritage called the removal an act of vandalism, while University of Warwick professor Katherine Astbury said the plaque was intended to provide a visible memorial of the prisoners, and a reminder of “an important, forgotten part of Caribbean history”.
The vandalism came during Black History Month and amid renewed debate over slavery reparations. Campaigner and author Sir Patrick Vernon said vandalism of memorials representing Black British history had occurred repeatedly over decades, citing damage to other memorials.
He described the theft as symbolic of an “ongoing battle and the legacy of enslavement”.
Jacqueline Roberts, SV2G chief executive, said the theft could not erase history, and stressed the importance of continuing research to uncover more hidden stories.
“Our history is intertwined with British history,” she said. “It’s important to understand that part of our journey, because it is part of the complexity of our identity, and affects our sense of belonging.”
Anthony Severin, St Lucia’s high commissioner and chair of the Caribbean community diplomatic caucus in the UK, described the theft as a “desecration of the memory and spirit of our commemorated ancestors”.
He pledged that the plaque “whether returned or replaced, will remain affixed to the walls of Portchester Castle”.
