US corporate lobbyists mounted ‘blitz’ to dilute landmark EU deforestation law, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:31 UTC
20:00:31 KST

US corporate lobbyists launched a two-year “blitz” to postpone and weaken the world’s most progressive legislation to protect forests, according to a new investigation by the environmental watchdog Mighty Earth.
Major US firms and trade associations, including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz and the US Soybean Export Council, as well as numerous other US firms and organizations, sought to influence the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) in more than 350 meetings, the advocacy group found.
US company representatives and industry groups deny there was a concerted campaign to derail the deforestation rules, saying their meetings with EU officials raised legitimate concerns around implementation.
The EUDR prohibits imports of commodities such as cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood from deforested land. When the ban was put forward in 2003, the then European environment commissioner, Virginijus Sinkevičius, described it as “the most ambitious legislative attempt to tackle these issues worldwide ever” and some US lawmakers said it should be a model for similar rules in the United States.
In the years since, its official implementation has been delayed twice and the original goal to rigorously trace the origin of commodities has been revised so much that some of its initial supporters claimed the policy has been in effect “dismantled”. The law will come into effect in December.
Lobbyists from many countries, including Brazil and several EU nations, are known to have contributed to this dilution. Mighty Earth has provided the most detailed analysis yet of the role of organisations from the United States.
It found 24 major US companies, trade associations and industry organizations discussed the EUDR in at least 173 meetings with members of the European parliament and 178 meetings with senior European Commission officials between July 2024 and July 2026.
The US organisations with the highest number of meetings with the European Commission were the National Alliance of Forest Owners, Advanced Woody Biomass Alliance, the US Soybean Export Council, Bunge, the American Chamber of Commerce to the European Union and Cargill.
Cargill had two meetings, Bunge one meeting and Mondlēz eight meetings.
Mighty Earth said lobbying was also conducted through the US Congress, the US Department of Agriculture, the Office of the US Trade Representative and the White House.
Two weeks after a July 2025 meeting at a Scottish golf course between Trump and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, the two sides released a joint statement that promised the US special treatment with regard to the EUDR.
The commission stated the US “poses negligible risk to global deforestation” (even though many of its biggest financial and trading companies have been repeatedly implicated in destruction of the Amazon and similar biomes). The statement also talked about the EU working “to address the concerns of US producers and exporters regarding EUDR, with a view to avoiding undue impact on US-EU trade”.
Mighty Earth said its investigation highlighted the need for the EU to adopt greater transparency about lobbying activities and to give more access to civil society to ensure balance.
“Our analysis found a relentless and aggressive campaign by major US businesses, trade bodies and government officials, going all the way to President Trump, who offered to personally intervene, to further pressure EU policymakers,” Isabel Fernandez, senior adviser for Mighty Earth, said. “Some of the companies lobbying the EU, include the most egregious who are still linked to the illegal clearing of forests for commodities, such as soy that make their way into European markets.”
Earlier this year a delegation of Trump administration officials went to EU capitals arguing the law would put the US off exporting to the European market because it would raise costs for US producers. In an opinion piece published in Agence France, Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, said the law was: “… sold as a bold strike against global forest loss. In reality it will impose significant regulatory compliance costs while producing inconsequential environmental benefit when enforced against countries that pose no deforestation risk.”
US corporate organisations said their engagement was designed to better understand and enhance the EUDR.
The American Chamber of Commerce to the EU said it had raised concerns about EUDR implementation challenges, such as IT system shortcomings and a lack of clarity around the obligations of companies. But a spokesperson said its role had been constructive: “AmCham EU has consistently supported the EUDR’s objective of tackling global deforestation and promoting sustainable supply chains ... We have asked to allow sufficient time for companies and authorities to prepare and ensure the regulation can be effectively enforced without undermining its environmental objectives.”
The US Soybean Export Council said it was focused on ways to support industry compliance with the EU’s rules. “USSEC does not seek delay or exemption; rather we favour a transition period as the Regulation comes into force. This would allow companies, control authorities, the European Commission, and the entire value chain to gain experience and learnings on how compliance works in practice, allowing for greater understanding and adaptations to implementation if needed moving forwards,” a spokesperson said.
The agribusiness company Bunge said it was committed to deforestation-free supply chains and was investing in monitoring and traceability that had, it said, achieved 100% traceability to farm for both direct and indirect soy sourcing in priority areas of Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay. A spokesperson said: “Bunge supports the objectives of the European Union Deforestation Regulation while observing our own non-deforestation commitment and strengthening responsible sourcing. We are also in contact with relevant EU bodies and national competent authorities via sector organizations and directly to request clarification on certain specific complex scenarios regarding the practical implementation requirements of the EUDR.”
Cargill and Mondelēz did not send an on-the-record response to the Guardian’s request for a comment.

====================================================================================================

Fake Linda and me: the Agatha Christie-worthy mystery of the fraudster who stole my byline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:30 UTC
20:00:30 KST

It started with an entirely ordinary interaction on LinkedIn. Someone had tagged me in a post, saying how much they’d enjoyed contributing to a New York Post article I’d written about “chronoworking”. As the author of a book about circadian rhythms, it was exactly the sort of subject I might write about. Except I’d never heard of this person, let alone interviewed them.
I clicked on the link and my stomach dropped. There, above an article about people who organise their working lives around their biological clocks, was my name: Linda Geddes.
It was the latest in a string of increasingly bizarre events that had begun three weeks earlier, when a friend who works as an editor at the scientific journal Nature texted to ask whether I’d been pitching stories to one of her colleagues. I hadn’t.
It turned out that someone had been approaching Nature editors using my name and an email address that wasn’t mine, referencing articles I’d previously written to make their pitches more convincing. Worse, the journal had recently encountered another impersonator posing as Caroline Williams, a former colleague of mine. That person had convinced an editor at Science to commission and publish an article under Caroline’s name, receiving about $1,000 for it.
Further digging revealed that Fake Linda had also pitched a story to Science, unsuccessfully. Then, last week, an editor at Nature Medicine contacted me to ask whether I’d been pitching to them and Nature Health as well.
I donned my sleuthing cap and discovered a potential link between Fake Linda and Fake Caroline. Entering my impersonator’s email address into Outlook.com’s account recovery system revealed a partially obscured Gmail recovery address. An editor at Science had independently discovered the same address pattern associated with Fake Caroline’s email.
As someone whose livelihood depends on the reputation I’ve spent decades building, I find this deeply unsettling. Someone is potentially making money by passing themselves off as me, while putting my professional credibility at risk. Apart from one interview conducted by email, the quotes in the New York Post article were lifted from previously published features, without attribution. Many of Fake Linda’s pitches also bear the hallmarks of AI-assisted writing. Even unsuccessful pitches could damage relationships with editors.
The New York Post has since removed the article, conducted an internal review and referred the matter to the appropriate authorities, a spokesperson said.
What I find particularly baffling is the motive. Freelance science journalism is hardly a lucrative profession, and is quite niche. My best guess is that a struggling freelancer is impersonating more established peers to boost their earnings, perhaps using AI to make the process more efficient. But how would they receive payment without revealing their identity?
Other possibilities have crossed my mind. Could it be a PR professional trying to secure coverage for a client, or someone testing how easily publishers can be fooled? Perhaps it is someone with a personal grudge. But as Caroline put it: “Why us? We’re nice!”
Dr Simon Miller, the director of policy, strategy and communications at the UK fraud prevention service Cifas, is equally bemused. “Ordinarily, if you’re seeking to defraud, you’re seeking to do it at scale, in a relatively light-touch way, using mechanised, industrialised processes,” he said. “This is tantalisingly unusual. It’s almost the stuff of Agatha Christie, but with 21st-century technology.”
Journalists are far from the only people finding their names attached to work they didn’t produce. In April, Prof Eric Topol, of the Scripps Institute in California, discovered his name on a scientific paper he knew nothing about. Four of his five supposed co-authors were similarly unaware of the paper, while the fifth could not be identified. Within hours of Topol flagging the incident on X, the journal’s website had disappeared.
Topol, who is a bestselling author, said he has discovered at least 12 books on Amazon with his name on that he didn’t write, including several cookbooks. “I don’t even know how to cook,” he said. Particularly upsetting was when a patient told him he’d read his supposed memoir. “They said: ‘I was reading it, and a lot of those things don’t seem to be accurate.’ That’s how I found out about it.”
Dr Leslie McIntosh, a vice-president of research integrity and security at Digital Science, said someone might add a respected name to a scientific paper without permission to make the work appear more credible. Fraudsters also sometimes added respected researchers as editors to make bogus journals appear legitimate and attract publication fees.
Even more nightmarish would be someone deliberately publishing misleading information under someone else’s name to damage their reputation. “If their name ended up on a retracted paper, they would then have to explain that retraction,” she said.
Employers are encountering yet another form of impersonation. Jamie Collier, a researcher at Google Threat Intelligence, said criminals had used stolen personal information to secure remote jobs under other people’s names, sometimes without the victim’s knowledge.
Generative AI is making such deception easier, “mainly by stripping away the usual tell-tale red flags that hiring managers relied on to spot fraud,” Collier said. Large language models can generate convincing CVs, tailored cover letters and fabricated evidence of professional experience.
“Real-time video filters and voice-cloning tools are the next step. While live deepfakes are still relatively nascent … threat actors are already testing them to bypass quick video screenings and mask regional accents,” Collier said.
The Society of Authors and the Writers’ Guild of Great Britain have warned of increasingly sophisticated scams involving people impersonating literary agents and publishers, in an attempt to get writers to part with money or sign away their rights.
The Society of Authors’ chief executive, Anna Ganley, said she personally received between five and 10 scam emails a day, supposedly from book festivals, literary agents, publishers and others. Some writers had lost thousands of pounds after responding to genuine-sounding offers. “It’s incredibly difficult for writers, because you are often looking for opportunities to market your books,” she said.
Unlike those scams, Fake Linda’s activities seem like a lot of work for relatively small financial gain. But the latest technology could make such impersonations easier. Miller said: “AI is allowing criminals to create sophisticated impersonations at unprecedented speed and scale.”
Or multiple impersonations. I’ve since identified a third science journalist, Sara Novak, with a potential link to Fake Linda and Fake Caroline. Fake Sara apparently pitched a story to Chemical and Engineering News in August, which was declined. When Real Sara shared her impersonator’s email address with me, I discovered it links to the same masked recovery address.
The consequences extend beyond those being impersonated. “The risk for journals and publishers is huge,” said Dr Ben Johnson, the chief editor at Nature Health, who turned down a pitch by Fake Linda. “People trust the Nature brand as a source of evidence-based quality information. If an AI-generated story from a fake journalist is submitted then I will likely spend hours editing it from AI slop into Nature prose, including all the fake quotes from people never interviewed.”
All of this raises uncomfortable questions about how you can be sure you know who you’re dealing with when communicating online. When I emailed the New York Post about my impersonator, it agreed to help rectify the situation, then asked: “I see that you’re emailing me from a Guardian email address. Is there any other info you can provide to verify who you are?”
After discovering that Science had inadvertently published a news story by Fake Caroline, its managing news editor, John Travis, said his team had started running all pitches and drafts through AI detectors, “though they are not perfect”. “We also require Zoom calls for any new writers,” he said.
The experience has also put editors at Nature on higher alert. “Sadly, for early career freelancers, this makes me less likely to commission news stories from journalists that I haven’t worked with before,” Johnson said. “I will also have to try to find the time to have a call with new freelancers before they write, to check they are who they say they are.”
Even video calls are no guarantee of identity. Google Threat Intelligence recently documented North Korea-linked hackers using real-time deepfakes to lure executives into Zoom calls with trusted peers. “They faked video and audio glitches to get the target to download a ‘troubleshooting tool’ that wiped out their credentials and wallets,” Collier said.
Miller advises independently checking unexpected approaches through an established email address or telephone number. McIntosh advocates several layers of verification, like the multiple identity checks at airports. “You have to have multiple ways to ensure and triangulate that you’re speaking to the person you think you’re speaking to,” she said.
For people whose identities have been hijacked, Miller advises warning professional networks and monitoring for further impersonation attempts.
There may also be legal remedies. Rupert Earle, senior counsel at the London law firm Bates Wells, said that under UK law, impersonating someone to secure paid work could constitute fraud. Victims could also have civil claims for “passing off” – misleading people into believing that work or services come from an established person or business – or false attribution, if work they didn’t create was published under their name.
However, identifying the perpetrator and taking legal action can be difficult, particularly when the publications are overseas and the impersonator’s location is unknown. Despite uncovering several clues linking Fake Linda and Fake Caroline, we still don’t know who is behind the accounts.
But the hunt for Fake Linda continues. I’ll be reporting the incident to the UK’s Report Fraud service. I’ve also sent a cease-and-desist email to my impersonator, demanding they stop.
For such a prolific writer, they’ve gone surprisingly quiet.

‘We are in hiding’: Briton with severe health issues fears deportation from Sweden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:30 UTC
20:00:30 KST

A seriously ill British man living in Sweden has been forced into hiding amid fears he will be deported as a result of what he says is a government Brexit residency error.
Mark Smith, 60, who has had heart attacks, strokes, severe headaches and chronically high blood pressure that has been difficult to treat, was told on the phone he should leave Sweden by 17 October as he was an “alien” without permission to stay.
Terrified of deportation, he and his wife have moved out of their home in Falkenberg, in south-west Sweden, to a caravan park. “We are in hiding, we daren’t go back to our apartment. We are scared to go out as we don’t know if the police will come and take us,” Smith said.
A court ruled on 12 October that a decision on deportation would not be suspended but gave him until 20 October to “submit his application for a retrial” in relation to “the grounds for the decision on indefinite deportation”.
Smith has been in Sweden since 2017 and says he was told by authorities he did not need to do anything to stay after Brexit in 2020. He worked, had private health insurance, supported his wife and registered on the population register administered by the national tax authority, as required under Swedish rules.
He was unaware, however, that Sweden was among 13 of the 27 EU member states that required Britons living in the country before Brexit to make a formal application to remain. Other countries, such as Spain, did not opt for that system and just required Britons to declare they were a resident.
Smith said: “I asked the tax authorities three times on different occasions if I had to do anything because of Brexit and they said no, telling me I had to wait for five years to apply for permanent residency.
“Because it was the tax authority, a government body, I took it for granted that what they told me was correct,” he added.
David Milstead, a British-Swedish volunteer citizens’ rights activist working through the Brits in Sweden group, said Smith’s case was typical of many Britons living in Sweden.
Milstead said: “Mark’s experience is far from unusual. I have encountered many British citizens who actively sought information from the Swedish authorities about their residence rights after Brexit, only to receive vague, unhelpful answers, sometimes being told that they needed to do nothing.”
They include the 78-year-old widow Joyce Thomas, whose husband also inquired about Brexit residency and was told by the tax authorities there was nothing to do, and who is now fighting a removal order.
Smith had a minor heart attack on Wednesday night but wanted his situation publicised because he said the British government needed to know what was happening to expats in Sweden, “not just to me but others”.
His wife, Petra, said his health conditions had left him so vulnerable she was not sure “if he will last until Christmas”.
She said: “He has been told he can’t drive, he can’t fly – what do they expect him to do? Get up and walk to England? Come on, Sweden, we need to step back from all of this and be better.”
After 12 years together, she said deportation would be devastating for her and her 15-year-old son who has special needs, who Smith co-parents. “It is wrong what they are doing, I feel ashamed to be Swedish. What they are doing is racist to British people,” Petra said.
Milstead said Smith’s case was “depressingly familiar” and should warrant the urgent attention of the European Commission, which has previously said Sweden was not breaking any laws.
“A gentleman with Mark’s serious health conditions should not be having to fight deportation. It is difficult to understand how the European Commission has concluded that Sweden’s treatment of late applications under the [Brexit] withdrawal agreement does not warrant a challenge,” he said.
“Sweden stands out so starkly from other EU countries, and there are serious questions that remain unanswered, particularly about proportionality and the treatment of vulnerable people. These are precisely the kinds of cases where the protections of the withdrawal agreement ought to matter most.”
The Scandinavian country has found itself under mounting pressure over its approach to the withdrawal agreements having deported 458 Britons, including one man who had been in the country since he was 10 years old, and a 65-year-old man married to a Swede with no family or property in the UK.
Sweden has also issued removal orders to a man with dementia who is in 24-hour care and who has been in the country for 25 years.
Under the legally binding treaty, it was agreed governments would communicate the Brexit residency rules, consider late applications on reasonable grounds, and exercise “proportionate” decisions including in the case of vulnerable people.
Smith’s troubles began in 2021 when he started to get ill and applied for sickness benefit. He was told by officials that he should have applied for post-Brexit residency. The couple immediately did so; they recall making the application at the end of 2021, in time for Sweden’s 31 December 2021 deadline.
They waited more than two years to hear back and when they did it was a rejection on the grounds that they were not married and therefore did not have a family connection to merit his residency in Sweden.
They were married in 2023 and had been living together since 2017.
It is not clear if Smith applied for the specific Brexit residency or through the usual immigration route, an important difference and one that may not have been made clear to British protected by the withdrawal agreement. Family connections are not a criteria under free movement rights, which apply to any individual regardless of marital status, so campaigners believe they have a strong case.
Smith said: “We were so much in love, we lived together, we did everything together, even now we hold hands walking down the streets. We wanted to get married, we wanted to do it the right way. I wanted to ask Petra’s father for permission and have him give her away, but two weeks after he gave me permission to marry his daughter, he passed.
“So we were looking into marriage but things just kept happening. But we don’t understand why this matters.”
They also said they had not been given the full court paperwork from the first case appealing against the migration agency’s decision, so they appealed to a higher courtwithout the full arguments against them.
After speaking to a judge this week, Petra has had assurances that all the paperwork will be sent to them by post, but they feel angry that they were not apprised of the information that the migration agency was arguing before the courts.
Sweden’s migration agency has said there is no evidence Sweden has taken an extreme approach to the withdrawal agreement.
The UK Foreign Office has raised concerns about Sweden’s approach to the withdrawal agreement with the European Commission on numerous occasions, but has been told Sweden is not breaching the agreement.
A spokesperson said: “We are in touch with Mr Smith and are providing consular support. We know this is a distressing and challenging time for those concerned and we are urgently raising the situation with both the Swedish authorities and the European Commission.”
The Foreign Office welcomed a statement by Sweden’s former migration minister Johan Forssell in August that Sweden would examine “additional measures” that would address the issue of Brexit deportation, and a similar declaration by Magdalena Andersson, who is on track to form the new government.

‘Drones all night. By morning, you smell the smoke’: life in the last hotel on Ukraine’s frontline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:30 UTC
20:00:30 KST

There is one important rule in the Richelievsky, Kherson’s last functioning hotel: close the curtains before dusk. Less than a kilometre away lies the Dnipro, the river that has formed the frontline since Ukrainian forces liberated Kherson in November 2022; Moscow’s troops are on the opposite bank.
In a city where Russian drone operators hunt civilians in what is now widely known as the “human safari”, even a sliver of light escaping through a window may be enough to reveal someone’s location after dark.
In the lobby, Yevhen Emtsov, the hotel’s manager, sits at a small round table almost buried beneath papers. Outside, explosions punctuate the evening, joined at intervals by the mechanical hum of drones patrolling the streets in the red zone. Inside, residents pass through, pausing with questions and requests at the table that now serves as Emtsov’s office.
In more peaceful times, the Richelievsky accommodated tourists and business travellers attending conferences. The three-star hotel belonged to a different Kherson, one in which the river drew visitors rather than marking a frontline.
But in March 2022, as Russian forces closed in, Emtsov began taking in people fleeing heavily shelled communities along the Dnipro without waiting for the hotel owners’ approval. By the time the city came under occupation, the building had already begun its transformation from a commercial hotel into a refuge.
In the months that followed the invasion, between 200 and 300 people were staying, far beyond its intended maximum capacity of 120. Russian patrols would enter the building, questioning residents and recording their fingerprints. “Imagine you are sitting at home, strangers come in and begin doing whatever they want,” Emtsov says.
Today, the hotel is home to 41 displaced people, with rooms and three meals a day provided free of charge. “People come to us,” Emtsov says. “You can sleep here today, and tomorrow we will see. Nobody sleeps on the street. Nobody.”
It is close to midnight when the power cuts out, leaving the hotel and the city in complete darkness. “Drones and artillery can be heard throughout the night,” Emtsov says. “By morning, you will be able to smell the smoke.”
Hours later, kept awake by the noise of bombing outside, I make my way towards the top of the building, where the seventh floor lies deserted.
From up here, Kherson is almost entirely dark, its streets and buildings barely distinguishable in the blackout. Brief flashes flare among the stars, while explosions and the buzz of drones carry through the night.
When daylight returns, the building shows no sign of stirring. At this hour, the Richelievsky feels like a ghost hotel, mirroring the emptied neighbourhoods of Kherson’s red zone.
The first people to emerge are in the hotel kitchen: Natalia Yastreb and Iryna Rybalchenko reheat fishcakes and stew from the previous evening. Residents drift wearily into the adjoining dining room with their plates, exchanging few words as detonations continue outside.
While some residents have already left for work, Nina and Viktor Tsokurenko begin the day in room 43 with exercises and tea. Since suffering a stroke, Viktor has struggled to speak. “There was a powerful explosion at one o’clock,” Nina says. “After that, I did not sleep again until morning.” Still, she offers coffee and honey; before the war, the couple kept bees.
One floor below, four cats pad around room 37. Tatyana Nesterchuk, one of the hotel’s longest-standing residents, has returned from a shift at a laundry in Kherson’s Dniprovskyi district. The minibus journey to work takes her through some of the city’s most dangerous streets, with an emergency bag always at her side.
“It is like a one-way road,” she says. “You do not know whether you will return. Before setting out, it is as though I am leaving a will behind.”
When warnings of incoming guided aerial bombs reach the hotel, she heads to the shelter with family photographs and other keepsakes packed into her suitcase, which weighs about 10kg. “It is heavy,” she says. “My son tells me to take half of it out. I tell him, ‘I can’t.’”
Nesterchuk has been told that her house has since burned down. Even the fences are gone. “But the land, at least, will remain, I suppose.” She remembers drinking coffee on a small terrace before leaving for work or taking a hoe into the garden to tend fruit and vegetables.
“I always loved the mornings at home,” she says. “The birds were singing. It was quiet and peaceful. There was no buzzing, no humming.”
Another air raid siren cuts across the city. In room 54, Alisia Logvinenko, 11, the only child among the hotel’s residents, answers my knock. She speaks in a breathless rush that makes her difficult to follow. Her mother, Iryna, stands behind her.
The 50-year-old tries to put the war into words a child can understand. “Someone wants to take away our home.”
“To conquer a country,” Alisia adds. “Did I say that correctly?”
“Yes, you did,” her mother says.
When Iryna mentions the few friends they still have in Kherson, Alisia cuts in. “Not mine, hers.”
Most of the children she knew before the war have left Kherson. “I don’t really miss them,” she says, opening her YouTube channel and turning the screen towards me. What makes her happy now, she says, is “lots of likes on my videos”.
Before the invasion, Iryna had planned to take Alisia camping in Ukraine’s nature reserves. The landscape her daughter has learned to navigate instead is governed by a different set of rules.
“Look at the sky. Listen and try to go where there are more trees and walls,” Iryna says. The hotel may offer a measure of shelter, but she has no illusions about its limits. “There is no feeling of safety anywhere.”
Downstairs, Svitlana Salii, Emtsov’s right hand, is behind the reception desk when her phone rings. As she listens, her expression tightens. A Russian FPV drone has struck the van carrying the hotel’s manager and several helpers on their way back from collecting groceries.
Outside, the mechanical hum rises and fades, and I find Emtsov and the others about 15 minutes away, gathered around the white Mercedes. “What can I tell you?” he says. “We heard the buzzing, saw the drone ahead and got out in time to take cover before it crashed into the vehicle.”
The attack is another reminder of what it costs to keep the place running. “As a hotel, we will not be able to operate. But as a hub, we will continue for as long as we have enough strength.”
As conditions in Kherson continue to deteriorate, Emtsov is trying to find a way out of the city for Iryna and Alisia; charities are seeking a place for them in Odesa. For now, mother and daughter remain in room 54, behind curtains drawn before dusk.

‘I spent five years with criminals’: dissident Cuban artist embraces new life in US after prison release
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:30 UTC
20:00:30 KST

When Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara was pushed into the back of a police car on 11 July 2021, during the biggest protests Cuba had seen in nearly three decades, he expected to be in custody for “one, maybe two days”. Instead five years would pass before he was free, and only then after he’d agreed to exile.
“I remember that Sunday,” he says as he opens a beer in El Espacio 23, an art gallery in the Allapattah neighbourhood of Miami. “I was at my girlfriend’s. Friends started writing to tell me there were demonstrations in the streets. It felt like the day we all longed for had arrived – the end of the dictatorship – and I went out into the street.”
He walked for an hour to Old Havana, but was suddenly picked up by Cuba’s revolutionary police. First he was taken to a former seminary in Havana’s suburbs, the much-feared state security interrogation centre of Villa Marista; then, after two days, to Cuba’s maximum security prison, in Guanajay.
There he became the best known of the more than 1,000 political prisoners believed to be incarcerated in Cuba.
He also became the most corrosive to the reputation of Cuba’s government. In contrast to José Daniel Ferrer, the 56-year-old hard-fighting and political former prisoner who was released in October 2025, Otero Alcántara is an artist: unruly certainly, but young, mischievous, mixed race, self-taught and from a poor background.
For many Cubans on the island, the treatment he received encapsulated a sense that the state had come down too hard on young people following 11 July. There’s no doubt that in the run-up to the protests, Otero Alcántara had been troublesome to Cuba’s embattled government. In 2018 he had co-founded the San Isidro collective in a poor part of Old Havana, protesting against a new law, decree 349, that required all artistic endeavours to be pre-approved by the state.
His performance pieces were pointed. He mocked a new $500-a-night hotel that none of his neighbours could afford by asking what had happened to the statue of Julio Antonio Mella, student leader and Marxist, which had previously stood outside. Or he hung out under a balcony in a hard hat after one collapsed, killing three young girls.
These pieces cut through. He believes the authorities would have tolerated such work if he’d agreed to show it in galleries. “I refused, because no one who mattered to me would see it,” he says. “Instead, I tried to speak directly to people on the street, and that wasn’t acceptable.”
The San Isidro collective was cut off by police and surveilled, its occupants harassed. Otero Alcántara says those within drew confidence from each other as the pressure, and the public interest, increased.
“There were so many points of view in San Isidro,” he says now. “There was a babalao [a high priest of Santeria, Cuba’s syncretic religion], a Muslim, a gay person – all the layers that make up a society. San Isidro united them, and from there it generated a ripple effect.”
The reality of prison, he says, was horrific. “The first month I spent with people taken on 11 July. But then they were released, and I spent five years with criminals, often murderers – people who aren’t normal, people who are sadistic, people who are cruel, people who kill women, kill children.
“You come to terms with the fact that you’re in an extremely violent place, and begin to understand the different ways. That normalisation is where confinement is the worst. I think it’s one of the worst experiences a human being can have.”
Told he would never be free to walk the streets of Cuba, he accepted exile in the US, and arrived in Miami on 18 July in good physical shape, having disappeared for the week after his prison term ended. It turned out he had been taken to a beachside state security safe house, where he was allowed to see family and drink Chinese whiskey with his guards.
Once in the US, he appeared in Washington to receive the 2026 Democracy Award from the National Endowment for Democracy, an institution that’s a bugaboo for supporters of the Cuban government. More bizarrely, former president George W Bush, who has also taken up art, painted his portrait for a forthcoming book about political prisoners and dissidents.
His exit from Cuba did not play well with sections of the exile community in Miami, some of whom accused him of having sold out. “Who drinks beer and toasts with their captors right before being exiled? This looks like a staged performance by G2 (Cuban state intelligence),” said Alexander Otaola, a popular Cuban American commentator.
“There was a lot of pre-judgment,” says Michael Bustamante, chair of Cuban and Cuban American studies at the University of Miami.
Otero Alcántara only added to the fire during a round of interviews with exile media. During one, with the 87-year-old former political prisoner Ángel de Fana, he said that, no longer living in Cuba, he would miss the “taste of a woman on the island” (“la sabrosura”).
The remark caused laughter among some in Havana, but less so in Miami. “His form of speaking is very off the cuff,” says Bustamante. “It’s very Cuban-everyman, and relatable, but for guardians of certain traditions it’s seen as a departure. And it’s hard not to see a subtext about race.”
Otero Alcántara blames the criticism on the prevalence of social media, something that has exploded in the five years he was in prison. “There’s this phenomenon where a lot of influencers are actually making a living off likes, and views, so they get caught up in an algorithm that keeps the conversation going, without even assuming any civic responsibility toward Cuba.”
He does, however, agree he received better treatment than some others, that the authorities were in some ways frightened of him. “There were moments when, especially when state security wanted to get me out, they eased up a bit, because I went on more than six hunger strikes in prison, and they knew they could cause me to have a mental breakdown, so they started to give in.”
“I could come here and say, ‘Oh, in prison they beat me senseless, they broke my head,’ but that wouldn’t be honest,” he adds. “I can’t give a speech for the cameras just to keep influencers happy.”
On the floor of EL Espacio 23 is a pile of paintings he made in jail, which he was allowed to bring with him (another black mark in some eyes). A triptych shows the bars of the jail with various things in front: a tree or a cross. “It’s about what you think about in jail,” he says.
The gallery, which belongs to the Cuban American billionaire and Democrat Jorge M Pérez, is something of a sanctuary: it offers month-long residencies to young artists from around the world so he is among friends.
Meanwhile, back in Cuba, the authorities have a new problem on their hands. Anna Sofía Benítez, 21, better known as Anna Bensi, was sentenced last week along with her mother to two years of “restriction of liberty”, which means having to report regularly to police and inform them of any travel plans.
An enthusiastic Christian, Benítez had been using social media to rail against the Cuban government and the collapsing conditions in Cuba. She was charged with “acts against personal and family privacy” after filming a police officer serving her a summons, and this subsequent sentence means she could be jailed for any further infraction. The sentence has been heavily criticised by religious leaders, and on Wednesday Mike Hammer, the US chargé d’affaires in Havana, visited the family, further stirring up the situation.
Young Cubans are watching her closely, as they still are Otero Alcántara. He said he wants to move to New York, where he can slot into an artistic crowd outside the Miami exile bubble – perhaps a smart move given the issues facing young Cubans in Florida, many of whom are now actively hiding from ICE.
In the US today it’s hard to see how he won’t get himself into further trouble. He says he would have been a Cuban revolutionary if he’d been born 50 years earlier. “But I’m almost certain I would have gone to prison when the revolution triumphed. Like many who realised the revolution had become a dictatorship, I would have rebelled against it.”
Given Cuba’s turbulent history, has there been any period where he wouldn’t have ended up in prison? “In the future,” he says.

‘Is this too little, too late?’: Cornell students on school’s response to gang-rape allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:30 UTC
20:00:30 KST

In the wake of a lawsuit over an alleged gang-rape that took place at Cornell University in 2024, the school announced this week that it would be suspending parties and social gatherings at fraternity houses for the remainder of the academic year.
Last month, a former student, referred to in court documents by the pseudonym “Jane Doe”, filed a civil lawsuit against multiple parties, including the university, accusing seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity of sexually assaulting her at a party at their fraternity house on campus in October 2024. All of the men named in the lawsuit have denied wrongdoing, and none have been criminally charged.
In a letter to the Cornell community, the school’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, said that the ban on frat parties will be “provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue”.
The Guardian spoke with several undergraduate students at Cornell about the university’s decision, as well as their handling of the alleged assault and its aftermath. The measure, which Kotlikoff referred to as an effort to “strengthen campus safety”, was announced on 13 October in a letter to the Cornell community. While some students welcome the ban on frat parties, others argue that the move is an attempt by the administration to avoid a perception of culpability in the case.
When asked for comment, Cornell referred the Guardian to Kotlikoff’s letter to the community from 13 October, in which he said: “I have spent the past weeks listening to students, faculty, staff, parents, alumni, and trustees, who have shared their feelings of deep connection and sympathy with Jane Doe, anger and frustration that this could happen at Cornell, and outrage at the broader prevalence of sexual violence against women in our society. These conversations, and campus protests, have underscored my deep conviction that we must do better: that the time for meaningful and lasting change at Cornell, and at campuses across the country, is now.”
A sophomore at Cornell’s school of industrial and labor relations, who asked to remain anonymous, supports the school’s latest decision. She acknowledged that Greek life “wasn’t something that really added to my experience at Cornell” and that the ban was “so necessary in light of Jane Doe’s experience”.
The student added that while she is not in Greek life herself, many of her friends are. “I think it’s been upsetting for people that are super involved in Greek life,” she said, noting that some members of Greek life feel that they’re being penalized for the actions of others. They “think that [the ban is] somewhat unnecessary because this happened two years ago, and it’s a completely different group of people”.
“I have many friends that have opposing viewpoints,” she said.
Some students argued that the opposition is the point, and believe that the administration’s decision was intended to further a divide between the student body.
“The fact that [the administration] thinks a one-year moratorium will solve this is, I wouldn’t say it’s misguided. I would say it is purposefully manipulative to the student body,” said Jack Huber, a sophomore at the school of industrial and labor relations and member of Students for a Democratic Cornell (SDC), an independent, student-run organization that advocates for free speech on campus. “I believe it’s a very intentional choice, because what it’s done is create a sentiment that many students are angry, and are blaming protesters for their inability to party.
“Cornell is not ready to commit itself to institutional change, and is using this moratorium to essentially scapegoat fraternities when this is a campus-wide issue,” he added. Huber added that issues of sexual assault will remain until the school has implemented an independent judicial system, which was previously in effect from 1969 to 2020.
Huber said that school’s current judiciary process operates as “a tool to be used to sweep incidences of sexual violence under the rug because they harm Cornell’s reputation, and persecute protesters because they harm the board of trustees’ investments”.
“That’s the system that allowed essays to get written by two of the [Cornell 7]” he said.
SDC is demanding that the administration rewrite a portion of its student code of conduct to require independent hearings and minimum sanctions for sexual assault.
Darius Pierce, a sophomore at Cornell’s college of architecture, art and planning, remembered hearing about the incident, which had resulted in Chi Phi being disbarred and removed from campus during his first few weeks of college in 2025.
“I was walking past the Chi Phi house, heading back to campus, and a person in my group pointed out [the house] and I asked why I’ve never heard of them, and they explained that there was an issue with ketamine and assault at that house, and that was it,” he said.
“No one ever expanded upon that. I hadn’t heard anything about it until the story broke with the Cornell Sun.”
Like Huber, Pierce believes that the administration’s decision to ban frat parties is an attempt to “cover up for their own faults and own mistakes”.
“They’re trying to make it seem like they’re actually responding to [the alleged assault] and taking action instead of addressing the real issue,” he said.
Following the alleged assault, Cornell issued a statement in November 2024 informing the community that there would be an internal investigation while the Cornell University Police Department continued their criminal investigation. Per Jane Doe’s lawsuit, Cornell University Police did not end up pursuing criminal charges. The investigation was reopened in September 2026 in response to public outrage. None of the defendants in the civil lawsuit have been charged and all have denied wrongdoing.
Pierce, who rushed a fraternity but decided not to join one, also spoke of the endemic culture of drinking and substance use he has witnessed within Greek life at Cornell. He recalled an experience at a fraternity party where “this group of girls kept screaming that it was their first time doing coke at that frat party, and that these frat guys were just handing out lines of coke like candy”.
“If you go to a frat, you plan on drinking,” Pierce said. “But it seems like for women specifically who go to these frats, they’re kind of pressured to do more.”
The Guardian previously reported on how Jane Doe’s lawsuit has reignited debates over Greek life and the relationship between fraternity parties, drinking culture and sexual assault. A 2019 survey from the Association of American Universities revealed that a quarter of undergraduate women reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual conduct, with fraternities being the setting where it was most likely to occur.
At Cornell, 35% of undergraduate women reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact since arriving at school, according to a 2025 survey conducted by the university.
Saya Taylor, a sophomore who is also a member of SDC, believes that the frat ban is a “Band-Aid” solution to a much deeper problem. “They’re trying to give the appearance that they are changing when they are not,” she said. “Cornell University does not want this to [have] a lasting impact.”
In addition to the fraternity ban, Kotlikoff also announced that the university would be adding a case manager to Cornell’s office of civil rights to help those who report sexual misconduct at the school navigate the processes. He also pledged that Cornell would work with the New York state police and allow their trauma-informed criminal investigators, who are independent of Cornell, to investigate allegations.
The sophomore believes that this week’s announcement is a step in the right direction. “For the vast majority, people like me, we want justice and we want the administration to change the structural way that they address sexual assault,” she said.
But others need more convincing.
“Is this too little, too late? The answer there is a resounding yes,” said Huber. “Jane Doe never got the justice she deserved in the moment.”

How the quirky puffin became a symbol of the climate crisis – and hope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:29 UTC
20:00:29 KST

For centuries human beings have exploited puffins, harvesting them by the thousand on their breeding grounds for their food and feathers. Over time, though, this relationship has changed, so that today we have come to love them, celebrating their quirky character and comical appearance and giving them a central place in our affections – a journey described by the environmental historian Dr Rob Lambert as the shift “from use to delight”.
How ironic, then, that just as we have come to truly appreciate them, our own existence now threatens theirs. The climate crisis threatens almost all the world’s roughly 11,000 species of birds, but its consequences have particularly dire significance for seabirds, whose life cycle is so intimately connected to the timing and abundance of their food supplies.
Warming oceans result in fish such as sand eels shifting their range into cooler waters, and thus either declining or disappearing from the seas around seabird breeding colonies. If puffins need to travel further to their feeding areas, or take longer to find and catch food once they get there, then their chicks have a lower chance of fledging.
Even if they do, they are less likely to survive the following winter. Our changing climate has already led to an increase in the frequency and severity of extreme weather events such as autumn and winter storms, which leads to a higher mortality of birds outside the breeding season.
It is often forgotten that the climate crisis is not the only negative factor affecting these birds’ lives. As we have seen, increased marine pollution, especially from oil and plastic, along with less severe yet still serious issues such as disturbance and predation, are already reducing the puffin’s breeding success at many once-thriving colonies.
The dire prediction that nine out of 10 puffins could disappear before the middle of this century is hopefully pessimistic, yet we do know that serious declines are already occurring.
In early 2026, BBC News reported that following that winter’s severe storms hundreds of dead and dying puffins, guillemots and razorbills had been washed up on beaches in Cornwall, Scotland and north-east England. Conservation organisations have also reported more than 20,000 stranded birds, mostly puffins, along the Atlantic coasts of France, Spain and Portugal.
Samuel Wrobel, the RSPB’s senior marine officer, noted that this was the worst wreck for over a decade, since the catastrophic events of winter 2013-14, and warned that “after the impact of avian flu this is the last thing our seabirds need”. Moreover, as most birds are likely to have died at sea, so will never be found, the true death toll is likely to be much higher.
Peter Harrison has spent his life watching, painting and studying seabirds, and has a special affection for the puffin. I asked him what he thought about the species’ future, and he began by confirming the many threats the birds face, including a reduction in their prey due to the climate crisis, threats to nest sites and the resulting lower breeding success.
Rather to my surprise, however, Harrison feels some optimism for the puffin’s future, pointing to that famous legal victory that stopped industrial sand eel fishing in the waters around England and Scotland. He is also enthusiastic about the use of technology to track the movements and survival of all seabirds, including the puffin, since this began in the 1980s.
“Prior to that time, there was a huge void in our knowledge of what puffins and other seabirds did in their non-breeding period,” he says. “They simply went to sea, only to reappear again in their breeding areas the following season. Rapid technological advances over the last four decades have greatly increased our understanding of their movements, revealing details of seabird distribution and behaviour at sea, including important foraging areas.”
And as he points out, this knowledge does not just benefit the puffin. “Auks – including puffins – fulfil a role as important canaries in the cage, indicators of global health and sustainability. If auks are doing well, the oceans will be doing well,” Harrison says.
The one thing we have on our side, Harrison believes, is that, unlike landbirds which often only live for a few years, even small seabirds can live for several decades. As he notes, although they might have gone through bad times, seabirds have in the past shown that they can make a rapid comeback, especially if we are able to rid their breeding islands of invasive predators.
Scientists have a crucial role to play, too. In 2004 BirdLife International developed the BirdLife Seabird Tracking Database (STDB) to collate tracking data using a range of different, and rapidly improving, technologies that can track the presence and movements of seabirds when they are away from their breeding colonies, as they are for most of their lives.
The records enabled them to identify six previously unrecognised oceanic routes used by the birds on their journeys: the Atlantic Ocean, North Indian Ocean, East Ocean, West Pacific Ocean, Pacific Ocean, and the Southern Ocean Flyways. The data obtained is also used for seabird research and conservation by BirdLife scientists and their collaborators throughout the world.
As Dr Stephen Kress, the scientist who has devoted his life to successfully bringing back puffins to the US, points out: “Seabirds were once abundant along the coastlines of North America and throughout the world, but the declines we’re seeing in their populations are directly related to things humans are doing – they would be fine if we weren’t tampering with their world and messing things up.
“And so I feel that we have an ethical responsibility as stewards of the Earth to do something where we can. That’s why we’ve developed these restoration techniques. If we hadn’t done that, we wouldn’t be documenting puffin recovery, we’d be documenting extinction.”
Yet perhaps we can maintain at least a small fragment of hope for the future not just of the puffin, but of all the world’s seabirds. They may be outside our day-to-day experience for much of our – and their – lives, yet the huge affection for the puffin, held by millions of people around the world, must surely count for something.
- This is an edited extract from The Puffin by Stephen Moss published by Vintage at £14.99. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Key player in false Talarico rumor has history of online posts invoking Nazi Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:29 UTC
20:00:29 KST

An influencer who played a key role in hoax claims that James Talarico was in a mental health facility has a long history of social media posts that favorably invoke Nazi Germany, express antisemitism and anti-Black racism, criticize miscegenation and call for “remigration” of refugees.
On X, the Lake Oswego, Oregon, resident Ryan Amacher, known online as Rhein Amacher, has described Muslims as “sub-human”, claimed that Black Africans are “monkeys” with low IQ, characterized immigrants as “vermin” and expressed support for the far right, including Germany’s AfD and the UK’s Tommy Robinson.
His attempt to damage Talarico’s campaign with false claims about a supposed inpatient admission to an Ohio facility fell apart quickly on Sunday night, but not before his claims were boosted by a staffer on the campaign of Talarico’s Republican rival, Ken Paxton. Since working for the Trump campaign in 2024, he has remained in the milieu of Republican politics and rightwing influencers.
Following the publication of this reporting, Amacher contacted the Guardian to reiterate his claim that he had called the facility, and that “a representative told me that James Talarico had been released from the facility”, even though later in the day the Lindner Center “issued an official statement categorically denying that Talarico had ever been a patient there”.
He called these “contradictory statements”, but conceded that “more thorough fact-checking and independent verification should have occurred on my end before the information was shared publicly”.
He added: “I stand by the authenticity of my phone call, but I also recognize that the information conveyed during that call was subsequently contradicted by the facility itself. Those are two distinctions worth making.”
Amacher concluded: “That said, my original reason for making the phone call remains a separate question: where was James Talarico during his approximately two-week absence from the campaign trail?”
The Paxton campaign did not respond to requests for comment.
Last week, Amacher phoned the Lindner Center of Hope, a psychiatric hospital in Mason, Ohio, three times, trying to confirm a false rumor that Talarico had been admitted there. The rumor apparently began with a 9 October post by an anonymous X account, TickleTexts, which claimed Talarico had been “hospitalized at Lindner Center for HOPE”, and was picked up by the Republican fundraiser Caroline Wren, who falsely tied it to a private flight between Ohio and Austin. Before calling, Amacher had posted as fact that Talarico “was hospitalized at the @LindnerCtrHope” and tagged the hospital asking it to confirm.
In the full recording of the second call, he gives his name as “Tim”, says he wants to send a care package to his cousin, and offers a four-digit patient code. “I simply made one up (2244) in an attempt to bypass the facility’s security restrictions to discuss the patient,” he later wrote on X. For most of the six-minute call the employee tells him she has no record of Talarico. In its final seconds she says a man that looks like Talarico “was just discharged this evening”.
An excerpt of the recording was incorporated into a 47-second clip that Nick Sortor posted on Sunday afternoon under the headline “Ohio mental hospital CONFIRMS James Talarico was discharged from the facility earlier this week”. Amacher posted his own version minutes later, and Elon Musk replied with a characteristic “!!”. Amacher had first offered the recording to Blaze Media and the Daily Mail, which reportedly declined to run it, and said in an X Space that evening that influencers are “not held to the same journalistic standards”. By Tuesday he had reportedly pulled out of an interview with the writer and podcaster Jesse Singal, saying his attorney had given him a “stand down order”.
The purported legal advice coincides with coverage of the fiasco, which has included speculation that Amacher’s attempt to access private health information may land him in legal trouble.
Previous coverage, however, has not probed Amacher’s long history of extremist commentary.
‘Modern Freikorps volunteers are needed’
Amacher often invokes Nazi Germany, and the paramilitary movement that preceded it, with apparent admiration.
“In 1919, Germany’s defeated soldiers came home only to be stabbed in the back by socialists and communists who wanted to burn the nation down and install a Soviet-style dictatorship,” he wrote on 29 July, over an AI-generated image of German soldiers beneath Soviet flags beside uniformed men under crescent moons at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate. In a follow-up post he wrote: “Modern Freikorps volunteers are needed to step up to purge the German nation of the filth destroying it from within.” An AI-generated image accompanying it showed a masked soldier wearing “Freikorps” and “Deutsches Reich” patches, with the black, white and red flag of imperial Germany flying over the Reichstag.
The Freikorps were paramilitary units of demobilized soldiers that crushed leftwing uprisings in Germany after the first world war. In January 1919, Freikorps troops murdered the communist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht. In June, Amacher told critics to “read up on the German Freikorps after 1919–and what became of Luxemburg and Liebknecht”.
“History has a way of repeating itself when revolutionary movements collide with a nation pushed to the brink,” he added. The Freikorps are widely seen as an ideological ancestor of Adolf Hitler’s Nazi party, though he later turned against them.
In July, replying to a post that said “we fought the wrong enemy in WW2, just like General Patton said before the jews assassinated him in 1945”, Amacher wrote: “We should have immediately re-armed the German Wehrmacht and auxiliary troops and joined forces to defeat Soviet communism, once and for all!”
Patton died in December 1945 after a car crash in occupied Germany; conspiratorial claims that he was assassinated have long been debunked.
When fellow influencer Cam Higby complained in February that saying Nick Shirley was not a Nazi had led others to call him one, Amacher replied that “a colleague’s great-grandfather served as a paramilitary adjunct in Germany’s ‘other’ military force (not the Wehrmacht)”. He went on: “By your logic, does that make him a Nazi? Asking for a friend…” and attaching an “OK” emoji.
He has captioned a photo of a figure skater with her right arm raised “Heil yes!” and offered to recruit a man “straight into my elite Panzer division”. Panzer divisions were armored tank units in Nazi Germany’s army. In July 2025 he joked that his ancestors “fled to Argentina as well, but way back in 1945, departing from the Deutsches Reich”.
He has also called for the return of the late Spanish dictator Francisco Franco, writing: “Bring back Francisco Franco!” in July under a post claiming that “African military-aged males by the THOUSANDS” were entering the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. And he has praised Germany’s AfD, which the country’s domestic intelligence agency labeled a “confirmed rightwing extremist” force last year. “The @AfD is the ONLY party left that will actually SAVE Germany from destruction,” he wrote in April. “We will restore traditional German societal norms, identity, and culture.”
‘He looks like a Jew’

Family Matters: The Secret History Behind Why Vincent van Gogh Cut Off His Ear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

After riding a series of escalators to the fifth floor of New York’s Museum of Modern Art, I stepped into a gallery where, on display, were a dozen paintings and lithographs by late-nineteenth and early twentieth-century artists, including Pablo Picasso, Paul Cézanne, and Georges Seurat.
But most visitors were gathered around one explosively colorful painting in swirling shades of light and dark blue, bottle green, and pale gold.
Instantly recognizable.
One of the most famous paintings in the world.
The Starry Night by Vincent van Gogh.
These were the early days of my research about a little-known woman who is key to shedding light on three inevitable questions when it comes to Vincent van Gogh. Why did he cut off his ear? Why did he commit suicide? And how, after dying in obscurity, did he eventually become regarded as one of the world’s greatest artists?
Gauging Van Gogh
Watching and talking to people as they engaged with this particular masterpiece seemed an apropos way to gauge the interest of Van Gogh lovers.
I, for one, could remember, as a child, first seeing The Starry Night reprinted in one of my parents’ art history books. It was my modern art “aha” moment. No one was standing over my shoulder telling me to pay it special attention, but I was mesmerized. The painting became imprinted on my young imagination, and I never forgot it.
As I observed the gallery, I quickly learned my reaction is hardly unique.
A man from Southern California named Paul Duelo was laughing. “I know this painting, and I don’t know anything about art,” he said with a chuckle, nodding at the crowd standing around The Starry Night. “Look at everyone!”
A woman from Seattle stood gazing quietly with her arms folded. Sheri Larison first saw a picture of The Starry Night more than 30 years ago in her high school art class. A reproduction of the iconic painting hung in her office. This was her very first time seeing the original.
“It’s overwhelming,” Larison whispered, with tears in her eyes. “It evokes something. It’s magical.”
She was interested in the painting’s origin story. “His mental health was declining,” she said, and that was true, although perhaps also misleading.
Van Gogh painted The Starry Night in June of 1889 during a year he spent in a mental asylum in the south of France.
It does not represent an actual place but a compilation of elements—a village, starry sky, moon, dark hills, and a cypress tree—all things that Vincent had seen at one time and brought together in this composition. The sight of stars, he said, always made him dream.
Hanging just to the left of The Starry Night was a Paul Gauguin’s painting, The Moon and the Earth. The juxtaposition provoked a curious thought. Gauguin and Van Gogh lived and worked together in Vincent’s yellow house in Arles in the south of France for several weeks. What would the hot-tempered, competitive Gauguin have thought seeing so many people gathered around Vincent’s painting at this moment while his was comparatively ignored? And what would Vincent have made of all the attention given to The Starry Night?
It is generally believed that it was an argument with Gauguin, who was threatening to quit Arles (in effect abandoning Van Gogh), which spun the mentally unstable Vincent into such a state of despair and frustration that he mutilated himself by slicing off his left ear.
The fine art of family matters
But, as I was learning, family matters also very likely played a part in the most notorious instance of self-harm in art history.
It’s a tragic story of dependence and the limits of love. And it’s where Jo van Gogh-Bonger comes in. Biographical details about her—revealed in her diaries and letters—have only recently been made public by the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam. They paint a picture of a determined woman to whom the world of art owes a tremendous debt.
Jo was married to Vincent’s younger brother, Theo, who was an art dealer in Paris and Vincent’s only source of income. Theo supported Vincent with a monthly allowance, and in exchange Vincent gave Theo his paintings to try to market and sell. The financial arrangement, as it would in most families, put an emotional strain on both brothers. Theo was not rich, and Vincent constantly complained about being broke, with not even enough money for food, and often practically begged his brother for more money.
Over the course of 10 years, Vincent created more than 800 paintings and 700 drawings, desperately hoping for financial independence and commercial success. But in Vincent’s lifetime, Theo is known to have sold just one painting: Red Vineyard at Arles.
In July of 1890, believing himself a failure as an artist and a man, Vincent shot himself in the chest. He was only 37.
Six months after Vincent’s suicide, Theo died from the ravages of syphilis, leaving Jo a young widow with a baby to support, not much money, and an unusual inheritance—Vincent’s paintings—more than 400 in total.
They filled the walls of their Paris apartment, were stored in closets, under beds, and at a nearby art supply store. The Potato Eaters, Irises, Sunflowers, self-portraits, and The Starry Night. Celebrated as masterpieces today, at the time they were regarded as the unpolished works of a depressed, crazy man and commercially worthless. Jo thought differently. She had no formal art training, but she loved his work and her instincts told her that Vincent was (as Theo had come to believe) a genius.
Jo also inherited hundreds of letters that Vincent wrote and received, most exchanged with Theo. Jo read and re-read those letters, initially to feel closer to Theo, but she was also captivated by Vincent’s compassion and intelligence. She decided the world should read them too. It was part of her plan: to organize exhibitions, lobby critics, and publicize the letters, which showed how vulnerable and anguished Vincent was, yes, but also how deliberate he was in his craft and how close Vincent and Theo were to each other. Eventually, in 1914, Jo succeeded in publishing Vincent’s letters in an ambitious three-volume book, which today is considered one of the most revealing and important works of art history.
An infamous ear
As much as she would play a vital role in propelling him to fame, Jo was also someone who unwittingly played a part in Vincent’s self-destructive descent, something she at times admitted feeling guilt about after his death. Jo understood Vincent was lonely and that he became more isolated after she married his brother.
That infamous act of self-mutilation, when Vincent cut off his ear, happened the very day Vincent likely received the surprising news that Theo and Jo were engaged, triggering what some Van Gogh experts, including Martin Bailey, suspect were unquenchable fears that Theo might eventually abandon him.
And Vincent shot himself just days after a stressful visit with Jo and Theo in Paris. Theo was thinking about quitting his job to start his own business, which meant, for a time, no income. The couple (who by now had a baby son they named after Vincent) hoped to rent a better apartment on a lower floor. But budgets were tight, arguments ensued, and Vincent eventually rushed out of the apartment, unable to shake the thought that he was a burden that Theo would or could no longer bear.
Jo didn’t seek to put herself at the center of this story, but she is there, nonetheless. A surprisingly relatable woman (at times insecure, at times doggedly persistent), she courageously stood up to the male-dominated art world as a champion for Vincent and spent 30 years of her life promoting his work and life story in Holland, Germany, France, England, and even, for a time, in America.
Interestingly, of all the paintings Jo inherited, no one—not Jo or Theo or Vincent—considered The Starry Night one of Vincent’s best. Vincent didn’t even sign it. Research recently published by the Van Gogh Museum points out that Vincent signed only about 16% of his paintings, hypothesizing he did so usually when he was completely satisfied or wanted to make them a gift to friends or family. In the brothers’ correspondence, The Starry Night was referred to rather than named. Theo called it simply “the village in the moonlight,” critically writing to Vincent that “I feel that the search for style takes away the real sentiment of things.”
Vincent conceded the painting lacked character and considered it a mistake that “…once again I’m allowing myself to do stars too big…new setback, and I’ve had enough of that.”
Jo also didn’t seem to consider The Starry Night as especially important. She sold it early on but reacquired it briefly in time for a major exhibition she organized in Amsterdam in 1905. It was painting number 199, called De Sterren (The Stars), and it changed hands two more times before MoMA acquired it in 1941. By then, it had been rechristened The Starry Night. The name stuck.
There is a world of personal stories behind the paintings of Vincent van Gogh, and they reaffirm an old adage: we can’t separate the art from the artist. I believe Jo would agree.
Paul Duelo, the man from California I met while admiring MoMA’s The Starry Night, lit up when I told him about Jo van Gogh-Bonger.
He had never heard of her before.
But he wanted to know more.
If you or someone you know may be experiencing a mental-health crisis or contemplating suicide, call or text 988.

Slovak PM says Slovakia and Hungary will not fund EU aid for Ukraine in 2027
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has said that Ukraine has asked the EU to provide an additional €70 billion in assistance for 2027, but Slovakia and Hungary will not participate in the initiative.
Source: European Pravda, citing Denník N
Details: Fico said it would be "dangerous" to link negotiations on the EU's future budget to financing for Ukraine.
He said Slovakia wanted to support Ukraine in other ways, such as through projects in education, road infrastructure and energy interconnections, but would not participate in another potential EU loan.
Fico said Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar shared this position.
Nevertheless, Fico criticised what he saw as insufficient discussion of peace initiatives and ways to end Russia's war against Ukraine at the EU summit in Brussels on Thursday and Friday.
The Slovak prime minister also reiterated that it would be "dangerous" to link negotiations on the EU's future budget to financing for Ukraine.
Background:
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at the Brussels summit that the war would cost Ukraine €155 billion next year. He asked EU leaders to find an additional €70 billion to support Ukraine.
- The European Commission acknowledged that Ukraine's 2027 budget does indeed face a €70 billion shortfall that will need to be covered by international partners.
- The European Council instructed the European Commission to prepare proposals for covering Ukraine's €70 billion budget shortfall in 2027.
