Ukraine’s grain trap: where to put the 2026 harvest and what prolonged export restrictions could lead to
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:59:00 EEST
19:59:00 KST

Ukraine’s grain trap: where to put the 2026 harvest and what prolonged export restrictions could lead to
Kyiv • UNN
Russian attacks and logistics problems have reduced grain exports from Ukraine. Surpluses could lower farmers’ incomes and the 2027 harvest.
Ukraine is harvesting a decent grain crop, but selling it is becoming increasingly difficult due to Russian strikes on ports, railways, and other logistics routes. There is currently a high probability that the grain may remain in storage instead of generating funds for farmers for the next sowing campaign.
The farms most at risk are those without their own storage facilities and forced to sell their produce to intermediaries at reduced prices. What could be the scale of grain accumulation, and what consequences could this have for the 2027 harvest? The CEO of the Ukrainian Agrarian Confederation (UAC), Pavlo Koval, explained to UNN.
The 2026 grain harvest — how much Ukraine has already collected and what volumes need to be exported
As of October 13, Ukrainian farmers had harvested 37.14 million tonnes of grain and leguminous crops, covering 65.2% of the planned area. According to Pavlo Koval's estimate, by October 15, up to 38 million tonnes had been collected from the fields. Separately, according to the Ministry of Agrarian Policy, about 13.9 million tonnes of oilseed crops had been harvested, including sunflower, rapeseed, and soybeans. It should be noted here that the previous state forecast projected a grain harvest of approximately 60.4 million tonnes.
Pavlo Koval explains that the discrepancy arose because of corn: its gross harvest may reach 30–31 million tonnes, but by mid-October only about 3.5 million tonnes had been harvested. Therefore, the final figures summarizing this year's grain harvest will emerge once farmers harvest this crop. And this is precisely where major problems begin.
"Due to the rain and high grain moisture, part of the harvest may remain in the fields until winter. Drying requires additional funds, which not every farm can afford," the expert warned.
Speaking about the wheat harvest, the UAC CEO estimated it at 26.2 million tonnes, of which approximately 12 million tonnes are planned for export. (For corn, the benchmark is 22 million tonnes of exports out of an expected production volume of 30 million tonnes.) However, these volumes represent export potential, because it is not enough to sell grain abroad — it must also be physically delivered to the buyer.
Maritime exports under threat — how much Ukrainian grain could remain in the country due to supply restrictions
According to the State Customs Service, as of October 16, since the beginning of the 2026/27 marketing year, Ukraine had exported 5.929 million tonnes of grain and leguminous crops. This is 24.9% less than during the corresponding period of the previous season.
Koval calculates that current shipments amount to approximately half of the required pace, given the size of the harvest. According to him, additional wheat stocks of 5–6 million tonnes could accumulate by the end of the season. If significant logistics restrictions persist during the period of mass corn deliveries, the risk of grain accumulation will increase sharply.
"The Danube route is of particular concern. In 2022, it made it possible to transport up to 2.5 million tonnes of cargo per month and partially offset restrictions on the operation of major seaports. Now it is being affected by strikes on terminals, infrastructure problems, and shipping disruptions. In the area of the Sulina Canal alone (the middle of the three major straits of the Danube Delta and the main navigable channel at the mouth of the Danube in Romania — ed.), about 150 grain vessels have accumulated," the expert said.
Rail crossings with the EU and road routes also cannot fully replace maritime transport: their capacity is limited, and transportation is more expensive. As a result, even when buyers are available, farmers cannot always ship their produce on time.
This season, Ukraine reduced wheat exports but increased corn exports12.08.26, 17:03 • 17890 views
Will Ukraine have sufficient storage capacity for the harvest, and what will happen to the surplus?
As of the end of 2025, Ukraine’s total grain storage capacity was estimated at 52.67 million tonnes of simultaneous storage. However, it is important to understand that some storage facilities are already occupied, some are located far from producers, and grain transportation and elevator services cost money. Therefore, under the most difficult scenario, according to a source speaking to UNN, if the current pace of exports and corn accumulation is maintained, carryover stocks could reach 30–35 million tonnes. As a result, the grain may have to wait for sale, while keeping it throughout this period will require the farmer to have storage space and financing.
"Having grain in the storage facility does not yet guarantee money in the account," Pavlo Koval emphasized.
According to him, small and medium-sized farms often have only three options:
-  pay for storage at an elevator;  
-  sell directly from the field at an unfavorable price;  
-  leave the produce in their own unsuitable facilities. 
Each of them entails its own costs and risks.
Additionally, excess supply within the country will put pressure on purchase prices. Even if grain becomes more expensive on the global market, Ukrainian producers will not necessarily benefit, as higher logistics costs and transportation risks may absorb the difference.
Export restrictions and farmers’ losses — how the grain crisis will affect sown areas and grain production in 2027
Ukrainian farmers have already felt the consequences of the current difficulties during the autumn sowing campaign. In an exclusive comment to UNN , Pavlo Koval said that by mid-October, approximately 3.5 million hectares of winter wheat had been sown. If the area reaches 4 million hectares by the end of the campaign, he will consider that an acceptable result. The situation is worse with winter barley: according to the expert’s estimate, about 280,000 hectares have been sown, compared with approximately 500,000 hectares planned.
"Amid difficulties selling grain, producers may cut spending on fertilizers, crop protection products and technological operations, which will affect next year’s yields. Some farms will also revise their crop structure in favor of crops that have higher margins and require less logistics capacity," the UAC director general forecast.
Among such options, he named rapeseed and sunflower. However, according to him, changing the "cropping map" will not solve the problem of the destruction of export routes.
The situation is quite difficult. I do not want to say that it is catastrophic, but it is quite challenging
He emphasized that the most vulnerable remain small producers without their own transport or financial reserves. For them, a delay in selling grain may result in lower profits and the risk of being unable to finance the next sowing campaign. Therefore, if export restrictions continue, the Ukrainian economy could suffer a double blow: lower foreign-currency revenues now and weaker grain-production potential in 2027.
How Russian attacks threaten Ukraine’s exports and whether alternative routes exist
Russian attacks on Black Sea ports threaten to cause grain accumulation and losses for farmers. Whether there is an alternative to maritime exports and what will happen if restrictions persist was explained in an exclusive comment to UNN by TEUS logistics company owner and director Dmytro Kazanin.
According to the expert’s estimate, Ukraine needs to export about 5 million tonnes of grain per month to avoid accumulating excess stocks.
"When it is necessary to ship about five million tonnes per month, we are shipping approximately two and a half million," Kazanin said.
Instead, he estimates current shipment volumes at only 2.5 million tonnes: the shortfall amounts to nearly half of the requirement.
Overall statistics also point to a slowdown in exports. According to the State Customs Service, as of October 16, since the beginning of the 2026/27 marketing year, Ukraine had exported 5.929 million tonnes of grain and pulses, 24.9% less than during the corresponding period of the previous season. The reason is that, due to higher transportation costs, farmers are forced to choose between selling at a loss and storing their crops.
Alternative export routes—can railways, road transport, and Danube ports replace the Black Sea ports?
At present, grain exports through the western borders, by rail, by truck, and via the Danube remain possible. But there is an important caveat: according to Kazanin's assessment, the combined capacity of these routes is insufficient to compensate for what Ukraine is losing because of the downtime at the Black Sea ports, which are constantly being attacked by the Russian armed forces.
"This cannot be compensated for. Our ports are designed (specifically—the editor) for this kind of work. All the border crossings and the Danube ports together cannot compensate for it," the logistics expert explained.
On the railway route that can be used to export grain, congestion is emerging, according to Kazanin. At crossings with EU countries, there are not enough European railcars to transfer grain from Ukrainian rolling stock. In addition, specific transshipment rules in the EU further complicate movement.
There are also problems with transporting agricultural cargo along the Danube.
"Danube shipping is being constrained by low water levels. Look, a barge with a capacity of 2,000 tonnes can load only about 1,000 tonnes in shallow sections in order to travel along the route to the Romanian port of Constanța. The movement of vessels from the Upper Danube to the Lower Danube is also limited," Dmytro Kazanin explained.
He clarified that some routes are nevertheless operating and cited his own company's experience as an example. Kazanin noted that in September, TEUS sent 72 containers of wheat to Indonesia via Gdańsk. At the same time, he immediately emphasized that this would not replace bulk shipments and would not significantly affect the global logistics problems that domestic farmers have faced this year.
More expensive logistics and loss of competitiveness—how Russian attacks are affecting the cost of Ukrainian grain exports
According to Kazanin's assessment, logistics costs have increased three- to fourfold recently. Since Ukrainian producers do not determine global grain prices, the additional costs of delivering it effectively reduce the amount that the farmer ultimately receives for their work.
Our farmer is losing income. Today, they have to sell grain at a loss because logistics costs have increased three- to fourfold
As an example, he cited a grain production cost of $150–160 per tonne, while sales revenue for a farm may amount to $120–125. If the situation does not change going forward, Dmytro Kazanin assumes that grain exports may become even more unprofitable. Moreover, Ukraine will feel the consequences of this as early as the next sowing season.
Due to a lack of funds, farmers are cutting back on fertilizer purchases. This could reduce yields in 2027, as well as export revenues and budget income. And because of unprofitable prices, some of the corn may remain in the fields over the winter altogether
The threat of grain accumulation—is it relevant for Ukraine, and why?
In response to questions from UNN journalists, Dmytro Kazanin explained that if the gap between the harvested crop and its exports—2.5 million tonnes per month—persists, it will mathematically amount to about 5 million tonnes after two months and 7.5 million tonnes after three. At the same time, the expert cautioned against equating delayed exports with the physical loss of grain. He emphasized that, for now, the issue is primarily the inability to deliver the necessary volumes to buyers on time.
"This is not about loss, but about the possibility of exporting it (the grain — Ed.). At present, there is no possibility of exporting the amount that is needed," he emphasized.
According to Kazanin, problems with exporting the harvest arise for Ukrainian farmers simultaneously in all directions: there is a shortage of railcars and railway capacity, transshipment at the border slows things down, while the Danube is constrained by shallow waters. Therefore, no single alternative route will save exports.
The available corridors need to be used simultaneously, along with the stable operation of Black Sea ports. Because prolonged restrictions could also affect next year's harvest
As a reminder
Russia is increasingly targeting Ukrainian grain export corridors in the Black Sea, increasing security risks for the entire region. Romania and Bulgaria are already asking NATO to strengthen protection against drones from the Russian Armed Forces.

Pro-Palestinian politician threatens Berlin left's election victory over Israel stance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:56:15 UTC
19:56:15 KST

Until a month ago, no one outside Germany's internal left-wing politics had heard of  Vanessa Emde. This week, she became a central figure in German and Berlin politics, with her positions threatening to deny her party, Die Linke (The Left), which won the Berlin elections in late September, the opportunity to form a government. Moreover, the controversy Emde sparked this week threatens to tear Die Linke apart from within, triggering a genuine struggle over the party's fundamental identity. At the heart of the dispute, unsurprisingly, is its attitude toward Israel.
After Die Linke won more than a quarter of the vote in Berlin, it was clear that forming a coalition under its leadership would require negotiations with the Greens and Social Democrats (SPD), its two natural partners in establishing a left-wing government.
However, before agreeing even to enter talks with Die Linke, the leaders of both parties demanded clarification and unequivocal commitments on two main issues: that the party distance itself from any ties to criminal clans in Berlin and, above all, that it commit to combating antisemitism, protecting Jewish lives, acknowledging the October 7 massacre, opposing Hamas and unequivocally recognizing Israel's right to exist.
Die Linke found itself in a trap. Signing such agreements would run counter to a central principle held by its voters, particularly younger voters and immigrant communities. But refusing the conditions would reinforce the public perception that it was an antisemitic party. Without the Greens and SPD, it had no chance of forming a coalition. Die Linke's representatives in Berlin signed the memorandum of understanding on the issue, and the parties agreed to begin talks.
But the agreement began to unravel almost immediately afterward, when Die Linke decided to admit Vanessa Emde to its parliamentary group. Although she had been directly elected in the Neukölln district with nearly 50% of the vote, the SPD and Greens had demanded that she not be admitted to the group. For them, she was a red line.
Emde, a queer feminist activist, rode a wave of political success largely on the strength of her explicitly anti-Israel platform. She belongs to a group called Palestine Solidarity Working Group (AG Palästina-Solidarität), whose members have previously claimed that "the Palestinian struggle will end when Tel Aviv is in Palestinian hands." On election night, she proudly posed for a photograph with Ibrahim Ibrahim, a prominent supporter of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) in Germany who is active in the United Palestinian National Committee, which also includes Hamas supporters.
She is best remembered for a statement she made in May, when she said she "does not believe in the right of states to exist, only in the right of human beings to exist." Although the statement did not refer directly to Israel, its context was clear. She supports a one-state solution and explained her friendly photograph with Ibrahim by saying she rejects the authority of Germany's domestic intelligence agency to determine who may establish political ties in the country.
Within Die Linke, the Berlin branch is considered the most radical, particularly regarding policy toward Israel. Within the Berlin branch, Neukölln, a district with a large Muslim immigrant population, is regarded as the most radical of all. Die Linke cannot afford to lose its support, either electorally or because of the work local activists do to bring voters to the polls.
Now, the local branch and its voters have demanded that the party not give in. Calls have grown louder to preserve the party's policies and the positions that brought it electoral victory at all costs, particularly on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, even if that means remaining in opposition.
The grassroots pressure worked. On Thursday, Emde posted a three-minute video on her Instagram account in which she repudiated her signature on the memorandum of understanding with the other two parties and reaffirmed all her previous statements, including her rejection of the right of states to exist.
"The fact that I, as an individual, am being used as a bargaining chip in the talks is, to put it mildly, a democratic scandal that must be investigated," she wrote in the accompanying post.
According to Emde, "The starting point for this madness: A few months ago, I published a video in which I paraphrased a self-evident principle of international law: 'States do not have a right to exist — people have a right to exist.'
"I also said: 'The demand for a democratic one-state solution with equal rights for all people, regardless of their ethnic origin or religion, is a legitimate political demand and must not be criminalized.'"
The SPD and Greens announced the cancellation of coalition talks, saying they suspected Die Linke was conducting two parallel sets of negotiations and signing separate memorandums of understanding: one in coalition negotiations with them and the other in internal party negotiations, with each agreement undermining the other.
Die Linke's leaders have now announced that the parliamentary group distances itself from Emde's remarks and disavows her political positions. Discussions about her future in the group are scheduled to begin Tuesday, with Emde in attendance.
The Palestinian issue and the war in Gaza have dominated Berlin's streets for the three years since October 7 and were an important factor in the city's election campaign. Now, they threaten both the stability of a potential local coalition and the unity of the radical left-wing party, confronting it with a fateful question: Does Die Linke have an identity without its distinctly anti-Israel stance?
It remains to be seen whether the party's argument that its position constitutes criticism of Israeli policy rather than antisemitism will be accepted, and whether it can preserve its unity and its chances of governing without abandoning that position.

Gilad Schalit’s release, 15 years later: Why Israel must remember joy of his homecoming - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:51:26 UTC
19:51:26 KST

Last Sunday, October 11, an important anniversary passed almost unnoticed.
On June 25, 2006, a 19-year-old Israeli soldier was abducted during a Hamas attack near the Gaza border. For the next five years, his name became part of the daily consciousness of Jews worldwide.
We saw his photograph everywhere. We watched the demonstrations. We followed every rumor of negotiations, every hopeful report and every subsequent disappointment.
We prayed for him in our synagogues, attended rallies, and signed petitions. His name became familiar to people who had never met him and probably never would.
I was living in Britain at the time, and I remember vividly how deeply his captivity affected Jewish communities far beyond Israel’s borders.
Gilad Schalit was not simply another soldier. He was somebody’s son, somebody’s brother, a young man who should have been enjoying the ordinary experiences of early adulthood.
Instead, he was being held in isolation, deprived of his freedom, and separated from everyone he loved.
For five long years, we prayed and hoped he would somehow return.
And then, suddenly, the extraordinary news came.
There was an agreement. He was coming home.
On October 11, 2011, 15 years ago, Israel announced that an agreement had finally been reached to secure Gilad’s release after more than five years of hell on earth. One week later, on October 18, he came home.
It was a moment of almost indescribable national joy. And perhaps, amid everything that has happened since, we should pause to remember it.
Of course, the Schalit prisoner exchange has been analyzed, criticized, and debated endlessly.
Much has been written about the price Israel paid, the prisoners who were released, the precedent it established, and the possible consequences for the horrific events of October 7, 2023. These are serious questions, and history has made some of them even more painful.
I do not dismiss the argument. But that is not what I want to write about today.
I want to remember something simpler, something profoundly human. I want to remember how it felt when we heard that Gilad was coming home.
I remember the overwhelming relief, happiness, excitement, and, above all, gratitude. After years in which hope had repeatedly been raised and dashed, something truly wonderful was happening.
For a brief moment, it seemed that an entire nation could share in one family’s happiness. The joy was almost overwhelming; we wanted to laugh out loud and greet perfect strangers with a grin and a hug.
When Gilad finally appeared on our television screens on October 18, thin, pale, and visibly affected by his ordeal, the emotion was extraordinary.
Here was the young man whose photograph we had studied for years. Here he was, alive. Here he was, back on Israeli soil.
And then came the images of him reunited with his family.
How could anyone watch without being moved?
We had never met him, yet somehow we felt we knew him. His parents’ relief became our relief. Their happiness became our happiness. The prayers of five years seemed to find their answer in that single embrace.
Of course, even then there were families for whom the release of convicted terrorists brought renewed anguish rather than celebration. Their pain was real and deserves recognition.
Remembering the joy of Gilad’s return does not require us to dismiss their suffering or ignore the difficult decisions involved, far from it.
But surely we can acknowledge that, whatever our views about the agreement, the return of a young man from captivity was itself something worth celebrating. And there are two people whose extraordinary contribution should never be forgotten.
A place for gratitude
Noam and Aviva Schalit, Gilad’s parents, refused to allow their son to disappear from public consciousness.
For five years, they campaigned tirelessly. They attended meetings, confronted politicians, spoke to journalists, and kept their son’s photograph before the eyes of the nation.
Noam, in particular, became the public face of a family’s determination never to give up. He was not a professional campaigner or a politician. He was a father who wanted his son back.
What could be more human about that simple truth?
In 2022, Noam died after a battle with cancer. He was only 68. But he lived to see his son return, embrace him again, and, in 2021, accompany him to his wedding.
What a blessing that was. What a reward for years of anguish and perseverance.
And what of Gilad himself?
Thankfully, after the extraordinary public attention surrounding his captivity and release, he has largely chosen, and achieved, a quieter life.
He married Nitzan Shabbat and has worked as a sports journalist, pursuing an interest that existed long before his abduction.
In many ways, that is perhaps the most heartening part of his story.
We sometimes imagine that the happy ending to a dramatic story must itself be dramatic. But perhaps the greatest victory for someone who has endured years of captivity is the ability to live an ordinary life.
To go to work. To enjoy sport. To spend time with family and friends. To marry, laugh, make plans, and wake up each morning without fear of what the day might bring.
Most of us take these things for granted. For somebody who has had them forcibly taken away, they must assume an entirely different significance.
We cannot know everything that Gilad has experienced since his release, nor should we presume to understand the lasting effects of his captivity. He deserves his privacy and the freedom to build his life away from the public gaze.
But it brings great joy to know that the young man whose face once appeared on countless posters has been able to move forward with his life.
The events of October 7 brought the terrible reality of hostage-taking back into our lives on a scale that none of us could have imagined.
Once again, we became familiar with photographs, names, families, and campaigns. Once again, prayers for the return of captives became part of our daily existence.
And once again, we were reminded how precious a single human life can be.
We live in an age of relentless argument. Every event is immediately subjected to political analysis. Every decision is judged, often with considerable bitterness, and every moment of happiness seems destined to be overshadowed by the next crisis.
There is a place for criticism, accountability, and historical reflection. But there must also be a place for gratitude.
Not every memory needs to become an argument. Not every anniversary needs to reopen a political battle.
Sometimes we should allow ourselves simply to remember that something good happened.
Fifteen years ago, after 1,941 days in captivity, a young Israeli soldier returned to his family. A mother embraced her son. A father saw the culmination of five years of tireless effort. And millions of people, in Israel and across the Jewish world, shared a moment of extraordinary happiness.
Whatever happened afterward should not erase that moment.
As we approach the anniversary of Gilad’s homecoming on Sunday, let us remember the tears of joy, the relief, and the gratitude.
Let us remember Noam and Aviva and the extraordinary love that sustained their campaign.
And let us wish Gilad many more years of peace, happiness, and the ordinary pleasures of a life lived in freedom.
The world has enough darkness. Sometimes we need to remind ourselves that there is light, too.
And do you know what? Fifteen years later, it is still worth stopping to say thank you.
The writer is a rabbi and physician. He writes and teaches on Jewish ethics, leadership, and resilience. His work appears on rabbidrjonathanlieberman.substack.com and youtube.com. @rabbidrjonathanlieberman

Details
"Automatic extensions of mobilization deferments have begun. More than 90% of current deferments may be extended automatically—without repeat applications or visits to government institutions. The grounds for extending deferments are being verified according to uniform rules based on data from state registers. After that, users will be able to see in Reserve+ whether the deferment has been extended and for what period," the ministry said in a post.

Deferments will be updated gradually, so notifications will not arrive for everyone at the same time.Automatic extension is available for 22 categories of citizens. For this, the grounds for the deferment must remain valid and be confirmed by data from state registers.
How can you find out the result?
"You will receive a notification in Reserve+ in any case—both if the deferment is extended automatically and if it is not. If you have not received a notification yet, wait for the verification result. After the extension is successfully completed, update your electronic military registration document and check the new validity period," the post says.
The ministry also said that the absence of an automatic extension of a deferment does not necessarily mean that a person has lost the right to a deferment.
"This does not necessarily mean that the right to a deferment has been lost. The reason may be missing or outdated data in state registers. Check the data and update it if necessary. After that, you can submit a new request through Reserve+ if your category is available for online processing, or visit a CNAP with the relevant documents. The current deferment remains valid until its expiration date," the post says.
Reminder
The Office of the Military Ombudsman prepared legislative proposals that provide for stricter requirements for obtaining a mobilization deferment for parents of children with disabilities, husbands and wives, and other relatives of people with disabilities.

Rare pink diamond goes on display in France 100 years after amateur heist
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:46:41 BST
19:46:41 KST

Rare pink diamond goes on display in France 100 years after amateur heist
- Published
A rare pink diamond is going on display in France for the first time since it was stolen almost 100 years ago to the day - the last time it was shown to the public.
The nine-carat, pear-shaped gemstone known as the "Grand Condé" was pilfered in an overnight raid on the Château de Chantilly in October 1926 and concealed in a hollowed-out apple.
The diamond - one of few royal jewels to survive the French Revolution - was recovered a few weeks later when a hungry maid at the hotel in which the thieves were staying took a bite of the apple.
It will once again be on display in the Condé Museum at the Château de Chantilly until 3 January.
The museum's director Mathieu Deldicque said that while the apple story may sounds far-fetched, it was widely covered by newspapers at the time.
Deldicque has faced questions about whether the exhibition may be tempting fate, especially given the string of heists on European cultural institutions in the past 12 months, including the daring daylight robbery of jewellery from the Louvre museum in Paris.
While he declined to reveal to CNN how much the diamond was insured for, he noted that extensive academic study into the properties of the diamond had taken place to make it uniquely identifiable.
The results of this analysis, as well as previously unseen archive material about the gem's history and theft, form part of the exhibition, according to the museum.
Naturally occurring pink diamonds are exceptionally rare and often sell for tens of millions of dollars. The highest price ever fetched for one at auction was $71.2m (£53.6m) in 2017, according to Sotheby's.
The exact origins of the Grand Condé remain a mystery.
It was first mentioned in 1740 in an inventory of Louis Henri de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, drawn up following his death, the Château de Chantilly said.
It then became part of the collection of Queen Marie-Amélie of Bourbon-Sicily, the wife of French King Louis Philippe I, and then her son, Prince Henri of Orléans, the Duke of Aumale.
He bequeathed it to the Institut de France, which now owns the Château de Chantilly, 50km (31 miles) north of Paris, along with thousands of artworks and manuscripts which became the Musée Condé collection.

Yerevan Declaration urges faster action to halt biodiversity loss
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
18:42:39 CST
19:42:39 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- The Yerevan Declaration was adopted at a biodiversity leaders' summit in the Armenian capital on Friday, calling for stronger international cooperation and accelerated efforts to halt and reverse biodiversity loss.
Held ahead of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), the summit brought together heads of state and government, alongside representatives of international organizations, local communities and other stakeholders.
Armenian Environment Minister and COP17 President-designate Hambardzum Matevosyan presented the declaration, entitled "Taking Action for Nature," as the summit's outcome document.
The declaration reaffirmed commitments to the Convention on Biological Diversity and to the effective implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, with its mission of halting and reversing biodiversity loss by 2030 and its vision of living in harmony with nature by 2050.
While welcoming growing global mobilization for biodiversity, it said the first global report on the framework's implementation showed that collective efforts and progress remained insufficient and that accelerated implementation was urgently needed.
In the declaration, leaders committed to strengthening national implementation through whole-of-government and whole-of-society approaches, in accordance with national circumstances, priorities and capabilities. They also committed to integrating biodiversity considerations into public policies and economic sectors and strengthening the conservation, restoration, management and sustainable use of terrestrial, freshwater, coastal and marine ecosystems.
The declaration also set out commitments to strengthen monitoring, planning, reporting and review, improve biodiversity data and knowledge systems, and promote science-based decision-making and the responsible use of innovative technology.
On financing, it stressed the need to mobilize increased public and private funding for biodiversity from all sources, ensuring that funding is adequate, predictable, timely and accessible. It also emphasized capacity-building, scientific and technical cooperation, access to and transfer of technology, and innovation, alongside stronger international partnerships to support implementation in developing countries, particularly the least developed and small-island developing ones.
It looked ahead to the first global review of collective progress in implementing the framework as an important milestone for strengthening transparency, accountability and collective learning, addressing implementation gaps, promoting effective solutions and accelerating action.
The declaration also called for an effective, results-oriented outcome in Yerevan, with a clear pathway toward accelerated implementation of the framework and achievement of its targets. ■

US strikes $25M UNICEF deal to avert medicine shortages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:40:00 UTC
19:40:00 KST

The U.S. government has reached an agreement to continue providing some of the world’s poorest countries with free, lifesaving medicines and medical equipment for mothers, infants and young children, following months of uncertainty and supply disruptions.
The U.N. Children’s Fund, or UNICEF, will procure the supplies, a State Department spokesperson told Reuters by email, without disclosing further details. UNICEF said the one-year agreement is worth $25 million.
The funding represents only a fraction of the assistance affected by the Trump administration’s aid cuts and dismantling of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID).
However, the deal should prevent another sudden interruption in supplies that some of the world’s most vulnerable countries depend on as they negotiate new health assistance agreements with Washington.
Nine former U.S. aid officials, nongovernmental organization representatives and government officials told Reuters that an interruption had been a significant concern because the existing contract between the now-defunct USAID and its supplier was due to expire last month.
The agreement covers the procurement and delivery of maternal and child health supplies, as well as some nutrition supplies, to at least 15 countries previously covered by the program, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti and Mali, UNICEF said.
It follows nearly 18 months of disruption after Washington moved to freeze and then scale back many U.S. aid programs as part of its “America First Global Health Strategy.”
In countries such as Congo, shortages resulting from the disruption have already emerged.
At Nyangezi General Hospital in eastern Congo, health workers said they had run out of lifesaving medications, including oxytocin, used to prevent and treat postpartum hemorrhage, and amoxicillin, an antibiotic used in pediatric care and during childbirth.
“It was a donation we received (previously) from USAID, and at the moment, there is none,” midwife Alice Bulambo told Reuters.
The main government-run warehouse in the area has experienced stockouts for more than a year, said Olivier Kabarati Amani, chief medical officer for the Nyangezi health zone.
As a result, health facilities have been forced to buy medicines at market prices. Over the past six months, “the cost of care has doubled, if not tripled,” Amani said, as the health care system in eastern Congo continues to struggle with Ebola.
The State Department said it “has prioritized ensuring all lifesaving commodities have continued to be made reliably available.”
Maternal and newborn health supplies accounted for less than 1% of the more than $5 billion spent by the USAID Global Health Supply Chain Program between 2016 and 2023, according to the most recently available annual report. The spending was channeled through private contractor Chemonics.
Reuters first reported plans to close the program, which also managed the donation and delivery of supplies to combat malaria and HIV, in April, with aid officials warning that the Sept. 30 shutdown could cause shortages.
The planned closure of the Chemonics supply chain program is part of the broader U.S. global health strategy, which aims to move countries toward self-reliance while scaling back U.S. support and reducing reliance on contractors.
The U.S. has instead signed more than 30 bilateral health aid agreements with recipient countries, including Congo. The agreements require countries to contribute funding and are worth billions of dollars combined.
However, the details of the agreements are still being worked out, and it had been unclear what would fill the gap in the ordering process in the meantime.
Although many countries were already moving toward taking responsibility for their maternal and child health needs, order lead times can reach a year or more, five former USAID officials said.
The Congolese government aims to take over by next year but has struggled with the recent uncertainty, said Polydor Kabila, coordinator of the universal health care program in the president’s office.
Alongside the UNICEF agreement, U.S. authorities have extended the deadline for Chemonics to deliver some key malaria and HIV supplies, the State Department spokesperson told Reuters. The U.S. has also signed an agreement with the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria that allows countries to order new U.S.-funded HIV and malaria supplies through the fund’s ordering platform.
In a statement, UNICEF said it would work with the U.S. to “keep health and nutrition supplies moving so more children receive lifesaving care.” The agency added that no orders had yet been placed but were expected shortly.

The aerial incursions prompted Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency, Rosaviatsiya, to enact emergency ground stops and flight restrictions across Moscow’s primary airport cluster shortly before midnight.

Compounding disruptions to Russian civil aviation

Civil aviation data released by Rosaviatsiya head Dmitry Yadrov indicates that recurring airspace closures and drone threats have contracted commercial passenger traffic, with Russian carriers transporting 39.5 million passengers between May and August – a 7 percent decline compared to 42.6 million passengers carried during the corresponding period in 2025.
Ukrainian officials have stated that interdiction operations do not target civilian aircraft, but aim to constrain military transport and highlight the risks of utilizing Russian sovereign airspace during wartime.

Poland moves to allow more municipalities to charge tourist fee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:37:35 UTC
19:37:35 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Many more municipalities in Poland will be allowed to charge a daily fee for tourists and other overnight visitors after a change to the law dropping environmental requirements for levying such charges.
Kraków, which received 8.7 million overnight tourists last year, had in particular been pushing for the change. However, Poland as a whole has seen a recent boom in visitor numbers, recording the EU’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights in tourist accommodation last year.
#Krakow #opłataturystyczna #ustawa 🚨🔥Z OSTATNIEJ CHWILI! 🔥🚨
📢 Prezydent RP podpisał nowelizację przepisów dotyczących podatków i opłat lokalnych, PIT oraz PCC.
🏨 Najważniejsze zmiany dla branży turystycznej dotyczą opłaty miejscowej i uzdrowiskowej.
🗓️ Od 2027 r. za jej… pic.twitter.com/9ATvENvNol
— Kraków (@krakow_pl) October 15, 2026
Until now, a “visitor’s fee” could be levied by municipalities with beneficial climatic features, “scenic qualities” and the capacity to accommodate people visiting to benefit from these attributes, as well as localities in areas with the status of a “spa protection area”. In practice, this largely applied to seaside and mountain resorts.
Kraków did charge a visitor’s fee between 2004 and 2015, but was subsequently unable to do so due to a toughening of environmental requirements. The city has long suffered from bad air pollution, though it has taken significant steps to tackle the issue.
Now, under new legislation proposed by the government earlier this year and signed into law by President Karol Nawrocki this week, the requirement for beneficial climatic features has been scrapped, meaning many more places will be able to charge the visitor’s fee.
From 1 January, municipalities with scenic qualities will be able to charge visitors up to 5 zloty (€1.14) for each night they stay in hotels, guesthouses and short-term rental accommodation for up to one month, a rise on the current maximum of 3.46 zloty.
Additionally, whereas previously only people visiting for the purposes of tourism had to pay, the fee now applies to all visits, including for work or health purposes, reports broadcaster TVN. People with significant disabilities, children with certified disabilities and their carers will be exempt from the fee.
In another change, fees will be collected directly by accommodation providers, who will be required to maintain detailed records, reports the Infor news service. Passing fees on in a timely manner will entitle providers to receive at least 10% of the money they collect.
Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026
In 2024, Kraków appealed to the government to be allowed to charge tourists a fee, noting that “overtourism leads to tensions and social discontent”, as the “local community suffers” and “residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”.
With its UNESCO-listed Old Town, Wawel royal castle, and former Jewish district of Kazimierz, Kraków is regularly named as one of Europe’s best tourist destinations. Last year, a record 16.25 million people visited the city, of whom 8.7 million stayed overnight.
While that is a boon to the local economy, it also often causes tensions with residents, who complain about noise and disruption. In 2024, the city created the new position of “night mayor”, whose role is to reconcile the needs of tourists, businesses and residents.
Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb.
Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026
Following this week’s change to the law, Kraków city hall confirmed that it would now again be able to collect a visitor’s fee “if the statutory conditions are satisfied and the municipal council adopts an appropriate resolution”.
The city’s recently elected new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, who will be sworn in next week, said before Sunday’s election that he was in favour of a tourist tax of at least 20 zloty per night, four times the new maximum.
“In western European cities there are rates of that size and higher,” Gibała said, quoted by financial news service Money.pl. “Maintaining the city in the face of the influx of tourists is costly. In Kraków, private business owners profit from tourism, whilst the city and its residents foot the bill.”
Poland as a whole has also experienced a boom in tourism. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%).

A protest calling for the resignation of Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko is under way outside Kyiv City State Administration building in the centre of the capital.
According to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, several hundred participants had gathered outside the administration building at 36 Khreshchatyk Street as of 12:20. The rally began with speeches by activists and organisers.
The protesters are holding cardboard signs reading "Klitschko, resign," "Glass bus stops won't protect us from missiles and drones," "It's Time," "Mayor or Looter," "Kyiv Isn't Ready Even for Autumn," "Klitschko, It's Time for You to Go," "Who to Call When the Mayor Steals Money," "Schrödinger's Mayor – Klitschko exists separately from his powers," "Russia strikes, and you just add to it," and others.
The protesters are also chanting "Resign!"
Passing cars occasionally honk in support of the protesters.
At the same time, a small number of participants supporting the current mayor and opposing President Volodymyr Zelenskyy are also present outside Kyiv City State Administration building. They are holding signs reading "Klitschko – Our Mayor" and "Hands Off Klitschko." Police asked them to move away from the main protest, but they refused.
Seven police minibuses and five patrol cars are parked near Kyiv City State Administration building. More than three dozen officers from the National Police, Patrol Police and Dialogue Police are present at the rally site, while others remain in patrol vehicles.
In addition, representatives of the OZON civil society organisation and the Red Cross Society are monitoring the protest.
"Klitschko has had the authority and resources for all 12 years. He must bear political responsibility and step down from office," a statement issued by the rally organisers the previous day said.
In particular, the statement points to what the protesters describe as systemic, long-standing problems in city governance, including the city's lack of preparedness for the challenges of war, such as insufficient mobile and stationary shelters, a lack of alternative water, heating and sewage systems, and failures to address the consequences of destruction and assist those affected. It also cites allegations of corruption involving the mayor's team, favouring developers' interests, the lack of decisions to protect valuable historic buildings, deterioration of the public transport system, disregard for petitions and public opinion among city residents, and other problems.
The organisers said populist strategies were being developed without any intention of implementing them, decisions were being postponed for years and responsibility was constantly being shifted. They said the division of powers between the city authorities and district administrations could not serve as an excuse for the lack of results.
According to the protest organisers, the mayor could resign voluntarily, lose office as a result of a court ruling or an election, transfer his powers to a military administration, or leave office as a result of voluntary mobilisation.
The organisers' demands were signed, among others, by the All-Ukrainian Association Automaidan, the Green Teremky Initiative, the Legal Platform Kyiv Ecological and Cultural Center NGO, the March for Kyiv Association, the Passengers of Kyiv NGO, the Right to the City NGO, the Repair Together NGO, the Seven-Tiered Mountain Youth Center, the Kyiv Heritage NGO and the Spalah! NGO.
Ahead of the event, the UDAR Vitali Klitschko faction in Kyiv City Council, citing the security situation, called on Kyiv residents to refrain from mass gatherings on Saturday, October 17.
The faction said those calling on people to gather for protests should consider who would bear responsibility if a Russian attack occurred during the gathering and people were harmed. It said destabilising the situation in the capital, which Russia was attacking and seeking to deprive of electricity, heat and water, would only benefit the enemy. It added that responsibility, unity and joint efforts were needed to ensure Kyiv's resilience.
In response, the rally organisers published instructions on what participants should do in the event of an air raid alert.
The organisers said people with access to a map showing enemy aerial targets would be present at the rally and would be able to provide additional warnings about potential threats to the city centre. In the event of a threat, the rally would be suspended and participants would be asked to take shelter. They identified the TSUM shopping centre car park, Khreshchatyk and Teatralna metro stations, as well as nearby underground passages if there was little time, as the nearest shelters.
As previously reported, Vitali Klitschko, who was serving as Kyiv mayor at the time, won the first round of the October 2020 local election with 50.9% of the vote. Klitschko was first elected mayor of the capital in a special election in May 2014.
Under the Law of Ukraine On Local Self-Government, a mayor's powers may be terminated early in the event of a personal resignation; loss of Ukrainian citizenship; a conviction becoming final; a final court ruling holding the mayor liable for a corruption-related offence or declaring assets to be of unjustified origin; recall through a popular initiative; a court ruling declaring the mayor legally incapacitated, missing or presumed dead; or the mayor's death.
The mayor's powers may also be terminated early if the mayor violates the Constitution or laws of Ukraine or the rights and freedoms of citizens, or fails to exercise the powers granted to the office, based on a local referendum or a decision by the relevant council adopted by secret ballot with at least two-thirds of council members voting in favour. Early termination is also possible in cases provided for by the laws of Ukraine On Military-Civilian Administrations and On the Legal Regime of Martial Law.

Iran women’s wheelchair basketball suffer loss against Thailand
TEHRAN - Iran’s women’s wheelchair basketball team suffered a 64–33 defeat to Thailand in their second Group Stage match at the fifth edition of the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games on Saturday.
Despite showing improved performance in the second quarter, Iran were unable to overcome Thailand, who maintained control throughout the contest to secure a convincing victory.
Thailand made a strong start, taking the opening quarter 16–6. Iran responded with a more competitive display in the second quarter but still fell 16–13, leaving Thailand with a 32–19 lead at half-time.
The third quarter saw the two sides compete more evenly in the opening stages, but Thailand gradually pulled away, winning the period 15–7 to extend their advantage.
Thailand then closed out the game strongly, taking the final quarter 17–7 to seal a 64–33 victory.
The result marked Iran’s second consecutive defeat in the group stage. The Iranian side had opened their campaign with a 65–20 loss to hosts Japan in their first match.
Iran will look to bounce back when they face Cambodia on Monday in their next group-stage fixture, aiming to deliver a stronger performance and secure a better result.
The Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games are being held in Japan, bringing together athletes from across Asia to compete in a wide range of para sports.

Pope Leo returns to Vatican four days after lung cancer surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:35:22 UTC
19:35:22 KST

Pope Leo returns to Vatican four days after lung cancer surgery
Pope Leo XIV was released from the hospital on Saturday after lung cancer surgery. Doctors removed part of the 71-year-old's right lung last week to extract a cancerous tumour.
Pope Leo XIV will leave the Rome hospital on Saturday, where he has been recovering from lung cancer surgery after doctors deemed him "fit for discharge", the Vatican said.
Leo, 71, has been at the Gemelli hospital in Rome since Tuesday, when doctors removed part of his right lung to extract a cancerous tumour.
"Considering the blood tests, the chest X-ray done this morning, and evaluating the clinical picture, the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge," doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora wrote in a note published by the Vatican.
Read moreWhat we know about Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer diagnosis
The Vatican said that Pope Leo "will leave the hospital in the early afternoon and return to the Vatican. Tomorrow he will recite the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment".
The Angelus prayer is typically given by the pope from the Apostolic Palace overlooking St Peter's Square.
But in past years, former popes John Paul II and Francis similarly hospitalised at the Gemelli have delivered the prayer from the window of their hospital rooms.
The Vatican press office said that Leo celebrated Mass on Saturday, as he has in recent days, in a room on the 10th floor of the hospital where he has been recovering.
Outside the hospital, 12-year-old Ukrainian Varvara Struck said she was rooting for the pope.
The former cancer patient said she had met the pope last year in Rome, "and he blessed me for a successful treatment".
"With his support, I’ve now overcome my illness, and I want to give him my positive energy so that he, too, can overcome his illness as quickly as possible," she said.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Up in air
News that the otherwise active pope had a cancerous tumour removed from his lung has rattled the Vatican and the world's 1.4 billion Catholics.
But his doctors have said Leo's recovery has been progressing normally as they await the results of tests that will determine the course of action to take.
Leo has resumed some work, making a call on Friday to Russian President Vladimir Putin to urge a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
Up in the air, however, is a planned papal voyage to South America, scheduled for November 6-17 to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
Vatican watchers say that Leo – who spent two decades as a missionary in Peru – is anxious to make the long journey, but will likely follow the recommendations of his doctors.
Leo has cancelled all his audiences until October 20.
The pope announced to the public in St Peter's Square last Sunday, following the Angelus prayer, that a routine medical examination had revealed a nodule that doctors recommended should be removed.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

G7 plans to allocate €260 million for restoration at the Chornobyl NPP following Russian strike
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:35:11 EEST
19:35:11 KST

G7 plans to allocate €260 million for restoration at the Chornobyl NPP following Russian strike
Kyiv • UNN
G7 countries plan to allocate €260 million for the restoration of the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant’s confinement structure. The total need is estimated at at least €500 million.
The G7 countries plan to allocate €260 million for the restoration of the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant’s New Safe Confinement, which was damaged as a result of a Russian strike. This was reported by Ukraine’s Ministry of Energy on October 17, UNN reports.
Details
The G7 countries plan to allocate €260 million for the restoration of the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant’s New Safe Confinement
Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal called the G7 countries’ decision an important step toward restoring nuclear safety at the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant, which was compromised as a result of the Russian strike.
According to him, the total funding required to restore the New Safe Confinement amounts to at least €500 million. Thus, the announced funding is expected to cover part of the necessary costs.
"I thank France and, personally, Minister Roland Lescure for leading the mobilization of international support. I am grateful to the G7 countries for their readiness to contribute to the restoration. We expect to secure the necessary funding to cover the remaining needs during the donors’ conference, which will be held in Paris under the joint chairmanship of Ukraine, France, and the EBRD," Denys Shmyhal emphasized.

Gallery: Central Estonia's upgraded Mäo junction reopens to traffic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17

19:35:00 KST

Gallery: Central Estonia's upgraded Mäo junction reopens to traffic
Mäo's upgraded highway junction has reopened with five bus stops, two roundabouts and a 30-space parking lot, improving long-distance bus connections in Central Estonia.
A Lux Express bus made the symbolic first stop at Mäo on Friday, marking the completion of construction and the launch of bus service at the junction.
"By Monday morning, ten Lux Express routes en route to Tallinn and another ten en route to Tartu will be stopping here," said Urmas Kupp, executive director of the Järva County Public Transport Center (JÜTK).
Other bus operators are also interested and could begin stopping there as early as November 2.
One key amenity, however, is still missing. Despite assurances at the opening that the upgraded junction is safer and ready to accommodate long-distance buses, passengers have no proper public bathroom at Mäo, with only a temporary portable toilet installed next to one of the bus shelters.
The Transport Administration says building a passenger terminal is not its responsibility.
"Our job is to maintain and develop national roads," said Transport Administration director general Priit Sauk, adding that it's up to public transport centers and local governments to build stops and passenger terminals.
JÜTK plans to sell an unused terminal and use the proceeds to build a new one at Mäo, which would also solve the bathroom problem. Infrastructure Minister Kuldar Leis (Reform) said the project should be a joint effort with the state.
"I think the most logical approach for projects like this is for the state and local governments to work together," Leis said.
Next stretch of Tallinn–Tartu Highway roadwork begins
Friday also marked the start of reconstruction on an eight-kilometer stretch of Tallinn–Tartu Highway between Käsukonna and Imavere. The work, expected to take about two years, includes a multilevel interchange at Imavere that will connect traffic from Viljandi to the highway.
Sauk said another 15 to 16 kilometers between Mäo and Käsukonna also need rebuilding.
"It's included in our road maintenance plan and long-term plans," he noted. "If the next funding period allows, we'd like to get started on it within the next couple of years."

Germany news: Berlin's leftist parties move step closer to forming government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:34:00 UTC
19:34:00 KST

Left, Greens, SPD move a step closer to governing Berlin
Published October 17, 2026last updated October 17, 2026
What you need to know
- Members of The Left, the Greens and the SPD reached an initial agreement to begin formal coalition talks
- German Chancellor Friedrich Merz addresses conservative CDU/CSU national youth-wing conference
- Germany's development minister asks that debt borrowing rules be eased to allow further critical Ukraine funding
- In the northern state of Schleswig-Holstein, police expect 3,000 participants to show up for an Alternative for Germany (AfD) youth rally and a pro-democracy counter-rally
Here is a roundup of the main news from and about Germany for the weekend of October 17-18:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Berlin coalition hopefuls to focus on housing
Berlin's Left Party, the Greens and the Social Democrats (SPD) revealed details of what they hope will be their governing policy, should the coalition be approved by their parties' members.
Among the policies, the possible left-wing Berlin state government could bring around 160,000 apartments under public ownership.
The Left's Elif Eralp, who is seeking to become leader of Berlin, said the compromise would affect five companies, including Germany's largest property company, Vonovia.
It all comes as voters made unaffordable housing a central issue, one that The Left campaigned on, as rent costs in Berlin have spiraled in recent years and public apartments have been in short supply.
Eralp said the three parties also agreed on a "very ambitious new building program" for public housing, where they hope to get 100,000 planning permissions by 2031, which will then lead to 100,000 new affordable flats.
The coalition hopefuls would also work to implement a rent cap for publicly owned apartments.
German-Israeli Society president blasts possible Berlin coalition
Volker Beck, the president of the German-Israeli Society, sharply criticized the prospect of a Left/Green/SPD coalition in Berlin, labeling the Left "a bunch of anti-Zionists."
Beck leveled his criticism in an interview with German national broadcaster Deutschlandfunk (DLF).
The interview will be broadcast Sunday but a manuscript has been made available in which Beck tells DLF that anti-Zionism forms the identity of some in Berlin's Left Party, adding "for them, anti-Zionism is their world view, their passion."
"It forms their identity and it is extremely dangerous for society," he said.
Although Beck vouched for Left Party top candidate Elif Eralp's integrity, saying, "she's riding an anti-Zionist wave but she doesn't control it," he said, "she's overwhelmed with the situation."
Finally, Beck blasted an antisemitism statement released by the Left, Greens and SPD this week to quell fears as, "unclear," reminding Greens and SPD that Berlin is "now the most radical state chapter the Left Party has."
Berlin: Left, Green and SPD leaders wrap inital talks
The leaders of Berlin's Left, Green and Social Democratic parties wrapped up exploratory talks ahead of official negotiations to form a potential coalition on Saturday, four weeks after state and municipal elections in which the Left was the big winner, taking 25.7% of the vote.
On Saturday, party leaders informed Germany's DPA press agency that the initial talks, which began in earnest on October 8, had been completed and that an agreement had been reached to put the prospect of coalition negotiations up for a vote in their respective parties.
The party votes are scheduled to begin with the Greens on Monday. The SPD has not announced a date, and the Left will vote on October 31.
Should the party bases agree to the proposal, coalition government negotiations could begin in early November.
Party leaders scheduled a group press conference outlining the results of negotiations for Saturday afternoon.
Talks between the three broke down early this week in a fight over accusations of antisemitism among the ranks of the Left Party. The Greens and SPD demanded a clear commitment to sanctions against such transgressions before resuming talks.
New polling sees AfD and CDU/CSU down, Left and BSW up slightly
This week's INSA "Sonntagstrend" poll, commissioned by the tabloid Bild, showed a one percentage point drop for both the far-right AfD and the conservative CDU/CSU, and one percentage point gains for the Left Party and the left-wing populist BSW.
The AfD remains the most popular party in nationwide polling, with 29% favorability.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU/CSU is polling second at 18%.
The Greens remained steady at 14%, as did the junior coalition partner SPD at 13%.
The Left, which recently won Berlin's mayoral race but has struggled with its handling of questions of antisemitism, bettered its favorability to 11%; and BSW, which has thrown in its lot with the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, picked up a point to 4%.
The liberal FDP rounded out the field unchanged at 4%, while support for other parties amounted to 7%.
INSA founder and CEO Hermann Binkert said the results of the poll trace a dramatic slide by the country's biggest establishment parties the CDU/CSU and the SPD, noting that their combined 31% meant they had lost "nearly a third of their voters" since the last parliamentary election in 2025.
INSA, which placed the margin of error at plus/minus 2.9 percentage points, conducted its survey among 1,206 registered voters between October 12 and 16.
Development minister urges debt spending to finance Ukraine aid
German Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan has called for a debt-spending exemption for her ministry in order to keep up aid to Ukraine amid deep budget cuts.
Speaking to Reuters news agency on the sidelines of annual International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, Alabali Radovan said much of Germany's civilian spending for Ukraine comes from her ministry's budget.
About €330 million ($371 million) in Ukraine funding will come out of her ministry's budget this year, down from €670 million in 2022, and €750 million in 2023.
In asking for relaxation of Germany's constitutionally anchored debt brake, which limits government borrowing, Alabali Radovan underscored the gravity of the situation: "Russian attacks are more severe than ever, leading to more deaths, more destruction, more suffering. But as budget cuts for development assistance continue, we simply will not be able to maintain our support for Ukraine."
"At this point," she added, "it is not a political decision, we just face massive cuts and it will no longer be possible."
Alabali Radovan's plan has support from Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul but faces broad pushback from parliamentarians opposed to further borrowing exemptions.
Alabali Radovan told Reuters that she supports German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's call for other countries to increase Ukraine aid, saying, "We are the strongest supporters, and I believe others can and should contribute more."
Merz pushes reform agenda
Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Saturday acknowledged that his administration's reform plans "shake up the country, shake up our party," but insisted that they are the only choice for the CDU going forward.
Speaking of his plan for a fundamental overhaul of Germany's retirement, nursing care and health insurance systems, Merz said: "If we can't show that we've gotten our economy growing sustainably again before the next parliamentary election, that we've sustainably reformed and future-proofed our welfare system by the next parliamentary election, we won't stand a chance in the next parliamentary election."
Merz insisted that his Cabinet should sign off on the reforms by the end of the year.
Among these is a controversial reform that would raise Germany's retirement age.
Social Democrat (SPD) coalition partners in the federal government are against the move, as are three CDU state premiers in eastern Germany.
Merz addresses party youth at annual convention
Chancellor Friedrich Merz was in Bonn Saturday to address an annual national meeting of his Christian Democratic and Christian Social Unions' (CDU/CSU) youth wing, the Young Union (Junge Union/JU).
Things were testy the last time Merz addressed the 90,000-member group — when they fought over pension policy— and he will now face them with dwindling approval numbers and growing dissatisfaction over the way he has led Germany and his party.
Merz will greet a youth wing that is self-confident as he himself reels from disastrous election results in recent state and municipal elections.
On Friday, the JU overwhelmingly re-elected Johannes Winkel as their chairman, with the CDU federal parliamentarian taking 94.3% of the vote.
"Our generation still has big plans," said Winkel as he spoke to JU attendees, "and we will be the ones who successfully continue to write the history of the CDU and CSU as a people's party."
On Friday, North Rhine-Westphalia State Premier Hendrik Wüst, a rising star within the party, addressed attendees. On Sunday, Bavarian State Premier Markus Söder will take the stage. Both represent potential replacements for Merz.
Despite the number of prominent party leaders addressing the JU amid talk of Merz's possible political demise, Johannes Winkel vowed: "We're not some applause meter. This isn't a casting show for the chancellorship."
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Morgen from the DW news team in gray and blustery Bonn, where, just across the street, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is addressing the Junge Union (JU) youth wing of his CDU and its Bavarian sister party CSU at an annual national conference.
Last time Merz spoke to the group, things got confrontational over pension policy. The chancellor will have a number of thorny issues to navigate this time around, not least whether the party thinks it can survive under his leadership.
As Germany struggles with budget cuts, the country's development minister asked for a debt spending exemption to cover shortfalls in critical funding assistance for Ukraine. Reem Alabali Radovan warned that Ukraine is suffering more death and destruction than ever but "as budget cuts for development assistance continue, we simply will not be able to maintain our support."
In the northern state of Schleswig-Holstein, "Generation Deutschland," the youth wing of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), is holding a rally under the motto: "Secure the Future — Safeguard Identity." A "Rally for Democracy" counterdemonstration will also take place. Police say they expect roughly 3,000 participants in all.
Stay tuned for the latest on these angles and plenty more from Germany this weekend.

Israeli firm exploited online ads to spy on Al Jazeera and Palestinian sites, researchers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:33:10 UTC
19:33:10 KST

Israeli digital advertising agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a sprawling network of online ads that it used to track targets and help hack their devices, two research groups said on Thursday.
Its services gave Israel's Candiru – a spyware company blacklisted by the U.S. government – as well as other Israeli surveillance firms access to advertising platforms run by Google, Comcast, Russia's Yandex and others, according to separate reports from Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab and New York advertising security firm Confiant.
The reports show how the online advertising business, long a subject of privacy concerns, can also serve as a channel for sweeping espionage campaigns.
Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025, something it said it was able to confirm because the media group had shared its network logs with the group.
In a statement, Al Jazeera said it "condemns the spyware attacks targeting a number of its staff" and that it was taking steps to protect its employees and its systems. "Those responsible must be held accountable," it said.
"The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Christl, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike."
Discover-Tech's online ads – often for ordinary products such as phones or earbuds – reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said.
Users who visited sites or used apps with the malicious ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes also try to extract phone numbers from some smartphone users, the researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur.
Some ads would be used to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, both research groups said, though Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume.
Malicious ads shown in hundreds of sensitive networks
Confiant cofounder Jerome Dangu said Discover-Tech was pumping out at least 10 million ads per day all around the world and that data-sharing arrangements – called cookie matching – allowed it to track people even beyond the reach of its advertisements.
"Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said.
Discover-Tech, which was founded in 2020, did not return messages left via its contact form. A LinkedIn message and emails sent to its chief executive, Dekel Boni, were not returned.
Reuters' attempts to reach Candiru's owners were similarly unsuccessful. The U.S. Commerce Department blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for allegedly supplying spyware that was used to maliciously target government officials, journalists, activists and academics.
Dangu of Confiant said that the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, like the Palestinian territories, were particularly saturated by the Israeli firm's ads.
"You go to almost any site in Palestine – any site – you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he said.
Citizen Lab also said it had similar evidence showing the malicious ads were shown to people in the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission, and more than a dozen national governments. Other networks the ads appeared in included chip-related firms such as Nvidia, Sandisk, Broadcom and Micron, as well as several media organizations in Mexico, Israel, and Europe that were not identified.
In addition to identifying Candiru and a couple of other surveillance vendors, Citizen Lab said it was able to glean some details about where Discover-Tech's users might be based because the firm inadvertently exposed its authentication logs to the internet, showing people logging in from internet protocol addresses in Israel, Europe, and the Gulf.
Measures against Discover-Tech
Discover-Tech is now being frozen out of parts of the online ad market.
Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant's investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies."
IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved vendors last week after an audit identified policy violations.
Comcast ad tech subsidiary Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its platform "following recent activity," Comcast said in a statement. Yandex did not return Reuters messages seeking comment.
Advertising-driven surveillance is increasingly being seen as a national security threat. Earlier this year, the Pentagon said it had received reports that U.S. forces deployed to war zones had been targeted using location data harvested by ad tech firms and data brokers. Branches of the military have since disabled ad tracking on some devices.
