Pope Leo XIV to leave hospital after lung cancer surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:07:16 UTC
19:07:16 KST

Pope Leo XIV is being released from the hospital on Saturday, four days after lung cancer surgery, and will deliver the traditional noon blessing Sunday from a window overlooking St. Peter's Square, the Vatican announced.
The 71-year-old Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
His personal physician and surgeon said in a separate statement that Leo was “deemed fit for discharge from the hospital” based on blood test results and a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning along with an assessment of his clinical condition.
He is set to leave the hospital in the early afternoon and return to the Vatican, the Vatican said in a brief statement.
During his recovery, Leo continued some of his official duties, including a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin and meetings with senior Vatican aides. Medical bulletins indicated that his condition was steadily improving and that he could carry out normal daily activities independently.
On Friday, the Vatican released the first images of the pontiff since his surgery, showing him celebrating Mass in a hospital chapel while wearing green vestments. Leo distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes and thanked hospital staff for their care.
Leo underwent surgery Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital after doctors discovered a small, localized nodule in his right lung during routine medical examinations. The 71-year-old pontiff had publicly disclosed the finding during his Sunday noon prayer, explaining that doctors recommended removing the growth because it had been detected at an early stage.
The operation, led by Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, lasted approximately 90 minutes, although Leo spent about three hours in the operating room. Surgeons removed the entire lower lobe of his right lung in an effort to eliminate the suspected cancerous tissue. Tests conducted during surgery confirmed lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer, a diagnosis doctors had suspected based on preliminary examinations.
The Vatican said the procedure was completed successfully, on schedule and without complications. Leo regained consciousness after the operation and returned to his hospital room, where he spent a peaceful night, according to a Vatican statement issued Wednesday.
Doctors have not disclosed the tumor's precise size or whether cancer cells were found in nearby lymph nodes, factors that could influence the pope's prognosis and determine whether additional treatment is necessary. Before the operation, oncologists said his outlook could be excellent because the growth was detected early and appeared to be localized.
The pope's next major scheduled engagement is a November 6-17 trip to Latin America, involving about a dozen flights and two helicopter journeys. The Vatican has continued preparations for the visit, although Leo's ability to travel will depend on his recovery.
Meanwhile, doctors are awaiting further test results to establish the cancer's molecular and genetic characteristics, determine whether it has spread beyond the removed lung lobe and assess whether additional treatment will be necessary.
The American pontiff arrived at Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday morning, walking through the main entrance and waving to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered outside. His decision to publicly disclose the diagnosis and planned surgery marked an unusual degree of transparency surrounding the first major health problem reported during his papacy.
Elected in May 2025, Leo has generally maintained an active lifestyle, including playing tennis, and is not known to smoke. He had no previously disclosed major health problems since becoming pope.
The Vatican initially expected Leo to remain hospitalized for approximately one week and canceled all his public engagements through October 20. Unlike previous popes who stayed in the hospital's dedicated papal apartment, Leo was accommodated in a nearby room because the apartment was undergoing renovations.

Trump-Zelenskiy rift threatens vital support for Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:05:35 UTC
19:05:35 KST

Trump-Zelenskiy rift threatens vital support for Kyiv
WASHINGTON/KYIV, Oct 17 - From US threats to cut off intelligence support for Ukraine to a waiver of tariffs on Russian exports and a diesel deal that could help Russia fund its war, it has been a damaging week for ties between Kyiv and its most important ally, Washington.
US President Donald Trump, frustrated by high energy costs he blames partly on Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, has repeatedly criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. A disruption of US-provided satellite internet services raised fears that Ukraine could be vulnerable as it prepares for another winter of Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.
Zelenskiy responded to Trump's barbs with an unusually sharp series of public criticisms of Trump, suggesting the US was now favoring Russia. He said Ukraine would defy Trump's demand to stop striking Russian energy targets, citing Russia's continued attacks.
Intensifying the discord, Trump waived key US Russia-related sanctions and tariffs on Friday, shortly before they were scheduled to take effect. That prompted Zelenskiy to say in social media posts that Trump's action would encourage Russia to continue attacks on Ukraine.
The widening rift has sparked concerns that Trump and Zelenskiy's tumultuous relationship could lead to even worse outcomes for Kyiv. Trump could yet restrict the supply of weapons to Ukraine, follow through on threats to stop sharing battlefield intelligence, or strike more economic deals with Moscow.
Despite Zelenskiy's remarks, Kyiv wants to continue dialogue with Trump's envoys, his friend Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, two Ukrainian officials familiar with the talks said, speaking on the condition of anonymity.
Denys Sienik, chargé d'affaires at Ukraine's embassy in Washington, told Newsmax on Friday that Ukraine was grateful to Trump and his team for their efforts to end the war and said Ukraine was willing to engage in talks with Russia.
Trump told reporters on Friday he would continue to deal with both Zelenskiy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “I want that war to end,” he said.
'MISSED OPPORTUNITY': FORMER US OFFICIAL
Daniel Fried, the senior State Department official on Europe from 2005 to 2009, said it was unclear whether Washington was making a lasting shift away from Ukraine, but the fallout was damaging prospects for an end to the war that began with Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion.
"It's not only a missed opportunity, it causes genuine suffering in Ukraine and encourages Putin to continue the war, so it's not cost-free," said Fried, now at the Washington-based Atlantic Council think tank.
Trump's relationship with Zelenskiy has long been uneasy. Trump and US Vice President JD Vance publicly upbraided Zelenskiy during an Oval Office meeting in February 2025. Washington has paused or slowed military assistance to Ukraine under Trump, while allowing European allies to purchase US weapons for Kyiv.
The relationship had steadied until Ukraine's strikes this year on energy sites in Russia began contributing to rising fuel prices. High gasoline and diesel prices are a political headache for Trump ahead of November's midterm elections, in which his Republican Party could lose its majorities in the US Congress, according to analysts.
Experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz.
Frustrated by Zelenskiy, however, Trump turned to Russia to increase fuel supply and contain prices, according to a person familiar with the internal debate, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Trump said on October 9 he had reached a deal with Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel.
In an executive order released by the White House on Friday, Trump also waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs shortly before they were supposed to take effect under the Graham Act, which Trump signed last month.
Although the law, named for the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, called for new penalties on Russia starting next week, it also allows the president to waive them if it is in the US national interest to do so.
Zelenskiy said Trump's latest action undercuts the Graham Act's main goal and will fuel Russia's "desire to keep killing people."
The US diesel deal with Russia and the waiver are the latest steps in what Zelenskiy said he expects to be continued sanctions relief on Moscow.
The prospect of the US continuing to pressure Russia to end the war has dimmed since Graham's death in July, Zelenskiy said. Graham, a South Carolina Republican and a confidant of Trump, strongly supported Ukraine.
"It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest," the Ukrainian president wrote.
HIGH STAKES FOR UKRAINE
For Kyiv, the stakes are high and immediate. Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukraine had received no warning from Western partners before a deadly Russian attack on the capital.
Without US intelligence, Ukraine could face greater difficulty detecting and countering Russian missile and drone attacks, particularly against energy infrastructure that Moscow has repeatedly targeted during previous winters.
Trump has said the US is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. But Zelenskiy told NPR that US officials had warned Ukrainian commanders intelligence could be reduced or cut off.
Ukraine's Starshield system, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink service, was disrupted after what two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter said was an order originating from the White House, Reuters reported on Thursday.
The service has been partially restored, but the episode highlighted the vulnerability created by Ukraine's dependence on technology controlled by US companies and subject to decisions by the Trump administration.
Trump may face resistance if congressional Republicans see his approach as weakening Ukraine while benefiting Russia. Ukraine retains support among Trump's fellow Republicans, some of whom argue that Washington should not pressure Kyiv into accepting a settlement on terms favorable to Moscow.
Zelenskiy's tough responses to Trump were risky, but he may be counting on a power shift on Capitol Hill after the midterm elections to make it harder for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia and further reduce military assistance to Kyiv, said Brett Bruen, a former foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration and head of the Global Situation Room consultancy.
“Zelenskiy knows who he’s dealing with,” he said. “Trump’s threats don’t have the same kind of effect as they did when JD Vance tried to shame him in the Oval Office.” REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Nostalgia for a party’s past cuts both ways when it comes to support for political violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:00:57 UTC
19:00:57 KST

A recent study suggests that longing for a political party’s past is tied to support for political violence in opposite ways, depending on how people relate to their party. Among partisans whose commitment is obsessive, stronger collective nostalgia went along with a stronger link to support for violence, while among those whose commitment is harmonious, it went along with less support. The findings, published in Journal of Applied Social Psychology, suggest that nostalgia for “the good old days” does not carry the same meaning for everyone who feels it.
The way people commit to a political cause can take two distinct forms. Harmonious passion describes a freely chosen involvement that coexists easily with a person’s other life commitments, such as family or hobbies. Obsessive passion describes a more compulsive attachment where the political cause becomes deeply tied to a person’s sense of self-worth. In this state, people often feel inner pressure to defend their beliefs and struggle to step away from politics when they need to.
This distinction helps researchers understand the psychological roots of radicalization. For instance, a 2019 study by Bélanger and colleagues found that obsessive passion for a cause was linked to moral disengagement, a way of justifying harmful actions as acceptable, and to support for political violence, whereas harmonious passion was linked to peaceful activism.
Separately, psychologists have examined collective nostalgia, which is a sentimental longing for the past of a group that a person belongs to. For example, a 2015 study found that a collective longing for a nation’s past can unite people around their own group while also being linked to hostility toward outside groups. In addition, a 2020 study found that the effect of collective nostalgia on attitudes toward outsiders depends on what kind of past people long for, such as whether they yearn for an open society or a more uniform one. Relatedly, a study covered by PsyPost in 2022 showed that collective nostalgia is associated with populist attitudes.
These two lines of inquiry left an open question about why only a small fraction of people who feel longing for a past era come to view violence as acceptable. The research, led by Jocelyn J. Bélanger, an associate teaching professor at Carnegie Mellon University in Qatar and co-author of The Three Pillars of Radicalization, sought to connect these ideas. The authors proposed that collective nostalgia might widen the gap between the two forms of passion, going along with more support for violence among the obsessively passionate and less among the harmoniously passionate.
“Politicians on every side sell voters a golden age to reclaim, yet research on collective nostalgia had left a puzzle: longing for the group’s past sometimes breeds hostility and sometimes breeds belonging,” Bélanger told PsyPost. “We suspected the answer lay not in the nostalgia itself but in the kind of passion a person brings to their cause.”
To test this idea, the researchers surveyed 417 adult political partisans in the United States, recruited online in March 2022. The sample was split into two groups, consisting of 263 Democrats and 154 Republicans. Participants answered questions about their political party, rating how much their involvement felt harmonious and how much it felt obsessive.
The survey also measured participants’ feelings of collective nostalgia, asking how often they longed for the “good old days” of their party or past presidents from their side of the aisle. In addition, the authors assessed willingness to support or engage in hostile actions against the rival party, from physically attacking opponents to cutting off friendships with rival supporters. The researchers accounted for participants’ overall ideological commitment, so that the results would reflect how people internalized their beliefs rather than simply how much they cared about their party.
The initial results were consistent across both the Democratic and Republican groups. Obsessive passion was linked to greater support for political violence against the opposing party, while harmonious passion was not. Support for political violence was low overall, averaging about 1.7 to 1.8 on a 7-point scale.
When the researchers looked at collective nostalgia, they observed that the two forms of passion diverged. For participants with high levels of obsessive passion, increased feelings of nostalgia went along with even stronger support for political violence. The authors describe this as an amplification pattern, while stressing that the term describes the shape of a statistical relationship, not cause and effect.
But among participants high in harmonious passion, the pattern ran the other way. When nostalgia was low, harmonious passion was unrelated to support for violence, but when nostalgia was high, people with more harmonious passion reported less support for violence.
“We predicted it, but I was still struck by how cleanly nostalgia cut both ways: the same longing tracked greater openness to violence among obsessive partisans and less among harmonious ones,” Bélanger noted. “That crossover appeared among Democrats and Republicans alike, which tells me we are looking at the psychology of devotion rather than the psychology of one party.”
The researchers interpret this divergence through nostalgia’s bittersweet nature, though they did not measure these feelings directly. For the obsessively passionate, a longed-for past might feel like something stolen that must be forcefully reclaimed. For the harmoniously passionate, reflecting on a shared past might evoke connection and belonging, which could encourage restraint.
“How you care about a cause matters more than how much you care,” Bélanger explained. “Among people whose politics is a freely chosen part of life they can set aside at the dinner table, longing for the group’s glory days went with less support for political violence; among people whose politics has swallowed their identity, the same longing went with more.”
“In statistical terms the effects are modest (the interplay between nostalgia and passion explains an extra 1 to 2 percent of the variation in support for violence), yet the link between obsessive passion and support for violence was roughly twice as strong among highly nostalgic partisans as among less nostalgic ones,” Bélanger said. “Support for violence was low on average, so picture nostalgia as a force that pulls the most zealous toward the dangerous end of the scale, not as a nation primed for conflict.”
The findings align with earlier research covered by PsyPost in 2024 by members of the same research team. That study also examined American political partisans and found that obsessive passion was linked to support for political violence, whereas harmonious passion was not.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. “The misreading I’d most like to head off is ‘nostalgia breeds violence,’ because its main role was to magnify whichever kind of passion a person already had, for better or worse,” Bélanger pointed out. “We can show that these things travel together but not that nostalgia causes them, and agreeing with violence on a questionnaire is a long way from committing it.”
It is also possible that an underlying factor drives both, or that a person’s willingness to support violence colors how they remember the past. Collective nostalgia also tends to accompany feelings of threat, anxiety about the group’s future, and grievance, none of which were measured, so these related feelings could account for the pattern. Additionally, the researchers did not directly measure whether participants felt their party had fallen into decline, a perception that often travels alongside nostalgia and might help explain the pattern among the obsessively passionate.
The study also measured how people felt about political violence rather than observing actual behavior. The leap from endorsing aggressive tactics on a survey to carrying out physical harm in the real world is a large one, and future studies would need to track actions over time to see if these patterns hold.
“Next, we want to induce nostalgia in the lab to see whether it causes these shifts, and to test our hunch about why: obsessive partisans may dwell on the bitter half of nostalgia, what was taken from the group, while harmonious partisans savor the sweet half, what the group shared,” Bélanger said. “The long-term goal is practical: if we can help people hold their convictions more harmoniously, we may blunt the political appeals that turn longing into rage.”
“Nostalgia is among the oldest tools of political persuasion, and our findings suggest its effect depends less on the message than on who hears it,” the researcher added. “The same appeal to a golden age that steadies a calm partisan may embolden a zealous one.”
The study, “Collective Nostalgia Widens the Gap Between Obsessive and Harmonious Passion in Support for Political Violence,” was authored by Jocelyn J. Bélanger, Daniel Snook, Danaiym Talantbekova, and Jais Adam-Troian.

====================================================================================================

‘Countries are defying gravity at all income levels’: how long can global economy resist chaos?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:00:27 UTC
19:00:27 KST

Inside the vast, glass-walled Queen Sirikit conference centre in Bangkok, the air-conditioned atmosphere was calm as policymakers from more than 100 countries gathered this week for the International Monetary Fund’s annual meeting – and contemplated the surprising strength of the global economy.
A small army of smiling, uniformed Thai staff were on hand to explain the baffling geography of the heavily guarded building, where lunch options were as cosmopolitan as the delegates – including, improbably, a Burger King.
“Resilience” was the buzzword at one event after another, after six months in which sky-high oil prices and geopolitical chaos have made less of a dent in the global economy than first feared.
Growth has not fallen off a cliff, buoyed up by the AI investment boom; stock markets haven’t crashed. “We had Covid, the war in Ukraine, supply-chain shocks, the war in Iran, and the alarm bells go off. And yet we haven’t had that massive synchronised crisis. So I think there’s this feeling that a lot of countries are sort of defying gravity at all income levels,” said Clemence Landers, the vice-president of the Washington-based Center for Global Development.
Yet the IMF was also keen to remind delegates that the resilience of the past six months had been bought at a cost and may not last. The message – “Resilience under strain, urgent choices” – leapt out from the front page of its flagship publication, the World Economic Outlook (WEO).
According to IMF experts, the cost of the energy support measures governments have put in place to protect their citizens from soaring oil prices, as a result of Donald Trump’s war in Iran, has been an extraordinary 0.5% of global GDP.
It said many countries would be unable to sustain support on this scale for much longer – and some had already begun to phase out subsidies, exposing the public to more of the costs of the conflict.
The IMF urged governments to limit the costs and let market signals do their work, by sticking to temporary, targeted measures, rather than across-the-board subsidies.
Aside from how to cope with the practicalities of a conflict that has persisted far longer than many governments had hoped – and whose end point remains elusive – the IMF was also keen to highlight two pressing risks.
The first was what it sees as the unsustainable state of the public finances, particularly in the world’s richest countries. The WEO projected the highest budget deficits this year for advanced economies since the depths of the Covid pandemic.
That means government debt in these countries is expected to keep rising – from 108% of GDP last year, to 115% of GDP in five years’ time.
“Public debt is high in many economies, and fiscal buffers that could otherwise have helped meet rising spending pressures from ageing populations, climate change and national security needs have instead been used to absorb the repeated shocks,” the WEO said.
Anxiety about spendthrift governments appears to have been one factor driving the recent sell-off of government bonds – pushing up yields, or interest rates, to their highest levels in decades; though it also reflects higher expectations for inflation and growth.
The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, lamented: “Too many countries, they did not use the post-pandemic recovery to rebuild fiscal buffers, and each new shock has pushed debt levels higher.”
Fretting that this leaves governments exposed when the next shock comes, as well as pushing up the share of tax revenues required just to service debt, Georgieva repeatedly implored governments – not least Washington – to tighten their belts. “What is our loudest call to policymakers right now? Make urgent repairs to the fiscal house before the cracks widen,” she said. It seems a message unlikely to land well with voters buffeted by one shock after another.
The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, did not bother to travel to Bangkok to hear it; nor to oversee the meeting of G20 finance ministers, of whom he is formally the chair this year.
The UK chancellor, John Healey, stepped in to chair the meeting instead. He spent much of his brief time in Bangkok stressing the importance of standing shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine – which the US has notably not been doing of late. Russia’s delegation was allowed to attend the G20 meeting, to the deep discomfort of UK delegates.
The UK received a positive review from Georgieva and her colleagues, for setting out a plan to balance the books; though she conceded the bond markets had not rewarded its prudence.
“The UK is actually one country where action to reduce the deficit has been taken decisively,” she said. Asked why the UK’s bond yields have not fallen accordingly, Georgieva said London’s status as a global financial centre tended to put the UK under additional scrutiny.
“Traditionally we’ve seen more attention, in relative terms in the UK, to what the government is doing. [There is] a bit more sensitivity, and I think the government recognises they need to stay the course.”
Unusually, no communique was issued after the G20 meeting: a stark signal of how difficult it has become to reach multilateral agreement in the current fissiparous period.
The UK will take over the G20 presidency next year and has ambitious plans, on AI regulation and international development; but Bessent’s no-show was a reminder of the tough task they face in rekindling multilateralism.
The other alarming message the IMF was keen to land, concerned the threat of an AI market crash. As Georgieva put it in a blogpost on Friday: “The risk is that expectations may run rapidly ahead of productivity gains, setting the stage for near-term disappointment.”
The Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, while professing himself an optimist about the long-term gains of “superintelligence”, as he insisted on calling it, put it another way: “We really don’t know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies. Who’s going to get to make the money? What are the consequences for those that bet that they were going to make money, but the market structure doesn’t allow it?”
And AI is not just a stock market phenomenon but a huge driver of real-world exports, of the hardware and infrastructure necessary – albeit the benefits are heavily concentrated in a small number of economies, including Taiwan and South Korea. The knock-on effects, then, would be significant.
It is a familiar fear; but in its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Review, the IMF laid out in detail the rising levels of debt being used to finance the AI boom; the intricate financial linkages between the companies involved; and the increasingly leveraged position of the investors – including hedge funds – backing them up.
As far back as the Wall Street crash of almost a century ago, the economist JK Galbraith was highlighting the fact that leverage – betting with borrowed money, effectively – tends to amplify booms and busts.
And as ministers met in the Thai capital, elsewhere in Asia there were tremors that may suggest Georgieva’s fear of “near-term disappointment” may already be gripping some investors.
South Korea’s Kospi share index recorded its biggest weekly loss since October 2008, at the height of the financial crisis, tumbling by 14.5% during the week, as traders ditched chip manufacturers such as Samsung and SK Hynix.
Analysts reported that questions around the borrowing, spending commitments and future profitability of AI companies unsettled the markets. Bonds issued by the datacentre CoreWeave slumped almost to distressed levels as these worries swirled.
Expectations of future increases in US interest rates also rose, after data showing that consumer price inflation rose in September, as did inflation at the US factory gate. US tech stocks were also hit, knocking 2% off the Nasdaq index between Monday and Thursday.
It was just the latest of a series of market wobbles of late, and finance ministers and central bankers probably gave it little thought as they were whisked in air-conditioned comfort back to their capitals this weekend.
But if the boom does turn to bust, sending shock waves through the global economy, they won’t be able to say they weren’t warned that the “resilience” we have been enjoying rests on shaky foundations.

Zest is a Key Ingredient to Good Living
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Approaching life with positive expectations, a get-up-and-go attitude, and eagerness is related to many good things in life. This individual asset is often referred to as zest, and it can be purposefully developed to assist us in managing daily stressors as well as creating meaningful lives.
True zest is not due to hyperarousal or too much caffeine. It is a cultivated cheerfulness and joy. When we are stressed or not feeling well, it’s hard to avoid doing things halfway or halfheartedly. But there are ways we can increase zest even when it seems like the deck is stacked against us, the world is filled with conflict, and our social media feeds are thick with chaos and gloom.
Psychologists Christopher Peterson and Martin Seligman pioneered the field of positive psychology, the scientific study of human flourishing. One of the highlights of their initiatives was published in 2004, Character Strengths and Virtues, a groundbreaking text on the 24 universal character strengths. Zest is one of the 24 strengths.
When you cultivate zest, you’ll want to fully engage in life and not just view it from the sidelines, look forward to each day, and wake to anticipation over the day’s possibilities. Zest has also been referred to as vitality, exuberance, and joie de vivre, the French phrase for the joy of living.
In an analysis of data from 130 studies involving more than 275,000 people around the globe, most character strengths were associated with greater mental health. But zest was one of just two strengths (the other is hope) that had the strongest relationship to mental well-being across countries and age groups. Zest contributes to life satisfaction among children, adolescents, and adults. In addition, in a study of nearly 10,000 employed adults, those who scored high on zest had higher work satisfaction and were more likely to view work as a calling. People who score high on measures of zest are also more likely to view their lives as meaningful.
I reached out to Ryan Niemiec, a psychologist and author of several books, including The Power of Character Strengths and Character Strengths Interventions: A Field Guide for Practitioners. Niemiec is the chief science and education officer at the VIA Institute on Character, a non-profit focused on the science and practice of character strengths. I asked him about the most effective ways people can increase zest in their own lives.
“In terms of boosting zest, I turn straight to behavioral activation, one of the most proven strategies for depression,” Niemiec said. “In practical terms, this means to take action in some way to boost oneself—to take that one step forward in lifting one’s energy.” He encouraged people to engage every day in one healthy pleasure, one form of physical activity, and one action that makes you feel like you accomplished something.
Some of us seem to naturally have this irresistible aliveness, often invigorating those around us. Others work hard to cultivate zest. Research supports the idea that we are never too old to change. And we can learn how to cultivate zest.
We can learn to savor pleasures, set good intentions, and try to view life as an adventure. Other intentional ways to potentially lift our spirits include taking a brisk 10-minute walk every morning, doing cardiovascular or strength-building challenges, practicing Reiki or yoga, laughing with friends, and engaging in stimulating tasks and work. The VIA Institute on Character has activities, workbooks, videos, webinars, and courses—some of them free—on improving all the character strengths, including zest.
To be sure, practicing a zest for life can be harder for those who have physical illness and pain and those who engage in unhealthy lifestyle behaviors. And those striving for zest under these circumstances may benefit from assistance from a mental health professional like a psychologist, a physical health provider like a physician, or a personal trainer or fitness instructor.
For some of us, being hard on ourselves is second nature. We expect our mental health to stretch under strain. Rather than exclusively focusing on what’s wrong with our mental health, one approach is to develop skills, traits, and perspectives that can help us. Acquiring zest is a worthwhile investment and may help us not only through challenging times, but also help us to see beauty and soar in our lives and workplaces.

Bulgarian Nickolay Mladenov Emerges as Possible Contender for UN Leadership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Bulgarian citizen Nickolay Mladenov, the High Representative for Gaza within the US-backed Peace Council, is among the potential candidates being discussed for the next United Nations secretary-general, Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported following the Security Council’s sixth informal vote on October 16.
Seven candidates have been officially nominated so far, but the field could expand because every contender has received at least one negative vote from a permanent member of the Security Council. The five countries with veto power are the United States, Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom.
Alongside Mladenov, AFP cited Lana Nusseibeh, the United Arab Emirates’ minister of state for foreign affairs, and Feridun Hadi Sinirlioğlu, secretary-general of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), as names circulating in diplomatic circles. None of the three has officially announced a candidacy.
“If countries wish to put forward more candidates, that is entirely within their sovereign right,” US Permanent Representative to the UN Mike Waltz said after the vote.
The sixth informal ballot did not produce a candidate acceptable to all five permanent Security Council members. For the first time in the selection process, ballots were differentiated by color, allowing members to identify whether any candidate faced opposition from a country holding veto power.
Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica received the most support, with nine votes, but also faced five negative votes, including two from permanent members. Rafael Grossi of Argentina and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana likewise received negative votes from two permanent members.
Current Secretary-General António Guterres is due to complete his second five-year term on December 31, 2026. The Security Council must recommend a successor for appointment by the UN General Assembly.
Under established diplomatic tradition, the secretary-general’s position rotates among the world’s regions, giving Latin American candidates an expected advantage in the current selection. Pressure is also increasing for a woman to become the UN’s first female secretary-general.

Gaza shelters deteriorate after repeated displacement as winter approaches: IOM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:54:15 UTC
18:54:15 KST

Repeated displacement during three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has left shelters across the enclave increasingly deteriorated, while restrictions and funding shortages are hampering preparations for winter, a senior UN migration official said late on Friday.
Karl Baker, regional crisis coordinator for the Gaza response at the International Organisation for Migration (IOM), said some Palestinians have been displaced as many as eight times, damaging or destroying tents and other temporary shelters each time families are forced to move.
“When they move, all those goods that they currently have or did have either get destroyed, or they have to seek new shelter,” Baker told UN News.
Even basic materials such as tarpaulins need to be replaced roughly every six months, but humanitarian agencies have been unable to bring replacements into Gaza at the required scale, he said.
Baker said agencies now need to move beyond temporary solutions toward more durable transitional shelters.
Materials needed for stronger roofing, concrete floors, and more substantial walls, however, are affected by Israel’s “dual-use” restrictions over security concerns.
“After three years of war, we do need to improve the level of shelter which is inside, and move further away from temporary and more toward transitional type of shelter,” he said.
Baker said IOM remains in constant contact with Israeli authorities, but some durable materials continue to be denied entry over security concerns.
He also cited funding shortages and disruptions to international shipping as obstacles, saying IOM relies on suppliers in countries including China, India, and Pakistan.
Although funding has begun to arrive, it remains insufficient to meet the needs of an estimated 1.8 million to 1.9 million people requiring shelter assistance, he added.
Baker said only around 30 percent of Gaza is currently accessible to most of the population, forcing displaced Palestinians into increasingly crowded and often flood-prone areas.
“The 30 percent in which they currently live is a very large displacement camp,” he said.
With winter rains already beginning, humanitarian organisations are working to address flood-prone areas and deploy water pumps, but Baker warned that getting displaced Palestinians through the winter would be the biggest challenge.
Earlier this month, IOM said available and incoming shelter supplies covered only 17 percent of Gaza’s winter needs, while more than half of tents and makeshift shelters were in poor condition.
A ceasefire has been in effect since October 10 2025, but Israeli attacks and restrictions on the entry of humanitarian and shelter supplies have continued.

BANDAR SERI BEGAWAN, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) --The contribution of Brunei's non-oil and gas sector to gross domestic product (GDP) increased from 46 percent in 2015 to 55 percent in 2025, a government minister said recently.
The share of non-oil and gas commodities in the country's exports also rose significantly from 7 percent to 60 percent over the same period, said Haji Abdul Manaf Haji Metussin, coordinating minister for economic policies and minister of economy, trade and industry, according to official media Pelita Brunei on Friday.
Speaking at the Baiduri Momentum Summit 2026 held near the capital, he attributed the increase largely to the expansion of downstream petroleum and chemical products.
The minister stressed that Brunei must move beyond reacting to global economic developments and instead anticipate emerging trends, strengthen economic resilience and seize opportunities to diversify its economy.
He said economic diversification remained central to achieving the third goal of Brunei Vision 2035, which aims to build a dynamic and sustainable economy.

====================================================================================================

As Israel blocks PA funding, the West Bank’s healthcare system is failing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:47:55 UTC
18:47:55 KST

As Israel blocks PA funding, the West Bank’s healthcare system is failing
Hospitals across the occupied West Bank have been hit by a funding shortage.
Beit Jala, occupied West Bank – Khaldoun Atwan starts each day in the oncology ward at Beit Jala Government Hospital, not knowing what barriers will come his way.
The Nabi Yunis checkpoint in Halhul seems to be “always closed”, so the head of the daytime oncology unit at the hospital leaves his car and finishes the commute from Hebron by taxi.
“More than once, by God, I found the mirror broken. I found the wiper broken,” he said about his journey through an area where settlers are now active.
Traversing a dizzying array of gates and checkpoints opening or closing at will, he does not know whether he will reach the hospital, whether his patients will, or whether the drugs they need will be on the shelf when they do.
Beit Jala is the only government hospital in Bethlehem governorate, home to some 320,000 people. Inside his tiny, spartan office, Atwan is struggling to keep up with his cancer patients who have regressed because they missed crucial appointments or essential drugs needed for their chemotherapy treatment.
Not even during the second Intifada, he recalls, was drug supply an issue. Now, it’s inescapable.
“Everything’s short … whatever’s available we give,” he said. “It’s a disaster.”
The Palestinian Authority (PA)’s finances have collapsed over the last three years due to a reduction in international aid and disruptions in Israel’s transfers of tax receipts. Israel’s actions in the occupied West Bank since October 2023, including widespread road closures, checkpoints and a series of settler pogroms against Palestinian communities, have also impacted the economy.
As a result, the occupied West Bank’s healthcare system is rapidly deteriorating, with staff receiving just half their salaries, while the PA can’t pay for essential medications.
‘Emergency cases only’
Alongside others nervously pacing in the courtyard, an older cancer patient from a village in Bethlehem governorate stood at the entrance of the hospital, weighing with his son what to do. “Every month they do their best, the doctors and the cleaning staff, but they aren’t provided with anything,” he said.
Ministry clinics are now operating part-time, with doctors seeing well more than 100 patients a day when they are. Now, even a doctor’s visit is rushed and unaffordable: “If we want to go to the doctor for a checkup, we need 200 shekels [$65],” said an older cancer patient.
“It’s not a story of there being no staff,” said Iyad Dari, the attending physician at the dialysis unit at Beit Jala. Getting paid only half their salaries, “the government employee is working just two or three days a week, because he hasn’t got enough to come in for his full hours,” he added. As a result, the hospital ends up covering emergency cases only.
“At first, [patients] were [angry]. But now everyone understands: Everyone’s suffering,” Dari said.
The medical supplies crisis in Beit Jala and across the West Bank is the result of Israel’s withholding of tax revenues earmarked for the PA, an action spearheaded by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
“This crisis is very predictable, and we saw it coming 100 percent,” said Milena Ansari of Physicians for Human Rights Israel. Even before the genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, Israel was periodically withholding tax revenues, endangering the Ministry of Health’s coffers, Milena said.
According to Yosef Ojra, an internal medicine specialist at Beit Jala, the withheld revenues have depleted the Health Ministry’s funds to pay medical suppliers, who are now withholding their services. The ongoing borrowing of supplies between the public and private arms of healthcare has greatly strained private clinics, pharmacies and hospitals.
Hisham Amle, an oncologist at the hospital, said shortages are “an old problem, not a new one”, but that about 90 percent of important items – for chemotherapy, above all – used to be there. Now, even immunotherapies and biologics are missing, and cancer treatment runs on an unbroken chain. “If the patient misses a session or two, he’s lost all the treatment before it,” he said.
“When I first took over the department, the drugs were available,” said Atwan, the lead oncology nurse. He then began to list all the crucial drugs he was now missing for his patients. “There’s not one single complete protocol I’ve got.”
Khuloud Dweib, the hospital’s director of pharmacy, said the ministry recently managed to obtain eight previously missing oncology drugs and four biologics. This should be enough for between a month and a half and two months. But many other drugs are still out of stock, she said.
Unlike in Gaza, Israel is not blocking medicines from entering the West Bank, Ansari noted. The problem is “strictly” that the PA has no money to buy them. But “Israel has the primary legal obligation as an occupying power,” she notes, to ensure adequate medical care and access to occupied populations.
Denied movement, denied care
For all of the southern West Bank, Beit Jala’s hospital is the only public option available for cancer and dialysis treatment, with patients coming from Bethlehem and Hebron governorates, parts of occupied East Jerusalem and sometimes Jericho.
But as Israeli checkpoints and gates multiply, reaching the hospital has become a nightmare. Dari described a dialysis patient from Nahalin, with an appointment at seven or eight in the morning, whose village was sealed. “He sat about four, five hours at the checkpoint,” Dari said. Then he took the long way round, through Jaba, Surif, Halhul and Hebron, and reached the unit at four in the afternoon. A normal journey costs about 10 shekels. “A detour like this costs more than 100 shekels,” Dari said, and some patients need dialysis four times a week.
The ministry’s central supply warehouse, meanwhile, is in Nablus, Dweib said – and an hour-and-a-half drive can now take six to 10 hours when closures hit.
Often, Atwan’s patients require treatments split between his unit and the Augusta Victoria Hospital in occupied East Jerusalem. Before the war, cancer patients from the West Bank routinely received medical permits to enter Jerusalem. Some treatments are in Beit Jala, while others are only available in East Jerusalem. But there are no guarantees any more that patients can reach Jerusalem. “I’ve got a cancer patient … He waited on a referral, and there’s no treatment, and after all the running around it comes back he’s security-rejected, too,” Atwan said. “I mean, he doesn’t get a permit to go to [Augusta Victoria]? Where’s he supposed to go?”
Atwan recalled patients who became neutropenic due to missed treatment sessions, and one was lucky not to end up with sepsis. “These are disasters.”
He’s not sure exactly how many cancer patients he’s lost due to missed and incomplete treatments; many of the poorer patients, he said, simply go home and die there.
‘I’ve started cutting back, not taking much’
As crowds swell at front desks and people wait at the hospital’s entrance, a nervous exhaustion percolates through the hospital’s aged halls. “People are really tense. Everyone’s scared,” Dari said.
Atwan, who receives half his salary, struggles to cover his commute from Hebron and help support his daughters at university.
“Let’s not talk about our state of mind – we’ll start crying, for God’s sake,” said Atwan. “Our morale is at rock bottom … We smile in spite of ourselves.”
Amid mass unemployment with labour permits systematically revoked, more sick Palestinians are pushed towards public hospitals just as those hospitals have less to give. Hospitals “will prioritise someone who will actually pay them”, Ansari added.
Ahmed, a Palestinian from Bethlehem with a medical degree, would check every couple of days with the pharmacist to see if they had Humira, an injection every two weeks that his sister with Crohn’s disease needs. For three months, the pharmacists were out of stock. Buying directly from the pharmaceutical company would cost about 2,000 shekels ($650) for one or two injections. “We couldn’t afford that,” he said. “So we just struggled until it became available again.”
The elderly cancer patient from a village facing settler pogroms has cut back on his own medication. “It’s not supplied regularly,” he said. A course of it costs 20,000 shekels ($6,500). “I’ve started cutting back, not taking much,” he added.
Amid supply and staffing shortages, surgery backlogs have piled up. Sayed Ayyad, 22, from al-Eizariya, fell during an accident, fracturing his ankle badly last month. With serious operations taking priority, he waited three weeks for a slot.
“They told me there’s 60 people waiting for an operation,” he said. “One day we couldn’t do the surgery because there were no medicines, no painkillers, no anaesthetic, nothing.”
Fates left to chance
Khuloud Dweib, who heads the pharmacy department at Beit Jala, has to manage the worsening crisis as patients struggle with their health and finances. “There’s no security. We don’t have political, or health, or even financial security,” she said.
She’s left thinking of cases like a young man with multiple sclerosis studying medicine in Egypt. The Health Ministry used to provide his medicine through private purchase until the company stopped supplying without payment. His mother came to see her. “I want to sell my house so I can get the injection for my son,” the mother told her. “Because he’s in Egypt, away from home, studying, and … he’s stopped seeing, stopped walking.”
“So, what can I tell you,” Dweib said, fighting back the tears. “God help people.”
The medical staff fear that with their supplies being hollowed out, they could face a similar fate to their colleagues in Gaza who have been kidnapped or killed.
“We know that at any moment we could be targeted as medical staff, just because we’re medical personnel providing services to people,” Dweib said. “We’re a father and a mother in this society.”
Nobody in the ageing hospital wards sees an end in sight. “The longer we stay, the worse the situation gets,” said Dari.
At three o’clock each afternoon, Atwan has to leave in the hope that he can reach Bab az-Zawiya in Hebron, where he waits for a shared taxi.
“Maybe there’ll be a checkpoint for me, maybe there won’t be,” he said. It’s not so different from the conundrums his patients face. “When a patient gets sick, it’s his luck if the medicine’s there,” he said. “We’ve got no future. I swear: We’ve got no future.”

EU Blames Russia for Drone Attacks on Ships in Bulgaria’s Black Sea Waters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:46:04 UTC
18:46:04 KST

Bulgarian Power Exports Double as Battery Storage Expands
Bulgaria’s energy storage capacity has reached 6 gigawatts this year, approaching the country’s electricity demand of 7.4 GW and reshaping domestic and regional power markets
The European Council has formally blamed Russia for drone attacks on commercial vessels in the exclusive economic zones of Bulgaria and Romania in the Black Sea, describing the strikes as a serious breach of international law in the conclusions of its two-day summit in Brussels.
The document condemns Russian attacks on Ukraine’s agricultural infrastructure, Black Sea and Danube ports, border crossings, export facilities and vessels, as well as the blockade of shipping routes and destruction of grain storage facilities. It accuses Moscow of using food as a weapon again and threatening global food security, particularly in Africa, Asia and the Middle East.
“Attacks against civilian shipping, cargo, and commercial vessels—including those flying the flags of EU member states, such as the recent attacks within the exclusive economic zones of Bulgaria and Romania in the Black Sea—are unacceptable. They constitute a serious violation of international law and the law of the sea, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS),” the conclusions state.
Club Z reported on the wording yesterday after obtaining a copy of the document. The European Council is calling for safe passage to be restored immediately for all civilian, cargo and commercial vessels operating in the Black Sea to prevent further escalation.
European Council President António Costa also accused Russia of increasing its hybrid operations across Europe, citing sabotage and repeated violations of EU member states’ airspace and territorial waters.
“These actions will not go unanswered. We will redouble our efforts to implement our defense strategy through 2030,” Costa said.
Discussions on Ukraine continued throughout the summit. Costa said EU leaders had asked the European Commission to draw up a plan to meet Ukraine’s needs in 2027.
During a meeting with EU leaders, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv needed an additional 70 billion euros, in addition to the 90-billion-euro loan already agreed upon.
Fuel prices were another major issue. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the war in the Middle East had driven up the cost of imported fossil fuels, while Europe had received no additional energy supplies.
“Since the start of the war in the Middle East, the cost of imported fossil fuels has risen by 106 billion euros—without us receiving a single additional molecule of energy. Furthermore, gas prices have increased by about 140% since the end of February, and the price of diesel has doubled,” von der Leyen said.
To respond to migrant emergencies such as the situation in Ceuta at the end of July, the European Commission plans to propose a new EU framework for emergency response. Sudan’s army claims dozens of RSF fighters killed in Nyala attack
Rapid Support Forces accuse army of killing 30 civilians in attack on Nyala’s busy livestock market.
The Sudanese army says it has killed dozens of fighters from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in a series of air attacks on the southwestern city of Nyala, but the paramilitary group says the military has killed civilians.
The targets of Friday’s attack were RSF positions and command centres in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state and the seat of the paramilitary group’s self-declared administration, the army said in a statement.
However, the RSF said the army carried out a drone attack on a busy livestock market, killing 30 civilians, including 17 women and five children.
The group has not confirmed or denied whether separate attacks by the army killed some of its fighters and destroyed its command centres.
Separately, the human rights group Emergency Lawyers said in a post on X that a market was hit on Friday in Nyala and the drone used was “affiliated” with the Sudanese army.
Reporting from the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, Al Jazeera’s Almigdad Alruhaid said on Saturday that the fighting between the army and RSF has “intensified”.
“In South Kordofan, a source in the Sudanese government told Al Jazeera that the RSF carried out drone attacks on mining sites with the exchange in fire intensifying in many parts of Sudan in the past 24 hours.”
The army has repeatedly targeted the Darfur region in western Sudan with drones to try to retake territory controlled by the RSF, which holds most of the area.
This month, Sudanese military chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan promised to seize “every inch” of territory under RSF control.
The Sudanese civil war began in 2023 and has killed tens of thousands of people. The United Nations has described the situation in Sudan as the world’s worst humanitarian crisis.

Indian police arrested Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), on Saturday, according to multiple media reports, a day after detaining him ahead of a rally in Delhi that drew hundreds of protesters waving national flags and demanding the resignation of the country's election chief.
Dipke was arrested to prevent a breach of the peace and was due to appear before a special executive magistrate on Saturday, broadcasters NDTV and India Today reported.
Delhi police did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment.
The CJP, opposition groups and student organizations have staged near-daily protests this month, calling for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign over a revision of voter lists that they allege favors Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
More than 130 million voters were deleted from the lists during the revision. The Election Commission has denied favoring any party and said voters who were wrongly removed can re-enroll. The BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Student activist Neha Bora, a prominent face of the protests, was also detained Friday as she tried to reach central Delhi with dozens of supporters. She was released Saturday.
"Please, spare the people of India. Impeach Gyanesh Kumar and halt SIR (special intensive revision), so that the ordinary citizens of this country can breathe a sigh of relief, feel at ease, and have their voting rights ensured," Bora told the ANI news agency after her release.
Dipke was detained Friday as he left a house in central Delhi. Police forced him into a police car and drove away after a brief argument.
Dipke had called Friday's protest in support of two CJP leaders who were detained and sent to jail for five days this week for demonstrating at a protest site in violation of a ban.
Earlier Friday, police had met with Dipke and warned him against proceeding with the protest.
The Cockroach movement has emerged as a significant source of political pressure on Modi and the BJP during the prime minister's 12 years in power.
A weeks-long sit-in by the movement's supporters earlier this year forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign over exam paper leaks.

Pope Leo cleared for discharge 4 days after lung cancer surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:42:00 UTC
18:42:00 KST

Pope Leo XIV will be discharged from the hospital Saturday, four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, and is expected to deliver his traditional noon blessing Sunday from a window overlooking St. Peter’s Square, the Vatican said.
The 71-year-old pope had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Tuesday after doctors identified a nodule suspected of being cancerous. The operation confirmed a diagnosis of adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
His personal physician, Luigi Carbone, and surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement released by the Vatican that blood tests, a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning and an assessment of his clinical condition showed he was fit to leave the hospital.
Leo is expected to return to the Vatican in the early afternoon, according to the statement.
The discharge comes earlier than the Vatican’s initial estimate of a weeklong hospital stay and follows several indications that the pope has been recovering well. His audiences had been canceled through Tuesday, but Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said the timing of his release would depend on his medical team.
Leo disclosed his condition last Sunday during his traditional appearance before the faithful gathered in St. Peter’s Square, telling them that doctors had found a nodule in his lung that would need to be removed.
Since undergoing surgery, he has continued several official and religious activities from Rome’s Gemelli Hospital, including a telephone conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin, meetings with senior aides and the celebration of Mass in the hospital chapel.
Medical updates from his physician and surgeon have described a positive postoperative recovery, saying Leo has been able to carry out his normal daily activities independently.
The Vatican released the first images of the pope since his surgery Friday, showing him standing at an altar in a hospital chapel wearing green liturgical vestments. Doctors said the latest tests confirmed his continued improvement.
Leo presided over the liturgy himself and distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes attending the service, Bruni said.
During his homily, the pope thanked hospital staff for their daily work caring for sick people and for the attention they had given him during his treatment, Bruni said.
His recovery will be closely watched ahead of a planned trip to Latin America from Nov. 6-17. The journey, scheduled to begin about three weeks after his discharge, includes 12 flights and two helicopter trips.
The Vatican has signaled that preparations for the visit are continuing. On Friday, it published the names of journalists accredited to travel aboard the papal plane.
Oncology surgeons say patients can generally be cleared to fly about three weeks after surgery, provided their recovery allows it. Whether Leo will be fit for the demanding trip will depend on his continued progress and his doctors’ assessment.
Medical teams are still awaiting test results that will establish the cancer’s precise molecular and genetic characteristics, determine whether it has spread beyond the removed lung lobe and clarify whether further treatment will be necessary.

Repeated displacement leaves Gaza shelters deteriorating ahead of winter: IOM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:41:48 UTC
18:41:48 KST

Repeated displacement during three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has left shelters across the enclave increasingly deteriorated, while restrictions and funding shortages are hampering preparations for winter, a senior UN migration official said late Friday.
Karl Baker, regional crisis coordinator for the Gaza response at the International Organization for Migration (IOM), said some Palestinians have been displaced as many as eight times, damaging or destroying tents and other temporary shelters each time families are forced to move.
“When they move, all those goods that they currently have or did have either get destroyed, or they have to seek new shelter,” Baker told UN News.
Even basic materials such as tarpaulins need to be replaced roughly every six months, but humanitarian agencies have been unable to bring replacements into Gaza at the required scale, he said.
Baker said agencies now need to move beyond temporary solutions toward more durable transitional shelters.
Materials needed for stronger roofing, concrete floors, and more substantial walls, however, are affected by Israel’s “dual-use” restrictions over security concerns.
“After three years of war, we do need to improve the level of shelter which is inside, and move further away from temporary and more toward transitional type of shelter,” he said.
READ: Gaza residents face another winter amid shelter shortages, dwindling aid
Baker said IOM remains in constant contact with Israeli authorities, but some durable materials continue to be denied entry over security concerns.
He also cited funding shortages and disruptions to international shipping as obstacles, saying IOM relies on suppliers in countries including China, India, and Pakistan.
Although funding has begun to arrive, it remains insufficient to meet the needs of an estimated 1.8 million to 1.9 million people requiring shelter assistance, he added.
Baker said only around 30% of Gaza is currently accessible to most of the population, forcing displaced Palestinians into increasingly crowded and often flood-prone areas.
“The 30% in which they currently live is a very large displacement camp,” he said.
With winter rains already beginning, humanitarian organizations are working to address flood-prone areas and deploy water pumps, but Baker warned that getting displaced Palestinians through the winter would be the biggest challenge.
Earlier this month, IOM said available and incoming shelter supplies covered only 17% of Gaza’s winter needs, while more than half of tents and makeshift shelters were in poor condition.
A ceasefire has been in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, but Israeli attacks and restrictions on the entry of humanitarian and shelter supplies have continued.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Japan’s government has approved plans for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. to build the country’s first 3-nanometer chip plant, reports said Saturday.
The Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry announced Friday it agreed to the proposal to establish a second fab for the TSMC-led joint venture with Japan Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing in Kumamoto Prefecture, per CNA. The original plan had been to produce 12 nm and 6 nm chips at the new factory, but in February, TSMC announced it was planning for the more advanced 3 nm semiconductors.
The plant will turn out 6,000 wafers per month instead of the 48,000 projected under the previous plans, according to an Asahi Shimbun report. The Japanese government also agreed to changes for the existing first TSMC plant, ending the production of 12 nm to 16 nm chips. Instead, the fab will produce 45,000 wafers per month made with 22 nm to 28 nm technology.
Some of the changes were motivated by TSMC seeing an increased demand for chips for the development of AI products, Asahi Shimbun reported. The second plant is scheduled to start operations in December 2028.
Final production figures will be decided based on the scale of government subsidies, per CNA. The original plan was to provide NT$150 billion (US$4.63 billion) in subsidies.

After more than seven hours of inspections, a specialized team and a tugboat began moving the vessel toward Burgas. Following a sleepless night for the teams involved, the ship entered Burgas Bay early this morning and was secured at Berth 25.
The operation was complicated by poor weather, the vessel’s damaged hull and the risk that further structural damage could cause it to sink. The ship was described as effectively a wreck and no longer operational.
“The actual boarding was the most complex and dangerous part of the operation,” said Capt. Zhivko Petrov, director of the Maritime Administration in Burgas, explaining the risks involved in approaching the ship and securing it to a tugboat.
A visual inspection identified three breaches in the hull, on the starboard side, the port side and at the stern. A major opening was also clearly visible near the bow after the vessel docked. The exact nature and extent of the damage will be established through expert assessments.
Transport and Communications Minister Georgi Peev said Bulgarian authorities had taken all necessary steps to bring the uncontrolled vessel to safety despite the weather conditions.
“As the Ministry of Transport, we have a responsibility to ensure that drifting, uncontrolled vessels are not left in our waters. That is why we did everything possible to bring the ship here,” Peev said.
The investigation will examine the circumstances of the attack and seek to identify the drones used. Investigators are expected to search around the damaged sections for drone debris that could help establish who was responsible.
The Military Prosecutor’s Office in Sofia has opened a probe into a suspected war crime linked to the attack. Peev said investigators had working hypotheses about the origin of the strike, but stressed that responsibility must be established through evidence.
“We have working hypotheses, yes, the attack most likely originated from Russia, as it is highly improbable that Ukraine would attack its own vessels. As you know, the ship sails under the Ukrainian flag. However, we must definitively prove this; our conclusions must always be based on evidence,” the minister said.
The recovery operation was carried out by Bulgarian teams, with assistance from the Chelsea 2, a vessel owned by the same owner as the damaged ship. Peev rejected claims that cargo could have been unloaded while the Chelsea 3 was still at sea, saying it reached Burgas empty.
“We have taken measures to prevent anyone from boarding the ship. No one has boarded the vessel, and no cargo has been removed. I am absolutely certain of this,” Peev said.
The Bulgarian state is paying for the rescue operation. Peev also announced that European funding had been secured to purchase the country’s first specialized rescue vessel, with the procurement process expected to start next year.

“The year 2030 will mark the end of my presidential term. This matter is completely settled,” Sisi said during a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital.
Sisi said the Egyptian constitution “will not be touched,” stressing the need to prevent any violation of constitutional and democratic principles.
He said the constitution defines the role of the armed forces in protecting the constitutional order, democracy and the fundamental pillars of the state.
“I will not leave the Egyptian state until it is brimming with its own people capable of shouldering responsibility,” he added, saying a new generation of leaders is currently being prepared through the Egyptian Military Academy.
Egypt ready to defend Saudi Arabia
Sisi also said Egypt is prepared to take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to defend the kingdom’s security and sovereignty.
“We will take any measure to protect Saudi Arabia,” he said, adding that he would call on parliament to convene an emergency session to authorize such action if requested.
“We stand firmly to protect and defend the territories of our brothers in the Gulf,” he added.

An international forum on the reconstruction of Ukraine will take place in Bucharest on October 22–23
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:32:34 EEST
18:32:34 KST

The international forum “Rebuilding Ukraine: Security, Opportunities, Investment” will take place on October 22–23, 2026, in Bucharest, Romania, at the ROMEXPO exhibition center, Pavilion C2. The event will bring together representatives of government agencies from Ukraine, Romania, and other European countries, as well as international financial organizations, investors, the business community, and experts.
The forum is organized by the Romanian think tank New Strategy Center in partnership with the Romanian Chamber of Commerce and Industry. The academic partner of the event is the University of Agronomic Sciences and Veterinary Medicine in Bucharest (USAMV).
According to the updated program, 31 thematic panel discussions are scheduled over the course of two days, focusing on attracting international capital for Ukraine’s reconstruction, the development of transportation and energy infrastructure, industrial cooperation, defense technologies, food security, and cross-border cooperation.
One of the forum’s key focuses will be a discussion of Romania’s role as a regional logistics and investment hub for Ukraine’s reconstruction. In particular, participants will examine the prospects for developing transport corridors between Ukraine, Romania, and Moldova; expanding the capacity of Danube ports; and creating new rail and road routes between the Baltic and Black Seas.
Special attention will be given to investment opportunities in Ukrainian regions. The program includes special presentations on projects in the Kyiv, Zakarpattia, Ivano-Frankivsk, Vinnytsia, Chernivtsi, Odesa, and Kherson regions. Representatives of local authorities, regional development agencies, and the business community will discuss attracting foreign investors, implementing infrastructure projects, and developing cooperation with Romanian partners.
On October 22, the main focus will be on economic recovery, financing, and investments. Participants will examine mechanisms for attracting private capital, opportunities offered by international development banks, support programs for Ukrainian businesses, and prospects for the restoration of residential and industrial infrastructure.
Among the announced participants for the first day are Gennadiy Chizhikov, President of the Ukrainian Chamber of Commerce and Industry; Marina Khlistun, Executive Director of UkraineInvest; Kateryna Glazkova, Executive Director of the Union of Ukrainian Entrepreneurs; and representatives of the European Investment Bank, the German development bank KfW, Japan’s JBIC, Poland’s BGK, and other international financial institutions.
As part of the discussion on financing the reconstruction, a remote presentation by a representative of the Ukrainian government is scheduled. Separate panels will be dedicated to the development of the agricultural sector, ensuring global food security, the modernization of the energy sector, and the development of renewable energy sources.
Also on October 22, there will be a presentation of the “Together for Ukraine” platform, initiated by the New Strategy Center to foster cooperation and support for Ukraine.
Human capital issues will be the subject of a separate discussion featuring Ella Libanova, director of the M.V. Ptukha Institute of Demography and Social Studies of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine. Participants will discuss challenges related to the return of Ukrainian citizens from abroad, workforce supply for the economy, and the training of specialists for reconstruction.
On October 23, the forum’s program will focus on security challenges, the development of the defense industry, energy resilience, and cross-border cooperation.
In particular, panel discussions are planned on international security guarantees for Ukraine, the prospects for ending Russian aggression, the use of unmanned systems, and the development of joint production of defense products by Ukrainian and European companies.
Participants in the discussion on security guarantees will include Igor Zhovkva, Advisor to the President of Ukraine on Foreign Policy; Kiril Petkov, former Prime Minister of Bulgaria; and representatives from the United States, Japan, and European think tanks.
A separate session will be dedicated to the reintegration of veterans and the utilization of their professional potential in economic recovery. Among the participants listed is Ruslan Prykhodko, Ukraine’s Deputy Minister for Veterans’ Affairs.
The energy segment on the second day will include discussions on preparing Ukraine’s power grid for the winter, protecting critical infrastructure, cooperation in the Black Sea region, and prospects for involving international companies in energy projects. Among the announced participants are representatives of Naftogaz of Ukraine, OMV Petrom, ROMGAZ, Japan’s JICA, and other energy companies and organizations.
Issues related to the participation of Romanian businesses in Ukraine’s reconstruction will play a significant role in the program. A special panel will be dedicated to financial instruments, institutional support, and opportunities for implementing joint investment projects.
The forum’s concluding discussions will address the prospects for post-war security in Europe, the development of defense-industrial cooperation, Russia’s international responsibility, and mechanisms for compensating Ukraine for damages caused by the war.
The organizers note that the forum’s goal is to create a practical platform for dialogue between Ukrainian and international companies, financial institutions, and representatives of government agencies and local authorities. Particular emphasis is placed on identifying specific investment opportunities and forming partnerships aimed at Ukraine’s long-term economic recovery.
The New Strategy Center is an independent Romanian think tank specializing in security, defense, foreign policy, energy, and regional cooperation. The organization hosts international conferences and expert events dedicated to strategic challenges in the Black Sea region and Central and Eastern Europe. This forum continues a series of events on Romania’s role in Ukraine’s recovery, organized by the New Strategy Center in 2023 and 2025.
The detailed forum program and information about participants are available on the event’s official website.
The Interfax-Ukraine news agency is a media partner of the event.

IMF urges support for poorer nations facing high inflation, war spillovers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:31:47 UTC
18:31:47 KST

IMF urges support for poorer nations facing high inflation, war spillovers
Low-income countries spend up to 14 percent of their revenue on debt repayments, IMF chief says.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has a responsibility to help poorer nations struggling with rising debt, high inflation and price shocks caused by war spillovers, the head of the global lender says.
Speaking as the IMF’s annual meetings in Bangkok wrapped up on Saturday, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said discussions with global policymakers showed both “optimism and worry”.
“Optimism from the resilience of the global economy, the promise of AI, the dynamism of Asia,” Georgieva told reporters. “But AI is also recognised to be a source of worry and so are inflation, high levels of debt, wars, climate risks.”
Georgieva said vulnerable nations are missing out on the AI investment boom that is driving growth in richer countries while at the same time dealing with higher borrowing costs.
Higher global interest rates mean low-income countries now spend 8 to 14 percent of their revenue on debt repayments, up from previous years, she said.
“I can tell you that people everywhere, but especially in poorer countries, don’t like inflation. Inflation is like a tax on the poor,” Georgieva said.
The warnings came as low-income, oil-importing countries take the strongest hit from rising global energy costs. Prices have soared since February when the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran, leading to retaliatory strikes in the Middle East and disrupted oil and gas flows.
“Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security,” said a statement issued by Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, the chairman of the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC).
The IMFC is the main steering committee for the 191-member crisis lender.
Debt relief and regional support
Georgieva said her organisation has a responsibility to help countries restructure debt if needed to assist with domestic resource mobilisation, bring in international finance and create conditions for private investment.
Such countries need to set spending targets that prioritise growth and protect the most vulnerable people, she said, adding that the IMF has a “relentless pursuit of more resources for low-income countries”.
“When we do our best, it translates into better lives for people,” she said.
Georgieva also said the IMF plans to back Iraq “very firmly” with a requested loan programme while talks with Lebanese authorities are making progress.
“We will get to Iraq both money and policy support,” she said. “In the case of Lebanon, we are in very intense discussions with Lebanese authorities. We have made significant progress towards the programme. We have still a bit more work to do together, and I’m confident we will be successful.”
