Hunting in the wilderness, embracing Zionism: Inside a Montana cowboy family's extraordinary life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:47:18 UTC
17:47:18 KST

They hunt elk in snow-covered mountains, raise children who know how to use a lasso by age 7 and sell horses to finance trips to Israel. Documentary photographer Dan Lior and his friend, adventurer Noam “Nofi” Genet, encountered a rugged Montana cowboy family and got a firsthand look at a life defined by hard work, faith and an extraordinary love for the Jewish people.
Their journey included firing revolvers in the wilderness, an exhausting hunting expedition through the snow and a visit to a remote log cabin with a giant Star of David at its entrance. Along the way, they met people of few words who nevertheless know how to extend a heartfelt welcome.
In the vast expanses of Montana, far from major highways and tourist attractions, even a routine drive through the state known as Big Sky Country can turn into an adventure.
"We set out in two vehicles toward the grazing area to put out salt for their cattle," Dan recalls. "Suddenly, there's no reception, no phone service. We lost our way, lost track of them and got completely lost," he says with a laugh. "We're driving off-road, trying to find our bearings and getting nowhere, and there are grizzly bears and dangerous wildlife out there."
The solution seemed to come straight out of a Western.
"While we're trying to figure out how to get ourselves out of this mess, suddenly we hear gunshots in the air," Dan says excitedly. "So we drive toward the sound and see them standing on the roof of their vehicle, firing their revolvers into the air."
As it turns out, the revolvers familiar from classic Westerns remain an essential part of life in the Montana wilderness.
"You walk into their house and there's a shelf with revolvers and hunting rifles, just like in the Wild West," Dan says. "And they carry them on their belts. It's really a matter of safety because they live in what's known as Bear Country."
After the two groups reunited, the gunfire incident turned into an amusing encounter between the Israelis and the cowboys.
"There are these big cowboy revolvers out there, so we say, 'Come on, let's shoot,'" Dan recalls. "We take the revolvers and start shooting at trees. Then one of them, Ephraim, brings out a shotgun, and someone throws a bottle into the air. We shoot and miss, shoot and miss."
Then it was Ezekiel's turn to show the visitors how things are done in Montana.
"They throw the bottle into the air for him — and boom, he hits it."
Noam “Nofi” Genet, an American Jew who grew up in Florida and now lives near the Sea of Galilee, met the pro-Israel cowboy family through a rehabilitation initiative he launched. As part of the program, he brings small groups of Israeli military reservists, some of whom are coping with post-traumatic stress, on wilderness expeditions in Montana.
He learned about the family after some of its sons traveled to Israel during the war to show their support. The family later invited him to visit their ranch in Montana's Bear Country.
Six hours on horseback: A hunting expedition in Montana's snowy mountains
Noam, an expert fisherman with wilderness survival skills, joined the pro-Israel cowboys on a challenging four-day hunting expedition in the Montana mountains.
For the locals, this was no tourist adventure. It was part of the family's efforts to stock up on meat for the winter.
"We rode for six hours to their hunting camp, and there was a lot of snow along the way," he recalls. "For the first hour, riding through the snow is fun. These guys were practically born in the saddle. But after that, my whole body was in serious pain."
“Some people hunt for sport, but these people hunt to survive. A deer like that can feed a family for several months.”
And what does a typical day on such a hunting trip look like? 
"They work incredibly hard. They get up very early in the morning and look for signs of elk, one of the largest species in the deer family, because it's their mating season."
But the hunt did not unfold quite as they had hoped.
"We didn't see any elk, but we found another very large deer that they shot from 300 meters (about 330 yards) away. It was a very special and very sad moment for me, but also deeply meaningful and educational."
After the animal was shot, another demanding stage of the hunt began.
"I watched Ezekiel, the cowboy, cut open the deer's belly with a large knife and then work incredibly hard to carry it on his back, antlers and all, down from the mountaintop toward their camp," Noam says.
"I carried his enormous rifle and heavy coat so he could carry the deer meat, weighing about 150 kilograms (330 pounds), back to camp. And that was after he'd removed all its internal organs."
Noam emphasizes the distinction between hunting for recreation and hunting for food.
"Some people hunt for sport, but these people hunt to survive," he says. "An animal like that can feed your family for several months. You butcher it and put everything in the freezer."
A Star of David in the heart of bear country
The Montana cowboy family's home looks as though it came straight out of the nostalgic television series Little House on the Prairie.
But a large, illuminated Star of David hangs on the front of the log cabin, while inside, pictures of Israel and biblical symbols adorn the walls. The family members are not Jewish but devout Christians.
"They have a love for God, a love for Israel, a love for their land and a love for hard work," Dan says. "They don't have time for small talk. They get up in the morning and go straight to work."
So what inspired their love for Israel?
"It was their father, may he rest in peace," says Noam, who tried to trace the roots of the family's special connection. "He taught them the Torah and instilled in them a love for the Jewish people."
They hunt for their own food, wear tzitzit and Stars of David, and support the Jewish people and Israel.
According to Noam, the extended family includes more than 10 children, along with another generation of grandchildren bearing biblical names.
"They're strong, extraordinary people. They hunt for their food, wear tzitzit [ritual fringes traditionally worn by observant Jewish men] and Stars of David, and support the Jewish people and our country."
To illustrate the depth of their connection to Israel, Noam imitates the family's thick cowboy accent as he repeats something he heard them say:
"I love God. God loves Israel. I want to love what God loves."
And their love for Israel goes far beyond the Star of David on the wall.
"The sons work outdoors all day, training wild horses and selling them," Noam explains. "If they want to fly to Israel to help, like they did after October 7, they sell a horse and use the money to come to Israel."
Lunch with the Israel-loving cowboy family in the heart of Montana looks like a scene from the hit television series Yellowstone, starring Kevin Costner.
The family raises horses and cattle, goes on hunting expeditions, makes a living through manual labor and teaches its children to take part in ranch work from a very young age.
"They have a plastic steer for roping practice in the field next to their house," Dan says. "I watched Elisheva, a 7-year-old girl, walk up to it, pick up a rope from the grass and start swinging her lasso."
"Every time she throws it, from a distance of 10 or 15 meters [about 33 to 49 feet], she lands it right on the horns. She also goes out to do chores around the ranch on her pony, and her little sister, who's 2, is already collecting eggs from the chicken coop."
Arriving in such a remote place and watching the children, Dan says, offers a striking perspective on modern life.
“If you dropped me out there in the middle of nowhere, my chances of survival would be much lower than theirs.”
"You get to this remote place, look at the kids and realize two things," he says admiringly. "You realize this is how we lived 150 years ago. You don't buy your food. You grow it, harvest it and store it."
"On the one hand, you realize how privileged your own children are. On the other hand, if you dropped me out there in the middle of nowhere, my chances of survival would be much lower than theirs."
Few words, plenty of hospitality
In Montana's Wild West, people are not particularly inclined to talk about their feelings.
Even when posing for a photograph with a visitor from Israel, members of the cowboy family will not necessarily put an arm around his shoulder or display affection in the way Israelis are accustomed to.
But that does not mean they are any less warm.
"It's not that they're cold," Dan explains. "They served us tons of food, steaks and dessert fresh out of the oven. And they're constantly asking what you need, asking about Israel, asking about your experiences and who you are."
According to Dan, these are people who express their feelings primarily through actions.
Noam was equally struck by the family's reserve and dry sense of humor.
"They're simple, down-to-earth people who don't talk much, but they're funny," he says.
"The women are very strong, and from what I experienced, they talk more than the men. They work incredibly hard in the kitchen and with the children. They're wonderful mothers, and they support the men 100% in everything they do. It's like living with a strong, hardworking wife and stepping back in time."
Despite the family's heartfelt hospitality and deep love for Israel, however, the isolated ranch is not a tourist destination, and Dan believes it should stay that way.
Behind the rugged landscapes, the horses and the lifestyle that seems lifted from a Western movie lies a demanding reality of relentless physical labor.
Every visit from guests means a day of work the family must sacrifice, even as the cattle, horses and rest of the ranch continue to require constant attention.
"When we come to visit, that's an entire day when they're not doing what they need to do to actually survive the next day, or two days down the road," Dan explains.

Third Corps posts footage of first strike on Russia's new Dragon thermobaric weapon system – video
Soldiers from the 3rd Army Corps have struck a Russian TOS-3 Drakon (Dragon) thermobaric rocket launcher system for the first time. The system was hit by a drone.
Source: 3rd Army Corps on social media
Details: The Drakon was struck during Operation Vivaldi. The weapon, classified as a heavy flamethrower system by the Russians, was hit by a drone operated by the Muramasa unit from the Kraken Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment.
The system was attacked 12 kilometres from the line of contact after the Drakon had been observed firing.
The attack on the Russian TOS-3 Drakon thermobaric rocket launcher system
"We have struck a Russian TOS-3 Drakon heavy flamethrower system for the first time – the enemy's latest development. This is yet another result of the 3rd Corps' systematic efforts to destroy enemy weapons and weaken its combat capabilities," the 3rd Army Corps commented on the strike.
According to the 3rd Army Corps, the TOS-3 Drakon is the latest development in the heavy flamethrower system family, which includes the Solntsepyok and TOS-2 Tosochka. The new model is equipped with slat armour and explosive reactive armour.
The system fires unguided thermobaric rockets from 15 launch tubes. The TOS-3 Drakon has an estimated range of 15 km and needs a crew of three.
Background:
- Earlier, Oboronka, Ukrainska Pravda's defence section, reported that Ukrainian troops had deployed ground robotic systems behind Russian lines during Operation Vivaldi in northern Donetsk Oblast. The manoeuvre enabled Ukraine's defence forces to liberate two villages and clear a third.
- During the 3rd Army Corps' Operation Vivaldi, fighters from the NC13 strike ground robotic systems unit upgraded ground-based kamikaze drones with two grenade launchers and used new strike tactics.

Scotland must earn its NATO place, says SNP defence MP
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:43:38 BST
17:43:38 KST

EXCLUSIVE – An independent Scotland would hold the Greenland Iceland gap on NATO’s behalf and would have to demonstrate what it brings to the alliance beyond its geography, the SNP Westminster leader told me when I sat down with him to chat all things defence.
Dave Doogan, the member for Angus and Perthshire Glens, said his party’s policy of NATO membership carries obligations that cannot be assumed. “You can’t just want to be in NATO. You have to demonstrate that you’re worthy to be in NATO. NATO is a collective assurance and defence pact, and so if we are asking those current members of NATO to let us into that club, then we need to know, they need to know rather, that, well, what are you going to do over and above your geography, Scotland? And we need to be able to answer that question and answer it clearly.”
The geography itself would change name and meaning on independence, and Doogan set out what that would leave Scotland responsible for in the North Atlantic approaches: “If you look at an independent Scotland, the Greenland Iceland UK gap would then be the Greenland Iceland Scotland gap, and you and I both know that the corridor of principal tension between Russia and NATO is in that environment, that Euro-Atlantic region. So Scotland would have, working with their allies, a role in that.”
Doogan argued that Scottish membership would be an addition to the alliance and not a subtraction from it. “An independent Scotland within NATO makes the United Kingdom greater than the sum of its parts. There’s an additionality with an independent Scotland. We won’t be spending that five and a half billion annually, recurring and growing, on something else. We’ll be spending it on defence of the realm and defence of the Euro-Atlantic zone in cooperation with our allies, just like Denmark does, just like Norway does, just like Finland and Sweden do, and the UK do.”
He warned against treating the Typhoon force at Lossiemouth as a Scottish asset in all but name, arguing that the station exists for a job wider than Scotland: “Let’s not think for one minute Lossiemouth is there to defend Scotland alone. Lossiemouth is there to protect the UK’s northern flank.”
Doogan has already done the arithmetic behind that offer, having drafted and costed a plan for an independent Scotland with an army, a navy and an air force funded by around five and a half billion pounds a year. He wrote it about two and a half years ago, said it now needs updating, and corrected the suggestion that the work was unfinished, saying it simply needs a refresh. He is holding it back until the next independence referendum debate.
Asked why he has not published it, he said: “All of these things are about timing, and you know we can’t all see defence as a priority. I accept that, but actually, if we unpack these things, if we don’t have security, then we don’t have anything. And security isn’t just about territorial integrity and freedom of movement. It’s about food security, energy security, and a whole range of other things.”
He added that the document is written to answer a question that has not yet been asked in earnest: “Why not release the defence plan now? Well, a good reason is that it needs a refresh, but it’s designed to answer a question when enough people are asking that question, and that will come when we’re having the next independence referendum debate. Because I believe that it’s a cogent and sensible plan.”
Doogan described the document as “a signpost and a clarion acceptance that Scotland has a responsibility to defend itself as an independent state, and it has a responsibility to be a responsive and reliable partner to our allies.”
On the shape of the force, he said the plan assumes a conventional structure built up over a number of years: “The proposal that I’ve drafted and costed shows Scotland with a traditional three main service, army, navy and air force, and of course that needs generated over time. You don’t start with that, but you can have it on the drawing board.”
The budget comes from Scotland’s existing share of British defence spending, money he says is already being spent on Scotland’s behalf: “Scotland would be in a position to spend what it currently is exposed to in terms of the UK fiscal environment on defence, which is circa five, five and a half billion per share of the UK defence budget. That would be on a rolling year-on-year recurring with inflation, a budget that would generate a substantial defence force across three services.”
Doogan argued that the headline percentage tells you very little on its own, telling me “I often think two or three per cent of GDP is pretty abstract. Sometimes it’s not what you do, it’s the way that you do it. And the same is true, it’s not what you spend, it’s what you spend it on.”
He made the case for the naval component on industrial grounds, arguing that Scotland is among a small group of countries with the yards to build its own warships: “If you look at the amount of countries around the world that could have a stab at building a complex warship, there’s about twenty maybe at a push, and Scotland’s one of them. In fact, we’ve got two sites that can build complex warships on each side of the country.”
Doogan said he would be happy to go into where an independent Scotland would source combat aircraft, train its pilots and secure interoperability, while declining to treat those as prior conditions. “These are all legitimate operational questions, which I would quite like to answer, but I don’t feel the need to answer them because actually these are challenges that every sovereign state faces, and every sovereign state has to shop around for these platforms.”
On the division of existing British military equipment, he said the ownership position is clear but the practical answer is not. “It’s important to remember that we own the assets, all of them proportionately, at the disposal of the UK defence forces, and so we’ve got a call on them. But why would we make problems for the UK by taking our share?”
He set that against the state of the British inventory, where he argues the margin for giving anything away has long gone: “You know as well as I do that there is very little redundancy in any platform in the United Kingdom. You know, just look at what they were trying to do to get a functioning Type 45 out to the Mediterranean recently. If we think that there are squadrons of Typhoons up and down these islands ready to go at a moment’s notice, that’s not how it is.”
On that basis he ruled out pressing a claim that damaged what remained of the UK, telling me “So if we were to claim our share of eight per cent or whatever of UK assets, and that caused major difficulties for the UK, well, we just wouldn’t do it because it’s not intelligent.”
Division of assets has been one of the hardest parts of the independence argument to pin down since 2014, when the Scottish Government’s white paper assumed a share of equipment would transfer and the then British government declined to negotiate before a vote. The eight per cent figure Doogan uses reflects Scotland’s rough share of the British population, which was the basis the 2014 prospectus worked from.
On relations with what would remain of the United Kingdom, Doogan expects cooperation to follow from mutual interest. “Let’s not pretend for one minute that the United Kingdom, once all the heat has gone out of an independence debate and Scotland has chosen to be independent, the rest of the UK will cooperate with Scotland just in the same way it cooperates with every other entity and jurisdiction that used to be governed from London. It’s entirely predictable, because it’s to England’s and the rest of the UK’s self interest to cooperate with Scotland, and it’s in Scotland’s interest to cooperate with the rest of the UK.”
He added that the hostility between the two governments is a product of the constitutional argument itself: “This enmity that exists just now is a function of trying to keep the UK together. Once Scotland’s out of the UK, that enmity has no purpose anymore, and we’ll work together like grown-up and respectful states.”
Doogan said that losing jurisdiction over the northern half of the island would present the rest of the UK with a problem, and that he would not want it handled adversarially. “If the SNP or I have got anything to do with that, that won’t be a challenge because we’ll approach it in a cooperative way. How we do that is up for discussion. A brand new independent Scotland would not want to be undefended, but the rest of the UK would not wish a brand new independent Scotland to be undefended either.”
On the deterrent, he said Scotland would have no further say once the system left Scottish waters. “We have got no locus with the deterrent once it’s removed from Scottish waters. It’s not a Scottish asset or system, it’s a UK asset or system. And so what they choose to do with it, where they choose to berth it, whether they choose to sustain and renew it going forward into the future, that’s entirely up to the rest of the UK. Scotland will have no role in that. We’ll respect their sovereignty and their freedom of decision, and they’ll respect ours.”
Where the deterrent goes after independence would be settled in London, and Doogan accepts Scotland would have no say in it once the system leaves Scottish waters. The rest of the case is his to make, and it comes down to a navy and air force built around the North Atlantic, five and a half billion a year spent on conventional defence, and a neighbour the alliance can rely on. On his own test, that is what Scotland would have to show over and above its geography. He says he has the plan to prove it, and he is waiting for the moment to publish it.
Doogan spent his career in defence engineering before entering Parliament in 2019 and has pushed conventional defence up the SNP’s agenda, work he describes as still in progress.

Planting hope in Samaria: A journey through vineyards, springs, and ancient history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:41:20 UTC
17:41:20 KST

We heard Jeremiah’s words three times on this trip: on Har Kabir, at Tura Winery, on Har Bracha (Mount Gerizim), and in a stone cellar beneath an organic farm at Givot Olam. Each time, the person quoting the verse was standing next to a vineyard planted within the last 25 years.
I write about healing tourism: places in Israel where people can heal the soul and refresh the body; places that can hold a couple, a family, or a group that has been through something hard. This time I brought my own family.
My wife Adi, our sons Lavie and Eitam, and I spent two days in Samaria, the Shomron, to see what the region offers a family that needs rest and open space. Since most people know Samaria only from headlines, I set myself one rule: listen to the people who live here, and let them tell the story of their land in their own words.
Two guides showed us the way. Lilian Zaitman from the tourism department of the Samaria Regional Council has lived in Kedumim for 44 years. Baruch Odeser, a field coordinator for the Council, has been guiding here for more than 15 years.
Twenty years ago, Baruch said, people in these communities drove out to work in the morning and came home only to sleep. Then local leaders saw that farming and tourism could carry the region, and wineries, farm shops, and coffee carts began to take root.
“What I have learned in Samaria is that agriculture and culinary culture are the path to bring outsiders from all walks of life and create meaningful connections,” Lilian told us. Almost every stop proved her right.
Our anchor on Har Kabir
Every good journey needs a base, and ours sat atop a mountain. Kabir Winery, on Har Kabir in Elon Moreh, close to 800 meters above sea level, brings a visitor center, a working winery, a dairy restaurant, and couples’ zimmers (guesthouses) together in a relatively large complex.
You park once, unpack once, and spend your days driving out to springs, farms, lookouts, and wineries. In the evening you return to vineyards, a cool mountain wind, and real quiet.
The zimmers are usually meant for couples: two dome-tent suites, each with its own jacuzzi or tub, a kitchenette with an espresso machine, and a private garden facing the vines. The complex is wheelchair accessible and ready for Shabbat-observant guests, with a synagogue a short walk away.
We had dinner at the winery’s kosher dairy restaurant, and the next morning a buffet breakfast, both built on fresh local produce and served on a wide terrace that overlooks the vineyards and down to the valley that reaches Nablus. On Fridays, from 9:00 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., the restaurant serves a rich brunch. We were not the only ones impressed.
On one Israeli booking site, every review of the zimmers gives a perfect score. One guest wrote that the Friday meal at the winery “would not shame a five-star hotel,” and another praised both the food and the hosts’ warmth and patience.
The complex is the life’s work of Itamar Weiss and his wife, Chani. They came to Elon Moreh 26 years ago as newlyweds. Itamar studied in yeshiva, but he wanted to connect people to the land the way his late grandfather had farmed it. When I asked what the mountain looked like when they arrived, he answered without hesitation.
“This mountain was bare. We came to no house, no tree, no vineyard, and no garden,” he said. “Today this mountain blossoms. We build houses and plant vineyards.”
They started with what they had. “We started small, with seven dunams. We took our wedding savings and put them straight into the ground,” Itamar said. “When I planted those vines, I knew I was starting to create a path that connects agriculture, wine and tourism.”
With his friend Eliab and a third partner, he now farms more than 150 dunams of wine grapes, plus table grapes in the Emek Tirza valley.
About the zimmers, he is clear: “My cabins are built specifically for a couple to come, disconnect, and recharge.”
The mountain itself is the main attraction. From the ridge, you look straight down into Emek Tirza, about 100 meters below sea level, a drop of roughly 900 meters, the sharpest change in height in the country. Kabir’s jeep and EasyRider tours cover it in about 15 minutes, past old stone terraces and wine presses cut into the rock thousands of years ago.
Nearby, a short, family-friendly trail of about 600 meters leads to the Mitzpe Kabir lookout and its ancient oaks.
Itamar hosts guests from all over Israel and abroad, including American groups several times a week, and he refuses to let Samaria be defined by hardship.
“There is a mistaken idea that if we talk about how hard things are, it will bring something good. It doesn’t,” he said. “The reality here is the exact opposite. It is pastoral, peaceful, and joyful. When people hear ‘Samaria,’ I want them to feel what they feel when they hear ‘the Golan.’”
More than 95% of his guests, he told us, leave saying they wish they could live there.
Croissants and a balcony over the country
Our first morning began further west, with breakfast at Atelier Florin, a new coffee cart and patisserie in Elei Zahav. It is named for the owner’s grandmother, whose portrait hangs inside and whose love of beauty and food shaped every hand-painted corner. Three months earlier, the plot was bare.
“Before this, there was nothing here, absolutely nothing,” we were told. Every Sunday, the team makes all of its dough from scratch.
Over coffee and homemade rich muffins, a regional representative explained how land is handled in western Samaria. It falls into three kinds, he said: survey land, state land, and private land. “Where it is private land, we obviously do not touch.”
A few minutes away, at Peduel, we stood on Mirpeset HaMedina, the Balcony of the State. Tel Aviv’s towers, Rosh Ha’ayin and, on a clear day, Hadera and Haifa University spread out below, while planes slid toward Ben-Gurion Airport. A visitor center with a glass-walled hall is rising over the ridge.
“Wellness arrives here naturally,” our host said. “It is a huge word, but here each person feels its unique qualities organically, through the crisp air, the open horizon, and the quiet space.”
Below, at the Byzantine ruins of Deir Qala, bereaved families and Duvdevan veterans build wooden benches in memory of friends who loved these hills.
Driving on toward Rehelim, Lilian told us how Professor Shivi Drori of Ariel University, founder of Gvaot Winery, studied ancient grape seeds to revive the region’s biblical grape.
“There used to be so many vineyards here,” she said. “Later, when the Muslims arrived and didn’t drink wine, they took out all the vines and planted olives. But Shivi succeeded in reaching the biblical grape.”
Ariel’s medical school, named for Dr. Moshe Leiter, a graduate who fell in Gaza, now has a rehabilitation department, so patients no longer have to travel all the way to Sheba Medical Center, Tel Hashomer.
Tura Winery: From an army tent to the world
Vered Ben Sa’adon was born in Holland. Her father’s mother survived the Holocaust. After her family converted and made aliyah, they laid roots in Kochav Hashahar, next door to the family of Erez, the man she would marry. She was 19, and he was 21. Like Itamar and Chani, they put their wedding money into the ground and bought 20 dunams of vines on Har Bracha.
After four years of orlah, when Jewish law forbids harvesting, wines made from their grapes won international awards. Then boycotts came, and outside wineries stopped buying grapes from Samaria. So Erez studied winemaking and became Tura’s winemaker, while Vered took over sales abroad and created her “Roza” rosé, named for her Dutch birth name.
Tura began in Rehelim inside an army shelter tent, curved like Noah’s Ark, with four barrels and 1,200 bottles. Today it makes nearly 280,000 bottles a year and exports half – to the United States, Europe, Dubai, and Australia. At 850 meters, the vines fight fog, heat, frost, and rocky soil.
“There is a saying that when the vine suffers, the grape excels,” our guide said. The tasting is slow on purpose: hold the stem, swirl, breathe, wait, all the way to the flagship Mountain Peak blend, aged 22 months in oak.
Clay and mud with Batya
On the hilltops of Itamar, Lilian brought us to Botz Bagiva, the ceramics studio of Batya Erdstein. Born to Yemenite parents who had moved to the United States, Batya is a nurse who made aliyah from San Diego 12 years ago. A decade ago, her husband gave her pottery tools, and her home studio began shipping Land of Israel designs to Jewish communities abroad.
Three months before our visit, she put her life savings into a large new workshop, built so that people with disabilities can take part too.
“We don’t rely on formal strategy. We operate on faith, prayer, and heart,” she said. The week before we came, groups of 40, 50, and 100 people arrived, all by word of mouth.
She sat the boys at the wheel. “Keep your elbows down on your knees, bring your hands together soft as butter, and let the wheel guide you,” she instructed gently. As the wet clay smoothed beneath their fingers, Batya looked out across the sweeping hilltop.
“For me, creating here is living a dream,” she reflected. “It’s the space, the heights, and the open horizon. It isn’t just physical – it spiritually expands the heart. Waking up at five in the morning to see the sunrise in this deep quiet – that is where real healing happens.”
She sees the hill itself as part of the lesson: “Taking clay out of earth that was once full of thorns and stones, and seeing with your own eyes that a couple with a few kids managed in 10 years to build something real on the map. It gives people so much inspiration.”
“Batya invested her soul, her best money, and her whole heart here,” Lilian said. When our plans shifted that afternoon, nobody minded. As someone in our group put it: “We just flow with it.”
The horseman of Itamar
In Itamar, Roy Mandelowitz built MRH Ranch, Mandelowitz Roy Horsemanship, “with my own 10 fingers.” A national champion in Extreme Cowboy Racing, he has worked with horses for more than 30 years. He grew up poor and with severe dyslexia.
“I was born into a very unhealthy environment and grew up among crime families,” he told us. “I know what horses gave me in my life. They saved me.”
At the recent national championships, Roy won bridleless riding, guiding his horse through obstacles with no reins, while his daughter took second among the youth. His 80-centimeter-deep arena footing was lab-tested to protect the horses’ joints.
“When we compete across the country, my team doesn’t just represent me. We represent Samaria,” he said. “There are so many stigmas out there. When people see the professionalism, skill, and sportsmanship coming out of Itamar, it breaks down barriers and shifts perceptions entirely.”
Trophies are not the point. “If I have a flag, a true core purpose for this place, it is working with youth at risk,” Roy said. Lone soldiers find a coffee corner with fresh-baked goods, and young people use his recording studio. For our boys, the ride was what Roy calls therapeutic tourism: “A deep inner journey.”
Cheese, coffee, and a cellar in the rock
Givot Olam, the organic farm Avri Ran founded on hilltop 851, is known across Israel for its free-range eggs and goat cheeses. At Cafe Shamayim, Sara served us organic yogurt, the farm’s cheeses, coffee, and fresh-baked goods. Everything here, even the small synagogue with its carved stone ark, is built from local stone.
“When Avri first started, people thought he was crazy,” Lilian said. “But he taught everyone what true sustainable agriculture means.”
Avri sat with us at a wooden table outside. When he arrived, he said the hill was bare rock and stone terraces, and he pointed to the old photographs on the walls and to Mark Twain’s account of the empty, desolate hills he crossed in the 1860s.
“People come with pre-packaged scripts,” he said, “but history and physical facts on the ground speak for themselves.”
Baruch put it even more plainly: “Here at Givot Olam I can tell you unequivocally: there was no Arab village here.” What the hills do hold, he explained, are ruins of ancient settlements, most likely from the Second Temple period.
A guide then led us to a rock-cut winepress and down stone stairs into a hand-carved wine cellar and a bell-shaped cistern that stays cool all year. “Over 2,000 ancient wine presses have been surveyed across these hills,” he said. Standing in the farm’s new organic vineyards, he told us, you are watching the prophecy come true in real time.
Givot Olam is also a place of mourning. Near the old wooden watchtower lies Or, a Duvdevan soldier who fell defending the country, buried on the hill among his family and comrades. Nearby, a young widow built a lookout for her husband, who fell in Gaza.
Sitting there, I told our hosts what I look for in my work: something deep and real, beauty in the people and the land, shared without judgment, without prejudice, and without politics.
A sanctuary in the vineyards
At Khan Ben Hakramim, Naomi Ronsky and her husband Moshe run air-conditioned Mongolian-yurt glamping built for recovery.
In holiday seasons, they give the whole site to one extended family at a time, up to 80 people. They have hosted families evacuated from Gush Katif, reservists, and wives of wounded soldiers. Groceries wait in the fridge on arrival, and a Sefer Torah sits in the main yurt so families can pray on site.
“Wellness isn’t just massage tables or saunas,” Naomi told us. “It’s a unit of reservists sitting together around a grill at night, talking through what they’ve experienced. It is giving people a place that can hold their story, give them air to breathe, and let them leave refreshed.”
Springs at dawn
Baruch drove us down white switchbacks into the Samaria Desert, past Wadi Atala, the path Jacob chose to Shechem so his flocks would not harm anyone’s crops. At the bottom lies Ein Fuka, also called Ma’ayan Arnon, a clear spring pool under a towering eucalyptus, on the ancient border between Ephraim and Manasseh. We picked wild figs straight from the branches.
“When you come down here early in the morning, you are completely alone with nature,” Baruch said. Gazelles and foxes come to drink.
Climbing out, we stopped at Mitzpe Matan, a lookout built by the father of Matan Zagron, a young officer killed in a 2002 terror attack. Below lay Nahal Tirza, where, Baruch said, the Israelites came up into the land under Joshua.
“You aren’t just looking at scenery,” he said. “You are looking at the gateway through which our ancestors entered the Land.”
The next morning at 7:00, mist still hung over Elon Moreh as we drank coffee with Baruch at Ein Kabir, a spring pool shaded by fig, willow, and mulberry trees. The local teenagers care for it, draining it once or twice a year and scooping out the mud by hand.
“When you keep a place truly clean, the next person who arrives feels hesitant to leave trash behind,” Baruch said. There are no lights at night. “Nighttime belongs to the animals.”
A kollel head from Bnei Brak once called him; until then, they had always gone to the Golan. Now haredi families come by the busload. To me, this is wellness at its simplest: a cold morning swim with your children and a ripe fig picked off the tree.
Where a nation was born
At the new Elon Moreh Heritage and Visitor Center, director Shira began with Abraham, whose first stop in the Land of Israel, she reminded us, was “the place of Shechem, unto the oak of Moreh,” in the valley below. She told us about archaeologist Adam Zertal’s discoveries on Mount Ebal and about the 1970s pioneers who tried eight times to settle here.
Quoting pioneer Menahem Felix, she said: “They put their head against the wall, and on the eighth time, the wall broke.” Lavie and Eitam lingered in front of Uri Sa’adya’s photographs of golden eagles, foxes, and gazelles on the cliffs just outside town. “The nature here is wild and breathtaking,” Shira said.
Our last stop was Mount Gerizim, the biblical Mount of Blessing, facing Mount Ebal across the valley of Shechem. On its summit lives the Samaritan community, about 850 people between here and Holon, who still write in ancient Hebrew script and carve their mezuzahs into stone.
Baruch shared a story from Yefet, longtime director of the Samaritan Museum, about his 90-year-old mother, who kept the full Yom Kippur fast against a doctor’s advice and came through it. We left with jars of Har Bracha tahini, made by Samaritan producers.
From the mountain we could see the vineyards of Tura and Kabir, where two young couples planted their wedding savings. A few ridges away, a nurse from San Diego shapes clay on faith, a horseman saved by horses teaches teenagers to ride, and a couple keeps a Torah scroll in a yurt so tired families can rest.
Jeremiah promised that the planters would plant and enjoy the fruit.
In Samaria, they are also setting a table and inviting the rest of us to sit down.
The writer is a travel photojournalist mapping Israel’s natural landscapes at the intersection of wellness, healing hospitality, and sustainable tourism. He was a guest of the places mentioned.

The gate of Eden: In Israel’s Valley of Springs, ancient history offers a new journey of healing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:41:14 UTC
17:41:14 KST

More than 1,700 years ago, the Talmudic sage Reish Lakish looked out over the Beit She’an basin and left a line the valley still lives by: “If the Garden of Eden is in the Land of Israel, its gate is Beit She’an.”
We came to see for ourselves, as a family, with our two boys: two nights, and a valley that seems to be made mostly of water.
Emek Hama’ayanot, the Valley of Springs, lies beneath the ridge of Mount Gilboa, inside the long scar of the Syrian-African Rift. About 40 natural springs rise here from deep underground, holding steady between 24 and 28 degrees Celsius in every season. Water is the reason people came, and the reason they stayed.
Under the Greeks and Romans, Beit She’an became Scythopolis, the leading city of the Decapolis, a league of 10 Greco-Roman cities, and the only one of them west of the Jordan River. Its builders turned spring water into public fountains, cascading staircases, and great heated baths. Long before anyone coined the phrase “wellness tourism,” this valley was practicing it.
What we found 2,000 years later is a region still in the business of healing: fish ponds returned to wetland, kitchens reopened by reservists home from war, and a holiday village that uses running water to quiet the world.
A village built to slow you down
Our base for both nights was Kama Resort, and it shaped everything that followed.
Its founder, Khen Shalem, never planned to be a hotelier. Trained as a physicist, he moved into filmmaking and won a Student Emmy Award for his short film Abe. After securing the film rights to Meir Shalev’s bestselling A Russian Novel (Roman Rusi), he realized that independent cinema in Israel would not pay its own way. Kama was meant to be a quiet business that would fund the screenplay.
Then the place took hold of him. Today, he says that even with a large budget in hand, he would put every resource back into Kama rather than return to a film set.
Shalem grew up on nearby Kibbutz Nir David, and Kama feels like a memory of that childhood. At its center is a wide green lawn in the spirit of the old kibbutz commons, framed by an avenue of trees. Every unit faces inward, toward the grass, the reflection pools, and the shallow wading pool. He kept the creative work in the valley. Architects Hava Pasder and Ami Dvir, of the firm Artista, drew the plans. Lilach Lempel designed the interiors. Visual artist Dana Stempler Asael photographed the rooms.
The valley is working farmland, and tractors start early. Instead of building walls, Shalem turned to the memory of his father, an archaeologist who studied the Roman water systems of this region and who passed away when Shalem was a boy. A stone aqueduct now runs across the grounds and spills into a waterfall over the wading pool. Its steady rush covers the sound of farm machinery and settles over the whole village like white noise.
The suites are unlike anything else in the valley: rounded vaults modeled on arched aircraft hangars, built with curved-steel Quonset engineering. To get them right, Shalem found Rami, an Israel Air Force veteran who spent his military career building these exact hangars. Inside, the ceiling curves overhead without a single hard angle, and the effect is one of shelter.
Each suite has 42 sq.m. of insulated living space and an 18-sq.m. private terrace. It sleeps up to six, with a double bed and two to four singles, a large bathroom with a walk-in shower, and a kitchenette with a refrigerator, microwave, and espresso machine. There are no televisions, by design. The idea is that you step outside and listen to the valley instead.
Even the safe rooms tell a story. Israeli law requires a fortified room, a mamad, and Shalem shaped Kama’s to echo the 1930s Tower and Stockade (Homa U’migdal) settlements, a nod to the nearby historical outposts of Tel Hashlosha and Migdal George.
Kama Resort has 23 units today, with zoning approval for up to 250. Its lawn can hold corporate retreats of 250 people and gatherings of up to 600. Many guests book their next stay before they check out. From here, the valley’s springs, nature reserves, ruins, and restaurants are all minutes away, and Kama guests receive benefits at leading local restaurants and attractions.
Dawn with the flock
Spring and summer in the valley set their own hours. If you want to be outside, you go at dawn.
At 6 a.m., with the sun rising crimson and gold over the mountains of Jordan, we arrived at Havat Nokdey Ruppin, known across the valley as Dir Balak, on the edge of Kibbutz Kfar Ruppin. Ile Shevach, with a background as an emotional therapist, runs the farm with her husband, Tsachi, its master cheesemaker. They built it as an educational farm as much as an agricultural one. The kibbutz children who work here, known as the “Dirnikim,” care for the young goats, handle daily chores, and set much of the barn’s rhythm.
We walked out to pasture with the herd, some 40 mothers and kids, and our two sons found their places on their own.
Eitam, seven, took the front. With a rough wooden staff in hand, he led the herd forward, steering it through body language, low calls, and small shifts in position. His small frame was a silhouette against the rising sun, and the flock moved with his steps. Lavie, 10, took the rear, and the farm’s puppies with it. He watched the ground, kept the pups watered as the heat climbed, and carried them when the desert thorns cut their paws.
Walking beside us, Shevach said that shepherding was humanity’s first school of leadership and responsibility. Animals read the person guiding them instantly: the anxiety, the hesitation, the calm. For a child to earn that trust from a flock, and to show that kind of care on rough ground, is a lesson no classroom can teach. Watching our boys that morning, I understood exactly what she meant.
The farm’s coffee truck was waiting when we came back: excellent espresso, warm, flaky pastries, and cheese made on site from the milk of the goats we had just walked across the fields. It was sharp and clean, with a trace of the wild herbs the herd grazes each morning. Animal, land and table, with nothing in between.
Water finding its way home
Our guide to the valley’s wild eastern edge, along the Jordanian border, was Chen Ravon Sherry, a ranger with the Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI). Her field is rewilding, a conservation approach that pulls back from heavy human intervention and lets natural processes repair damaged ecosystems on their own terms. By the end of our trip, her way of seeing had become the thread running through everything we experienced.
For decades, commercial fish ponds dominated this landscape. They broke up migration routes and disrupted the native springs. Under the Startup Nature campaign, Chen and the SPNI are reversing that, one careful step at a time. They clear old blockages and use gravity and the land’s natural slope to send spring water back into abandoned ponds. The result is a growing chain of wetlands that eventually returns clean water to the Jordan River.
The land has answered. Thick walls of reeds, sweet cane, and native plants have reclaimed the banks. Songbirds fill the air, and native fish move through water that feels untouched.
Along the border fence, the quiet is so complete that the loudest sounds are a fish breaking the surface and the wind in the reeds. That stillness has drawn combat veterans, civilians carrying the invisible wounds of war, and people living with severe PTSD. Many come to volunteer alongside the SPNI rangers, clearing stream paths, tracking wildlife, and checking water levels. It is slow, repetitive work under an open sky. With no sudden city noise and the constant presence of running water, frayed nervous systems slowly settle.
Winter transforms these ponds again. The valley sits on the great migration corridor linking Europe, Asia, and Africa, and ranks as the second most important bird-watching destination in Israel. Thousands of great white pelicans land here in tight formation, alongside black storks, glossy ibises, herons, and raptors riding the thermals off Mount Gilboa. Picture a January morning at the edge of a border pond, pelicans feeding in unison beneath the desert mountains. That is our next reporting trip.
The valley at the table
A landscape can’t fully restore you unless it feeds you too. Every table we sat at in this valley told a story of return: to the soil, home from the front lines, or straight into ancient stone.
Meshek Eliyahu, Moshav Beit Yosef: Our culinary journey began at this family-run farm restaurant, where chef Eliran Ishran cooks farm-to-table in the truest sense. For more than a decade, the family worked at the top of Israel’s competitive restaurant scene. When the war broke out, many of them were called up for months of reserve duty on the front lines, and came home wanting what mattered most: family, soil, and honest cooking.
The kitchen buys directly from valley farmers and has no fixed menu. Each day is built around what was harvested that morning from their own plots and neighboring farms. We ate charred root vegetables with raw tahini and local honey, crisp field greens, and slow-baked bread made from heirloom grains. Every plate felt alive.
Artichoke, at the foot of Mount Gilboa: Where the mountain meets the valley floor, Artichoke puts regional farming at the center of the plate. Artichokes, beets, and fresh herbs are the stars, cooked with real creativity. Children and adults can step off the patio straight into the fields and walk among the rows of crops, while the sheer cliffs of the Gilboa rise behind the tables. Readers who show this article receive a special discount through Yaniv.
Zoara Distillery (Jordan Spirits): Zoara was founded to solve an agricultural problem. Valley packing houses reject millions of kilograms of good dates every year for cosmetic flaws alone. Zoara rescues them, ferments and distills them into a clean, high-proof base, and then turns to the land for flavor: Mount Gilboa pine needles, local ashwagandha, mint, and lemon verbena. Its lineup revives the heirloom Yosef Effendi mandarin, which took silver at the 2024 London Spirits Competition, alongside a bright mulberry gin and Arak Mansour, aged three years in oak barrels in the valley heat. A glass here sums up Emek Hama’ayanot: taking what was discarded or scarred and making it whole again.
Dinner among the ruins
In Beit She’an’s old city, history isn’t behind glass. You eat beside it, and sometimes inside it.
Even Harosha: This wine bar and meat bistro carries one of the valley’s great stories of resilience. Its founder, Shimon Oshri, a retired IDF commander, spent most of his career leading elite units, including the Duvdevan unit. After leaving the army, he bought an old, grease-stained garage along the historical market streets, planning to turn it into a fine bistro.
His first day of construction was set for October 8, 2023. Instead, he went straight back into uniform and spent months commanding troops on the southern front. When he finally came home, he poured himself into finishing the space. He named it for the keystone that locks an arch together and dedicated it to his late mother, a beloved local kindergarten teacher for 42 years.
The setting is extraordinary. The dining room sits inside the moat that Crusader knights cut some 900 years ago to protect their fortress. Its walls are the original hand-cut basalt and limestone arches, softened by sleek industrial steel. The kitchen pairs premium meats with regional wines, but the dish already entering local lore is Shimon’s Schnitzel: huge, golden, wafer-thin, with an unbelievable crunch. It is comfort food raised to an art, and best eaten with a glass of crisp local wine.
Helena: For lunch, Helena gives the most honest taste of the town. It has the bustle of a beloved workers’ lunch spot, and it treats its food with real pride. Helena backs onto the ancient stone of the old quarter, steps from a 2,000-year-old Roman amphitheater where, in the golden age of Scythopolis, gladiators fought lions. The moment you sit down, the table fills with house-made salads, bright pickles, smoky grilled eggplant, and fiery chili sauces, followed by thin, crisp schnitzels and tender grilled meats. Fast, generous, and done with care, it’s easy to see why locals line up every afternoon.
That amphitheater has never been excavated. The region holds so much history that the Israel Antiquities Authority has left it as it is, wild and silent under the brush. To trace the stone gates where fighters and lions once entered the arena, from your seat at a lunch table, is an experience no museum can offer.
Basilia: For dinner, we went to Basilia, an upscale dairy and Italian restaurant. The kitchen works closely with local growers, so the menu shifts with the valley’s harvests: pasta rolled by hand each day, wood-fired pizzas with blistered, airy crusts, and garden salads built around artisanal valley cheeses. The service is warm, but the real magic is on the open terrace, where the night breeze moves through wheat fields that stretch into the dark. Here, fine dining and fertile earth share the same breath.
The city beneath the city
Early one morning, before the gates opened to the public, we walked Beit She’an National Park with its longtime director, Nissim Bados. He has spent about 40 years excavating and preserving this site. He first arrived in 1986 as a young student, when a large government project brought 450 local workers to the dig to fight unemployment in the region.
Few cities on earth, Nissim told us, can match Beit She’an’s unbroken record: nearly 7,000 years of continuous settlement, with 20 layers of civilization stacked on the central tel alone, from the Chalcolithic through the Canaanite, Egyptian, and Persian eras. The valley’s soil was so fertile it was said to yield seventy times the seed sown.
Under the Greeks and Romans, the city was reborn as Scythopolis, named, as Nissim tells it, for Scythian horsemen from the cold steppes who settled here for the water despite the summer heat. It became the capital of the Decapolis and a crossroads between the Mediterranean and the East. As we walked the great stone avenues of the Cardo and the Decumanus, Nissim pointed to the spot where his team found 32 perfectly preserved gold coins buried beneath fallen columns.
The whole city was built as a celebration of water. Stone aqueducts carried millions of cubic meters from the valley’s springs into public fountains and down monumental staircases. The western bathhouse alone spread over more than seven dunams, warmed by a hypocaust heating system beneath the floors. Wellness, it turns out, was always a pillar of civilization here.
Scythopolis also feels unusually real. Its Roman theater, with remarkable acoustics, is more than 90% original stone, unlike the heavily reconstructed ruins at Caesarea. And what visitors see today, Nissim explained, is only 7%-8% of the ancient city’s 1,700 dunams. The rest lies under the valley floor, frozen as it stood on January 18, 749 CE, when an earthquake leveled the city in seconds. There is enough buried city left, he says, for another 90 years of digging.
Standing in that empty theater as the morning light climbed the stone, I thought back to Chen’s ponds, to water slowly finding its way home to the Jordan. Reish Lakish called this valley the gate of Eden. Two thousand years on, the springs are still running, and the valley is still restoring the people who walk through it.
The writer is a travel photojournalist mapping Israel’s natural landscapes at the intersection of wellness, healing hospitality, and sustainable tourism. He was a guest of the places mentioned.

Controversy erupted in the Kfar Ganim neighborhood of Petah Tikva on Friday, with several synagogues reportedly refusing to host Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich amid objections to political activity during religious services.
According to residents and congregants in the neighborhood, numerous synagogues declined requests to host Smotrich or allow him to address worshippers. Others agreed to welcome the minister, including one synagogue where the decision to let him speak sparked a heated dispute among congregants.
Organizers of the visit told Maariv that Smotrich is expected to visit approximately 10 synagogues across Petah Tikva that invited him to speak. They acknowledged that several synagogues had requested that politics be kept out of their services and would therefore not be included in the itinerary.
The organizers nevertheless emphasized that Smotrich was visiting one of Petah Tikva's liberal strongholds and was receiving a warm welcome from local residents.
Among the synagogues reportedly excluded from the itinerary were Young Israel, Heichal Gavriel, Ohel Yitzhak, and Nigunei Chaim.
Numerous failed efforts to convince synagogues to host Smotrich, sources say
Sources familiar with the arrangements claimed that their absence was not coincidental. According to the sources, efforts had been made to coordinate Smotrich's visit, but numerous synagogues refused to host him. They also claimed the opposition left Smotrich with the option to address residents in a public garden in the afternoon.
The controversy intensified over the decision to allow Smotrich to speak at one of the synagogues, with some congregants arguing that political activity had no place during prayer services, particularly with Israel in the midst of an election campaign.
One congregant opposed the appearance, writing, "Politicians should not be brought into a synagogue."
Another questioned the decision, writing, "Why bring division into the synagogue at all? Why? Who exactly does this serve?"
Others questioned whether the visit was intended to deliver a religious message or advance Smotrich's political interests.
One message challenged the stated purpose of the appearance, reading, "Let's not pretend otherwise; he's not coming to deliver a Torah teaching, even if that's how it's presented. He's engaging in politics on Shabbat, and we need to ask the rabbi whether he's even allowed to do that, because it's work for him."
Several congregants oppose withdrawing Smotrich's invitation to speak
However, not all congregants supported canceling the appearance. Some argued that withdrawing the invitation after it had already been extended and publicly announced would be inappropriate, particularly since the synagogue had hosted other speakers in the past.
They also warned that canceling the event at this stage could be seen as a personal insult to Smotrich.
One congregant raised concerns about the embarrassment that withdrawing the invitation could cause, writing, "There's also the issue of publicly humiliating someone. After it's already been announced everywhere that he will speak at our synagogue, preventing it is a form of insult."
As the disagreement continued, some congregants proposed a compromise that would separate political activity from religious services. Under the proposal, Smotrich would speak in the synagogue hall outside prayer times, allowing only those interested to attend.
The dispute remained unresolved ahead of Shabbat, with some congregants insisting that politics should be kept out of synagogues, while others argued that once an invitation had been extended and publicly announced, it should not be withdrawn.

Murder in Malaysia: Justice for Altantuya Shaariibuu

Pro-Palestinian protesters demand cancellation of Israeli dance performance at Madrid theater

2026-10-17

17:40:46 KST

Approximately 200 pro-Palestinian protesters gathered outside the Teatros del Canal theater in Madrid on Thursday night to protest a performance by Israel's Batsheva Dance Company.
The demonstrators waved Palestinian flags and displayed a large banner reading in Spanish, "Israel dances while it kills in Gaza." They called for a boycott of the company and demanded that its performances be canceled. Some shouted "Murderers" and "Shame on you" at audience members arriving at the theater.
Despite the demonstration, the performance went ahead as planned and, according to the Israeli Embassy in Spain, ended with a standing ovation.
Batsheva is performing Sadeh21, a work by Israeli choreographer Ohad Naharin, as part of a three-show engagement in Madrid scheduled for October 15, 16, and 17 at the theater's Concha Velasco auditorium.
The opening performance took place Thursday night, with two additional shows scheduled for Friday and Saturday. Spanish media reports say all three performances sold out.
Prominent Spanish choreographer, actress join protests
Among the demonstrators was prominent Spanish choreographer and dancer Nacho Duato, who had previously called for Batsheva's performances to be canceled in social media posts.
Duato argued that while Russian dance companies faced boycotts after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, an Israeli company receiving public funding was invited to perform in Madrid.
Spanish actress Goizalde Núñez also joined the protest, while filmmaker Javier Fesser criticized the funding for the performances.
Duato sparked further controversy after a video circulated on social media in which he described Hamas as a "liberation movement" and refused to classify it as a terrorist organization.
The Israeli Embassy in Spain responded sharply on Thursday, posting on X/Twitter that Duato was leading the boycott against Batsheva while supporting Hamas, the terrorist organization responsible for the October 7, 2023, massacre in southern Israel.
On Friday, the embassy issued another statement congratulating Batsheva on the success of its opening performance, the standing ovation it received, and the fact that all three shows had sold out.
Meanwhile, a different response emerged from the dance academy that bears Duato's name.
Following Thursday's performance, the academy posted a photograph on Instagram showing its students alongside Batsheva dancers. It thanked the Israeli company for an unforgettable evening and called for peace, mutual respect, and continued artistic cooperation.
The academy's message contrasted with Duato's public calls to boycott the performances.
The demonstration was organized by the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement and pro-Palestinian solidarity groups, which argued that the Israeli government's financial support for Batsheva made the company a tool for promoting Israel's image abroad.
The theater's workers' committee also opposed hosting the Israeli company.
Theater director rejects protesters' demands, says program not political
However, the theater's director, Ruperto Merino, rejected demands to cancel the performances, saying decisions about the artistic program were based on professional, not political, considerations.
Merino said the theater would not censor artistic works based on their creators' country of origin.
Batsheva, one of Israel's most internationally recognized dance companies, told the Spanish newspaper El País that it is not a political organization and that its members hold differing views.
A spokesperson for the company said Batsheva had publicly called for a ceasefire, the release of the hostages, and an end to the bloodshed in Gaza since October 7.
She also emphasized that Naharin has opposed the Israeli occupation for years and has been a vocal critic of Israeli government policies.
According to the spokesperson, Batsheva is accustomed to facing protests outside its performance venues and knows how to handle them without being drawn into confrontations.
She added that previous Israeli governments had attempted to cut the company's funding because of its political positions, stressing that public funds belong to citizens, not the government.
The protests in Madrid come approximately two weeks after the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) published an extensive study on October 1 titled State of the Arts, documenting what it described as the widespread and systematic exclusion of Jewish, Israeli, and Zionist artists from cultural industries across the United States.
The study examines incidents involving music, dance, theater, film, literature, publishing, museums, and the visual arts.
One chapter, titled "Dark Stage," documents 65 incidents at 41 locations across the United States in which Jewish and Israeli performing artists faced protests, harassment, disruptions to performances, or cancellations.
Batsheva is specifically mentioned in the report, alongside Jewish singer Matisyahu and the Israel Philharmonic Orchestra.
Similar incidents have also targeted Jewish comedian Jerry Seinfeld, whose performance in Chicago was recently disrupted by pro-Palestinian activists.
Seinfeld has faced protests over the past three years amid criticism of his support for Israel and the sympathy he has expressed for victims of the October 7 massacre.
In May 2024, dozens of students walked out of Duke University's commencement ceremony in protest as Seinfeld delivered a speech. In August, the ADL documented a campaign calling for the cancellation of his Washington performances.
Singer Regina Spektor has also faced heckling during a performance, while comedian Judy Gold was subjected to antisemitic shouts on stage.
These incidents are among a growing number of reported boycotts and protests targeting Jewish and Israeli performers.
According to the ADL, however, some of the most concerning forms of discrimination occur away from public view.
ADL CEO Jonathan Greenblatt said when the study was published that discrimination extends beyond public demonstrations to decisions made behind the scenes by cultural institutions, publishers, and event organizers.
The organization warned that Jewish artists are being pushed out of American cultural life, blacklisted, and denied professional opportunities.
The ADL also highlighted a phenomenon it described as "silent boycotts," in which invitations are quietly withdrawn, performances are never scheduled, collaborations are abandoned, and cultural institution directors are reluctant to hire Israeli or Jewish artists associated with Israel.
Israeli singer Noga Erez, for example, has said she lost opportunities to perform abroad because she is Israeli.
The report also describes cases in which authors were asked to remove Hebrew words from their work, change the Jewish names of characters, or avoid setting their stories in Israel to improve their chances of publication.
In the visual arts sector, 12 of the 40 leading museums examined in the United States received the ADL's lowest rating because of shortcomings in their policies and representation of Jews.
None of the 40 museums surveyed explicitly included Jewish identity in their diversity and inclusion commitments.

“The investigation must establish the facts, including who initiated the violence,” the office said.
“We will not allow disputed incidents to be exploited to demonize the hundreds of thousands of law-abiding Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria,” it added.
Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot responded to the confrontation, saying in a post on X, “We condemn criminal violence and call for the investigation and prosecution of those “This handful of rioters does not represent the public in Israel,” Eisenkot said. “The actions of this handful stain an entire nation and severely harm the security of all Israeli citizens and IDF fighters.”
'Hell for us': Palestinian mayor describes the incident
Nazem Saleh Shuman, the mayor of Abu Falah adjacent to the site of the violence, also reacted to the incident, telling The New York Times that, “This place became unlivable.”
“This is a residential place, where the people live next to their fields, next to their land.”
“But it's become a hell for us,” he added.
“This is our land, we were born here, our ancestors came from here, and we've lived here all our lives,” he added. “We believe in this place, and we take care of it. We have nowhere else to go.”
The NYT cited numbers from Israeli human rights group Yesh Din, which monitors settler violence, which said it had documented 82 violent incidents against olive harvesters, 135 instances of crop theft and 39 cases of damage to or destruction of trees.
The investigation into the Abu Falah confrontation was ongoing as officials and lawmakers called for those responsible to be identified and held accountable on Saturday.
The Mateh Binyamin Regional Council, which administers Israeli settlements in the area, blamed the Palestinian Authority for the confrontation.
The council said the Palestinian Authority had “led hundreds of anarchists and terrorists into a direct confrontation with Israelis near Abu Falah, all under the cover of the olive harvest.”
"Footage from the scene shows terrorists launching fireworks directly at people and hurling stones at Israelis, while journalists stand behind them, documenting this deliberate provocation," it said.
The council also alleged that the PA orchestrated the incident, claiming PA patrol vehicles were present at the scene.
The council said clashes between Israelis and Palestinians had eventually been dispersed by Border Police officers and that several activists had been injured.
Levine describes being kicked and having equipment taken
Levine, a veteran photojournalist who was covering the olive harvest, said she was knocked to the ground and repeatedly kicked during the confrontation by masked and hooded attackers.
The identity of the attackers remains unknown as an investigation into the incident continues.
“After about 10 minutes, they tried to make me get up; they pushed me back to the ground and continued kicking me,” she said.
“I tried to hold on to my cameras and my side bag, but in the end they just ripped everything from me and kept kicking me,” she added.
Levine underwent surgery on Saturday on a finger on her left hand that was nearly severed in a settler attack in the West Bank on Friday.
Her daughter, Ashley Milner, told the Associated Press that the finger was severed to the bone, leaving a tendon exposed. Levine also suffers from a broken rib, fractures to several vertebrae, and cuts throughout her body, the daughter said.
Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray condemned the incident in a statement reported by N12 News, saying Levine wore visible identification marks that clearly identified her as a journalist.
“We are appalled by this unjustified attack on a journalist who was doing her job,” Murray said. “We call on the authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and act on its findings.”
The US Embassy in Jerusalem told N12 that it was aware of the incident and was monitoring the situation.

Nearly one in five children in Switzerland at risk of poverty
Some 114,000 children in Switzerland are affected by poverty in Switzerland and another 315,000 children are at risk of poverty. Children from single-parent households and large families are particularly at risk.
The Swiss Network for Children’s Rights is therefore calling for a national strategy to combat child poverty.
In a press release, the Swiss Network for Children’s Rights states that child poverty not only affects living standards but also impairs educational, developmental, and health opportunities as well as social participation. It therefore calls for binding targets and systematic performance reviews, a separate child-specific component in the National Poverty Monitoring System, and nationwide minimum standards for family benefits.
+ Swiss drama unmasks the country’s invisible working poor
However, the statement noted that the support a family receives currently depends on the canton of residence and residency status. A national strategy is therefore needed as a solution instead of a patchwork of cantonal benefits.
According to the press release, other key children’s rights in Switzerland are still not being satisfactorily implemented five years after the recommendations of the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child. The child rights impact assessment is limited to a mere mention in the message guidelines, and key data gaps persist such as those regarding children placed outside their families or the reasons for child protection measures.
According to the network, the shortfall is most evident in the Ombudsman’s Office for Children’s Rights. Parliament had already issued a clear mandate for this in 2020, and during the consultation process, a clear majority also spoke out in favor of an independent body that advises children individually and mediates when necessary. However, the federal government is “sticking to a watered-down solution that omits precisely these elements”.

Language matters in Hong Kong’s birth rate debate, not just money
Hong Kong’s fertility woes are not just about affordability. They might also involve language use and how it shapes our views of the future
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
Dr Zhisheng (Edward) Wen is an associate division head and senior lecturer in the College of Professional and Continuing Education at Hong Kong Polytechnic University, where he researches and teaches second language acquisition, translanguaging and cognitive science. 
When Hong Kong debates how to raise its birth rate, the conversation usually revolves around money: bigger baby bonuses, tax concessions, housing support, cheaper childcare and so on. These economic measures are necessary. Lowering the cost of raising a child removes some real and immediate barriers.
However, there is another, lesser-known factor that works more subtly and implicitly. It comes not from economics but from the structure of the language or languages we speak each day.
Consider a simple contrast. In English, one says, “Yesterday it rained. Now it is raining. Tomorrow it will rain.” In Chinese, the same three sentences need no such grammatical marking. The verb does not change. The future is not grammatically separated from the present.
