Israeli raids and arrests in southern Syria push population to the brink
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:17:06 UTC
16:17:06 KST

Israeli raids and arrests in southern Syria push population to the brink
Survivors recount brutal prison conditions, enduring beatings, restraints, and psychological abuse by Israeli soldiers.
Qatana, Syria – In the living room of his home, Ahmed explains in a low voice how he was beaten and tortured in an Israeli prison after he was arrested at a checkpoint the Israeli military had set up on the street in his village in Syria.
“They stopped me, they asked for my name, asked where I’m from,” he says. “I gave my name and village. They said, ‘You need to come with us for five minutes, and we’ll bring you back.'”
He says he then spent more than one year detained in Israel. For 90 days, he was in handcuffs and describes being thrown to the cell floor, beaten with sticks while restrained with his hands behind his back.
“They tighten the cuffs by stamping on them with their feet, until the cuffs bite into the flesh of your wrists and also your buttocks. Sometimes they leave them tightened like this for one or two days until your hands are extremely swollen. Your hands go green, and you can’t feel them at all.”
After his release this month, dozens of people gathered outside his home to congratulate him on his return, and to seek any scrap of information about their own relatives who are still missing. Al Jazeera has ascertained that there are at least 51 Syrians still detained inside Israel. Many were held in the notorious Sde Teiman military prison, but have since been transferred to facilities run by the Israel Prison Service. Al Jazeera has confirmed Syrians have been moved to Ofer, al-Jalama (Kishon) and Megiddo. A small number have been released.
The impact is ongoing. Mahmoud – a pseudonym – had been home for nine days when Al Jazeera interviewed him. “Until now I feel unstable; I’m not normal. I feel crazy sometimes in the night. I go to look at my kids because I can’t believe I’m really home.”
Mahmoud pauses as his six-year-old son carries in a tray of wobbling tea glasses and sets it carefully on the carpeted floor. The glasses clink, and the window shakes. The children turn their heads towards the sound of artillery. Since early August, the Israeli military has fired shells into the fields most days, preventing farmers and shepherds from working, occasionally killing livestock and regularly terrifying the population. In September, the Sijil Center, a Syrian organisation that monitors Israeli activity, documented 280 Israeli violations of the 1974 agreement between the two countries, including incursions, raids and arrests, as well as artillery and machine-gun fire.
UN forces have patrolled a demilitarised zone between the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights and the rest of Syria since the 1974 agreement, but Israel occupied more Syrian land in the immediate aftermath of the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime in December 2024. The peacekeepers remain, but have limited capacity to restrain Israeli military activity, which continues to increase.
In one incident in late August, two Israeli tanks and five other armoured vehicles descended from one of their hilltop bases and blocked the only access road to United Nations Disengagement Observer Force base 37, near the village of Jubata al-Khashab. A man who works for the local council called the UN base, which houses a peacekeeping mission established in 1974 to maintain the Israeli-Syrian ceasefire, and asked if they needed assistance.
“I think they were offended,” he laughed. “And they told me ‘, No, stay where you are; don’t you or anybody else come down here. We’ll call for help from another base if we need it.'”
UNDOF confirmed to Al Jazeera that the movement of their personnel continues to be “restricted on occasion” by the Israeli military, and that Israel’s practice of setting up roadblocks and checkpoints is “preventing UNDOF from conducting its planned and mandated patrol activities”.
Residents sometimes seek help from peacekeepers when people are detained at checkpoints, but there is little they can do about the midnight raids.
Mahmoud was detained at 3:30am when Israeli troops surrounded his home, calling for him by name and brandishing a photo of him from social media. Nine days after his release, he crouches, kneeling and pressing his forehead to the ground with his hands behind his head.
“They make us sit like this for hours,” he says, noting that he ended up with infected wounds on his knees from the cell floor. He has scars on his wrists and ankles from being restrained.
“They cuff you so you can’t move and then release the dogs,” he says. “They have muzzles on, but they ran into us, like a body slam.” The metal muzzles, he explains, made the impact stronger and caused bleeding.
“I want to tell you about the ‘disco room’,” he says. “It’s a room full of speakers; they put detainees in there, and the music is very loud.” He described seeing Syrian, Palestinian and Lebanese prisoners throwing up when they were allowed out.
Mahmoud was never charged, and says he does not know why he was released. He says that he was never granted access to a lawyer throughout his detention. The Red Cross has been denied access to detainees in Israeli detention since October 7, 2023, the date of the Hamas-led attack on Israel and the start of Israel’s subsequent genocidal war on Gaza.
“They make sure you understand the moment you enter that you are stripped of all your rights; they tell you this explicitly.”
Al Jazeera has contacted the Israeli military for comment, but has yet to receive a response. Israel says that its occupation of Syrian land and incursions deeper into Syria are necessary for security reasons, and to defend Syria’s Druze community, which it says is threatened by the authorities in Syria – a claim the Syrian government rejects.
Detained without charge
Ahmed was bewildered by this treatment. He told Al Jazeera that he was not even questioned until nearly five months into his detention. He was asked whether he, or anyone he knew, was a member of Hezbollah, Hamas, ISIL (ISIS) or a list of other armed groups which had little in common and fought on opposite sides during the war in Syria.
Mohammed Seyyed was detained in 2025. Israeli troops had conducted an incursion the previous day, wreaking destruction on his home and farm. He, his son, his brother and his nephew had gone to make repairs when they were detained and taken into Israel. He was brought to the interrogation room bound and blindfolded. When an Israeli officer freed his eyes, they showed him maps and photographs of his home and neighbourhood.
“Even the barber who cuts my hair, they knew his name, his address,” he said. “They were letting me know they knew everything about me. That any question they might ask, they already knew the answer and would know if I was lying.”
But when the questions came, they were general. The Israeli officers seemed to know everything about him, except what he was accused of. Mohammed told Al Jazeera that one of the officers admitted he had been detained based on false information, which he attributed to reports made by those in his community who inform for Israel.
A community under siege
The fallout of Israeli military activity is wide-ranging. Impromptu checkpoints mean many residents are afraid to leave their homes. Road closures have an impact long after the Israeli soldiers leave: students who need to travel for university consider relocating to Damascus to guarantee they can attend classes, and people with health conditions worry about being blocked from reaching care.
The Syrian government is in a difficult position; Israel has blocked its forces from operating in the south, and it doesn’t have the military strength to confront its neighbour even if the authorities wished to. Instead, they have been attempting to negotiate a security agreement, but talks have largely stalled since the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran.
Residents are losing patience and have begun to protest. In Qatana, local sheikhs gathered after Friday prayers.
“They tested our patience in Daraa,” said Sheikh Mamdouh Tahhan, referring to an incident in Abidin where locals confronted Israeli troops. “As a state we don’t have the ability to get into a war with Israel, but as people we are ready.”
The families of some of those detained feel abandoned by their government. They complain about the lack of legal or financial assistance, noting that with their breadwinners missing, they have run up debts worth hundreds of dollars at local grocery stores.
The families have created a WhatsApp group to exchange news and information, sometimes looking for signs in a sky that is heavy with the sound of Israeli warplanes flying low, and the persistent buzz of a surveillance drone. “From the morning I’ve been listening, and I’ve been hearing the drone,” one mother says. “I have a hunch that because the drone is up, maybe there will be a release today.”
For several weeks in a row, people were released on Wednesdays. It has become a day of pained anticipation. Hassan Ahmed’s son, then 16, was taken into Israel in April 2025. Israeli troops razed his 400 olive trees shortly after. He has become pivotal in organising protests and hunting for information along with the other parents – in October, Israeli forces raided his farm again, destroying solar panels. Sitting on his balcony, the late afternoon sun filtering through the leaves of a walnut tree, he plays voice notes from other parents that land every minute or so.
“Since this morning, any message that pings on the phone, any new notification I check, hoping somebody has been released,” another mother explains. “Our hearts are on fire. We’re waiting.”
“I’m full of grief,” Hassan says, putting the phone down. “I’ll never be able to describe the pain, it’s very tough. Even trying to describe it makes my heart tighten. I feel like my heart will stop. I feel I will explode.”

Feature: Family memories bring Vietnamese general's Long March legacy to life
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:16:07 CST
16:16:07 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 1, 2026 shows a sculpture and a portrait of Vietnamese general Hong Shui in Hanoi, Vietnam. (Xinhua/Liu Ying)
HANOI, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- For the family of Vietnamese general Hong Shui, known in Vietnam as Nguyen Son, the Long March in China is a journey they never witnessed, yet one that has lived on through stories about the man who walked it.
Between 1934 and 1936, the Red Army, led by the Communist Party of China (CPC), trekked up to 12,500 km to break through the encirclement of Kuomintang forces, a journey later known as the Long March.
Hong Shui joined the CPC in 1927 at the age of 19 and dedicated himself to the Chinese revolution.
He was later conferred the rank of general by both Vietnam and China, becoming the sole foreign national to be commissioned as a general of the Chinese People's Liberation Army after the founding of the People's Republic of China -- a distinction that earned him the revered title of "two-nation general."
Among the stories passed down in the family is one about a belt that was boiled and eaten when food ran short, a detail that has come to symbolize the hardships Hong Shui and his comrades endured.
When Hong Shui set out on the Long March in October 1934, food and water were scarce, and the rugged terrain and punishing weather added to the hardships.
"He crossed the snow mountains three times. Sometimes he traveled on horse and sometimes on foot, without warm clothing," recalled Nguyen Mai Lam, his fourth daughter, born in 1948.
Lam also remembered how her father described the odyssey in a poem when speaking to trainees at a military school in Vietnam's central province of Thanh Hoa in 1948.
"Many comrades sacrificed their lives
Blood reddened the snow
Blood flowed and turned into fire
Lighting the road of the Long March," she recited.
Her younger sister Nguyen Thanh Ha, born in 1949, lived with their father in China from age one until his death when she was seven.
Though she could not recall details of the Long March, she remembered his stories about Chinese comrades and ordinary families who helped him during the revolutionary years.
"My father had very warm feelings toward the Chinese people," she said, recounting how he frequently spoke of the close bonds among them, describing the relationships as "almost as if they were family."
That sense of connection has also shaped the younger generations.
For his great-grandson Nguyen Minh Quan, Hong Shui's experience has become a source of strength.
"The difficulties and hardships I face are nothing compared with what General Hong Shui experienced during the Long March," Quan said.
Remembering his great-grandfather's experiences gives him confidence and courage to move forward, he added.
Quan said inheriting his great-grandfather's legacy also means putting the greater good and justice ahead of small personal interests.
The family has sought to keep that legacy alive by publishing more than 10 books about the general and working with the Chinese Embassy in Vietnam this year to republish a photo book.
It also maintains the Nguyen Son-Hong Shui two-nation general scholarship fund, providing scholarships for excellent Vietnamese students learning Chinese and students from disadvantaged backgrounds.
Two years ago, Quan traveled to Beijing to donate his great-grandfather's handwritten poetry notebook to a Chinese museum, keeping a copy to preserve as a family heirloom.
"I'm trying to promote the story of General Nguyen Son so that what he contributed during his lifetime to the revolutions of Vietnam and China will live on," he said. ■

Vocational education supplies nearly 10 mln skilled workers annually in China: white paper
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
15:15:34 CST
16:15:34 KST

The White Paper on Vocational Education in China is released during the closing ceremony of the World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference in Tianjin, north China, Oct. 17, 2026. The conference closed here on Saturday. (Xinhua/Zhao Zishuo)
TIANJIN, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- In recent years, China's vocational education system has provided an annual average of almost 10 million skilled personnel to various industries, according to a white paper released on Saturday.
The white paper on China's vocational education was issued at the 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference in Tianjin Municipality in north China, which ran from Thursday to Saturday this week.
The white paper revealed that the average length of education among China's newly added skilled personnel had reached 14.35 years.
In 2025, 5.82 million students graduated from higher vocational education institutions, while nearly 5.22 million graduated from secondary vocational schools, the white paper said.
China has the world's largest vocational education system, with 9,151 secondary vocational schools, 1,554 higher vocational colleges and 124 vocational undergraduate institutions.
Higher vocational institutions account for more than half of the country's higher education institutions. In addition, 52 regular higher education institutions offer vocational undergraduate programs.
As of the end of 2025, China's catalog of vocational education majors covered 19 major categories, 97 categories and 1,491 majors, spanning virtually all sectors of the national economy and all 41 major industrial categories.
At the Tianjin conference's closing ceremony, the Framework of World Vocational and Technical Education Standards, the development of which was led by China, was jointly released by 45 countries.
The framework calls for improving vocational school systems, establishing a lifelong education and training system for all, developing teaching materials through industry-education collaboration, building teaching teams via school-enterprise partnerships, and using AI to drive reform in education and teaching.
Four national standards for Luban Workshops, proposed by China's Ministry of Education, were also unveiled at the closing ceremony.
They cover development requirements, teaching equipment requirements and operational quality assessment, among others. These standards will take effect on April 1, 2027.
Luban Workshops are overseas vocational education projects jointly established by Chinese and foreign educational institutions, offering academic programs and skills training.
China has established 38 Luban Workshops in 32 countries, which have provided academic education to more than 30,000 students and skills training to over 160,000 participants. ■

Huge queues at the border with Poland amid air raid alerts: trucks are waiting for up to two days

Unknown Publisher

Huge queues at the border with Poland amid air raid alerts: trucks are waiting for up to two days
Kyiv • UNN
In Dorohusk, the queue reached 900 trucks on October 16, with a waiting time of around 40 hours. Border crossing operations are suspended during air raid alerts.
Huge queues have been recorded at Poland's border with Ukraine. Border crossing points suspend operations during alerts related to Russian airstrikes on Ukraine. Poland's PAP news agency reported this on October 16, UNN writes.
Details
The waiting time for trucks at the Dorohusk border crossing is reportedly almost two days, while at Hrebenne it is about two days. Traffic usually increases on weekends and holidays, but border crossing points also suspend operations during alerts.
Michał Derus, a spokesperson for the Chamber of Tax Administration in Lublin, said that on Friday, October 16, truck drivers had to wait about 40 hours to leave Poland through the border crossing with Ukraine in Dorohusk. The estimated waiting time at the other border crossing in Hrebenne is 25 hours.
The spokesperson noted that queues at border crossings usually grow ahead of weekends and holidays. Friday is the day when traffic and the number of vehicles waiting to leave can increase by several dozen percent, the publication notes.
Recently, additional disruptions have been caused by frequent Russian airstrikes in western Ukraine, which are warned about in alerts sent to local residents and government officials.
These alerts require the suspension of customs clearance and, if necessary, evacuation. Evacuations have occurred less frequently recently, but the number of alerts leading to the suspension of customs clearance in Dorohusk and Hrebenne may range from several to dozens during a twelve-hour shift, the publication indicates.
The spokesperson for the Chamber of Tax Administration in Lublin explained that these breaks usually last from a dozen to several dozen minutes, but if there are, for example, around ten of them during a single shift, the total suspension of customs clearance may last up to several hours.
He said that although border guards may and do carry out various customs clearance procedures during an alert, vehicles cannot leave the border crossing area because a special air-threat regime is in effect in Ukraine. "Ukraine, of course, no longer accepts vehicles at that time," he added.
According to border guards, approximately 900 trucks were waiting in line in the afternoon of October 16 to leave Poland through the border crossing in Dorohusk. "The queue is very long. It starts even before Chełm. We estimate that it will take about two days to clear the vehicles through customs," Derus added.
It was estimated that 250 trucks were waiting in line to cross the border in Hrebenne.

U.S. Army takes drone killers to Africa for testing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:14:24 UTC
16:14:24 KST

- The U.S. Army will test up to 15 counter-drone and force protection systems in Tan-Tan, Morocco, in early 2027, aiming to field winners within 180 days.
- Soldier-led demonstrations in February and March will be followed by an operational assessment during African Lion 2027 in April and May.
The U.S. Army plans to test up to 15 counter-drone and base protection systems in Morocco next spring and aims to get the ones that work into soldiers’ hands within 180 days, under a new fast-track effort run by its Africa-focused command and a rapid acquisition team.
U.S. Army Southern European Task Force, Africa, known as SETAF-AF, is teaming with the service’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate, or G-TEAD, on what they call an accelerated capability event. The first one will take place in Tan-Tan, in southern Morocco, and will focus on protecting early-entry command posts and small operating locations from Group 1 to Group 3 drones, a range that runs from hand-launched quadcopters to unmanned aircraft weighing several hundred kilograms.
Soldiers will put the candidate systems through demonstrations in Tan-Tan in February and March 2027. The systems will then go through an operational assessment in April and May during African Lion 2027, U.S. Africa Command’s largest joint military exercise on the continent, which Morocco co-hosts each year.
G-TEAD plans to validate up to 15 solutions, with the U.S. Army’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Fires lined up as the office that would take the winning systems into wider service.
“The ACE is structured around five capability categories,” said U.S. Army Maj. Katlin VanWye, a G-TEAD representative embedded with SETAF-AF. “An overarching, completely integrated fly‑away kit and four subcategories focused on sUAS detection, kinetic defeat, nonkinetic defeat and passive protection. Solutions will integrate into the Army’s C-UAS command and control Integrated Battle Command System-Maneuver.”
The categories cover the full chain of drone defense: spotting small drones, shooting them down, jamming or otherwise disabling them, and hardening positions so drones that get through do less damage. The fly-away kit is meant to package those pieces into a single set a unit can deploy quickly.
The U.S. Army chose Africa partly for its testing conditions. The command says open radio spectrum, uncongested airspace and varied terrain give soldiers room to test drone detection and jamming equipment in ways that crowded training ranges in the United States and Europe cannot easily match.
G-TEAD operates under the U.S. Army Pathway for Innovation and Technology and places small teams inside the service’s regional component commands, including U.S. Army Europe and Africa, U.S. Army Pacific and U.S. Army Central, to turn commanders’ urgent needs into requirements that acquisition offices and prize-authority partners can act on. It assigned a team to SETAF-AF in summer 2026.
“ASCCs always had priorities, they’ve always had capability gaps, but the two things they’ve never had is acquisition authority and research, development, test and evaluation dollars,” said U.S. Army Col. Christopher Hill, director of G-TEAD.
Hill said that because G-TEAD has visibility across several commands, it can line up modernization efforts, stretch funding and push systems that prove themselves in one theater out to the rest of the U.S. Army. Each event follows three phases: submission and preparation, soldier-led demonstrations, and follow-on operational evaluation.
“ACEs are driven by real, urgent, theater-specific technology gaps,” said VanWye.
Small drones have become one of the main threats to command posts and bases after their mass use in the war in Ukraine and in attacks on U.S. forces in the Middle East, and the U.S. Army has been buying and testing counter-drone systems at a rapid pace to keep up.
“Soldiers need capability,” Hill said. “We have to come in, and we have to actually perform and produce.”
The demonstrations in Tan-Tan begin in February 2027, with the operational assessment at African Lion running through May.

'Internet access is fundamental right': SC suggests ‘child mode’ for social media accounts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:06:21 UTC
16:06:21 KST

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Saturday declared access to and use of the internet a fundamental right for every individual, including children, under Articles 21 and 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, observing that “The safety of our children and their freedom are not at odds with each other.”The bench of Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice K Vinod Chandran also suggested that children’s online safety should be strengthened through measures such as a ‘child mode’ for social media accounts, rather than denying them access to the internet altogether, LiveLaw reported.A bench comprising Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice K Vinod Chandran made the observations while issuing directions to strengthen mechanisms for detecting and removing child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) from social media platforms and other online services.According to LiveLaw, the bench said: "..we have no hesitation in saying that the right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right of every individual under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. Our children, irrespective of their age enjoy the same rights, and to deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a conscience worth protecting or a freedom of speech worth expressing.
The safety of our children and their freedom are not at odds with each other. Our children are entitled to both."Blanket restrictions are not the answerThe bench acknowledged that the internet, in its present form, poses safety risks to children. However, it said restricting children's access because online platforms had failed to detect and remove harmful material would amount to mistaking the victim for the problem.The court examined whether children should be completely shielded from the internet and social media in the interest of their safety. It noted that the right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) includes the right to know, receive and impart information and ideas.Describing the internet as a marketplace of ideas, creative expression and information, the court said its value extended beyond the material available online to the opportunities it provided for learning, communication and access to information."For many children, particularly in remote areas, it is often the only source of learning and information," the court observed.It also noted that the internet could be particularly important for children with special needs, for whom online platforms might be the only place to find companionship with others facing similar circumstances.
Building on earlier rulingsThe bench referred to the Supreme Court's 2020 judgment in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, which held that "the freedom of speech and expression and the freedom to carry on any trade or business through the medium of the internet is constitutionally protected as a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution."In that judgment, the court had refrained from expressing a view on whether the right to access the internet, by itself, constituted a fundamental right.The bench also referred to the 2025 judgment in Pragya Prasun & Ors. v. Union of India, in which the court recognised the right to digital access as a fundamental right under Article 21.

His reporting focuses on elections, national security, and institutional affairs, tracking the decisions and conflicts that shape public life. He specialises in sharp explainers and in-depth feature stories that go beyond headlines to decode political shifts, defence strategy, geopolitical flashpoints, and changing public sentiment. Greece Rules Out Compromising Defenses for Ukraine Patriots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:02:00 UTC
16:02:00 KST

Greece will do everything possible to support Ukraine but will not take steps that compromise its own national defense capabilities, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said in Brussels on Friday, Oct. 16.
Speaking to Radio Liberty on the sidelines of the European Council summit, Mitsotakis addressed questions regarding whether Athens would transfer Patriot surface-to-air interceptor missiles from its military stockpiles to Kyiv.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Mitsotakis declined to comment publicly on whether the Ukrainian government had submitted a formal request for the systems, while emphasizing Greece’s security priorities in the Eastern Mediterranean.
“You know that we have supported Ukraine by providing significant air defense assets from our stockpiles,” Mitsotakis told reporters.
“At the same time, I want to be completely candid: we will do everything possible to support Ukraine without undermining Greece’s defense capabilities. We are also in a security-sensitive region, we have other obligations, but we stand by Ukraine and always try to do everything possible.”
While Greece has previously transferred shorter-range air defense systems to Ukrainian forces, Athens has not officially announced or authorized deliveries of long-range Patriot interceptors.
According to Greek newspaper Kathimerini, Kyiv approached Athens with a request to acquire up to 200 Patriot PAC-2 missiles.
General Staff Reports 222 Clashes on Wednesday as Russia Continues Pressing Pokrovsk Axis
Ukrainian defense planners noted that after 23 years of operational service in the Hellenic Air Force, portions of the Greek PAC-2 stockpile are nearing the end of their certified operational shelf life.
Allied pressure on aging Southern European stockpiles
The statements by the Greek head of government follow coordinated diplomatic efforts by NATO and EU defense officials to persuade Greece and Spain to transfer aging surface-to-air missiles to Ukraine.
Athens and Madrid maintain some of Europe’s largest national inventories of Patriot PAC-2 interceptors, systems that Ukrainian defense planners require to defend urban population centers and electrical grid infrastructure from Russian ballistic and cruise missile strikes.
Military data cited by The Telegraph indicates that Greece holds at least 200 Patriot PAC-2 missiles whose certified 23-year lifespan is approaching expiration.
Allied defense coordinators have argued that transferring aging munitions before they exceed statutory operational limits represents a practical arrangement, noting that expired missiles require expensive, logistically complex factory recertifications.
“We know that some countries have interceptor missiles that will expire soon,” EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas stated during multilateral consultations in Ireland last month. “So it would be very good if they were transferred to Ukraine.”
While Spanish military stockpile figures remain classified, Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares confirmed last month that Madrid agreed to deliver five Patriot interceptors to Kyiv.
Zelensky appeals for 300 Patriot interceptors ahead of winter
The Greek position comes as President Volodymyr Zelensky delivered an urgent appeal to EU heads of state in Brussels on Friday, Oct. 16, calling for 300 Patriot interceptors alongside €70 billion ($79 billion) in financial assistance for the upcoming year.
Addressing the European Council summit, Zelensky warned that Ukrainian forces have depleted critical stockpiles of surface-to-air interceptors capable of neutralizing Russian ballistic missiles, leaving civilian energy networks vulnerable as winter temperatures approach.
“I ask you to really focus on helping us get PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors,” Zelensky said in his address to EU leaders. “Ukraine can’t get by on just two or four missiles from a country every few months. We need a winter package – we always spoke about it between us – of missiles: 300 Patriot interceptors specifically against ballistic missiles.”
Ukrainian officials have emphasized that defending regional electrical generation and distribution nodes against combined ballistic missile and turbojet drone strikes requires steady munition supplies, warning that piecemeal transfers remain insufficient to ensure persistent airspace defense.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:00:37 UTC
16:00:37 KST

A senior Hamas official told the London-based Saudi newspaper Asharq Al-Awsat that Ali al-Amoudi, who is considered the terrorist organization's leader in the Gaza Strip, was wounded in an Israeli strike targeting him two weeks ago.
According to the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, Amoudi, dubbed "Sinwar's successor," was inside the apartment targeted in the strike but survived because he was in a separate part of the residence.
According to the report published Saturday morning, the official said Amoudi was in good condition and receiving treatment at a secure location. This marks the first time a senior Hamas official has acknowledged that Israeli intelligence correctly identified the target of the strike.
Amoudi, Hamas' former head of public relations, was released in the 2011 Gilad Shalit prisoner exchange and has emerged over the past year as one of the central figures overseeing Hamas' affairs in Gaza. He is competing against Nizar Awadallah for the leadership of the terrorist group's political bureau in the Strip.
The strike, carried out on a Saturday morning two weeks ago in western Gaza City, exactly three years after the October 7 massacre, reportedly killed five people, including four women. At the time, Asharq Al-Awsat quoted three Hamas sources who expressed doubts that Amoudi had been killed. One believed he had been at the scene but may have survived.
The assassination attempt was part of an Israeli military campaign targeting senior Hamas figures in recent weeks, including the commander of Hamas' northern Gaza brigade, Izz al-Din Bik, the head of Hamas' finance department, Mohammed Abu Alwan, and the commander of Hamas' Rafah Brigade, Nael Abu Obeid.
Two days after the strike, senior Hamas official Ghazi Hamad said Amoudi had survived. Speaking to the Saudi news channel Al Arabiya, Hamad accused Israel of violating the Gaza ceasefire agreement by continuing its policy of targeted killings. "The Israeli assassinations are putting the Gaza agreement at risk of collapse," he said. He also placed responsibility on Washington, saying, "The United States is responsible for saving the Gaza agreement and must pressure Israel to stop the assassinations."
Amoudi was born in the Gaza Strip and lives in Khan Younis. He was linked to the murder of Shin Bet security coordinator Noam Cohen and was arrested in 1994 by troops from the IDF's undercover Duvdevan unit in the village of Abu Dis, east of Jerusalem. While his accomplices exchanged fire with the soldiers surrounding the house, Amoudi emerged with his hands raised and sustained only minor injuries in the incident.
He was sentenced to life in prison but was released in the 2011 Shalit prisoner exchange, along with Yahya Sinwar and approximately 1,000 other terrorists.
His ties to Sinwar are considered a defining feature of his career within Hamas. The two met while serving prison sentences in Israel and maintained their relationship after their release. During Sinwar's first term as head of Hamas' political bureau in Gaza, from 2017 to 2021, Amoudi served as his bureau chief.
In 2021, Amoudi was elected to Hamas' political bureau and was appointed head of the group's public relations department that same year. In that role, he helped formulate Hamas' communications strategy and messaging and coordinated between the group's political leadership and operational units.
Following Sinwar's killing in October 2024 and the deaths of numerous other senior Hamas leaders in Gaza during the war, Amoudi's standing within the organization grew. According to reports, he assumed responsibility for managing the affairs of Hamas' political bureau in Gaza and became a central figure in overseeing the group's operations on the ground.
During this period, his name was linked to a series of organizational changes and appointments within Hamas' structures in Gaza. Reports also indicated that some of these moves sparked disagreements among senior officials, with questions raised within Hamas over how he had acquired his authority.
Amoudi is now competing with Nizar Awadallah for Hamas' top leadership position in Gaza. The first round of voting ended without a clear winner, and the decisive round was suspended after Awadallah appealed aspects of the election process.
According to sources cited by Al Arabiya and Al Hadath, Khaled Mashal and Zaher Jabarin support Awadallah, while Amoudi has the backing of Khalil al-Hayya, head of Hamas' political bureau. However, Asharq Al-Awsat reported that it remains unclear whether al-Hayya supports either candidate.
Despite his longstanding ties to Sinwar and his involvement in managing Hamas' affairs in Gaza, Amoudi is not regarded as a commander of the group's military wing. Rather, he is a senior political and organizational figure whose influence has grown significantly following the killing of much of Hamas' top leadership during the war.

‘I cannot carry all of this alone’: the couples kept apart by the war in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:00:24 UTC
16:00:24 KST

Wijdan Abu Matar, 43, was forced to leave Gaza in November 2023 with her eight children for medical treatment, while her injured husband, Hatem, remained behind.
Wijdan and her family were living in the Nuseirat refugee camp when the Gaza war began with the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel. Ten days later, on 17 October that year, an Israeli strike hit the al-Muhandseen tower, near their home, injuring Wijdan and every member of her family.
“We were sitting together, just about to start lunch when the bombing happened,” Wijdan recalled. “The ceiling collapsed over our heads. Everything went dark. I couldn’t see anything. I just started screaming the names of my sons and daughters.”
Her daughter Nour, 15, suffered the most serious injuries, including a fractured skull and bleeding in the brain. Five-year-old Amna suffered severe burns to her chest. The family was initially separated after the strike.
Nour spent about 33 days in intensive care, with Wijdan by her side. Amna and Aysel, three and a half, were at a different hospital for 15 days.
On 30 November 2023, Wijdan travelled with Nour to a hospital in Egypt for treatment. For months, the family remained scattered across Egypt, receiving medical treatment and staying with other relatives.
“I felt completely helpless,” Wijdan said. “There was a fire in my heart because I was away from my husband and my family was scattered.”
Eventually, Wijdan managed to bring her children together in an apartment in Egypt. Three years on, however, she is still separated from her husband, who remains in Gaza. “I have become both the mother and the father to my children,” she said. “The responsibility is exhausting me, and I am constantly worried about my husband.”
Hatem suffered a serious leg injury that limits his mobility and is now displaced in a tent in Nuseirat. Even speaking to him is difficult because of Gaza’s unreliable internet connection. “When he manages to get online, he calls me and the children. He tells me, ‘I am counting the days until I can see you again.’ I can see the tears in his eyes,” Wijdan says.
Wijdan has no regular source of income and relies on donations. Hatem stopped receiving a salary 10 months ago and his injury prevents him from working.
In Egypt, life is difficult for Wijdan and her family. She says she cannot afford transportation to send five of her children to school. “I see my children’s future slipping away in front of me, and there is nothing I can do.”
Nour still requires medical treatment, but Wijdan often cannot afford her medication. She sometimes considers returning to Gaza to be with Hatem, but fears exposing her children to further suffering.
“I dream of getting my children the treatment they need, and I hope we can reunite with my husband as soon as possible so he can also receive treatment,” Wijdan said. “I cannot carry all of this alone. Psychologically, I am exhausted. I have lost 35 members of my family in this war.”
Since the war began with Hamas’s attack on Israel that killed 1,200 people, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the health ministry. Earlier this year an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continues to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.
Sami Abu Tabaq, a 29-year-old Palestinian photojournalist, was forced to leave the Gaza Strip in April 2024, leaving behind his family and his fiancee, Ola.
“Loneliness kills me every day,” he said. “Life away from the woman I love and my family is incredibly hard. I’m desperately waiting for the day God brings us together again.”
Sami became engaged to Ola five months before the war began. They had met by chance when he chose her family’s home as a location for a photoshoot. Before the war, they saw each other constantly. They went to the sea, had dinner at restaurants in Gaza, and spent months preparing the house where they planned to live after their wedding, which was scheduled for November 2023.
Sami and his family fled their home in Tal al-Zaatar, Jabaliya, early on in the war. Their home was badly damaged and later destroyed, along with the house Sami and Ola had been planning to move into once they got married.
When his sister decided to flee south with her children, Sami accompanied her but he could not reach Ola to say goodbye.
The separation became unbearable. Days, sometimes weeks, passed without Sami knowing whether Ola was alive. Once, he saw reports that an entire residential block near her home in Gaza City had been bombed. “I almost lost my mind. I had never felt so helpless,” he said. Unable to return north, he asked his brother to check on her. Eventually, his brother confirmed that she and her family were alive.
Sami continued working as a photojournalist from southern Gaza. Four journalists who had shared his tent were later killed, including Hamza al-Dahdouh, a son of the Al Jazeera journalist Wael al-Dahdouh.
As Israel threatened a ground invasion of Rafah in 2024, Ola began urging Sami to leave Gaza, fearing he would be killed. Sami paid a company coordinating exits at the time for both of them to cross into Egypt. But Ola could not reach southern Gaza to travel through Rafah. “She told me, ‘You go, and I’ll follow you,’” Sami said. “And here we are, still waiting, nearly two and a half years later.” They still have not managed to get married.
By his second day in Egypt, Sami was overwhelmed by guilt. “The overthinking kills me,” he said. “I felt ashamed to turn on the lights or eat proper food while my fiancee and my family were struggling to find the most basic things.”
In Egypt, his life has become dominated by loneliness and sleeplessness. “There is safety in Egypt and there are beautiful places, but I stay home. Happiness has no meaning without her. I cannot enjoy anything while she is not here,” he said.
Despite the war, Ola completed her bachelor’s degree in nursing at the Islamic University of Gaza. She has also endured enormous loss: her cousin, the journalist Ayat Khadoura, was killed, along with about 50 other members of her extended family.
From Egypt, Sami tries to create moments of happiness for her. For her latest birthday, he contacted her brother in Gaza and secretly arranged a cake, gift and flowers. “When she woke up and saw everything, she was so happy. I love her reaction when she’s happy.” The only problem was the flowers. “They were artificial,” he said. “I wasn’t happy with them, but natural flowers can’t get into Gaza because Israel does not allow them in.”
Sami says he has tried every possible way to get Ola out, without success. She is now applying for scholarships abroad, hoping education might provide a route to evacuation and, eventually, to him.
Sami recently travelled to Mecca for Umrah, where one prayer remained constantly on his mind. “I prayed, ‘God, please bring us together soon,’” he said. “But one thing I know for sure: I will wait for her for the rest of my life, until God brings us together.”

Plan to make firms pay more to train older workers than youth apprentices in England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:00:24 UTC
16:00:24 KST

Employers in England are to be forced to pay more to train an older worker than a youth apprentice under plans being drawn up by the government to tackle the youth jobs crisis.
The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’s apprenticeship funding scheme to increase the cost of training by 25% for a worker over the age of 25 in order to encourage businesses to train young people instead.
Aiming to reverse a 40% drop in youth apprenticeship starts over the past decade, the proposal is being developed as part of the government response to Alan Milburn’s review into why so many young people are out of work.
With his final report delayed until after the budget, the former Labour cabinet minister this week signalled that boosting access to apprenticeships would be critical for fixing the first rungs of the career ladder for young people.
The chancellor, John Healey, is preparing to include measures to tackle soaring youth unemployment in his highly anticipated tax and spending statement to the Commons in less than a fortnight’s time.
After a rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training to almost 1 million, Andy Burnham has made supporting youth job opportunities central to his agenda for power, including sweeping changes to retool technical education and apprenticeships.
Ministers have been clear they want to rebalance the apprenticeship system back towards younger people. More than half of new starts are now for over-25s and the number of under-19s enrolling has almost halved in a decade.
Under the changes being planned to the growth and skills levy – the £4bn a year tax used to fund the national apprenticeship system – employers in England will face a new “co-investment” rule restricting the funding they can access.
Aiming to tip the balance to incentivise youth apprenticeships, the change is controversial because employers have for years been told by successive governments they were free to spend their levy funds on training as they saw fit.
“Employers are not going to like it,” said one senior policy expert close to the government. “They were told ‘it’s your money, you get to decide’. But the system is not working at the moment.”
Earlier this year Labour revamped the apprenticeship levy introduced by the Conservatives in 2017, with changes handing more flexibility to employers over the types of training the system can be used for – including new foundation apprenticeships and shorter courses.
Under the levy, large employers (those with yearly wage costs totalling more than £3m) must pay 0.5% of their total annual pay bill into a dedicated digital pot that they can draw from to fund training and assessment costs.
Following the proposed change, money from the pot would still be available to cover eligible training costs for apprentices aged 16 to 24. However, for older apprentices, the funds would cover only 75% of the cost and employers would need to pay for the remainder. It is believed the measure is under consideration for a phased launch from the start of the next academic year, in September 2027.
Labour has been warned that its skills strategy to tackle youth unemployment risks failure without a change in course. Official figures show its flagship foundation apprenticeship scheme has enrolled just 160 young people in the first eight months, against an ambition for 30,000 starts over the course of the parliament.
This month the Fabian Society thinktank called on ministers to increase the rate of the growth and skills levy to 0.7% to raise an additional £2.5bn, which could be used to target more funding towards youth apprenticeships.
However, it is understood that ministers are wary of heaping additional costs on businesses after the backlash suffered over employer national insurance contributions and as firms press for budget support to help them hire more young people.
Alongside tight constraints on the public finances, this has shifted the focus to restricting levy funds as a way to support young people without further adding to the costs for the public purse.
A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said: “We remain determined to address the 40% decline in apprenticeship starts among young people and give them the skills they need to succeed.
“We are already pivoting the system towards the next generation, including by creating 50,000 additional apprenticeships for young people, and introducing a new hiring payment of £2,000 for SMEs who take on a 16-24-year-old apprentice.
“The Milburn review is due in the autumn. We will not pre-empt its findings.”

No money for Ukraine and EU budget cuts: What could a Le Pen victory mean for the EU?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:00:24 UTC
16:00:24 KST

Le Pen is campaigning on a platform that would reshape France’s relationship with the EU ahead of the 2027 presidential election, potentially setting Paris on a collision course with Brussels with far-reaching implications.
Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, is seeking to become France’s next president on a hardline anti-EU platform, pledging to cut the country’s contributions to the EU budget and end funding for Ukraine.
On Ukraine, Le Pen has repeatedly pledged to end financial assistance. Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Wednesday, she said that if elected, France could only sustain funding for six months because of the “perilous” state of its public finances.
“This funding will stop, and it is a matter of honesty to tell [Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy] the truth,” she told Euronews.
Zelenskyy hit back in an interview with the Financial Times on Thursday. “The price to pay is not as high as the value of people’s lives,” he said. “That is why I think Ms Le Pen is not fully familiar with certain details.”
He added that, if Le Pen were elected president, she should have access to “the most powerful European system that works”, stressing that Ukraine’s battlefield experience could benefit European countries.
Le Pen has also called for an end to EU sanctions against Russia, while saying France could continue training Ukrainian troops and supplying military equipment to Kyiv.
Her comments signal that Le Pen is prepared to take a hardline stance, pledging to end French funding for Ukraine in a position similar to that of US President Donald Trump.
Her stance also contrasts sharply with that of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who is often compared to Le Pen but has advocated continued support for Kyiv.
Speaking in the Italian Senate on Wednesday ahead of an EU summit in Brussels, Meloni delivered a forceful defence of Ukraine’s right to self-defence.
“Supporting Ukraine is not an alternative to peace, it’s what makes it possible,” Meloni said. “The peace we want is one that is sustainable, just and also safeguards Europe and our interests.
“Therefore, the position of this government will not change: support for Ukraine, pressure on Russia and Euro-Atlantic unity.”
‘France’s support for Ukraine goes far beyond aid’
“France’s support for Ukraine goes far beyond aid alone. It is primarily diplomatic,” Elie Tenenbaum, director of the French Institute of International Relations’ Centre for Security Studies, told Euronews.
He highlighted France’s leading role in initiatives such as the Coalition of the Willing, launched alongside the United Kingdom, as well as other mechanisms that “help keep Ukraine afloat”.
These include the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan (USL), whose implementation and disbursement depend on the political backing of major countries, including France.
Tenenbaum stressed that cuts to EU-level funding would have a greater impact on Ukraine than a reduction in France’s bilateral aid.
“If France were not only to stop providing bilateral aid and contributing to the EU budget, but also to actively oppose these kinds of mechanisms, then the entire framework of European assistance to Ukraine would be put at risk.”
According to figures from the German think tank Kiel Institute, France has committed an estimated €27 billion to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. This includes €7.9 billion in bilateral aid and €19 billion through European mechanisms.
Germany remains Europe’s largest provider of aid to Ukraine in absolute terms, having pledged more than €50 billion since February 2022, well ahead of France, Italy and the Netherlands. Relative to GDP, however, Denmark and Estonia provide the highest levels of bilateral aid.
Cutting France’s contributions to the EU budget
With six months to go before France’s presidential election, Le Pen is campaigning on a platform centred on tighter immigration controls, greater national sovereignty and measures to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, as rising fuel prices fuel public discontent.
Her party has backed capping France’s net contribution to the EU budget at €5 billion a year, down from €8 billion, according to figures published by the French Senate. Such a move would mark a departure from recent years, during which France’s contributions have generally increased, despite annual fluctuations.
Under President Emmanuel Macron, France has backed a larger EU budget, unlike countries such as Germany, which favour tighter spending limits. Paris has also called for new EU own resources, meaning additional sources of revenue beyond member state contributions.
Although France is a net contributor to the EU budget, it also receives substantial funding for its farmers through the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).
“France stands out among the major contributors as it is the only one that has so far supported an ambitious EU budget,” Eulalia Rubio, a senior research fellow at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.
She said Le Pen’s proposals reflected a “lack of understanding” of EU institutions.
“Spending varies slightly every year, so you can’t say, ‘We’re only going to pay €5 billion every year from now on’,” she commented.
Rubio warned that if France overcame the legal obstacles to cutting its contributions, other member states would have to make up the shortfall. Such a prospect could prove particularly contentious given that France is the largest recipient of farming subsidies.
On Wednesday, France’s National Assembly rejected the National Rally’s proposal to unilaterally reduce the country’s contributions to the EU budget for 2027, instead backing the government’s planned level of funding.
Thierry Chopin, an adjunct professor of European studies at Sorbonne University, said a National Rally victory could mark a break with France’s traditional role as a driving force within the EU and with the “intellectual contributions championed by Paris” in recent years, which had gained traction in response to global events.
Chopin pointed to France’s role in promoting European sovereignty, strategic autonomy in defence and trade protection measures. However, he said France’s influence had waned during Macron’s second term as its economic credibility declined.
“This credibility was not particularly strong to begin with, but it has worsened given the country’s budgetary situation, public debt and the difficulties facing its public finances. And then, once again, there are political considerations, because the executive branch has been weakened,” he said.
EU budget for 2028-2034
Speaking to the Financial Times on Wednesday, Le Pen described efforts to reach an agreement on the EU’s 2028-2034 budget by the end of 2026 as "anti-democratic."
She accused the European Commission of undermining “democratic processes” by advancing the budget ahead of elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland.
Ahead of the vote, Macron has moved to secure key positions, including at the central bank, by appointing allies. On Thursday, the French president told EU leaders during a closed-door meeting that Paris favours reaching a deal this year.
Beyond the timeline, Le Pen is also focused on the substance of the EU budget. Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, she said she hoped to “build new coalitions” with like-minded parties to challenge what she described as an anti-growth mindset in Brussels.
She also suggested that the European Central Bank (ECB), led by Christine Lagarde, should revise its mandate to give greater weight to economic growth. The ECB is independent and its primary mandate is to maintain price stability.
Experts told Euronews they are sceptical that member states would support another major overhaul of EU fiscal rules following the sweeping reform of the Stability and Growth Pact in 2024.
“In my view, member states show little appetite for another major reform,” Andreas Eisl, a senior research fellow in European economic policy at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.
He added that “future changes are likely to involve reinterpretations of the existing rules rather than a fundamental overhaul of their legal foundations”.
Le Pen has repeatedly criticised EU regulations and standards, describing them as “regulatory hell” or a “regulatory shantytown”, and has pledged to strip them back to the bare minimum. Such an approach could undermine the bloc’s legal framework if adopted across member states.
“Obviously, if every member state does this, the EU can no longer function as a union based on the rule of law,” Chopin said.
The National Rally leader has also vowed to “stop” the European Green Deal, the EU’s flagship programme to cut emissions and achieve climate neutrality by 2050.
Le Pen argues that the Green Deal undermines economic growth. She has also proposed abolishing institutions such as the European Committee of the Regions (CoR), an advisory body representing local and regional authorities involved in implementing EU policies, including climate measures.
“The dismantling of the European Green Deal is already underway. If Marine Le Pen were to be elected, this would only be further accentuated, according to certain analyses,” Phuc-Vinh Nguyen, head of the Energy Centre at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.
Maria Tadeo contributed to this report

EU working on multiple fronts to limit Russians from entering bloc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

The European Union is working on multiple fronts to limit the number of Russian citizens that can enter the bloc, including the nuclear option of a total ban on all non-essential travel into the club’s Schengen zone.
This comes as Brussels and several EU member states have flagged that individuals using either Russian diplomatic cover or travelling on tourism visas have played key roles in various types of hybrid attacks in the bloc.
Most recently, German authorities revealed that the main suspect in the drone attack on Leipzig airport in August, which caused major traffic disruptions, was a Belarusian-Russian citizen who entered the EU using an Italian-issued Schengen tourist visa.
In a leaked EU presidency policy paper on various Russian visa options, seen by RFE/RL, it is noted that the “only long-term and effective solution would appear to be the possibility to adopt visa restrictive measures, which would ban non-essential travel for one nationality of applicants.”
The document notes that changes to the EU visa code would be necessary for such a move and that “these visa measures would be applied in a uniform way as EU law”. A change to the visa code would be made via qualified majority, constituting 55 percent of all member states, representing 65 percent of the total EU population.
A bigger overhaul of the EU visa code could come later in the year, but several EU member states, notably in southern Europe, are still reluctant to completely shut down various avenues of people-to-people contact with Russian citizens.
Shortly after the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the EU fully suspended the EU-Russia visa facilitation agreement that allowed for cheaper visas, multiple-entry visas and simpler procedures to obtain them.
Brussels also issued guidelines to EU member states on how to deal with Russian visa applications, prioritizing so-called “essential travel” requests such as applicants going for humanitarian reasons, including civil society representatives, political dissidents and independent journalists or family reunification.
Patchwork approach
These guidelines are nonbinding, giving each EU member state wide discretion on how they would treat Russian visa applications. And the result has created a European patchwork of approaches to Russian visa requests.
While many countries on the EU’s eastern flank, bordering Russia, imposed very strict rules by hardly allowing any Russian nationals to enter, southern member states, keen on summer visitors, were more generous in issuing Schengen tourist visas for Russian citizens.
In 2025, a record since the full-scale invasion was reached, with 477,878 visas being issued to Russian nationals for tourism purposes. The vast majority of those were authorized by Greece, Italy, France, and Spain.
Until a potential decision on a full entry ban could be taken, the EU is working in parallel on three separate tracks on how to reduce the number of Russian visitors -- banning ex-combatants in Ukraine, reducing Russian diplomatic movement and so-called “limited territorial validity (LTV)” visas, which only allows you to stay in the country that issued the visa while prohibiting the holder from travelling to other Schengen zone countries.
The presidency paper notes that “LTV visas are presented as an interim measure, pending the future implementation of a full ban on travel for non-essential purposes.” Germany has argued for this approach and the paper notes that the rationale behind the push is to let the countries that still issue non-essential visas to Russian to “assume full responsibility for doing so, in a context where other Member States adopt a much stricter approach.”
But the paper also points out the limits with this move, noting that “this runs against one of the basic principles on which the Schengen area is based, ie mutual trust. It amounts to a re-nationalisation of short-stay visa policy”.
Limited effect
The very fact that there hardly are any internal EU border controls also make an LTV visa have limited effect, with the document stating that “an LTV visa issued to a Russian national with malevolent intent does not seem to offer sufficient security guarantees against further movements inside the Schengen Area.”
Regarding ex-combatants travelling on tourist visas, movement is expected soon.
Various European consulates in Russia will most likely be required to check military service documents as part of the visa issuance routine. There are still some issues, however, such as the fact that many of the consulate staff are Russian citizens and that Moscow, according to European diplomats familiar with the matter, has threatened them with legal action if they ask about such documentation.
In a separate diplomatic note, seen by RFE/RL, the case for restricting the movement of Russian diplomats and consular staff within the EU is also being explored.
The common practice right now stipulates that Russian diplomatic personnel in the EU are only required to notify authorities when traveling to another member state, but there is now a push to introduce a requirement to obtain prior authorisation from the country they intend to visit.
Another idea gaining traction in Brussels is to limit how long Russian diplomats and officials can remain in their host countries as European counterintelligence services are keen to curb long-established spy networks, in which diplomats stationed in one place for extended periods often play a key role.
This story was originally published by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), partners of LRT English.

Taiwan plans US industrial parks to support suppliers

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan plans to establish industrial parks in the US to help smaller domestic suppliers set up local operations and strengthen semiconductor and AI supply chains, Economics Minister Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said.
Kung told Bloomberg Monday that the first park is planned for Texas, with construction costs of up to NT$129.8 billion (US$4 billion). The government aims to develop additional sites across the US, with each subsequent park expected to cost between NT$64.9 billion and NT$129.8 billion, according to CNA and Anue.
The initiative is intended to help smaller suppliers expand overseas to support major manufacturers such as TSMC and Foxconn, which provide critical hardware for data centers worldwide. Both companies are key partners for US AI chipmakers Nvidia and AMD, as well as cloud service providers such as Meta and Microsoft.
However, AI data centers also require components such as chip packaging substrates, cooling modules, and other equipment supplied by smaller Taiwanese firms. Unlike their larger customers, these suppliers often lack the financial resources to independently cover the high costs of setting up overseas facilities.
Kung said the government would offer comprehensive assistance to companies setting up operations in the parks. Support would include credit guarantees for loans and helping them communicate with US federal and local authorities on issues such as visa applications and land acquisition.
People familiar with the matter said Taiwan had already secured a plot of land in Texas for an industrial park. The Ministry of Economic Affairs said it would release further details at a later date.

Iran’s U23s face an uncertain future
TEHRAN - Iran’s U23 football team are approaching another crucial stage in their development without a head coach, a settled management structure or a clearly defined roadmap towards the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.
Nearly three weeks after the team’s disappointing exit from the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, the search for a successor to Hossein Abdi has yet to produce a final decision, with Yahya Golmohammadi now emerging as the leading candidate.
The uncertainty is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Iran travelled to Japan with ambitions of making progress but bowed out in the group stage after a 4-1 defeat by North Korea in its final match.
Abdi resigned after returning from Japan, leaving the Football Federation of Iran (FFIRI) to begin another search for a coach. Afshin Ghotbi was initially linked with the position, while other domestic and foreign names were also discussed. Those options have failed to produce an appointment, and Golmohammadi has moved to the front of the queue.
FFIRI president Mehdi Taj has confirmed that talks have taken place with Golmohammadi, saying the former Persepolis coach appears to be the closest candidate to the job. Golmohammadi, however, is currently in charge of Iraqi club Duhok, whose management has reportedly resisted the prospect of his departure. Iranian officials are therefore seeking the club’s approval before they can turn preliminary discussions into a final agreement.
 
The process has also raised questions about the federation’s decision-making structure. With the youth committee and national teams department assigned responsibilities under the federation’s statutes, the extent of their involvement in selecting the team’s coach remains unclear.
 
In a statement following the Nagoya elimination, the federation apologized to supporters and promised a thorough review, candid assessment and decisive action. Yet the gap between that pledge and the continuing uncertainty over the team’s leadership remains evident.
Abdi, meanwhile, challenged the federation’s account of the team’s preparation. He said the squad had gone 47 days without a training camp or access to players between early August and September 17, contradicting claims that adequate facilities and preparation had been provided.
Iran’s Olympic campaign requires sustained access to players, cooperation with clubs, a coherent schedule of training camps and international friendlies, and clear performance targets. Appointing an experienced coach may be a necessary first step, but it cannot substitute for a long-term strategy.
With qualification for Los Angeles 2028 the ultimate objective, Iran’s U23 team remain in limbo. The federation has acknowledged the failure in Nagoya and promised corrective action, but until a coach is appointed and a credible program is established, the road to the Olympics remains uncertain and the same cycle of late decisions and unmet expectations risks repeating itself.

Why Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty

Why Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty
For more than three decades, Michael Gove has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible, the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam.

U.S. Air Force adds drone-mimicking firm to adversary pool
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:48:44 UTC
15:48:44 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded KestrelX, A2G International and Fleet Adversary Support and Training places on a $5.4 billion adversary air and close air support contract.
- Work runs across the continental United States through Oct. 8, 2029, with only $3,000 obligated at award and funding to follow through task orders.
The U.S. Air Force has added three small companies to a contract worth up to $5.4 billion for privately flown “Red Air” adversary aircraft and close air support training, including a firm that flies small planes made to mimic enemy drones and cruise missiles.
KestrelX of Driggs, Idaho, A2G International of Melbourne, Florida, and Fleet Adversary Support and Training of St. Augustine, Florida, each received a place on the indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract for the Combat Air Force Contracted Air Support program, the U.S. Department of War said. The Air Combat Command Acquisition Management and Integration Center at Langley Air Force Base, Virginia, awarded the deals on Oct. 15 after a competition in which three offers were received. Only $3,000 was obligated at signing, with money to flow later through individual task orders.
Under the program, private companies supply aircraft and pilots that play the enemy, or Red Air, against U.S. fighter crews in training, and fly close air support sorties so joint terminal attack controllers on the ground can practice calling in airstrikes. Work will take place across the continental United States through Oct. 8, 2029.
The new awards carry the same $5.4 billion ceiling and a nearly identical end date as the second Combat Air Force Contracted Air Support contract, which the U.S. Air Force awarded in September 2024 to eight established adversary air companies, including Airborne Tactical Advantage Company, Draken International, Top Aces and Tactical Air Support. Those firms compete with one another for task orders under the vehicle, and the original version, awarded in 2019, had a $6.4 billion ceiling.
KestrelX brings a different kind of aircraft to that pool. The company, founded by former U.S. Navy fighter and test pilot Don Moseley, flies small jets and light propeller planes modified to replicate drones and cruise missiles, and it has played those threats in exercises such as Northern Strike in Michigan. Last month, the U.S. Navy hired KestrelX under a contract worth up to $9.99 million to supply low-observable target aircraft and engineering support for training exercises.
A2G International describes itself as an operator of manned and unmanned aircraft that provides airborne intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance services to U.S. and foreign government customers.
Contracted Red Air grew as the U.S. Air Force ran short of its own aggressor aircraft and did not want to tie up front-line fighters, particularly F-35s, playing the enemy in training. A 2021 Government Accountability Office report found that the U.S. Air Force planned for adversary air contracts to serve as a bridge, with their use expected to phase out around 2030 as the service builds up its own aggressor squadrons and explores new crewed and uncrewed adversary aircraft.
Each of the three new companies will now be able to compete for task orders under the contract through October 2029.

Hypersonic-armed stealth destroyer nears sea trials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:44:05 UTC
15:44:05 KST

- The U.S. Navy added $99.1 million to an Ingalls Shipbuilding contract to cover sea trials for USS Lyndon B. Johnson, the last Zumwalt-class destroyer.
- The ship is being fitted in Pascagoula with Conventional Prompt Strike hypersonic missiles, following USS Zumwalt, which finished sea trials in January 2026.
The U.S. Navy is paying Huntington Ingalls Industries another $99.1 million to take USS Lyndon B. Johnson (DDG 1002), the last of its three angular Zumwalt-class stealth destroyers, through sea trials as the ship is fitted to carry hypersonic missiles.
The contract modification, announced by the U.S. Department of War, raises the ceiling on an existing Ingalls Shipbuilding contract to cover the destroyer’s sea trials. About 95% of the work will take place at the company’s shipyard in Pascagoula, Mississippi, with completion scheduled for October 2028, and the U.S. Navy obligated about $59.3 million at signing, split between fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2026 shipbuilding funds.
During sea trials, a new or heavily modified warship leaves the yard to run its propulsion, steering, combat systems and other equipment at sea before the U.S. Navy accepts it. For Lyndon B. Johnson, they will follow years of work in Pascagoula to turn the ship into one of the first U.S. warships able to fire Conventional Prompt Strike, a hypersonic missile designed to reach targets thousands of kilometers away at more than five times the speed of sound.
The Zumwalt class was originally designed around two 155 mm Advanced Gun Systems meant to bombard targets ashore, but the U.S. Navy canceled the guns’ special long-range shells in 2016 after costs soared, leaving the destroyers with guns they could not use, and later decided to remove them and give the three ships a new strike mission with hypersonic missiles.
General Dynamics Bath Iron Works in Maine built Lyndon B. Johnson, which was christened in April 2019 by the late president’s daughters, before moving to Ingalls for combat system activation. In January 2025 the ship entered dry dock in Pascagoula to start installing the large missile tubes for Conventional Prompt Strike, and the U.S. Navy said at the time that it planned to commission the destroyer in 2027.
The lead ship, USS Zumwalt (DDG 1000), went through the same conversion first. Ingalls replaced its forward gun with four large-diameter tubes that each hold three hypersonic missiles, giving the ship 12 in total, and Zumwalt completed builder’s sea trials in January 2026 after nearly three years in the yard, HII said. The second ship, USS Michael Monsoor (DDG 1001), is set to receive the same missile system during a future yard period.
Conventional Prompt Strike shares its hypersonic glide body with the U.S. Army’s Dark Eagle long-range hypersonic weapon, which the U.S. Army fields on truck-mounted launchers. The missile boosts its warhead to high speed and altitude, then releases a glide vehicle that maneuvers toward the target, making it harder for air and missile defenses to intercept. Lockheed Martin, the program’s prime contractor, received a $1.36 billion contract modification earlier this year to support missile and launcher production for the system.
Ingalls is due to finish Lyndon B. Johnson’s sea trials and related work by October 2028, which would make it the second Zumwalt-class destroyer to go to sea with hypersonic missile tubes.
