The chatbot murder guide: AI’s struggle between privacy, reporting violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:50:37 UTC
14:50:37 KST

The chatbot murder guide: AI’s struggle between privacy, reporting violence
The deadly Tumbler Ridge shooting in Canada raises questions about when AI companies should report threats of violence to police, and the potential risks to an individual’s privacy.
For months before carrying out Canada’s deadliest school shooting in almost four decades, Jesse Van Rootselaar was consulting an unlikely adviser on how to perpetrate mass murder.
“In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 [Remington shotgun] is brutal … Close quarters is its playground,” OpenAI’s ChatGPT guided the 18-year-old, according to reports.
On February 10, 2026, Van Rootselaar shot his mother and half-brother at home before going to a school in the small British Columbia town of Tumbler Ridge, where he killed another six people – including five students – before taking his own life.
Earlier this week, on October 14, US authorities charged a Washington State man with allegedly conspiring with Van Rootselaar to plan the attack. But the mass shooting incident has raised questions that go beyond the traditional legal understanding of culpability.
The British Columbia government in September filed a civil lawsuit against OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman, accusing them of failing to prevent the incident and claiming they were aware of the conversations that turned deadly. Families of the victims also filed separate lawsuits. OpenAI’s leadership issued a public apology for their failure to notify authorities.
The company has not responded to requests from Al Jazeera for its comments on the lawsuits.
But as the case against OpenAI progresses, it has spurred a familiar debate: Where should a line be drawn between reporting potentially dangerous behaviour and protecting an individual’s privacy?
“The question of whether companies should be required to turn such information over to law enforcement is extraordinarily difficult, particularly if they don’t already screen chats for indications of such types of threats,” United States-based civil liberties lawyer Jenin Younes told Al Jazeera.
“Forcing companies to implement a surveillance system implicates very serious civil liberties concerns, and that’s probably a bridge too far for me,” Younes added.
“On the other hand, AI gives individuals access to types and quantities of information they didn’t have previously that may facilitate the commission of mass casualty events, a concern it’s not easy to dismiss.”
AI’s ability to distinguish thoughts from threats
One of the biggest challenges facing AI companies is determining whether a user expressing violent thoughts actually intends to act on them.
In August, Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, flagged a user to San Francisco police after discovering conversations allegedly threatening its CEO, Dario Amodei.
According to the San Francisco Standard, citing a police report, the user had claimed to possess an AR-15 gun and suggested he had Amodei “in his sights”.
However, when contacted by the newspaper, the man said he was joking and had no intention of carrying out any form of violence. The person was neither charged nor detained, the Standard said.
Fazl Barez, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford specialising in AI safety and governance, said current AI models cannot “reliably” determine whether an interaction with an AI chatbot “is purely hypothetical or is likely to lead to harmful behaviour”.
“Suppose you are a creative writer working on a fictional story and want to explore how a murder plot might unfold. From the context, it may be clear that this is simply a fictional narrative. If the threshold for flagging potentially harmful content is too low, such a writer could be wrongly flagged,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Similarly, consider a graduate student in biology or chemistry studying pathogens that, if misused, could have serious consequences. They might be trying to understand the risks associated with these pathogens and how to mitigate them. Such discussions may be necessary for legitimate research and education. Even when the subject matter is sensitive, they should not automatically be flagged without considering the broader context.”
The researcher said identifying a credible threat may require examining a user’s interactions across multiple conversations, rather than relying on isolated statements.
Barez said someone experiencing intrusive violent thoughts might turn to a chatbot for support, while another person planning an attack may reveal their intentions gradually across several conversations.
“Distinguishing between the two requires careful consideration of context, intent and patterns of behaviour, rather than relying on individual statements alone,” he added.
Chinmayi Sharma, a law professor at Fordham University, said the debate has parallels with the duty imposed on mental health professionals to warn identifiable third parties about credible threats.
However, she said there was a key difference – therapists have professional training, knowledge of their patients and enforceable standards governing their conduct. AI companies do not necessarily have comparable safeguards.
“My concern with AI companies is that right now there’s not a concerted effort to hire mental health professionals, sociologists, individuals that would have the unique expertise on what the indicators of threat are here,” Sharma told Al Jazeera.
“Secondly, licensed professionals are accountable to concrete, legally enforceable standards in their discipline. We don’t have something like that for AI companies.”
The privacy dilemma
The privacy implications extend beyond whether AI companies can accurately identify threats. Millions of people use chatbots to discuss relationships, emotional distress, mental health concerns and deeply personal experiences.
Civil liberties lawyer Younes said many users may not realise how vulnerable those conversations could be to disclosure.
“They often reflect a person’s innermost thoughts, questions, and desires. The majority of people assume that these dialogues will never be viewed by another person,” Younes, president and legal director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, said.
Younes warned that the consequences of greater monitoring could extend well beyond those planning violence.
“If people fear their chats can be turned over to law enforcement simply because they express disturbing thoughts/violent fantasies etc, many will be dissuaded from using them,” she told Al Jazeera.
Younes argued that forcing companies to establish systems for monitoring users and reporting conversations could raise serious constitutional concerns in the US, including protections against unreasonable searches.
Meanwhile, Fordham’s Sharma also raised an issue about who could be disproportionately affected by heavy monitoring by AI chatbots.
“The concern is always there about either intentional or unintentional targeting, because if you have models trained on what we consider dangerous speech, they’re almost always going to reflect biases,” she said. “Certain minorities’ speech is over‑flagged as a threat, while other comparable speech is not.
“Even in a world in which everyone is benevolent, we should still be concerned about disparate outcomes,” she said, warning that machines could reproduce such disparities at scale.
‘Not a licensed therapist’ – When do AI companies become liable to report?
While AI companies may face moral pressure to prevent violence, their legal obligations are less clear, legal experts say.
Bryan Choi, a professor of law at the University of Colorado Boulder, said US law recognises a duty to warn in certain circumstances, including when mental health professionals become aware of imminent threats or when a special relationship exists between parties.
But those principles do not necessarily apply to AI companies.
“Under present case law, it seems unlikely that a company such as OpenAI would be held to have such duties to warn,” Choi told Al Jazeera. “The chatbot is not a licensed therapist. There is no special relationship between the company and the victims.”
Choi said existing negligence and product liability laws could potentially be applied to AI companies, but proving responsibility would present significant challenges.
Finding a balance
Fordham’s Sharma suggested that independent institutions could help establish reporting standards rather than leaving decisions entirely to private companies or requiring immediate disclosure to police.
Such bodies she said could develop procedures for assessing threats and explore ways of sharing only relevant information while protecting users’ identities and other personal details.
Meanwhile, Younes argued that users should, at a minimum, be clearly informed about whether their conversations are monitored and what circumstances could lead to information being shared with law enforcement.
“This is almost certainly an issue that will be wrestled with over the coming years, and I’m not sure anyone knows the solution at this particular point in time,” she said.
“Events that have not yet occurred will likely influence how these policies are shaped.”

Font size
Bulgaria offers a true culinary journey in mid-October, bringing together traditional recipes, local producers, folklore and cooking demonstrations. Bulgarians celebrate autumn with Elena dry-cured ham, Smilyan beans, roasted chestnuts and a variety of pumpkin delicacies.
PHOTO facebook.com/elenski.byt
The popular Elena Ham Festival takes place in the town of Elena in northern Bulgaria from October 16 to 18. Visitors can sample a traditional Bulgarian dry-cured pork delicacy made from a hind leg of pork and characteristic of the Elena region.
Locals say the recipe is simple: meat, salt, spices and a little patience. Yet the ham’s distinctive flavour is closely tied to the local climate, traditional curing methods and generations of experience among local producers.
PHOTO BTA
Vegetarian food lovers may be tempted to visit the Rhodope village of Smilyan, home to the traditional Smilyan Bean Festival, held from October 16 to 18.
PHOTO Facebook/ People and traditions - Brezhani
Meanwhile, the village square in Brezhani in southwestern Bulgaria hosts the Brezhani Chestnut Festival. The famous local chestnuts are smaller and have lighter-coloured shells than other varieties, but boast a much sweeter taste. Roasted on the spot, they are served with young wine made from the latest grape harvest.
PHOTO kazanlak.com
The 11th National Walnut Festival will take place this weekend in the centre of Golyamo Dryanovo, a village in the Kazanlak region. The event was first held in 2014 in honour of what was once the oldest walnut tree on the Balkan Peninsula, estimated to be 500 years old and which survived until 1993. A special postage stamp was issued in Bulgaria in 1965 in three print runs in honour of the tree. Today, Golyamo Dryanovo is still home to one of Bulgaria’s largest walnut plantations featuring local varieties, covering an area of more than 2,500 decares (250 hectares).
PHOTO nesebar.bg
The flavours of the sea will take centre stage at the 13th Autumn Fish Festival, “Autumn Shoals”, in Nessebar from October 16 to 18.
PHOTO facebook.com/festivalnazhitenatapitka
To mark World Bread Day and World Food Day on October 16, the town of Strazhitsa is hosting the Wheat Loaf Festival. The event is inspired by The Wheaten Loaf, a popular fairy tale by Angel Karaliychev, a writer born in Strazhitsa.
PHOTO BTA
The Pumpkin Festival is being held for the seventh time in the village of Dalboki, near Stara Zagora in southern Bulgaria. The programme includes a cooking competition, a variety of pumpkin dishes and a tasting of traditional rachel, a sweet pumpkin preserve.
PHOTO BTA
No visit to the town of Radomir, known as the boza capital of Bulgaria, would be complete without sampling this distinctive sweet, fermented drink popular across the Balkans. Located near Sofia, the town will host its 11th Boza Day on October 17, featuring a farmers’ market and a craft fair.
PHOTO visit.varna.bg
Varna is the destination of choice this weekend for lovers of Bulgarian wine. The coastal city is hosting the Urban Wine Fest 2026 on October 16–17, one of a series of events dedicated to Bulgarian wines in the run-up to International Mavrud Day on October 26.

The ‘Maid of Ghent’ has been the city’s symbol for 700 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:48:00 UTC
14:48:00 KST

The ‘Maid of Ghent’ can be seen in various places around the city, but fewer and fewer people are familiar with the figure that has adorned the city’s coat of arms since 1991. “She first appeared as early as the 14th century. She is not a single person, but a symbol. She embodied both the rebellious city and nationalism,” says Nina Uelpenich of Ghent University, who has now delved into her history.
In the city centre, there are several references to the Maid of Ghent. There is the café ‘De Maecht van Ghent’ on the Korenmarkt, the Corn Market. Her image adorns the tower door of the post office building and the base of the statue of Jacob of Artevelde on the Vrijdagmarkt, the Friday Market.
Historian Nina Uelpenich researched the origins of the figure and the meanings it has taken on over the past centuries. “The very first mention dates back as far as the 14th century, in a poem by Boudewijn van der Lore. At that time, the Maid was a symbol of Ghent during a conflict with the Count of Flanders.”
From a figure of the Virgin Mary to a nationalist symbol
The female figure is based on the Virgin Mary. She does not refer to any real person. “Several cities were depicted as a virginal figure. They appear everywhere: in books, during ceremonies – in Ghent and elsewhere.” She is also a popular figure in works of art from that period.
‘Even during the Calvinist period – when idols were destroyed – she endured. She is no longer merely a Catholic symbol.’ When Napoleon came to power, most city maidens lost their significance. ‘In Ghent, however, there was a revival during the 19th century.’
“At the time of Belgium’s formation, the Maid was a symbol of the region’s medieval history. Images began to appear in which she is depicted waving the tricolour. She was the face of the illustrious past that was to shape Belgian identity. She became a nationalist figure.”
The female figure was used on posters advertising the 1913 World Exhibition in Ghent. In this way she also became an international symbol of Belgium during the period between the wars.
“Chosen to tell a particular story”
The Maid lost that significance in the decades that followed. “All sorts of maidens emerged, co-existing side by side: there is a liberal Maid of Ghent, a socialist Maid of Ghent… It really became a popular symbol that could serve any form of identity formation.”
“The Maid of Ghent shows how symbols are used to shape identity. This is not a fixed reality, but a construct. They are chosen and magnified to tell a story.” A story that still resonates today, for since 1991 the Maid has adorned Ghent’s official coat of arms.

Indian woman jailed over son’s fatal stabbing faces possible deportation from UK

Vickrum Digwa's mother Kiran Kaur was jailed for three years in July for assisting an offender
An Indian woman jailed for helping her son after he fatally stabbed an 18-year-old student in Southampton could face deportation to India following her early release from prison, British authorities have indicated.According to new agency PTI, the UK Home Office said it would seek to deport foreign criminals at the earliest opportunity, although it did not refer specifically to Kiran Kaur, 53. Foreign nationals sentenced to at least 12 months in prison are generally considered for deportation, subject to exceptions and legal challenges.Kaur was sentenced to three years in prison in July for assisting an offender by removing the weapon used by her son, Vickrum Digwa, to kill Henry Nowak on December 3, 2025. She is expected to be released early under a government scheme aimed at reducing overcrowding in British prisons.Digwa, 23, was sentenced to life imprisonment in June, with a minimum term of 21 years before he becomes eligible for parole.Both Kaur and her son have been granted permission to challenge their sentences, with their appeals scheduled to be heard by the UK Court of Appeal on November 5.Kirpan argument sparks controversyThe case drew widespread attention after Digwa sought to invoke a religious self-defence argument involving the kirpan, a ceremonial knife that Sikhs are legally permitted to carry in the UK.
During Kaur’s sentencing, Justice William Mousley stressed that the kirpan was a symbol of religious faith and was not intended to be carried for offensive purposes. He said any use of the weapon in self-defence would have to be justified by circumstances involving great seriousness and urgency.The judge also criticised Kaur for removing the weapon rather than challenging her son’s actions and encouraging him to do the right thing.He acknowledged that she had experienced a difficult life in India before marrying and moving to the UK nearly 30 years ago. He said she had acted to protect her son rather than for personal gain and was unlikely to reoffend, while making clear that her actions warranted punishment.British Sikh organisations and parliamentarians subsequently condemned what they described as the misrepresentation of the kirpan, stressing that religious protection did not justify the violence in this case.Police conduct under investigationThe killing also triggered scrutiny of police conduct after body-worn camera footage showed officers handcuffing Nowak following Digwa’s allegations that he had been subjected to racism. Those allegations were subsequently rejected in court.
The Independent Office for Police Conduct is investigating the officers’ handling of the incident amid allegations of “two-tier” policing, referring to claims that different communities were treated unequally.The case has heightened tensions in Southampton and the wider Hampshire and Isle of Wight area.Kaur’s potential deportation remains subject to the applicable immigration process, while the outcome of the appeals against her sentence and Digwa’s life term is awaited.

Iranian, Algerian central banks governors discuss enhancing economic cooperation
TEHRAN- The Governor of the Central Bank of Iran met and held talks with Mohand Bouri, Governor of the Central Bank of Algeria, on the sidelines of the Annual Meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
At the meeting, the two sides discussed and exchanged views on the latest status of monetary, banking, and trade relations between the two countries. Enhancing the level of joint economic cooperation and utilizing mutual capacities to strengthen bilateral trade interactions were among the most important themes of the meeting.
The Governor of the Central Bank of Iran, referring to the historical and political commonalities between Iran and Algeria, emphasized the serious determination of the Islamic Republic of Iran to develop and consolidate economic relations with friendly and brotherly countries.
The Governor of the Central Bank of Algeria, while expressing satisfaction with the meeting, emphasized his country’s readiness to expand economic and banking cooperation with Iran and the need to follow up on mutual agreements in line with the interests of the two nations.
In late December, Saeed Zare’ Haghighi, the head of Iran Trade Center in Algeria, said that Algeria’s infrastructure needs offer significant opportunities for exporting technical and engineering services, making the North African country a largely untapped economic market.
He said Africa — and Algeria in particular — should be seen as a strategic destination for the private sector, noting that limited numbers of commercial counsellors made targeted entry into new markets essential.
He described Algeria as a geopolitically secure country with a strategic location close to Europe, adding that after the decline in Russian energy exports, about 20 percent of Europe’s oil and gas is now supplied by Algeria.
Zare’ Haghighi said Algeria’s foreign currency revenues had risen from around $50 billion to more than $300 billion in recent years, generating a trade surplus of $20 billion to $30 billion and creating broad scope for economic cooperation.
He pointed to strong demand in Algeria for technical and engineering services, infrastructure projects, and the construction of silos and storage facilities linked to food security, saying Iranian companies had the technical know-how and experience to meet these needs.
He also highlighted Algeria’s industrial and mining potential, including steel and phosphate, and said the trade center was ready to identify opportunities, guide exporters and promote participation in specialized exhibitions, drawing on models used by countries such as Turkey that combine trade with on-the-ground investment.

Russian missile strikes on Kharkiv injured 15 people, including three children, late Friday evening, Oct. 16, damaging residential high-rises and warehouse infrastructure, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) reported.
According to emergency responders, Russian forces launched a missile strike targeting the city’s Nemyshlianskyi district, with one kinetic impact directly striking a commercial storage warehouse.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The blast ignited a fire spanning 100 square meters and caused structural damage to neighboring multi-story residential apartment buildings and adjacent facilities.
In total, the strikes produced four distinct fires across the impact perimeter. Specialized firefighting units and rescue teams from the DSNS contained and extinguished all four blazes during overnight operations.
Medical personnel and first responders treated 15 injured civilians at the scene and in municipal medical facilities, confirming that three children were among the wounded.
Overnight nationwide barrage and air defense operations
The strikes on Kharkiv formed part of an expansive overnight aerial assault conducted between Friday evening and Saturday morning, Oct. 17, combining ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and strike drones across several Ukrainian regions.
According to an operational summary issued by the Ukrainian Air Force Command, Russian forces launched ballistic missiles – including Iskander-M and KN-23 systems – from Russia’s Voronezh and Rostov regions alongside occupied Crimea, Kh-22 and Kh-32 cruise missiles from Crimean airspace, four sea-launched Kalibr cruise missiles from Novorossiysk, and 332 unmanned aerial vehicles from multiple staging bases across Russia and occupied territories.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 16, 2026
The drone assault incorporated a mix of Shahed loitering munitions – including 31 turbojet-powered variants – alongside S-8000 Banderol compact cruise munitions, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya decoy platforms.
Ukrainian air defense units, combat aviation, electronic warfare teams, and mobile interceptor groups downed or suppressed 293 aerial targets by 8:00 a.m. local time, including all four Kalibr cruise missiles and 289 strike and decoy drones, 23 of which were jet-powered models.
Military authorities confirmed that incoming munitions struck 22 distinct locations nationwide alongside falling debris from intercepted weapons.
Morning strikes on Zaporizhzhia
The Friday evening injuries in Kharkiv were followed early Saturday morning by strikes targeting urban infrastructure in southeastern Ukraine.
Russian forces launched several missiles at the city of Zaporizhzhia shortly after 4:30 a.m. on Saturday, striking an open area surrounded by residential blocks. Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Head Ivan Fedorov confirmed that at least two civilians were injured in the attack, while the blast damaged three residential buildings and set multiple parked vehicles on fire.
The missile arrivals in Zaporizhzhia coincided with widespread air defense alerts issued across central and southern Ukraine, with air defense commands tracking ballistic trajectories toward Kryvyi Rih, Kamianske, and Dnipro in the Dnipropetrovsk region.
Concurrently, the Kyiv City Military Administration declared a red-level emergency alert for the capital as incoming Russian loitering munitions approached from the north, prompting authorities to urge residents to remain in designated shelters until interception operations concluded.

2026-10-17
05:33:54 UTC
14:33:54 KST

For years, Danielle Abraham worked to bring Israel's agricultural expertise and innovation to countries struggling with water shortages, food insecurity and harsh climate conditions. After October 7, that mission took a new direction. Instead of taking Israeli expertise abroad, she sought to bring it home and put it to work for farmers whose livelihoods had been devastated.
Just days after the Hamas attack, Abraham launched ReGrow Israel, an initiative aimed at rebuilding farms and agricultural infrastructure in communities near the Gaza border. Initially, she envisioned it as a consulting service for farmers, with a team of experts assessing their needs and developing long-term recovery plans. But the reality on the ground was far more urgent. Farmers had been left without tractors, equipment or the infrastructure needed to resume operations. Before planning for the years ahead, they needed help getting their farms running again.
What began as an emergency response in southern Israel has since expanded to farms and communities affected by the war in the north. The initiative supports farmers by providing equipment, restoring infrastructure and bringing in professional expertise and technology, while also working to strengthen Israeli agriculture over the long term.
For this work, Abraham will receive the Nefesh B'Nefesh Sylvan Adams Bonei Zion Prize at a ceremony this coming Sunday, marking Aliyah Day. The event will be broadcast live on ynet. Now in its 12th year, the award recognizes immigrants from English-speaking countries who have made exceptional contributions to Israeli society across a range of fields. Abraham was selected in the Global Impact category.
Abraham's journey began more than 15 years ago in a lecture hall in London. An Oxford University music graduate working at Britain's Home Office, she was 23 when she attended a lecture by Israeli agronomist Yitzhak Abt. Abt, who had helped establish Israel's international agricultural assistance program through MASHAV, the Foreign Ministry's Agency for International Development Cooperation, spoke about immigrating to Israel from South Africa and his work advancing agriculture in Israel and developing countries.
When Abraham returned home from the lecture, she told her family: "When I grow up, I want to be him." The encounter changed the course of her life. Abraham left her job, sold her car and immigrated to Israel in 2010.
Israel was not entirely unfamiliar to her. She had visited during summer vacations as a child and had relatives living in the country. She grew up in a Zionist household, was active in a Zionist youth movement and had visited Israel at 16. At Oxford, she led a Jewish student society and defended Israel in public debates. Still, leaving a sought-after job in London to begin life as a new immigrant in Israel was a leap into the unknown.
'Just for a year'
When Abraham accepted a position at Israel's Foreign Ministry, she had not yet fully committed to building her life in the country. She told everyone back home that she was coming for just one year. "Only after six months did I start saying I was thinking about making aliyah," she recalled. "My family and friends said, 'We knew from the moment you got on the plane.'"
Her parents, she said, never told her what to do and supported whatever decision she made. But there was one moment when they realized she was not coming back. "When I bought a piano for my home, they said, 'Now that you have that, you're not coming back.'"
One of her first challenges in Israel was the language. She would write down unfamiliar words she heard and send text messages to a friend asking what they meant. On weekends, she went to the beach with vocabulary lists from her Hebrew classes and memorized them. She also taped the lists to cabinets in her office. "My vocabulary was mostly agriculture and developing countries," she recalled. "I couldn't order food in a restaurant, but I could talk about irrigation."
At the Foreign Ministry, Abraham joined MASHAV and later served as a senior policy adviser, representing Israel at the United Nations, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and the German Development Bank. In many ways, she had fulfilled the ambition sparked by Abt's lecture: using Israeli expertise to solve real-world problems around the globe.
In 2017, she began leading Volcani International Partnerships, an organization that draws on Israeli agricultural knowledge and innovation to address challenges such as food security, water scarcity and farming in difficult climate conditions. Agriculture, she explained, is one of the fields in which Israel is a world leader, combining the Zionist vision with practical benefits.
Bringing the expertise home
After October 7, Abraham decided to use the experience, experts and international connections she had accumulated to help Israeli farmers. "When the extent of the destruction in the Gaza border communities became clear, I saw that some countries facing similar situations turn to outside assistance," she said. "I told everyone, 'We have everything right here: researchers, agronomists, innovation and high-tech. We just need to bring it all together.'"
ReGrow Israel began by providing emergency assistance to farmers in communities near Gaza, including replacing agricultural equipment and repairing damaged infrastructure. The initiative later expanded to farms and communities affected by the war in northern Israel.
Since its establishment, it has raised tens of millions of dollars to help rebuild Israeli agriculture. But Abraham said the goal was not simply to repair what was destroyed. She wanted to use the recovery process to build a stronger, more advanced and more resilient agricultural sector.
For Abraham, agriculture is more than an economic industry. It is closely tied to Israel's food security, the livelihoods of residents in outlying regions and the ability to sustain communities along the country's borders. "If agriculture isn't strong there, we won't have communities on the border," she said. Yet she believes Israel still does not sufficiently recognize agriculture as a strategic asset. "I still don't see enough effort being made to use it to strengthen Israel, both at home and abroad."
Despite everything October 7 changed in her life and work, Abraham has no doubts about her decision to immigrate. "Of course," she replied when asked whether she would choose Israel again. "You have to be a little crazy to live here, but you have to believe."
Looking back at the young woman who arrived alone in 2010, barely speaking Hebrew, Abraham sees a quality she is still trying to preserve. "I see a brave young woman with a kind of naivety that's important today. Everything was possible. I wasn't willing to take no for an answer," she said. "That's the spirit I try to hold on to, even as reality changes. We need people with big visions and hope, who make decisions that aren't crazy but are a little courageous, and who start with small things."
Alongside Abraham, several other immigrants will receive the Nefesh B'Nefesh Sylvan Adams Bonei Zion Prize. Naomi Stuchiner, founder of Beit Issie Shapiro, will receive the award in the Community and Non-Profit category; Dr. Philip Klipstein, a senior researcher in science and technology, will be honored in the Science and Medicine category; Rabbanit Chana Henkin, founder and dean of Nishmat, the Jeanie Schottenstein Center for Advanced Torah Study for Women, will receive the Education award; and Ami Baran, president of the Israel Athletics Association and CEO of the Israel Softball Association, will be recognized in the Culture, Arts and Sports category.
Professor Marta Weinstock-Rosin, a neuropharmacologist who developed Exelon, a drug used to treat Alzheimer's disease, will receive the Lifetime Achievement Award. Barak Swarttz, a content creator and founder of GRIT for Good, will receive the Young Leadership Award, while former ambassador Ron Dermer, who served as Israel's ambassador to the United States and strategic affairs minister, will receive a special recognition award.
For Abraham, the honor provides a platform not only for her work but also for Israeli agriculture and for immigrants seeking to find their place in the country. She said she still feels like "a little girl from London who made a small effort." To her, the message behind the award is simple: "You can come here and make a contribution, whether big or small."

Trade unions push for EU law to address menopause at work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:32:41 UTC
14:32:41 KST

The European Trade Union Confederation wants menopause enshrined in EU workplace legislation, as the European Parliament examines the issue and the Commission stops short of proposing a dedicated strategy.
The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC), which represents 45 million members across 41 European countries, is pushing for menopause to be recognised in EU workplace law, arguing that a lack of support is costing women earnings, career opportunities and pension income.
“Women’s work-related health risks remain largely ignored by the law, which remains orientated around male-dominated jobs,” said ETUC Deputy General Secretary Isabelle Schömann. “It’s high time that the law caught up with the reality of the whole workforce today and the risks facing them.”
The push comes as the European Parliament examines a report calling for menopause to be treated as an economic, employment and social issue, while the European Commission has stopped short of proposing a dedicated EU menopause strategy.
Menopause, which typically occurs between the ages of 45 and 55, affects a significant proportion of the workforce. Around 30% of women experience symptoms that affect their capacity to work, including fatigue, sleep disruption, hot flushes, joint pain, anxiety and difficulties concentrating. Around 85 % of women experience at least one of those symptoms.
Research cited by the confederation found that women's earnings in Norway fell by 7.4% by the fourth year after a menopause diagnosis, with reduced working hours, sick leave and missed promotions contributing to the decline.
“Loss of pay, lost promotions, and lower pensions is the price being paid by millions of women for the failure to adapt work to the menopause,” Schömann said.
Pressure builds for EU action
The campaign comes amid growing recognition of menopause in the EU's gender equality agenda, although concrete workplace protections remain largely a matter for national legislation and employers.
In November 2025, Equality Commissioner Hadja Lahbib said the Commission was not planning a dedicated EU strategy on menopause, while pointing to research projects funded through Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe addressing its medical and social impacts.
The Commission has since included menopause in its Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2030, published in March. The strategy commits to exchanging national best practices on tackling menstrual and menopause poverty and to a study, planned for 2028, on the economic and societal benefits of closing the women's health gap, including menopause.
The commitments mark a shift towards recognising menopause in the EU's wider equality agenda, but stop short of proposing dedicated legislation setting out workplace rights for menopausal employees.
The European Parliament is seeking to push the issue further. Spanish Socialist MEP Lina Gálvez is leading a draft report titled Menopause beyond a health issue: turning menopause into an economic, working and social priority.
The draft, which will be further discussed at the plenary session only next year, calls for a dedicated EU strategy, broader research, public campaigns to challenge stigma, better workplace support and improved access to healthcare.
“It is therefore essential to have an EU strategy that includes broader and more inclusive EU research, evidence-based public campaigns to change the social perceptions, improved workplace support and improved access to healthcare,” Gálvez wrote in the draft report. “It is time for the EU to tackle menopause.”
The report remains a parliamentary initiative, rather than adopted EU policy.
Unions want changes at work
For the ETUC, the priority is to ensure that menopause is reflected in the way workplaces are organised and regulated.
Its demands include risk assessments covering workplace temperature, ventilation and facilities; flexible hours and remote working; training for managers and human resources staff; and physical adjustments such as temperature controls and ergonomic equipment.
The confederation also wants menopause policies negotiated with trade unions, then implemented and monitored, alongside free menstrual and menopause products at work.
“The way work is organised can make a crucial difference in deciding the impact of the menopause,” Schömann said, adding that unions are already negotiating collective agreements covering workplace adjustments and flexible arrangements.

Lapland airports expect 5–10% passenger growth this winter
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:31:59 EEST
14:31:59 KST

Airports in Finnish Lapland expect passenger numbers to increase by 5–10% during the coming winter season, prompting airport operator Finavia to recruit 20% more seasonal workers and expand facilities to accommodate growing international tourism.
Finavia announced on Wednesday that airline operations at Lapland's airports are forecast to increase by 4–8%, driven by direct international flights and passengers connecting through Helsinki Airport.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The company has spent the year preparing its airports in Rovaniemi, Kittilä, Ivalo and Kuusamo for the winter tourism season, investing in infrastructure, passenger services and staffing.
Finavia opened 120 seasonal positions across the four airports in June, representing a 20% increase from 2025. The recruitment campaign attracted 460 applications, nearly 60% more than the previous year.
The additional employees will more than double Finavia's workforce at the airports during winter. The recruits include returning seasonal workers and people beginning their careers in aviation.
"We believe that tourism in Lapland will continue to grow, which is why we are developing our airports proactively," said Henri Hansson, Finavia's Senior Vice President for the Airport Network.
The company has also introduced measures to manage increasing flight volumes, particularly at Rovaniemi and Kittilä airports.
Both airports adopted international slot coordination during the 2025–2026 winter season. Under the system, an independent coordinator allocates arrival and departure times to airlines according to available airport capacity.
Finavia said the arrangement distributes flights more evenly throughout the day, reducing congestion and allowing airport operators to allocate staff and equipment according to demand.
"Slot coordination has worked well. It spreads air traffic more evenly over different hours of the day, which prevents air traffic congestion," Hansson said.
Infrastructure improvements have also been completed at several airports.
At Rovaniemi Airport, Finavia finished a ground transport development project in September, adding approximately 4,000 square metres of parking space for 130 cars.
The project also reorganised areas used by taxis, buses and private vehicles to improve traffic flow outside the terminal.
Rovaniemi and Kittilä airports have received replacement self-service check-in machines, allowing passengers to complete check-in procedures and print baggage labels.
At Ivalo Airport, Finavia installed self-service baggage drop machines to reduce reliance on staffed counters during peak periods.
The airport operator said maintaining punctuality remains a priority as passenger numbers increase.
According to Finavia's operational data from 2023 to 2026, punctuality at Lapland's airports has generally remained between 98% and 100%, including during periods of heavy snowfall and runway maintenance.
Finavia said Rovaniemi Airport achieved higher operational punctuality during the record-breaking 2025–2026 winter season than in the previous year, despite handling more passengers.
The company also reported maintaining customer satisfaction levels during the period.
Hansson said Finavia intends to continue developing airport infrastructure and operational processes as demand for travel to Lapland increases.

Xiplomacy: Xi's decades-long commitment to poverty reduction
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:29:00 CST
14:29:00 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Poverty eradication is "a common ideal of humanity," Chinese President Xi Jinping has once said.
Five years after China declared a complete victory in the fight against absolute poverty in 2021, its approach continues to inspire poverty reduction efforts worldwide.
Xi's dedication to poverty alleviation spans decades, from his early work in poor rural communities to the nationwide campaign he led and his efforts to promote international cooperation -- a long-running endeavor that resonates as the world marks the International Day for the Eradication of Poverty on Saturday.
A DECADES-LONG PURSUIT
"A weak hatchling bird can be the first to fly, and the poorest can be the first to become rich," Xi wrote in a 1988 essay on the development of Ningde Prefecture in east China's Fujian Province.
The following summer, Xi, then Ningde's Party secretary, traveled by car and on foot to reach Xiadang, a remote mountain township that had no road access.
Xi returned to Xiadang twice, helping tackle problems with roads, electricity and water supplies. In 2019, residents wrote to tell him that their township had shaken off poverty, and he replied with congratulations.
After becoming China's top leader, Xi continued his hands-on approach to poverty reduction. He conducted more than 50 inspections and research visits related to poverty alleviation, traveling to all 14 of the country's contiguous areas of extreme poverty.
In February 2018, Xi visited impoverished Yi families in Zhaojue County, Sichuan Province, asking about their livelihoods and discussing ways to tackle poverty with villagers and local officials.
"Not a single ethnic group or family should be left behind in building a moderately prosperous society in all respects," he said during the visit.
On Feb. 25, 2021, Xi declared a "complete victory" in China's fight against absolute poverty. Over eight years, nearly 100 million rural residents had been lifted out of absolute poverty, enabling the country to meet the poverty reduction target of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development a decade ahead of schedule.
In a congratulatory letter to Xi, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called the achievement "a reason for hope and inspiration to the entire community of nations."
LESSONS BEYOND BORDERS
China's poverty reduction experience has attracted attention from leaders around the world, some of whom have sought inspiration from Xi's writings and visited places where his ideas were put into practice.
Xi's early ideas on poverty reduction and economic development were collected in "Up and Out of Poverty," a collection of speeches, articles and interviews from 1988 to 1990 during his tenure in Ningde. Explaining the title, Xi wrote that its significance lay first and foremost in uprooting the "poverty mentality" and "poverty thinking."
In a foreword to the book's Uzbek edition published in 2023, President of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev said the work remained an important source of guidance for state and social governance more than three decades after its initial publication.
During his visit to China this month, President of Botswana Duma Gideon Boko traveled to Fuzhou and Ningde in Fujian Province, where Xi once worked, and visited an exhibition on poverty reduction. During talks with Xi in Beijing, Boko depicted China's development as "an economic and political miracle never seen in history."
In June 2018, Bounnhang Vorachith, then President of Laos, visited Shibadong Village in central China's Hunan Province to learn about China's approach to poverty reduction. In villager Shi Basan's home, he paused before a photograph showing Xi chatting with her beside a fire pit.
During that November 2013 visit, Xi first proposed "targeted poverty alleviation" in a discussion with villagers, calling for measures tailored to local conditions and each household's needs.
After retracing Xi's route and speaking with residents, Bounnhang voiced hope of bringing the village's experience back to Laos. In reply to a letter from the villagers the following year, he praised Shibadong's success as offering invaluable lessons for his country.
In September 2026, Prime Minister of Madagascar Mamitiana Rajaonarison also visited Shibadong, where he witnessed first-hand residents' changing lives and watched demonstrations of traditional Miao ethnic embroidery. He said the visit shown him Xi's deep concern for the people and provided inspiration for Madagascar.
TURNING EXPERIENCE INTO ACTION
Xi's efforts to share China's poverty reduction experience abroad date back to his early tenure in Fujian Province.
There, he promoted Juncao technology as part of Fujian's poverty reduction cooperation with northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. In 2000, he introduced the technology to a visiting governor from Papua New Guinea and later helped establish a China-aided Juncao demonstration base in the Pacific island country.
Juncao technology uses grass to cultivate mushrooms and provide livestock feed. The technology has spread to more than 100 countries, creating hundreds of thousands of jobs.
In Zimbabwe, farmer Mandiudza Masvongo has earned 330 U.S. dollars from selling mushrooms since taking up Juncao cultivation in June 2025. The proceeds have helped her start a small cleaning products business, which she said could mark a turning point in her life.
Beyond agriculture, China's development assistance has also improved basic services and created opportunities for small businesses. In Cambodia's Tanorn village, a China-aided project brought better roads, clean water and solar power. Por Sokhim, once dependent on rice farming, now runs a grocery store, while her husband operates a motorcycle repair shop.
In 2021, Xi proposed the Global Development Initiative, with poverty reduction and food security among its priorities. In the five years since its launch, cooperation projects under the initiative have taken root and delivered tangible results in more than 120 countries.
At the 2024 G20 summit in Rio de Janeiro, Xi drew upon China's experience to express confidence in the prospects for poverty reduction across the developing world.
"If China can make it, other developing countries can make it too. This is what China's battle against poverty says to the world," he told world leaders. ■

Pärnu to swap public recycling for curbside pickup in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:23:00 UTC
14:23:00 KST

Pärnu to swap public recycling for curbside pickup in 2027
Pärnu is switching to curbside pickup for sorted household waste in 2027, eliminating public paper and recycling dumpsters from across the city.
Pärnu City Council unanimously approved the city's 2027–2031 waste management plan on Thursday, paving the way for a new system that shifts recycling from public dumpsters to curbside pickup.
Under the new plan, only public glass collection dumpsters will remain. Deputy Mayor Robert Kiviselg said producer responsibility organizations (PROs) will cover much of the cost of the new system.
"Under state rules, [households] will have to pay 50 cents per quarter for paper and cardboard and another 50 cents for the remaining mixed packaging," he said.
Residents will be free to choose between special bags and dedicated recycling bins.
Public recycling dumpsters have often been plagued with issues, including considerable amounts of waste being dumped in the wrong dumpsters. Curbside pickup, however, will make it easier to ensure residents are sorting their waste correctly.
Ivo Jaanisoo, deputy secretary general at the Ministry of Climate, said many households across the country have already gotten better at sorting their waste.
"Since last year, we've been offering separate biowaste pickup right from people's homes, and that's already shown results," he said.
Pärnu's new waste management plan will take effect next fall.

US 'cuts off' Iran from maritime trade as pressure campaign targets oil revenue, military funding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:20:35 UTC
14:20:35 KST

US Central Command (CENTCOM) Commander Admiral Brad Cooper claimed on Friday that Iran has been cut off from maritime imports and exports as Washington intensified its campaign against Tehran's oil revenue and military funding.
In a video message, Cooper said US efforts focused on three areas: restricting Iranian oil exports, disrupting digital financing and weakening the ability of Iran's security forces to pay their personnel.
"As a point of emphasis, with the exception of the humanitarian assistance we've allowed in, Iran has no exports and no imports by sea," Cooper said.
He said US forces have prevented Iran from exporting at least $25 billion worth of crude oil in recent months.
"CENTCOM has also supported US interagency partners in freezing nearly $350 million in digital cryptocurrency assets, further constricting Iran's ability to fund terrorism or replace weapons and factories that we destroy," he said.
Cooper claimed that Iran-aligned groups operating across the region had begun withholding payments to their fighters to redirect funds to the IRGC, which he said was also struggling to pay its personnel.
According to Cooper, the IRGC was also struggling to pay its personnel.
"The Islamic regime is clearly feeling the economic pain, and the IRGC is increasingly showing signs of greater desperation as a result," he said.
US claims Strait of Hormuz remains open
Despite the restrictions on Iranian maritime trade, Cooper said commercial shipping continued through the Strait of Hormuz.
He accused Iran of attacking commercial vessels and said US forces were working with regional allies and shipping industry partners to strengthen maritime security.
"Let me be clear: the Strait of Hormuz is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran, and it remains open for business," Cooper said.
He said approximately 400 merchant ships had transited the strait over the previous seven days.
He added that US forces had assisted Gulf partners in transporting more than 100 million barrels of crude oil through the waterway during the same period, bringing the total volume shipped with US assistance in recent months to more than 1.3 billion barrels.

Russian attacks in Ukraine kill at least 8, cut power to 1 million
Russia strikes Kharkiv, Kramatorsk, Volyn and Rivne as Russia presses its campaign against Ukraine’s power grid.
Russian attacks killed at least eight people and injured 60 across Ukraine, hit two shopping centres and cut power to more than a million people, Ukrainian officials have said.
The attacks on Friday struck nine regions. In the eastern city of Kharkiv, a 71-year-old woman and a 58-year-old man were killed and 12 people were wounded in strikes on three districts, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
Two people were killed in Kramatorsk, a frontline city in the Donetsk region, and two more in the southeastern Dnipropetrovsk region.
In the northwestern Volyn region, which borders Poland, a drone strike on a food-processing facility killed one person and wounded eight, Governor Roman Romaniuk said.
Drones also hit a customs terminal and set fire to about 10 trucks in the town of Kovel, on a major road from Kyiv to Poland.
In Rivne, drones hit a major shopping centre and other sites, killing one person and wounding seven, regional governor Oleksandr Koval said.
A shopping centre in Sumy, close to the front line, was also hit.
Power cuts
Ukraine’s Ministry of Energy said repair crews had restored power to more than a million people who lost it on Friday.
In Volyn, about 370,000 households lost power, with supply since restored to at least 100,000 of them.
The blackout could last at least 24 hours in the regional capital, Lutsk, Mayor Andriy Razumovskyi said.
Large parts of Rivne were also left without power.
Russia’s military chief told President Vladimir Putin on Friday that the military had allocated the assets needed to press its aerial campaign against Ukraine’s energy system.
Civilian toll
Meanwhile, the United Nations said on Friday that civilian casualties in Ukraine had climbed steeply.
According to UN human rights monitors, at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 wounded in Ukraine last month, 85 percent more than in September 2025.
Between January and September 2026, 2,570 civilians were killed and 15,211 wounded, almost 60 percent more than in the same period last year and more than twice the 2024 level, the report said.
“The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest periods for civilians in years,” said Danielle Bell, head of the UN’s human rights monitoring mission in Ukraine.

Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:14:50 UTC
14:14:50 KST

Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain
Scientists have uncovered a hidden brain circuit linking deep sleep, growth hormone, and wakefulness, revealing why a good night's sleep is essential for both body and brain health.
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising two-way relationship between sleep and growth hormone, revealing how the brain carefully balances physical recovery with wakefulness. The findings could help explain why poor sleep harms metabolism and brain health, potentially opening the door to new treatments for sleep and neurological disorders.
- Share:
A good night's sleep does much more than leave you feeling refreshed. During deep sleep, the body releases growth hormone, a powerful chemical messenger that helps build muscle, strengthen bones, and regulate fat metabolism. For teenagers, getting enough sleep is especially important because growth hormone plays a major role in reaching their full height potential.
Scientists have long known that insufficient sleep can interfere with growth hormone production. What remained unclear was exactly how the brain controls this process, particularly during non-REM sleep, the deep, restorative stage that typically dominates the earlier part of the night.
Now, researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have uncovered the brain circuitry behind this relationship. In a study published in the journal Cell, the team identified the neurons that regulate growth hormone release during sleep and discovered a previously unknown feedback system that helps maintain a delicate balance between hormone levels and wakefulness.
The discovery reveals that the relationship works in both directions. Sleep stimulates growth hormone production, but growth hormone also sends signals back to the brain that influence when we wake up.
The findings could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to treating sleep disorders associated with metabolic diseases such as diabetes, as well as neurological conditions including Parkinson's and Alzheimer's.
"People know that growth hormone release is tightly related to sleep, but only through drawing blood and checking growth hormone levels during sleep," said study first author Xinlu Ding, a postdoctoral fellow in UC Berkeley's Department of Neuroscience and the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute. "We're actually directly recording neural activity in mice to see what's going on. We are providing a basic circuit to work on in the future to develop different treatments."
Why Deep Sleep Matters for Growth and Metabolism
Growth hormone is best known for its role in childhood development, but its importance extends well into adulthood. It supports the maintenance of muscle and bone, helps the body regulate how it uses stored fat, and influences blood sugar levels.
When sleep is consistently disrupted, growth hormone regulation can suffer. Because this hormone helps control glucose and fat metabolism, inadequate sleep may contribute to an increased risk of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.
To understand how the brain coordinates these processes, the Berkeley researchers focused on a region called the hypothalamus. Located deep within the brain, this small but essential control center helps regulate hunger, body temperature, hormone production, and the daily cycle of sleeping and waking. Its basic functions have been preserved throughout mammalian evolution.
Within the hypothalamus, the researchers examined neurons that produce growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) and two distinct types of neurons that produce somatostatin.
These chemical messengers have opposing functions. GHRH encourages growth hormone secretion, while somatostatin suppresses it. Together, they help control how much growth hormone enters the bloodstream, largely by regulating its release from the pituitary gland, a small hormone-producing structure at the base of the brain.
The scientists also investigated how growth hormone influences the locus coeruleus, a region in the brainstem involved in alertness, attention, thinking, and the drive to explore new or unfamiliar experiences.
Disruptions in the activity of this region have been linked to several psychiatric and neurological disorders.
"Understanding the neural circuit for growth hormone release could eventually point toward new hormonal therapies to improve sleep quality or restore normal growth hormone balance," said Daniel Silverman, a UC Berkeley postdoctoral fellow and study co-author. "There are some experimental gene therapies where you target a specific cell type. This circuit could be a novel handle to try to dial back the excitability of the locus coeruleus, which hasn't been talked about before."
Scientists Map the Brain Circuit That Controls Growth Hormone
The research was conducted in the laboratory of Yang Dan, a professor of neuroscience and of molecular and cell biology at UC Berkeley.
To investigate how the circuitry works, the team studied mice using electrodes implanted in their brains. The scientists recorded neural activity while using light to stimulate specific neurons in the hypothalamus, allowing them to observe how different parts of the system responded.
Mice are particularly useful for studying sleep regulation because their sleep patterns differ significantly from those of humans. Rather than sleeping through one long stretch each night, mice typically sleep in brief episodes lasting only several minutes, scattered throughout the day and night.
This gave the researchers repeated opportunities to examine how neural activity and growth hormone regulation changed as the animals moved between sleeping and waking.
Using advanced techniques to trace connections between brain cells, the team discovered that GHRH and somatostatin behave differently depending on the stage of sleep.
During rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, the stage commonly associated with vivid dreaming, activity involving both GHRH and somatostatin increases. Although these hormones normally exert opposing effects, their coordinated activity during this stage contributes to increased growth hormone release.
During non-REM sleep, the pattern changes. Somatostatin activity decreases, reducing its inhibitory influence, while GHRH activity rises moderately. This combination also promotes growth hormone secretion.
The discovery helps explain how different sleep stages can support the release of the same essential hormone through distinct patterns of brain activity.
Growth Hormone Also Helps Control When We Wake Up
Perhaps the most surprising finding was that growth hormone does not simply respond to signals from the sleeping brain. It also influences the brain circuits that control wakefulness.
As growth hormone gradually builds up during sleep, it stimulates neurons in the locus coeruleus, increasing their activity and helping promote the transition toward waking.
This creates a feedback loop in which sleep encourages growth hormone release, and the resulting hormone activity helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.
The researchers also identified an unexpected complication. Although greater activity in the locus coeruleus generally promotes alertness, excessive stimulation can have the opposite effect.
In an earlier study published the same year, Silverman demonstrated that when neurons in this region become overexcited, they can paradoxically promote sleepiness rather than wakefulness.
Together, these findings reveal a carefully regulated system in which the brain must balance competing signals to maintain healthy sleep and hormone activity.
Scientists describe this type of self-regulating process as homeostasis, the body's ability to maintain stable internal conditions even as its environment and physiological demands change.
"This suggests that sleep and growth hormone form a tightly balanced system: Too little sleep reduces growth hormone release, and too much growth hormone can in turn push the brain toward wakefulness," Silverman said. "Sleep drives growth hormone release, and growth hormone feeds back to regulate wakefulness, and this balance is essential for growth, repair and metabolic health."
A Surprising Connection Between Sleep and Brain Health
The newly identified feedback system may have implications that extend beyond physical growth and metabolism.
Because the locus coeruleus helps regulate attention, alertness, and cognitive function, growth hormone's influence on this region suggests it could also play a role in how effectively the brain functions after waking.
This raises the possibility that maintaining healthy sleep and growth hormone rhythms may support both physical recovery and mental performance.
"Growth hormone not only helps you build your muscle and bones and reduce your fat tissue, but may also have cognitive benefits, promoting your overall arousal level when you wake up," Ding said.
By identifying the specific brain cells and signaling pathways involved, the researchers have provided a foundation for exploring therapies that target disrupted sleep and hormone regulation.
Such approaches could eventually prove useful for people with sleep disturbances related to metabolic disorders or neurological diseases. However, the experiments were conducted in mice, and additional research will be needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans and whether they can be safely targeted with treatments.
The findings underscore a fundamental principle of sleep biology: Rest is not simply a period when the brain switches off. It is an active, carefully coordinated process in which hormones and neural circuits constantly communicate to support growth, repair, metabolism, and wakefulness.
Research Funding and Contributors
The research was supported by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI), which supported Dan as an HHMI investigator until the year of the study's publication, and the Pivotal Life Sciences Chancellor's Chair fund.
Dan holds the Pivotal Life Sciences Chancellor's Chair in Neuroscience.
Additional co-authors include Peng Zhong, Bing Li, Chenyan Ma, Lihui Lu, Grace Jiang, Zhe Zhang, Xiaolin Huang, Xun Tu, and Zhiyu Melissa Tian of UC Berkeley, along with Fuu-Jiun Hwang and Jun Ding of Stanford University.

Journal Reference:

Neuroendocrine circuit for sleep-dependent growth hormone release. Cell, 2025; 188 (18): 4968 DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2025.05.039

PARIS – Clashes broke out between police and protesters in cities across France on Oct 17 as tens of thousands of people angered by living costs and declining public services took to the streets in some of the country’s most violent protests in years.
The Interior Ministry said 272 people had been arrested by mid-afternoon after violent incidents involving hooded individuals, including in Paris, Marseille in the south, Toulouse in the south-west, Angers in the west and Lyon in east-central France.
The protesters said most people were protesting peacefully and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police.
The ministry said, however, that violence was increasing, and that there had been “confrontations with law enforcement, looting or attempted looting of shops, attacks on and damage to public buildings”.
It blamed the unrest on what it described as the “ultra-left”.
In some parts of Paris, police occasionally fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks and goggles to protect against tear gas.
Some tourists at a fashionable department store near the Paris opera were seen spluttering when they were caught in clouds of tear gas, and shops nearby were hastily shuttered.

In Lyon, protesters torched the tourist office.

Police response under scrutiny

“We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions,” said a 19-year-old protester in Paris who gave her name as Lola.
A large police presence had been deployed in central Paris, especially near landmarks such as the Champs-Elysees and the Arc de Triomphe, which were excluded from the routes of two authorised demonstrations.
Protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, recalling the Yellow Vest movement that marked President Emmanuel Macron’s previous term in office.
Police tactics have drawn criticism following a series of injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who had his hand blown off after picking up a stun grenade. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said more than 900 police personnel had also been injured.
The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen cases of alleged police violence. France suspended the use of stun grenades for the student demonstrations, but Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said they could be used in the protest on Oct 17.
The Yellow Vest movement started in 2018 as a protest against taxes on diesel before expanding into an outpouring of anger at high living costs and income inequality.
The movement subsided after Macron announced billions of euros in tax cuts. REUTERS

German minister seeks debt-brake exemption to sustain Ukraine aid
BANGKOK, Oct 17 - Germany's development minister is seeking an exemption from the country's debt brake, a constitutional limit on government borrowing, for Ukraine funding, arguing that much of Germany's civilian support for Ukraine comes from her ministry's budget.
"The Russian attacks are more severe than ever, leading to more deaths, more destruction, more suffering. But as budget cuts for development assistance continue, we simply will not be able to maintain our support for Ukraine at this level," Reem Alabali Radovan told Reuters on Friday, on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank meetings.
Funding for Ukraine in her ministry's budget amounts to about €330 million ($371 million) this year, down from €670 million in 2022 and €750 million in 2023.
"At this point, it is not a political decision; we just face massive cuts and it will no longer be possible," Alabali Radovan said. "This is especially hard as the money is wisely invested in Ukraine's and Europe's stability."
Alabali Radovan is a member of the Social Democrats, the junior partner of the governing coalition led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU.
Her proposal has the backing of Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, a member of the conservative CDU, but faces opposition from other members of the party who oppose further exceptions to borrowing rules beyond those already approved, such as for defence spending.
"I am already prioritising support for Ukraine, but there are many other crises and conflicts, too. And we work in the long term, which means large parts of our budget are already committed," Alabali Radovan said.
"That means the cuts hit crisis instruments above all, because – naturally – they work with flexible funds that are not yet pre-committed."
Alabali Radovan added that she supports Merz's call for other countries to contribute more.
"We are the strongest supporters, and I believe others can and should contribute more," she said. REUTERS

746 aftershocks recorded in Panama after 7.5 earthquake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17

746 aftershocks recorded in Panama after 7.5 earthquake
More than 740 aftershocks have been recorded across Panama since a powerful magnitude 7.5 earthquake struck on Oct. 9, with scientists monitoring ongoing seismic activity and investigating reports of significant changes along the country's Pacific coastline, Qazinform News Agency cites Anadolu Agency.
Nestor Luque, director of the Institute of Geosciences at the University of Panama, said aftershocks from an earthquake of this magnitude could continue for up to two months. The shallow quake, which occurred at a depth of less than 10 kilometers, released enough energy to trigger ongoing adjustments within the Earth's crust, though aftershocks are gradually weakening.
Authorities stressed that recent tremors detected in the provinces of Chiriquí and Bocas del Toro appear to be linked to separate fault systems and are not necessarily connected to the Oct. 9 earthquake.
Meanwhile, geologists are assessing reports from coastal communities where residents have observed exposed rock formations and what appears to be a retreat of the sea. Experts say tectonic movements can cause land to rise or sink, potentially altering coastal landscapes.
Scientists are also examining unusual changes in seawater color, including grayish shades reported by some residents. One possible explanation is that underground water mixed with minerals released during the earthquake, although laboratory analysis will be needed to determine the exact cause.
On Isla Cañas in Los Santos Province, residents have reported that the island may have developed new fractures following the quake. Researchers plan to conduct field studies to determine whether any cracks extend across the island and into surrounding waters, which could indicate fault displacement.
The Institute of Geosciences has called for stronger seismic monitoring infrastructure, estimating that around 150 additional instruments would be needed to improve earthquake observation nationwide. A comprehensive early-warning network, meanwhile, could require as many as 700 sensors across the country.
Earlier, an earthquake with an intensity of up to four magnitude points was registered in Kamchatka.

Trump waives several Russia sanctions as new US law takes effect
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:02:50 BST
14:02:50 KST

Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
- Published
Donald Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.
The sanctions were passed by the Congress and signed into law the president in September.
But Trump issued an executive order Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US national interest, prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.
Trump and Zelensky have exchanged sharp words about one another. Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy by giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.
It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.
- Trump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network 
  - Published1 day ago
- Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC 
  - Published22 hours ago
Many of these provisions have now been waived by Trump.
Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev called the waiver "an important and truly historic moment".
Posting on X, he said the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage", primarily on the US and global market, and that economic cooperation benefits both nations.
Democrats including the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer criticised the move, accusing Trump of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky.
"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer wrote on X.
A handful of Republicans, too, have come out against the move.
Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, a Trump ally, called waving sanctions against Russia a mistake, saying on Fox News: "I wish the president hadn't done it."
He added there were other ways to could address diesel prices and "the current path, unfortunately, just... benefits Putin and that's not a good idea."
Senator John Cornyn, also of Texas, said on X: "Helping Putin in Ukraine is reckless. He would not stop with Ukraine and our NATO allies would be next."
North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis called it "beyond irresponsible", noting the sanctions legislation passed the chamber with bipartisan support and a large majority - only 11 senators voted against it.
Trump could bring down energy prices "by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin," he said.
Nebraska Representative Don Bacon said many lawmakers will resist funding the president's agenda "knowing he is propping up a dictator's invasion and throwing an ally under the bus".
The move is likely to draw further anger from Ukraine, where Zelensky has long stressed the need for stringent sanctions to limit funding Russia can use in its war effort.
Zelensky said on Saturday morning that the sanctions "could have helped enormously" and that the law was "supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end".
He pointed to Russian overnight attacks on 15 Ukrainian energy facilities that had caused power cuts in several regions and said: "Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter."
Zelensky said it was "important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening" on the ground.
He later told reporters that he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.
Negotiators from Ukraine spoke to their US counterparts on Friday and that both teams could meet next week, he also said.
Trump was initially criticised by Zelensky and Ukraine's European allies for temporarily suspending some US sanctions to import Russian diesel in a bid to bring down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war. His Republican party is at risk of losing control of the US Congress, in next month's midterm elections, largely due to voters' sour mood about affordability.
Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.
A few days later, Trump claimed that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to facilitate the export of Russian diesel.
Both nations have been intensively striking one another's energy infrastructure. Kyiv says this is to limit revenue for Russia's war machine, while Moscow claims it only targets facilities used by the Ukrainian military.
Zelensky initially expressed surprise at Trump's announcement, and said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same. After three days of fresh attacks from Russia, Kyiv resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Trump, condemned Ukraine's strikes as a disgrace, but Zelensky said he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests".
Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine.
Last week Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield missions, Ukraine said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks.
During the slowdown, Russia launched several deadly strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying these came with no prior warning.
Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that Ukraine had been told by US officials the speed restrictions were linked to technical issues.
However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found "these problems do not exist" and the system was operating at higher speeds.
Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing and deliberately slowing down the network.
Ukrainian authorities have confirmed that at least nine people have been killed and around 60 injured in Russian strikes across the country over the past 24 hours. That included an ambulance driver killed and 20 others injured in a Russian strike on the city of Kherson, they said.
Russia's defence ministry said it had targeted industries linked to Ukraine's defence industry - including steel works, an electrical sub-station and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.
Additional reporting by Helen Sullivan and Sareen Habeshian
