Trump imposed "hellish" sanctions on Russia and immediately suspended their implementation – BBC
Kyiv • UNN
Donald Trump formally introduced sweeping sanctions against Russia but postponed their implementation indefinitely. He explained the decision by citing U.S. national interests.
U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order imposing sweeping sanctions against Russia, but immediately suspended their implementation for an indefinite period. The restrictions are provided for by a law passed by Congress to increase economic pressure on the Kremlin over the war against Ukraine. BBC reports, UNN writes.
Details
The law, known as the Graham Act, required the U.S. president to impose new sanctions by October 18. At the same time, the document allows the White House chief to temporarily suspend their implementation if this serves the national interests of the United States.
Trump invoked precisely this provision. On Friday, he signed an executive order formally imposing the new restrictions, but at the same time postponed their implementation without setting an end date.
Why Trump abandoned new sanctions against Russia
“By this, I am suspending the implementation of the sanctions, restrictive measures, and tariffs provided for by the Graham Act. I have sent Congress official confirmation that granting such a delay at this stage serves the national interests of the United States,”
The new law provides, in particular, for the possibility of imposing tariffs of up to 100% on goods from countries that purchase Russian oil and gas or help Moscow evade sanctions. The document also concerns Russia’s shadow fleet and financial sector.
Experts link Trump’s decision to the energy crisis caused by the war with Iran. Earlier, the U.S. president had already authorized the purchase of Russian diesel fuel, explaining this as necessary to curb rising fuel prices in the United States.
At the same time, the existing U.S. sanctions against Russia were not lifted. The new law codified some of the restrictions imposed earlier, but additional sanctions mechanisms remained suspended. Experts estimate that such a policy could weaken the West’s economic pressure on the Kremlin.

Azerbaijan announced plans to resume purchasing Russian natural gas from Gazprom during Russian Energy Week in Moscow on Friday, Oct. 16, signaling renewed energy cooperation with Moscow as Western countries seek to curb the revenues financing Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Elshad Nasirov, vice president of Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR, told participants at the Moscow forum that Baku was interested in restarting gas purchases and exchange operations with Russia’s state-controlled energy giant.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“SOCAR is the only company in the world which started out buying gas from Gazprom and then began supplying gas to Gazprom, and now we want to start buying and exchanging gas with Gazprom once again,” Nasirov said, according to Interfax’s report from Moscow.
Nasirov acknowledged that the two sides had not agreed on specific purchase volumes or delivery dates.
The declaration is particularly significant because Azerbaijan has positioned itself as an alternative supplier of natural gas to Europe since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Azerbaijani gas flows to European markets through the Southern Gas Corridor, a pipeline network supported by the European Union as part of its strategy to reduce dependence on Russian fossil fuels.
The prospect of renewed Russian gas imports into Azerbaijan raises questions about how Baku intends to balance its expanding commercial relationship with Gazprom against its commitments to European energy diversification.
Zelensky: Starlink Still Not Fully Restored, Disrupting Drone Defense and Frontline Supplies
In July 2022, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed an agreement to expand cooperation on natural gas supplies.
The European Commission’s memorandum envisaged increasing the Southern Gas Corridor’s annual capacity to at least 20 billion cubic meters by 2027.
Brussels presented the arrangement as part of its REPowerEU strategy to reduce dependence on Russian energy following Moscow’s invasion.
“We will double the supply of gas from Azerbaijan to the European Union,” von der Leyen said when the agreement was signed.
She described the Southern Gas Corridor as an important route for replacing Russian supplies and strengthening European energy security.
Moscow seeks new energy opportunities as Washington eases sanctions
Russian Energy Week, held in Moscow from Oct. 14–16, brought together Russian officials, energy executives and international partners to discuss oil and gas markets, investment and energy cooperation as Moscow seeks to maintain exports despite Western sanctions over its invasion of Ukraine.
Azerbaijan announced plans to resume Russian gas purchases on the forum’s final day, hours before US President Donald Trump signed an executive order waiving sweeping sanctions and tariffs against Russia.
The legislation, known as the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, targeted Russian energy revenues, financial institutions, defense companies and major foreign buyers of Russian oil and gas.
Trump invoked a national interest exemption to suspend the new penalties, following his controversial diesel agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
04:00:20 UTC
13:00:20 KST

Shortly before midnight last Sunday, the digital thermostats controlling hundreds of supermarket cold aisles across France began to flicker and rise.
In a “bizarre and unprecedented” cyber-attack, hackers had remotely overridden the temperature settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F).
Over the next four to six hours, the food inside first defrosted, then slowly began to cook.
Shop staff arriving early to restock shelves reported catching a blast of hot air, like opening an oven, when they went to fill freezers. One Normandy supermarket reported a number of its freezers had been pushed to 80C (176F). In certain stores, the extreme temperature rise had sparked fires triggering sprinklers and water damage.
“It was a catastrophe,” said one worker at the large Intermarché supermarket in the south-west suburb of Issy-les-Moulineaux in Paris. “They pushed the freezers here up to 62C. Everything had to be thrown away. It was such a waste.”
After removing tons of spoiled food, staff at the store worked until almost midnight on Monday to reorder and restock shelves. “Thankfully, we were able to get things almost back to normal the same day,” another shop worker added. “But we had to clear out everything in the freezers.”
If shop managers first assumed it was an isolated failure, it soon became clear up to 700 stores – including those from the Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains along with a number of smaller independent shops – had been victims of a cyber-attack.
Dominique Schelcher, the president of Coopérative U, said 80 of its 2,000 supermarkets had been targeted. “This is a completely unprecedented, unexpected, and extremely serious attack. In my entire professional career, I’ve never seen anything like it,” the shocked executive told French radio.
The Paris public prosecutor’s office immediately opened an investigation into the latest in a series of cyber-attacks that have made France the most hacked country in Europe.
Gérôme Billois, a partner in the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said the hack had the hallmarks of political sabotage.
“The two most feasible scenarios are either it was a group of youngsters or activists who wanted to blow up a few freezers to prove what they could do, or it was a destabilising attack, what we call sabotage, by internal or external state actors,” he said.
“As for the attack’s signature, the most likely scenario is still a destabilisation attack – one designed to convey the message to populations that they are not safe, to convey the impression that the government is falling apart, and ultimately to instil fear.
“Currently there are two international actors known for doing this sort of thing: Iran and Russia.”
The hackers had pirated the controllers supplied by the Danish company Danfoss that controls the freezers and fridges. Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. Initial investigations suggest the hackers disabled alarm systems before tampering with the thermostats, or extended the defrost programme by several hours to avoid triggering alarms.
Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” that customers install updates or replace obsolete unsupported systems. The affected refrigeration units were “running outdated firmware”, it said. In the days following the first wave of attacks, France’s cyber-attack alert centre ANSSI confirmed supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted.
Marta Rybczyńska, a cybersecurity specialist and researcher, said she had found previous security warnings about old supermarket freezers running out-of-date software and newer models not having firmware updated.
“Some of these freezers hadn’t been supported by the manufacturers for several years and there were notices saying they should be replaced. Other freezers were newer but the software hadn’t been updated,” Rybczyńska said.
“The hackers found these weaknesses and used them.”
She added: “Many of the freezers appear to have been running with a default password. The hackers were able to modify or turn off the alerts so the shops only realised when the first person arrived in the morning and saw the damage that had been done.”
The most recent French cyber-attack mirrors a similar incident in the US in August when connected fridges and freezers at a dozen military commissaries – on-base food stores – went into unscheduled defrost cycles overnight causing massive food loss.
France is the most heavily pirated country in Europe by the volume of records exposed by hackers, according to the cybersecurity and risk management company Upguard.
In the last three years, hackers have breached France’s health system, France Travail, the government-run jobseekers agency, the National Agency for Identity Documents (ANTS) and most of the big mobile phone companies. This summer, the economy and finance ministry lost the personal and fiscal records of 678,000 taxpayers to a series of cyber-attacks.
Billois says France has fallen behind in addressing cybersecurity and has still not adopted the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (2024) that introduced mandatory security for internet-connected devices.
“It’s a text that’s not political and that everyone agrees on but is delayed because there’s always more urgent legislation or there are quibbles about amendments, and this has been a disaster,” he said.
In the UK, the cyber security and resilience (network and information systems) bill to tackle cyber threats, is wending a similarly tortuous way through parliament. However, it fails to directly cover the food industry.
Supermarket boss Schelcher was quick to shift the blame for the attack on to unnamed refrigeration contractors who maintain the cold aisle equipment. “Our supermarkets are not customers of Danfoss,” he told RTL radio.
As yet, no individual or group has claimed responsibility for the supermarket cyber-attack; Paris prosecutors have instructed detectives from its anti-cybercrime unit but Billois says finding the hackers will take time.
“It’s possible they’ll be identified eventually, but it could take weeks if not months to be certain because hackers know how to hide their tracks,” Billois said.
Rybczyńska added: “Whether it’s possible to trace the hackers depends on their level of capability; if it’s a handful of youngsters, it’s easier because they probably won’t have thought to remove traces. If they are professionals it’s more complicated and will take longer. If they’re in a foreign country, it’ll be extremely difficult.”
The total cost of the cyber-attack has yet to be calculated but Thierry Cotillard, the CEO of Intermarché, said losses could run to “tens of millions of euros”, which store companies say is unlikely to be covered by their insurance.
“It’s a bizarre story,” Billois added. “There’s a shared responsibility between the supermarkets, the refrigeration companies who are sub-contractors and who maintain the material, and the software company. We cannot say who is to blame except, of course, the hackers.
“But in the end it comes down to freezers connected to the internet without being adequately secured. And that must be a wake-up call to everyone.”

French schoolchildren have been treated like enemies to be crushed – for telling the truth | Rokhaya Diallo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
04:00:20 UTC
13:00:20 KST

As a secondary school pupil in 1994, I took part in protests against a reform that would have allowed French employers to pay young people below the minimum wage. Our campaign was successful, but if we had had to face the terrifying police response unleashed on student protesters in France over recent weeks, I would have stayed at home.
A 14-year-old boy, Eden, suffered a fractured jaw and had teeth knocked out after a police teargas grenade struck him in the face. Sixteen-year-old Maël lost the sight in one eye allegedly after being struck by a shot from an LBD, a form of rubber-bullet launcher. Evan, 15, had his hand blown off in an explosion involving a police stun grenade. And in Dunkirk, a police SUV is alleged to have driven repeatedly at groups of secondary school pupils, as an officer could be heard saying: “Come closer, we’ll smash their fucking faces in.” Accounts from children left terrified by brutal treatment in police custody describe traumatic experiences with severe psychological and physical consequences.
France, the self-styled home of human rights, is now attracting the kind of international legal scrutiny you would expect if this were an authoritarian regime gone mad. The human rights organisation Ligue des droits de l’Homme has condemned the alarming “brutalisation of young people”, and the threat to their freedom of expression.
A UN special rapporteur has called on the French authorities to respect the physical safety of protesters. The UN human rights office says it is following incidents surrounding the protests in France “with concern”. Amnesty International has called for the suspension of rubber-bullet launchers at school protests, condemned the disproportionate use of force and reminded the authorities of their duty to protect children. The Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, whose activism increasingly encompasses struggles against oppression and state violence, travelled to France this week to support school pupils.
It is often argued that France is broke, and that crippling debt levels make the student demand for €10bn of investment to improve their learning conditions a non-starter. But even in our difficult fiscal position, public spending is a political choice: to reduce debt you can cut public spending or you can raise revenue.
Economists Élise Huillery and Romane Paris have come up with a credible proposal for investing an additional €11.8bn a year in education, funded through tax reform targeting large inheritances, raising €12.7bn in 2026 and increasing taxes only for the wealthiest 1% of heirs. This would make money available to raise teachers’ pay, improve support for pupils, student grants and housing, and expand university places.
But the debate about public spending does not invalidate the legitimate grievances of pupils, teachers and parents, which are not new. Nor does it justify a vicious law and order response. Learning conditions in some of the most disadvantaged schools have been deteriorating to shockingly poor levels for a long time. I highlighted school conditions in France in the Guardian three years ago, arguing then that the state education system was among the most unequal in the developed world. The lack of resources assigned to such basic things as teaching vacancies has been glaringly apparent for years, with jobs in some districts sometimes left unfilled for months.
More than 20m teaching hours were lost in state secondary schools in 2024-25, equivalent to almost one in 10 lessons. More than 15m of those hours were lost because no replacement teachers were provided. Schools in designated priority education areas, which serve disadvantaged communities, have been particularly affected, according to France’s National Audit Office.
In Seine-Saint-Denis, the poorest part of mainland France, two-thirds of school doctor posts were vacant in 2023. As early as 2022, the Créteil education authority reported a shortfall of 60 school nurses and 20 social workers, with 90% of the unfilled posts in Seine-Saint-Denis. In 2025, 49 suicides were recorded among staff in the national education system. While these deaths cannot all be attributed to work, it is hard to avoid thinking of the severe deterioration in working conditions across the sector.
Then there are the schools that are physically falling apart: water that is unsafe to drink because of bacterial contamination, pupils reporting rats and cockroaches, filthy toilets, and in one case, a septic tank that overflows when it rains. There are power cuts, missing furniture and some classrooms are so poorly insulated that temperatures fall below 14C in winter and hit 40C during heatwaves.
In Mayotte, where protests began, a secondary school built for 900 pupils is accommodating 2,300. The protests then spread to mainland France through a school in Créteil that began the academic year short of 13 teachers and other staff, as well as a deputy headteacher.
Another issue at the core of pupils’ anger is Parcoursup, the system through which school leavers apply for higher education. Seen as discriminatory, it has left 126,000 applicants – many from disadvantaged backgrounds – without a place this year.
Rather than deal with this crisis as justified social protest based on legitimate demands, the government has invoked a doctrine set out in its Operational Guide to Urban Violence. It has treated school pupils as internal enemies to be neutralised. This sets up a coercive response, disregarding the possibility of resolving the conflict through constructive measures.
By 8 October, 6,877 people had been taken into police custody, about 80% of them children. On 1 October alone, police made 1,949 arrests, exceeding the highest single-day total recorded since 1961, says the historian Éric Anceau. According to the Syndicat de la magistrature, a French judges’ leftwing union, the numbers reflect a clear determination to crush the movement. So overwhelming has the police deployment been that teachers and parents have had to form human chains to protect children.
The police operations are also driven by a focus on arrests, which encourages forceful confrontations and fuels the escalation. This in turn draws more people into rioting. About 700 police officers and a number of teachers have been injured since the start of the unrest.
The sociologist Olivier Fillieule points out that policing protests requires an assessment of risk. If the swift break-up a blockade exposes teenagers to serious injury, you have to consider alternatives. Temporarily accepting a degree of disorder when immediate intervention risks creating more of it should remain a guiding principle of policing protests, Filleule says, noting that the French authorities know how to apply restraint when farmers stage blockades.
Yet while the police have opened internal investigations into 36 allegations of officer violence, the interior minister Laurent Nuñez said he had given the forces “no instructions to exercise restraint”. This is a shameful and contemptuous way to respond to young people’s healthy expression of dissent. Such violence towards citizens has no place in a democracy.
- Rokhaya Diallo is a French journalist, film-maker, activist and Guardian Europe columnist

Trump Halts Sweeping Russia Sanctions, Citing US National Interest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
03:43:03 UTC
12:43:03 KST

US President Donald Trump signed an executive order Friday, Oct. 16, suspending sweeping sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia just two days before they were due to take effect. Trump cited US national interests despite growing concerns that easing economic pressure on Moscow could help finance its war against Ukraine.
The executive order published by the White House waives major provisions of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Trump signed into law on Sept. 18.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The suspended measures include additional 500% tariffs on Russian imports and 100% duties targeting the five largest buyers of Russian oil and natural gas, as well as countries facilitating Moscow’s sanctions evasion.
The restrictions were scheduled to take effect Sunday, Oct. 18, under legislation designed to cut the energy revenues sustaining Russia’s invasion.
“As described further in section 4 of this order, I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Trump wrote.
The decision follows his controversial diesel agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, which eased restrictions on Russian fuel exports amid rising global energy prices.
It also comes as relations between Washington and Kyiv have deteriorated, with President Volodymyr Zelensky warning that allowing Russia to earn more from energy sales could strengthen Putin’s ability to continue the war.
Zelensky: Starlink Still Not Fully Restored, Disrupting Drone Defense and Frontline Supplies
Trump suspends 500% tariffs and penalties on Russian oil buyers
Under the Graham Act, Congress authorized extensive economic measures against Russia’s energy and defense industries, financial institutions, senior officials and networks helping Moscow circumvent Western sanctions.
The legislation also provided for steep tariffs against countries continuing to purchase Russian energy, extending the financial consequences of Moscow’s invasion to its major trading partners.
Trump’s order sets out three major tariff categories:
- An additional 500% duty on goods imported from Russia.
- A 100% duty on imports from the five largest buyers making new purchases of Russian oil or natural gas beginning Oct. 18.
- A 100% duty on goods from the five leading countries facilitating Russian oil sanctions evasion.
However, the order simultaneously waives those duties, preventing their immediate application.
The decision shields major Russian energy customers, potentially including China and India, from new US trade penalties as long as the waiver remains in effect.
The measures also targeted Russia’s so-called shadow fleet – tankers used to transport Russian oil despite Western efforts to restrict Moscow’s energy exports.
Trump’s order suspends specified new sanctions provisions but does not remove restrictions already imposed under separate executive authorities.
Trump invokes national interest exemption
The president relied on Section 115 of the Graham Act, which allows sanctions, restrictions and tariffs to be waived if the administration certifies that doing so serves US national interests.
“I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States,” Trump stated.
The legislation also requires a report explaining the basis for that determination.
The executive order confirms that the certification and accompanying report were submitted to Congress, but does not publicly provide a detailed explanation of why suspending the additional penalties would serve US interests.
The waivers will remain in effect until Trump or designated administration officials determine that further action is appropriate.
The order directs the US Trade Representative, working with the State, Treasury and Energy departments, to continue monitoring Russian energy purchases and sanctions evasion.
Although the administration retains authority to reconsider the waivers, no timetable for restoring the measures was announced.
Bipartisan backlash over sanctions relief
Trump’s decision follows mounting criticism from lawmakers in both parties over the administration’s earlier agreement to ease restrictions on Russian diesel.
In a bipartisan letter to the administration, senators warned that allowing Russian energy exports could provide Moscow with additional revenue to finance military operations against Ukraine.
The criticism has extended beyond Democrats to Republicans who supported stronger economic pressure on Putin.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina has questioned the administration’s approach to the Russia diesel agreement and its implications for legislation championed by the late Lindsey Graham.
Democratic lawmakers have also challenged Trump’s decision to suspend sanctions Congress approved.
Representative Don Beyer accused the president of yielding to Putin, while Senator Elizabeth Warren criticized the administration for undermining congressional efforts to pressure Russia.
The dispute raises broader questions about the effectiveness of sanctions legislation when its implementation depends on presidential discretion.
Although the Graham Act remains law, its national interest waiver gives the administration substantial authority to prevent the new restrictions from taking effect.
Diesel deal with Putin precedes broader sanctions reversal
The decision comes one week after Trump agreed to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports in exchange for additional fuel supplies intended to ease pressure on international energy markets.
The agreement was presented by Washington as a response to rising fuel prices, which have been affected by the ongoing US-Israeli war against Iran and disruptions to global energy supplies.
Under the arrangement, Russia agreed to release hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel into international markets.
The White House has defended the cooperation as necessary to stabilize prices for American consumers and businesses.
However, critics argue that increasing Russian energy sales could replenish Moscow’s revenues at a time when Western sanctions are intended to limit its ability to sustain the invasion of Ukraine.
Kyiv condemns sanctions relief as Russia continues attacks
President Volodymyr Zelensky has criticized Washington’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian energy, warning that additional revenues could strengthen Moscow’s ability to finance its invasion.
He called the diesel arrangement a “weak decision” and insisted that Russia should face increased economic pressure rather than concessions.
The dispute has coincided with Trump’s criticism of Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries.
Trump described Kyiv’s renewed attacks as a “disgrace,” arguing that they were contributing to higher global energy prices.
Zelensky has defended Ukraine’s efforts to weaken Russian oil infrastructure, which generates revenue supporting Moscow’s military operations.
Ukraine has also accused Russia of continuing to target Ukrainian energy facilities despite discussions about a possible mutual halt to attacks on energy infrastructure.
During Friday’s EU summit in Brussels, European Council President António Costa rejected the idea of easing pressure on Moscow.
“This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” Costa said.
“Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.”

Avi Nesher's ‘Our Loves’ turns tragedy into immersive cinema - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
03:35:42 UTC
12:35:42 KST

Avi Nesher’s latest movie, Our Loves, opened in theaters across Israel on Thursday and is a beautiful, moving film about ordinary people in extraordinary circumstances.
It tells a story that is suspenseful, sad, sometimes even funny, and always human. It may even change the way you see the world – and yourself.
Nesher has described it as the story of seven people who all think they are having the worst day of their lives on October 6, 2023.
That’s really all you need to know about it going in, and yes, it does encompass the October 7 massacre, but it isn’t “an October 7 movie.”
It’s different from the television series Red Alert and One Day in October, for example, because it follows fictional characters living their lives who happen to get caught up in the massacre, while those series were dramatized versions of specific stories about real people.
Some Oct. 7 dramatizations are like watching news reports, but this one is truly cinematic
They were like watching news reports acted out, while Our Loves is a different experience, a truly cinematic one.
The idea of people who thought they were as stressed as they could be on October 6 is a smart lens for tackling October 7. You get to know each character and are drawn into their stories.
The attack begins only after you have been engrossed in the movie for nearly an hour and have almost forgotten what is in store for the protagonists.
Our Loves opens with the quote: “Love is always immersive, anytime and anyplace, but it is more intense the nearer it comes to death,” by Gabriel Garcia Marquez from Love in the Time of Cholera.
This sets the tone for the characters’ stories, which, as the title suggests, are all about love in one way or another.
Playing with our expectations, the movie opens at a concert that turns out not to be the Nova Music Festival, but a rock concert on October 5 that most of the main characters attend for different reasons, and we get to know them gradually.
Among these characters is Shabi (Shalom Michaelshvili), an aggressive retired general who is divorced and suing his ex-wife to force her to sell their house, which she and their children don’t want to give up.
He tells himself he’s doing the right thing, but when he sees his strong-willed daughter, Liri (Noa Cohen), she can barely look at him.
Deep down, he knows he’s lost something, but he still can’t stop himself from continuing the court case, and there is a painful hearing on the morning of October 6.
Liri attends the rock concert to support her new boyfriend, Matan (Nevo Katan), a sound engineer working there, whose parents, Katya (Lena Fraifeld) and Gadi (Lior Miller), are splitting up because Katya has decided she needs to try living on her own.
Katya is moving into the young people’s section of the kibbutz in the Gaza border communities region where they live, right near Liri and Matan.
A policewoman, Mili (Magi Azarzar), on security duty at the event, is nervous because she plans to introduce her girlfriend, Sandra (Hadas Yaron), a nerdy nuclear scientist at the Dimona reactor, to her very traditional Moroccan mother (Evelin Hagoel).
Niso (Yaniv Biton), one of Mili’s police colleagues, is reluctantly quitting to move to Europe with his wife and take a lucrative marketing job.
Another one of the main characters, Sapir (Daniel Gimpel), a young religious woman, desperately wants to get married and start a family, but enjoys trance music and dancing, which the guys she dates see as an unwelcome wild streak.
On the morning of October 6, the boyfriend she thought she was getting engaged to dumps her.
Her friend (Kim Or Azulay) convinces her it’s time to have some fun despite the religious laws of Shabbat and Simchat Torah by attending the Nova festival.
Torn between religious duty and the need to rebel, Sapir agrees to attend the festival. She even takes a pill her friend buys from Yoyo (Leib Levin), a sexy drug dealer who keeps his stash in his underwear.
Personalities don't change under threat
Suddenly, starting at 6:29 a.m. on October 7, the world around them changes at breakneck speed, and everything they do becomes a life-or-death choice.
But their personalities don’t change because they are under threat, and Nesher’s playful sense of humor and the absurd don’t disappear just because he is depicting a tragedy.
Shabi heads south to save Liri as soon as he learns her kibbutz is under attack, but he needs a rifle and some backup.
Stopping by an army base, he picks up four of the most clueless recruits in the history of cinema, all of whom have names starting with the same letter, which makes it even harder for him to tell them apart.
Only it may be better that way, he mumbles, because the likelihood that any of them will make it home alive is slim.
The comedy and tragedy of the four guys and Shabi continue throughout the day, and slowly, this arrogant general begins to truly question how he uses people, perhaps for the first time in his life.
Unexpected comedy comes up at other times, too, but I don’t want to risk revealing spoilers by giving away too much.
One moment that has stayed with me and exemplifies Nesher’s approach to the day’s events is when Matan’s former girlfriend (singer-actress Neomi Aharoni Gal, aka Nunu, who also performs the title song), who runs a hot-dog stand at the Nova, tries to flee carrying her hot-dog steamer.
A police officer, desperately trying to fight off dozens of terrorists with a handgun, yells at her to leave it and run, but she keeps trying to hold onto the heavy contraption, protesting that she can’t live without it.
Knowing what happened at the festival, we can see how foolish she is being, but at the same time, it’s understandable that she couldn’t switch gears instantly during the attack.
So many of us had trouble making the switch that day, and this moment in particular put me into the heads of the people at the music festival.
The excellent acting (Shalom Michaelshvili, best known as a comic actor, as the general, and newcomer Daniel Gimpel as the young religious festival-goer are standouts in a fine ensemble), original music, and stunning cinematography all flow together to tell the story.
The movie had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival last month, despite the anti-Israel sentiment roiling the international cultural world.
Some of the reviewers there criticized the movie for not telling its story from the point of view of Hamas terrorists as well as the Israeli characters.
Nesher has said in interviews that he could not write from the point of view of a terrorist who would burn a family alive, and the truth is that, had he even attempted to tell the story from the terrorists’ point of view, he would have been accused of cultural appropriation.
Another point about the critical reception of the movie abroad is that reviewers full of staunch opinions on how Nesher should have portrayed the terrorists seem to have missed the fact that in a scene late in the movie, when several characters arrive at a hospital, the head doctor (Hisham Suleiman) is an Arab.
These reviewers do not know enough about the region to discern when characters are speaking Hebrew or Arabic, but they still think they know how this story should have been told.
One reviewer wrote, from the comfort of a Toronto hotel room, that “quite a few of the characters seem less distraught than one might expect given the circumstances,” as if she were intimately familiar with how people act during a day-long terror attack.
The remark also suggests she was unaware that Hamas fired tens of thousands of missiles at Israel prior to October 7, and that at first the attack seemed routine to many people.
But it’s the director’s triumph that he manages to get those of us who do know the facts about the conflict to forget the headlines and just get into the story.
In the key scene, when rockets fired by Hamas begin to fly toward the festival venue, we are so much in Sapir’s head that for a moment, when the light streaks across the sky, we, too, wonder whether we are seeing fireworks that are part of the festival.
In that moment, and several others, in an ambulance or on the road during a brief respite from the killing, we embrace life along with the characters.
Seeing this movie can be transformative, and after you watch it, you may look at your own life differently, just as the survivors in the movie do at the end of the day.
Nesher, one of Israel’s most acclaimed and popular directors, knows how to tell a story, or, in this case, stories. He started his career over 40 years ago with the classic army entertainment group movie, The Troupe.
He has also made such modern classics as Turn Left at the End of the World and, more recently, another drama based on Israeli history, Image of Victory, which told the story of both sides in the battle of Nitzanim in the Independence War.
It makes sense that he would be the director to find the human truth in the tragedy of this infamous day and turn it into immersive cinema.

Southern California wildfire engulfs homes, prompts evacuation orders
The fast-spreading Norte Fire in Orange County is fuelled by intense warm winds and unseasonably high temperatures.
A fast-spreading wildfire in Orange County, in Southern California, has engulfed several coastal properties and prompted widespread evacuation orders.
The Orange County Fire Authority said on Friday that the Norte Fire had scorched about 188 hectares (465 acres), with the state’s Cal Fire agency putting it at about 231 hectares (570 acres) by the evening, and that at least six homes had been damaged or destroyed in the San Juan Capistrano area.
The fire authority said firefighters were “aggressively attacking the fire from the ground and air” and issued pleas for people to stay clear of the area.
Unseasonably high temperatures and low humidity are fuelling the rapid growth of the fire, the AFP news agency reported.
The Norte Fire started in the coastal city of San Clemente on Friday and moved to the city of San Juan Capistrano, with some 6,000 homes and 16,000 residents under evacuation orders by the evening. An evacuation shelter has opened in each city while helicopters attempt to douse the flames.
Intense warm winds
The Norte Fire is one of several in the region driven by Santa Ana winds, intense warm gusts that blow from the southwest US interior towards the California coast.
The Santa Ana winds typically arrive in the autumn, right when Southern California’s vegetation is at its driest after a long, rainless summer, according to The Weather Channel.
Forecasters said winds blew at between 55km/h and 90km/h (35mph and 55mph) within coastal areas.
The strongest winds were expected through Friday, but the high heat and low humidity conditions that contribute to the growth of the fire are expected to last through Saturday night.
Tens of thousands of people in Los Angeles County were left without power as authorities attempted to lessen the possibility of electrical sparks that the heavy wind gusts could carry.
Other ongoing fires
California firefighters were also busy battling the Bryson Fire, which broke out on the outskirts of the Malibu beach community in Los Angeles County on Thursday. As of Friday, the fire had burned about 59 hectares (147 acres) and was 17 percent contained, according to Cal Fire.
The Henderson Fire was 20 percent contained and had burned 842 hectares (2,080 acres) in San Diego County by Friday, Cal Fire said. The blaze impacted Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton and prompted freeway closures.

Why one of NYC’s longstanding symbols is set to disappear

Why one of NYC’s longstanding symbols is set to disappear
New York City’s horse-drawn carriages could disappear under legislation proposing a ban from June 2028, as concerns over passenger safety and animal welfare fuel efforts to end the familiar tourist attraction, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent.
The proposal, known as Romanch’s Law, is named after 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who died after being thrown from a runaway carriage in Central Park in June. He was visiting New York to celebrate his high school graduation. His death brought renewed urgency to the debate over whether carriage rides should continue operating in the park.
“His death was heartbreaking, and it was preventable,” City Council Speaker Julie Menin said in an official statement announcing her support for the legislation in July.
Menin became the first sitting City Council speaker to publicly endorse ending horse-drawn carriage rides in Central Park. She said the transition should protect New Yorkers, international visitors and the horses, while providing employment opportunities for people whose livelihoods depend on the industry.
The teenager’s death followed the death of a carriage horse in Central Park a week earlier. The incidents intensified scrutiny of an industry already facing longstanding concerns over animal welfare and public safety.
Under the proposed legislation, sponsored by Council Member Christopher Marte, horse-drawn cab operations would be prohibited from June 1, 2028. The measure would wind down the industry by stopping the issuance of new operating licenses, with existing driver licenses eligible for limited renewals until the deadline.
The proposal also addresses what would happen to the animals. Carriage horses could not be sold or transferred for slaughter, or sent to another horse-drawn cab business.
For drivers and other affected employees, the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection would administer a workforce development program to help them move into other fields of employment.
Menin has identified hospitality and tourism among the sectors where displaced workers should have access to quality jobs. The planned phaseout therefore seeks to combine an end to carriage rides with protections for both workers and horses.
The ban has not yet become law and remains subject to legislative approval.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that site preparation is underway for a 102-meter-tall detention facility in New York City’s Chinatown, expected to become the world’s tallest correctional facility.

New menopause guidelines designed to cut through misinformation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
03:21:20 UTC
12:21:20 KST

Australia has new guidelines for managing menopausal symptoms
Hot Flushes. Night sweats. Vaginal dryness. Painful sex. A frequent need to wee.
Menopause marks the end of a woman's reproductive years and is associated with a range of symptoms that can affect their quality of life.
There's a lot of information and misinformation about the best treatments to help ease the severity of symptoms.
In a bid to make things easier, the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG) has developed a new set of clinical guidelines.
Loading...
The guidelines clarify when to use menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) over other medicines and what options are available for those with a history of breast cancer.
RANZCOG guideline development group chair Catriona Melville said they wanted to "cut through the noise" and provide clear, evidence-based recommendations for clinicians to discuss with their patients.
"If your clinician is not clear about where the evidence lies and what's safe and what isn't safe, and what's recommended and what isn't recommended, then they're not in a position to have that patient-centred discussion about what the available [treatment] options are," she said.
What do the guidelines cover?
The new guidelines provide evidence-based advice for managing the symptoms of menopause, which begins 12 months after a woman's last period.
The guidelines cover vasomotor symptoms (such as hot flushes and night sweats) and genito-urinary symptoms (such as vaginal dryness and the frequent need to urinate) of menopause in women 40 years and above.
They do not cover the management of bone density, joint pain, libido, depression or anxiety.
Magdalena Simonis, a practising GP and women's health expert from the University of Melbourne, said not all women experienced the same type or severity of symptoms.
While she was not involved in developing the guidelines, she said they reinforced the need for clinicians to treat the whole person in front of them, not just the symptom.
"We should also be looking at lifestyle and other risk factors around the time of the menopause," Dr Simonis said.
"This is a really important time to talk about [cholesterol] lipid control, bone density management and lifestyle activities.
"Looking at family history of other cancers, breast screening, cervical screening and having that conversation around chronic conditions."
How do the guidelines work?
The guidelines list a range of possible treatment options for different menopausal symptoms, including menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), acupuncture and hypnosis, ranking available evidence on a scale of very low to high.
The guidelines recommend that women taking MHT have an annual review with their doctor.
But there's not enough evidence that weight loss or physical activity alone will improve hot flushes or night sweats, or that hypnosis will improve sleep.
Dr Melville, a specialist gynaecologist and sub-specialist in sexual and reproductive health, said the new guidelines would hopefully make it easier for clinicians and patients to understand their options.
For example, women with a history of breast cancer can be offered vaginal oestrogen to ease menopausal symptoms.
Although RANZCOG had previously released statements about managing menopausal symptoms, Dr Melville said these were their first evidence-based guidelines.
How will it improve patient care?
Women should receive the same standardised recommendations no matter who they see or where they live if clinicians across Australia use the same guidelines.
Jean Hailes for Women's Health chief executive Sarah White, who was not involved with the guidelines, said this was important because clinicians wanted to give their patients the very best support, but there was a lot of online misinformation to wade through.
"It really will help the health professional to have these new guidelines sitting in front of them so that they can talk them through and reassure women that they are getting the very best advice," she said.
The guidelines also encourage clinicians to ask women approaching menopause if they experience any "troublesome" symptoms, especially if patients are First Nations, Māori and Pacific Islander women and others who may experience barriers to treatment.
This will make it easier for women to get help, even if they find it hard to ask.
Won't there be new national guidelines soon?
The Australian government has funded separate perimenopause and menopause guidelines expected to be released next year.
These guidelines, which RANZCOG is contributing to, will be continually updated as new evidence emerges.
Dr Simonis welcomed the spotlight on the health of menopausal women.
She encouraged anyone experiencing troublesome symptoms to book an appointment with their GP and advised women approaching mid-life to schedule a check-up.
"Menopause is not a stage to be afraid of or to dread; it's a natural phase of life,"
she said.

Cameroonians await government reshuffle after Biya’s return
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
03:14:28 UTC
12:14:28 KST

Cameroonians await government reshuffle after Biya’s return
After 10 weeks abroad, Biya returned to Cameroon but has yet to appoint a new government or vice president.
Yaounde, Cameroon – Every weekday at 5pm, Elvis Mbi tunes in to the state broadcaster’s flagship radio bulletin, hoping to hear an announcement from President Paul Biya that could signal a change in Cameroon’s political leadership.
Biya, 93, returned to Cameroon on August 20 after spending about 10 weeks abroad. His prolonged absence fuelled speculation about his health and whereabouts, including unverified claims that he had died.
His return raised expectations of a government reshuffle, but no new government had been appointed by October 6. The vice presidency, restored through a constitutional amendment in April, also remained vacant.
“Every Cameroonian was expecting that upon his return home, he was going to change government, but nothing up to this moment,” 39-year-old Mbi told Al Jazeera.
In his December 31, 2025, address to the nation, Biya promised that a new government would be formed “in the coming days”. More than nine months later, the promised change had yet to materialise.
Succession fears grow
The vacant vice presidency has drawn particular attention since politicians approved a constitutional amendment in April restoring the position abolished in 1972.
Under Law No. 2026/002, promulgated on April 14, the president may appoint and dismiss a vice president.
The amendment provides for the vice president to assume the presidency on an interim basis if the office becomes vacant because of the president’s death, resignation or permanent incapacity.
The vice president serves the remainder of the seven-year presidential term under the conditions set out in the Constitution.
The reform establishes a formal succession mechanism while leaving the appointment of the vice president to Biya. The amendment does not set a deadline for filling the post.
“We all know the president needs assistance in order to execute state duties and that’s why we are anxiously waiting for the appointment, but nothing has happened yet to our greatest dismay,” Mbi said.
A disputed presidential decree purporting to appoint a vice president has added to the speculation.
In June, an individual delivered a sealed envelope to Cameroon Radio Television (CRTV) in Yaounde containing a purported presidential decree appointing a vice president.
The document appeared to bear the official seals of the presidency and a signature attributed to Biya, according to a government statement published by state newspaper Cameroon Tribune on July 1.
CRTV did not broadcast what the document said. The government said the decree had not been issued through the proper official process and confirmed that the individual had been detained and an investigation was under way.
For Jude Mutah, a Washington-based governance and democracy expert and director of member relations at the Corporate Council on Africa, the attention paid to the state broadcaster’s evening bulletin reflects public expectations of political change.
In the absence of clear information, rumours can gain traction, he said.
Cabral Libii, leader of the Cameroon Party for National Reconciliation and an opposition figure in the 2025 presidential election, has argued that appointing a vice president would matter beyond filling a vacant post.
“The vice presidency is not just another administrative post to be filled. Appointing your vice president means securing your leadership,” Libii said in a public appeal.
“A vice president of this calibre could help to mitigate the succession struggles that are currently paralysing collective action,” he added.
Economic uncertainty
The leadership questions are unfolding as Cameroon faces other challenges, including a separatist conflict in its English-speaking regions and an armed rebellion linked to Boko Haram around the Lake Chad Basin.
Jason Healy, a sub-Saharan Africa country risk analyst at BMI, part of Fitch Solutions, said uncertainty over political leadership could weigh on investor confidence.
Healy warned that prolonged uncertainty could discourage some investors from committing to large, long-term projects. He also suggested that delaying appointments could be a political calculation by Biya, allowing him to retain control over the timing and composition of any changes.
Mbi Aziseh Azimboh, executive director of the Policy Lab for Civic Innovation and Community Solutions (POLITICOS), said prolonged uncertainty could slow government decision-making and delay reforms and public policies.
Government defends president’s prerogative
The government has defended Biya’s authority to decide when to make appointments.
In an interview with RFI in August, Communication Minister and government spokesperson Rene Emmanuel Sadi said the president had the authority to form a new government and determine when to do so.
“It is surely quite normal for him to take his time when entrusting such a high office to one of his fellow citizens,” Sadi said.
Elvis Ngolle Ngolle, a former minister and coordinator of the ruling Cameroon People’s Democratic Movement’s academy, said citizens’ concerns were legitimate but maintained that the president had the constitutional prerogative to act when he chose.
The presidency did not respond to an Al Jazeera request for comment.
For Mbi, his radio-listening ritual continues.
“No one knows anything any more. It is so disheartening when I tune in each time but don’t get the big news,” he told Al Jazeera.

Judge Joseph Montano said prosecutors could pursue new charges against Busfield.
The actor has strongly denied allegations of improperly touching two young boys – twin brothers – on the Albuquerque set of Fox TV drama The Cleaning Lady.

He steadfastly professed his innocence, calling the allegations against him “lies”, and his attorneys asked for the charges against him to be dismissed.
In Friday’s ruling, Montano said the prosecution did not properly instruct members of the grand jury on procedures for requesting testimony from additional witnesses. In part, the prosecutor incorrectly informed the grand jurors that at least eight of them would have to agree to wanting to hear from a witness for that person to be called.
“The prosecuting attorney failed to act in a fair and impartial manner,” Montano wrote, adding that the lawyer’s actions “had the practical effect of unilaterally withholding witnesses requested by the grand jurors”.
Busfield, 69, is best known for his prime-time television roles as a White House reporter on the NBC political drama The West Wing and as an advertising agency executive on ABC ensemble series Thirtysomething. He also appeared in the baseball film Field of Dreams starring Kevin Costner.

====================================================================================================

Trump pauses new Russia sanctions passed by Congress amid deepening row with Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
02:53:38 UTC
11:53:38 KST

Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.
In an executive order on Friday, the US president said he was waiving many sanctions, restrictions and duties on Russia, in a move that comes as he has been publicly criticising Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including suggesting that Ukraine needs a new leader.
The move was greeted by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who wrote on social media: “The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment.”
Trump signed the legislation last month, after Congress passed the measure in an act of rare bipartisan agreement. It sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fuelling Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The legislation – whose primary backer in Congress was the late senator Lindsey Graham – sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving and was due to be implemented in two days.
It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Friday’s announcement comes a week after Trump said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.
Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1m tons “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional 3m tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
The president has face widespread criticism after making the announcement, with a dozen US senators – including six Republicans – calling on Trump to rescind his diesel deal.
A letter from the bipartisan group of lawmakers sent on Tuesday urged Trump to execute the sanctions authorities included in the legislation passed last month, called the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026”.
Under the legislation he signed into law, Trump had until 18 October to impose the sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy, or waive them. The administration had not told lawmakers whether it would impose the sanctions or issue a waiver.
Zelenskyy said on Friday the diesel deal would mean cash “will start flowing back into Russia”, as he met European leaders in Brussels.
Trump blindsided Zelenskyy last weekend by announcing that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities. Facing midterm elections next month, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing up energy prices that could cost his Republican party its thin majorities in the US Senate and House of Representatives.
Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph (161km/h). Neither has officially been confirmed.
The US sanctions legislation has also become a campaign centerpiece for Senator Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham’s sister appointed to serve out the remaining months of his term, who is also running to replace him in the Senate more permanently.
In a debate earlier this week with South Carolina Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham – who has Trump’s endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week – said she had been “so proud” to help get the measure passed but acknowledged it was Trump’s purview as to how he implemented it.
“It gives the president tools that he can use, if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions,” Graham said during the debate in Columbia. “So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall.”
With Reuters and the Associated Press

Prosecutors had requested damages of more than $100,000 but the judge ruled against it and said any compensation would have to be pursued through civil proceedings.
The brothers’ parents, Martin and Debra Robinson, travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.
They have established a foundation in their sons’ names to carry on their legacy.
The Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation aims to “help people live bigger, shine brighter and love harder in their honour”.
Callum, the older of the two brothers, moved to the US as a professional lacrosse player and has been remembered for his loving nature and passion for the environment, having been involved in coastal cleanups.
Jake, a doctor, was set to take up a position at Geelong hospital after returning to Australia.
He has been remembered for his academic success, his passion for sport, particularly cricket and surfing, and his compassion.
Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

Brazil’s Amazon deforestation hits lowest level on record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
02:49:21 UTC
11:49:21 KST

Brazil’s Amazon deforestation hits lowest level on record
Data show a 42 percent drop in forest clearance from a year earlier, giving Lula a boost before the election run-off.
Deforestation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest has fallen to its lowest level since records began in 1988, according to official figures that give a boost to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva days before a presidential run-off.
Brazil’s space research agency, Inpe, said on Friday that 3,335 square kilometres (1,288 square miles) of forest were cleared in the 12 months through July, about 42 percent less than the year before.
The previous record low was 4,571 sq km (1,765 sq miles) in 2011-12, while annual losses peaked at nearly 30,000 sq km (nearly 11,600 sq miles) in the mid-1990s, according to Inpe’s Prodes satellite programme, which measures from August to July because cloud cover is lower in mid-year.
“It’s an absolutely stratospheric drop…it’s like a dream,” Environment Minister Joao Paulo Capobianco said at a news conference in Brasilia.
Marcio Astrini of the climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima called the figures “a historic achievement” and said they show that “with political will, it is possible to curb deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions”.
President Lula wrote on X: “Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030.”
Lula took office in 2023 pledging to end illegal deforestation by 2030, after clearing soared to a 15-year high under his far-right predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro. The Amazon lost about 11,600 sq km (about 4,480 sq miles) a year on average during Bolsonaro’s 2019-2022 term, almost 60 percent more than in the previous four years.
Deforestation has fallen every year since 2022 and is down 71.2 percent over four years. The AFP news agency attributes the drop to greater monitoring and stiffer penalties for illegal logging.
Lula faces Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, in the election run-off on October 25, with polls showing them neck and neck.
Flavio pledged in his manifesto to strengthen environmental oversight in the Amazon, focus enforcement on organised crime rather than extractive workers and small farmers, and end “illegal deforestation” by 2029.
He has also praised his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for coup plotting, for opposing what he calls a “radical environmental agenda”.
Deforestation in the Cerrado savanna, south of the Amazon, also fell by about 24 percent, to 5,517 sq km (2,130 sq miles), the lowest since records began in 2001.

Trump waives ‘bone-crushing’ Russia sanctions

Trump waives ‘bone-crushing’ Russia sanctions
US President Donald Trump has suspended sweeping new sanctions against Russia that he signed into law just a month ago, invoking a national-interest exemption to waive penalties targeting Moscow’s economy and countries purchasing Russian energy.
In an executive order issued on Friday, Trump waived sanctions and tariffs mandated by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, including proposed 500% tariffs on imports from Russia and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
“I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States and a report explaining the basis for the certification,” Trump wrote.
China and India, the two largest buyers of Russian crude oil, were expected to be among the countries hardest hit by the legislation.
The bill, championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, has been described by supporters as a “bone-crushing” measure aimed at driving Russian energy exports out of the global market. Hawkish US lawmakers argued that existing restrictions had allowed Moscow to circumvent economic pressure.
Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports earlier this month in an effort to curb rising energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections. The move sparked outrage in Ukraine and among America’s European allies, prompting a bipartisan group of US senators to accuse Trump of betraying Kiev.
According to US media reports, Trump decided to ease sanctions after Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky refused to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities, which Trump blamed for high energy prices.
On Friday, US Representative Gregory Meeks introduced a bill in Congress seeking to block the diesel agreement with Russia. The Democrat accused Trump of “cozying up to [Russian President Vladimir] Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine.”
Trump has defended the agreement as beneficial to American consumers and consistent with his “America First” agenda. In response to the backlash, he attacked Zelensky as “not a good guy for us to deal with” and suggested that Ukraine needed “a new president.”
Russia has maintained that it has adapted to mounting Western economic pressure, while describing the Graham bill as a hostile move that would undermine Trump’s efforts to broker peace between Moscow and Kiev.
“[Russian] diesel has begun reaching global markets, and it will have a certain positive effect on stabilizing oil markets,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Thursday.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s investment envoy and a negotiator on Ukraine, hailed the waiver as “an important and historic moment.” Economic cooperation serves the interests of both countries, “contributes to global economic stability, and lays the foundation for building trust and achieving lasting peace,” he wrote on X.

“I don’t know whether that’s true or not. If it is, we are very grateful.”

Russian Shaheds outpace restricted Ukrainian interceptors
Zelensky offered a detailed explanation of how Starlink restrictions undermined Ukraine’s defense against jet-powered Shahed drones, which Russia has increasingly deployed against Ukrainian cities.
“We use Starlink to intercept jet-powered Shaheds that come and strike our civilians and kill our families,” he said.
“We use special interceptors that move at very high speeds – interceptor drones that operate specifically with Starlink.”
According to Zelensky, Ukraine’s satellite terminals were subjected to restrictions that prevented high-speed drones from maintaining the connections required for their missions.
“Starlink was not switched off. The speed was reduced,” he said.
“And when the speed was reduced, we were unable to shoot down some of the Shaheds.”
Zelensky said Russian jet-powered drones were flying at speeds exceeding 400 km/h (249 mph), while Ukrainian Starlink-equipped systems had faced a movement-speed threshold of approximately 70 km/h (43 mph).
The consequences, Zelensky said, were particularly serious because the affected drones were intended to stop Russian attacks before they reached civilian areas.
“We were unable to use a tool to protect civilians,” he said.
“This is very painful and unpleasant.”
Starlink restrictions disrupted food and water deliveries to Ukrainian troops
Zelensky said the Starlink restrictions also disrupted food and water deliveries to Ukrainian soldiers holding frontline positions under constant Russian drone surveillance, where conventional supply vehicles cannot safely reach them.
“Our most important thing is people,” Zelensky said.
“Food and water are delivered to our soldiers, who spend weeks and months on the front line, using drones equipped with Starlink,” he said.
Those operations require drones capable of traveling at high speeds, making satellite communication restrictions particularly disruptive.
Zelensky said the limitations interfered with these deliveries while simultaneously weakening Ukraine’s ability to intercept drones targeting civilians.
“They were cutting off our logistics and the protection of the civilian population,” he said.
Ukraine seeks independence from US-controlled military technology
Zelensky acknowledged that Ukraine continues to rely on US intelligence for early warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches, despite receiving intelligence from dozens of other countries.
“Regarding ballistic missiles, specifically information about their launches, we receive that information from the United States,” he explained.
“As you can see, there are many challenges, particularly those related to ballistic missiles.”
Zelensky said Ukraine was working to reduce such vulnerabilities by strengthening its own technological capabilities and cooperation with European partners.
“We are working on every possible option to make Ukraine as independent as possible,” he said.

How Culver City is quietly emerging as a new mecca for AI filmmaking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
02:33:28 UTC
11:33:28 KST

How Culver City is quietly emerging as a new mecca for AI filmmaking
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Culver City’s mix of Hollywood studios, tech companies and available office space is drawing a growing cluster of AI filmmaking startups eager to reshape the industry.
- The companies tout new creative possibilities, using generative tools for everything from short-form crime shows to commercials and film effects.
- But unions and many Hollywood workers fear AI will take jobs, even as studios explore hybrid productions and secure protections against fully synthetic performers.
The heart of Screenland is cozying up to artificial intelligence.
The open space in Culver Steps typically hosts community events and movie nights. But on Wednesday, it turned into a job fair for companies looking to hire talent for AI studios.
Companies showed off their life-like AI videos, urging emerging talent — and out-of-work creatives — to join them as they worked to reinvent traditional filmmaking.
“It’s a great breeding ground for this new filmmaking,” Dave Clark, cofounder of AI film production studio Promise, said about Culver City. “To the independent filmmakers here, it’s time to take back power.”
The event was part of LA Tech Week, a citywide event organized by venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.
Culver City has emerged as a magnet for companies and consumers.
Culver City is already home to big names in Hollywood and technology like Amazon MGM Studios, TikTok, Apple, and Sony Pictures Entertainment. Recently, a growing cluster of AI studios, including Promise, TrueShort, Native Foreign, and PhantomX, are expanding in the neighborhood.
Luma AI, a $4-billion Palo Alto startup that makes generative AI video software, opened a facility in Culver City last year. The company’s Dream Lab occupies a 7,000 square feet space and employs a team of 13.
“Culver City is the future of AI and filmmaking,” Caroline Ingeborn, Luma AI’s chief operating officer, said in a statement.
The companies said they are drawn by the legacy studios they hope to rival. The fact that space is available and affordable thanks to the general decline of the entertainment business in L.A. also helps.
Proponents of AI see it as an antidote to high production costs and say it allows creatives to make films that otherwise would never be made. However, many in Hollywood, its unions, and the public at large are suspicious of the surge in AI use, worried it is stealing the work of human creatives and taking people’s jobs.
The new wave of AI filmmakers have accepted the rise of AI as inevitable, and are forging ahead, increasingly in Culver City.
The city is not opposed to it.
“We’re a hub for the creative economy that is continuing to evolve,” said Adam Troy, Culver City assistant city manager, in a statement. “We look forward to what’s next in the space and what businesses see their future here in Culver City.”
Job postings reveal studios are quietly adopting AI.
TrueShort moved into Culver City last month, taking over most of a 5,000-square-foot office space near Amazon’s studio. The AI studio has raised $17 million and employs about 45 people. Around 75% of them are creatives: filmmakers, editors, sound designers and composers.
Its streaming app hosts short-form true crime audio and video shows that are fully AI-generated. On average, a 10-minute episode costs about $10,000 to make and takes about 10 days to go from idea to release.
“The next Netflix or the next Disney is going to come out of AI this time,” said Nate Tepper, cofounder of TrueShort. “And, in a way, it kind of needs to be a startup because the big incumbents are not going to move as fast. They’re going to be afraid of backlash.”
The company outgrew its Santa Monica office and is now located near Culver Theater.
“It is cool being next to the other bigger lots like Sony and Amazon, only because it’s inspiring,” Tepper said. “We want the lot. We want to become the big studio.”
A California e-commerce platform is fueling the rise of live shopping in the United States, taking on giants such as TikTok and tackling concerns that the app is draining people’s bank accounts.
Culver City-based creative studio Native Foreign makes AI commercials for brands that are more open than Hollywood about AI use. It has done ads for Virgin and Toys R Us.
It made one of the first AI-animated shorts, “Critterz,” using OpenAI’s software and planned to help make a movie based on it, but OpenAI pulled out of the project and canceled its video-making AI model.
“We don’t have the kind of opportunities that maybe some huge huge studios and companies have, so we are able to bag above our weight with these tools,” Nik Kleverov, co-founder of the company, said on a panel at LA Tech Week.
Amid rapid technological change, a growing number of filmmakers and companies in Southern California are using AI tools to radically rethink how films and TV shows are made.
Google-backed Promise is another Culver City-adjacent AI studio that’s a proponent of hybrid productions, where human actors work with AI specialists. The company uses AI to generate backgrounds, visual effects, and synthetic humans for its slate of films, but a lot of the performances are shot on soundstages across L.A. using actors.
In late 2024, the studio acquired Curious Refuge, an online AI school that teaches traditional artists and newbies to use generative AI tools for filmmaking. Promise moved close to Culver from Venice in June.
Excitement about AI grows even as the industry puts up guardrails to contain it. The actors’ guild SAG-AFTRA has secured special protection against fully synthetic performers in the union contract signed this year.
However, some Hollywood veterans point out that the industry has fought over technology before. Alex Cancado, who spent years in visual effects and has worked on over 80 movies, now works in the AI Studios division of Amazon MGM Studios.
Tech giant Google has been quietly making overtures to major studios as it tries to find ways to get Hollywood to use its AI technology.
Pitching the crowd of creatives on Wednesday, he said the transition from practical effects to computer graphics was equally fraught.
“It was a challenge getting CG to be accepted by directors and producers,” Cancado said.
Much of the buzz around AI use for big productions started with a conference in Culver City called “AI on the Lot,” which started in 2023. It has since grown to thousands of attendees.
The organization also sponsored the job fair on Culver Steps and a networking happy hour for media AI companies in Culver City. It estimates that AI media companies with $2 billion in backing have converged on the city.
Mike Gioia, a founder of AI on the Lot, attends City Hall meetings and is trying to build momentum around the concept of a “Culver cluster” — bringing more companies and individuals working in AI to the neighborhood.
“We want to make Culver City the capital of AI media,” said Gioia.

US records 4,410 measles cases as outbreak grows

US records 4,410 measles cases as outbreak grows
The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has recorded 4,410 measles cases so far in 2026, an increase of 330 in a week, and has dispatched an investigator to the state of Pennsylvania to help contain the country’s largest outbreak, Al Jazeera reports.
CDC figures also show 451 measles-related hospitalisations nationwide this year. Children and teenagers aged five to 19 account for 42 percent of cases, followed by adults aged 20 and older, who make up 41 percent. Seventeen percent of cases were among children under the age of five.
Pennsylvania reported 1,222 cases across 42 counties as of Wednesday, including 86 new infections since October 9, according to the state health department. The outbreak has led to 225 hospitalisations and five confirmed measles-associated deaths. State officials are actively investigating a sixth reported death.
The CDC is sending a so-called “disease detective” from its Epidemic Intelligence Service to work with state health officials on the Pennsylvania outbreak. The deployment follows Pennsylvania’s request for federal assistance, known as an Epi-Aid.
Pennsylvania has expanded vaccination efforts in affected communities. State health centre staff have administered more than 5,900 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine doses at 202 pop-up clinics since the outbreak began in late April.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency on October 5 as measles cases rose in nearby Pennsylvania. The order is effective until November 4 and expands the number of healthcare professionals authorised to administer vaccines and allows nurses greater flexibility to order measles testing.
Measles vaccination coverage among US kindergarteners fell from 95.2 percent in the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4 percent in 2025–2026, according to data from the CDC. The agency estimates that about 280,000 kindergarteners are at risk because of gaps in vaccination coverage.
