James Webb reveals a strange bulge in an alien planet's atmosphere
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
23:27:29 UTC
08:27:29 KST

James Webb reveals a strange bulge in an alien planet's atmosphere
- Date:
- October 16, 2026
- Source:
- University of Bristol
- Summary:
- Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have discovered that a distant alien planet's atmosphere is surprisingly lopsided. Located 1,300 light-years away, the scorching gas giant WASP-17b experiences powerful winds that redistribute heat, causing one side of its atmosphere to bulge outward. A groundbreaking new mapping technique revealed these hidden distortions, confirming predictions about how extreme temperatures and winds shape alien worlds.
- Share:
Astronomers have long depicted distant exoplanets with smooth, circular outlines. But new observations reveal that the atmospheres surrounding some of these scorching alien worlds can have surprisingly uneven shapes.
Using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), researchers have discovered that the atmosphere of WASP-17b, a giant planet roughly 1,300 light-years from Earth, extends farther outward on one side than the other. Although its overall outline remains approximately circular, its atmosphere is noticeably asymmetrical. The distortion provides new evidence of how extreme temperatures and powerful winds reshape the atmospheres of distant planets.
The discovery, published in Nature Astronomy, comes from a study jointly led by Cornell University in the United States and the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom. Researchers used an innovative technique called 'transmission strings', developed by Bristol astrophysicists Dr. David Grant and Dr. Hannah Wakeford, to investigate the planet's atmospheric structure in unprecedented detail.
James Webb Reveals the 3D Structure of an Alien Atmosphere
WASP-17b belongs to a class of planets known as 'hot Jupiters', enormous gas giants that orbit close to their host stars and experience intense heating. Its unusual atmospheric shape offers a new perspective on how heat moves around these extreme worlds.
Lead author Dr. Lili Alderson, a Klarman Postdoctoral Fellow at Cornell University, began the research while studying at the University of Bristol, where she earned her doctorate in physics.
"This is proof of concept that planets are in fact 3D objects, and that consistently, as they go around their star, what we predict should be happening is happening. To move beyond computational exercises and see it for real is a different matter."
The observations provide valuable information about WASP-17b's atmospheric chemistry and temperature variations, including differences between its equator and poles and between its permanently illuminated and dark hemispheres.
These results closely match earlier theoretical predictions and computer models. Together, they offer one of the most detailed three-dimensional pictures of an exoplanet's atmosphere yet produced, establishing a useful reference point for studying the more than 6,000 exoplanets confirmed so far.
Co-author Dr. Hannah Wakeford, Associate Professor in Astrophysics at the University of Bristol, said: "Planets are temperamental, their atmospheres complex and chaotic. The fact that all of these numbers came together and showed us this very structured, dynamical picture of this giant world over 1,000 light-years away was just really exciting."
A New Technique Uncovers Hidden Atmospheric Features
James Webb's extraordinary sensitivity has already enabled scientists to investigate alien atmospheres using a method called eclipse mapping. This approach examines subtle changes in light as a planet moves behind its parent star, helping researchers determine how conditions vary across the planet.
The new "transmission strings" technique, also called transit mapping, examines the opposite part of the planet's orbit. As an exoplanet passes in front of its star, some starlight travels through the outer edges of its atmosphere before reaching the telescope.
By analyzing that light from different angles, scientists can investigate the atmosphere's composition and determine how far it extends at different locations around the planet. This outer atmospheric boundary is known as the limb.
Traditional methods generally combine light measurements from the entire limb into a single average spectrum. The new approach instead separates information from different regions, allowing researchers to identify atmospheric variations that would otherwise be concealed.
"Rather than assuming your atmosphere is a circle with the same radius all the way around, our technique allows you to pull out different distances from the center to the edge of the planet," Dr. Alderson said. "We're able to go around the edge. So, we've gone from a ring to understanding where on the ring the gemstones are, so to speak."
Powerful Winds Create a Lopsided Atmosphere
The new measurements revealed a particularly interesting feature near WASP-17b's equator, precisely where previous models predicted it would appear.
The distortion occurs on the planet's "evening" side, where powerful atmospheric winds carry heat away from the hemisphere that permanently faces its star and toward the hemisphere locked in darkness.
This movement of hot gas causes the atmosphere on the evening side to expand farther outward than it does on the cooler "morning" side. As a result, the planet's atmospheric outline is not perfectly symmetrical.
The findings confirm a major prediction about the temperature differences between these regions. The transit mapping measurements also supported other previously identified characteristics of WASP-17b.
Dr. Alderson added: "Theory predicts that the morning and the evening sides should have a strong temperature difference, and WASP-17b fits really nicely in that trend -- pretty much bang-on what we thought it would be."
A Breakthrough for Mapping Weather on Distant Planets
Successfully applying transmission strings to WASP-17b demonstrates that the technique could be used to study the atmospheres of many other exoplanets.
Until recently, much of what astronomers could determine about these distant atmospheres came from measurements averaged across large regions. The new method offers a way to distinguish conditions at different latitudes, as well as between the day and night sides of a planet.
Eventually, this approach could help scientists investigate atmospheric structures on smaller scales, bringing them closer to mapping weather patterns on worlds far beyond our solar system.
Dr. Wakeford said: "Having this very robust mathematical model that we can apply to this state-of-the-art data is incredibly exciting. The results are a really beautiful demonstration of the dynamics that are going on in these multidimensional and multifaceted worlds."
The study used observations gathered through JWST's Telescope Scientist Deep Reconnaissance of Exoplanet Atmospheres through Multi-instrument Spectroscopy (TST DREAMS) Guaranteed Time Observations program.
Funding was provided by NASA, the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), and the Klarman Fellowship.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Bristol. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Lili Alderson, Hannah R. Wakeford, David Grant, Nikole K. Lewis, Avinash Verma, Jayesh Goyal, Mark Hammond, Daniel Valentine, Natalie H. Allen, Ana Glidden, Amélie Gressier, Jingcheng Huang, Maura Lally, Dana R. Louie, Jacob Lustig-Yaeger, Cathal Maguire, Elijah Mullens, Kristin S. Sotzen, Jeff A. Valenti, Roeland P. van der Marel, Tiffany Kataria. A spatial map of the atmospheric limb of a hot Jupiter. Nature Astronomy, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-02986-4

Albanian PM blames ‘foreign hands’ for unrest as student protests intensify
Riot police clash with protesters for fourth day, as young Albanians protest corruption and poor university conditions
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has blamed “foreign hands” for the increasingly violent student-led protests that are calling on him to resign.
Riot police clashed with protesters outside the education ministry for the fourth day in a row, as thousands of young Albanians marched through the capital, Tirana, on Friday to protest government corruption and poor university conditions.
“This is not a student phenomenon,” Rama said in a video address on Friday. He said there were “foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace”.
Rama insisted that the protest had “absolutely nothing to do with the hardships, problems or legitimate aspirations of anyone who desires a better life”.
Police officers used water cannon and tear gas as demonstrators hurled rocks.
The protests have spread beyond the capital to Elbasan, Shkodra and Korca, where demonstrators broke windows and set fire to rubbish bins, local media reported.
The ongoing escalation follows months of mostly peaceful demonstrations, originally sparked by the sale of part of Albania’s coastline to a luxury resort development linked to Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.
Days of unrest have increasingly targeted banks and government buildings. Protesters hurled bricks and concrete blocks at the education ministry on Tuesday. They also set fire to several buildings across the city, including the prime minister’s office, the finance and justice ministry buildings and branches of several banks.
According to a police statement, 160 people were detained over alleged acts of violence on Thursday evening.
The EU question
Demonstrators are demanding Rama’s resignation, as well as electoral and education reforms.
The prime minister, whose government denies corruption, said he would be ready to discuss rising education costs but rejected the calls to resign.
He said on Thursday, “My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward.”
His dismissal “would be a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership”, he added.
Corruption scandals have complicated Albania’s efforts to join the EU. Analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking.
Rama won a fourth term last year on promises to take Albania into the EU, aiming for membership as early as 2028.

Grynspan holds lead for next UN chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
23:16:30 UTC
08:16:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Grynspan holds lead for next UN chief as race enters decisive stage
An informal poll by the United Nations Security Council on Friday placed former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race to become the 10th UN secretary-general, two people close to the process said.
But there was no clear winner as all candidates received two or more opposing votes from the ultimately decisive five permanent members of the council — Russia, China, the US, France and Britain — opening the door for new candidates to join the race, diplomats and observers said.
Whoever wins will have to tackle multiple crises, including several wars, cutbacks in American contributions to the UN, and the 193-member body's declining political relevance as Washington has pulled out of dozens of its agencies.
This was the sixth secret ballot organized by council officials, who have less than three months to pick the successor to UN chief Antonio Guterres, whose term ends on December 31.
Securing the council's recommendation requires at least nine positive votes of the 15 countries and no "discourage" votes from the five permanent members.
The race has entered a decisive stage, as Friday's poll for the first time used color-coded ballots revealing whether a veto power opposes a candidate.
Four of five polls in recent months showed Grynspan, 70, narrowly ahead, with one poll in August placing Guyana's UN ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett in the top spot.
This dynamic did not fundamentally change on Friday, with Grynspan receiving nine "encourage," five "discourage" and one "no opinion" vote, with two of the five opposing votes coming from the Security Council's permanent members, people close to the process said.
Rodrigues-Birkett received eight votes in favor, six against, and one "no opinion," with two opposing votes from the permanent members.
Rafael Grossi, director general of the UN nuclear watchdog, received a near-identical result to Rodrigues-Birkett, but with one fewer permanent member supporting his bid.
Four more former UN officials and senior diplomats are vying for support, but they have received more opposing than supporting votes, indicating waning enthusiasm for their candidacies.
Diplomats say several senior figures, including former and current foreign ministers and country leaders, are considering entering the race. Any new entrant will face a steep challenge of convincing the divided council in short order.
On the question of new contenders joining the race, Washington's envoy to the UN, Mike Waltz, said after the vote: "Countries, if they want to put more candidates in, that's certainly within their sovereign rights."
When Guterres was chosen in October 2016, it took six straw polls for the council to reach agreement.
In the more than 80-year history of the UN, there has never been a female secretary-general.
In an interview with Reuters on Thursday, Grynspan said she "wouldn't be surprised" to receive a veto and said that it would be just the start of negotiations as such blocking votes have been overcome by winning contenders in past races.
"The game is not over -- we will have to continue working," she said.
The Costa Rican economist added that the UN has become too risk-averse and its next leader must be prepared to bear the cost of diplomatic failure and try again.
She also said the UN must cut top jobs, curb bureaucracy and stop agencies duplicating work, arguing that cost-cutting alone would not revive an institution struggling with shrinking resources and declining political clout.

Italy and the U.S. Strengthen Cooperation with the ‘Accelerator on Trusted Technologies’
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
01:12:11 CEST
08:12:11 KST

Italy and the U.S. are strengthening their cooperation and launching the “Accelerator on Trusted Technologies,” a plan designed to connect companies, researchers, and investors from both sides on opportunities in the fields of artificial intelligence, energy, and life sciences. The initiative took shape during the third “Italy-U.S. Dialogue on Trustworthy Technologies for Democracies,” held at the Italian Embassy in collaboration with the Transatlantic Harmonic Foundation and the Krach Institute for Tech Diplomacy at Purdue.
                                    
The event brought together numerous institutional representatives, researchers, and as many as 90 companies from both countries. In addition to Marco Peronaci, Italy’s ambassador to the U.S., participants included Giorgio Mulè, vice president of the Chamber of Deputies; Attilio Fontana, president of the Lombardy Region; Francesco Rocca, president of the Lazio Region; and Barbara Cimmino, vice president of Confindustria. Also present via video messages were Anna Maria Bernini, Minister for Universities and Research, and Alessio Butti, Undersecretary to the Prime Minister’s Office with responsibility for innovation and technology. On the American side, participants included Jacob Helberg, Under Secretary for Economic Affairs at the State Department, and David Fogel, Assistant Secretary for Commerce.
                                    
The initiative comes at a favorable time for Italy-U.S. relations in the technological and economic spheres. On September 21, Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Antonio Tajani and Senator Marco Rubio signed the agreement on critical minerals in New York; in July, Italy joined the Pax Silica initiative.
                                    
Italian companies are making significant investments in the United States: Pirelli will expand its plant in Georgia; in addition to acquiring a U.S. electric utility, Prysmian will invest in North Carolina; Angelini has acquired an American pharmaceutical company; Enel Green Power has done the same in the renewable energy sector by acquiring Excelsior Energy Capital.
                                    
“The U.S. and Italy boast a long-standing partnership in the technology sector. Collaboration is already well advanced, for example, in the space sector: Italy is among the main partners of Artemis and will contribute to the lunar exploration plan by participating in the development of habitation modules. “Just consider that NASA has valued Italy’s contribution to the lunar exploration program at $5 billion,” noted Ambassador Peronaci, also highlighting the advanced collaboration in fundamental physics and quantum technologies.
                                    
“Lombardy,” emphasized President Fontana, “is ready to play a leading role in strengthening technological cooperation between Italy and the United States. Local companies, universities, and research centers represent a model of excellence, thanks to their high level of technical and managerial expertise. This leadership can gain further momentum through international partnerships of this kind.”
  The Accelerator will last 18 months and will focus on three strategic sectors: AI and advanced technologies, energy, and life sciences.

Drone strike kills 30 at cattle market in Sudan's Darfur

Breadcrumb
Drone strike kills 30 at cattle market in Sudan's Darfur
A drone strike on a cattle market in Sudan's Nyala killed 30 people on Friday, AFP reported, in one of the deadliest attacks on the paramilitary stronghold in the western Darfur region.
The Rapid Support Forces blamed the attack on the army, while a military source acknowledged an uptick in strikes on the area, without claiming responsibility.
Both the RSF and the army, at war since April 2023, have increasingly used drones to launch far-reaching attacks without sacrificing their fighters.
Nyala, Sudan's second-largest city and the capital of South Darfur state, serves as the seat of the self-declared administration established by the RSF last year.
"The drone strike on the city's cattle market today killed 30 people and wounded 47 others, who are receiving treatment at the hospital," a medical source at Nyala Hospital told AFP on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to brief the media.
The source did not say who was responsible for the attack.
The strike hit the livestock market on a Friday morning, when traders and shoppers typically crowd the area and roadside stalls serve grilled meat, a popular breakfast in Darfur.
The RSF accused the Sudanese army of carrying out Friday's attack using a Turkish-made drone.
In a statement, the paramilitary group said the strike targeted a densely populated civilian area, adding that preliminary reports indicated 17 women and five children were among the dead.
A military source, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that the army had intensified strikes against RSF positions inside Nyala on Friday.
The source said the military had also targeted Nyala airport 48 hours earlier, adding that all attacks were aimed at military objectives.
Drone warfare
Sudan's war, now in its fourth year, has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced more than 11 million and triggered what the United Nations has described as one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
More than 1,100 people were killed in drone attacks across Sudan during the first half of this year alone, according to the UN.
Nyala has come under repeated drone attacks in recent months as the army seeks to challenge RSF control over Darfur.
The paramilitary group seized most of the region last year after capturing El-Fasher, the last major Darfur city previously held by the army, in an offensive that UN experts said bore "the hallmarks of genocide".
The latest strike comes as fighting intensifies in several parts of the country, including the strategic Kordofan region linking Darfur to central and eastern Sudan.
On Thursday, an army Antonov aircraft struck a house in the paramilitary-controlled village of Abu Zaeima in North Kordofan, killing five children from the same family and wounding their mother, according to the rights group Emergency Lawyers.
Recent attacks in Kordofan have also hit a shelter for displaced people and a university dormitory, killing at least 15 people, the group said.

Ukraine could strip critical workers of draft exemptions – PM
Ukraine could reduce mobilization exemptions for employees of companies deemed critical to the country, Prime Minister Sergey Koretsky has said, arguing that employers are exploiting the current system.
The country declared mobilization shortly after the escalation of the conflict with Russia in February 2022, barring most military-age men from leaving the country.
However, approximately 1.4 million Ukrainians currently hold employment-based exemptions from military service, according to Economy Minister Aleksandr Kravchenko.
Speaking during a Q&A session in the Ukrainian parliament on Friday, Koretsky said the government is considering stripping critical-sector employers of the right to exempt 100% of their staff. He cited cases in which companies had significantly expanded their workforces, with all employees automatically shielded from conscription.
“Unfortunately, there are many abuses, and additional exemptions continue to be granted every month,” Koretsky said.
“If you have a 100% exemption, it means you can expand your workforce indefinitely and exempt people from mobilization, regardless of whether they actually work as repair technicians, energy workers or in other roles. Unfortunately, this practice has already become widespread,” he added.
Koretsky said some companies had received blanket exemptions despite not meeting the criteria for being classified as critical. As an example, he cited an unnamed contractor for Ukrenergo, the national power grid operator. “When we looked into the details, it turned out that only 20 out of 100 employees were actually working for Ukrenergo. Yet all 100 were exempted,” Koretsky said.
The prime minister called for audits to determine how many employees at a given company perform tasks essential to its operations and the country’s needs. He added that stricter criteria could be applied to businesses as a whole, with only those supporting Ukraine’s defense capabilities and other essential state functions qualifying as critical.
Earlier this week, opposition MP Yaroslav Zhelezhnyak published what he claimed was a draft of the proposed changes, reducing exemption quotas for defense and energy companies from 100% to 85%, and for housing and utility companies from 75% to 60%.
Multiple lawmakers and businesses have warned that such measures would exacerbate existing staffing shortages in critical industries.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian outlet Strana UA reported on Thursday, citing sources, that relations between Koretsky and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky had deteriorated. The outlet claimed that Zelensky could dismiss Koretsky in the spring of 2027 and blame him for government failures during the winter months.
Koretsky, who was appointed prime minister in a government reshuffle in July, has been linked by local media to disgraced businessman and former close Zelensky associate Timur Mindich, who fled to Israel amid an investigation into an alleged $100 million embezzlement scheme involving state nuclear power operator Energoatom.
According to Strana UA, Koretsky has defied Zelensky’s expectations by developing political ambitions, disregarding some of his requests and communicating directly with European partners without Zelensky’s involvement.
Amid mounting battlefield losses and desertions, Ukraine’s conscription drive has been marred by incidents of draft officers forcibly detaining military-age men on the streets, sparking spontaneous protests, clashes and outrage on social media.
While Kiev does not regularly publish figures on its battlefield losses, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk claimed last month that Ukrainian forces had recently been suffering around 27,000 killed and wounded per month. Russia’s Defense Ministry, meanwhile, claimed that Ukrainian casualties reached 500,000 in 2025 alone.

Colombia deepens ties with Israel, considers Holocaust alliance membership after embassy opening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:12:35 UTC
07:12:35 KST

As Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar affixed a mezuzah to the entrance of Colombia’s new embassy in Jerusalem on Wednesday, the two countries were exploring another step in their rapidly improving relationship. Colombia is considering applying to join the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA), Israeli Ambassador to Colombia Vivian Aisen revealed to The Media Line.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Aisen said Sa’ar and Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar discussed the possibility during Bula’s visit to Jerusalem. Colombia adopted the IHRA working definition of antisemitism in June 2022, but it is not currently a member or observer country. No formal application has been announced.
The alliance promotes Holocaust education, remembrance, and research. Countries seeking full membership must first obtain observer status and then proceed through an intermediate liaison stage.
Colombia inaugurated its Jerusalem embassy on October 14, becoming the 10th country with an embassy in the city, according to Israel’s Foreign Ministry, and the fourth Latin American country to do so, following Guatemala, Honduras, and Paraguay.
The opening was the most visible part of a broader diplomatic reversal under Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, whose government has restored full relations with Israel, lifted reciprocal visa requirements, removed restrictions on coal exports, and renewed implementation of the countries’ free trade agreement.
At a Foreign Ministry reception later Wednesday, attended by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Bula announced that Colombia had formally requested to withdraw from the Hague Group, a coalition established to coordinate diplomatic and legal measures against Israel over the war in Gaza. He also announced plans for a national initiative to combat antisemitism.
Colombia's Jerusalem embassy signals diplomatic reversal
The embassy opening fulfilled a promise made before de la Espriella’s election. Sa’ar said the two met in Buenos Aires in November 2025, when the future president pledged to relocate Colombia’s embassy to Jerusalem if elected.
“He made a promise, and he kept it,” Sa’ar said. “Just two months after he took office, we inaugurated the Embassy of Colombia in Jerusalem.”
The embassy occupies a stone building dating to 1920. The inauguration brought together Bula, Sa’ar, Colombian Ambassador to Israel Tania Gilinski Bacal, Aisen, and Jerusalem Mayor Moshe Lion.
Palestinian officials criticized the decision. Palestinian Vice President Hussein Al Sheikh condemned the move, saying it disregarded international law and Jerusalem’s disputed status. Jordan’s Foreign Ministry also objected, describing the embassy opening as a violation of international law and relevant resolutions.
Israel considers all of Jerusalem its capital, while the Palestinians seek East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state. Most countries maintain their embassies in Tel Aviv or nearby, arguing that Jerusalem’s final status should be determined through Israeli-Palestinian negotiations.
For Aisen, who arrived in Bogotá eight weeks ago, the initial assignment was to rebuild diplomatic ties after former Colombian President Gustavo Petro severed relations with Israel in May 2024 over the war in Gaza.
“We did not come with the intention of returning to what we were,” Aisen said. “We came to strengthen our relations and go much further.”
The countries have since restored their diplomatic representation, appointed ambassadors, and resumed practical cooperation. Reciprocal visa requirements ended on September 1, while Colombia lifted Petro’s prohibition on coal exports to Israel.
Israel and Colombia restore trade and security cooperation
The free trade agreement required a more technical process. On October 13, the governments completed an exchange of diplomatic notes restoring the agreement, which originally took effect in August 2020.
Israel’s Foreign Ministry described the move as reversing Petro’s termination of the agreement. Aisen explained that the previous Colombian government had attempted to cancel the treaty but had not completed the country’s domestic procedure for withdrawing from an international agreement. The new government therefore needed to reactivate the existing accord rather than negotiate a replacement.
The renewed economic relationship builds on decades of commercial and security cooperation. Colombia has long used Israeli military equipment, and the governments are discussing expanded ties in cybersecurity, technology, agriculture, and other fields.
In a recorded message to Wednesday’s reception, de la Espriella described Israel as a friend and strategic partner. He identified security, intelligence, counterterrorism, organized crime, agriculture, science, innovation, and trade as priorities.
Colombia distances itself from international action against Israel
Colombia’s diplomatic realignment also extends to international institutions.
On September 18, Bogotá notified the International Court of Justice that it was withdrawing its declaration of intervention in South Africa’s case accusing Israel of violating the Genocide Convention during the Gaza war.
The court confirmed the withdrawal four days later. Colombia had intervened in April 2024 to submit its interpretation of the convention. Its withdrawal does not end South Africa’s case against Israel, which rejects the genocide allegations.
The court decision is separate from Colombia’s request to leave the Hague Group, which Bula announced at Wednesday’s reception.
“We reject that approach,” Bula said of the coalition.
He presented the request as another step toward restoring a relationship that began when Colombia recognized Israel in 1949 and established diplomatic ties in 1957.
Antisemitism concerns emerge amid renewed Israel ties
Bula said Colombia’s Foreign Ministry would work with other government ministries and the Confederation of Jewish Communities of Colombia to develop a national initiative against antisemitism.
The effort would also draw on advice from the US State Department’s Office of the Special Envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism, he said, while seeking Israeli participation.
During Wednesday’s reception, Bula criticized the previous administration for what he described as its failure to condemn terrorism clearly and accused it of contributing to “what may be the most virulent wave of antisemitism in Colombia’s recent history.”
“The government of President de la Espriella, this Foreign Ministry and this foreign minister will not remain silent,” Bula said. “We will not let this scourge go unchecked and unchallenged across the country.”
Aisen said attitudes toward Israel became increasingly polarized after the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, and the subsequent war in Gaza. She said some anti-Israel rhetoric had drawn on longstanding antisemitic conspiracy theories.
“If you open my Twitter account, you will see comments that go back to medieval antisemitism,” she said.
One example she cited concerned Israel’s humanitarian response to Colombia’s devastating earthquake in August. Israel deployed approximately 80 rescue and medical personnel and sent additional medical equipment following the disaster.
Aisen said online allegations had circulated claiming that Israeli rescue personnel had come to Colombia to take children. She described the claims as an example of antisemitic conspiracy theories directed against Israel.
Her particular concern is that hostility toward the Israeli government can extend to Colombia’s Jewish population, with Jews held responsible for Israeli policies or actions.
“The Colombian Jewish community became guilty for everything that the State of Israel does,” she said. “That antisemitism has to be confronted.”
Yet Aisen said her personal experience in Colombia had been markedly different from the hostility she encountered online.
“I feel extremely welcome by everyone I meet, not only people in the government but also members of the general public,” she said. “They thank me for Israel being back in Colombia. They feel that Israel can contribute a great deal to the country and that those two lost years were regrettable.”
Marcos Peckel, executive director of the Confederation of Jewish Communities of Colombia and commissioner to combat antisemitism at the Latin American Jewish Congress, attended both the embassy inauguration and Wednesday evening’s reception.
“For those of us who know the history of what this means, it gave us goosebumps,” Peckel told The Media Line. “It shows that President Abelardo de la Espriella is completely determined to take the relationship between Israel and Colombia to its highest level.”
Peckel, who has served on the World Jewish Congress Executive Committee since 2013, said Colombia’s population, regional influence, and history of commercial and security cooperation with Israel give the embassy decision considerable diplomatic weight.
Peckel's concern is whether the renewed relationship can survive future changes of government.
Thousands of demonstrators took to the streets in Colombian cities on October 14 to protest de la Espriella’s domestic policies, with some also opposing his renewed partnership with Israel and closer ties to the United States.
Aisen acknowledged that Israel has become part of Colombia’s domestic political divide. The Jerusalem embassy, one of de la Espriella’s most visible foreign policy decisions, could become a target for his opponents, she said.
“As an Israeli, it hurts me to see that Israel became an issue that divides the public,” she said. “It should not be that way.”
Peckel believes cooperation in agriculture, water management, scientific research, trade, and other practical fields could make bilateral relations more resistant to political shifts. He wants partnerships with institutions and influential sectors of Colombian society that can endure beyond the current administration.
“These changes have to outlast governments,” Peckel said. “The challenge in Latin America is to create very strong roots with the people and with important sectors such as agriculture and water, so that if another government comes, it cannot simply undo what is being built.”

'Sad we are fighting in public': Ex-Shin Bet deputy director demands full October 7 inquiry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:12:25 UTC
07:12:25 KST

Former Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) deputy director Israel Hasson called for an investigation into the failures surrounding the October 7, 2023, Hamas massacre, following statements by the then-Prime Minister's military secretary, Maj.-Gen. Avi Gil and then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar that contradict Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's accounts of events before and after the attack.
Speaking on 103FM, Hasson addressed the conflicting accounts and questioned how Israel had reached a point where senior security officials and political leaders were publicly disputing responsibility rather than conducting a comprehensive examination of the failures.
"I sat through the Shin Bet's investigation for four and a half hours," Hasson said. "An investigation is measured by whether there are questions that were not asked."
"I told them, 'I salute you. I don't have a single additional question that you haven't asked yourselves, but I'm leaving here without an answer.'"
Hasson pointed to the scale of the October 7 attack and the absence of specific intelligence warning beforehand.
"Three thousand people participated in this attack, and we had no concrete warning," he said.
Former Shin Bet deputy chief explains intelligence available to Netanyahu's military secretary
Hasson emphasized that the prime minister's military secretary has access to a broader intelligence picture than any single intelligence agency possesses at a given moment.
"Avi Gil has the complete intelligence picture, which is not available at every moment within the Shin Bet," he explained.
"There are 15 officers in the military secretariat. All of Israel's intelligence information is available to them. His picture is much more comprehensive and complete."
According to Hasson, the military secretariat is responsible for consolidating intelligence assessments from different agencies and presenting them to the prime minister in an organized manner.
"To avoid a situation where, in quotation marks, everyone is confusing the prime minister, the information goes through a channel that can say: 'This is what the Shin Bet says, this is what Military Intelligence says, this is what the Mossad says, and what another hundred bodies are saying.'"
Hasson says inquiry must establish responsibility for October 7 failures
Hasson expressed frustration over the public disputes surrounding the events of October 7, arguing that a formal investigation is needed to determine where the failures occurred.
"It is so sad that we have reached this point," he said. "It is so sad that we are fighting in public instead of going and investigating this matter."
He said a commission of inquiry might not necessarily uncover information unfamiliar to experienced security officials, but would provide the public with a clearer understanding of the failures and their causes.
"A commission of inquiry probably won't discover something I don't already know," Hasson said.
"But it will show the public where the problem was and what caused it. Conclusions will have to be drawn and corrections made to prevent something like this from happening again."
Hasson cites Agranat Commission on political and military responsibility
Hasson acknowledged that not all intelligence sources can be disclosed to the public, but questioned whether withholding certain information would undermine the ability to establish responsibility.
"It is perfectly legitimate that you and I are not given access to all our intelligence sources," he said. "The question is whether that currently affects the conclusions."
He referred to the Agranat Commission, which investigated the failures surrounding the 1973 Yom Kippur War, and its findings regarding intelligence assessments and political responsibility.
"The Agranat Commission said that when there is intent and capability, you do not wait for a warning," Hasson said.
"They established that. They also established that if the military echelon says one thing, it does not absolve the political echelon of responsibility."
Hasson argued that security decision-makers should prioritize precautionary action rather than wait for definitive intelligence before responding to a potential threat.
"It is better to call off a state of heightened readiness than to start looking for a reason to act," he said.
He also referred to previous recommendations to target Hamas leaders in the years leading up to October 7.
"I know how many times in the five years before 2023 there were demands to strike Hamas leaders," Hasson said.
"There were demands to neutralize them. They said the money was going toward armament. They said everything they said."
Former Shin Bet deputy chief addresses Ronen Bar's lawsuit against Netanyahu
Hasson also addressed the lawsuit filed by former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar against Netanyahu, describing the dispute as extending beyond the former agency director personally.
"In my view, this is not Ronen Bar filing a lawsuit against the prime minister. This is the Shin Bet filing a lawsuit against the prime minister," Hasson said.
He sharply criticized Netanyahu's allegations against Bar, calling the extremely serious.
"He attacked him at a level that amounted to betrayal," Hasson said.

Did Netanyahu’s phone call with Sharaa change Israeli-Syrian relations? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:12:18 UTC
07:12:18 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday that he spoke by telephone with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa during deadly clashes in southern Syria in July 2025, claiming the conversation helped stop the killings. Damascus has not confirmed the call, which Netanyahu disclosed less than two weeks before Israel’s parliamentary elections.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Netanyahu made the announcement on October 15 at a Likud campaign gathering with members of Israel’s Druze community in Yarka, a northern Israeli town. He described the conversation as brief and tense but did not explain how it was arranged or provide further details.
The Israeli prime minister also discussed Israeli military operations during the violence in Syria’s predominantly Druze Sweida Governorate, including airstrikes against the Syrian Defense Ministry building and a target within the presidential palace compound in Damascus.
Violence erupted in July 2025 following clashes between Druze and Bedouin groups, with Syrian government forces and tribal fighters subsequently becoming involved. Israel carried out strikes against Syrian military positions, saying it was acting to protect the Druze community.
In its first response to Netanyahu’s announcement, the Syrian government neither confirmed nor denied the conversation. An unnamed official source quoted by the state-run Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) rejected attempts to involve Syria’s Druze community in Israeli election campaigning, describing it as an integral part of the country’s national fabric.
The source accused Israel of interfering in the July 2025 violence and arming an unauthorized armed group to destabilize Sweida. The allegation has not been independently verified.
According to the Syrian government, Israeli airstrikes during the clashes prevented Syrian forces from intervening to restore order. Damascus maintained that US mediation, rather than Netanyahu’s reported conversation with Sharaa, had brought those strikes to an end.
Syria also reaffirmed its cooperation with the United States and Jordan on a roadmap intended to restore stability in Sweida and called for international pressure on Israel to comply with the 1974 Disengagement Agreement.
The Media Line sought comment from Ahmad Mowaffaq Zaidan, media affairs adviser to Sharaa, and Mohammad al-Jafal, adviser for Afro-Asian affairs at Syria’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates. Neither had responded by publication time.
Israel, Syria continuing to pursue security negotiations
The disclosure comes as Israel and Syria pursue US-mediated security negotiations despite continuing disagreements over Israeli military deployments and Syrian sovereignty.
Israel captured the Golan Heights from Syria in 1967 and expanded its military presence in southern Syrian territory following the fall of Bashar Assad’s government in December 2024. Damascus demands that Israeli forces withdraw from areas entered after Assad’s removal and that both countries return to the arrangements established under the 1974 agreement.
Israeli authorities maintain that their military operations and deployments are necessary to protect the country's northern border.
Although Israel and Syria have no formal diplomatic relations, contacts between senior officials have become an important part of efforts to prevent further confrontation.
In August, Reuters reported, citing informed sources, that Mossad chief Roman Gofman spoke with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani on August 14 about Turkey’s military presence in Syria.
Jordan subsequently hosted US-mediated talks between senior Syrian and Israeli delegations on August 23, according to SANA. Those discussions addressed Israeli military operations, measures to reduce tensions, and the possibility of reaching a security agreement.
Netanyahu’s disclosure suggests that contact may also have occurred directly between the countries’ leaders, although Damascus has yet to acknowledge such an exchange.
Netanyahu-Sharaa call could signal willingness to reduce tensions
Syrian political analyst Firas Allawi told The Media Line that the reported conversation could signal a willingness to communicate despite the deep disagreements between Damascus and Israel. He cautioned against interpreting it as evidence of an approaching peace agreement.
“Any political contact between the two sides could represent an initial step toward reducing tensions, but it does not necessarily mean that a peace agreement is close,” Allawi said.
“The issue depends on the willingness of both sides to address outstanding matters, foremost among them Syrian sovereignty and the Israeli military presence. The timing of Netanyahu’s announcement also calls for an examination of his domestic political calculations, without overlooking the possibility that these contacts are part of broader efforts to reshape the regional landscape.”
Allawi’s comments come as Netanyahu campaigns ahead of Israel’s October 27 parliamentary elections. The prime minister made his announcement before Druze voters while describing his government’s efforts to protect members of their community in Syria.
The timing raises questions about the political purpose of the disclosure, although the contacts reported between Israeli and Syrian officials in recent months suggest that discussions have continued beyond the immediate circumstances of the 2025 clashes.
For retired Syrian military pilot and analyst Khaled Mansour, the value of direct political communication depends on whether it can lead to practical arrangements that reduce the risk of further fighting.
“Moving from military confrontation to political understandings requires tangible measures on the ground, including ending escalation, limiting military operations, and establishing clear security arrangements that prevent renewed clashes,” Mansour told The Media Line. “The success of any negotiation process will also remain tied to addressing the Israeli military presence inside Syrian territory and providing mutual security guarantees that do not undermine Syrian sovereignty.”
The dispute over the buffer zone established under the 1974 agreement remains a central obstacle. Syria seeks the withdrawal of Israeli forces from territory entered after December 2024, while Israel insists on security arrangements intended to prevent hostile forces from operating near its border.
Mansour said sustained negotiations would require more than occasional direct contacts between senior leaders.
“Political contacts may help prevent military miscalculations and establish channels for containing crises, but building lasting peace requires enforceable understandings and clear mechanisms for monitoring compliance, not merely contacts or political statements.”
Despite continued US diplomatic involvement, Israel and Syria have yet to reach a comprehensive agreement governing military deployments and security arrangements along their shared frontier.
Beyond those disagreements, the possibility of direct communication between Netanyahu and Sharaa has raised hopes among some Syrians that dialogue could eventually help end decades of conflict.
Bakhour Shmantoub, head of Syria’s small Jewish community, told The Media Line that he hoped contacts between the governments could develop into a broader peace process.
“Yes, it could open the door to peace. The region is tired of wars, and peace is necessary,” Shmantoub said.

Israel risks winning the war while losing the world - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:12:06 UTC
07:12:06 KST

The decision to award the Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay – who chaired a UN commission that concluded Israel was committing genocide in Gaza – should be a wake-up call. Whether intended or not, the award signals how receptive the world has become to that accusation. Israel’s strategic environment is changing dramatically, and our future is at stake.
Israelis are divided into two camps. One believes the country is doing well. After recovering from the October 7 massacre, Israel’s security position is stable – even stronger than before, as the Yellow Lines in Gaza and southern Lebanon attest. The economy is thriving despite three years of war – witness the strong shekel. And despite our bitter divisions, civil society remains vibrant, enterprising, and marked by solidarity – witness Israel’s high ranking in the World Happiness Report.
The other camp sees a country in crisis. The war drags on, with no diplomatic settlement in sight to ensure lasting stability. The flawed strategic assumptions that preceded October 7 remain unexamined, as no official commission of inquiry has been established to date. This leaves us vulnerable to another disaster. The ultra-Orthodox community shirks its share of the national burden, threatening our economic and security future. Trust in state institutions is eroding, and social tensions are mounting – to the point that some fear civil war.
Yet both camps must confront a danger that transcends their differences: Israel stands on the brink of severe international isolation. That could trap us all in a harsh new reality with potentially grave consequences. This strategic warning demands a fundamental change of course at home, across political lines.
Israel is on the brink of international isolation
Europe, Israel’s largest trading partner, is moving toward sanctions that could seriously damage our economy. Britain and 11 other countries, including Canada, have announced or are considering restrictions on trade in settlement goods. But Israel’s economy does not stop at the Green Line. Almost every major Israeli company could find itself exposed to looming sanctions.
That could trigger a chain reaction. Businesses worldwide might avoid trading with Israel for fear of being branded sanctions violators. Even friends of Israel could pull back – not out of hostility but out of commercial caution. A creeping de facto boycott could transform BDS – boycott, divestment, and sanctions – from a radical fringe cause into a sweeping movement that reshapes life in Israel. We could become a pariah state alongside Russia, North Korea, and Iran.
The United States is Israel’s principal security and diplomatic anchor. Relations with American administrations have sometimes been tense, but broad bipartisan public support held firm. Today, the reverse is true – and this is the heart of the strategic warning.
Cooperation with the current administration is impressive. But it offers tactical reassurance while obscuring a troubling strategic shift: American sympathy for Israel is eroding. The decline extends beyond Democrats, reaching younger Republicans and even young Evangelical Christians.
Anti-Israel attitudes once associated with the radical Left and the fascist Right have gained a foothold in the mainstream. For the first time in decades, Americans are no more likely to sympathize with Israelis than with Palestinians. They are David; we are Goliath.
Israel is on a slippery slope toward a dangerous defeat – economic and diplomatic, and perhaps even in the security arena when a new US administration takes office in just over two years. No one can know how likely each part of this scenario is to materialize.
Shifts in public opinion, national interests, and governments abroad could still work in our favor. But we cannot cling to the complacent belief that “everything will be okay,” or to the illusion that an isolated, self-sufficient “Sparta” could survive. A sudden diplomatic collapse – a “6:29 a.m.” moment echoing the shock of October 7 – is a real possibility.
The forces driving these developments are complex, and not all are within Israel’s control. Still, coalition and opposition alike have a duty to weigh every action, every statement, and every failure to act in light of the long-term implications for Israel’s diplomatic standing, national security, and economy.
This is not a call for Israel to sacrifice its vital interests to appease world opinion. But there is ample room for constructive action. We can take steps most Israelis support – such as stamping out Jewish terrorism – and refrain from rhetoric most Israelis reject, including calls to flatten Gaza or force its residents to emigrate. Israelis in both camps share an overriding interest in preventing this strategic warning from becoming a tragic reality.
The writer is president of the Jewish People Policy Institute (JPPI) and professor emeritus of law at Bar-Ilan University.

The coalition said on Friday it had also destroyed two cruise missiles over the Red Sea and three drones in Saudi Arabia's Southern and Riyadh regions. It did not identify those behind the attacks.
In Aden, two missiles launched by Houthi militia landed on the airport grounds, the Aden Security Department said. It said the incident was the second attack on the facility in less than a week.
The Houthi militant group did not immediately claim responsibility.
No casualties were reported. A Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo was preparing for takeoff when the missiles landed, the security department said.
Yanbu is a key outlet for Saudi oil exports, allowing the country to ship crude to international markets via the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz, where heightened regional tensions and security threats have raised concerns over the safety of shipping.
Brent crude briefly touched $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May, as worries over escalating Middle East tensions raised concerns about tighter global supplies.
Saudi Civil Defense authorities earlier issued alerts in the Jazan region and the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, where such warnings have become frequent since fighting resumed last month.
Humanitarian crisis in Yemen
Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government has raised fears of a further deterioration in the country's humanitarian crisis.
Aid agencies have warned that conditions are worsening rapidly.
The Yemen conflict has become another front in the wider regional war that began with US and Israeli war on Iran in February.
Yemen's war began in 2014, when the Houthi militia seized the capital Sanaa. A Saudi-led intervention began the following year, leading to years of stalemate before a 2022 truce that held until this year.
The Houthis have repeatedly launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia since the conflict reignited, targeting airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure.
In recent days, the militant group has also targeted sites in government-held parts of Yemen, including Aden airport and the presidential palace in the interim capital.

Yemen’s government says Houthis fired two missiles at Aden airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
21:56:07 UTC
06:56:07 KST

Yemen’s government says Houthis fired two missiles at Aden airport
Attack comes as Yemeni gov’t forces claim advances in Marib province and say they ‘neutralised’ 430 Houthi fighters in 24 hours.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government says the Houthis have launched missiles at the airport in Aden, a day after carrying out a deadly attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city.
Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said two missiles landed near the runway at Aden International Airport on Friday, 500 metres (1,640 feet) from an aircraft that was preparing to take off.
All passengers and crew were safe, he said on X, thanking “divine providence” for preventing a potential “horrific humanitarian catastrophe” and calling the attacks on the airport “a grave violation of international laws and norms”.
The Houthis, in a statement attributed to a military source, said on Friday that they launched an attack on “the Saudi forces’ command headquarters in the Badr camp in Aden province” as well as a weapons depot, the AFP news agency reported.
The latest attack in Aden, which is the seat of the internationally recognised government, comes amid continued heavy fighting in Yemen’s reignited civil war between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned Houthis.
Yemeni government forces said earlier on Friday that troops had advanced in Marib province northeast of Sanaa.
Military spokesman Majed al-Nazili said Yemeni government forces, with air support, had made significant “territorial gains” in the eastern part of the province, securing “key positions”.
He also said Yemeni forces had “neutralised” more than 430 Houthi fighters in 24 hours, while destroying or disabling more than 100 of their vehicles and military assets.
Elsewhere, in Taiz governorate, which has emerged as a key battlefront in the war, Yemeni government forces claimed to have fended off several “large-scale” Houthi attacks, inflicting “heavy losses” on the group.
Yemeni government forces also claimed to have captured a specialised drone team affiliated with the Houthis in the Taiz area.
In recent weeks, Houthi forces have encircled the city of Taiz — Yemen’s third largest urban centre — by cutting its main road south to Aden, causing widespread displacement and worsening a humanitarian crisis.
Missiles over Riyadh
Elsewhere on Friday, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said it had downed missiles and drones over Riyadh and other parts of Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging Houthi attacks against the kingdom, including by arming and training the group.
But Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Friday rejected the accusation, saying Tehran had not played a role in any Houthi operations. The ministry also reiterated a proposal to mediate between the Houthis and Riyadh.
The war in Yemen erupted in 2014 when the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized the capital, Sanaa, and forced the government to flee.
An international military coalition led by Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the internationally recognised government in 2015, leading to years of fighting between the warring sides.
A 2022 UN-backed truce halted most fighting, but tensions have been high in Yemen since the Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabian ports and shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in July.
In September, the Houthis carried out a lightning ground offensive on Mocha, pushing back forces loyal to Yemen’s government from the Red Sea port city.
The same month, the group’s forces again swept through and seized territory along the western coast and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, including the strategically located Mayyun Island in the strait.

US not to supply Ukraine with weapons at expense of its own security — columnist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

06:55:00 KST

WASHINGTON, October 17. /TASS/. The United States will not send weapons to Ukraine at the expense of security of its own armed forces in the Middle East, said Jude Russo, a columnist for the US magazine The American Conservative.
Commenting on reports about Ukraine’s shortage of missiles for Patriot air defense systems, the possible cessation of Washington’s transfer of intelligence data to Kiev, and the restriction of the Starlink satellite system, he said: "This is bad for Ukraine, although not altogether surprising. For months, the press has been full of ominous stories and analyses about the dire state of American munitions stockpiles after the US began its latest little jaunt in the Middle East."
"Reality is beginning to bite," the observer noted. In his opinion, even in the current conditions, the United States can continue the war with Iran without any special risks, but this "will come at the cost of readiness in other theaters." He said that a war with Iran "will always tend to demand more attention and resources than the proxy conflict in Europe. The US is not going to sacrifice the safety of its own military personnel and its own economic security for Ukraine."

Text description provided by the architects. For decades, Surat's relationship with the Arabian Sea was shaped by a fragmented and underutilized shoreline. The Dumas Sea Face Masterplan reimagines this edge as a living coastal landscape, transforming a neglected waterfront into a resilient public realm where ecology, civic life, and urban identity converge. Located along the historic Dumas coastline, the project responds to the growing demand for high-quality public open space in one of India's fastest-growing cities. Despite its long-standing cultural and recreational significance, fragmented development, limited accessibility, and the absence of a cohesive vision have constrained the shoreline's potential. The masterplan addresses these challenges by stitching together disparate segments into a continuous waterfront experience that reconnects the city with the sea.
